topics.title: Math and classical ML
topics.about: Linear algebra, probability, optimization, and the classical models that still win on tabular data.

questions.title: A decision tree with no depth limit scores 99% on training data and 71% on validation. What do you try first?
questions.answer: A 28-point gap between training and validation is the textbook sign of high variance: the tree has memorised the training set. Constrain it (max_depth, min_samples_leaf, pruning), or average many trees (a random forest). More data also helps, if you can get it.
options: Limit the tree: a maximum depth, or a minimum number of samples per leaf.
Train for more epochs.
Add more features so the tree has more to work with.
Switch to a deeper model, such as a neural network.

questions.title: A 10-class image classifier gets 64% on training data and 63% on validation. People score 95% on the same task. What's the problem?
questions.answer: Both numbers are low and close together: high bias (underfitting). Add capacity (a bigger model, better features), reduce regularisation, or train longer. Collecting more data is the classic wrong move here.
options: The validation set is too small.
Not enough training data.
High bias: the model is too simple to fit even the training data.
High variance: it's overfitting.

questions.title: You run 5-fold cross-validation on 10,000 rows. How many rows does each of the five models train on?
questions.answer: Each fold holds out one fifth for validation and trains on the other four fifths: 10,000 × 4/5 = 8,000 rows. Every row is used for validation exactly once across the five runs.

questions.title: A demand forecast scores 0.92 R² with random 5-fold cross-validation and 0.55 in its first month in production. What's the most likely cause?
questions.answer: Validation has to mimic deployment. A forecaster always predicts the future from the past, so validate the same way: train on everything before a cut-off date and test on what follows (a rolling or expanding window). Random folds let neighbouring days, which are highly correlated, sit on both sides of the split.
options: Five folds is too few.
The model needs more regularisation.
Production data is always noisier.
Random folds let the model train on days after the ones it's tested on.

questions.title: In a churn model, the most important feature by far is `account_closure_reason`. Validation AUC is 0.99. What do you conclude?
questions.answer: For every feature, ask: would I know this value at prediction time? A closure reason is written when the account closes, which is the event being predicted. Remove it and anything derived from it, then expect validation AUC to fall to something believable.
options: The model is overfitting, so add regularisation.
Target leakage: that field only gets filled in once a customer has churned.
Drop the feature, because one feature shouldn't dominate.
It's a strong feature. Ship the model.

questions.title: A colleague oversamples the minority class with SMOTE, then splits the data into train and test. Test recall is excellent. What's wrong?
questions.answer: SMOTE creates new minority points by interpolating between real ones. Done before splitting, a test example's near-copies land in training, and the model gets credit for recognising them. Split first, then resample only the training portion, ideally inside a pipeline so cross-validation does it per fold.
options: The test set is too small.
Nothing. SMOTE is the standard fix for imbalance.
Synthetic points built from test examples' neighbours end up in training, so the test set is contaminated.
SMOTE should be applied to the test set too.

questions.title: Out of 1,000 transactions, 20 are fraud. Your model flags 50 transactions, and 15 of those are fraud. What is its precision?
questions.answer: Precision = true positives ÷ everything flagged = 15 ÷ 50 = 0.3. Of the transactions the model flags, 30% are fraud.

questions.title: Same model: 20 frauds in the data, 15 of them flagged. What is its recall?
questions.answer: Recall = true positives ÷ all actual positives = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75. The model catches three quarters of the fraud.

questions.title: Same model, precision 0.3 and recall 0.75. What is its F1 score? (Three decimals is fine.)
questions.answer: F1 is the harmonic mean: 2 × 0.3 × 0.75 ÷ (0.3 + 0.75) = 0.45 ÷ 1.05 = 0.429. The harmonic mean is pulled towards the lower of the two, so a model can't score a high F1 by being good at only one of them.

questions.title: 1% of users are fraudulent and your model has 99% accuracy. What should you report instead?
questions.answer: With heavy imbalance, accuracy mostly measures the majority class. Report precision and recall at your operating threshold, and use PR-AUC to compare models, because it's dominated by performance on the rare class. ROC-AUC counts true negatives in its false-positive rate, and with 99 negatives per positive that rate stays small even when most flags are wrong.
options: Accuracy is fine, because 99% is high.
Precision and recall at the threshold you'll use, plus PR-AUC.
ROC-AUC alone.
Mean squared error.

questions.title: A test catches 99% of a rare condition and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. The condition affects 1 in 1,000. If someone tests positive, what's the probability they have it? (As a decimal.)
questions.answer: Out of 100,000 people, 100 have the condition and 99 of them test positive. Of the 99,900 healthy people, 1% (999) also test positive. So 99 ÷ (99 + 999) = 0.090, about 9%. Even a very accurate test has low precision when the condition is rare. Bayes' rule is the formal version of this count.

questions.title: The fraud team can review 200 cases a day. How do you choose the model's threshold?
questions.answer: When a person acts on each flag, the operational constraint sets the threshold. Rank by score and take the top k, then evaluate with precision@k. If the cost of missed fraud is known, compare it with the cost of a review to decide whether the team needs more capacity.
options: Pick the threshold that maximises F1.
Use 0.5, the default.
Pick the threshold that maximises accuracy.
Rank each day's transactions by score and send the top 200: the threshold follows from capacity.

questions.title: Your model has a ROC-AUC of 0.95, and its predicted probabilities will be used to set insurance prices. What else do you check?
questions.answer: AUC is about ranking, calibration is about the probabilities. Check a reliability diagram (bucket the predictions, compare the average prediction with the observed rate in each bucket) or the Brier score. If the curve is off, fit Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. Boosted trees and naive Bayes are often poorly calibrated out of the box.
options: Nothing. 0.95 AUC is excellent.
Calibration: whether a predicted 20% risk really happens about 20% of the time.
Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold.
Feature importance.

questions.title: A model predicts 0.9 for an example that turns out positive. What is the log loss for that one prediction? (Natural log.)
questions.answer: Log loss for a positive is −ln(p) = −ln(0.9) = 0.105. Compare with a confident miss: predicting 0.1 for the same positive costs −ln(0.1) = 2.30, more than twenty times as much. Log loss punishes confident wrong answers hard.

questions.title: You have 500 features and suspect only about 20 matter. You want a linear model that uses few of them. Which regularisation?
questions.answer: The L1 penalty's corners sit on the axes, so the optimum often lands where many weights are exactly zero. Use elastic net (L1 + L2) when the important features are correlated with each other: plain lasso tends to pick one of a correlated group arbitrarily.
options: Dropout.
L1 (lasso): it pushes many weights to exactly zero.
L2 (ridge): it shrinks every weight.
No regularisation, then drop features with small weights.

questions.title: Your features range from 0–1 (a ratio) to 0–1,000,000 (income). Which of these models doesn't care about the difference in scale?
questions.answer: Anything based on distances, dot products or penalties on weights needs standardised features: kNN, SVMs, regularised linear models, neural networks. Tree-based models don't, because each split only compares values within one feature.
options: Logistic regression with L2 regularisation.
Gradient-boosted trees.
An SVM with an RBF kernel.
k-nearest neighbours.

questions.title: A random forest's built-in feature importance ranks `zip_code` (30,000 distinct values) at the top. Should you believe it?
questions.answer: Mean decrease in impurity is computed on training data and is biased towards high-cardinality and continuous features. Permutation importance on held-out data asks a cleaner question: how much worse does validation get when this feature is shuffled? If zip code still matters, consider target encoding (computed within folds) or grouping to region.
options: Not yet. Impurity-based importance favours features with many distinct values. Check with permutation importance on validation data.
Yes, if the forest has many trees.
No. Zip codes are never useful.
Yes. The forest found it most useful.

questions.title: k-nearest neighbours works well on 5 features but poorly once you add 195 more mostly-irrelevant ones. Why?
questions.answer: With many dimensions, the nearest and farthest neighbours end up at nearly the same distance, so "nearest" stops meaning much. Each irrelevant feature adds noise to every distance. Select features, reduce dimensions (PCA), or learn a metric. Or use a model that weights features, such as boosted trees.
options: k is too small.
kNN needs more training epochs.
The features need one-hot encoding.
In high dimensions, distances become similar for all points, and the irrelevant features drown out the useful ones.

questions.title: Two features in a linear regression have a correlation of 0.98. Their coefficients flip sign between training runs on resampled data. What's happening?
questions.answer: When two features carry nearly the same information, many combinations of their weights fit equally well, so small changes in the data swing them around. If you need interpretable coefficients, drop or combine one of them, or use ridge regression, which spreads the weight stably. The variance inflation factor (VIF) measures the problem directly.
options: The model is underfitting.
One of the features must be leaking the label.
Multicollinearity: the model can trade weight between the two almost freely, so individual coefficients are unstable.
The learning rate is too high.

questions.title: Income is missing for 30% of loan applicants, and applicants with missing income default twice as often. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: Here data is not missing at random. Not reporting income tells you something. Impute (the median, or a model-based estimate) so the model has a number, and add an indicator so it can learn that missingness matters. Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values natively by learning which branch they go down.
options: Fill with the mean and say nothing else.
Drop the rows with missing income.
Drop the income feature.
Impute a value, and add a binary "income was missing" feature.

questions.title: Explain the bias-variance trade-off. How do you tell which problem you have?
questions.answer: Expected test error decomposes into bias squared, variance, and irreducible error. Bias is systematic error from an under-parameterized model that cannot capture the underlying structure; training and validation error are both high and close. Variance is sensitivity to fluctuations in the training sample; training error is low but the validation gap is large. Irreducible error is the noise floor from unmeasured variables or label noise, bounding performance regardless of model complexity. To diagnose, plot learning curves against training set size. If adding data asymptotes with high error, you have high bias—add capacity, features, or unfreeze layers. If validation error keeps improving as data grows, you have high variance—regularize, collect more samples, or reduce feature count.
keyPoints: High bias gives high training and validation error.
High variance gives low training error and a large validation gap.
Learning curves distinguish capacity limits from data sensitivity.
More capacity reduces bias; more data or regularization reduces variance.

questions.title: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: L2 regularization (Ridge) adds a squared weight penalty $\lambda \sum w_i^2$, shrinking weights smoothly toward zero without setting them to zero. Geometrically, its spherical loss contour meets the loss surface off-axis, handling multicollinearity by distributing weight across correlated features. L1 regularization (Lasso) penalizes absolute values $\lambda \sum |w_i|$; its diamond contour has non-differentiable corners on the coordinate axes, driving weights to exact zero and performing embedded feature selection. L1 struggles when features are collinear: it arbitrarily selects one and zeroes the rest. ElasticNet resolves this with a convex combination $\alpha L_1 + (1-\alpha) L_2$, retaining L1's sparsity while grouping correlated predictors via L2.
keyPoints: L1 penalizes absolute weights and can produce exact zeros.
L2 penalizes squared weights and shrinks correlated features together.
L1 can select arbitrarily among correlated predictors.
ElasticNet combines sparsity with L2 stabilization.

questions.title: Your fraud dataset is 0.1% positive. How do you train and evaluate the model?
questions.answer: Never use raw accuracy: predicting the majority class trivially yields 99.9%. Evaluate with Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC) and set operational thresholds using recall at fixed precision or expected cost. Keep validation and test splits on the true 0.1% base rate to reflect deployment reality. For training, apply focal loss or class weights in the loss function, or use stratified undersampling of negatives on training folds only. If you resample training data, predicted probabilities will be systematically distorted; you must adjust the output log-odds back to the true prior or calibrate probabilities using Platt scaling or isotonic regression on unskewed validation data before feeding scores into downstream business logic.
keyPoints: Accuracy hides failure on a rare positive class.
Evaluate precision-recall and choose a threshold using business costs.
Keep validation and test data at the deployment class prevalence.
Apply class weights or resampling only during training.
Calibrate probabilities on data with the true class prevalence.

questions.title: When is PR-AUC more useful than ROC-AUC?
questions.answer: ROC-AUC evaluates True Positive Rate against False Positive Rate. Because FPR's denominator is all actual negatives, a surge of false positives in a 0.1% positive dataset barely changes FPR, making ROC-AUC misleadingly optimistic. PR-AUC evaluates precision ( / (TP + FP)$) against recall, directly exposing false positive contamination. ROC-AUC is baseline-invariant with a random guess scoring 0.5, allowing comparison across varying populations. PR-AUC has a random baseline equal to the positive prevalence  / (P+N)$, meaning 0.001 in fraud. Use PR-AUC for rare-event detection where false alerts carry real operational cost, and reserve ROC-AUC for ranking evaluation where class distribution is balanced or stable.
keyPoints: ROC plots true positive rate against false positive rate.
Many negatives can hide costly false positives in ROC metrics.
Precision-recall exposes false alerts for rare positive classes.
Random PR performance equals positive prevalence; random ROC AUC is 0.5.

questions.title: How do bagging and boosting differ? Compare random forest with XGBoost.
questions.answer: Bagging trains deep, low-bias trees independently in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them, reducing variance without altering bias. Feature subsampling decorrelates the trees, making Random Forest resilient to hyperparameter misconfiguration. Boosting trains shallow, high-bias trees sequentially, with each tree fitting the pseudo-residuals of the current ensemble to systematically reduce bias. XGBoost extends gradient boosting using second-order Taylor expansion (gradients and hessians), an exact or approximate greedy split finder with histogram binning, explicit leaf-weight regularization, and default split directions for missing values. Random Forest is parallel and hard to break; XGBoost delivers higher accuracy on tabular data but requires early stopping to avoid overfitting noisy labels.
keyPoints: Bagging trains models independently and averages to reduce variance.
Random forests use bootstrap samples and feature subsampling.
Boosting sequentially fits errors or loss gradients.
XGBoost uses gradient and Hessian information with regularization.
Boosting needs tuning and early stopping to control overfitting.

questions.title: How does an SVM work, and what does the kernel trick do?
questions.answer: Support Vector Machines find the hyperplane maximizing the geometric margin between classes. Only points lying on or within the margin slab—the support vectors—determine the decision boundary; non-support vectors can be moved or deleted without changing the boundary. The hyperparameter $ balances margin width against training violations: high $ enforces a hard margin with low bias and high variance, while low $ allows slack for better generalization. The kernel trick computes inner products in a high-dimensional feature space using a kernel function (x, z) = \langle \phi(x), \phi(z) \rangle$ without evaluating the mapping explicitly. Because solving the dual problem scales between (N^2)$ and (N^3)$ with sample count $, SVMs do not scale to millions of rows.
keyPoints: SVM maximizes the margin between classes.
Support vectors determine the decision boundary.
The C parameter trades margin size against training violations.
Kernels compute feature-space inner products without explicit mapping.
Kernel SVM training scales poorly to very large sample counts.

questions.title: Why does logistic regression use log loss rather than squared error?
questions.answer: With a sigmoid output, squared error gives a non-convex problem and very small gradients when the model is confidently wrong. Log loss is the negative log likelihood of a Bernoulli model, it is convex in the weights, and it penalizes confident mistakes heavily. Weights are read as changes in log odds, which is why the model stays popular when explanations matter. It needs scaled features for regularization to treat them fairly.
keyPoints: Log loss is the negative Bernoulli log likelihood.
Logistic log loss is convex in the linear model weights.
Squared error with sigmoid can give weak gradients for confident mistakes.
Logistic weights describe changes in log odds.

questions.title: What does PCA do, and when does it fail?
questions.answer: PCA computes an orthogonal linear transformation projecting centered data onto directions of maximum variance, using eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix or singular value decomposition (SVD). Retaining the top $ components minimizes reconstruction mean squared error. Features must be standardized first, or variables with larger numerical units dominate the projection. PCA fails in two common scenarios: when class separability lies along low-variance directions rather than high-variance ones—where Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is appropriate—and when data lies on non-linear manifolds, where methods like UMAP, t-SNE, or autoencoders are required. The components are also linear combinations of all original features, reducing interpretability.
keyPoints: PCA projects centered data onto orthogonal directions of maximum variance.
Top principal components minimize linear reconstruction error.
Feature scales can dominate PCA without standardization.
High variance need not preserve class separation.
Linear projections cannot represent a nonlinear manifold.

questions.title: How does k-means work, what are its limits, and how do you choose k?
questions.answer: K-means minimizes within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) by alternating between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as cluster means. It is guaranteed to converge to a local minimum; running k-means++ initialization with multiple random restarts avoids poor initializations. Because it uses Euclidean distance, it assumes isotropic, spherical clusters of similar size and density; it fails on non-convex manifolds or clusters with varying variances, where Gaussian Mixture Models or DBSCAN excel. Features must be scaled to avoid metric distortion. Select $ by combining the elbow curve, silhouette analysis for cluster separation and cohesion, and operational constraints such as downstream capacity.
keyPoints: K-means alternates nearest-centroid assignment with centroid recomputation.
It minimizes within-cluster squared distance and may reach a local optimum.
Initialization and multiple restarts affect the result.
Euclidean distance favors scaled, spherical, similarly sized clusters.
Choose k using validation metrics and operational constraints.

questions.title: How does a decision tree choose a split, and why do trees overfit?
questions.answer: At each internal node, a decision tree evaluates all candidate feature splits and selects the threshold maximizing impurity reduction—Gini impurity or entropy for classification, and variance reduction for regression. Trees overfit because greedy recursive partitioning can continue until every leaf contains a single sample, memorizing noise and outlier points. Greedy splitting also has no lookahead: it cannot detect multi-feature interactions that provide no marginal gain in isolation. High-cardinality categorical features artificially inflate impurity reduction and cause severe overfitting. Mitigate this through pre-pruning (capping max depth, min samples per split, and min samples per leaf) or cost-complexity post-pruning ($\alpha$), or ensemble methods.
keyPoints: Tree splits maximize impurity reduction.
Deep leaves can memorize noise and overfit.
Greedy single-feature splits can miss interactions.
Depth and minimum leaf size or pruning control complexity.

questions.title: How do you approach feature engineering for a tabular model?
questions.answer: Start from what would be known at prediction time, since anything later is leakage. Use domain ratios, time-window aggregates and recency features. Encode high-cardinality categoricals with target encoding fitted inside folds, or hashing. Treat missingness as a possible signal. Scale only for models that need it. Add features one group at a time, keep those that improve validation, and check that serving can compute each one within its latency budget.
keyPoints: Features must be available at prediction time to avoid leakage.
Domain ratios, window aggregates and recency can expose useful signal.
Target encodings must be fitted within training folds.
Validate feature groups incrementally.
Serving must compute features within its latency budget.

questions.title: How do you handle missing values? When is dropping rows wrong?
questions.answer: Diagnose the missingness mechanism first. Under Missing Completely at Random (MCAR), missingness is independent of both observed and unobserved data; dropping rows is valid though wasteful. Under Missing at Random (MAR), missingness depends on observed features; dropping rows introduces selection bias, so use multivariate or model-based imputation with an explicit missingness indicator flag. Under Missing Not at Random (MNAR), missingness depends on the missing value itself (e.g., high-income earners withholding salary); imputation cannot fully correct this without modeling the missingness process. Always fit imputation parameters strictly on training splits to prevent data leakage, and ensure tree-based models leverage their native missing-value routing.
keyPoints: MCAR missingness is independent of observed and unobserved values.
MAR missingness depends on observed data.
MNAR missingness depends on the missing value itself.
Dropping rows can bias results when missingness is not completely random.
Fit imputation only on training data and consider missingness indicators.

questions.title: Design an A/B test for a new ranking model. What can go wrong?
questions.answer: Choose one primary metric and guardrails such as latency. Fix the minimum detectable effect, then compute sample size from baseline variance, power and significance before starting. Randomize by user, not request, and run full weekly cycles. Problems include peeking at results, novelty effects, sample ratio mismatch, interference between users, and testing many metrics. A sample ratio check should run first, because it can invalidate the entire result.
keyPoints: Randomize at a unit that avoids interference or contamination.
Choose a primary outcome and safety guardrails before the test.
Plan sample size and test duration using a minimum detectable effect.
Avoid repeated significance peeking and account for multiple comparisons.
Check sample ratio mismatch and delayed or seasonal effects.

questions.title: What does a p-value actually mean, and what is a common misreading?
questions.answer: It is the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and it says nothing about effect size. With very large samples, tiny useless effects become significant, so report a confidence interval and judge practical impact. Running many tests inflates false positives, so correct for multiple comparisons.
keyPoints: A p-value is a tail probability under the null hypothesis.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Statistical significance does not measure effect size or business value.
Repeated tests and optional stopping can inflate false positives.

questions.title: A feature strongly predicts churn. Can you tell the business that changing it will reduce churn?
questions.answer: No. Prediction shows association, which may come from a confounder or reverse causation. For example, support tickets may predict churn because unhappy users file them, and reducing tickets would not fix the cause. To estimate an effect, run an experiment. If you cannot, use methods such as difference-in-differences or propensity matching, and state their assumptions. Uplift models target who responds to an action rather than who is at risk.
keyPoints: Prediction alone does not establish a causal effect.
Confounders or reverse causality can explain an association.
A randomized intervention can identify the effect of changing a feature.
Observational causal estimates require explicit identification assumptions.

questions.title: Why can't you use random k-fold on a time series, and how do you validate instead?
questions.answer: Random folds let the model train on the future and predict the past, and nearby points are correlated, so the score is too optimistic. Use rolling or expanding-window validation, with a gap between train and test when features use lag windows. Compare against naive baselines such as last value or seasonal last value. Report error by horizon, because accuracy usually falls the further ahead you predict.
keyPoints: Random folds can leak future information into training.
Use chronological holdouts or rolling-origin validation.
Fit preprocessing using only each training window.
A gap may be needed for overlapping features or delayed labels.

questions.title: What is model calibration and when does it matter?
questions.answer: A model is calibrated when predicted probabilities match observed event frequencies: among events predicted at 0.8, 80% should be positive. Complex models like gradient-boosted trees and deep networks often rank well (high AUC) while outputting overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities. Calibration is essential when probabilities drive expected-value calculations, ad auction bidding, or multi-class ensemble weighting. Measure calibration with reliability diagrams and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Fix it using Platt scaling (fitting a logistic sigmoid on logits) for smooth shifts, isotonic regression for non-parametric monotonic mapping, or temperature scaling for multiclass models. Fit calibration parameters strictly on a separate holdout set to prevent overfitting.
keyPoints: A calibrated probability matches the observed event frequency.
Calibration matters when decisions use probabilities and costs.
Reliability diagrams and proper scoring rules assess calibration.
Fit Platt scaling or isotonic regression on separate validation data.
A model can rank well while its probabilities are miscalibrated.

questions.title: A colleague builds a dense layer that takes 784 inputs and gives 128 outputs. The first forward pass stops with a shape error. Which dimensions does the weight matrix need, and how do you read an error like this one?
questions.answer: The matrix is 128 by 784: one row for each output and one column for each input. A matrix product needs the inner sizes to agree, so a 128 by 784 matrix times a 784 by 1 input gives a 128 by 1 output. An error means the inner sizes differ, and the fix starts with the shapes of every operand written on paper.
followUps: Level 1: What shape does the bias have? Expected: one value for each output, so 128 values, stored as a 128 by 1 column so that it adds to each output column.

Level 2: A batch of inputs arrives as rows instead of columns. What changes? Expected: the order of the product changes, so the batch matrix times the transposed weight gives one output row for each input.

Level 2: Why does a transpose appear in the backward pass? Expected: the gradient for the input needs the weight matrix with its rows and columns swapped, so that the shapes agree in the reverse direction.

Level 3: How does broadcasting hide a shape bug? Expected: a dimension of size 1 is stretched to fit, so a wrong shape can run without an error and give wrong values. An assertion on the shape catches it.
wrongAnswers: "The weight matrix is 784 by 128 because inputs come first." With a column input the matrix needs 128 rows and 784 columns. The order of the product decides which form is right, not the order in which you name the sizes.
"Shapes do not matter, the framework fixes them." Broadcasting repeats only a dimension of size 1. A 784 against a 128 inner size is an error, or a silent wrong result after a reshape.
"Transpose things until the code runs." A transpose that makes the code run can multiply the wrong pairs of numbers. Write the shapes down first and then change the one that is wrong.

questions.title: A language model scores a sentence as the product of the probability of each word. For long sentences the score is exactly zero, and two long sentences can no longer be compared. What went wrong, and what do you compute instead?
questions.answer: The product of many small probabilities underflows to zero in floating point. Add the log probabilities instead, and the sum stays a finite negative number. A more negative sum means a less likely sentence, and the order of the sentences is unchanged.
followUps: Level 1: Why is every log probability zero or negative? Expected: a probability is between 0 and 1, and the log of such a number is at most 0.
Level 2: How do you compare two sentences of different length? Expected: compare the mean log probability per token, or the perplexity, not the raw sum.
Level 2: Where does this appear in a loss function? Expected: cross-entropy is the negative log probability of the correct class, so training already runs in log space.
Level 3: How do you get log probabilities from logits without forming the probabilities first? Expected: log-softmax, which subtracts the log-sum-exp of the logits from each logit.
wrongAnswers: "Use a wider float type and the product will be fine." A wider format only moves the point of underflow. Fifty words with probability 0.01 give 10 to the minus 100, and a longer sentence pushes it further down.
"Multiply the probabilities and take the log at the end." The product is already zero before the log, and the log of zero is minus infinity.
"Clip each probability to a minimum value." That changes the score of every rare word and still underflows for a long enough sentence.

questions.title: A regression report shows a negative R-squared on the test set. A teammate says the metric code must be broken, because R-squared lives between 0 and 1. How do you answer?
questions.answer: R-squared is one minus the ratio of the residual sum of squares to the total sum of squares around the mean. It is 1 for a perfect fit, 0 for a model that only predicts the mean, and below zero when the model does worse than that constant. A negative value is a real result, and it says the fitted model hurts on this data.
followUps: Level 1: What value does a model that predicts the training mean get on the test set? Expected: near 0 when the test mean is close to the training mean, because the residual and total sums are almost the same; below 0 when the two means differ.

Level 2: Training R-squared is high and the test value is negative. What does the gap say? Expected: the model fit the training data and does not transfer; suspect overfitting or a shift between the sets.
Level 2: Why report R-squared next to RMSE? Expected: RMSE is in the units of the target and shows the size of a typical error; R-squared is a fraction of variance and has no units.
Level 3: The target has a heavy tail. What else do you check? Expected: MAE next to MSE, because squared errors let a few outliers dominate both MSE and R-squared.
wrongAnswers: "R-squared cannot be negative, so the code has a bug." The formula has no lower bound. A model that predicts worse than the mean gives a negative value.
"Negative means the slope is negative." R-squared compares residuals with the variance around the mean. It carries no sign of a slope.
"Clip it to zero in the report." That hides the fact that the mean would beat the model.

questions.title: Your classifier trains on a cross-entropy loss. A reviewer asks why you do not train on the KL divergence between the labels and the predictions instead. Explain how the two quantities relate and what would change, if anything, in training.
questions.answer: Cross-entropy of P and Q equals the entropy of P plus the KL divergence from P to Q. The labels fix P, so their entropy is a constant during training, and the two objectives have the same gradient. With one-hot labels the entropy is zero and the two numbers are equal: minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class.
followUps: Level 2: Why is KL not a distance? Expected: it is not symmetric; each direction weights the log ratio by a different distribution.

Level 3: With label smoothing the loss never reaches zero. Why? Expected: the soft target has positive entropy, and cross-entropy is at least the entropy of the target; KL would reach zero at a perfect match.
Level 3: Differentiate the loss by each logit. What form do you get? Expected: the predicted probability minus the target, for each class.

Level 4: In distillation the target is a teacher's softmax. Which of the two numbers do you log? Expected: KL, because the teacher's entropy is a constant offset per sample that hides how close the student is; the gradient is the same either way.
wrongAnswers: "They are different objectives and give different models." They differ by the entropy of the labels, which does not depend on the model, so the gradients are equal.
"Cross-entropy is a distance between two distributions." It is not symmetric, and it is not zero when the distributions match; it equals the entropy of P at a match.
"KL is smaller, so it is the better loss." KL is cross-entropy minus a constant. The optimizer sees the same slope.

questions.title: You minimize the Rosenbrock function from the point (-1, 1). Plain gradient descent creeps along the curved valley and needs thousands of steps. The same run with momentum arrives much sooner. Explain what the valley does to plain descent and what momentum changes.
questions.answer: In a narrow valley the gradient points across the valley, not along it, so each plain step jumps from one wall to the other and makes little progress toward the minimum. Momentum keeps a velocity that sums past gradients. The across components flip sign and cancel, the along component keeps its sign and builds up, so the path is smooth and fast.
followUps: Level 2: What does beta control? Expected: how much of the past velocity survives each step; 0.9 keeps roughly the last ten gradients.

Level 3: Momentum overshoots the minimum and comes back. Why? Expected: the velocity carries the point past the bottom when the gradient has already changed sign; a smaller beta or a decaying learning rate damps it.
Level 3: How does this zigzag show up in a real training run? Expected: the loss drops fast and then plateaus while the weights oscillate; a smaller learning rate or momentum smooths it.

Level 4: Why does Adam help on the same valley beyond what momentum does? Expected: it scales each weight's step by the inverse of its running gradient size, so the steep direction takes small steps and the flat direction takes large ones.
wrongAnswers: "Raise the learning rate until plain descent moves faster." A larger step jumps further across the valley and diverges before it speeds up the along direction.
"Momentum is a bigger learning rate." The velocity grows only where gradients keep their sign and cancels where they flip, which a scalar learning rate cannot do.
"The valley is a local minimum, so the optimizer is stuck." The gradient is not zero on the valley floor. The point moves at every step, slowly.

questions.title: Automatic differentiation can push derivatives forward from the inputs or pull them backward from the output. Training frameworks pick the backward direction. Why, and in which situation would the forward direction be the better choice?
questions.answer: A network has millions of parameters and one scalar loss. Reverse mode seeds the output with a gradient of 1 and gets the gradient of every parameter in one backward sweep. Forward mode needs one sweep for each input variable, so it wins only when the inputs are few and the outputs are many.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the backward sweep need a topological order? Expected: a node must receive the full gradient from every consumer before it passes gradient to its children.
Level 3: How many forward-mode sweeps does a model with one million weights need for one gradient? Expected: one million, one per input variable, which is why nobody trains that way.

Level 3: What is a dual number and how does it carry a derivative? Expected: a pair of a value and a derivative, where the derivative part squares to zero, so each arithmetic rule carries the derivative along.

Level 4: Name a case in an ML system where you would pick forward mode. Expected: a function with one or two inputs and a large vector output, where one sweep gives the derivative of the whole output along one input direction.
wrongAnswers: "Reverse mode is more accurate than forward mode." Both are exact up to floating point rounding. The difference is the cost, not the result.
"Forward mode cannot handle a composition of functions." Both modes apply the chain rule through every link. Forward mode pushes the derivative from the input side.
"Backpropagation is a different algorithm from reverse-mode autodiff." Backpropagation is reverse-mode autodiff applied to the network graph, with the loss as the single output.

questions.title: A teammate standardizes the whole table with a scaler, then splits it into training, validation and test rows, and reports a test score. In production the score is well below that number. Name the fault in the pipeline and describe a setup where the test number predicts production.
questions.answer: The scaler saw the test rows, so the mean and standard deviation carried information from the test set into training. That is data leakage, and it makes the reported score optimistic. Split first, fit every preprocessing step on the training rows only, and apply the fitted transform to the other two sets.
followUps: Level 2: How does the same fault appear inside k-fold cross-validation? Expected: a transform fit on all rows before the folds leaks across every fold; fit it inside each training fold.
Level 2: Why does reading the test score many times also inflate it? Expected: each change after a look fits the test set, so it becomes a second validation set.
Level 3: The data has a time axis. What changes in the split? Expected: split by time, so the model never trains on rows after the ones it predicts; a shuffled split lets future rows into training.

Level 4: How do you tune hyperparameters and still report an honest number? Expected: nested cross-validation with an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop for the estimate, or a validation set for tuning and a test set used once.
wrongAnswers: "Scaling is a harmless transform, so the order does not matter." The mean and standard deviation are statistics of the data. Fitting them on test rows moves test information into training.
"A leak this small cannot move the score much." The size is unknown until you remove it, and other leaks, such as a target-derived feature, hide behind the same habit.
"Run the test set after each change to be safe." Each look and change fits the test set, and the number stops predicting production.

questions.title: A from-scratch cross-entropy passes its unit tests on small logits. On real batches the loss comes back as inf. You print the batch and one logit vector is [100, 101, 102]. Walk me through the cause and the fix, and say why the fix is not an approximation.
questions.answer: The exponential of 100 is about 2.69 times 10 to the 43, far past the float32 maximum of about 3.4 times 10 to the 38, so each term of the softmax denominator overflows and the ratio is inf or nan. Subtract the largest logit from every logit before the exponential. The probabilities are identical in exact arithmetic, and the largest term is now exp(0), which is 1.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the shift leave the probabilities unchanged? Expected: the factor exp(c) appears in the numerator and the denominator and cancels.

Level 2: What goes wrong when every logit is very negative? Expected: every exponential underflows to 0 and the log of the sum is minus infinity; the same shift fixes it because the largest term becomes exp(0) = 1.

Level 3: Why compute the loss from log-softmax rather than from the log of a softmax? Expected: a probability that underflowed to 0 has a log of minus infinity; log-softmax subtracts the log-sum-exp and never forms the probability.

Level 3: A framework loss function takes logits, not probabilities. Why? Expected: it fuses log-softmax and the negative log-likelihood in one stable step, so the caller cannot overflow or underflow on the way in.
wrongAnswers: "Clamp every logit at 80 and move on." A clamp changes the probabilities whenever a logit crosses it. The shift gives the exact same probabilities with no bound on the logits.
"Switch to float64." A wider exponent only moves the overflow point. Logits grow during training and will pass it.
"Add a small epsilon inside the log." The inf comes from the exponential, before the log. An epsilon does nothing about an infinite denominator.

questions.title: A binary classifier reports 95 percent accuracy on a dataset where 95 percent of the rows are negative. The product owner is happy. You are not. Which numbers do you ask for, and how do you choose the decision threshold for this product?
questions.answer: A model that always says negative also gets that accuracy, so the number proves nothing. Ask for the confusion matrix, then precision, recall and F1 at the current threshold, and the AUC-ROC for the ranking. Move the threshold from the default of 0.5 toward the error that costs the product more: raise it when a false positive is expensive, lower it when a missed positive is expensive.
followUps: Level 2: What precision and recall does the always-negative model get? Expected: recall is 0, because it finds no positives, and precision is undefined or set to 0 because it predicts none.
Level 2: Why is F1 a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean? Expected: the harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot hide a near-zero recall behind a high precision.
Level 3: How do you keep the threshold choice honest? Expected: pick it on the validation set, not the test set, and report the test metrics at that fixed threshold once.

Level 3: When is AUC-ROC the wrong summary? Expected: when the positive class is rare and the product cares about the precision of the top predictions; a precision-recall curve shows that part of the picture.
wrongAnswers: "Accuracy is 95 percent, so the model is good." The always-negative model gets the same number. Accuracy hides the minority class.
"Keep the threshold at 0.5 because that is where the sigmoid crosses." The default is only the point where the model is unsure. The product's costs decide the cut.
"Pick the threshold that gives the best test F1." That fits the test set. Choose it on validation data and report the test score once.

questions.title: A node in a classification tree holds 6 cats and 4 dogs. Give its Gini impurity and its entropy in bits, and explain how a tree uses either number to choose a split.
questions.answer: The class shares are 0.6 and 0.4. Gini is 1 minus the sum of squared shares, so 1 minus 0.36 minus 0.16, which is 0.48. Entropy is minus the sum of share times log base 2 of share, which comes to 0.971 bits. The tree tries every feature and threshold and keeps the split with the largest drop from the parent's impurity to the weighted impurity of the two children.
followUps: Level 2: What is the gain of a split that puts all the cats on one side and all the dogs on the other? Expected: the children are pure, so their impurity is 0 and the gain equals the parent's impurity, 0.48 for Gini.
Level 2: Why weight the children by their sample share? Expected: a pure child with one sample should not count as much as a mixed child with the rest of the data.
Level 3: How does the tree turn a continuous feature into candidate thresholds? Expected: sort the values and try the midpoint between each pair of distinct neighbors.

Level 3: What stops the recursion before every leaf holds one sample? Expected: pre-pruning limits such as a maximum depth, a minimum number of samples per leaf, or a minimum gain, or post-pruning after the full tree is grown.
wrongAnswers: "Gini is 0.6 times 0.4." That product is half of the two class Gini. The formula is 1 minus the sum of squared shares, which gives 0.48 here.
"Entropy of a 6 to 4 node is 1 bit because there are two classes." One bit is the maximum, reached only at equal shares. Unequal shares give less, 0.971 bits here.

"Pick the split with the lowest child impurity, and the parent does not matter." The parent's impurity is the same for every candidate split at that node, so the ranking is the same, but the gain is what the tree stores and reports as feature importance.

questions.title: A language model has a vocabulary of V tokens. On a held-out text, its mean cross-entropy per token, measured in nats, equals the natural log of V. Estimate the perplexity and say what the number tells you about the model.
questions.answer: Perplexity is the exponential of the mean cross-entropy, so here it equals V. On average the model is as uncertain as a uniform pick over the whole vocabulary. A trained model should sit far below V. The mean alone does not prove that the model learned nothing, because other per-token predictions can give the same average, so check per-token predictions and the data.
followUps: Level 2: The loss is reported in bits instead of nats. What changes? Expected: raise 2 to the loss instead of e; the perplexity is the same number.
Level 2: What does a perplexity of 50 mean in words? Expected: on average the model is as uncertain as a uniform pick among 50 tokens.
Level 3: Two models use different tokenizers. Can you compare their perplexities? Expected: not directly; the token count and the vocabulary differ, so the per-token numbers measure different things.

Level 3: A perplexity equal to V shows up on in-domain text after training. What do you suspect first? Expected: a pipeline bug, such as labels that do not line up with inputs or weights that did not load, because the model is doing no better than chance.
wrongAnswers: "Perplexity equal to V means the model is perfect." A perfect model has perplexity 1. V is what a uniform guess gets.
"Divide the loss by V to get the perplexity." Perplexity is the exponential of the loss, not a ratio.
"A lower perplexity on any text means a better model." Only on the same text with the same tokenizer. A different text or vocabulary moves the number without any change in the model.

questions.title: You have a tabular dataset and two candidate base learners: deep decision trees that fit the training rows almost perfectly, and decision stumps that barely beat a constant. You can afford one ensemble method for each. Which one gets bagging and which one gets boosting, and why?
questions.answer: Bag the deep trees and boost the stumps. Deep trees have low bias and high variance, and averaging many of them trained on bootstrap samples cancels the variance without adding bias. Stumps have high bias and low variance, and boosting builds them in sequence so each new one corrects the errors of the ensemble so far, which drives the bias down.
followUps: Level 3: Why does bagging the deep trees not fix bias? Expected: the average of many models that miss the same pattern misses it too; averaging only removes their disagreement.
Level 3: What does the learning rate do in gradient boosting? Expected: it scales each tree's contribution; a smaller rate needs more trees and generalizes better.

Level 4: Boosting's training error keeps falling while validation error rises. What happened and what do you do? Expected: later rounds fit noisy or mislabeled rows; stop early on the validation loss, or lower the learning rate and the tree depth.

Level 4: Why does a forest's test accuracy plateau but not fall as trees are added? Expected: each tree lowers variance and none adds bias, so more trees cannot overfit the way more boosting rounds can.
wrongAnswers: "Boost the deep trees, since boosting is the stronger method." A low bias, high variance learner has little bias to remove, and boosting amplifies its variance.
"Bag the stumps to make them strong." Averaging stumps that all underfit still underfits; bagging leaves bias where it is.
"Any ensemble of enough models beats a single one." Gains need diverse errors; models that make the same mistakes do not cancel them.

questions.title: Your training stack can run in float16 or in bfloat16. A teammate picks float16 because it keeps more digits. Which format do you pick for training, which for inference, and what extra mechanism does one of them need?
questions.answer: Pick bfloat16 for training. It has the same 8-bit exponent as float32, so it covers the same range up to about 3.4e38, and activations, logits and gradients that spike past 65,504 do not overflow. float16 has 10 mantissa bits and more precision, but its 5-bit exponent caps at 65,504 and underflows gradients below about 6e-8, so it needs loss scaling to train. For inference, where values are bounded and precision matters more, float16 is the usual choice.
followUps: Level 3: Why do small gradients vanish in float16 and not in bfloat16? Expected: float16's smallest normal values sit near 6e-8 and smaller gradients round to 0; bfloat16's exponent reaches float32's range.
Level 3: What does dynamic loss scaling do when a gradient turns inf? Expected: skip the step, halve the scale, and double it again after a run of clean steps.

Level 4: You moved from float32 to float16 and validation accuracy fell by a few percent with no error. What happened? Expected: gradient underflow zeroed small updates; enable loss scaling or move to bfloat16.
Level 4: Why is bfloat16 cheap to convert from float32? Expected: it is the top 16 bits of a float32, so conversion drops the low mantissa bits and the exponent is unchanged.
wrongAnswers: "More mantissa bits means better training, so float16 wins." Training is limited by range; a logit spike past 65,504 becomes inf in float16 and is fine in bfloat16.
"Loss scaling changes the training result." Dividing the gradients by the same factor before the update gives the same update; the scale only lifts small values above the underflow floor.
"Use bfloat16 everywhere, inference included." Inference values are bounded and the extra float16 precision helps there; the lesson makes float16 the inference default.

questions.title: You add a new layer to a from-scratch network and run a gradient check. The relative error between the analytical and the numerical gradient is about 1e-3 for one weight. A teammate says the backward pass has a bug. Before you agree, how do you decide whether the fault is in the backward pass or in the check itself?
questions.answer: A relative error near 1e-3 is in the warning band, so first make the check trustworthy. Use the two-sided difference, set the step to the range from 1e-5 to 1e-7, run the check in float64, and compute the relative error with the max of both magnitudes in the denominator. If the error stays near 1e-3 or grows under those conditions, the backward pass is wrong; if it drops below 1e-5, the check was at fault.
followUps: Level 3: Why prefer the two-sided formula over the one-sided one? Expected: its error falls with h squared instead of h, so a moderate h gives a close estimate without cancellation.
Level 3: Why not run the check on every step of production training? Expected: it needs two forward passes for each parameter, so it is far too slow; it belongs in unit tests and in debugging.

Level 4: The error is tiny for most weights and large for a few in one layer. What does that pattern say? Expected: the layer's backward pass is right in general and wrong on one path, such as a shared input whose contributions were overwritten rather than added, or a kink at those weights.
Level 4: How do you check a layer that contains a random mask? Expected: fix the seed so both loss evaluations use the same mask, or run the check in evaluation mode where the mask is off.
wrongAnswers: "Make h as small as possible for the most accurate derivative." Below the rounding scale the subtraction cancels and the result is noise. There is a floor on h, around 1e-7 in float64.
"A relative error of 1e-3 is close enough, ship it." The lesson puts 1e-3 at the bug boundary. A stable error there means a wrong gradient that will slow or break training.
"Use the absolute difference instead of a relative one." A large gradient and a tiny one need different tolerances. The relative error with a floored denominator handles both.

questions.title: You fit a logistic regression with gradient descent on a small dataset where one line separates the two classes with no errors. The loss falls at every epoch, the weights grow at every epoch, and the run never settles. A colleague proposes a squared error loss instead, because it has a clear bottom. What is happening, and what do you do?
questions.answer: On separable data the log loss has no finite minimum: scaling the weights up pushes every probability closer to its label and the loss closer to zero, so descent walks forever. Squared error through a sigmoid is a worse trade, because that cost surface is not convex and has flat regions where the gradient dies. Keep the log loss and add an L2 penalty, which gives one finite, unique minimum.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the cross-entropy convex for this model while squared error is not? Expected: the log of the sigmoid combines with the linear score into a convex function; squaring the gap between a sigmoid and a label creates flat regions and several local minima.

Level 3: What does the decision boundary do while the weights grow? Expected: the line w x + b = 0 barely moves; only the steepness of the sigmoid across it grows, so predictions become overconfident.

Level 4: How does the L2 penalty change each gradient step? Expected: it adds a term proportional to w to the gradient, so each step also shrinks the weights, and the shrinking balances the pull toward larger weights at a finite point.

Level 4: The data is nearly separable instead. Does the problem go away? Expected: a finite minimum exists, but the weights are large and the probabilities overconfident; the penalty still helps calibration, and a validation loss shows it.
wrongAnswers: "The falling loss means the model is still improving, let it run." The boundary stopped improving; only the confidence grows, until the weights overflow or every probability saturates.

"Switch to squared error for a well-defined minimum." That surface is not convex with a sigmoid output, so descent can stop in a poor local minimum, and the gradient vanishes where the sigmoid saturates.
"Add early stopping and call it solved." Stopping fixes the run time but leaves the weights wherever the clock ran out; a penalty gives a defined answer that does not depend on the epoch count.

questions.title: A random forest's feature importance puts a user id column near the top of the list. The column is an integer with a different value in almost every row. The team wants to build a product rule around it. What do you tell them, and how do you check?
questions.answer: The default importance is the mean decrease in impurity, summed over every split that used the feature. A column that is distinct on nearly every row offers a huge number of candidate thresholds, so trees split on it to carve out small pure groups by chance, and those impurity drops add up on the training data. Run a permutation importance check instead: shuffle the column on held-out data, measure the drop in accuracy, and expect close to zero for an id.
followUps: Level 3: Why do many distinct values make it easy for a tree to find a good-looking split? Expected: more thresholds mean more chances that one of them separates a few rows by luck; the gain is real on the training sample and absent on new data.

Level 3: Permutation importance for the id is near zero and the validation score is fine. What does that say? Expected: the id carried no signal the model depends on; it absorbed training noise, and the other features do the work.
Level 4: The permutation importance of the id is large as well. What now? Expected: suspect leakage; the id tracks the target through time or source, and that link breaks in production.

Level 4: How do you compute permutation importance so it is not optimistic? Expected: on held-out data, shuffle only the one column, repeat several times and average, and keep every other column fixed.
wrongAnswers: "The forest found the id useful, so it is useful." The impurity sum counts splits that fit training noise; a column with many distinct values collects them.
"Drop every integer column to be safe." Integers such as counts carry real signal. Test the one column with a permutation.
"The two importance methods always agree." The lesson's exercise builds a case where the impurity method ranks a noise feature highly and the permutation method does not.

questions.title: A feature pipeline computes the variance of a column with the formula mean of x squared minus the square of the mean, in float32. On a column with values near one million the result is far from the true value and sometimes negative. Explain the cause and propose a formula that holds.
questions.answer: The two terms are each about 10 to the 12 and almost equal, and their difference is the small true variance. In float32 the spacing between neighboring numbers at that size is far larger than the variance, so the subtraction returns rounding noise, which can be negative. Compute the variance from centered values instead: subtract the mean first, or use the running update that the lesson calls the Welford algorithm.
followUps: Level 3: Why can the naive result be negative when a variance cannot? Expected: the result is rounding noise, and nothing in the formula bounds the sign of noise.

Level 3: Would float64 fix the pipeline? Expected: it moves the problem to larger values, around 10 to the 15 digits of precision, but the same inputs scaled up break it again; the centered formula fixes it at any scale.

Level 4: The column arrives as a stream and you cannot hold it in memory for two passes. What do you do? Expected: use the Welford update, which keeps a running mean and a running sum of squared deviations in one pass.

Level 4: Where does this same cancellation hide inside a normalization layer? Expected: a layer norm or batch norm that computes variance as mean of squares minus squared mean on activations with a large mean; implementations center first for this reason.
wrongAnswers: "The formula is correct algebra, so the code must have a typo." The algebra is exact and the arithmetic is not. The two terms are correct to about 7 digits each, and the variance lives below that.
"Clamp the result at zero." That hides the sign and keeps the wrong magnitude.

"Divide the column by one million first and multiply the variance back." Scaling helps here, but it moves the mean, not the problem; a column with a large mean and a tiny spread still cancels. Center first.

questions.title: Two variants of a classifier differ by one hyperparameter. On one held-out split, variant B beats variant A by a small margin, and the team wants to ship B. Design the evaluation that decides whether B is better, and say what you would report.
questions.answer: One split gives one noisy number, so the gap could be chance. Run k-fold cross-validation with the same folds for both variants, keep the per-fold differences, and test whether their mean is far from zero with a paired t-statistic. Report the mean and spread of each variant's fold scores, the mean difference and the statistic, and keep the test set out of the comparison.
followUps: Level 3: Why must both variants use the same folds? Expected: pairing removes the fold-to-fold variation from the difference, so the test asks only about the variants.
Level 4: What does an absolute t above 2.78 mean with five folds? Expected: with 4 degrees of freedom the mean difference is unlikely to be zero at the 5 percent level, so the gap is probably real.

Level 4: How do you avoid tuning on the folds you report? Expected: nested cross-validation; the inner loop picks the hyperparameter and the outer loop measures it, so the reported folds never saw the choice.
Level 4: The difference is significant and tiny. Do you ship B? Expected: weigh the effect size against the cost of the change; significance says the sign is reliable, not that it matters.
wrongAnswers: "One held-out split is enough if it is large." A single split still depends on which rows landed where; folds show the spread.
"Compare the two mean scores and pick the higher one." Without the per-fold pairing and the spread, a gap smaller than the fold noise looks like a win.
"Use the test set to break the tie." The test set is single use; a choice made on it turns it into a validation set.

questions.title: A team keeps growing a model. Test error falls, then spikes as the parameter count approaches the number of training rows, then falls again as they keep going. The classical U-shaped curve predicts the spike but not the second fall. Explain what the curve shows, and give the team a rule about model size.
questions.answer: The spike sits at the interpolation threshold, where the model has just enough capacity to fit every training row and is forced into one specific, noise-sensitive solution, so variance peaks. Past it, many solutions fit the training data and gradient descent's implicit regularization picks a simple one, so error falls again. That is double descent. The rule: stay well below the threshold with explicit regularization, or go well past it; the worst place to sit is on it.
followUps: Level 3: How do you recognize the threshold in a training log? Expected: training error reaches zero and test error is at its worst at about the same model size or epoch.
Level 4: Why can adding data hurt in this regime? Expected: more rows move the threshold; a fixed model that was past it can land on it, which is the sample-wise form.
Level 4: What does regularization do to the peak? Expected: it smooths and lowers the peak but does not remove it.
Level 4: Does this make the bias-variance trade-off wrong? Expected: no; it holds below the threshold and is incomplete above it, where the implicit bias of the optimizer takes over.
wrongAnswers: "The second fall is a measurement error." It appears in linear models, trees and networks, and in both the sample-wise and epoch-wise forms.
"Make the model as big as the budget allows and stop thinking about it." Bigger past the threshold works, but sitting on the threshold is the worst outcome; size the model deliberately away from it.
"Regularization removes the problem." It smooths and lowers the peak; it does not remove it.

questions.title: Take-home. Build a stacking ensemble on a tabular classification dataset with three base models from different families and a logistic regression meta-learner. Deliver the training code, a comparison with each base model alone, and a written argument that the meta-learner was never trained on a prediction made for a row the base model had already seen. Describe how you structure the work and what you check before you submit.
questions.answer: Generate the meta-features with k-fold cross-validation: for each fold, fit the base models on the other folds and predict the held-out fold, so every training row gets base predictions from models that did not train on it. Fit the meta-learner on those out-of-fold predictions, then refit the base models on all training rows for test time. Compare on a test set that neither level touched, and report the base models and the stack side by side with fold spreads.
followUps: Level 3: Why soft predictions rather than hard labels as meta-features? Expected: probabilities carry confidence, so the meta-learner can weight a sure base model above an unsure one.

Level 4: The stack beats every base model on the training folds but not on the test set. What is the first check? Expected: whether any meta-feature came from a base model that had seen that row; an in-sample prediction teaches the meta-learner to trust an overfit model.
Level 4: How do you show the base models are diverse enough to help? Expected: compare their errors on the validation folds; models that fail on the same rows add nothing.
Level 4: When would you not ship the stack? Expected: when the gain over the best base model is inside the fold spread, or below the cost of running three models.
wrongAnswers: "Fit the base models on all training rows, predict those rows, and train the meta-learner on that." Those predictions are in-sample and too good; the meta-learner learns to trust the base model that overfits most.
"Use three random forests with different seeds." Same family, similar errors; the stack needs models that fail on different rows.
"Set the meta-learner's weights by hand." The point of stacking is to learn which base model to trust where; fixed weights are a voting ensemble.

topics.title: Deep learning
topics.about: Backpropagation, losses, optimizers, initialization and how to debug a network that does not learn.

questions.title: A freshly initialised 10-class classifier should predict roughly uniform probabilities. What cross-entropy loss should you see on the very first batch? (Natural log.)
questions.answer: Uniform predictions give each class probability 1/10, so the loss is −ln(1/10) = ln 10 = 2.303. It's a free sanity check. A language model with a 50,000-token vocabulary should start near ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8. A first loss far above that means the initialisation is too large (confident wrong predictions). A first loss far below it means the labels are leaking into the inputs.

questions.title: Training loss sits at 2.30 for a 10-class problem and doesn't move for 1,000 steps. What's your first debugging step?
questions.answer: Loss stuck at ln(classes) means the outputs are still uniform: gradients aren't reaching the weights, or they don't change anything. The classic causes are a learning rate of 0 or tiny, the optimiser not given the model's parameters, a forgotten optimizer.step() or zero_grad(), frozen layers, or inputs and labels that don't line up. Overfitting one batch separates "the code is broken" from "the problem is hard" in a couple of minutes.
options: Add more layers.
Try to overfit a single batch of 32 examples. If it can't, the bug is in the code, not the data.
Collect more data.
Train for 10,000 more steps.

questions.title: Training loss keeps falling. Validation loss falls until epoch 5, then rises every epoch. What's happening, and what do you do?
questions.answer: Training loss falling while validation loss rises means the model is fitting noise specific to the training set. Stop at the best validation epoch, then reduce the gap: weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, a smaller model, or more data.
options: Train longer and validation will come back down.
Overfitting from epoch 5: keep the epoch-5 checkpoint (early stopping), then add regularisation or augmentation.
The learning rate is too low.
Validation data has a bug.

questions.title: Loss jumps up and down by a lot from step to step and doesn't trend down. What do you change first?
questions.answer: Wild oscillation with no downward trend is the classic sign of a learning rate that's too high. Lower it, add warmup if you haven't, and check the batch isn't tiny (very noisy gradients look similar). A learning-rate range test, increasing the rate gradually over a few hundred steps and watching where the loss starts to blow up, finds a sensible value quickly.
options: Lower the learning rate, by 3–10×.
Use a bigger model.
Raise the learning rate to escape a bad region.
Remove the learning-rate warmup.

questions.title: Training in fp16, the loss suddenly becomes NaN after 200 steps. What's the most likely cause?
questions.answer: fp16's range is narrow, so a spike in activations or gradients overflows to inf, and the next operation produces NaN. Fixes, roughly in order: use bf16 if the hardware supports it (fp32's exponent range), use dynamic loss scaling with fp16, clip gradients, lower the learning rate, and look for an unstable operation such as a softmax or log on unclamped values.
options: The model is too small.
Too much weight decay.
The dataset contains NaN labels.
Values overflowing fp16's range, which tops out around 65,504: exploding activations or gradients.

questions.title: Evaluating the same checkpoint twice on the same validation set gives 81.2% and then 79.6%. What did you forget?
questions.answer: In training mode, dropout randomly zeroes activations and batch norm uses the current batch's statistics, so outputs change from run to run. Call model.eval() before evaluation (and wrap it in torch.no_grad() to save memory), then model.train() before training resumes.
options: Turning off gradient calculation.
Setting a random seed for the validation loader.
Switching the model to evaluation mode, so dropout is still active.
Shuffling the validation set.

questions.title: The learning rate warms up linearly from 0 to 3e-4 over the first 2,000 steps. What is it at step 500?
questions.answer: Linear warmup: lr = 3e-4 × 500 ÷ 2,000 = 7.5e-05. Warmup avoids huge, badly-directed updates in the first steps, before Adam's moment estimates have settled. It matters most for transformers trained with large learning rates.

questions.title: After warmup, the learning rate follows a cosine decay from 3e-4 down to 0 over the remaining steps. What is it exactly halfway through the decay?
questions.answer: Cosine schedule: lr = min + ½ (max − min)(1 + cos(π t ÷ T)). At t = T/2, cos(π/2) = 0, so lr = ½ × 3e-4 = 1.5e-04. The rate falls slowly at first, fastest in the middle, and slowly again at the end.

questions.title: Why do most transformer fine-tuning recipes use AdamW rather than Adam with an L2 penalty added to the loss?
questions.answer: In plain Adam, an L2 term becomes part of the gradient, then gets rescaled by the per-parameter adaptive denominator, so the effective regularisation varies by parameter in ways nobody intended. AdamW subtracts lr × weight_decay × w separately from the adaptive update, so decay behaves like true weight decay. In practice it generalises better and its settings transfer more reliably between models.
options: AdamW is faster per step.
AdamW doesn't need a learning rate.
With Adam, an L2 penalty gets divided by the adaptive denominator, so weights with large gradients are barely regularised. AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights.
Adam can't train transformers.

questions.title: You raise the batch size from 256 to 1,024 on the same SGD setup. What's a common starting point for the learning rate?
questions.answer: For SGD, the linear scaling rule (multiply the learning rate by the batch-size ratio, with warmup) is a good starting point up to fairly large batches. For Adam-style optimisers, square-root scaling is a common heuristic. Either way, treat it as a starting point and check with a short sweep.
options: Divide it by 4.
Keep it the same.
Multiply it by 4 (linear scaling), with a warmup.
Learning rate doesn't depend on batch size.

questions.title: A transformer trains well but the loss spikes sharply every few thousand steps, then slowly recovers. What's a standard fix?
questions.answer: Occasional loss spikes usually come from a rare batch producing a huge gradient. Gradient-norm clipping rescales the whole gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold, so the direction is kept but the step is bounded. If spikes continue, lower the learning rate, check for bad data in those batches, and look at the Adam epsilon and beta2 settings.
options: Remove the warmup.
Raise the learning rate.
Switch from AdamW to plain SGD.
Clip the global gradient norm, often to 1.0.

questions.title: With He initialisation for a ReLU layer that has 512 inputs, what is the standard deviation of the initial weights? (Three decimals.)
questions.answer: He initialisation draws weights with variance 2 ÷ fan_in, so std = √(2 ÷ 512) = 0.0625. The factor of 2 makes up for ReLU zeroing half its inputs, which keeps the variance of activations roughly constant from layer to layer. Xavier (Glorot) uses 1 ÷ fan_in, or 2 ÷ (fan_in + fan_out), which suits tanh.

questions.title: You train a segmentation model with batch norm, and memory limits you to 2 images per GPU. Results are poor and noisy. Why, and what do you do?
questions.answer: Batch norm normalises with the mean and variance of the current batch. With 2 examples those estimates are mostly noise, and the running statistics used at evaluation time don't match what training saw. GroupNorm and LayerNorm normalise within each example, so they don't depend on batch size. SyncBatchNorm computes statistics across all GPUs.
options: Remove all normalisation.
Use a larger learning rate.
Batch statistics computed from 2 examples are very noisy. Use group or layer normalisation, or synchronised batch norm across GPUs.
Batch norm doesn't work with images.

questions.title: A plain 50-layer network trains worse than an 18-layer one, even on the training set. What's the usual fix?
questions.answer: Worse *training* accuracy with more layers is the degradation problem, not overfitting. Residual connections (x + f(x)) make the identity function easy to represent and give gradients a direct path back through the network. Normalisation and careful initialisation help too. This is the ResNet result, and it's why every transformer block has two residual connections.
options: More dropout.
More training data.
A larger learning rate.
Residual (skip) connections, so each block learns a change to its input.

questions.title: What causes vanishing and exploding gradients, and how are they fixed?
questions.answer: Backpropagation computes gradients via the chain rule, multiplying Jacobian matrices across layers. When weight matrices or activation derivatives have singular values below 1—such as sigmoid or tanh whose maximum derivative is 0.25—gradients vanish exponentially with depth. If singular values exceed 1, gradients explode. Mitigate vanishing gradients using non-saturating activations (ReLU, GELU), residual connections that provide an additive gradient highway, normalization layers (LayerNorm, RMSNorm), and proper variance initialization such as He initialization for ReLU ((W) = 2/n_{in}$). For exploding gradients, enforce L2 gradient norm clipping (typically threshold 1.0) and monitor per-layer gradient norms during warmup.
keyPoints: Repeated Jacobian multiplication can shrink or amplify gradients.
Saturating activations and poor initialization worsen gradient flow.
Residual paths and suitable initialization improve propagation.
Gradient clipping controls exploding gradients but does not fix vanishing gradients.

questions.title: Why do LSTMs handle long sequences better than plain RNNs, and why did transformers replace them?
questions.answer: Plain RNNs apply the same transition matrix at each step, causing gradients to vanish or explode over long time horizons. An LSTM introduces a dedicated cell state updated via an additive highway:  = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot 	ilde{c}_t$. When forget gate  pprox 1$, the gradient $ rac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}$ equals $, preserving gradient flow across hundreds of steps without exponential decay. Transformers replaced recurrent architectures because RNNs require sequential step-by-step computation that cannot parallelize across time during training. Self-attention connects any two token positions in O(1) operations and computes all interactions across the entire sequence in parallel on GPUs.
keyPoints: LSTM gates control what memory to retain, write and expose.
An additive cell path helps gradients travel across time.
Recurrent computation is sequential and limits training parallelism.
Attention offers shorter paths to distant tokens at a memory cost.

questions.title: Why do CNNs work so well for images? Explain convolution and pooling.
questions.answer: CNNs succeed on images due to two inductive biases: translation equivariance and spatial locality. Locality assumes neighboring pixels share strong semantic correlation, captured by small convolutional kernels. Translation equivariance means shifting an object in the input shifts the resulting feature map identically, allowing shared weights to detect features anywhere in the image. Hierarchical stacking grows the effective receptive field from local edges to complex object semantics, while pooling or strided convolutions reduce spatial dimensions. Vision Transformers lack these built-in spatial priors: they treat image patches as arbitrary tokens with global attention from layer one, requiring far larger pretraining datasets to learn spatial structure from scratch.
keyPoints: Convolution shares local filters across image positions.
