Weight sharing reduces parameters and gives translation equivariance.
Deeper layers combine local features into larger receptive fields.
Pooling reduces spatial resolution and can discard precise location.

questions.title: What problem do residual connections solve?
questions.answer: Deep plain networks fail not from overfitting, but from an optimization barrier: as depth increases, training error degrades because gradients struggle to propagate through non-linear layers. ResNet introduces identity shortcut connections where a block learns a residual mapping (x) = H(x) - x$, producing output (x) = F(x) + x$. When weights are initialized near zero, the block defaults to the identity function. During backpropagation, the gradient $ rac{\partial L}{\partial x} =  rac{\partial L}{\partial H}(1 +  rac{\partial F}{\partial x})$ passes back directly through the +1 term, ensuring gradient signal reaches early layers regardless of network depth and enabling models with hundreds of layers to converge.
keyPoints: Deep plain networks can be harder to optimize even without overfitting.
A residual block learns a correction added to its input.
The identity path improves gradient flow.
Projection shortcuts handle changes in feature dimensions.

questions.title: Compare batch normalization and layer normalization. Why do transformers use layer norm?
questions.answer: Batch Normalization computes mean and variance across the batch dimension for each feature, tracking running statistics for inference. It degrades when batch sizes are small, and it fails in NLP because variable sequence lengths and autoregressive single-token decoding distort mini-batch statistics. Layer Normalization computes mean and variance across the hidden channel dimension {model}$ for each token independently (0 	o$ normalize over $). Because LayerNorm performs zero cross-sample or cross-token pooling, it behaves identically during training and single-token serving, handles dynamic sequence lengths naturally, and operates cleanly in distributed pipelines. BatchNorm remains effective for CNNs with large, fixed-size image batches.
keyPoints: Batch norm uses batch statistics per feature channel.
Layer norm normalizes features within each example or token.
Batch norm uses running statistics at inference.
Layer norm works without dependence on batch size and suits variable-length transformers.

questions.title: Compare SGD with momentum, Adam and AdamW. What would you start with?
questions.answer: Momentum accelerates gradient descent by accumulating an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients, dampening oscillations across steep ravines. Adam adds adaptive per-parameter learning rates by tracking both first moments (momentum) and uncentered second moments (variance). However, standard Adam couples L2 regularization with the gradient update: weight decay is divided by the square root of historical squared gradients, penalizing frequently updated weights far less than infrequently updated ones. AdamW fixes this by decoupling weight decay, subtracting $\lambda 	heta_{t-1}$ directly from the weights after the adaptive step. Use AdamW with linear warmup and cosine decay for transformers, and SGD with momentum for convolutional architectures.
keyPoints: Momentum accumulates gradients to smooth SGD updates.
Adam adapts learning rates using first and second gradient moments.
AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive gradient update.
Optimizer choice and learning rate must be validated on the workload.

questions.title: How does dropout work, and how does it behave at inference?
questions.answer: During training it zeroes each unit with probability p, which stops units relying on each other and acts like training many thinned networks. Common implementations scale the kept activations by 1/(1-p) so expected values match, then disable dropout at inference. Forgetting eval mode is a common bug that makes predictions noisy. Keeping dropout on at inference, Monte Carlo dropout, gives a rough uncertainty estimate.
keyPoints: Dropout randomly zeros activations during training.
It reduces reliance on particular co-adapted features.
Inverted dropout scales retained activations during training.
Ordinary inference disables dropout without random masking.

questions.title: Why do we pair softmax with cross-entropy, and how should you compute it safely?
questions.answer: Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution, and cross-entropy is its negative log likelihood. Together they give a simple gradient, predicted probability minus target, times the input features at the last layer, and it stays large when the model is confidently wrong. Compute the loss directly from logits using a log-softmax function, because computing softmax first and then a log can underflow and produce infinities or NaNs.
keyPoints: Softmax converts logits into a categorical probability distribution.
Cross-entropy penalizes low probability on the correct class.
Compute loss from logits with log-sum-exp for numerical stability.
Applying softmax before a logits-based loss is incorrect.

questions.title: Training loss is NaN after a few hundred steps. How do you debug it?
questions.answer: Isolate the failure systematically. First, log gradient norms, loss components, and activation scales right before the NaN step. Common root causes are: 1) Data anomalies (unhandled NaNs, infs, or zero-length sequences in a batch). 2) Numerical instability in loss functions (log of zero, unscaled logits in cross-entropy, or division by variance without epsilon). 3) Mixed-precision underflow or overflow in FP16, where dynamic loss scaling fails. 4) Unstable learning rates without warmup. To debug, enable PyTorch anomaly detection (torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)), overfit on a single deterministic mini-batch, inspect whether gradients or activations blew up first, and enforce gradient norm clipping at 1.0.
keyPoints: Find the first non-finite activation, gradient or loss.
Check data, labels and invalid operations before changing the model.
Inspect learning rate and gradient norms.
Compare with full precision to isolate overflow or loss-scaling problems.
Use clipping or stable loss implementations when the diagnosis supports them.

questions.title: How does distributed data parallel training work, and what limits it?
questions.answer: Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) replicates the full model across all GPUs; each GPU computes forward and backward passes on an independent data micro-batch. During the backward pass, gradients are averaged synchronously across workers via ring or tree All-Reduce, keeping weights synchronized. DDP is bounded by inter-GPU network bandwidth (NCCL), straggler effects, and GPU memory capacity. In mixed-precision training, model weights, gradients, and AdamW optimizer states consume 16 bytes per parameter. When a model exceeds single-GPU VRAM, transition to ZeRO or FSDP: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states (4x memory reduction), ZeRO-2 shards gradients (8x), and ZeRO-3/FSDP shards model weights, gathering them on-demand during forward and backward passes.
keyPoints: Data parallel workers hold model replicas and process different batches.
Workers all-reduce gradients before a consistent optimizer step.
Communication and synchronization can limit scaling.
Gradient accumulation or larger batches trade throughput against optimization behavior.
Model states may require sharding when replicas do not fit.

questions.title: What is mixed-precision training and what can go wrong?
questions.answer: Mixed precision uses 16-bit floating point (FP16 or BF16) for matrix multiplications and activations while maintaining FP32 master weights and optimizer states. FP16 has a 5-bit exponent and 10-bit mantissa (max value ~65,504, min subnormal $\sim 6 	imes 10^{-8}$); small backpropagated gradients easily underflow to zero, requiring a dynamic loss scaler that multiplies loss by a scale factor and skips optimizer steps on overflow. BF16 shares FP32's 8-bit exponent and has a 7-bit mantissa, offering the same dynamic range (0^{38}$) with reduced precision. BF16 eliminates gradient underflow and loss scaling entirely, making it the modern standard on Ampere and newer GPUs.
keyPoints: Mixed precision uses lower precision for selected compute with higher precision where needed.
FP16 can underflow gradients or overflow activations.
Loss scaling protects small FP16 gradients.
BF16 has a wider exponent range than FP16.
Check numerical stability rather than assuming lower precision preserves results.

questions.title: How do GANs train, and why did diffusion models overtake them?
questions.answer: GANs frame generative modeling as a minimax game between a generator producing synthetic samples and a discriminator distinguishing real from fake data. Training optimizes Jensen-Shannon divergence (or Wasserstein distance with a 1-Lipschitz critic). GANs suffer from non-convergence limit cycles, vanishing generator gradients, and mode collapse where the generator outputs limited repetitive variations. Diffusion models replace adversarial competition with denoising score matching: a forward Markov process adds Gaussian noise across discrete timesteps, and a reverse neural network learns to predict the added noise using a stable mean squared error loss. Diffusion guarantees stable training and full mode coverage, trading one-step inference for multi-step sampling.
keyPoints: A GAN trains a generator against a discriminator.
Adversarial training can be unstable or collapse to a few modes.
Diffusion learns to reverse progressive noise corruption.
Diffusion trades iterative sampling cost for more stable training and coverage.

questions.title: What does a VAE optimize, and how does the reparameterization trick help?
questions.answer: A VAE maximizes the evidence lower bound, made of a reconstruction term and a KL term that keeps the latent distribution near a prior. Sampling is not differentiable, so the trick writes the latent as the mean plus the standard deviation times independent noise, which lets gradients flow to both. Too much KL weight can make the decoder ignore the latent, which is known as posterior collapse.
keyPoints: A VAE optimizes a reconstruction term and KL regularization toward a prior.
The encoder predicts a latent distribution.
Reparameterization samples noise and transforms it using differentiable parameters.
The KL-reconstruction balance affects latent usefulness and reconstruction quality.

questions.title: With only 2,000 labelled images, how would you build a classifier?
questions.answer: Start with a pretrained backbone, freeze it, and train a new head. Then unfreeze the top layers at a lower learning rate if validation improves. Use strong augmentation and a split that prevents near-duplicate leakage. Check class balance and label quality, since label errors matter more with small data. Compare against simple features plus logistic regression, and consider active learning to spend further labelling budget where it helps most.
keyPoints: Start from a pretrained image model rather than training from scratch.
Use a clean representative split and appropriate augmentation.
Train a classifier head then selectively fine-tune with a smaller learning rate.
Use regularization and validation to control overfitting on limited labels.

questions.title: In PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), why is gradient synchronization strictly synchronous, and how does gradient bucketing overlap communication with backprop?
questions.answer: In Distributed Data Parallel, each GPU holds a full model replica and computes backward gradients on its own data shard. Gradient synchronization is strictly synchronous because all replicas must apply identical parameter updates at every step to keep weights mathematically identical without diverging. To hide communication latency, PyTorch does not wait until the entire backward pass finishes. It organizes parameters into buckets in reverse layer order. As soon as backward autograd completes the gradients for a bucket, DDP initiates an asynchronous Ring-AllReduce across all GPUs while earlier layers are still computing gradients. Ring-AllReduce shares gradients in logical rings of chunks: each GPU sends and receives simultaneously, transferring two times the gradient size divided by the number of ranks. The trade-off is bucket size tuning: large buckets achieve high network bandwidth utilization on InfiniBand, but small buckets start communication earlier to overlap with backward computation.
followUps: What happens if your model parameters are not executed in deterministic order during the forward pass?
How does Ring-AllReduce communication volume scale as you increase cluster size from 8 to 1,024 GPUs?
wrongAnswers: Claiming DDP uses asynchronous parameter updates like Parameter Server architectures, ignoring that DDP enforces strict synchronous lockstep.
Believing Ring-AllReduce transfers the entire model size from every GPU to every other GPU sequentially, rather than in ring chunks.
tradeOffs: Bucket pipelining overlaps communication with computation, but setting buckets too small increases per-message kernel launch overhead.
Strictly synchronous AllReduce guarantees mathematical equivalence to single-GPU training, but forces fast GPUs to wait for the slowest straggler node.
keyPoints: DDP replicas must apply identical synchronized gradient updates.
Bucket gradients and start asynchronous all-reduce as buckets become ready.
Overlap communication with remaining backward computation.
Large buckets favor bandwidth while small buckets begin overlap sooner.

questions.title: Compare ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3 in terms of memory reduction and inter-node communication overhead.
questions.answer: ZeRO eliminates redundant memory across data-parallel ranks in three stages. In standard training, every GPU stores identical optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters. In ZeRO Stage 1, we shard the optimizer states across GPUs, which reduces memory by roughly four times with zero extra communication. In ZeRO Stage 2, we also shard the gradients, so each GPU reduces and stores only its slice of gradients, again with no extra communication cost. In ZeRO Stage 3, we shard the actual model parameters. Each GPU keeps only its partition; during the forward pass, it gathers layer parameters via an all-gather, computes the activations, and immediately discards the gathered weights. The backward pass repeats this all-gather and runs a reduce-scatter on gradients. The trade-off is memory capacity against interconnect bandwidth: ZeRO-3 lets you train massive models without model-parallel code, but it introduces 50% more communication, making training network-bound on slow ethernet networks.
followUps: How does ZeRO-Offload extend ZeRO-3 by utilizing host CPU memory and NVMe storage?
Why does ZeRO-2 have identical communication volume to standard DDP?
wrongAnswers: Asserting that ZeRO-1 increases network communication overhead, when optimizer state sharding requires zero extra collective traffic.
Thinking ZeRO-3 permanently holds gathered parameters in GPU memory, missing that weights are discarded immediately after layer computation.
tradeOffs: ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 reduce memory significantly with 0% communication overhead, whereas ZeRO-3 requires 50% extra communication for layer all-gathers.
ZeRO-3 eliminates the need for tensor or pipeline model-sharding code, but requires high-bandwidth interconnects like NVLink or InfiniBand.
keyPoints: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states and ZeRO-2 additionally shards gradients.
ZeRO-3 also shards model parameters.
Gather layer weights for computation and reduce-scatter gradients.
Greater memory savings require more interconnect communication.

questions.title: Walk through how PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) shards model states across forward and backward passes. What is the communication cost?
questions.answer: Fully Sharded Data Parallel shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across ranks at the granularity of individual transformer layers. During the forward pass, before executing a specific layer, FSDP executes an all-gather collective so all ranks receive the full un-sharded weights. It computes the forward activations and immediately frees the un-sharded parameters from memory, keeping only its assigned shard. During the backward pass, FSDP all-gathers the layer weights a second time to compute input gradients, frees the weights again, and performs a reduce-scatter on gradients so each rank holds only its shard of the gradient. To minimize overhead, FSDP overlaps the all-gather of the next layer with computation of the current layer. The trade-off is memory efficiency against communication volume: FSDP scales model capacity linearly with GPU count, but communication volume increases by roughly 50% compared to standard DDP, requiring high-bandwidth interconnects like NVLink or InfiniBand.
followUps: What is the difference between FSDP FULL_SHARD and SHARD_GRAD_OP?
How do you implement activation checkpointing inside an FSDP-wrapped transformer block?
wrongAnswers: Believing FSDP gathers the entire model weights all at once before the forward pass, which would immediately cause an out-of-memory error.
Assuming FSDP eliminates the backward all-gather because parameters were already gathered during the forward pass.
tradeOffs: FSDP achieves linear memory scaling with cluster size, but increases communication volume by roughly 50% relative to standard DDP.
Wrapping layers too granularly creates thousands of small collective launches; wrapping too coarsely spikes peak memory.
keyPoints: FSDP shards parameters, gradients and optimizer states by layer.
All-gather layer weights before forward and backward computation.
Free full weights after use and reduce-scatter gradients.
Overlap next-layer gathering with current computation to reduce overhead.

questions.title: What causes the pipeline bubble in pipeline parallelism, and how do 1F1B scheduling and interleaved micro-batching reduce idle GPU time?
questions.answer: In pipeline parallelism, we split model layers sequentially across multiple GPUs. When Rank 0 is running the first layer on a batch, downstream GPUs sit idle waiting for activations to arrive; similarly, during backward passes, upstream GPUs sit idle waiting for gradients. This idle time is the pipeline bubble. If a batch is split into m micro-batches across p pipeline stages, the bubble fraction is approximately p minus one divided by m plus p minus one. To minimize this bubble, 1F1B scheduling alternates one forward micro-batch with one backward micro-batch. Once the pipeline warms up, each GPU immediately runs a backward pass as soon as gradients arrive, freeing activation memory before launching the next forward micro-batch. The trade-off is activation memory versus bubble overhead: increasing micro-batches shrinks the bubble percentage, but keeping more micro-batches in flight increases peak activation memory across intermediate stages.
followUps: How do you combine pipeline parallelism with tensor parallelism and data parallelism in 3D parallelism?
What happens to the pipeline schedule when layers have uneven computation times?
wrongAnswers: Believing pipeline bubbles can be eliminated completely without micro-batching, ignoring sequential data dependencies across layers.
Assuming 1F1B and GPipe have identical peak memory footprints, ignoring that GPipe delays all backward passes until all forwards complete.
tradeOffs: 1F1B scheduling caps peak activation memory to p micro-batches, whereas standard GPipe retains all m micro-batches in memory.
Interleaved 1F1B reduces the bubble further by assigning multiple virtual stages per GPU, at the cost of additional P2P communication.
keyPoints: Pipeline stages idle while awaiting activations or gradients.
Splitting batches into more micro-batches reduces the bubble fraction.
1F1B alternates forward and backward micro-batches to release activations sooner.
More in-flight micro-batches increase activation-memory pressure.

questions.title: How does Megatron-LM split transformer attention and MLP matrices across GPUs with only two AllReduce operations per layer?
questions.answer: Megatron-LM tensor parallelism shards individual matrix multiplications across GPUs within a single node. In multi-head attention, the projection matrices for queries, keys, and values are split column-wise across GPUs. Each GPU computes attention heads for its slice independently with no communication. The output projection matrix is split row-wise: each GPU multiplies its local head outputs by its weight slice, and a single all-reduce sums the partial vectors across ranks to produce the final attention output. For the feed-forward network, the first linear layer is split column-wise, GeLU activation is applied locally, and the second linear layer is split row-wise, followed by a second all-reduce. This achieves tensor parallelism with exactly two all-reduce operations per transformer layer. The trade-off is high communication frequency: every single layer requires two all-reduces, so tensor parallelism is strictly confined to high-bandwidth intra-node NVLink connections and cannot scale efficiently across slow inter-node networks.
followUps: Why can we not apply tensor parallelism across nodes connected by standard 100 Gbps Ethernet?
How does Sequence Parallelism build on Megatron-LM to shard LayerNorm and Dropout activations?
wrongAnswers: Row-splitting QKV and column-splitting output projections, which forces an extra AllReduce between every internal layer operation.
Attempting to scale Megatron tensor parallelism across 64 nodes over standard TCP, resulting in 95% communication stall time.
tradeOffs: Column-then-row matrix decomposition eliminates inter-layer communication, but requires ultra-fast NVLink bandwidth (e.g. 900 GB/s on H100).
Splitting attention heads requires head counts to be cleanly divisible by the tensor-parallel degree.
keyPoints: Column-shard QKV projections so ranks compute separate heads.
Row-shard output projections and all-reduce partial outputs.
Apply column then row sharding to feed-forward layers.
Frequent layer collectives favor high-bandwidth intra-node links.

questions.title: How does gradient accumulation simulate a larger effective batch size without running out of GPU memory, and what happens at optimizer step boundaries?
questions.answer: Gradient accumulation lets you train with large effective batch sizes when a full batch does not fit into GPU memory. We divide the target batch into smaller micro-batches that fit into VRAM, run forward and backward passes sequentially, and accumulate gradients into the parameter gradient buffers without zeroing them. In distributed training with DDP, calling backward on every micro-batch would trigger an expensive all-reduce collective every time. To prevent this, we wrap intermediate micro-batches in PyTorch's no_sync context manager, which suppresses gradient synchronization until the final micro-batch of the accumulation cycle. At that boundary, DDP synchronizes gradients across all ranks, the optimizer steps, and gradients are zeroed. The trade-off is training throughput against wall-clock step time: gradient accumulation reduces communication overhead and avoids out-of-memory errors, but optimizer updates happen less frequently, which requires adjusting learning rate warmup schedules.
followUps: Why must you divide loss by accumulation_steps before calling loss.backward()?
How does gradient accumulation interact with batch normalization statistics?
wrongAnswers: Calling optimizer.step() and optimizer.zero_grad() inside the accumulation loop, which updates weights on single micro-batches instead of accumulating.
Omitting model.no_sync() in DDP, triggering an AllReduce collective on every single micro-batch and destroying training throughput.
tradeOffs: no_sync() avoids redundant AllReduce collectives on intermediate micro-batches, but gradients must be scaled by accumulation steps to avoid loss explosion.
Large effective batch sizes improve hardware throughput, but past a critical threshold, larger batches yield diminishing returns in sample efficiency.
keyPoints: Accumulate gradients over micro-batches without zeroing between them.
Use no_sync on intermediate DDP micro-batches.
Synchronize, step the optimizer and clear gradients at the accumulation boundary.
Less frequent updates require adjusted warmup schedules.

questions.title: Your distributed training job halts with an NCCL watchdog timeout error on node 4. How do you systematically isolate whether this is straggler compute, network packet drop, or silent GPU failure?
questions.answer: An NCCL watchdog timeout error indicates that an all-reduce or collective operation waited beyond its timeout limit, but the rank that timed out is rarely the root cause. Collective operations require all ranks to enter the call; if one rank hangs or runs slowly, every other rank eventually times out waiting for it. To isolate the issue, we set NCCL_DEBUG to INFO and enable asynchronous error handling. First, we inspect the logs to identify which rank failed to enter the collective. If one rank is delayed while others are waiting, we check for a compute straggler: uneven batch sizes, an un-sharded evaluation loop, or data loading bottlenecks on that host. Second, we verify GPU health by checking for thermal throttling, PCIe bus errors, or uncorrectable ECC memory errors using nvidia-smi. Third, if all compute ranks look normal, we test the network fabric with collective benchmarks like nccl-tests to check for dropped packets, InfiniBand link degradations, or route flapping. The trade-off is diagnostic verbosity against overhead: detailed tracing slows down execution, but it pinpoint the exact failing rank.
followUps: What is the difference between an NCCL barrier timeout and a silent kernel lockup?
How do you configure NCCL socket interfaces to ensure traffic routes over InfiniBand rather than secondary Ethernet interfaces?
wrongAnswers: Assuming the node reporting the timeout is the broken node, missing that healthy nodes time out waiting for a hung peer.
Immediately rebooting the host without checking GPU ECC errors, PCIe link speed degradation, or dmesg hardware logs.
tradeOffs: Enabling NCCL_DEBUG=INFO provides detailed ring topology and collective tracing, but generates substantial log volume on large clusters.
Asynchronous error handling halts jobs immediately upon collective failures, preventing GPU compute waste on dead runs.
keyPoints: A collective timeout can be caused by another rank failing to enter.
Enable NCCL diagnostics and identify the delayed rank.
Check data loading, uneven work and GPU health.
Test network collectives if compute ranks look healthy.

questions.title: How does activation checkpointing trade extra compute for GPU memory, and how do you decide which layers to checkpoint?
questions.answer: During the forward pass of training, standard backpropagation saves all intermediate layer activations in GPU memory so they can be used to compute gradients during the backward pass. For long sequences or deep models, these activations consume far more memory than the model weights themselves. Activation checkpointing discards intermediate activations during the forward pass, saving only the inputs to designated transformer blocks. During the backward pass, when gradients for that block are needed, we re-run the forward pass on that specific block from its saved input, recomputing the activations on the fly, and immediately compute gradients. This reduces activation memory from linear in the number of layers to roughly square root of the number of layers. The trade-off is compute against memory: activation checkpointing adds approximately 20 to 30 percent extra floating-point operations to training, but it lets you train significantly larger models or longer sequence lengths without out-of-memory crashes.
followUps: Why is activation memory quadratic in sequence length for standard attention without FlashAttention?
How does FlashAttention reduce the necessity of activation checkpointing for intermediate attention matrices?
wrongAnswers: Believing activation checkpointing saves parameter or optimizer memory, when it strictly targets forward intermediate activations.
Claiming recomputation doubles total training time, ignoring that backward passes account for the majority of baseline compute.
tradeOffs: Full activation checkpointing cuts activation memory drastically at the cost of roughly 25% to 33% recomputation overhead.
Selective activation checkpointing checkpoints only memory-intensive operations (like attention softmax) while caching linear layer activations.
keyPoints: Save block inputs instead of every intermediate activation.
Recompute discarded activations during backward before calculating gradients.
Checkpointing reduces memory at the cost of extra forward computation.
Use it to fit deeper models or longer sequences.

questions.title: Why has bfloat16 largely replaced FP16 for distributed pre-training, and when is FP16 still preferred?
questions.answer: Bfloat16 has largely replaced standard FP16 for distributed pre-training because of its dynamic range. Both formats use 16 bits, but FP16 allocates 5 bits to the exponent and 10 bits to the mantissa, giving a maximum value of 65,504 and underflowing below roughly ten to the minus five. Small gradients in deep transformer layers frequently underflow to zero, requiring dynamic loss scaling to prevent training instability. Bfloat16 allocates 8 bits to the exponent and 7 bits to the mantissa, exactly matching the dynamic range of single-precision FP32 up to ten to the thirty-eighth power. This preserves gradient magnitudes without loss scaling, greatly reducing underflow and making large-scale pre-training runs significantly more stable. The trade-off is mantissa precision: BF16 has fewer precision bits than FP16, resulting in slightly higher rounding error. FP16 remains preferred when numerical accuracy is more important than dynamic range, such as inference tasks on hardware without native bfloat16 tensor cores.
followUps: Why does FP16 require dynamic loss scaling during backward passes while BF16 does not?
What happens when you accumulate matrix products in BF16 versus accumulating in FP32?
wrongAnswers: Claiming BF16 completely eliminates all numerical underflow, ignoring that its lower mantissa precision creates higher rounding noise.
Believing FP16 and BF16 have identical dynamic ranges because both occupy 16 bits in memory.
tradeOffs: BF16 eliminates dynamic loss scaling and gradient overflow instability, but trades off three bits of mantissa precision relative to FP16.
FP16 achieves lower quantization noise and higher numeric precision, but requires careful loss scaling to prevent underflow to zero.
keyPoints: FP16 has a narrower exponent range and may need loss scaling.
BF16 matches FP32 exponent range and preserves small gradient magnitudes.
BF16 has fewer mantissa bits and more rounding error.
Hardware support and numerical needs affect the format choice.

questions.title: When training across 64 GPUs, how do you configure the DistributedSampler and random seeds to guarantee no duplicate data across ranks and reproducible resumption?
questions.answer: When training across multiple GPUs, each rank must process a unique, non-overlapping subset of the dataset in every epoch. We wrap the dataset in PyTorch's DistributedSampler, configuring the total number of replicas and the rank of each GPU. The sampler calculates the slice of data indices assigned to that rank so data is partitioned cleanly. Crucially, in our training loop, we must call sampler.set_epoch(epoch) at the start of every epoch. The sampler uses the epoch number to seed its deterministic shuffle; if you omit set_epoch, the dataset will shuffle once at the start of training and repeat the exact same ordering every subsequent epoch, reducing model generalization. For reproducible resumption, we save the global epoch, the global step count, and the random states for PyTorch, NumPy, and Python in our checkpoint. The trade-off is dataset size alignment: when the dataset cannot be divided evenly across ranks, the sampler pads samples to keep batch counts identical, which slightly over-samples border items unless drop_last is enabled.
followUps: What happens in DDP if one rank processes one fewer batch than the other ranks because drop_last was False?
How do you implement streaming webdataset sharding across thousands of workers without pre-computing index tables?
wrongAnswers: Omitting sampler.set_epoch(epoch), causing the DataLoader to produce identical data sample orderings across all epochs.
Seeding all dataloader worker processes with the identical random seed, causing all ranks to process identical data shards.
tradeOffs: DistributedSampler guarantees non-overlapping rank partitions, but requires calling set_epoch() every epoch to ensure shuffling across epochs.
Padding uneven datasets ensures equal batch counts per rank, avoiding deadlock in AllReduce, but introduces duplicate border samples.
keyPoints: Use DistributedSampler to assign data across ranks.
Call set_epoch each epoch to change the deterministic shuffle.
Save epoch, step and random states for reproducible resumption.
Uneven dataset sizes require padding or dropping samples.

questions.title: A junior engineer removes every activation function from a 10 layer network to make it faster and reports that training still runs and the loss still falls. What did they build, and why will it fail on XOR or on a spiral dataset?
questions.answer: Two linear layers compose into one: W2 (W1 x + b1) + b2 equals (W2 W1) x + (W2 b1 + b2), which is a single matrix and a single bias. Ten linear layers are one linear layer with extra parameters and the same decision boundary, a hyperplane. XOR and a spiral need a curved boundary, so the network cannot fit them at any width or depth.
followUps: Level 1: Which layer is allowed to have no activation? Expected: the output layer of a regression model, which must produce any real number.
Level 2: Does the deep linear network train faster than one layer? Expected: no; it computes the same function with more parameters and more matrix multiplies.
Level 2: Which activation would you add back for a plain MLP and for a transformer? Expected: ReLU for the MLP and GELU for the transformer.

Level 3: Why is the collapse not a proof that depth is useless? Expected: with a nonlinearity between layers the substitution fails and each layer adds capacity; deep networks fit the same functions with fewer parameters than wide shallow ones.
wrongAnswers: "Ten layers are deeper, so they represent more." Without a nonlinearity the product of the matrices is one matrix; depth adds nothing.
"The biases make it nonlinear." A bias shifts the hyperplane; it does not bend it.
"The loss went down, so it is learning fine." It learns the best linear fit, which for XOR or a spiral is near chance.

questions.title: A saved model gives a different test accuracy each time you evaluate it on the same test set with the same weights. The data loader does not shuffle. What is the most likely cause, and which two layer types are involved?
questions.answer: The model is still in training mode at test time. Dropout keeps zeroing random units, so each forward pass runs a different subnetwork, and batch normalization keeps using the mean and variance of the current batch instead of its running averages. Switch to evaluation mode before inference and turn gradient tracking off.
followUps: Level 1: What does dropout do in evaluation mode? Expected: nothing; it passes every value through unchanged, because the scaling was applied during training.

Level 2: Why can batch normalization not use batch statistics for a batch of one at test time? Expected: the variance of one sample is zero, so the statistics are meaningless; the running averages must be used.
Level 2: How does a container pass the mode to its children? Expected: its train and eval methods set the flag on the container and on every module inside it.

Level 3: You forget to switch back to training mode after validation. What happens in the next epoch? Expected: dropout stays off and batch norm stops updating its running statistics, so the model trains without regularization and its inference statistics go stale.
wrongAnswers: "Set a random seed before each evaluation." That hides the symptom; the model still evaluates with dropout and batch statistics active, so the accuracy is wrong, just repeatably wrong.
"GPU arithmetic is nondeterministic, this is normal." That gives differences far below one changed prediction, not a moving accuracy.
"Remove dropout from the architecture." Dropout is a training time regularizer; the fix is to switch modes, not to delete the layer.

questions.title: A single perceptron learns the AND and OR gates in a few epochs. On the XOR gate it never converges, even after 1000 epochs. Why not, and what is the smallest change to the model that makes XOR learnable?
questions.answer: A perceptron takes a weighted sum, adds a bias and applies a threshold, so its decision boundary is one straight line. AND and OR put their ones on one side of a line. XOR puts the ones at (0, 1) and (1, 0) and the zeros at (0, 0) and (1, 1), and no single line separates those two pairs. Add a hidden layer: two neurons that compute OR and NAND, and an output neuron that ANDs them, give XOR exactly.
followUps: Level 1: What does the learning rule do when a prediction is right? Expected: the error is 0, so no weight changes.

Level 2: Why does the step function block learning in the two layer version? Expected: it has no useful gradient, so backpropagation cannot assign blame to the hidden weights; the sigmoid is smooth and has a gradient everywhere.
Level 2: Why do weights of 20 and -20 work in the sigmoid version? Expected: large weights make the sigmoid act like a step, so each hidden neuron is a crisp OR or NAND.
Level 3: Is a three input majority function linearly separable? Expected: yes; output 1 when at least two inputs are 1 is a half space, so one perceptron learns it.
wrongAnswers: "Train longer or raise the learning rate." No line separates the XOR points, so no number of epochs finds one.
"Add more inputs or more neurons in the same layer." A wider single layer still draws one line through the same plane.
"A hidden layer with no activation fixes it." Two linear layers compose into one linear map, which is one line again. The hidden layer needs a nonlinearity.

questions.title: Adam keeps a running average of the gradient and a running average of its square, and divides each by one minus beta to the power t before the update. A teammate deletes those two divisions to simplify the code. What changes in the first steps of training, and when does the change stop mattering?
questions.answer: Both averages start at zero, so at step one the first moment is only (1 - beta1) times the gradient, a tenth of it with beta1 at 0.9, and the second moment is a thousandth of the squared gradient with beta2 at 0.999. The divisions rescale both to unbiased estimates. Without them the square root of the second moment is shrunk more than the first moment, so the ratio and the step come out too large while the averages warm up. The first moment's factor is close to 1 after about 50 steps, but the second moment's factor, 1 - 0.999 to the t, stays well below 1 for thousands of steps, so without the division the step stays too large for that long.
followUps: Level 2: What does the first moment estimate and what does the second? Expected: the running mean of the gradient, which is momentum, and the running mean of the squared gradient, which sets a per-parameter step size.
Level 2: With beta1 at 0.9, how many past gradients does the first moment roughly average? Expected: about ten, from 1 over (1 - 0.9).

Level 3: Why does Adam still want a warmup if bias correction exists? Expected: the correction fixes the scale of the averages, not their noise; a few steps of statistics are a poor estimate, so a small early learning rate limits the damage.
Level 3: Which Adam hyperparameter do you change first when training is unstable? Expected: the learning rate, then beta2; almost never beta1 or epsilon.
wrongAnswers: "The division is a numerical safety term like epsilon." Epsilon guards a zero denominator; the division by one minus beta to the t corrects the zero initialization of the averages.
"Without it the first steps are too small, so training is only slower." The second moment's square root is shrunk more than the first moment, so the ratio and the step come out too large.
"Both corrections stop mattering after about 50 steps." That holds for the first moment only. With beta2 at 0.999 the second moment's factor stays well below 1 for thousands of steps.

questions.title: You want weight decay on a transformer trained with Adam. One engineer adds an L2 penalty on the weights to the loss. Another uses an AdamW optimizer with a weight decay argument. They say the two are the same thing. Are they, and which do you choose?
questions.answer: They are the same only under plain SGD. In Adam, a penalty inside the loss becomes part of the gradient and is divided by the running gradient size like every other term, so weights with large gradient variance get less decay and weights with small variance get more. AdamW subtracts lr times lambda times w after the adaptive update, so every weight shrinks by the same fraction. Choose AdamW; the lesson makes it the default for transformers for this reason.
followUps: Level 2: Why is the decay uniform in AdamW? Expected: it is applied to the weights directly, outside the adaptive division, so the fraction removed per step is lr times lambda for every weight.

Level 3: Where exactly does the penalty go wrong inside Adam? Expected: it enters the gradient, so it is averaged into the first moment and squared into the second, and the division by the root of the second moment rescales it per parameter.
Level 3: What decay values does the lesson give? Expected: 0.01 for AdamW on transformers, 1e-4 for SGD on CNNs, up to 0.1 for a heavily overfit model.

Level 4: What experiment shows the difference in a few lines? Expected: start from weights of large magnitude, train both with the same decay, and plot the weight norm; AdamW shrinks it faster and more evenly.
wrongAnswers: "Weight decay and L2 are the same by definition." They coincide under SGD; under an adaptive optimizer the penalty is rescaled per parameter.
"Use Adam with L2 and a bigger lambda to compensate." A bigger lambda does not fix the unevenness; some weights still receive almost no decay.
"Adam adapts, so it does not need weight decay." Adaptation sets step sizes; it does not shrink weights. Overfit transformers still need decay.

questions.title: Xavier initialization sets the weight variance to 2 over the sum of fan in and fan out. Kaiming initialization sets it to 2 over fan in. Both are called variance preserving. Explain what each one preserves, where the 2 in Kaiming comes from, and what happens to a 50 layer ReLU network that starts from a plain standard normal.
questions.answer: A layer's pre-activation variance is fan in times the weight variance times the input variance, so a weight variance of 1 over fan in keeps the signal size constant through a linear layer. Xavier balances that condition between the forward and the backward pass, which gives 2 divided by the total of the two fan counts, and it suits sigmoid and tanh, which are near linear around zero. ReLU zeroes half of its inputs and halves the variance at each layer, so Kaiming doubles the variance of each weight to 2 over fan in to compensate. A standard normal with a fan in of 512 multiplies the variance by 512 at every layer, and the signal explodes within a few layers.
followUps: Level 2: Why does zero initialization fail even though its variance stays constant? Expected: every neuron computes the same function and receives the same gradient, so the layer has one effective neuron; random weights break the symmetry.
Level 3: Which initialization goes with GELU? Expected: Kaiming, as for ReLU.

Level 3: How do you verify an initialization without training? Expected: push random data through the network and log the mean activation magnitude per layer; it should stay in a band such as 0.5 to 2.0 at every depth.

Level 4: Why do residual networks need a further scale beyond Kaiming? Expected: each residual addition adds variance, so the stream grows with the layer count; the GPT-2 scheme scales residual weights by 1 over the square root of 2N.
wrongAnswers: "Random is random, the scale does not matter if it is small." Too small vanishes and too large explodes; the lesson shows both, and the margin is thin at 50 layers.
"Xavier works for ReLU too, the difference is minor." Xavier under-estimates the variance ReLU needs by a factor of 2, and over 50 layers the signal falls to about 8.8 times 10 to the minus 16.
"Kaiming's 2 stands for the forward and backward passes." That 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the activations; Xavier's 2 is the one that balances the two passes.

questions.title: A binary classifier trained with mean squared error on a balanced dataset settles on an output near 0.5 for every input. The loss is low and stable, and the optimizer reports no problem. Explain why the optimizer is content and which loss you switch to.
questions.answer: With two classes split evenly, a constant output of 0.5 gives a squared error of 0.25 on every row, which the lesson calls the minimum MSE a model can reach without learning anything, and the sigmoid's flat regions give MSE almost no gradient near a confident wrong answer. Cross-entropy charges minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class: 0.693 for 0.5, 0.01 for 0.99 and 4.6 for 0.01, so it pushes each prediction toward its label. Switch to binary cross-entropy.
followUps: Level 2: Write the derivative of binary cross-entropy with respect to p. Expected: minus y over p plus (1 - y) over (1 - p), which grows without bound when p is near 0 for a positive row.
Level 2: Why does a prediction of 0.5 cost 0.693 under cross-entropy? Expected: it is minus the natural log of 0.5.
Level 3: After the sigmoid, differentiate cross-entropy by the logit. What do you get? Expected: the prediction minus the target; the log cancels the sigmoid's derivative.
Level 3: When is MSE the right loss? Expected: regression on real valued targets; for heavy outliers, MAE or a Huber loss.
wrongAnswers: "Lower the learning rate so MSE converges properly." The 0.5 output is where MSE is content; a smaller step arrives there more slowly.
"MSE and cross-entropy have the same minimizer, so it does not matter." They agree only at a perfect fit. Away from it, MSE's gradient flattens where cross-entropy's grows.
"Use accuracy as the loss instead." Accuracy has no useful gradient; the optimizer needs a smooth loss.

questions.title: A network has ten hidden layers, each with a sigmoid activation. Estimate the largest factor that the sigmoid derivatives alone let a gradient keep on the way from the loss to the first layer, and say what that number means for training.
questions.answer: The sigmoid derivative is s times (1 - s), which peaks at 0.25 when the output is 0.5. Backpropagation multiplies by that derivative once per layer, so after ten layers the activation factors multiply to at most 0.25 to the tenth power, about one millionth. Each layer also multiplies by its transposed weight matrix, and weights with a norm above 1 can enlarge the gradient, so the figure bounds only the activation part. With the small initial weights of the lesson, the first layers receive almost no signal and stay near their initialization while the last layers learn, which is the vanishing gradient problem.
followUps: Level 2: Why is 0.25 an upper bound and not the typical value? Expected: the derivative is 0.25 only at an output of 0.5; saturated units near 0 or 1 have derivatives near 0, so the real shrink is worse.
Level 2: How does tanh compare? Expected: its derivative peaks at 1.0, four times better, but it still falls toward 0 for large inputs, so deep tanh stacks vanish as well.
Level 3: What does ReLU change in the calculation? Expected: the derivative is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so the gradient passes through unchanged and the product does not shrink.
Level 3: How do you observe the problem without the formula? Expected: log the mean absolute gradient per layer; the first layers show values orders of magnitude below the last.
wrongAnswers: "The gradient vanishes because the learning rate is too small." A larger learning rate scales every layer; the ratio between the first and the last layers stays near one millionth.
"Sigmoid outputs are between 0 and 1, so the gradient is between 0 and 1 and that is fine." The derivative, not the output, multiplies through the layers, and its maximum is 0.25.
"Backpropagation is broken for deep networks." Backpropagation computes the exact gradient; the gradient itself is tiny because of what it passes through.

questions.title: A network with a hidden layer of 512 units is initialized with every weight and every bias at zero. Training runs for thousands of epochs and the loss barely moves. Learning rate and data both check out. What is wrong, and why does a small random perturbation of each weight fix it?
questions.answer: Every neuron in the layer starts identical, so each computes the same output, receives the same gradient and takes the same update. They stay identical for the whole run: the layer holds the parameters of 512 neurons and the function of one. Random initialization gives each neuron its own starting point, so the gradients differ and the neurons learn different features. The scale of that randomness then decides whether the signal survives the depth.
followUps: Level 2: Is it fine to set the biases to zero? Expected: yes, when the weights are random; the lesson's layers do so.
Level 2: Would a nonzero constant for every weight fix it? Expected: no; the neurons are still identical and move in lockstep.

Level 3: After the fix, the loss moves but a deeper version trains badly. What do you check next? Expected: the scale of the random draw against the activation; Xavier for sigmoid and tanh, Kaiming for ReLU, verified by activation magnitudes per layer.

Level 3: How does the lesson show the symmetry in a few lines? Expected: four zero-initialized neurons on one input give four identical outputs, and it counts one effective parameter instead of eight.
wrongAnswers: "The learning rate is too low." Each neuron moves, but all move together; no learning rate separates identical gradients.
"Add more neurons." They are all the same neuron; width adds nothing without symmetry breaking.
"Zero init is fine for the first layer because the inputs differ." The neurons in one layer share the same inputs; what differs across neurons has to be the weights.

questions.title: After a few hundred steps at a high learning rate, a ReLU network's loss stops falling. You log the activations after each ReLU, and in two layers more than half of them are exactly zero on every batch. Explain what happened to those units, why they cannot come back on their own, and what you change.
questions.answer: First confirm that the units are dead and not only sparse: over a large sample, a dead unit is zero on every input. A ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input outputs zero and has a derivative of zero, so it receives no gradient and its weights never move again. A large update, driven by the high learning rate, pushed those units' weights and biases far enough negative that no input brings them back. Lower the learning rate, re-initialize the dead units or the dead layers, and move to an activation with a gradient on the negative side, such as a leaky variant or GELU.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the unit stay dead rather than drift back? Expected: zero output gives zero gradient to its weights, and nothing else in the loss touches them.

Level 3: How do you tell a dead unit from a sparsely active one? Expected: count the fraction of inputs on which it is positive over a large sample; dead is zero on all, sparse is positive on a small fraction.
Level 4: What links the high learning rate to the death? Expected: one large step moves the bias or weights far negative so every input lands below zero; clipping and a smaller rate limit the step.
Level 4: Can you revive the dead units without retraining from scratch? Expected: re-initialize their incoming weights with a Kaiming draw and continue; the rest of the network keeps its progress.
wrongAnswers: "Half zeros is normal sparsity for ReLU." Some zeros are normal; a unit that is zero on every input is dead and contributes nothing, and the lesson flags a layer above half zeros.
"Raise the learning rate so the units jump back." The gradient is zero regardless of the rate; no step reaches them.
"Switch to sigmoid to avoid zeros." Sigmoid trades dead units for vanishing gradients through depth; a leaky variant or GELU keeps the benefits of ReLU.

questions.title: A team ports a vision training recipe to a transformer and keeps batch normalization. Training is unstable, and text generation with one sequence at a time produces garbage. Explain why transformers use layer normalization instead, and when you would go a step further to RMSNorm.
questions.answer: Batch normalization normalizes each feature across the batch, so its statistics depend on the batch size and on which sequences share the batch; with small batches they are noisy, with a batch of one they are meaningless, and training and inference run different code paths. Layer normalization normalizes across the features of one sample, so it does not depend on the batch and is identical in both modes, which is what variable length sequences and single sequence generation need. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the shift parameter, keeps the accuracy, and saves about 10 percent of the normalization cost, which is why most recent large language models use it.
followUps: Level 3: What does batch normalization need at inference that layer normalization does not? Expected: running averages of the mean and variance collected in training; layer normalization computes its statistics from the sample itself.
Level 3: Where does a transformer block place the normalization? Expected: after each attention and feed-forward block in Post-LN, or before them in Pre-LN, which trains more stably.

Level 4: What does RMSNorm remove and what does it cost? Expected: the mean subtraction and the shift parameter; the lesson reports the same accuracy with about 10 percent less normalization overhead.

Level 4: Why did the original explanation for batch normalization fall out of favor? Expected: later work showed the gain comes from a smoother loss landscape with smaller Lipschitz constants, which lets the optimizer take larger steps.
wrongAnswers: "Batch normalization only needs a bigger batch." Generation runs one sequence at a time and sequence lengths vary; the fix is a norm that does not look across the batch.
"Layer normalization is a weaker regularizer, so it is a compromise." It normalizes across features, which is the right axis for sequences, and it removes the mismatch between training and inference.
"RMSNorm is an approximation that loses accuracy." The lesson reports the same accuracy; the re-centering adds little and costs compute.

questions.title: A ten class classifier trains for many epochs, and the cross-entropy loss sits at about 2.3 the whole time, on training data and on validation data. Nothing crashes. What does that number tell you, and in which order do you debug?
questions.answer: Minus the natural log of one tenth is about 2.3, the loss of a model that gives every class the same probability, and the lesson's table reads a loss stuck there as a uniform prediction with no usable signal. The mean alone does not say why. Run the one batch overfit test first: a failure points at the loss, the backward pass, the optimizer hookup or misaligned labels, and a pass sends you to the data path to check that labels line up with inputs. Only then look at the learning rate, the gradients and the architecture.
followUps: Level 3: Why uniform rather than some other wrong answer? Expected: with no usable signal, equal logits minimize the expected cross-entropy over a balanced label set, and that costs the log of the class count.

Level 3: What does the overfit one batch test tell you here? Expected: whether the model and loop can learn at all; a healthy setup drives a small batch to near zero loss in a few hundred steps, and a failure means a broken loss, backward pass, optimizer hookup or misaligned labels.

Level 4: The one batch test passes and full training still sits at 2.3. Where next? Expected: the full data path, such as a shuffle that breaks the pairing of inputs and labels, or unnormalized inputs, since the model can learn when given a consistent batch.

Level 4: What distinguishes this symptom from a loss that starts at 2.3 and falls slowly? Expected: a slow fall is a learning rate or capacity question; a flat 2.3 for many epochs means no signal reaches the model.
wrongAnswers: "Train longer, it is a slow start." A flat value at the uniform loss for many epochs means no signal, not a slow one.
"Make the model bigger." Capacity is not the issue when the model cannot beat a uniform guess on its own training data.
"Lower the learning rate." The rate changes how fast the loss moves, and here it does not move at all; check the data first.

questions.title: You are about to launch a multi-day training run on a new architecture with a new data pipeline. Design a check that runs in about 30 seconds and must pass before the run starts. List the classes of bugs it catches and the ones it does not.
questions.answer: Take one small batch of 8 to 32 samples and train on it alone for a few hundred steps. The loss must fall to near zero and the training accuracy must reach 100 percent. A pass shows that the loss function, the backward pass and the optimizer hookup work, and that the model can fit this batch, but not that each input has its correct label, because a model can memorize a wrong but consistent pairing as well. It says nothing about generalization, leakage or the full data loader, so it is the first gate and not the last.
followUps: Level 3: The loss on the one batch stalls well above the threshold. Name three suspects. Expected: a loss that does not match the output layer, an optimizer built before the model's parameters were created, or a model too small to fit the batch.
Level 3: Why 8 to 32 samples? Expected: small enough that a correct model memorizes it in a few hundred steps, so a failure is unambiguous and the test stays fast.

Level 4: The test passes and the full run later shows training accuracy at chance. What does the pass rule out, and what remains? Expected: the model and loop can learn, so what remains is the full data path: a shuffle that unpairs inputs and labels, or normalization computed differently for the full set.

Level 4: How do you turn this into a gate in a training script? Expected: run it on a fixed batch at startup, assert the final loss is below the threshold, refuse to start the long run on a failure, and rerun it whenever the architecture or pipeline changes.
wrongAnswers: "A passing test means the model will generalize." It proves the model can memorize one batch; generalization needs the validation curve.
"Skip it, the full run shows problems soon enough." The run shows a symptom hours later and the symptom fits many causes; the test isolates the loop in seconds.
"Use the whole training set for a few epochs instead." That is the full run; a small batch is what makes a failure unambiguous and fast.

questions.title: A transformer with Kaiming-initialized weights trains without trouble at 20 layers and diverges at 126 layers with the same recipe. Nothing else changed. Explain why depth breaks it even with a variance preserving initialization, and what the GPT-2 style fix does.
questions.answer: Kaiming keeps the variance constant through each sub-layer, but a residual block adds the sub-layer's output back onto its input, and the variance of a sum of independent terms adds. With N residual additions the stream's variance grows in proportion to N, so a deeper stack carries a larger residual signal, and the attention logits and feed-forward activations built from it grow with it. The GPT-2 fix scales the weights of the layers that write into the residual stream by 1 over the square root of 2N, so the accumulated variance stays the same at any depth.
followUps: Level 3: Why does Kaiming not account for this? Expected: it preserves variance through a matrix multiply followed by ReLU; it knows nothing about the addition that follows.
Level 3: Why 2N and not N? Expected: each transformer layer writes into the stream twice, once from attention and once from the feed-forward block, so N layers make 2N additions.

Level 4: How would you confirm the diagnosis before changing the initialization? Expected: push random input through the untrained model and log the residual stream magnitude per layer; growth with depth confirms it, and the scaled version should be flat.

Level 4: Does a Pre-LN layout remove the need for the scaling? Expected: it normalizes what enters each sub-layer and helps stability, but the additions into the stream sit outside the norm, so the lesson still applies the scaling to the writers.
wrongAnswers: "Deeper models just need a smaller learning rate." A smaller rate slows the growth of the weights; it does nothing about the variance that accumulates in the forward pass at initialization.
"Kaiming is variance preserving, so depth cannot be the issue." It preserves variance through each sub-layer, not through the sum of a sub-layer and its input.
"Divide the residual stream by N at the output." The fix has to act where the variance accumulates; scaling the writers keeps every intermediate layer in range, not only the last one.

questions.title: A transformer recipe starts the learning rate at zero and ramps it linearly up to the peak during the first steps, then decays it with a cosine. A teammate wants to start at the peak to save those steps. Explain what the ramp protects, how long it should be, and how to write it down so the recipe scales to a longer run.
questions.answer: The first updates are the fragile ones: the weights sit near their initialization, Adam's running estimates of the gradient mean and variance are built from a handful of samples, and the gradient norm is large and noisy. A full size step on that footing diverges or drops the model into a plateau it never leaves. Warmup keeps the effective step small until the statistics settle, over about 1 to 5 percent of the total steps, and the schedule should express that length as a fraction of the run rather than as a fixed step count.
followUps: Level 3: Why is Adam sensitive at step zero in particular? Expected: its moment estimates start at zero and the first steps use statistics from one or two gradients; bias correction fixes their scale but not their noise.

Level 3: What does the gradient norm look like during a healthy warmup? Expected: it rises roughly in step with the learning rate and settles after the peak; a norm that stays high after the ramp says the peak is too aggressive.

Level 4: Why does a fixed warmup step count break when the run gets longer? Expected: 2000 steps is 10 percent of a 20,000 step run and a vanishing share of a 200 million step run, so the same count gives two different schedules; a fraction keeps the shape.

Level 4: You change the batch size. What do you revisit? Expected: the warmup length and the peak; the schedules lesson lists the warmup period as the setting that must change when the batch size changes.
wrongAnswers: "Warmup wastes steps at a low rate." The lessons spend 1 to 5 percent of training on it, and a run that diverges in its first steps wastes all of them.
"Bias correction already handles Adam's cold start, so warmup is redundant." The correction rescales the averages; it cannot turn two samples into a good estimate.
"Set the warmup to 2000 steps, the big runs use that." That count was a fraction of one specific run; on a short run it is most of the training, and on a longer one it is nothing.

questions.title: Take-home. Implement a learning rate schedule as one function of the step: a linear ramp from zero to a peak, a cosine decay from the peak to a floor, and a fixed floor after the last step. Deliver tests that pin the value at every boundary, prove the curve has no jumps, and show that a resumed run lands on the right value. Describe your design and your tests.
questions.answer: Write one function with three branches: up to the warmup step, the peak times the step over the warmup length; between the warmup step and the total, the floor plus half the gap times one plus the cosine of pi times the progress since warmup ended; past the total, the floor. Test the fixed points: zero at step zero, the peak at the end of warmup from both branches, the floor at the last step and the floor one step later. Add a continuity test that bounds each one step change, and a resume test that computes the schedule from a saved global step.
followUps: Level 3: Why implement the three regions in one function? Expected: so the ramp endpoint and the cosine start share one formula for the peak, and a change to the peak or the step counts cannot open a gap at a boundary.

Level 4: What is the right bound for the continuity test? Expected: the larger of the ramp slope, peak over warmup steps, and the steepest cosine slope, pi times the gap over twice the decay length; a short cosine segment can be steeper than the ramp.

Level 4: Why pin at the floor after the last step instead of raising? Expected: a trainer that overshoots keeps a usable rate and logs a warning; extending training means changing the total in the config, not the loop.
Level 4: What makes a resumed run land on the right value? Expected: the schedule reads a monotonic global step saved in the checkpoint, not an epoch counter or a local loop variable.
wrongAnswers: "Set the floor to zero so the schedule finishes cleanly." The lesson keeps a non-zero floor near 10 percent of the peak so the optimizer keeps learning in the tail; a zero floor looks clean and leaves the model under-trained.

"Test a few steps in the middle, the boundaries follow from the formula." An off by one at a boundary is the bug the lesson warns about; it shows up hours into a run as a rate that is 1 percent off at the moment it matters.
"Compute the rate from the epoch and the batch index." Sharded datasets and restarted loaders break that mapping; the global step is the durable axis.

questions.title: A run trains for hours with a smooth loss. Then, within three logging intervals, the loss jumps, becomes inf, and every value after that is NaN. The same recipe worked on a smaller model. Give your ranked list of causes, the evidence that separates them, and the changes that keep it from happening again.
questions.answer: A clean run that dies late is almost always an oversized update: the peak learning rate is too high for the larger model, a rare batch produced a huge gradient, or the schedule reached its peak at a point where the model was already sensitive. The logs separate the cases: for an explosion the gradient norm spikes before the loss does, while a forward pass overflow, such as a softmax without the max shift or a normalization over a zero variance, shows a normal norm and a loss that goes to inf in one step. Fix with gradient clipping by norm at 1.0, a lower peak with warmup, and a loss computed from logits, then resume from the last good checkpoint.
followUps: Level 3: What in the logs separates an oversized update from a forward pass overflow? Expected: the gradient norm rises over several steps before the loss for an explosion; an overflow shows a normal norm and a loss that goes to inf in a single step.
Level 4: Why clip by norm rather than by value? Expected: clipping by norm scales the whole gradient and keeps its direction; clipping each element changes the direction.

Level 4: Why did the recipe work on the smaller model? Expected: the peak that was safe there sits near the edge for the larger one; a sweep on the small model is a prior, and the optimum shifts with size, so verify rather than copy.

Level 4: What do you add so the run never dies silently again? Expected: log the gradient norm beside the learning rate each step, alert on a NaN loss, checkpoint often enough to resume, and restart with clipping and a warmup.
wrongAnswers: "Add an epsilon to the loss and restart." An epsilon fixes a log of zero at step one; a late explosion comes from the update size, and the run will die again.
"Halve the learning rate and hope." Halving is a guess; the lesson's move is a 10 times reduction, together with clipping and a check of the schedule position.
"NaN means the data has a bad row." A bad row shows in the first epoch, not after hours of clean training; replay the failing batch on the checkpoint before you blame it.

questions.title: You inherit a model with no known good learning rate and a compute budget of a few hours. Design the procedure that picks the peak learning rate and the schedule for the run, and say what you log to defend the choice.
questions.answer: Run a learning rate range test first: train for about a hundred steps while the rate grows exponentially from 1e-7 toward 10 and record the loss at each rate. Take the rate where the loss falls fastest and set the peak about 10 times lower. Then run a linear warmup over 1 to 5 percent of the steps into a cosine decay with a floor near a tenth of the peak, or the 1cycle policy when the budget is short and the total step count is fixed. Log the range test curve, the schedule curve and the gradient norm beside the learning rate at every step.
followUps: Level 3: Why set the peak below the steepest point rather than at it? Expected: the steepest point is close to where the loss starts to diverge, and a long run needs a margin; one order of magnitude lower keeps it.

Level 4: When do you choose 1cycle over warmup plus cosine? Expected: a short, fixed budget where the total step count is known; it converges faster for a fixed compute and needs the step count in advance.

Level 4: The peak is right and the loss still oscillates near the end. What do you adjust? Expected: the decay, not the peak; a schedule that ends too high leaves steps too large for the final minimum, so lower the floor or lengthen the decay.

Level 4: How does the model's size change the plan? Expected: sweep the peak on a smaller version first as a prior, then confirm with the range test on the full model, because the optimum shifts with size.
wrongAnswers: "Use 3e-4 for Adam, it always works." It is the lesson's starting default when nothing is known, not a result; the range test takes minutes and replaces a guess with a measurement.
"Pick the rate with the lowest loss in the range test." The lowest point sits next to divergence; the lesson picks about 10 times lower than the steepest fall.

"A constant rate is fine if it is the right one." The right rate changes during training; a constant that fits the start is too large at the end, and the lesson keeps constant rates for small models and debugging.

topics.title: Transformers
topics.about: Attention, positions, the transformer block, the KV cache and the cost of long context.

questions.title: What is a foundation model, and how is it different from a regular ML model?
questions.answer: A foundation model is pretrained at very large scale on broad data, so it learns general representations instead of solving one narrow task. That makes it a shared base you can adapt to many tasks through prompting or fine-tuning, without training from scratch. A traditional model is trained on data for one specific task. Classical models such as XGBoost are still the better choice for structured tabular data, tight latency budgets, low cost, or when you need explainable decisions.

questions.title: What is a Large Language Model, and what is it actually trained to do?
questions.answer: A neural network (almost always a decoder-only Transformer) trained to predict the next token given everything before it. Nothing more exotic than that at the objective level — the wide range of downstream behavior (chat, code, reasoning) emerges from scale plus post-training on top of that one pretraining objective.

questions.title: What is tokenization, and why can't LLMs just read raw text?
questions.answer: Splitting text into a fixed vocabulary of subword units (tokens) the model actually operates on — characters are too fine-grained (long sequences, no semantic unit), whole words are too coarse (unbounded vocabulary, can't handle unseen words).

questions.title: A BPE tokenizer meets the rare word "unfathomability". What does it do?
questions.answer: The algorithm most LLM tokenizers use to build that subword vocabulary: start from individual characters/bytes, and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until you hit a target vocabulary size. Frequent words end up as one token; rare words fall back to smaller subword pieces.
options: It adds the word to the vocabulary on the fly.
It maps the word to a single unknown-word token.
It always splits the word into single characters.
It splits the word into smaller subword pieces that are in its vocabulary.

questions.title: What are embeddings?
questions.answer: Dense numeric vectors representing tokens (or whole sentences/documents) such that semantic similarity corresponds to geometric closeness — the representation everything downstream (attention, retrieval) actually operates on.

questions.title: Remove positional encoding from a bidirectional (encoder) Transformer. How does it see "dog bites man" versus "man bites dog"?
questions.answer: Self-attention on its own is permutation-invariant — it has no notion of token order. Positional encoding injects order information into the input so the model can tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog."
options: Attention weights encode word order on their own.
It still reads left to right, like an RNN.
It can't tell them apart: each token's representation is the same in both, because self-attention ignores order.
Only the first word's position is lost.

questions.title: What is self-attention?
questions.answer: The mechanism letting every token in a sequence look at every other token and weight how much each one matters for updating its own representation — computed from Query/Key/Value projections of the same input.

questions.title: What are Query, Key, and Value in attention?
questions.answer: Three learned linear projections of the same input: Query represents "what am I looking for," Key represents "what do I offer" for every other position, and the Query·Key similarity produces attention weights that combine the Values into the output.

questions.title: You drop the 1/√d_k scaling from attention in a model with d_k = 128. What goes wrong first?
questions.answer: Without scaling, dot products grow large as the key dimension grows, pushing softmax into a region with near-zero gradients (it saturates toward one-hot). Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores in a range where softmax stays well-behaved.
options: Nothing, because softmax normalises any scale.
Scores grow with the dimension, softmax saturates towards one-hot, and gradients through it nearly vanish.
Memory use grows.
Attention becomes uniform across tokens.

questions.title: What is multi-head attention, and why not just use one big attention head?
questions.answer: Running several smaller attention computations in parallel, each with its own learned projections, then concatenating the results — letting different heads specialize in different kinds of relationships (syntax, coreference, position) instead of one head averaging everything together.

questions.title: In an encoder-decoder translation model, where do the queries, keys and values in the decoder's cross-attention come from?
questions.answer: Self-attention: Query, Key, and Value all come from the same sequence. Cross-attention: Query comes from one sequence (e.g. a decoder), Key and Value come from a different one (e.g. an encoder's output) — how an encoder-decoder model lets its decoder attend to the source input.
options: Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder's output.
All three from the decoder.
Queries from the encoder, keys and values from the decoder.
All three from the encoder.

questions.title: Someone trains a decoder-only language model and forgets the causal mask. Training loss drops unusually fast. What happens at generation time?
questions.answer: Causal masking blocks a position from attending to future positions, which is what makes autoregressive next-token generation well-defined — without it, predicting token *n* could see token *n+1*, which doesn't exist at inference time.
options: It can no longer produce text of any kind.
It generates better, because it saw more context in training.
Nothing changes, because masking only matters during inference.
It fails: in training it could see the next token, so it learned to copy instead of predict.

questions.title: A model has 24 layers and 16 key-value heads of dimension 64, and stores the cache in fp16. How much KV cache does each token add? (KiB.)
questions.answer:
Keys and values, for every layer and KV head: 2 × 24 × 16 × 64 × 2 bytes = 98,304 bytes = 96 KiB per token. A 4,000-token conversation needs about 375 MiB for one user.

Storing each generated token's Key/Value projections so they don't get recomputed on every subsequent step — without it, generating token *n* would redo the attention computation for all *n-1* prior tokens from scratch. It's also the dominant consumer of GPU memory during serving, which is why techniques like GQA/MQA exist to shrink it.

questions.title: What is the difference between BERT and GPT?
questions.answer: BERT is an encoder-only architecture trained with bidirectional self-attention: every token attends to all tokens across both left and right context. It is pretrained using Masked Language Modeling (reconstructing 15% masked tokens), making it suited for classification, sequence labeling, and bi-encoder embedding retrieval. GPT is a decoder-only architecture utilizing causal masking, where lower-triangular attention matrices prevent tokens from attending to future positions. It is pretrained via autoregressive next-token prediction, optimizing the likelihood of the subsequent token. BERT cannot generate coherent open-ended text because it lacks autoregressive factorization, while GPT cannot condition on bidirectional context within a single forward pass.
keyPoints: BERT uses bidirectional encoder attention.
BERT pretraining masks tokens for reconstruction.
GPT uses causal attention with next-token prediction.
Encoder representations suit understanding tasks; causal decoders generate autoregressively.

questions.title: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide by the square root of d_k?
questions.answer: If query and key components have variance one, their dot product has variance d_k, so larger dimensions produce larger scores.
