Large scores push softmax into a nearly one-hot region where gradients become very small. Dividing by the square root of d_k brings the variance back to about one, which keeps attention trainable. It is a simple variance correction, the same reasoning behind careful weight initialization.
keyPoints: The dot-product variance grows with key dimension under unit-variance assumptions.
Large attention logits saturate softmax.
Dividing by square root of key dimension stabilizes logit variance.
Less saturated softmax gives healthier gradients.

questions.title: Why use multiple attention heads instead of one big head?
questions.answer: Rather than computing a single attention pattern over the full hidden dimension {model}$, multi-head attention projects Queries, Keys, and Values $ times into lower-dimensional subspaces of size  = d_{model} / h$. Each head runs scaled dot-product attention independently, and the outputs are concatenated and projected through ^O$. This allows the model to attend simultaneously to diverse representation subspaces at different positions—such as syntax, coreference, and positional proximity—which a single attention matrix would collapse into an average distribution. Computational complexity and parameter count remain identical to single-head attention because  	imes d_k = d_{model}$.
keyPoints: Each head has learned query, key and value projections.
Different heads can represent different token relationships.
Heads attend in parallel in separate representation subspaces.
Head outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension.

questions.title: Explain self-attention, cross-attention and causal masking.
questions.answer: In self-attention, queries, keys and values come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, queries come from the decoder and keys and values come from the encoder, which lets a translation model look at the source. Causal masking blocks attention to future positions during training, so the model cannot see the token it must predict. Decoder-only LLMs use masked self-attention and no cross-attention.
keyPoints: Self-attention takes queries, keys and values from one sequence.
Cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from encoder outputs.
Causal masking blocks attention to future target tokens.
Masking preserves autoregressive training without target leakage.

questions.title: What is the time and memory cost of attention, and how do models manage it?
questions.answer: Scaled dot-product attention requires (T^2 \cdot d)$ FLOPs and materializes an (T^2)$ attention matrix, creating quadratic compute and memory scaling with sequence length $. During autoregressive generation, recomputing previous keys and values would take (T^2)$ time; the KV cache stores past key/value tensors, reducing per-token generation to (1)$ operations at the cost of (T)$ memory per request. Mitigations include: FlashAttention, which tiles attention in GPU SRAM to eliminate HBM read/writes of the (T^2)$ matrix; Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), which shares key/value heads across query heads to slash KV cache size by 4x to 8x; and sliding window attention for bounded context.
keyPoints: Dense attention computes pairwise token scores with quadratic sequence cost.
Materializing the attention matrix requires quadratic memory.
FlashAttention reduces memory traffic without making exact dense attention linear.
Sparse or local attention changes connectivity to reduce cost.
KV caching avoids recomputing past keys and values during decoding.

questions.title: Explain temperature, top-k and top-p sampling. How would you set them?
questions.answer: Temperature $ scales logits prior to softmax ( / T$). Lowering temperature ( < 1.0$) sharpens the probability distribution, driving it toward deterministic greedy argmax selection, while higher temperature flattens entropy. Top-k sampling restricts the candidate pool to the $ most probable tokens. Top-p (nucleus sampling) dynamically computes the cumulative probability distribution and truncates candidates once the sum reaches threshold $. This adapts pool size to model uncertainty: confident predictions keep a tiny candidate set, while uncertain contexts widen the pool. Set  = 0.0 - 0.2$ for deterministic structured extraction and code generation; use  = 0.7$ with  = 0.9$ for conversational fluency.
keyPoints: Temperature rescales logits before softmax.
Top-k limits sampling to a fixed number of high-probability tokens.
Top-p keeps a variable-sized set reaching a probability mass threshold.
Lower temperature usually reduces diversity; settings require task evaluation.

questions.title: Walk me through how an LLM such as Llama is trained, from data to a chat model.
questions.answer: Modern LLM development follows a four-stage pipeline: 1) Pretraining: Self-supervised next-token cross-entropy over trillions of tokens of deduplicated, filtered web text and code, executed on thousands of GPUs using 3D parallelism and mixed precision. 2) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Training on tens of thousands of high-quality instruction-response demonstrations to teach multi-turn dialogue structure and task compliance. 3) Preference Alignment: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) or RLHF using reward models and policy optimization (PPO/GRPO) to enforce helpfulness and safety boundaries. 4) Serving Optimization: Post-training quantization (AWQ/GPTQ to INT4/FP8), KV-cache allocation (PagedAttention), and red-team safety evaluation before production routing.
keyPoints: Clean, deduplicate and tokenize pretraining data.
Pretrain with next-token prediction.
Instruction supervised fine-tuning teaches response behavior.
Preference optimization aligns responses with chosen preferences.
Evaluate quality and safety and monitor deployment behavior.

questions.title: What happens when a prompt exceeds the context window, and how do you design for it?
questions.answer: Exceeding the context window triggers API truncation or rejection, dropping vital instructions or context and causing severe hallucination. Production architectures handle context through four defenses: 1) Strict Token Budgeting: Deterministically reserving token budgets for system prompts, retrieved evidence, history, and generation buffers. 2) State Compaction: Evicting raw conversational turns into structured JSON summaries or key-value memory scratchpads. 3) Retrieval Precision: Reranking and filtering retrieved chunks to avoid the 'Lost in the Middle' phenomenon, where models fail to attend to facts placed in the center of long contexts. 4) Prompt Assembly: Placing static system instructions first to maximize prefix KV-cache reuse in vLLM or SGLang.
keyPoints: The context budget includes prompt and generated tokens.
Over-budget inputs require rejection, truncation or application-level reduction.
Retrieval and summarization can select or compress relevant content.
Long contexts still face cost and information retrieval failures.
Reserve output space and measure token use before requests.

questions.title: A new teammate has read the word "attention" a hundred times and still cannot say what a query, a key or a value is. Explain the three to them in one minute. Then tell me what changed between the 2014 encoder-decoder version and the version inside a transformer.
questions.answer: Attention is a soft lookup. Each token produces a query that asks for information, a key that says what the token holds, and a value that the token hands over when it is picked. The query is scored against every key, the scores go through a softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. In the 2014 version the query was the decoder state and the keys and the values were the same encoder states; a transformer takes all three from one sequence through three learned projections.
followUps: Level 1: What shape does the output have for one token? Expected: the value dimension, because the output is a weighted sum of value vectors.
Level 2: Why give keys and values separate projections? Expected: a token can be matched on one kind of information and return another kind.

Level 2: Why does the plain dot-product score need the query and the key to have the same dimension? Expected: a dot product is only defined for vectors of equal length; the general form inserts a matrix W to remove that constraint.

Level 3: Name the convention trap between the two classic score functions. Expected: one uses the decoder state before the current step and the other uses the state after it; mixing them produces subtly wrong gradients.
wrongAnswers: "The key and the value must be the same vector." They were in the classic version, but a transformer learns separate projections for them.
"Attention picks the single best matching token." The softmax gives a weight to every position, and the output blends all of the values.
"The query comes from the encoder." In encoder-decoder attention the query comes from the decoder and the keys and the values come from the encoder.

questions.title: Take a sentence and shuffle its words. Feed both versions through a self-attention layer that has no positional signal. How do the two outputs relate, and what are the three families of fixes you would name?
questions.answer: The output rows come back shuffled in the same way and nothing else changes, because attention only computes pairwise similarities between tokens. Order carries meaning in language and code, so the model needs a second signal. The three fixes are a position vector added to the embedding, a learned table or a fixed sinusoid, a rotation of the queries and keys by an angle that grows with position, and a distance penalty added to the scores.
followUps: Level 1: Why add the two vectors instead of concatenating them? Expected: the sum keeps D constant through the network and lets the model weigh token and position per feature.
Level 2: What does a learned position table cost that a sinusoid does not? Expected: max_context_length times D parameters, and it cannot be indexed past the trained length.
Level 2: Why do the high dimensions of the sinusoid encode coarse position? Expected: their wavelength is longest, so they change slowly across positions.
Level 3: Where in the block does the rotation apply? Expected: to Q and K inside attention, after the projection and before the score matmul, never to V.
wrongAnswers: "The softmax makes attention order-aware." The softmax normalizes a row of similarities; it has no idea which column is first.
"Add the position as one extra number on the embedding." One scalar cannot give the dot products a usable signal; the schemes spread position across many dimensions or into the scores.
"Position only matters for long sequences." A two-word sentence already changes meaning when its words swap.

questions.title: In the attention formula the raw scores go through a division before the softmax. A new engineer calls the division a convention and removes it to save one multiply. What happens to training, and how would you show the effect in ten minutes?
questions.answer: A dot product of two vectors grows with their length, so without the division the scores grow with the key dimension. Large scores push the softmax into a region where one key takes almost all of the weight and the gradient to every other key is close to zero, so learning stalls. The division by sqrt(d_k) keeps the variance of the scores about constant for any head size. Show it with random Q and K at d_k = 64: print the score range and the softmax weights with and without the division.
followUps: Level 1: What is the shape of the score matrix for a sequence of n tokens? Expected: (n, n), one row per query and one column per key.
Level 2: Why does the missing division cause a silent failure instead of an exception? Expected: the softmax saturates, the gradients become tiny, and the loss plateaus with no error.

Level 2: Does the division change what the layer can represent? Expected: no, the projections can absorb a constant; it changes the scale of the scores at initialization, which is where training happens or stalls.
Level 3: With eight heads of width 64 in a model of width 512, which number goes under the root? Expected: 64, the head width, because each head computes its own softmax over its own scores.
wrongAnswers: "The division keeps the attention weights summing to one." The softmax normalizes any scores to sum to one; the division controls their spread, not their sum.
"A larger learning rate recovers the lost gradient." When the softmax is saturated the gradient carries almost no information about the other keys, and a larger step does not create information.
"Scale the values instead of the scores." The values are summed after the weights are fixed, so their scale does not touch the softmax.

questions.title: A decoder generates 100 tokens one at a time from an empty prompt. Count the token states each loop computes for the prefix: a naive loop, and a loop that caches the key and value vectors of earlier tokens. Then count the query-key comparisons that remain with the store, and name what the store deliberately leaves out.
questions.answer: The naive loop runs every prefix token through the layer again at every step, so it computes 1 plus 2 plus 3 and so on up to 100 token states, which is 5050 and grows with the square of the length. With the stored keys and values, each step computes the state of the new token only, 100 in total. The new query still meets every stored key, so the cached loop still makes 5050 query-key comparisons: the store removes the recomputed key and value vectors, not the comparisons. The store holds no queries, because a past token never asks a question again; only the newest token does.
followUps: Level 1: What grows in memory as generation proceeds? Expected: the stored keys and values, per layer and per head, one entry per generated token.
Level 2: Why is a prefix token's key still valid after new tokens arrive? Expected: the causal mask means its hidden state only ever depended on earlier tokens, so later tokens cannot change it.
Level 2: You edit one word in the middle of the prompt. What happens to the store? Expected: everything from that position on is invalid and must be recomputed; the part before it stays valid.

Level 3: When does attention become bound by memory traffic instead of arithmetic? Expected: when the N by N score matrix is large enough that moving it through memory dominates; the lesson puts that at about 2K tokens and beyond.
wrongAnswers: "The store keeps the attention weights." It keeps keys and values; the weights are recomputed from the new query every step.
"The store saves memory." It costs memory and saves compute; the trade is memory for the recomputed key and value vectors.
"Queries must be stored too." A past token's query is never used again.

questions.title: Three products land on your desk: a search ranking model over documents, a coding assistant that writes code, and a speech-to-text system. Which transformer shape do you pick for each, and what does the pretraining loss have to do with the choice?
questions.answer: Encoder-only for ranking and embeddings, decoder-only for generation, and encoder-decoder when the input is a clear source sequence such as audio to transcribe. An encoder reads both sides of every position and trains on masked prediction, which gives strong representations and no way to generate. A decoder trains on next-token prediction behind a causal mask, so it can generate, and it scales cleanest, which is why it won language. The loss decides whether the model can produce text at all.
followUps: Level 2: Which sublayer exists only in the encoder-decoder shape? Expected: cross-attention, with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

Level 3: Why can a decoder-only model also do comprehension tasks? Expected: the same next-token model answers a question by continuing a prompt, and in-context learning lets it follow examples without a task head.

Level 3: When would you still choose encoder-decoder for a text task? Expected: when the input is a clear source sequence that the output transforms, such as translation or summarization of a fixed document.

Level 4: The ranking team wants to reuse the decoder they already serve. How? Expected: prompt it and read the logits of a label token, or attach a head and fine-tune; weigh the cost against an encoder that scores documents in one pass.
wrongAnswers: "A decoder-only model cannot classify." It can, by prompting or by adding a head; the point is that an encoder is often cheaper for that job.
"An encoder generates text one token at a time." It has no causal loss and predicts masked positions; it is not trained to continue a sequence.
"Every transformer block has cross-attention." Only the decoder blocks of an encoder-decoder model have it.

questions.title: An attention module between an encoder and a decoder runs without any exception, but the model's accuracy slowly falls behind the reference implementation. When you print the context tensor, its second dimension is the encoder length instead of the decoder length. Walk me through the diagnosis.
questions.answer: A module that runs and still produces the wrong shape is a broadcast bug, and a silent broadcast is the worst attention bug because it degrades accuracy instead of crashing. Write the expected shapes first: scores and weights are batch by decoder length by encoder length, and the context is batch by decoder length by the encoder state width. Then find the matmul whose operands were swapped or not transposed, fix it with one transpose or reshape, and add asserts on the shapes and on the weights summing to one.
followUps: Level 2: Which single test catches most attention bugs? Expected: the weights have shape batch by decoder length by encoder length and sum to one along the last axis.
Level 2: The score matrix comes out square in the encoder dimension. What happened? Expected: the keys were scored against themselves; the query tensor was replaced by the encoder states.

Level 3: Why does the plain dot score fail with a bidirectional encoder? Expected: the encoder state is twice the hidden width, so it no longer matches the decoder state; use the general form with a matrix between them.

Level 3: Why is the state convention a gradient problem and not a shape problem? Expected: both states have the same shape, so nothing fails; the gradient flows to the wrong step and the model learns a slightly wrong alignment.
wrongAnswers: "Reshape the output to the expected shape and continue." The values inside are wrong; a reshape only hides the mismatch.
"Lower the learning rate; the model is just unstable." The run is not unstable; it is computing the wrong quantity.
"Add a mask to fix the shape." A mask changes which positions get weight, not the layout of the tensor.

questions.title: A decoder must not read tokens that come after the current position. A teammate proposes to run the softmax first and then set the weights of later positions to zero. Why is that wrong, and where does the usual triangle of negative infinity really come from?
questions.answer: Zeroing weights after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to one, and the later tokens already shaped the normalization. The mask adds minus infinity to the scores before the softmax, so the exponential gives an exact zero there and each row is a distribution over the past alone. The triangle is not a patch on attention: a causal running average is a lower-triangular row-normalized matrix, and the mask is that same zero pattern written in the input domain of the softmax.
followUps: Level 2: Why not multiply the future scores by zero? Expected: a zero score still receives weight exp(0) before normalization, so the future still contributes.

Level 2: Where does the mask live in a real block and why? Expected: a registered buffer at the maximum context length, sliced per forward pass, so it sits on the right device and is not allocated on every call.
Level 3: Does an encoder need this triangle? Expected: no, an encoder is bidirectional; it needs a padding mask, which also uses minus infinity but follows the batch, not the diagonal.

Level 3: What does the mask have to do with parallel training? Expected: it lets one pass produce every next-token prediction at once while each prediction sees only its past, so the N losses are valid together.
wrongAnswers: "Set the future scores to zero." Zero is a legal score and still earns weight after the exponential; only minus infinity gives a zero weight.
"The mask is a training-only trick, so serving can drop it." The prompt is processed in one pass at serving time, and without the mask the prompt tokens would read their own future.
"Encoders also need the triangle." The encoder sees both sides by design; the triangle is what makes a decoder a decoder.

questions.title: A new decoder-only language model on a vocabulary of 64 tokens reaches a training loss near zero after only some hundreds of steps, and the sampled text is nonsense. Name the two most likely causes and the check that tells them apart.
questions.answer: On real text, a loss far below the logarithm of the vocabulary size this early, with nonsense samples, most likely means the model can see its own target. Either the causal mask is missing, so position i reads the token at i plus one through attention, or the targets were never shifted, so the input and the target are the same sequence. Check the attention weights: if any mass sits above the diagonal the mask is gone; if the weights are triangular, print one batch and compare the input and target columns.
followUps: Level 2: What loss do you expect at step zero, and why? Expected: about the logarithm of the vocabulary size, about 4.16 for 64, because a random model spreads probability evenly.

Level 2: How do you make the shift mistake impossible in the loader? Expected: slice one window of length T plus 1 and return window[:-1] and window[1:] from the same slice, with a test on one example.
Level 3: Write the causality unit test in one sentence. Expected: change the token at position j, run the block again, and assert that every output before j is unchanged.

Level 3: The mask and the shift are right, and the loss is still suspiciously low. What else leaks? Expected: a validation window that overlaps the training stream, or padding tokens counted as easy targets; check the split and the loss mask.
wrongAnswers: "The model is just learning fast." A loss near zero on natural text is not possible without seeing the target.
"Add dropout to regularize it." Dropout does not stop a leak; it only makes the copy slightly noisier.
"Lower the learning rate." The optimization is fine; the objective is broken.

questions.title: The 2017 paper placed the layer normalization after the residual add. Almost every model since about 2019 places it before the sublayer. What changed, how would you demonstrate the difference in one afternoon, and what does RMSNorm change on top of that?
questions.answer: Post-norm sends the gradient of the skip path through a normalization at every layer, so at depth the gradient shrinks and the run needs a warmup schedule to survive. Pre-norm keeps the skip path unnormalized, so the gradient reaches the embeddings cleanly and a deep stack trains without warmup tricks. Demonstrate it by stacking twelve layers of each variant with the same initialization and printing the gradient norm at the embedding after one backward pass. RMSNorm then drops the mean subtraction, one fewer operation, with the same stability in practice.
followUps: Level 2: Where exactly does the norm sit in a pre-norm block? Expected: inside each residual branch, before attention and before the MLP, plus one final norm before the head.
Level 3: Why does a pre-norm model need a final norm when a post-norm model does not? Expected: the pre-norm skip path is unnormalized, so the head would see an unbounded stream without it.

Level 3: Your six-layer post-norm model trains fine and the twenty-four-layer version diverges. Why? Expected: the skip-path gradient attenuates at every norm, and the effect compounds with depth; add warmup or switch to pre-norm.

Level 4: What would convince you to keep LayerNorm instead of RMSNorm? Expected: a measured quality or stability difference on your own run; the lesson's evidence is that RMSNorm matches it while being cheaper.
wrongAnswers: "The two placements compute the same function in a different order." The composition differs: one normalizes the stream, the other normalizes only the branch input.
"Warmup is a learning-rate detail unrelated to the norm." The lesson ties the need for warmup directly to the post-norm gradient path.
"RMSNorm needs the mean to be stable." It omits the mean on purpose and matches LayerNorm in practice.

questions.title: A transformer block has two skip paths, one around attention and one around the feed-forward network. What do they do for training, which of the two sublayers moves information between tokens, and why does a dropout layer placed on the skip path itself break something?
questions.answer: The skip path makes the gradient additive across depth, so its norm stays in scale through a twelve-layer stack instead of shrinking at every layer, and it lets each block learn a small update to a running representation instead of a full replacement. Only attention mixes tokens; the MLP applies the same two layers to every position on its own. Dropout belongs after the attention softmax, on the attention output before the residual add, and after the second linear of the MLP; on the skip path it breaks the identity that carries the gradient, and early stacks that did this trained brittly.
followUps: Level 2: Which sublayer would you remove if the model only needed per-token transformations? Expected: attention; the MLP never looks across positions.

Level 3: Why does the modern FFN use an expansion of about 2.6 instead of 4? Expected: SwiGLU has three weight matrices, so 2.6 times the width matches the parameter count of the two-matrix MLP at 4 times.
Level 3: Why do modern stacks drop the bias terms in the linear layers? Expected: the lesson reports a slight perplexity improvement and a smaller model.

Level 4: A reviewer wants to regularize a small model by dropping out the identity term. Your answer? Expected: no; keep dropout on the branch outputs, because the additive identity is what lets the gradient reach early layers.
wrongAnswers: "The skip path exists to keep the output shape equal to the input shape." The shape would match anyway; the skip path is about gradient flow and additive updates.
"Dropout anywhere inside the block is equivalent." Dropout on the identity term damages the gradient path; dropout on the branch outputs does not.
"The feed-forward network mixes information between tokens." It applies the same MLP to each position alone; mixing happens only in attention.

questions.title: You are choosing the attention variant for a new 70B-class decoder: full multi-head, multi-query, grouped-query, or MLA with its compressed latent. What does each one do to the memory that decoding holds per token, and what do you give up with each?
questions.answer: All four keep the same number of query heads; they differ in how many key and value heads exist, and only the keys and values are stored during decoding. Multi-query shares one key-value head across every query head, the smallest cache and some quality loss. Grouped-query uses a group of key-value heads, cuts the cache by n_heads / n_kv_heads and keeps nearly full quality, which is why it is the default. Latent attention compresses keys and values to a low-rank vector and decompresses at attention time, so it saves even more memory and pays extra FLOPs.
followUps: Level 2: Which numbers set the stored bytes per token? Expected: layers, key-value heads, head size and bytes per value, times 2 for the key and the value; the parameter count does not enter.
Level 3: Why does latent attention cost more compute per step? Expected: the stored latent has to be projected back to full keys and values at every decode step before the scores are computed.

Level 3: Can you move an existing multi-head checkpoint to grouped-query? Expected: yes, the grouped-query paper converts trained checkpoints and fine-tunes; measure quality on your own eval before you ship.

Level 4: The product wants 128K contexts at batch size one on a 40 GB card. Which variant and what else? Expected: grouped-query alone already fills the card at 128K, so latent attention or a smaller key-value type, and the weights still need their own memory.
wrongAnswers: "Grouped-query reduces the compute of attention." The scores are still computed for every query head; the saving is in the stored keys and values.
"Multi-query is free." It shares one answer set across all heads and the lesson records a quality loss.
"The cache size follows the parameter count." It follows the key-value heads, the layers, the head size and the data type.

questions.title: You change an attention layer from one head to eight heads and keep the model width fixed. What happens to the parameter count, to the compute, and to what the layer can represent? And why do practitioners refuse to make heads narrower than about 32?
questions.answer: The parameters do not change: the four projections are still d_model by d_model, and the heads are only a reshape of the same matrices into slices of width d_model / n_heads. The compute stays about the same because the per-head attention runs as one batched matmul over the head axis. Each head can specialize on its own relation, and the output projection is where the heads mix. The lesson's rule of thumb keeps a head at a width of 32 or more, because a narrower head sees too few dimensions, and above 256 you lose the benefit of many small specialists, while the sqrt scaling itself keeps the score variance constant at any width.
followUps: Level 2: Why is the fused QKV projection faster if the math is identical? Expected: one kernel launch and one matmul instead of three; the stacked weight gives the same result.
Level 3: What goes wrong if you remove the output projection? Expected: the heads can only mix through later layers, so the block loses expressive power even though the shapes still work.
Level 3: What is an induction head? Expected: a pair of heads that finds a previous occurrence of the current token and copies the token that followed it; the circuit behind in-context learning.

Level 4: Grouped-query attention keeps the query heads and shrinks something else. What and why? Expected: the key and value heads, because only they live in the decode-time cache; fewer of them cut cache memory while the query heads keep quality.
wrongAnswers: "More heads mean more parameters." The projections keep their size; the heads are a reshape of the same matrices.
"Heads exchange information while they attend." They work on separate subspaces; mixing happens only in the output projection and in later layers.
"Use as many heads as the width allows." Heads narrower than the lesson's rule of thumb of 32 see too little; the common widths are 64 and 128.

questions.title: The rotary scheme rotates every query and every key by an angle that is proportional to the token's absolute position. Yet everyone says it encodes relative position. Resolve the apparent contradiction, and tell me the one unit test you would write to prove the property.
questions.answer: The rotation acts on pairs of coordinates with the angle pos * theta_i. When a query from position m meets a key from position n, the dot product on each pair picks up cos((m - n) * theta_i), so only the gap survives and the two absolute positions cancel. The test: rotate two random vectors at positions (a, b) and again at (a + k, b + k), then assert that the two dot products agree within floating-point error.
followUps: Level 2: Why rotate Q and K but not V? Expected: position should shape the match between tokens, not the content that is returned once a token is picked.

Level 3: What happens at a position the model never saw in training? Expected: the fast-turning pairs reach angles the model never learned to read; scaling the base or interpolating positions brings them back into the trained range.
Level 3: How does linear-bias attention get relative position without any rotation? Expected: it adds a penalty proportional to |i - j| to the scores, one slope per head.

Level 4: Why does increasing the base help a longer context? Expected: a larger base lowers every frequency except the first pair, which always turns at one radian per position, so the high-frequency pairs are not squeezed into unseen angles when the context grows; the NTK-aware rule rescales the base by the extension factor raised to d / (d - 2).
wrongAnswers: "RoPE adds a position vector to the embedding." It rotates the queries and the keys inside attention; the embedding is untouched.
"RoPE needs a table of size maximum length times width." The angles come from a formula; there is no table and no parameter.
"Rotate the keys only and save half the work." Then the score depends on the absolute position of the key, and the relative property is gone.

questions.title: A paper draft shows attention heatmaps as proof that the model "reasons over the right tokens". You are the reviewer. What do you say about the heatmaps, and what would convince you that a given head does something specific?
questions.answer: Attention weights are a distribution over positions, and on their own they are not an explanation: for some tasks they can be permuted or replaced by arbitrary alternatives without changing the prediction, so a heatmap shows where mass went, not that it mattered. Ask for an ablation or a counterfactual, zero or shuffle the head and show that the prediction moves. The head roles that have survived probing are specific and testable: heads that attend to the previous token, copy heads, and induction heads that find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it.
followUps: Level 3: A head attends almost uniformly across positions. What does that tell you? Expected: little on its own; it may carry an average or nothing, and only an ablation says which.

Level 3: Describe a test for an induction head in one sentence. Expected: repeat a random token sequence and check that the head attends from each token to the token after its earlier occurrence, with ablation removing the copy behavior.

Level 4: Why can the weights be permuted without changing the output? Expected: the values at the attended positions may carry near-identical information, other heads may be redundant, and later layers can compensate.
Level 4: What replaces the heatmap as the headline figure? Expected: the change in loss or in the target probability under ablation and counterfactual edits, with a band across seeds.
wrongAnswers: "A high weight means the token caused the output." Weight shows where the lookup went; causation needs an intervention.
"Average the heads to get the model's attention." Heads do different things; the average hides the roles and still is not evidence.
"If the heatmap matches human intuition, the model reasons like a human." Agreement with intuition is not a test; the permutation result shows intuitive maps can be irrelevant to the output.

questions.title: Count the parameters of a decoder stack with a model width of 4096, 32 layers and a SwiGLU feed-forward network at an expansion of 2.6. Then add an untied embedding and output head for a vocabulary of 128K. Where does the total land, and why is the published model of that size a little different?
questions.answer: Per block, attention takes 4 d^2 for the four projections and SwiGLU takes 3 d (r d), about 3 r d^2. At the given width and expansion that is about 67M plus 131M, about 198M per block, and 32 blocks give about 6.3B. The untied embedding and head add about 1B, so the stack lands near the published 8B. The real model uses grouped-query attention, which shrinks the key and value projections, and a wider FFN at an expansion of 3.5, which moves parameters from attention to the FFN while the total stays close.
followUps: Level 2: Why are the norms negligible? Expected: each norm is one or two vectors of length d, thousands of parameters against millions per matrix.
Level 3: How does grouped-query attention change the per-block count? Expected: the K and V projections shrink to d by n_kv_heads * d_head, so attention holds less than 4 d^2.

Level 3: Why does an expansion of 4 with two matrices equal an expansion of about 2.6 with three? Expected: 2 * 4 d^2 = 8 d^2 and 3 * 2.6 d^2 is about 8 d^2; the modern block kept the parameter budget and changed the activation.

Level 4: The team ties the embedding and the head. What changes in the count and what do you check? Expected: about half of the 1B disappears; check that the output logits still use the transpose of the embedding and that quality holds.
wrongAnswers: "The parameter count grows with the sequence length." No weight depends on the sequence; the length changes activation memory and compute, not parameters.
"The embedding is a rounding error." At 128K by 4096 it is about 1B, more than a tenth of the model.
"Attention is where most of the parameters are." The FFN holds about two thirds of each block.

questions.title: This is the take-home we send: train a small decoder-only transformer on a character-level text corpus of about one megabyte, on a laptop, and return the code, the loss curves and a few samples. Tell me how you would approach it, what a reviewer checks in your submission, and which results prove that the model works.
questions.answer: Build the small reference shape: a character tokenizer over the 65 symbols of the corpus, a token embedding plus a learned positional embedding, a stack of pre-norm blocks with RMSNorm, causal multi-head attention and a SwiGLU network, a final norm and a head tied to the embedding, trained with a shift-by-one cross-entropy on random 256-character windows. Use AdamW, a cosine schedule with warmup and gradient clipping at 1.0, and hold out the last 10 percent of the text for validation. The bar from the lesson: a 4-layer, 4-head model of width 128, about 800K parameters, goes from about 4.2 to about 1.5 training loss in 2,000 steps, about 6 minutes on a laptop, with validation loss under 2.0 that tracks the training loss and samples that look like the corpus.
followUps: Level 2: What is the training loss at step zero and how do you know it is right? Expected: about the logarithm of the vocabulary size, about 4.2 for 65 symbols, because a random model is uniform.

Level 3: How does a reviewer know your causal mask works without reading the code? Expected: a test that changes a later character and asserts the earlier logits are unchanged, and a loss that starts at the random baseline.
Level 3: Why tie the head to the embedding at this size? Expected: it saves parameters and the lesson records a quality improvement; the head weight is the transpose of the embedding.

Level 4: A candidate swaps the character tokenizer for a subword vocabulary of about 50,000. What else must change? Expected: the embedding and head grow from 65 rows to about 50,000, the model needs more capacity to use them, and the windows now cover more text per token.
wrongAnswers: "Use a bigger model to reach a lower loss within the time budget." A larger model trains slower on a laptop and the lesson's bar is reached at 800K parameters in about 6 minutes.
"Skip the validation split; the corpus is tiny." The split is the only check against a leak and the reviewer looks for it first.
"Report the sample quality instead of the loss." Samples are evidence, not a metric; the curves and the held-out loss are what a reviewer compares across candidates.

questions.title: A model was trained with a context of 8K tokens. The product now needs 128K. You have a modest fine-tuning budget and no budget to pretrain again. Lay out the options by the way the model encodes position, and give me the plan you would run.
questions.answer: The answer depends on the positional scheme, so read the config first. A learned absolute table has no row past the trained length and cannot be extended without new parameters. With rotary embeddings you scale the base or interpolate the positions, with NTK-aware scaling, YaRN or LongRoPE, and fine-tune on long sequences; the lesson's reference is a model family that went from 8K to 128K this way. Linear-bias attention extrapolates by construction, but you cannot switch a trained model to it for free.
followUps: Level 3: Why does a rotary model fail when you just run it at 128K with no change? Expected: the fast-turning coordinate pairs reach angles the model never saw, so the scores at long distance are noise.
Level 3: What two measurements do you insist on before shipping? Expected: perplexity or task quality at the new length, and the same at the original length to catch a regression.

Level 4: The team proposes to switch the model to linear-bias attention because it extrapolates well. Your answer? Expected: that is a training-time choice; a checkpoint trained with rotation cannot be swapped to a score bias without retraining.

Level 4: What breaks on the serving side at 128K even if quality is fine? Expected: memory for each token's keys and values, which grows with the context; the attention stack needs grouped-query or latent attention and a tiled kernel.
wrongAnswers: "Set the maximum position in the config higher and ship." A learned table has no row for the new positions, and a rotary model needs its base scaled and a fine-tune.
"The sinusoid extends to any length, so the model works." The formula extends; the model was never trained to read those phases and its quality drops.
"Position interpolation needs no training." The lesson's recipe is to shrink the positions and then fine-tune for 1 to 5B tokens.

questions.title: A colleague refuses to enable Flash Attention on a quality-sensitive model because "approximate attention changes the outputs". Is it an approximation? Explain what the kernel changes and what it keeps, with the memory argument that motivated it.
questions.answer: It is exact. The kernel tiles the computation so the full N by N score matrix never lands in the GPU's main memory; each tile is scored, exponentiated and accumulated in on-chip memory with a running maximum and a running sum, and the final normalization matches the single-pass softmax up to floating-point reordering. What changes is the memory traffic: three round trips to main memory become one write per output tile, and the footprint drops from N squared to N. The numbers that leave the kernel are the same as standard attention.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the kernel keep a running maximum and not just a running sum? Expected: numerical stability; exponentials of raw scores overflow, so every exponential is taken relative to the maximum seen so far and rescaled when it changes.
Level 3: Why recompute values during training instead of storing the softmax output? Expected: storing it would mean materializing the N by N matrix, which is the thing the kernel avoids.
Level 4: The newest version is forward-only at launch. What does that mean for your stack? Expected: serving can use it, training keeps the previous version until the backward kernel ships.
Level 4: Is the output identical across batch sizes? Expected: not bit for bit, because the reduction order changes in 16-bit arithmetic; that is a determinism question, not an approximation.
wrongAnswers: "It drops small attention weights to save work." Nothing is dropped; every key contributes through the running sum.
"It only helps at very long context." It helps whenever attention is memory-bound, and the lesson reports 2 to 4 times on the earlier accelerator for ordinary lengths.
"It reduces the FLOPs of attention." The arithmetic is the same; the saving is in memory traffic.

questions.title: You inherit a decoder block written in the 2017 style: layer normalization after the residual add, a ReLU feed-forward network at four times the width, sinusoidal absolute positions summed into the input, bias terms on every linear layer, and full multi-head attention. Review it against what production decoders ship today and justify each change you ask for.
questions.answer: Move the normalization in front of each sublayer and switch it to RMSNorm; replace the ReLU network with SwiGLU at about 2.6 times the width so that its three matrices match the old parameter count; replace the sinusoid with rotation of the queries and keys; drop the biases; and use grouped-query attention to shrink the decode-time cache. Every change is one function substitution and the tensor shapes do not move. The evidence: pre-norm trains deep without warmup tricks, SwiGLU gains about half a point of perplexity in the published model papers, rotation gives relative position and a knob for long context, and grouped-query cuts cache memory by the ratio of query heads to key-value heads.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the SwiGLU expansion about 2.6 and not 4? Expected: three matrices instead of two, chosen so that the total parameters match the old network.

Level 3: Which of the six changes can be applied to an existing checkpoint without retraining? Expected: none cleanly; grouped-query can be converted with a fine-tune, the rest change the function and need training.
Level 4: What would you refuse to change in the review? Expected: the residual skeleton, the causal mask and the next-token loss; the modern block refined the pieces, not the frame.

Level 4: The team wants to keep the sinusoid because it has no parameters. Your answer? Expected: rotation also has no parameters, applies inside attention, encodes relative distance and extends to longer contexts by scaling its base.
wrongAnswers: "RMSNorm is a cheaper approximation that costs accuracy." The lesson records it as at least as stable with one fewer operation.
"SwiGLU doubles the feed-forward parameters." At about 2.6 times the width its three matrices match the old two-matrix count.
"Pre-norm removes the need for any final normalization." It adds the need: the residual stream is unnormalized, so the head needs a final norm.

questions.title: You lead a pretraining run with a fixed compute budget. One plan trains a 175B-parameter model on 300B tokens. Another trains a much smaller model on far more tokens. Which do you pick, how do you defend it to leadership, and when would you deliberately train past the point that the scaling law calls optimal?
questions.answer: Compute is about 6 times the parameter count times the training tokens, so the budget fixes the product and leaves the split open. The compute-optimal split is about 20 tokens per parameter; the first plan has about 1.7 tokens per parameter, which the lesson calls ten times undertrained, and a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beat that 175B model on every benchmark at 2.5 times less inference cost. If the model will serve a large volume, go past the optimum on purpose: train smaller and longer, because training is paid once and inference is paid forever.
followUps: Level 3: What is the E term and why can no budget remove it? Expected: the irreducible loss, the entropy of the data itself; the law approaches it but never crosses it.
Level 4: How does a sparse expert architecture change the plan? Expected: FLOPs follow the active parameters, so the optimal D is set against active N while total N sets memory.

Level 4: The web runs out of high-quality tokens for your budget. What are the levers? Expected: the lesson puts filtered English at about 5 to 10 trillion tokens; the levers are synthetic data, multilingual and multimodal data, and better curation.

Level 4: How would you check the law on your own stack before betting the budget? Expected: fit it on five small models from 100K to 10M parameters on the same data and compare the exponents with the published ones.
wrongAnswers: "The bigger model always wins at fixed compute." The 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beat the 175B model trained on 300B.
"Compute-optimal is also the cheapest model to serve." It minimizes training loss per training FLOP; serving cost scales with N, which is why production models over-train.
"A loss prediction is useless because abilities appear suddenly." The continuous loss is smooth and predictable; sudden benchmark jumps are mostly scorer artifacts.

questions.title: Between two model sizes a benchmark accuracy goes from near zero to high. The team calls it an emergent ability and asks for a larger budget to find the next jump. How do you evaluate the claim before you sign?
questions.answer: Ask what the scorer is. Exact match and thresholded accuracy are discontinuous: a model that gets most digits right scores zero until it gets all of them right, so a smooth gain in the underlying probabilities shows up as a cliff. Re-score the same checkpoints with a continuous metric such as the cross-entropy of the target answers; if that curve is smooth, the jump belongs to the scorer and not to the model. Plan the budget against the continuous curve, which the scaling law predicts reliably.
followUps: Level 3: Give an example of a discontinuous scorer and its continuous counterpart. Expected: exact match on a multi-digit answer against the log-probability or the digit-level accuracy of the same answer.

Level 4: How does this change the way you plan a training budget? Expected: predict the loss from the law, calibrate the benchmark against the loss, and place runs near the threshold instead of hoping for a jump.

Level 4: The product threshold really is binary for the user. Does the artifact argument still matter? Expected: yes; the threshold is real for the product, but its position is predictable from the smooth curve, which is what you need to budget.
Level 4: What would convince you that a jump is not a scorer artifact? Expected: the continuous metric also shows a kink at the same scale, replicated across seeds and data orderings.
wrongAnswers: "Accuracy is the ground truth and loss is a proxy." Accuracy with a hard threshold throws away the information that shows the trend; the loss is what the model optimizes and what the law predicts.
"Emergence means the scaling law broke." The law describes the continuous loss, which keeps its shape while the thresholded score jumps.
"Train the bigger model and see." That is the expensive experiment the analysis lets you avoid; re-score what you already have first.

questions.title: Design the attention stack of a new 70B-class decoder that must serve 128K-token contexts on a single 80 GB accelerator at batch size one. Cover the head layout, the positional scheme, the kernel, and the memory arithmetic that ties them together.
questions.answer: Start from the memory, because it decides the rest. With 8 key-value heads, 80 layers and a head size of 128 in a 16-bit type, the stored keys and values cost 4096 bytes per token per layer, about 10 GiB at 32K and 40 GiB at 128K before a single weight is loaded. So the head layout is grouped-query or latent attention, the stored type is reduced to FP8 to halve those bytes, the positional scheme is rotation with base scaling so that the model reaches 128K without a position table, and the kernel is a tiled one so that the N by N scores never touch main memory. Then count again: at 16 bits the weights of a 70B-class model alone are larger than the 80 GB card, so the weights also need a 4-bit type before the cache and the activations can fit beside them.
followUps: Level 3: Why not pick linear-bias attention for its extrapolation? Expected: it is a fair choice for a new model, but rotation has the long-context tooling and a base to scale, and neither can be swapped after training.

Level 4: The product later asks for batch size 8 at 128K. What changes? Expected: the cache multiplies by 8, so latent attention, a smaller stored type, a shorter maximum length or more cards; the weights do not change.
Level 4: Grouped-query from scratch or convert a multi-head checkpoint? Expected: from scratch for a new model; conversion with a fine-tune is for existing checkpoints and needs a quality check.

Level 4: Where does Flash Attention stop helping? Expected: it removes the N by N traffic; it does not shrink the cache, which still grows linearly with the context, so the cache math dominates at 128K.
wrongAnswers: "Use full multi-head attention for quality; memory is cheap." At 128K the full cache alone exceeds the card.
"The sinusoid handles any length, so the position scheme is solved." The formula extends but the model never saw those phases; rotation with base scaling is what reached 128K in practice.
"Skip the tiled kernel on a quality model because it changes the output." It is exact up to 16-bit reordering and it is what makes long context affordable.

topics.title: Tokenization, sampling and decoding
topics.about: How text becomes tokens, how a model picks the next token, and how speculation makes decoding faster.

questions.title: Walk me through one training step of byte-pair encoding on a small corpus, and tell me what the trained artifact actually is.
questions.answer: Start with every word split into base symbols, bytes or characters. Count every adjacent pair across the corpus, weighted by how often each word appears, merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol with the next free id, rewrite every occurrence, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The artifact is the ordered list of merges; the vocabulary follows from it, and the same list applied in the same order is what encoding uses later.
followUps: Level 1: Why weight pairs by word frequency instead of counting each distinct word once? Expected: the merges should serve the text the model will see, and common words appear many times.
Level 2: Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two training runs on the same corpus must produce the same table, or the same text would get different ids.

Level 2: What happens to the encoded length of a sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600? Expected: it falls, because more merges cover longer pieces; that curve is the compression curve.
Level 3: Why split the corpus into words before you count pairs? Expected: without it, merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with whole phrases that do not generalize.
wrongAnswers: "BPE picks the pair that makes the most meaningful piece." It picks the most frequent pair; meaning is a side effect, and the likelihood-based variant is a different algorithm.
"The vocabulary is the artifact; the merge list can be discarded." Encoding needs the merges in order; the vocabulary alone does not say how to split new text.
"All merges are chosen at once from the initial pair counts." Each merge changes the counts, so the loop recounts after every step.

questions.title: A customer in Korea reports that the same prompt uses up far more of the context window than the English version, and the bill is higher too. Why does this happen, and what does a model builder do about it?
questions.answer: The vocabulary was trained on English-heavy text, so its merges cover English and other scripts fall back to short pieces or raw bytes. Korean averages 2 to 3 tokens per word on an older vocabulary, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens than English for the same meaning; a Chinese character is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so without merges each character is several tokens. The builder's fix is a larger vocabulary trained on multilingual data, which is why one model family grew its vocabulary from 32K to 128K.
followUps: Level 1: Define fertility in one sentence. Expected: the average number of tokens the tokenizer produces per word, where higher means the model works harder for the same text.
Level 2: How do you measure the tax for a new vocabulary? Expected: tokenize matched sentences in several languages and compare tokens per character or per word.
Level 2: Why does a larger vocabulary help scripts other than English? Expected: more merges can be spent on their byte patterns, so each character or word needs fewer tokens.

Level 3: What does the tax do to a product's cost model? Expected: per-token pricing and per-token latency scale with the token count, so the same feature costs more and runs slower in affected languages, and the context budget shrinks.
wrongAnswers: "Korean is harder for the model to understand." The model sees ids; the extra cost comes from the tokenizer's merges, not from the language.
"Use a character-level tokenizer for Korean." Characters make every sequence longer; the fix is merges that cover the script.
"The model has a smaller context window for Korean." The window is the same number of tokens; the tokenizer spends more of them per word.

questions.title: Why does every current language model read subword tokens instead of whole words or single characters, and why do most of them build the vocabulary on top of raw bytes?
questions.answer: A word vocabulary cannot hold every word, so each new word becomes an unknown token and the model loses the signal. Characters never fail, but they make sequences several times longer and spend attention on spelling. Subwords keep common words whole and split rare words into meaningful pieces, and starting from the 256 byte values means any input in any script encodes with zero unknown tokens.
followUps: Level 1: What does fertility measure? Expected: the average number of tokens per word; 1.0 is one token per word and higher means the model works harder for the same text.
Level 2: Why does the unknown token disappear with byte-level vocabularies? Expected: every byte is itself a token, so any input decomposes into known tokens before any merge applies.
Level 2: What does a tiny vocabulary cost at inference? Expected: longer sequences, so more forward passes per answer and less text per context window.

Level 3: Why can you not fix a bad tokenizer after training? Expected: the embedding rows and every weight were trained against those ids; new ids have no learned meaning and old text would map differently.
wrongAnswers: "Characters are the safest choice because nothing is ever unknown." Bytes give the same guarantee, and characters make every sequence several times longer.
"A bigger word list solves the unknown problem." New words, misspellings, code and other languages keep appearing; no word list is complete.
"A token is a word." A token can be a byte, a piece of a word, a word, or a short phrase, depending on the merges.

questions.title: A fine-tuned chat model answers well in the training notebook. The deployed service, with identical weights, returns rambling text that runs until the token limit. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?
questions.answer: At the flat token sequence the model actually receives, not at the list of messages. A chat model was trained on one exact layout of role markers, special tokens and newlines; a missing newline, a swapped marker or an extra space puts the input outside the training distribution, and the end-of-turn token stops being predicted. Print the token ids of the same request from both paths and diff them, and check that the special tokens arrived as their reserved ids and not as the bytes that spell them.
followUps: Level 2: What does the end-of-turn token do at inference? Expected: it is the model's signal that the answer is complete; the server must stop on that id, or generation runs to the limit.

Level 3: A user types the literal string of a special token into the chat box. What should happen? Expected: with the allow flag off it becomes ordinary bytes, which is the safe default for user text; with it on, the user could inject a control marker.
Level 3: How do you test a template implementation? Expected: build the sequence for a fixed message list and compare it id by id with the output of the model's own template code.

Level 4: The template is correct and the ids still differ between notebook and service. What else? Expected: a different tokenizer file version, a different normalization step, or a different setting for adding special tokens at the start; hash the tokenizer file and compare the flags.
wrongAnswers: "The sampling temperature is too high in the service." Temperature changes which token is picked, not whether the stop token is ever predicted; the ids differ before sampling.
"The fine-tune overfit." The same weights behave in the notebook; the difference is in the input layout.
"Trim the output on the client." That hides the symptom and the model still wastes compute on text it should not generate.

questions.title: A classifier prompt asks for one of three labels and the model answers with a paragraph, so the parser crashes. Three layers of fix exist. Explain how the strongest one works at the level of the logits, and why it is often faster than free generation, not slower.
questions.answer: Prompting asks nicely, a vendor's structured-output API does it on the server, and constrained decoding does it locally by editing the logits. At each step a logit processor computes which vocabulary tokens can advance the target grammar, a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar compiled to a state machine, and sets every other logit to minus infinity, so the softmax puts probability only on valid continuations and an invalid output is unreachable. It can be faster because the search space shrinks and because tokens that the grammar forces, such as a fixed key name, are emitted without a model step.
followUps: Level 2: When does a finite-state machine not suffice? Expected: for recursive schemas; the machine flattens recursion to a fixed depth, and a context-free grammar engine is needed.
Level 3: What does a provider's plain JSON mode guarantee, and what does it not? Expected: valid JSON syntax, not conformance to your schema; always send a full schema.

Level 3: How does the retry library differ from the logit processor? Expected: it never changes the model's distribution; it validates after the fact and retries, which adds latency and cost per failure.
Level 4: The schema has an enum with 10,000 options and compilation times out. What do you do? Expected: predict a short list of candidates with a retriever first, then constrain the decode to those.
wrongAnswers: "Constrained decoding makes the answer correct." It makes the answer valid for the grammar; a well-formed wrong answer still passes.
"Checking the grammar at every token makes generation slower." The valid-token sets are precomputed per state, and forced tokens skip the model, so it is often faster.
"Enough examples in the prompt reach full compliance." The lesson's figure for prompting alone is about 80 percent; a contract needs the logits or the server.

questions.title: At encode time a BPE tokenizer holds the complete merge table. Why does it have to replay the merges in the order they were learned, and what goes wrong when two merges could fire at the same spot?
questions.answer: Encoding must reproduce what training did to the same text, and training saw the merges one at a time in that order. If merge one created "th" and merge five created "the" from "th" plus "e", then "the" can only form after "th" exists. When two merges could apply at one position, the one with the lower rank, learned earlier, wins; change that rule and the same text yields different ids, so the model sees a distribution of ids it was never trained on.
followUps: Level 2: Why is the naive loop slow? Expected: it scans the full merge table for every word, so the cost grows with the table size times the word length.
Level 3: How do production encoders get close to linear time? Expected: a rank lookup for each adjacent pair and a priority queue that always surfaces the lowest-ranked applicable merge.
Level 3: Two tokenizers were trained on different corpora to the same vocabulary size. Do they give the same ids? Expected: no; different corpora give different merge tables and different ranks.
Level 3: What test pins the order? Expected: encode a held-out word and compare with recorded ids; the capstone's tests also pin the round trip and the special-token reservation.
wrongAnswers: "Greedily take the longest token in the vocabulary that matches." That is a different algorithm and gives a different segmentation from the training run.
"Order does not matter because merges commute." A later merge depends on the symbols that earlier merges created, so they do not commute.
"Sort the merges by token length." Length is not rank; a long piece may have been learned early and a short one late.

questions.title: Before any merge runs, a production tokenizer cuts the text into chunks with a regular expression. Show me what the classic pattern does to Hello, world! Don't stop. and explain why the cut exists at all, given that the merges could run on the raw stream.
questions.answer: The pattern cuts the sentence into eight chunks, Hello, ,,  world, !,  Don, 't,  stop and .: each word after the first keeps the space in front of it, contractions split at the apostrophe, and punctuation stands alone. The merges then run inside each chunk and can never join symbols across a chunk boundary. Without the cut, training learns merges that span words, the vocabulary fills with whole phrases, and the pieces generalize worse to new text.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a prompt that starts without a space tokenize differently from one that starts with a space? Expected: the space is part of the word-initial token, so the first word maps to a different id; set the prefix-space behavior explicitly.
Level 3: Why does the regex module matter for this pattern? Expected: the Unicode letter and number classes cover scripts beyond ASCII, which the standard library's engine lacks.

Level 3: What is the trade in skipping the cut and running on raw text? Expected: no language rules and good behavior for scripts without spaces, against cross-word pieces that compress slightly better and are less interpretable.

Level 3: A tokenizer file is unchanged but ids differ between two machines. What in this stage can cause it? Expected: one machine fell back to the ASCII pattern because the regex module was missing, so the chunks differ.
wrongAnswers: "Pre-tokenization is just splitting on spaces." The pattern also handles contractions, digits, punctuation and runs of whitespace, and it keeps the space attached to the word.
"The cut is cosmetic; the merges would find the same pieces." Without the cut the merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with phrases.
"Attach punctuation to the word it follows." Then world! and world are different pieces, and the vocabulary pays for every punctuation variant.

questions.title: A team wants to grow the vocabulary of a new model from 32K to 128K tokens. The embeddings have 4,096 dimensions. Put numbers on what the change costs and on what it buys.
questions.answer: The embedding matrix goes from 32,000 by 4,096, about 131 million parameters, to 128,000 by 4,096, about 524 million, so about 400M more parameters from the tokenizer alone, and an untied output head costs the same again. In return the text compresses: an English paragraph of about 100 tokens at 32K takes about 70 tokens at 128K. Generating that same paragraph then needs about 30 percent fewer forward passes, and non-English scripts gain the most. The lesson's rule of thumb is 32k under 1B parameters, 50 to 100k from 1 to 10B, and 200k and above for multilingual or frontier models.
followUps: Level 2: Why do fewer tokens per word make inference faster? Expected: generation is one forward pass per token, so fewer tokens for the same text means fewer passes.
Level 3: What does a 128K vocabulary do to the output side of the model? Expected: the head has one row per token, so it grows with the embedding, and an untied head doubles the extra parameters.

Level 3: Why did the model family in the lesson move from 32K to 128K? Expected: fairer compression across languages; the English-heavy vocabulary gave other scripts a context window that was effectively half the size.

Level 4: How do you validate a vocabulary size before training? Expected: tokens per word per language on held-out text, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder, and a byte-exact round trip.
wrongAnswers: "A bigger vocabulary is always better." Under 1B parameters the extra rows dominate the model and rare rows are undertrained.
"The embedding is a rounding error next to the model." At 128K by 4,096 it is about 524M parameters.
"Vocabulary size does not affect the cost of a request." Tokens per word set the sequence length, and the sequence length sets the forward passes and the context budget.

questions.title: Three subword algorithms dominate: byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and Unigram. Contrast how each builds its vocabulary, tell me which one can give two different segmentations of the same word on purpose, and name the libraries you would reach for.
questions.answer: Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent adjacent pair, bottom up. WordPiece also merges bottom up but scores a pair by the count of the merged piece over the product of the counts of its parts, so it prefers pairs that co-occur more than chance, and it marks continuation pieces with a double-hash prefix. Unigram works top down: it starts from a large candidate set, assigns each piece a probability, and prunes the pieces whose removal hurts the corpus likelihood least, which is why it can also sample alternative segmentations for regularization.
followUps: Level 2: What is subword regularization? Expected: training on sampled segmentations from a Unigram model so the same word appears in several forms.
Level 2: What does the visible-space symbol buy? Expected: the space becomes an ordinary symbol, so the tokenizer needs no pre-tokenization and works for scripts without spaces.
Level 3: Which algorithm and setting for a multilingual vocabulary? Expected: Unigram trained on raw text with character coverage near 0.9995, so rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown.
Level 3: Why can an encode-only library not train your tokenizer? Expected: it ships pre-built vocabularies and a fast encoder; the training step lives in the other two libraries.
wrongAnswers: "WordPiece and byte-pair encoding give the same vocabulary on the same corpus." The criteria differ, so the merges differ; the likelihood ratio favors surprising pairs over merely frequent ones.
"Unigram is deterministic like the merge algorithms." It is probabilistic and can sample segmentations on purpose.
"The library that encodes the space as a symbol is itself an algorithm." It is a library that trains either the merge or the prune algorithm on raw text.

questions.title: Your creative-writing product samples at a high temperature and speculative decoding gives it no speedup at all, while the same setup flies on code completion. Explain the difference, and describe what the acceptance test becomes at temperature zero.
questions.answer: Acceptance depends on how often the verifier agrees with what the draft sampled. At a high temperature the target distribution is flat, the draft's samples spread across many tokens, and the acceptance ratio of verifier to draft probability falls toward one over the vocabulary size, so almost every draft is rejected and the draft's cost is paid for nothing. Code and structured output are predictable, so acceptance climbs above 0.9. At temperature zero the rule becomes a comparison: accept if the drafted token equals the verifier's most likely token, otherwise emit that token and stop.
followUps: Level 2: What does the acceptance ratio become when the draft and the verifier agree exactly? Expected: one, so every draft is accepted and each pass yields the full draft plus the bonus token.

Level 3: May the draft sample at a different temperature from the verifier? Expected: yes, as long as p is the distribution the draft actually sampled from; the output still follows the verifier's distribution, but a mismatch lowers acceptance.

Level 3: How would you implement the switch in a serving layer? Expected: read the request's temperature and output length, and disable speculation above a temperature threshold or below a length threshold, with the thresholds set from measured acceptance.

Level 4: Why is the loss worse at high concurrency than the formula suggests? Expected: a rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll that serialize under a full batch, and the batch already fills the memory bandwidth that speculation was exploiting, so the tail latency suffers.
wrongAnswers: "Lower the temperature so speculation works." The product chose the temperature for a reason; change the decoding path for those requests, not the product.
"The draft is too small; use a bigger draft." Size is not the issue when the target distribution is flat; a larger draft still cannot guess which of many acceptable tokens the verifier samples.
"At high temperature speculation changes the output." The rejection rule keeps the output distribution exact at any temperature; what changes is the speed.

questions.title: You review the schema of an extraction service. It is {"answer": ..., "reasoning": ..., "date": <a strict year-month-day regex>}, enforced by constrained decoding. Compliance is perfect, yet accuracy is poor and some dates are invented. What is wrong with the design, and how do you change it?
questions.answer: Two faults that no validator can catch. The answer field comes before the reasoning field, so the model commits to an answer before it has reasoned, and the strict date pattern leaves no legal way to say unknown, so the model complies by inventing a date. Put reasoning first and the answer last, and allow a null or a sentinel for a missing date; field order is logic, not formatting, and a grammar that is too strict forces a confident wrong value.
followUps: Level 3: How do you measure semantic validity when compliance is already perfect? Expected: a labeled sample scored by a judge or by rules on the content, tracked separately from schema compliance.
Level 3: The output needs a tree, such as nested comments. What changes? Expected: a state-machine library flattens recursion; move to a context-free grammar engine.

Level 4: The product streams the answer to the user and wants it first for latency. How do you resolve the conflict? Expected: name the trade; options are two calls, reasoning in a hidden field before a visible answer, or accepting the latency; never answer-first with the same accuracy expectation.

Level 4: How would the invented dates have shown up in monitoring? Expected: a field coverage rate near 100 percent on a corpus where the date is often missing is itself the alarm; compare the rate with the base rate of the field in the source.
wrongAnswers: "Tighten the regex so only plausible dates pass." The grammar is already the problem; a tighter one forces more invention.
"Add a line to the prompt asking the model to be honest." The mask forbids the honest tokens; no instruction can make the model emit a token with minus infinity logit.
"Validation passes, so the system works." Validation checks shape; it cannot see that the answer was committed before the reasoning or that a date was made up.

questions.title: A pretraining team wants to supervise each position on more than the next token. One design puts several independent output heads on the backbone. Another chains small modules, one per extra depth. Which design gives you a usable speculative draft at inference, and what does it cost during training?
questions.answer: The chained design. Module k takes the previous depth's hidden state and the embedding of the actual next token, runs its own small transformer block, and reuses the shared embedding and the shared output head, so its prediction of the token at t plus k plus 1 is conditioned on the token at t plus k, which is the same causal chain a decoder follows and lets the module draft tokens at inference with acceptance at depth one of 80 percent or more for about 1.8 times throughput. Independent heads all read the same hidden state and cannot condition on each other. The training cost is about 10 percent slower pretraining and about 14 h squared parameters per module, with a loss weight of 0.3 early and 0.1 later.
followUps: Level 3: Why share the embedding and the output head with the main model? Expected: no extra parameters, and the module predicts in the same vocabulary space as the backbone.
Level 3: Why is the published parameter overhead larger than the 14 h^2 estimate? Expected: the module's MLP has the same expert structure as the main model, which multiplies its parameters.
Level 4: With two modules, what does the second one take as input? Expected: the first module's hidden state and the embedding of the token two ahead, to predict the token three ahead.

Level 4: A team wants to add this to an existing dense model by fine-tuning a new head. Your answer? Expected: the module is not trained and the backbone was not shaped by the extra loss; the lesson's position is that it needs a pretraining run, and a post-hoc draft is the right tool for existing weights.
wrongAnswers: "The extra loss replaces next-token prediction." It is added to the main loss with a small weight; the main objective stays.
"The module can be bolted onto a trained model with a quick fine-tune." The design is a pretraining choice; existing weights get a post-hoc draft instead.

questions.title: This is a take-home we send: implement a byte-level byte-pair tokenizer with training, encoding and decoding, two reserved special tokens, and a test suite. Describe the design you would submit, the tests you would ship, and the one figure you would include in the write-up.
questions.answer: Reserve ids 0 to 255 for the raw bytes and a small block above them for the end-of-text and pad markers, split the corpus on whitespace and punctuation, train by counting frequency-weighted adjacent pairs and merging the top pair with a deterministic tie-break, encode by applying the lowest-ranked merge that fits until none fits, and decode by joining the byte expansions and decoding UTF-8 once. The tests pin the byte-exact round trip on an unseen sentence, on an emoji and on a literal special-token string with the allow flag on and off, plus the merge-order property and the reserved ids. The figure is the compression curve: the encoded length of a held-out sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600.
followUps: Level 2: Why do the raw bytes take ids 0 to 255 before anything else? Expected: every input can then be expressed in the vocabulary before any merge exists, so nothing is ever unknown.

Level 3: The input spells out the end-of-text marker as plain text. What does the allow flag change? Expected: off, the string is ordinary bytes and pieces; on, it maps to the reserved id and is skipped by the merge loop.
Level 3: Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two runs on the same corpus must give the same table, or the same text gets different ids across machines.

Level 4: Replace the simple split with the production regex pattern. What do you compare? Expected: the vocabularies and the encoded lengths on the same corpus, looking at how contractions, digits and leading spaces are handled.
wrongAnswers: "Use Unicode code points as the base symbols." Code points number in the hundreds of thousands and leave gaps for unseen characters; bytes are 256 and complete.
