"Decode each token to a string and join the strings." A token can hold part of a multi-byte character; join the bytes first and decode once.
"Skip the pre-split to get better compression." Merges then cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with phrases that do not transfer.

questions.title: After a routine dependency upgrade, an evaluation score for a deployed model fell sharply. No model weights changed. Give me a diagnosis plan that starts at the tokenizer, and the control you add so it cannot happen again.
questions.answer: A model trained with one vocabulary and served with another gets different ids for the same text and produces garbage, so first hash the tokenizer file in both environments and compare. If the hashes match, check the settings that change ids without changing the vocabulary: whether special tokens are added, whether a prefix space is added, and the normalization step, because a leading space or a ligature that normalizes differently moves whole tokens. Then freeze the tokenizer hash in CI and keep golden token ids for a fixed corpus so any change fails a test before it ships.
followUps: Level 3: How does a prefix space change the ids? Expected: the space is part of the word-initial token, so with it the first word gets one id and without it another, and the shift can continue through the merges.

Level 3: What does the compatibility normalization do, and when is it harmful? Expected: it maps compatibility characters to their plain forms, such as a ligature to two letters or a fullwidth letter to ASCII; it is lossy, so code or text that depends on the exact form changes meaning.

Level 4: The hashes match and the ids still differ on non-Latin text only. What moved? Expected: the pre-tokenizer engine; the environment without the Unicode-aware module fell back to the ASCII pattern.

Level 4: Design the CI gate in two sentences. Expected: a test that encodes a fixed multilingual corpus and compares against stored golden ids and a stored tokenizer hash; any difference fails the build and prints the first differing position.
wrongAnswers: "The weights did not change, so the model is the same." The model is the weights and the mapping from text to ids; change the mapping and the model sees different inputs.
"Retrain the model on the new tokenizer." A multi-week fix for a configuration bug; restore the training-time tokenizer and settings.
"Lowercase everything so the normalization does not matter." That changes the ids again and throws away information the model was trained with.

questions.title: Walk the line from a separate small draft model to the current generation of hidden-state drafts. What limitation did each step remove, and why does feeding the draft the verifier's internal features help so much?
questions.answer: A separate small model from the same family accepts around 0.6 of its tokens, because its distribution drifts from the verifier's. The first hidden-state draft replaces it with a one or two layer network that reads the verifier's last-layer features, so the draft starts from the verifier's own representation and acceptance rises to 0.7 to 0.8. The second generation proposes a tree of candidates and verifies every branch in one pass with a tree-shaped attention mask, lifting acceptance per accepted-path token above 0.85. The third drops the feature-matching loss, trains on direct token prediction, and feeds the draft its own previous outputs during training, which removes exposure bias and reaches 0.88 to 0.92.
followUps: Level 3: Why did matching the verifier's features cap the first generations? Expected: the feature loss asks the draft to reproduce hidden states rather than predict tokens, so more training data stopped helping; the third generation trains on tokens.
Level 3: What is exposure bias in this setting? Expected: the draft was trained on teacher-forced verifier inputs and run on its own outputs; the mismatch compounds over the draft steps.

Level 4: What does the tree cost? Expected: a non-causal attention mask that follows the tree topology, extra stored keys and values for the tree nodes, and scheduler complexity; the verifier still runs once.

Level 4: How do you compare the extra-heads design with the hidden-state draft? Expected: no second model to deploy and simpler serving, against a somewhat lower acceptance and a supervised fine-tuning stage on the verifier.
wrongAnswers: "A larger separate draft model is the main lever." Alignment with the verifier matters more than size; a one-layer draft on hidden states beats a far larger independent model.
"The hidden-state draft changes the verifier's output distribution to gain acceptance." The rejection rule keeps the output exact; the draft only changes how often it is right.
"A tree needs one verifier pass per branch." All branches are verified in one pass under the tree mask.

questions.title: A draft is accepted 80 percent of the time per token and proposes four tokens per step. How many tokens does one pass of the big model produce on average, how does the draft's own cost enter, and when does a longer draft stop paying?
questions.answer: The expected tokens per verifier pass are (1 - alpha^(K + 1)) / (1 - alpha); at an acceptance of 0.8 and K of 4 that is 3.36, so about 3.36 times fewer big-model calls. The wall time per token is (K c + 1) over that expectation, where c is the draft's cost relative to the verifier, so a longer draft adds cost linearly while the geometric series saturates; at 0.8 acceptance and c of 0.05 the optimum sits around 5 to 7 drafts for about 3.2 times. The lever that matters is the acceptance rate: at a fixed K, a rise from 0.6 to 0.9 about doubles the expected tokens per pass.
followUps: Level 3: At an acceptance of 0.95 and a draft cost of 0.02, where is the optimum? Expected: around 8 to 10 drafts, with the speedup pushing toward 5 times.

Level 3: Why does the expectation saturate as K grows? Expected: it is a geometric series; the probability that all drafts up to position K are accepted falls as alpha to the K, so late positions add almost nothing.

Level 4: How does batch size change the arithmetic? Expected: the verifier's extra work per draft is no longer hidden behind idle bandwidth, so the effective cost of verification and of a rejection rises, and the break-even acceptance climbs toward 0.45 to 0.55.
Level 4: What single measurement do you add to the dashboard? Expected: accepted draft tokens divided by proposed draft tokens, per traffic slice, so alpha is visible where the formula needs it.
wrongAnswers: "The speedup equals the draft length." Only if every draft is accepted; the geometric series and the draft cost cut it well below K.
"Doubling K doubles throughput." Beyond the optimum the extra drafts are mostly rejected and their cost is paid anyway.
"A draft ten times cheaper gives ten times the speedup." The draft cost sets c; the acceptance rate sets the expectation, and a cheap draft that is often wrong gains little.

questions.title: You are starting a 7B model that must serve many languages and also be strong at code. Design its tokenizer: the algorithm, the library, the vocabulary size, the coverage settings, and the validation plan you would gate the training run on.
questions.answer: Train a byte-fallback subword vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target mix of languages and code, with a pre-tokenizer that keeps leading spaces and separates digits and punctuation so that code tokenizes cleanly. For a model in the 1 to 10B range the heuristic is 50 to 100k tokens, and the multilingual requirement pushes to the top of that range or beyond it; set the character coverage near 0.9995 so that rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown. Gate on tokens per word per language, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder and a byte-exact round trip, and freeze the tokenizer file hash in CI before the first training step.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the corpus mix matter more than the algorithm choice? Expected: the merges or the pruned pieces follow the frequencies in the training text, so a script that is rare in the sample gets few pieces whatever the algorithm.

Level 4: What does whitespace handling do to code? Expected: indentation is runs of spaces or tabs; a pre-tokenizer that keeps whitespace runs as their own chunks lets them become stable tokens instead of being glued to the next word.

Level 4: The team wants to change the vocabulary after six months of training. What do you tell them? Expected: the embeddings and every weight were trained against the current ids; a change means a retrain, which is why the tokenizer decision is gated before the first step.
Level 4: How do you report the tokenizer with the model? Expected: the fertility table per language, the size and coverage of the vocabulary, the special-token list and the file hash.
wrongAnswers: "Pick 32k because earlier models used it." That size served monolingual models under 1B; a 7B multilingual coding model pays the tax in every language.
"Set character coverage to 1.0 to be safe." Full coverage spends vocabulary on characters seen once; near 0.9995 with byte fallback keeps rare scripts without wasting rows.
"Train on English now and add the other languages later." The vocabulary cannot change after training without a retrain; the languages must be in the tokenizer corpus from the start.

questions.title: Two changes shipped in one week: the target model moved to its next version, and a new customer whose traffic is mostly code was routed onto the same cluster. Speculative decoding has been on for months. Since then the mean inter-token latency fell 25 percent, the P99 rose 15 percent, and throughput at the usual concurrency is down. Diagnose it.
questions.answer: Both changes attack acceptance. The draft head was trained against the previous target version, so its distribution drifted and more drafts reject; the code traffic shifts the input distribution away from the general chat data the head was trained on, where acceptance falls into the 0.4 to 0.6 band. A rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll, two passes that serialize under a full batch, which is exactly a tail that worsens while the mean still improves. Read acceptance per traffic slice and per target version from the engine's speculative metrics, retrain or roll back to a head aligned with the new target, and gate speculation per request class.
followUps: Level 3: Why can the mean improve while throughput falls? Expected: the accepted requests get faster, but the rejected ones consume two target passes each, and at a full batch that extra work displaces other requests.

Level 4: Design the alert in two sentences. Expected: compute acceptance per slice and per target version over a short window and compare against the baseline recorded at rollout; page when a slice crosses the floor or drops a fixed share from its baseline.

Level 4: What is the fallback when acceptance drops on one slice only? Expected: switch that slice to an n-gram draft or to plain decoding while the head is retrained, and keep speculation where it still pays.

Level 4: How does this change your release process? Expected: a target upgrade ships together with a draft trained against it, and the benchmark that gates the release reports acceptance and P99 per slice.
wrongAnswers: "Increase the draft length to win back throughput." More drafts at low acceptance are mostly rejected and their cost is still paid; the tail gets worse.
"Turn speculation off everywhere." The chat slice may still pay; gate by slice and fix the head.

"The new target is just slower; speculation has nothing to do with it." A plain-decode benchmark of the new target settles that in minutes, and the mean improving while the tail worsens points at rejections.

questions.title: You are about to pretrain a model that will later serve a large volume using speculative decoding. Three ways to get a draft are on the table: bake sequential multi-token modules into pretraining, train a hidden-state draft head after pretraining, or reuse a small model of the same family. Give the decision with its costs, and name the gate you measure before you ship the flag.
questions.answer: If I control pretraining and the hidden size is at least 4096, I bake in the sequential modules: about 10 percent slower training buys a denser supervision signal and a draft that accepts 80 percent or more at depth one. If the weights already exist, I train a post-hoc head on the verifier's features with about 60 to 200B tokens; it is backward compatible and reaches 0.88 to 0.92 acceptance on general chat. A same-family small model needs no training and sits around 0.55 to 0.70. Whatever I pick, the gate is measured acceptance on my own traffic mix at production concurrency, with the flag off below about 0.55 and the tail latency watched, not the mean.
followUps: Level 3: The traffic is 70 percent chat at 0.7 acceptance and 30 percent code at 0.4. How do you decide? Expected: weight by traffic share, then check each slice against the floor; code alone is below it, so route code to a plain decode or train a code head.

Level 4: The target gets a new version next quarter. What happens to each option? Expected: the baked-in modules move with the model; the post-hoc head must be retrained against the new target; the small model drifts further; alert on acceptance per version.
Level 4: What does a hidden-state head read in the current generation? Expected: features from several target layers, not only the last, which is part of why acceptance rose.
Level 4: Where does the small-model option still win? Expected: a prototype with no training budget, or a CPU deployment where the engine ships only the plain draft path.
wrongAnswers: "Always use the latest hidden-state draft; it is strictly best." It needs training against your target and its acceptance on domain traffic can fall to 0.4; the baked-in modules give you a draft and a better model if you own pretraining.
"Bake the modules in later with a fine-tune." They are a pretraining choice; an existing dense model gets a post-hoc head instead.
"Pick by the speedup on a public benchmark." Acceptance depends on your traffic; the gate is measured on your own mix at your concurrency.

topics.title: Post-training
topics.about: Supervised tuning, preference tuning, LoRA and reinforcement learning on a trained model.

questions.title: When should you use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) versus fine-tuning, and how do you decide between them?
questions.answer: Use RAG when the model needs knowledge, especially facts that change often, because you can update documents without retraining. RAG also gives you citations and lets you enforce access controls at retrieval time. Use fine-tuning when you need to change behaviour, such as tone, output format, or a specialised task. Fine-tuned knowledge goes stale and needs retraining. Many production systems combine both: fine-tuning for behaviour and RAG for current facts.

questions.title: How does LoRA work under the hood, and how do you serve multiple LoRA adapters efficiently in production?
questions.answer: LoRA freezes the base model weights and learns each weight update as the product of two small low-rank matrices. Because only those small matrices are trained, the optimizer needs far less memory than full fine-tuning. Adapters can be merged into the base weights so inference has no added latency. To serve many adapters, you keep one shared base model in GPU memory and load or swap adapters per request, which is much cheaper than running a full model copy for each one.

questions.title: How does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) compare to traditional RLHF with PPO?
questions.answer: Traditional RLHF requires several stages: train a reward model on preference data, then optimise the policy with reinforcement learning such as PPO. That process is complex and can be unstable. DPO uses the same preference pairs but derives a direct loss, with an implicit reward defined relative to a reference model. It needs no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop, so it is simpler, more stable, and cheaper to train. You still need high quality preference data, and results depend on the task.

questions.title: How do you engineer high-quality fine-tuning datasets and prevent catastrophic forgetting?
questions.answer: Prioritise quality over quantity: a smaller set of clean, representative, expert-checked examples usually beats a large noisy one. Deduplicate data, remove low quality or contaminated examples, and keep train and test sets strictly separate so scores stay honest. To limit catastrophic forgetting, where new training erodes earlier abilities, mix in a portion of general or previous examples during training. Then evaluate on both the new task and older capabilities to catch regressions.

questions.title: A support bot must answer from a policy manual that changes every week. Fine-tune, or use RAG?
questions.answer: Rule of thumb: RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour. Retrieval keeps facts current and lets answers cite their source. Fine-tuning is good at teaching a format, a tone, a task-specific skill, or shortening prompts, and much less reliable at teaching facts. Many production systems use both: a lightly fine-tuned model that's good at answering from retrieved documents.
options: Fine-tune once, then never update.
Fine-tune every week on the new manual.
Neither: write a longer system prompt with the whole manual.
RAG: put the current policy in the context at query time.

questions.title: What does LoRA train?
questions.answer: For a weight matrix W (d × d), LoRA learns B (d × r) and A (r × d) with r much smaller than d, and uses W + (α/r)·BA in the forward pass. Only A and B get gradients and optimiser state, so memory and checkpoint size drop sharply. The adapter can be merged into W after training, so inference costs nothing extra, or kept separate and swapped per customer.
options: All the weights, at a lower learning rate.
Only the final classification layer.
Two small low-rank matrices per adapted weight matrix. Their product is added to the frozen original weights.
A new set of embeddings for special tokens only.

questions.title: LoRA with rank 16 on one 4,096 × 4,096 projection matrix. How many trainable parameters does that add?
questions.answer: A is 16 × 4,096 and B is 4,096 × 16: 2 × 4,096 × 16 = 131,072 parameters, against 16,777,216 in the matrix itself.

questions.title: As a percentage of that matrix's 16,777,216 parameters, how many does the rank-16 adapter train? (Percent, three decimals.)
questions.answer: 131,072 ÷ 16,777,216 × 100 = 0.781%. Across a whole model, LoRA typically trains 0.1–1% of the parameters. Optimiser state shrinks by the same factor, which is what makes a single-GPU fine-tune possible.

questions.title: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?
questions.answer: QLoRA quantises the frozen base weights to 4-bit NormalFloat, dequantises them on the fly in the forward pass, and backpropagates into bf16 LoRA adapters. Paged optimisers handle memory spikes. A 7B model's base weights take about 3.5 GB instead of 14 GB, so fine-tuning fits on one consumer GPU.
options: It quantises the adapters to 4-bit.
It removes the need for a GPU.
It trains a smaller model and then distils it.
The frozen base model is stored in 4-bit, while the LoRA adapters train in higher precision.

questions.title: You fine-tune on 10,000 examples averaging 1,500 tokens each, for 3 epochs. How many training tokens is that, in millions?
questions.answer: 10,000 × 1,500 × 3 = 45,000,000 = 45 million tokens. It's the number that sets both the cost (hosted fine-tuning is usually priced per training token) and the time (divide by your tokens per second).

questions.title: After fine-tuning on 5,000 legal Q&A pairs, the model is great at legal questions but worse at general instructions and basic maths. What happened, and what helps?
questions.answer: Training only on one narrow distribution overwrites general behaviour. Mitigations: replay (mix in 10–30% general instruction data), a smaller learning rate and fewer epochs, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, which change fewer weights, and an eval suite that includes general tasks, so you notice the regression before shipping.
options: Use a higher learning rate to finish faster.
The model was too small.
Catastrophic forgetting. Mix general instruction data back in, lower the learning rate or epochs, or use LoRA.
The legal data must contain wrong maths.

questions.title: Validation loss on your fine-tuning data keeps going down, but when people try the model, its answers are getting worse. What's the likely gap?
questions.answer: Validation loss uses teacher forcing: the model always sees the correct previous tokens. At inference it builds on its own outputs, and small errors compound. Lower loss can also come from learning the references' phrasing, without getting better at the task. Evaluate generated outputs on held-out prompts, with task metrics, human review, or a validated judge, and choose checkpoints by that.
options: The tokenizer changed.
Validation loss scores the next token on reference answers, which isn't the same as the quality of the model's own generated answers. Evaluate on generated outputs.
The model needs more epochs.
The validation set is too small.

questions.title: A fine-tuned chat model works in your training notebook but produces rambling text when served. What do you check first?
questions.answer: Chat models learn a precise format: role markers, special tokens, and an end-of-turn token. If the server's template differs, even by a missing end-of-turn token or a different system-prompt marker, the model sees an unfamiliar format and doesn't know where its turn ends. Use the tokenizer's chat template in training and serving, and test the served endpoint with a prompt from the training set.
options: That the server formats prompts with exactly the chat template and special tokens used in training.
The learning rate.
The GPU type.
Temperature.

questions.title: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?
questions.answer: RLHF with PPO trains a reward model on preference pairs, then optimises the policy with reinforcement learning against it, with a KL penalty to stay near the reference model: complex and finicky. DPO shows the same KL-constrained objective can be optimised directly, by raising the likelihood of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one (against the reference model). It's simpler and more stable, and widely used.
options: DPO only works for classification tasks.
DPO trains a bigger reward model.
DPO learns directly from preference pairs with a classification-style loss, with no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop.
DPO needs no preference data.

questions.title: You can fine-tune on 1,000 examples carefully written by experts, or on 100,000 scraped Q&A pairs of mixed quality. For teaching an instruction-following style, which is usually better?
questions.answer: For alignment-style tuning, the model already has the knowledge from pre-training. Fine-tuning mostly teaches the format and the manners. A small set of consistent, high-quality examples does that well, while large noisy sets teach inconsistency and errors. For teaching a genuinely new skill, you need more data, and quality still matters.
options: The 100,000 pairs, because more data always wins.
The 1,000 expert examples. For style and format, quality and consistency matter more than volume.
Neither. Fine-tuning can't change style.
Mix them equally.

questions.title: You have a small pretrained transformer and 800 labelled text messages, half of them spam. You need a binary classifier by tomorrow. Do you train only a new classification head, or do you update every weight? Defend the choice.
questions.answer: Swap the language-model head for a two-class linear layer and start with the body frozen. Head-only training is fast, costs almost no memory, and rarely overfits on this little data. Unfreeze the body only when the frozen run leaves accuracy on the table and the domain is far from the pretraining text.
followUps: Level 1: What does requires_grad=False on the body do to the optimizer? Expected: the optimizer receives only the head parameters, so the body weights never change.

Level 2: Why mean pooling and not the last hidden state? Expected: mean pooling with the mask is stable across lengths and needs no special token; last-token pooling suits decoder models that saw that pattern.
Level 2: Why keep the test split stratified? Expected: a known class balance lets you read precision and recall as honest numbers.

Level 3: The full update scores lower than the frozen run on this data. What happened? Expected: the body overfit the small set and lost pretrained structure; lower the body learning rate, unfreeze fewer blocks, or stay with the head.
wrongAnswers: "Train a fresh classifier from scratch, the model is small anyway." The pretrained body already encodes word identity, position and co-occurrence; a new model from 800 examples throws that away.

"Updating every weight is always more accurate, so do it." On 800 examples it lands within a couple of points of the frozen run and costs about three times the training time, with a real risk of overfitting.
"Report accuracy, the classes are balanced." Precision and recall tell you which error you make, and the confusion matrix shows the counts behind the score.

questions.title: An attention projection in your model is a square matrix with 4,096 rows and 4,096 columns. You add a LoRA adapter of rank 16 to it. How many values does the adapter train, and what share of the frozen matrix is that? Then say what changes when you double the rank.
questions.answer: The adapter is two thin matrices: A with 16 rows and 4,096 columns, and B with 4,096 rows and 16 columns. Each holds 65,536 values, so the adapter trains 131,072 parameters. The frozen matrix holds 16,777,216, so the adapter is 0.78 percent of it. A doubled rank doubles the adapter, because its size is linear in the rank.
followUps: Level 1: Why does B start at zero? Expected: the product B A is then zero, so the model starts from its original behavior and learns the change step by step.

Level 2: How does the count change for a matrix that is not square? Expected: A is r by the input width and B is the output height by r, so the count is r times the sum of the two sides; still linear in the rank.
Level 2: At what rank does the memory advantage start to fade? Expected: the lesson puts the point of diminishing returns past 64, where quality stops improving and the adapters stop being small.

Level 3: After training, how do you remove the cost of the second matrix product at inference? Expected: merge, compute W plus alpha over r times B A once, and save a full matrix of the original size.
wrongAnswers: "The adapter trains r squared parameters." It trains r times the sum of the two matrix sides; r squared would be a tiny block, not the two thin matrices.
"Doubling the rank doubles the quality." The gain flattens fast; the lesson finds rank 16 within about one point of full fine-tuning and little gain past 64.
"Alpha adds parameters." Alpha is a fixed scalar on the adapter output; it changes the effective step size, not the count.

questions.title: Your team has a budget to collect SFT data for a new assistant. One plan buys one million scraped question-answer pairs from the web. The other plan pays skilled writers for a much smaller set. Which plan do you pick, and how do you argue it?
questions.answer: Pick the smaller set from skilled writers. SFT teaches a behavior pattern, not new facts, so a few thousand to a few tens of thousands of clean examples are enough. The lesson's reference points are about 27,000 curated examples for the first SFT stage of a major open chat model, and 52,000 generated pairs that cost about 600 dollars and produced a usable assistant. Noise in scraped pairs is learned as behavior at the same weight as the good examples.
followUps: Level 1: What does SFT not teach the model? Expected: new facts; those come from pretraining, and SFT teaches the response pattern.

Level 2: How do you detect that a dataset teaches bad behavior before you train? Expected: sample and read it, score answer length and vocabulary diversity, check the ratio of instruction to answer, and drop the tail.

Level 2: After SFT the model answers well but lost some coding ability. What in the data plan addresses that? Expected: mix a few percent of raw pretraining text into the SFT batches and keep the run short.

Level 3: The writers produce long, detailed answers for everything. What is the risk? Expected: the model learns that length is the pattern, and later preference tuning can amplify it into verbosity; match the answer length to the product.
wrongAnswers: "More data always wins in machine learning." SFT learns a format on a model that already knows the content; a million noisy targets teach noise as behavior.
"Generated data is worthless, only human writing counts." The 52,000 generated pairs in the lesson produced a usable assistant for about 600 dollars; the issue is quality control, not the source.
"Train longer on the small set to make up for its size." More than three epochs on a small set leads to memorization, and the model repeats training examples word for word.

questions.title: You fine-tune a base model so that it follows instructions. A teammate's training loop computes cross-entropy on every token of each sequence, the instruction tokens included. Is that a problem? What do you change, and why?
questions.answer: Yes. Count the loss only on the answer tokens. The user always provides the instruction at inference time, so a gradient on it teaches the model to write questions, not to answer them. Set the label of every instruction position, every padding position and the answer boundary token to the ignore index, so they add no loss and no gradient.
followUps: Level 1: Which positions get the ignore index? Expected: the instruction, the padding, and the boundary token itself; the model predicts what follows the boundary, not the boundary.
Level 2: Why does the model still need the instruction in the forward pass? Expected: the answer is conditioned on it through attention; the mask removes its loss, not its context.
Level 2: How do you check the mask before a long run? Expected: print the tokens next to the labels for one example and confirm that only answer positions carry real labels, after the shift.

Level 3: A base model given a question keeps writing more questions. What does SFT change, and what does it not change? Expected: it teaches the conversation pattern, so the model answers after the response marker; it adds no facts, those come from pretraining.
wrongAnswers: "The loss on the instruction is extra signal, so keep it." It trains the model to generate instructions, and it shrinks the share of the gradient that comes from the answer.
"Divide the masked loss by the sequence length." A long instruction then dilutes the answer signal; divide by the number of answer tokens.
"Keep the loss on the response marker, so the model learns to emit it." The marker is part of the prompt template; the prompt provides it, and the model predicts what follows it.

questions.title: A GRPO run trains a small model on grade-school math with a binary reward. The reward per step jumps around, and the trend over many steps looks flat. The team wants to raise the learning rate. What do you read first, and what do you suspect?
questions.answer: Read the group statistics before you touch the learning rate. GRPO scores each answer against the mean of its group, so a group where every answer is right or every answer is wrong has a zero advantage for every member and teaches nothing. In the manual's runs, 10 of the 32 groups in the first step had one reward for all 8 answers, and about half of the groups did over 12 steps. If most groups are like that, the signal is thin, and the fix is the prompt mix or the dynamic sampling filter, not a bigger step.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a group with one reward give a zero advantage? Expected: GRPO subtracts the group mean and divides by the group standard deviation; equal rewards give a zero numerator for every answer.
Level 2: What else makes a math reward score 0 besides a wrong answer? Expected: an answer cut at the length limit before its final line; read the cut share next to the reward.

Level 3: The filter run shows a higher mean reward than the baseline. How do you decide if it learned more? Expected: compare the unfiltered reward, account for the bias from stopped long answers, and run a second seed against the spread of the baseline seeds.

Level 3: Your reward returns fractions, and a group with identical rewards still shows small nonzero advantages. Why? Expected: float32 rounding of the group mean leaves a remainder that the division by a near-zero standard deviation blows up; round rewards to values a float32 holds exactly.
wrongAnswers: "Raise the learning rate; the reward is flat because the steps are small." The signal is thin because many groups carry no advantage; a larger step amplifies noise and raises the gradient norm.
"Sample more answers per prompt to get a spread." In the manual's runs, 4, 8 and 16 answers per prompt gave reward gains inside one seed range, and more answers made each rollout longer.
"Read the reward of the last step." One step moves by up to a fifth of the scale; read the mean over five or more steps.

questions.title: You need a reward model for a helpfulness objective. A product manager suggests asking raters to score each answer from one to ten and regressing on the scores. Why do most pipelines collect pairwise comparisons instead, and what loss do you train with?
questions.answer: People are poor at absolute scores and good at relative judgments, so pipelines show two answers to one prompt and ask which is better. The reward model is the SFT model with its vocabulary head replaced by a scalar head. It trains with the Bradley-Terry loss, the negative log of the sigmoid of the reward difference between the preferred and the rejected answer. The difference in reward becomes a log-odds of preference, which turns many relative judgments into one consistent scale.
followUps: Level 2: Why read the last token's hidden state and not a mean over positions? Expected: with a causal mask the last position has attended to the whole sequence, so it holds the most complete summary; mean pooling is an alternative worth a test.

Level 2: Your reward model ranks 90 percent of the test pairs right. Good news? Expected: suspicious; with rater agreement near 73 percent, that score suggests a leak or a shortcut such as length, so check what the model keys on.

Level 3: How do you turn comparisons into a reward for several criteria at once? Expected: one reward model per criterion, such as helpfulness and safety, combined with weights; a single model learns a blur of the criteria.

Level 4: Why does the reward model need protection from the policy later? Expected: it saw only in-distribution answers; a policy under optimization moves off that distribution and finds answers that score high for the wrong reasons, which is why the RL stage carries a KL penalty.
wrongAnswers: "Regress on a one-to-ten score; it is more information per label." Absolute scores drift between raters and sessions; a pairwise judgment is cheap and consistent, and the Bradley-Terry fit recovers a scale from it.
"72 percent accuracy means the reward model is broken." The raters agreed only about 73 percent of the time; the model is near the agreement of its labels.
"Use a small reward model to save compute." A reward model that cannot represent the policy's outputs gives a noisy signal, and the policy exploits its blind spots.

questions.title: Your rater budget is gone. A colleague proposes to replace the human labelers with a model that reads a short list of principles and ranks the pairs, and to run the same RLHF pipeline on those labels. Is this just a cheaper RLHF? What changes?
questions.answer: It is the constitutional recipe, and it changes the failure modes rather than removing them. Phase one has the model critique and revise its own answers against sampled principles and trains on the revisions; phase two trains a reward model on pairs ranked by a feedback model and runs the usual RL stage. Rater psychology stops being the bias, and the reading of the principle set becomes the bias, applied uniformly over the whole dataset. Sycophancy toward a rater drops, and the proxy problem stays.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the recipe sample one principle per critique instead of giving the model the whole list? Expected: a focused critique is more specific and more useful as a training target; the list as a whole is covered over many samples.
Level 2: Which parts of the pipeline change and which stay? Expected: the label source and the SFT targets change; the reward model, the RL stage and the KL penalty stay.

Level 3: Name a sycophancy-like failure that still occurs with an AI labeler, and a check for it. Expected: the feedback model can prefer answers that quote the principles without following them; rate a held-out set with people and compare the two rankings.

Level 4: How do you argue for a priority order among principles? Expected: conflicts between principles need a resolution rule; a tiered order resolves them top-down, from catastrophic harm to platform rules to general ethics to helpfulness.
wrongAnswers: "The labels are free now, so collect ten times more pairs." More pairs with the same uniform bias make the bias stronger, not weaker; the volume gain does not fix the proxy.
"An AI labeler removes human bias from alignment." It replaces rater bias with principle-interpretation bias; the principles and the labeler's reading of them are now the proxy.

"This is only a safety trick; it does not touch helpfulness." The original work reports about the same helpfulness as RLHF with comparable data, and the same critique loop can target any principle you write.

questions.title: You have one GPU with 24 GB of memory and want to fine-tune a 7B model on your own instruction data. Walk me through the memory for a full update, for LoRA and for QLoRA, and say what makes the last one fit.
questions.answer: A full update of a 7B model needs about 56 GB: the weights in half precision, the gradients, and two optimizer states per parameter, all in half precision. LoRA keeps the half-precision weights but trains only small adapters, so the gradients and optimizer states shrink and the run takes about 18 GB. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit, about 3.5 GB of weights, and trains the adapters in half precision, so the run takes about 6 GB and leaves room for activations on a 24 GB card.
followUps: Level 2: Why does LoRA cut training memory so much more than it cuts weight memory? Expected: the gradients and the two optimizer states exist only for the adapter parameters, which are a fraction of a percent of the model.

Level 2: The adapters train in half precision while the base is 4-bit. Where does the forward pass compute? Expected: the base weights are dequantized block by block to the compute dtype for each matrix product, and the adapter path runs in half precision.

Level 3: When would you still pay for the full update? Expected: when the task needs changes that a low-rank update cannot express, when you have the data and the GPUs, or when the eval shows a gap that a higher rank does not close.
Level 3: How do you serve several QLoRA fine-tunes from one base? Expected: keep the adapters separate and load them on top of one base copy; merge only when you ship a single specialized model.
wrongAnswers: "Quantize the whole model to 4-bit and fine-tune it directly." Gradients and optimizer states still need higher precision; the base stays frozen in 4-bit, and only the adapters train.
"QLoRA halves the quality." The lesson's table shows a loss of a fraction of a point at rank 16 and parity at rank 64.
"Load the base in 8-bit with LoRA; it is the same thing." Eight-bit weights take twice the memory of NF4, and the double quantization and paged optimizers are what make the 6 GB figure.

questions.title: A colleague copies the pretraining configuration into an SFT run: the same peak learning rate, the same warmup, three epochs over 27,000 examples. The loss on the SFT set drops fast and everyone is happy. What do you expect to see when you test the model, and what do you change?
questions.answer: Expect catastrophic forgetting: the model answers in the training format, but its loss on raw text rises and it gets worse at code, math and anything outside the set. Pretraining used a peak rate about fifteen times higher than the SFT value in the lesson, 3e-4 against 2e-5. Cut the rate into the 1e-5 to 5e-5 range, keep one to three epochs, and track raw-text loss next to the SFT loss.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a rate that works for pretraining destroy an SFT run? Expected: pretraining starts from noise and averages over trillions of tokens; SFT starts from a working model and a small set, so each large step overwrites features that the set does not cover.
Level 2: How many epochs, and how do you decide? Expected: one to three; stop when the held-out instruction loss stops improving and the raw-text loss has not risen past the budget.

Level 3: The raw-text loss rose by a quarter, but the product team likes the answers. Ship it? Expected: not as it is; the model lost general ability that users will hit; rerun with a lower rate or a pretraining mix and compare on an eval outside the set.

Level 3: How does LoRA change this picture? Expected: the base weights stay frozen, so the damage is bounded to the adapter and a merge is reversible; the adapter also tolerates a higher rate than a full update.
wrongAnswers: "The SFT loss dropped, so the run worked." The loss on the set says nothing about what the model forgot; measure the raw-text loss and an eval outside the set.
"Warm up for 2,000 steps, like pretraining." The SFT set gives few steps in total; the lesson uses 0 to 100 warmup steps.
"Use a higher rate to finish faster, the data is small." A high rate on a small set overfits and overwrites pretrained knowledge; small data needs smaller steps, not larger ones.

questions.title: DPO is often described as RLHF without a reward model. Walk me through where the reward went. Start from the RLHF objective with its KL term and end at the loss you would implement.
questions.answer: The penalized objective has a closed-form optimum: the optimal policy equals the reference policy times the exponential of reward over beta, normalized per prompt. Invert it and the reward equals beta times the log ratio of policy to reference, plus a term that depends on the prompt alone. Put that reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability and the prompt-only term cancels, because both answers share the prompt. What is left is a loss in the policy's own log-probabilities: minus the log sigmoid of beta times the difference of the two log ratios.
followUps: Level 2: Why must the policy start as a copy of the reference? Expected: the derivation treats the optimum as the reference plus a learned shift, and a copy makes every implicit reward start at zero.
Level 2: What does a positive log ratio mean? Expected: the policy now gives that answer a higher probability than the reference does.

Level 3: Why does the derivation need both answers to share one prompt? Expected: the partition term depends on the prompt only; with different prompts it would not cancel, and the implicit rewards would not be comparable.

Level 4: Which assumptions of the derivation fail in practice? Expected: that the optimum is reachable, that the pairs are in-distribution for the reference, and that the reference is the true anchor; each later method in the family repairs one of them.
wrongAnswers: "DPO has no reference model, that is the point." It removes the reward model and PPO; the frozen reference stays in the loss, and the methods that drop it are a later variant.
"DPO maximizes the probability of the chosen answer." It maximizes the margin of two log ratios; the chosen absolute probability can fall as long as the rejected falls faster.
"Beta is a learning rate." Beta scales the implicit reward and sets how far the policy may move from the reference; the optimizer step size is a separate setting.

questions.title: In the PPO stage of RLHF, the objective subtracts a KL term between the policy and a frozen copy of the SFT model. A new hire asks why the pipeline keeps a second copy of the model in memory for that one term. Explain the failure it prevents and how you tune its coefficient.
questions.answer: The reward model was trained on answers that look like SFT output. Without the term, PPO moves the policy into regions the reward model never saw and finds strings that score high but that people dislike. The term charges the policy for leaving the SFT distribution, so it is a regularizer, not a hard constraint. Tune beta from the measured KL: too low and the reward climbs together with the KL, too high and the policy barely moves from SFT.
followUps: Level 2: Why is the term a regularizer and not a trust region? Expected: it adds a cost that grows with the distance; nothing stops the policy from paying it, so a large reward can still buy a large move.

Level 2: What two things must be true of the reference model in code? Expected: its weights never receive gradients, and it never shares parameters with the policy; a shared module silently removes the anchor.

Level 3: The reward rises, the KL rises, and human ratings stay flat. Which knob first? Expected: raise beta or stop early; then widen the reward model's training data so that the exploited region is covered.

Level 3: After RLHF the model scores lower on reading comprehension benchmarks. Is that the KL's job? Expected: no; that is the alignment tax, addressed by a pretraining log-likelihood term in the objective, as the PPO-ptx variant does.
wrongAnswers: "Drop the reference model to save memory and clip the PPO ratio harder." The clip bounds one update; it does not bound the drift over many updates, which is what the KL does.
"Set beta high to be safe." A high beta pins the policy to SFT, and the run buys nothing for its compute.
"KL is a safety filter for harmful text." It measures distance from the SFT distribution and knows nothing about content; a safe reference is what makes it useful.

questions.title: You left a one-GPU RL training run alone for an hour. When you come back, the GPU is idle, the process is still alive, and the log file has grown to more than a hundred megabytes. Nothing reports a failure. What happened, how do you confirm it, and what do you put in place so that it cannot happen again?
questions.answer: The rollout engine died and the trainer never noticed. The engine failed during startup, and the rollout client kept sending requests to it, got a 503 from the router on each one, and retried. The failed run in the manual wrote 200,533 such error lines in 63 minutes and never reported a failure. Confirm it by counting the error lines per minute and by reading the engine lines above the first error, then run every unattended job with a watchdog that stops the container when the errors do not stop.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the trainer not fail when the engine is gone? Expected: the rollout client treats the 503 as a transient error and retries each request; nothing in the loop limits the retries or the idle time.

Level 2: Where do you look for the reason the engine died? Expected: the engine lines above the first 503 in the same log; in the manual's case an attention backend assertion for a GPU outside its supported range.

Level 3: Why did the manual raise the watchdog from six checks to ten? Expected: a replay on a healthy run showed bursts 45 seconds apart that six checks mistook for a death; ten checks never fired on a healthy run and still caught a dead engine in about five minutes.

Level 3: What does the watchdog miss, and what do you add for it? Expected: a run that hangs with few errors, such as a reward import failure; add a check that the first step line appears within a time limit.
wrongAnswers: "Kill the run as soon as a 503 appears." A busy engine with hundreds of open requests writes bursts of these errors and recovers; the manual's busy run finished all its steps.
"Raise the client retry limit so the run survives." Retries are why the dead run lived for an hour; the engine will not come back by itself, and the GPU sits idle.
"The trainer crashed; look at the trainer lines." The trainer was alive and logging errors; the cause is in the engine startup lines above the first error.

questions.title: A team of four engineers with eight GPUs has about 20,000 preference pairs for a customer support assistant and wants it aligned in three weeks. One engineer wants the full RLHF stack with a reward model and PPO. Another wants DPO. Which do you pick, and under what conditions would you reverse the choice?
questions.answer: Pick DPO. With tens of thousands of pairs it matches or beats the full stack, it trains one model against a frozen reference in a supervised loop, it needs about a third of the compute, and each experiment takes hours instead of days. Reverse the choice when the signal has several dimensions and needs a learned reward you can inspect and reuse, when you want an online loop that rates fresh samples, or when DPO plateaus on your eval.
followUps: Level 3: What does the DPO run still need from the RLHF recipe? Expected: an SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, a held-out eval, and a beta choice that plays the role of the KL coefficient.

Level 3: The pairs come from an older model's outputs. Does that matter for DPO? Expected: yes; pairs that are rare under the reference produce arbitrary implicit rewards, so sample the pairs from the SFT model or filter them by reference likelihood.

Level 4: How would you turn the three weeks into an iterative loop without PPO? Expected: run DPO, generate from the new policy, collect preferences on those samples, run DPO again; the lesson's exercise calls this iterative DPO.

Level 4: Which failure mode do both methods share? Expected: over-optimization of a proxy, the reward model in one case and the ratio to the reference in the other; both need a blind eval and early stopping.
wrongAnswers: "RLHF is the proven path, so start there." The full stack is fragile to tune and needs three training loops; the lesson's practical guidance starts with DPO and switches only on a plateau.
"DPO needs no SFT stage." It needs a reference policy, and that reference is the SFT checkpoint; the single-stage methods are different losses.
"DPO has no hyperparameters to worry about." Beta decides how far the policy moves from the reference, and the lesson's sweep shows degenerate answers at a small value and no learning at a large one.

questions.title: Four teams bring you four datasets. One has thumbs-up and thumbs-down clicks on single answers. One has paired comparisons whose preferred answers are mostly twice the length of the rejected ones. One has no SFT checkpoint and wants a single training stage from the base model. One has pairs where some preferences are near coin flips and others are unanimous. Which preference loss do you recommend to each team, and why?
questions.answer: The clicks team gets the prospect-theory loss that works on single labels. The length-skewed team gets the reference-free loss that normalizes by length and adds a margin, so a longer winner does not win by its token count. The team without an SFT stage gets the odds-ratio loss, which adds a preference term to the SFT likelihood and trains from the base in one pass; the team with mixed preference strengths gets the identity-mapping loss, whose margin is bounded. Each one repairs one assumption that plain DPO makes.
followUps: Level 3: The clicks team also has a small paired set. Combine them? Expected: yes; train with the unpaired loss on the clicks and validate on the pairs, or weight the two losses; the pairs are the cleaner signal for the eval.

Level 3: Why does removing the reference save memory, and what does it cost? Expected: one model in memory instead of two; the cost is no anchor, so the policy can drift, and the margin term and early stopping carry that job.

Level 4: A team runs DPO and watches the probability of its chosen answers drop while the margin grows. Which row applies, and why is it not a tuning problem? Expected: the chosen-preserving variant; the gradient of plain DPO cares only about the difference, so no beta fixes the direction.

Level 4: How do you argue to a skeptic that these losses still over-optimize? Expected: the published curves of gold reward against KL for direct methods show the same peak and collapse as reward-model pipelines; the implicit reward queries out-of-distribution samples, and KL regularization does not stabilize it.
wrongAnswers: "Convert the clicks into pairs by matching a good and a bad answer for the same prompt." It keeps only prompts with both labels and invents comparisons the raters never made; the unpaired loss uses the labels as they are.
"Truncate the long winners so that the pairs are balanced." That destroys the answers people preferred; the fix is in the loss normalization, not in the data.
"Use DPO everywhere and tune beta per team." Beta cannot create pairs, remove a reference, bound a gap or supply an SFT stage; each of those is a different loss.

questions.title: During a DPO run the loss falls and the reward margin that the trainer logs grows every epoch. Yet the model's samples get shorter and less fluent, and the policy now gives the chosen training answers a lower probability than they had under the reference. Explain the mechanism and what you change.
questions.answer: The DPO loss cares only about the difference of two log ratios. It can lower the probability of the chosen answer as long as the rejected answer falls faster, and the margin still grows. This is the degraded chosen response failure: the policy moves probability mass away from both training answers, often toward short degenerate outputs. Log the absolute chosen log-probability, add a penalty on downward moves of the chosen term as the behavior-preserving variant does or switch to a loss with a bounded margin, and keep a generation eval next to the margin.
followUps: Level 3: Why does length matter in this failure? Expected: a long rejected answer has a more negative total log-probability by construction, so suppressing it is cheap and the gap grows for the wrong reason; length normalization removes that incentive.

Level 3: How does a reference-free, length-normalized loss change the picture? Expected: it scores the average log-probability per token with a margin, which removes the length bias and the reference, but it also removes the anchor, so drift needs its own guard.

Level 4: Which variant do you pick when preference strengths vary widely across pairs? Expected: the bounded one; it keeps the gap proportional to the preference, so strong pairs do not saturate the loss and weak pairs do not blow up.
Level 4: Does a lower beta help here? Expected: no; a lower beta lets the policy move further from the reference for the same margin, which makes the degradation worse.
wrongAnswers: "The margin grows, so training works; the samples are a decoding problem." The margin can grow while both answers lose probability; the generation eval is the objective, not the margin.
"Raise beta until the samples recover." A higher beta slows the drift but does not change the direction of the gradient on the chosen term; the penalty on that term does.
"Train more epochs; the chosen probability will come back." The loss has no term that rewards a higher chosen probability on its own, so more epochs push further the same way.

questions.title: Your RL run shows a steady disagreement between trainer and rollout engine on the probability of each sampled token. One engineer wants to turn on a capped importance weighting right away. Another says it is a kernel artifact and should be ignored. Lay out how you decide, and what you would try first.
questions.answer: Match the method to the source of the gap. Five sources exist: tokens re-encoded between turns, expert routing on a mixture model, a sampler that cuts the vocabulary, numeric differences between kernels or precisions, and stale samples. The first three have corrections that remove the cause; try those first, because a reweighting such as truncated importance sampling leaves the gap in place and adds variance to the gradient. A flat gap on a dense model with plain sampling is the kernel floor of that setup; measure it, keep it inside your range, and reweight only what remains after the causes are gone.
followUps: Level 3: Why does a reweighting add variance? Expected: tokens with a large ratio get a large weight, so a few tokens dominate the update; the cap limits that, but does not remove it.

Level 3: Replay needs both a top-k and a top-p set. Why is the top-k needed? Expected: the framework requires a positive top-k for replay, so a run with top-p alone changes the sampler without replaying the kept set.

Level 4: FP16 on the engine and BF16 on the trainer did not close the gap. Why? Expected: each side's own rounding sets a floor; the gap closes only when both sides round the same way, so the precision must match on both sides.

Level 4: When is the bit-exact mode the right answer, and when is it not available? Expected: when you need a gap of zero and your model and GPU are in its contract; it pins one attention kernel and batch-invariant operations for specific dense models on one GPU generation, and refuses the rest.
wrongAnswers: "Turn on importance sampling first; it is cheap." It leaves every cause in place, adds variance, and hides a setup error that the step-0 check would show.
"The gap is a kernel artifact, so it never matters." The sampler part was measurable and removable, and a gap that grows after a change is a cause you added.
"Deterministic inference is a correction method." It makes the engine repeat itself and leaves the gap where it was; the manual's four runs show the same gap with it on and off.

questions.title: You start a GRPO run with a new model checkpoint. At step 0, the metric that compares the trainer's log-probabilities with the rollout engine's reads several times higher than on your earlier runs with the same model family. A colleague suggests turning on the engine's deterministic mode to close it. What do you do?
questions.answer: Stop the run before it trains on wrong numbers. At step 0 both sides hold the same weights, so a value far above your healthy range means the two sides do not compute the same model: a wrong checkpoint path on one side, or a format that one side reads differently. Deterministic inference does not help; in the manual's runs it left the gap unchanged at about 0.015 and made the engine repeat itself, which is a different property. Fix the setup, then compare the step-0 value with the range of your healthy runs.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the gap never zero in a normal run? Expected: the two sides add the same numbers in a different order, with different kernels; across many layers and a large vocabulary the rounding adds up.
Level 3: What does the deterministic mode buy, then? Expected: the same rollout for the same seed, which is what you need to test a reward function on identical samples.

Level 4: Which levers move the floor of the gap itself? Expected: the precision on both sides, the tensor-parallel size of the engine, and kernels that add in one fixed order; each costs speed or work.

Level 4: The gap is fine at step 0 and grows step after step. What is different from the step-0 failure? Expected: the weights diverge after updates, so the weight update path is the suspect, not the checkpoint; read the update logs and run the weight equality check.
wrongAnswers: "Turn on deterministic inference to close the gap." The manual's four runs show the same gap with and without it; it makes the engine repeat itself and costs rollout time.

"A gap is normal; keep training and watch the reward." A step-0 value several times the healthy range means the trainer scores a different model than the one that sampled, so the run trains on wrong numbers from the first update.
"Add an importance-sampling correction." A reweighting hides a gap that comes from a setup error; remove the cause first.

questions.title: Four days into a PPO run, the mean score from the reward model keeps climbing. A blind human rating of samples from each checkpoint is flat, and the last two checkpoints read slightly worse. The team wants to keep training because the curve looks great. What do you say?
questions.answer: Stop, and treat it as reward hacking. The policy has found outputs that the reward model scores high but people do not prefer, because the reward model is a finite proxy with blind spots. Read the KL to the reference and the length and format of recent samples; a KL that climbs with the reward and answers that grow longer or more formulaic confirm it. Roll back to the checkpoint where the human rating peaked, raise the KL coefficient or stop earlier, and widen the reward model's training data to cover what the policy exploited.
followUps: Level 3: How do you tell reward hacking from a reward model that is right and raters who are wrong? Expected: read the samples; if people consistently dislike what scores high, the proxy is wrong, because the raters define the objective.

Level 3: The reward model is small to save compute. Does that matter here? Expected: yes; a reward model that cannot represent the policy's outputs has more blind spots, and the lessons warn against one smaller than the policy.

Level 4: You switch to DPO to get rid of the reward model. Does the problem go away? Expected: no; the implicit reward can be over-optimized the same way, with the same peak-and-collapse curve, so the blind eval and early stopping stay.

Level 4: Design a guard that stops a run on its own. Expected: a held-out human or trusted-judge eval on a fixed prompt set at each checkpoint, a KL budget, and a stop rule for an eval that falls while the reward rises.
wrongAnswers: "The human raters are noisy; trust the reward model." The reward model was fit to those raters; when they disagree with it on new samples, the model is extrapolating wrong.
"Lower beta so the policy can find even better answers." A lower beta lets the policy move further from the distribution the reward model knows, which is the cause of the problem.
"Keep training; the human eval will catch up." The lessons describe a plateau or a decline in human ratings while the reward climbs; more steps make the exploit stronger.

questions.title: Take-home. The RL framework you use scores each sampled answer with a reward function that you swap in by import path. Write a reward for a task with a numeric final answer, write a test plan for it, and explain how you would prove that your reward does not break the GRPO advantages before a long run. Keep the function and the plan short enough to read in five minutes.
questions.answer: Write an async function that receives the run arguments and one sample, extracts the last number from the answer and from the label, and returns 1.0 for a match and 0.0 otherwise, comparing as values so that 142 never matches 42. Test it on ten answers you scored by hand, with a correct one, a wrong one, an empty one and one cut at the length limit, because a reward that crashes on an empty answer stops the rollout of the whole step. Then check the advantages: a group where every answer gets the same reward must get an advantage of 0 for every member, and a fractional reward can fail that through float32 rounding.
followUps: Level 3: Why compare the numbers as values and not as strings? Expected: so that a trailing zero or a comma does not fail a right answer, and so that 142 does not match 42 by substring.

Level 3: The task has a free-text answer. What changes? Expected: the extraction; use a built-in overlap or multiple-choice scorer when one fits, because it is already tested, and keep the same ten-answer test plan.

Level 4: Which built-in reward gives minus one for a wrong answer, and what does that change downstream? Expected: the DAPO-style reward returns a dict with the score, so it needs the reward key flag; the sign changes the mean, not the zero-advantage property of a two-valued reward.

Level 4: How would you test a reward change without new rollouts? Expected: save the rollout samples of one run and replay them with the trainer alone, so that every candidate reward scores the same samples.
wrongAnswers: "Write a plain function; the flag help shows one." The framework awaits the result, so a plain function fails at the first call; write it as an async function.

"Return any float between 0 and 1 for partial credit; GRPO handles it." Fractions that float32 cannot hold exactly give groups of equal rewards a nonzero advantage; round to exact values and test such a group.
"Skip the empty-answer case; the model always writes something." A cut or empty answer reaches the reward every step, and a crash there stops the whole rollout.

questions.title: An engineer shows you two RL training runs. The new one, with a changed offload setting, finished its rollouts twelve percent faster and ended with a reward a few hundredths higher than the old one. They want to ship the change as the new default. Design the review: what do you ask for before you trust either number?
questions.answer: Ask for the spread of the baseline before you read the change. In the manual's three baseline seeds the final reward ranged from 0.736 to 0.766, so a gain of a few hundredths on one seed is inside the noise. Then ask what else differed: the manual's first offload pair also changed the engine memory fraction and compared different step numbers, and its twelve percent shrank to one to three percent in a same-day pair that changed one setting. Require two seeds, one change per run, the same step numbers, and times from steps that no thermal pause touched.
followUps: Level 3: Why compare against the spread of several baseline seeds and not against the best baseline? Expected: the best baseline is a lucky draw; the spread is the noise floor, and a change must clear it.

Level 3: The new run has no clean steps, because every rollout overlapped a pause. What can you still report? Expected: take the pause time out of each step and say so, as the manual did for one run, and mark the result as unconfirmed.

Level 4: How do you test a loss or reward change without paying for new rollouts? Expected: save the rollout samples of one run and replay them with the trainer alone; every replay sees the same samples, so a difference comes from the change.

Level 4: Two seeds show a gain outside the spread, but the step-0 gap moved too. What next? Expected: the change touched the setup, not only the setting; check that both runs load the same model and sampler before you credit the gain.
wrongAnswers: "Twelve percent is far above noise, ship it." The manual's twelve percent came from two settings changed at once and from different step numbers; one setting alone gave one to three percent.
"Average the rollout time over the whole run." The median follows the answer length, which falls as the model learns; compare the same step numbers.
"One seed is enough when the gain is clear." The three baseline seeds ended 0.03 apart with nothing changed; a few hundredths on one seed sit inside that.

questions.title: A staff engineer argues that moving every alignment run from PPO to direct preference methods ends the reward-hacking problem, because there is no reward model left to hack. Make the counter-argument with the mechanism, and say what survives in your pipeline either way.
questions.answer: Direct methods remove the explicit reward model, not the proxy. The quantity they optimize is the log ratio of policy to reference, an implicit reward that the preference data pins down only where the data has coverage. Under optimization the policy queries that ratio out of distribution, and the published curves of gold reward against KL show the same peak and then collapse as reward-model pipelines, with the KL regularization failing to stabilize it. What survives: a blind held-out eval, early stopping, broader preference data, and ensembles of signals.
followUps: Level 3: What does DPO remove from the PPO stack, concretely? Expected: a reward model to train and host, the PPO loop with its clip and value head, and an explicit KL coefficient; it keeps the frozen reference.

Level 4: Which variant bounds the gap, and what does that buy against this failure? Expected: the identity-mapping loss, whose margin target is one over two beta; it stops a weak preference from producing an unbounded implicit reward, which removes one path to collapse but not the out-of-distribution query.

Level 4: How do you detect over-optimization without a gold reward? Expected: a held-out eval with generation, the absolute chosen log-probability, the KL to the reference, and a comparison across checkpoints; a margin that grows while the eval falls is the signature.

Level 4: Does iterating, with fresh pairs from the current policy each round, help? Expected: yes, it moves the data coverage to where the policy lives, which is what the reference-ratio proxy lacks; it also reintroduces an online loop that needs its own stop rule.
wrongAnswers: "No reward model means nothing to hack." The implicit reward is a function the data pins down only on the pairs; the policy can push it anywhere else.
"The structural KL in DPO is enough regularization." The published curves show the same peak and collapse across KL budgets; beta changes the speed, not the shape.
"Use a smaller beta so the policy learns faster and you can stop earlier." A smaller beta lets the policy move further from the reference per unit of margin, which is the direction of the failure.

questions.title: Take-home. A company wants a support assistant built from an open 8B base model. They have about 50,000 past support conversations with customer ratings, two 24 GB GPUs, and three weeks. Write the post-training plan on one page: the stages, the data for each stage, the settings you start from, what you measure after each stage, and the three failure modes you guard against.
questions.answer: Three stages: first, SFT with QLoRA on the top-rated conversations in one chat template with the loss masked to the assistant turns, at a low learning rate for one to three epochs with a few percent of raw text mixed in, measured by held-out instruction loss, raw-text drift and a sample read. Second, DPO against the SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, on pairs built from high- and low-rated answers to the same prompt with a conservative beta, measured by a blind pairwise eval and the absolute chosen log-probability, not the training margin. Third, a release gate: a fixed prompt set rated blind, a refusal set, and a comparison with the base model on tasks the data never covered. The guards are catastrophic forgetting, length and agreement exploits in the ratings, and over-optimization of the preference proxy.
followUps: Level 3: Why DPO and not a reward model with PPO here? Expected: tens of thousands of pairs, two small GPUs and three weeks fit the DPO regime; a reward model and PPO need three loops and more memory.

Level 4: The ratings are one to five stars on single answers, not pairs. What changes? Expected: build pairs only where one prompt has answers at both ends of the scale, or use the unpaired loss that works on good and bad labels and keep the pairs for the eval.

Level 4: How do you prove that the DPO stage did not degrade the SFT behavior? Expected: the blind pairwise eval against the SFT checkpoint, the forgetting set, and the absolute chosen log-probability; a margin that grows while those fall is a stop signal.

Level 4: What would make you add an RL stage with a verifier? Expected: a part of the task with a checkable answer, such as a correct order number or a passing code snippet, where a binary reward and group-relative advantages give a signal the ratings do not.
wrongAnswers: "Skip SFT and run DPO on the base model." DPO needs a reference that already follows instructions; the single-stage loss is a different method, and the base model's pairs are out of distribution.
"Fully fine-tune the 8B model across both GPUs." A full update of a model this size needs about 56 GB with the optimizer states; two 24 GB cards hold it only with adapters and a 4-bit base.
"Use the star ratings as the reward and run PPO." A regression on absolute scores is the weak label the lessons warn about, and the full stack does not fit the compute or the timeline.

questions.title: You move an RL job from one GPU to a cluster where the rollout engines and the trainers run on separate devices. The team wants generation and training to run at the same time, so that neither side waits for the other. Design the async setup: which knobs matter, what new failure appears, and what you watch in the logs.
questions.answer: Async training lets the engines generate the next batch while the trainer updates, at the price of samples that come from older weights. Two modes exist: one step ahead, where every sample is at most one weight version old with the default update interval, and fully async, where a worker keeps generating and the trainer drains a buffer, so the age depends on how fast the trainer drains it. Set a limit on sample age, decide what happens to running requests at each weight update, and lower the learning rate as you allow older samples. Watch the weight version of each sample, the share of dropped samples, the clip fraction, and the gap between the two sides.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the clip fraction exactly 0 in a synchronous run with one update per rollout? Expected: the policy in the trainer is still the policy that produced the samples, so every ratio is 1 and nothing hits the clip range.

Level 4: Which pause mode do you choose, and what does the wrong one cost? Expected: retract keeps the work of running requests and continues them under new weights, which mixes weight versions inside one answer; abort throws the work away; in place changes the weights under a running request; the fully async mode refuses some of these, so read the flag help of your version.

Level 4: A partial answer started under version 5 and finished under version 7. Where does that show up? Expected: in the gap, because part of its tokens come from older weights than the trainer holds; watch the gap after you turn on partial rollout or raise the staleness limit.

Level 4: How does a dedicated evaluation fleet fit this design? Expected: it loads checkpoint snapshots and never takes part in the training weight updates, so its lag is reported in steps; in the version the manual read it does not combine with rollout fault tolerance.
wrongAnswers: "Run fully async on the single GPU too; it is the same code." With one GPU the two sides still take turns and generation stops during training, so you pay the staleness cost and get no overlap.
"Leave the staleness limit unset, so that no sample is wasted." Unset means no limit; very old samples pull the update in the wrong direction, and the gap grows without a cause in the kernels.
"Keep the learning rate from the synchronous run." The stable rate falls with the age of the samples; raise the update interval and you lower the rate by about the same factor.

topics.title: Inference and serving systems
topics.about: Batching, the KV cache, prefix caching, schedulers and how to measure a serving engine.

questions.title: How do you measure and optimize Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT)?
questions.answer: Time to first token mostly reflects queueing plus the prefill phase that processes the prompt. Time per output token reflects the decode phase, which generates tokens one at a time. Measure them separately, using percentiles and not just averages. To reduce time to first token, shorten prompts and use prompt caching so a shared prefix reuses its KV cache. To reduce time per output token, use efficient batching, quantization, or a smaller model. Streaming tokens as they are generated also makes the response feel faster.
keyPoints: Measure TTFT and output-token time separately using percentiles.
TTFT reflects queueing and prompt prefill.
Shorten prompts and cache shared prefixes for TTFT.
Improve decode with batching, quantization or a smaller model.

questions.title: Why does the KV cache bottleneck LLM serving memory, and how does PagedAttention solve it?
questions.answer: During generation, the model keeps the key and value tensors for every previous token in every layer, so that it does not have to recompute them. This KV cache grows with each token and each concurrent request, which often makes it the main GPU memory limit. Allocating contiguous memory for the maximum length wastes space and causes fragmentation. PagedAttention splits the cache into small fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like virtual memory pages, so more requests fit and throughput rises. It can also share blocks between requests with a common prefix.
keyPoints: KV cache stores prior tokens' keys and values in every layer.
Cache memory grows with tokens and concurrent requests.
Maximum-length contiguous allocations waste memory and fragment it.
PagedAttention allocates blocks on demand and can share prefixes.

questions.title: When a model generates tokens one at a time for a single user, what limits its speed on a GPU?
questions.answer: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel: big matrix multiplications, compute-bound. Decode produces one token per forward pass: for each token the GPU streams every weight through for a few operations each, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound. That's why batching many users together makes decode far more efficient: the weights are read once per step and used for every sequence in the batch.
options: Network latency between the user and the server.
Compute: the GPU's FLOPs.
Memory bandwidth: every new token has to read all the weights from GPU memory.
The tokenizer.
keyPoints: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel.
Large prefill matrix multiplications are compute-bound.
Decode generates one token per pass and is bandwidth-bound.
Batching reuses each weight read across sequences.

questions.title: A 7B model in bf16 (14 GB of weights) runs on a GPU with 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. What's the theoretical maximum decode speed for one sequence? (Tokens per second.)
questions.answer: Each token reads every weight once: 2 × 10¹² bytes/s ÷ 14 × 10⁹ bytes = 143 tokens/s. Real numbers land lower (the KV cache is read too, and kernels don't hit peak bandwidth), but this ceiling is the right first estimate, and it's why 7B models feel fast and 70B ones don't.
keyPoints: Estimate decode speed from memory bandwidth divided by weight bytes.
Use 14 billion weight bytes for the stated model.
Two trillion bytes per second gives about 143 tokens per second.
KV reads and imperfect bandwidth lower real throughput.

questions.title: Same GPU, same model, but quantised to int4 weights (3.5 GB). What's the new ceiling for one sequence?
