questions.answer: 2 × 10¹² ÷ 3.5 × 10⁹ = 571 tokens/s, four times the bf16 figure, because decode speed follows the bytes moved. Quantisation is mainly a memory-bandwidth optimisation for decode, which is why weight-only quantisation is so common in serving.
keyPoints: INT4 reduces the stated weights to 3.5 billion bytes.
Divide two trillion bytes per second by the weight size.
The ceiling is about 571 tokens per second, four times BF16.
Weight-only quantization reduces decode memory traffic.

questions.title: With 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and bf16 (2 bytes), how much KV cache does one token take? (KiB.)
questions.answer: Each layer stores a key and a value for each KV head: 2 × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. With full multi-head attention (32 KV heads) it would be 512 KiB. Grouped-query attention cuts the cache by 4× here.
keyPoints: Store both key and value tensors per KV head.
Multiply 2 by layers, KV heads, head dimension and bytes.
The stated configuration uses 128 KiB per token.
Using 32 KV heads instead gives 512 KiB, four times larger.

questions.title: How much KV cache does one sequence with an 8,192-token context need? (GiB.)
questions.answer: 8,192 tokens × 128 KiB = 1,048,576 KiB = 1 GiB per sequence. Long contexts are expensive mainly because of the cache, not the weights.
keyPoints: Multiply 8,192 tokens by 128 KiB per token.
That gives 1,048,576 KiB per sequence.
The cache is 1 GiB for each full-length sequence.
Long-context cost comes mainly from cache rather than weights.

questions.title: After loading the weights, 40 GiB of GPU memory is left for the KV cache. How many 8k-token sequences can run at once?
questions.answer: 40 GiB ÷ 1 GiB per sequence = 40 sequences. This is what really limits how many users one GPU can serve. It's why paged attention (allocating the cache in small blocks as sequences grow, instead of reserving the maximum up front) raises throughput so much: most sequences never reach 8k.
keyPoints: Divide the 40 GiB pool by 1 GiB per sequence.
The full-length upper bound is 40 sequences.
Paged attention allocates cache blocks as sequences grow.
Avoid reserving 8k for every request when most are shorter.

questions.title: Why do most recent open models use grouped-query attention (GQA)?
questions.answer: In decode, every step reads the whole KV cache. GQA lets groups of query heads share one key-value head, so the cache and the bandwidth it needs shrink by the group factor. Multi-query attention (one KV head) is the extreme case and costs more quality.
options: It improves accuracy over multi-head attention.
Several query heads share each key-value head, which shrinks the KV cache and the memory read per token.
It increases the context length.
It makes training faster.
keyPoints: Every decode step reads the prior KV cache.
GQA shares one KV head among several query heads.
Cache size and bandwidth shrink by the group factor.
MQA uses a single KV head with a larger quality trade-off.

questions.title: With static batching, a batch of 16 requests finishes only when the longest answer finishes. What does continuous batching change?
questions.answer: Output lengths vary widely. In static batching, a request that finishes early holds an empty slot until the longest one ends. Continuous (in-flight) batching schedules per decode step: it evicts finished sequences and inserts new ones straight away. Combined with paged KV caches, it's the main reason modern serving engines get several times more throughput from the same GPU.
options: Finished sequences leave the batch at every step and waiting requests join, so slots never sit idle.
It processes requests one at a time.
It makes each forward pass faster.
It compresses the KV cache.
keyPoints: Output lengths vary across requests.
Static batches leave finished slots idle.
Continuous batching replaces finished sequences each decode step.
Paged KV caches complement dynamic scheduling for throughput.

questions.title: Users say answers take a long time to *start*, but once text appears it streams quickly. Which metric is bad, and what are the usual fixes?
questions.answer: TTFT covers queueing plus prefill of the whole prompt. Long system prompts and retrieved context make prefill slow. Fixes: prefix caching (keep the KV cache of a shared system prompt and reuse it), trimming retrieved context, chunked prefill so long prompts don't block everyone, and enough capacity that requests don't queue. Report TTFT and time per output token separately. They have different causes.
options: Throughput: add more GPUs.
Time to first token (TTFT): reuse shared prompt prefixes, shorten prompts, and reduce queueing.
Time per output token: quantise the model.
Accuracy: fine-tune the model.
keyPoints: TTFT includes queueing and full-prompt prefill.
Reuse shared system prompts through prefix caching.
Trim retrieved context and chunk long prefills.
Provision queue capacity and report output-token time separately.

questions.title: Every request starts with the same 3,000-token system prompt. Which optimisation targets that directly?
questions.answer: Prefill for 3,000 identical tokens on every request is pure waste. Prefix caching stores the KV blocks for a common prefix and maps new requests onto them, cutting TTFT and compute. Many API providers bill cached input tokens at a discount for the same reason. Put the stable parts of the prompt first and the variable parts last, so the shared prefix stays as long as possible.
options: Quantising the KV cache.
Prefix (prompt) caching: compute the KV cache for the shared prefix once and reuse it.
Speculative decoding.
Increasing temperature.
keyPoints: Repeated identical prefix prefill wastes compute.
Cache shared-prefix KV blocks.
Map new requests onto those cached blocks.
Place stable prompt text before variable fields.

questions.title: In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes 4 tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. Each draft token is accepted with probability 0.8, independently, and checking stops at the first rejection. On average, how many tokens does each pass of the large model produce? (Two decimals.)
questions.answer: The large model always produces at least one token (its own correction or continuation), plus each accepted draft token. The expected count is (1 − α^(k+1)) ÷ (1 − α) = (1 − 0.8⁵) ÷ 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per pass of the large model. Decode is memory-bound, so checking 4 tokens costs about the same as producing 1. That's where the speed-up comes from: about 3.4× fewer large-model passes, minus the draft model's own cost.
keyPoints: The target emits at least one correction or continuation token.
Accepted drafts add tokens to each target pass.
Use the geometric expectation to obtain 3.36 tokens per pass.
Subtract draft-model cost from the reduced target-pass benefit.

questions.title: With temperature 0 in production, the same prompt sometimes gets slightly different answers. What's the usual explanation?
questions.answer: Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token, but the logits themselves vary by tiny amounts depending on which other requests share the batch, because kernel choice and reduction order change. When two tokens are nearly tied, that's enough to flip the choice, and the rest of the text diverges from there. Batch-invariant kernels can make serving fully deterministic, at some cost in speed.
options: The model has a bug.
Temperature 0 still samples randomly.
The tokenizer is non-deterministic.
Floating-point results depend on how requests are batched together, so tiny numerical differences can change which token wins a near-tie.
keyPoints: Greedy decoding chooses the highest-probability token.
Batch-dependent kernels and reductions slightly alter logits.
Near ties can flip a token and the continuation.
Batch-invariant kernels trade speed for determinism.

questions.title: How does iteration-level continuous batching differ from static request batching, and how does it maximize GPU tensor core utilization?
questions.answer: In static request batching, the model server groups several requests together, runs the forward pass until every single request finishes, and then emits responses. Because generation lengths vary widely, short requests finish early but remain trapped in GPU memory, while the server waits for the longest request to complete. Iteration-level continuous batching schedules requests at the granularity of individual generated tokens. At every decoding step, the engine removes requests that emitted an end-of-sequence token and inserts newly arrived requests into the running batch without pausing ongoing generations. The engine processes prompt prefill and token decoding dynamically across iterations. The trade-off is scheduling complexity versus hardware utilization: continuous batching adds a small CPU scheduling overhead to manage dynamic batch state at every iteration, but it increases serving throughput by three to four times and eliminates idle GPU tensor core stalls.
followUps: What happens when GPU memory fills up completely while several continuous batching requests are still generating?
How does iteration-level scheduling interact with CUDA graph execution?
wrongAnswers: Padding all requests to the maximum sequence length and waiting for all outputs to finish before returning any results.
Running separate GPU server instances for every individual incoming concurrent request, causing memory bandwidth starvation.
tradeOffs: Iteration-level scheduling maximizes GPU saturation across requests of diverse lengths, but requires dynamic KV-cache block allocation per token.
Co-scheduling compute-heavy prefill phases with memory-bound decode phases can cause brief tail latency jitter unless prefill is chunked.
keyPoints: Static batching waits for the longest request to finish.
Continuous batching schedules at individual token iterations.
Remove completed requests and insert arrivals at each step.
Dynamic scheduling adds CPU overhead while improving GPU utilization.

questions.title: How does chunked prefill prevent long prompt evaluations from causing time-to-next-token latency spikes for concurrent decode requests?
questions.answer: Prompt prefill is compute-bound, processing hundreds of input tokens in parallel, while token generation is memory-bandwidth bound, generating one token at a time. In standard continuous batching, when a user submits a long prompt of several thousand tokens, the engine runs the full prefill in one step. This monopolizes GPU compute for hundreds of milliseconds, stalling concurrent active decodes and causing sharp spikes in time-to-next-token latency. Chunked prefill solves this by dividing long prompts into fixed-size chunks, typically 512 tokens. At each iteration, the engine schedules a prompt chunk alongside running decode tokens, keeping the total token count within a balanced budget. The trade-off is time-to-first-token versus decode consistency: chunking slightly delays the initial response for that single long prompt, but it keeps time-to-next-token flat and predictable across all concurrent users.
followUps: How does chunk size affect GPU compute efficiency during the prefill phase?
What network bandwidth is required to transfer KV cache tensors between disaggregated prefill and decode nodes?
wrongAnswers: Processing long prompts all at once without chunking, accepting 500ms+ latency freezes for concurrent streaming users.
Splitting prompts across separate models without sharing intermediate KV states, forcing redundant recalculations.
tradeOffs: Chunked prefill bounds inter-token latency spikes for active decodes, but increases time-to-first-token for long incoming prompts.
Prefill-decode disaggregation separates prefill and decode onto different GPU pools, eliminating interference at the cost of network KV transfer.
keyPoints: Prefill is compute-bound while decode is memory-bandwidth bound.
Full long-prompt prefills stall concurrent decoding.
Schedule fixed-size prompt chunks alongside decode tokens within a token budget.
Chunking delays the long request's first token but stabilizes decode latency.

questions.title: How does PagedAttention manage block allocation tables, and what eviction policy should an engine use when GPU memory is saturated?
questions.answer: PagedAttention treats GPU memory like virtual memory in an operating system. Instead of allocating contiguous memory for the maximum sequence length, it partitions the KV cache into fixed-size physical blocks, typically 16 or 32 tokens. A logical-to-physical block table tracks which blocks belong to each sequence, allocating new blocks on demand as tokens are generated. When physical GPU memory is saturated and an active request needs a new block, the engine must resolve the memory pressure. It can preempt lower-priority requests using one of two strategies: recomputation or host swapping. In recomputation, the engine frees the request's KV blocks and re-runs prefill when capacity frees up. In swapping, the engine offloads the KV blocks over PCIe to host CPU RAM and pages them back when memory clears. The trade-off is memory utilization versus preemption recovery time: PagedAttention virtually eliminates external fragmentation, but CPU swapping introduces PCIe transfer latency during heavy burst traffic.
followUps: How does copy-on-write enable zero-memory branching during parallel sampling and beam search in PagedAttention?
What determines whether an engine should recompute prompt tokens versus swapping KV blocks to host RAM?
wrongAnswers: Pre-allocating max_tokens contiguous memory buffers for every request, wasting up to 80% of VRAM on unreserved space.
Terminating active user requests with fatal out-of-memory errors instead of swapping or preempting with recomputation.
tradeOffs: Non-contiguous block mapping eliminates external memory fragmentation, but introduces software page-table management overhead.
Swapping KV blocks to CPU memory preserves partial token progress, but PCIe transfer bandwidth limits how fast requests can be resumed.
keyPoints: Allocate KV cache in fixed-size physical blocks.
Map sequence logical blocks to physical blocks and allocate on demand.
Under pressure, preempt with recomputation or host swapping.
Swapping adds PCIe transfer latency.

questions.title: Walk through speculative decoding verification. Why does throughput degrade if the draft acceptance rate falls below fifty percent?
questions.answer: Speculative decoding accelerates inference by pairing a small, fast draft model with a large target model. The draft model autoregressively generates K candidate tokens cheaply. The target model then verifies all K tokens in a single forward pass, evaluating their conditional probabilities in parallel using modified causal attention masks. If the target model agrees with the draft token, the token is accepted; at the first mismatch, the target model samples a replacement token from a modified residual distribution and discards subsequent draft tokens. If the acceptance rate is high, the system generates multiple tokens per target forward pass. However, if the acceptance rate drops below approximately fifty percent, the target model rejects most draft tokens. The system still pays the latency of running the draft model and setting up verification tensors, but gains only one or two tokens per step. The trade-off is inference speedup versus draft compute overhead: speculative decoding achieves two times speedups when the draft aligns with target distributions, but degrades latency when drafting low-entropy code or math where draft models diverge frequently.
followUps: How does the target model sample from the residual probability distribution when rejecting a draft token?
What is Medusa and how does it generate draft tokens without a separate draft model?
wrongAnswers: Accepting all draft tokens without verification, altering the output distribution and producing lower-quality text.
Running the target model verification autoregressively token by token, losing the parallel matrix multiplication advantage.
tradeOffs: Speculative decoding achieves significant speedups without changing output distribution, but requires extra GPU memory to host the draft model.
A large draft token window K increases potential speedup, but wastes draft compute when early tokens in the window are rejected.
keyPoints: A draft model proposes K tokens for parallel target verification.
At the first mismatch, sample a residual replacement and discard later drafts.
High acceptance yields multiple tokens per target pass.
Low acceptance retains draft and verification overhead without enough progress.

questions.title: How does radix tree prefix caching reuse KV-cache tensors across multi-turn conversations and shared system prompts?
questions.answer: In multi-turn chat and agent workflows, consecutive requests frequently share identical token prefixes, such as system prompts, few-shot examples, or prior conversation history. Standard serving runtimes recompute the KV cache for the entire prompt on every single turn. Radix tree prefix caching organizes the physical KV blocks in a radix tree structure where edges represent token subsequences. When a new request arrives, the engine matches its prompt token IDs against the radix tree from the root. Any matching prefix branch is immediately reused, bypassing the prefill forward pass for those tokens and starting generation immediately. When GPU memory fills up, the engine evicts leaf nodes using a least-recently-used policy while keeping popular root prefixes resident in memory. The trade-off is memory retention versus tree indexing overhead: radix caching reduces time-to-first-token by 80% on long shared prefixes, but requires keeping cached blocks allocated in VRAM even when requests finish.
followUps: How do you implement cache eviction when multi-tenant requests compete for the same physical KV memory?
Why must prompt caching engines enforce deterministic tokenization across identical string inputs?
wrongAnswers: Re-running prompt prefill from scratch on every turn of a multi-turn conversation, wasting GPU compute on identical history.
Matching prompt prefixes using character substrings rather than token sequences, causing cache misses due to token boundary shifts.
tradeOffs: Radix caching eliminates redundant prefill compute on common prefixes, but retains KV memory across requests, reducing space for active batches.
Exact token prefix matching is required: modifying a single token early in the prompt invalidates the entire downstream cache branch.
keyPoints: Match incoming token prefixes against a radix tree of KV blocks.
Reuse matching blocks to skip prefix prefill.
Evict least-recently-used leaves while retaining popular roots.
Retained cache blocks consume VRAM after requests finish.

questions.title: How do you design a model router that optimizes the Pareto frontier across latency, cost, and output quality across multiple LLM tiers?
questions.answer: Not every user query requires a frontier reasoning model. Simple tasks like sentiment analysis, summarization, or entity extraction can be handled by smaller models at a fraction of the cost and latency. A model router evaluates incoming queries and directs them to the most efficient model that satisfies the task's quality bar. We train a lightweight classifier, or use embedding similarity against categorized reference queries, to predict task complexity. We establish strict routing rules: structured entity extraction and classification route to small local models; complex multi-step reasoning, mathematical derivations, and policy generation route to frontier models. We monitor the Pareto frontier by plotting average cost per thousand requests against benchmark accuracy. The trade-off is routing overhead and misclassification risk versus aggregate cost reduction: a classifier adds a few milliseconds of latency and can occasionally misroute a subtle query to a smaller model, but it reduces overall fleet API costs by 60% to 80% without degrading perceived quality.
followUps: How do you calibrate router confidence thresholds to prevent difficult edge cases from routing to small models?
What metric best captures the trade-off between cost savings and user dissatisfaction from misrouted queries?
wrongAnswers: Sending 100% of user queries to the most expensive frontier model regardless of task difficulty, wasting budget.
Routing solely based on query character length, assuming short queries are always easy and long queries are always hard.
tradeOffs: Dynamic routing cuts aggregate inference spend significantly, but introduces routing latency and the risk of under-powering difficult queries.
Embedding-based routing allows adding new categories without retraining, while fine-tuned classifiers achieve higher routing accuracy.
keyPoints: Route queries to the cheapest model meeting the quality bar.
Predict complexity with a classifier or reference-query embeddings.
Send simple extraction to small models and complex reasoning to frontier models.
Monitor cost versus accuracy while accounting for misrouting and router latency.

questions.title: How do you implement a fallback cascade that handles provider rate limits (HTTP 429) and latency timeouts without breaking client streams?
questions.answer: When building production applications on external LLM APIs, provider outages, regional rate limits, and unexpected latency spikes are inevitable. A fallback cascade routes traffic across multiple providers with graceful degradation. When a request begins, the gateway calls the primary model endpoint under an aggressive initial token deadline. If the primary provider returns an HTTP 429 rate limit error or fails to stream the first token within the deadline, the client cancels the primary connection and dispatches the request to a fallback provider or an on-premise open-source model. If the stream had already started emitting tokens to the user, cancelling is not an option; the gateway must maintain the connection and handle retries only at step boundaries. The trade-off is system availability versus output consistency: fallback cascades guarantee 99.9% uptime during third-party outages, but secondary models may differ in reasoning style, formatting compliance, or refusal boundaries.
followUps: How do you prevent a cascading thundering herd where failing traffic on Provider A immediately overwhelms Provider B?
What state must be preserved when falling back midway through a multi-step agent tool invocation?
wrongAnswers: Failing the user request immediately with a 500 error upon receiving a single upstream HTTP 429 rate limit response.
Attempting to switch to a fallback model after already streaming partial text to the user, creating disjointed responses.
tradeOffs: Provider fallbacks ensure high availability during outages, but secondary models can produce inconsistent formatting or tool-calling schemas.
Aggressive initial token deadlines catch slow provider hangs quickly, but can prematurely abandon valid slow-prefill requests.
keyPoints: Apply an initial-token deadline to the primary provider.
Cancel and fall back on rate limits or a missed first-token deadline.
Once streaming starts, retry only at step boundaries.
Secondary models may differ in formatting, reasoning or refusal behavior.

questions.title: Compare embedding cluster routing with fine-tuned transformer classification for intent dispatch in production query gateways.
questions.answer: When dispatching incoming queries to specialized domain models or prompt templates, gateways rely on either embedding clustering or fine-tuned sequence classification. Embedding cluster routing maps user queries into vector space using an embedding model and calculates cosine similarity against cluster centroids representing known intents. Its major advantage is flexibility: engineers can add, split, or update intent categories simply by adding reference examples, requiring zero model retraining. However, embedding models are computationally heavier than small classifiers and struggle to separate semantically similar queries with opposite intents. Fine-tuned classification uses a small encoder, such as ModernBERT, trained on labeled intent data. It runs inference in a few milliseconds and learns sharp decision boundaries on fine-grained keywords. The trade-off is operational agility versus inference efficiency: embedding routing allows instant runtime updates without redeploying models, whereas fine-tuned classifiers achieve lower latency and higher classification accuracy at the cost of retraining pipelines.
followUps: How do you handle out-of-distribution queries that do not match any known intent cluster?
What metric should you monitor to detect intent drift in production query streams?
wrongAnswers: Using regular expression keyword matching as the primary intent classifier, which breaks on natural language variations and typos.
Prompting a large generative model to classify the intent of every incoming query, adding 500ms of latency and unnecessary cost.
tradeOffs: Embedding clustering allows instant category updates without retraining, but requires maintaining vector indexes and embedding inference compute.
Fine-tuned classifiers achieve sub-10ms classification latency with high accuracy, but require labeled data and retraining when intents change.
keyPoints: Embedding routing compares queries with intent centroids.
Reference examples let intent categories change without retraining.
Fine-tuned classifiers learn sharper boundaries with lower inference latency.
Classifier updates require a retraining pipeline.

questions.title: How do you quantify model uncertainty in an automated classification pipeline to escalate ambiguous queries to human reviewers?
questions.answer: In high-stakes applications like content moderation, medical document triage, or loan classification, models must recognize when they do not know the answer. We quantify uncertainty using both prediction probabilities and output entropy. For classification models, examining the top softmax probability alone is misleading because neural networks are notoriously overconfident on out-of-distribution data. Instead, we compute the margin between the top two probabilities, and calculate Shannon entropy across the probability distribution: high entropy indicates that probability mass is spread across multiple conflicting classes. For generative models, we sample multiple completions at a low temperature and measure semantic consistency across outputs. When entropy exceeds a calibrated threshold or semantic agreement is low, the pipeline flags the item as high-uncertainty, halts automated processing, and routes the ticket to a human review queue. The trade-off is automated throughput versus decision risk: conservative uncertainty thresholds ensure safety but increase human review volume, while loose thresholds risk silent model errors.
followUps: How does temperature scaling or Platt scaling calibrate raw model logits into reliable probabilities?
What is the difference between aleatoric uncertainty (data noise) and epistemic uncertainty (model ignorance) in production?
wrongAnswers: Using raw uncalibrated softmax confidence scores as the sole escalation criterion, trusting overconfident false predictions.
Escalating a fixed arbitrary percentage of queries rather than using data-driven uncertainty thresholds.
tradeOffs: Multi-sample semantic entropy provides reliable uncertainty signals for generative models, but increases token compute costs.
Strict escalation thresholds reduce error rates on critical decisions, but increase human review staffing requirements.
keyPoints: Top softmax confidence alone can be misleading on out-of-distribution inputs.
Use top-two probability margins and entropy for classification uncertainty.
Measure semantic consistency across sampled generative outputs.
Escalate high uncertainty to humans with a review-volume trade-off.

questions.title: How do you implement dynamic prompt compression before routing long contexts to smaller, cost-effective models?
questions.answer: When routing complex queries to smaller models, passing full conversational history or retrieved documents can exceed their context windows or degrade their attention quality. Dynamic prompt compression removes redundant tokens and filler phrases while preserving key semantic information. We implement compression using extractive token scoring, such as calculating perplexity with a small distilled model. Tokens that contribute low information content—such as repetitive boilerplate, filler words, and predictable sentence structures—are pruned based on their information density. Alternatively, we use structured schema compression: stripping decorative markdown, converting verbose JSON arrays into compact delimited tables, and pruning unreferenced schema definitions. The compressed prompt is then dispatched to the smaller model. The trade-off is compression compute latency versus token cost savings: running a compression pass adds a few milliseconds of compute, but it reduces token volume by 30% to 50%, saving inference latency and cost on downstream models.
followUps: How do you evaluate whether compressed prompts degrade downstream task accuracy on complex reasoning benchmarks?
What is the difference between extractive prompt compression (LLMLingua) and abstractive summarization?
wrongAnswers: Truncating prompts by naively cutting off the beginning or end of text, destroying system instructions or user questions.
Using a large frontier model to summarize prompts before sending them to small models, negating all cost savings.
tradeOffs: Extractive prompt compression reduces context length and token spend significantly, but risks accidentally dropping crucial constraints.
Structured schema minimization preserves semantic guarantees, but requires format-specific parsing pipelines.
keyPoints: Prune low-information tokens with extractive scoring.
Remove decorative Markdown and compress verbose structured data.
Preserve key semantics before dispatching to a smaller model.
Compression adds compute but reduces downstream tokens and latency.

questions.title: How do you architect system prompts, tools, and few-shot examples to maximize provider-level prompt cache hit rates?
questions.answer: Provider prompt caching (such as Anthropic and OpenAI prompt caching) stores KV cache tensors for identical prompt prefixes across API calls. Because cache matching requires strict character-for-character prefix equality, any dynamic value inserted early in the prompt invalidates the entire cache for all subsequent text. We architect prompts in a strict static-to-dynamic hierarchy. At the absolute top, we place invariant system instructions, role descriptions, and policy rules. Immediately following, we place static tool definitions and canonical few-shot examples. Only at the very bottom of the prompt do we insert dynamic variables: the current timestamp, user profile attributes, conversation history, and the user's latest query. In providers that support explicit cache control breakpoints, we tag the boundary immediately after the static tools. The trade-off is prompt layout constraints versus API cost: standardizing prompt order requires disciplined template design, but it delivers up to 90% cost discounts and significant time-to-first-token reductions on cached prefixes.
followUps: What happens to prompt cache hit rates if you dynamically sort tool definitions alphabetically on every request?
How does prompt caching interact with temperature and top-p sampling parameters?
wrongAnswers: Inserting current timestamps or user IDs at the very top of the system prompt, invalidating the cache on every single request.
Randomizing or dynamically filtering tool schemas per request, causing prefix cache misses across team members.
tradeOffs: Strict static-to-dynamic prefix structuring achieves 80%+ cache hit rates, but prevents embedding dynamic timestamps early in system prompts.
Explicit cache breakpoint tags guarantee cache boundaries, but require managing provider-specific API parameters.
keyPoints: Identical prefixes are required for prompt-cache reuse.
Put invariant system instructions, tools and examples before dynamic data.
Place explicit cache breakpoints after static tools where supported.
Standardized prompt order constrains template design while saving cost.

questions.title: How do modern serving runtimes like vLLM and SGLang use radix trees to manage KV caches across multi-turn agent threads?
questions.answer: In multi-turn agent workflows, an agent repeatedly invokes tools, appends tool outputs to its history, and calls the model again. In naive serving, each turn recomputes the entire prompt history from scratch. Runtimes like vLLM and SGLang organize memory into a radix tree prefix cache where nodes represent sequences of tokens and store references to physical KV memory blocks. When an agent submits a multi-turn prompt, the serving engine walks the radix tree to find the longest matching prefix. It reuses the pre-computed KV blocks for all prior turns and runs the prefill forward pass only for the newly added tool result tokens. When branching into multiple speculative trajectories or parallel tool calls, the tree branches naturally, sharing ancestor KV blocks across child branches with zero memory duplication. The trade-off is tree maintenance overhead versus compute savings: managing radix tree lock structures adds minor CPU overhead, but it eliminates 70% to 90% of redundant prefill compute in agentic loops.
followUps: How does radix caching handle memory eviction when multiple agent threads exhaust total GPU VRAM?
What happens if two concurrent requests share a prefix that is currently being computed by the first request?
wrongAnswers: Discarding all KV cache memory after every turn of an agent loop and re-evaluating the full conversation history from scratch.
Using flat hash tables for prompt caching, which cannot match partial prefixes or shared hierarchical conversation branches.
tradeOffs: Radix tree caching eliminates redundant prefill FLOPs on multi-turn conversations, but requires keeping inactive KV blocks allocated in VRAM.
Shared prefix branching enables zero-copy tree search and parallel sampling, but requires reference-counted block eviction.
keyPoints: Walk the radix tree for the longest matching prompt prefix.
Reuse prior-turn KV blocks and prefill only new tool-result tokens.
Share ancestor blocks across branching trajectories.
Tree maintenance adds CPU overhead while reducing redundant prefill.

questions.title: When GPU VRAM is constrained, compare LRU eviction with cost-weighted prefix eviction for shared prompt caches.
questions.answer: When GPU memory fills up, the prompt caching engine must evict stored KV blocks to free space for incoming requests. Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction discards the prefix that has not been accessed for the longest time. While simple and effective for uniform workloads, LRU ignores the asymmetry of computation costs: recomputing a 50-token prefix takes negligible time, whereas recomputing a 4,000-token system prompt containing complex documentation wastes thousands of FLOPs. Cost-weighted eviction assigns an eviction score combining access recency, access frequency, and the computational cost required to regenerate the prefix (measured in token length and FLOPs). High-cost root prefixes like company-wide system prompts and large reference manuals are protected from eviction, while short, cheap leaf prefixes are evicted aggressively. The trade-off is eviction algorithm complexity versus recomputation FLOP savings: cost-weighted eviction requires maintaining priority queues and token metrics, but it minimizes total cluster compute waste under heavy memory pressure.
followUps: How do you prevent a very long, rarely-used prefix from permanently consuming memory under cost-weighted eviction?
What metric best quantifies prompt cache efficiency: token hit rate or request hit rate?
wrongAnswers: Evicting prefixes randomly when GPU memory is exhausted, frequently discarding heavily-used system prompt caches.
Measuring cache performance solely by request hit rate, ignoring that hitting a 10,000-token prompt saves 100x more compute than a 100-token prompt.
tradeOffs: Cost-weighted eviction protects expensive long prefixes from eviction, maximizing compute savings under memory pressure.
Maintaining priority queues with dynamic cost-decay scores introduces more scheduling complexity than a simple doubly-linked LRU list.
keyPoints: LRU evicts the least recently accessed prefix.
LRU ignores the different costs of recomputing short and long prefixes.
Weight eviction by recency, frequency and regeneration cost.
Protect expensive roots and evict cheap leaves using additional priority bookkeeping.

questions.title: What context ordering and schema standardization rules allow multiple teams to share a single prompt cache across multi-tenant tools?
questions.answer: In multi-tenant platforms, different teams often call shared internal tools while adding their own team-specific instructions. If each team formats tool schemas with different key orderings or places team identifiers at the top of the prompt, the serving engine treats them as completely distinct prompts, achieving zero cache sharing. We enforce organizational prompt standardization rules. First, all shared foundational instructions and global tool definitions are serialized using a canonical schema with sorted keys and identical whitespace. Second, we establish a strict slot-ordered prompt layout: Slot 1 is global system policy; Slot 2 is shared enterprise tool schemas; Slot 3 is tenant-level policy; Slot 4 is session history; and Slot 5 is the user query. This ensures that Slot 1 and Slot 2 form a massive shared prefix that hits the GPU KV cache across all teams and tenants in the company. The trade-off is developer autonomy versus platform efficiency: teams must adhere to platform schema rules, but the organization achieves 80% prompt cache hit rates across departments.
followUps: How do you detect when a team accidentally introduces non-standardized whitespace that breaks cross-tenant prompt cache hits?
How do tenant-specific security permissions interact with shared cached prefix blocks?
wrongAnswers: Allowing every developer team to format prompt headers and JSON schemas in arbitrary order, destroying cross-tenant cache hit rates.
Placing tenant API keys or user IDs at the start of prompts, isolating cache blocks to individual users.
tradeOffs: Canonical prompt ordering enables cross-tenant prefix cache sharing across the organization, slashing global GPU serving costs.
Enforcing standardized prompt layouts requires governance tooling and linting in developer CI/CD pipelines.
keyPoints: Canonicalize shared schemas with sorted keys and identical whitespace.
Order global policy and shared tools before tenant policy.
Put session history and user queries after shared prefixes.
Standardization restricts team formatting choices but enables cache sharing.

questions.title: A teammate posts in the team channel that the server does 255 tokens per second. Is that a result? What would you ask for, and what single number tells you where to stop adding users?
questions.answer: It is a slogan, not a result, because a throughput number without the latency that came with it describes nothing a user feels. Ask for the concurrency, the median and P99 first token and time per token at that concurrency, the client and the temperature, and the clock. Goodput is the number that sets the limit: the requests per second, or the share of requests, that met every latency target at once, and on the manual's GB10 the BF16 server's goodput was highest at a cap of 4 while its throughput kept rising to a cap of 64.
followUps: Level 1: Which numbers go next to a throughput figure? Expected: the concurrency or request rate, and the median and P99 of the first token and of the time per token at that point, with the client, temperature and clock as context.

Level 2: Goodput fell to zero at a cap of 8 while throughput still rose. How can both be true? Expected: the server wrote more tokens per second, but the median request took longer than 100 ms per token, so at least half of the requests missed the target and almost none met every bound; throughput counts tokens and goodput counts requests that arrived on time.

Level 3: Why is the mean the wrong statistic for the time per token? Expected: the distribution has a long right tail; a batch with one long prefill neighbour can ship most tokens near 7 ms and a few near 60, so the mean reads 9 ms while the P99 reads 65, and users hit the P99 regularly.

Level 4: Two tools report different time per token for the same run. Why, and what do you do? Expected: one excludes the first token from the inter-token calculation and the other includes it, 7.07 against 12.00 ms in the lesson's example; state the tool and the definition with every number, and keep one tool for every run you compare.
wrongAnswers: "255 tokens per second is the capacity of the server." The same server gave that throughput with a median time to first token of 0.8 s at one load and 3.9 s at another; the number without its latency is not a result.

"Add users until throughput stops rising, then stop." On the GB10 the BF16 throughput kept rising to a cap of 64 while goodput was 0 or close to it from a cap of 8; the latency target, not the throughput curve, sets the limit.
"Report the mean time per token." The distribution is right-skewed, so a mean of 9 ms can hide a P99 of 65; report the median, P90 and P99.
"The engine's own admission limit protects the users." The engine's limit comes from memory, which runs out long after latency is unacceptable; enforce the knee in the client or the gateway.
keyPoints: Throughput needs concurrency and latency context.
Report median and P99 first-token and per-token latency.
Record client, temperature and GPU clock.
Choose capacity by requests meeting every latency target.

questions.title: A user sends a chat request to a serving engine and the answer streams back, slowly at first and then word by word. Describe what the GPU does from the moment the request arrives until the last token. Name the phases, and name the numbers you would put on a dashboard for each of them.
questions.answer: A request has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values into the KV cache, so the GPU is busy with math. Decode then writes one token per request per step, and each step reads all the weights to do it, so the GPU waits for memory. Four numbers measure them: TTFT for the wait before the first token, TPOT and ITL for the stream, and output tokens per second for the whole server.
followUps: Level 1: Which of the four numbers matters most to someone who reads a long answer? Expected: TPOT, the mean gap between tokens, together with the P99 ITL for the worst stalls.

Level 2: Why is decode bound by memory and prefill by math? Expected: a decode step reads every weight to make one token per request, so the bytes moved dominate; a prefill step handles hundreds of prompt tokens per pass, so the math per byte is high.

Level 3: In the manual's run, 64 users got about eight times the output of one user. Why do the cost per token and the wait per user move in opposite directions? Expected: each decode step reads the weights once for all running requests, so more requests share one read; each request then waits for a longer step.

Level 4: The lesson describes a prefill phase and a decode phase. What does the vLLM scheduler have instead? Expected: one token budget per step; running requests take their next token first and prompt chunks fill the rest, so a prefill is a request with many tokens left to compute.
wrongAnswers: "Throughput is the number to optimize, and the rest follows." Throughput is what the GPU owner pays for; the users feel TTFT and the gaps between tokens, and at 64 users the manual's server wrote eight times the tokens while each user waited about 7.5 times longer per token.

"Prefill and decode run as two separate stages inside the engine." The vLLM scheduler has one token budget per step; running requests get a decode token first and prompt chunks fill the rest, so the two phases mix in one step.
"TPOT and ITL are the same number." TPOT is the mean time per output token for one request; ITL is each gap between two tokens, and its P99 shows the stalls that the mean hides.
keyPoints: Prefill processes the prompt and writes KV tensors.
Prefill is dominated by math.
Decode generates one token per request and reads weights.
Measure TTFT, TPOT, ITL and server output throughput.

questions.title: You serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one GPU with a maximum model length of 8,192 tokens. At startup the server prints a maximum concurrency of 2.94, and a manager asks if the GPU can serve only three users at a time. Your users send about 512 prompt tokens and get about 128 tokens back. How do you answer?
questions.answer: The startup number assumes that every user fills the full maximum model length, and real users hold much less. Count the KV bytes for one token, divide the KV pool by that number, and then divide the pool by the context that one user really holds. On the L4 in the vLLM manual, the pool of 24,096 tokens fits 37 users with 640 tokens each.
followUps: Level 2: What happens to a request that needs more blocks than are free? Expected: it waits in the queue. A running request that needs a block when none is free is stopped and computed again later.
Level 2: Why does the mixture-of-experts model use less KV memory per token than the dense model? Expected: it has fewer KV heads, and the KV heads, not the weights, set the bytes per token.
Level 3: How do you check your count after a start? Expected: read the memory line and the pool line in the startup log, and compare them with the count from the model config.
Level 3: What is the cost of the FP8 KV cache? Expected: a possible loss of quality, so measure it on your own eval before you ship it.
wrongAnswers: "Divide the GPU memory by the model size." The weights are only one part. The users that fit depend on the KV pool and on the context per user.
"The maximum concurrency in the log is the user limit." It assumes that each user fills the maximum model length, which real users do not.
"More parameters always mean more KV memory per token." The bytes per token depend on the layers, the KV heads and the head size.
keyPoints: Startup capacity assumes every user fills maximum length.
Compute KV bytes per token and total token capacity.
Divide the pool by realistic per-user context.
The stated 24,096-token pool fits 37 users at 640 tokens.

questions.title: A team runs long agent sessions on SGLang with hierarchical caching on. Their dashboards show #cached-token: 0 on requests that resend a long history. They have tuned the cache tiers and the write policy, and the hit rate barely moves. The prompt template looks stable to them. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?
questions.answer: Look at the first tokens of the request as the server sees them, not at the template. A relay or a chat template often adds something that changes on every request near the start, such as a request ID, a session hash or the date, and the tree matches from the first token and stops at the first difference. In the manual's incident a random hash in the system prompt cost 27.6 points of hit rate, and removing it moved the engine hit rate from 66.8 to 94.4 percent.
followUps: Level 2: The same random ID moves behind the fixed text instead. What does it cost now? Expected: about 45 tokens of prefill instead of about 3,027; in the experiment that was 43 ms more than the stable prompt instead of 28 times longer.

Level 3: After the prompt fix, one server hits well and the fleet still misses. What next? Expected: routing; a request that lands on a server without its prefix misses, and routing each conversation to the same server moved one report from 64.7 to 92.1 percent.

Level 4: The host tier still hurts other sessions after the prompt fix. What did the incident count, and what does it mean? Expected: 250,000 evict calls against 376 completed load-backs; a load-back that finds no room evicts other sessions from the GPU pool, so the pool size and the write policy need a look only after the prompt is fixed.
wrongAnswers: "Raise the hierarchical cache ratio until the hit rate recovers." No cache flag can recover a miss that starts at token 5; the first fix was a prompt edit, worth 27.6 points of hit rate.

"The template is stable, so the prompt is stable." The template is not what the server sees; a relay, a gateway or the chat template can insert a hash, a date or a snapshot, so compare the token sequences of two consecutive requests from the start.

"A changed field in the middle only costs the tokens of that field." Every token after the change is a different branch of the tree, because the attention values of later tokens depend on every earlier token.
keyPoints: Inspect actual serialized request prefixes.
Dynamic request IDs or dates can break prefix matching.
The cache stops matching at the first changed token.
Removing the incident's random hash restored cache hit rate.

questions.title: Every request to your service starts with the same long system prompt, and the prefix cache is on. The server reports almost no cached tokens, and the first token is slow. Last week a teammate added a request ID to the start of the system prompt for tracing. What happened, and what do you change?
questions.answer: The prefix cache matches a prompt from its first token and stops at the first token that differs. A new ID at the start makes every later token a miss, so the server computes the whole prompt again on each request. Move the parts that never change to the front and put the ID after them. Then prove the fix with the cached-token counters.
followUps: Level 2: The hit rate is still low after the fix. What is the next cause to check? Expected: a full pool, because the cache keeps old blocks only until a running request needs the memory.
Level 2: Where in a chat request does a change cost the least? Expected: in the newest message, because the template puts it last, so only that message is computed again.

Level 3: Two tenants send the same system prompt. What is the risk, and what is the control in vLLM? Expected: one tenant can learn from timing what the other sent. Send a different cache_salt for each tenant, so that their requests never share blocks.

Level 3: A team tunes the cache tiers and the eviction policy, and the hit rate does not move. What do you check first? Expected: the prompt text, for a value that changes on each request near the start, such as a random hash or a timestamp.
wrongAnswers: "Give the cache more memory." A bigger pool keeps more blocks, but a prompt that differs at the first tokens has no block to reuse.
"The cache matches the longest shared part anywhere in the prompt." The cache matches only from the first token, so a shared part after a difference never hits.
"Turn on hierarchical caching." A second tier stores more prefixes. It cannot match a prefix that is different on every request.
keyPoints: Prefix matching starts at token one.
An early changing ID invalidates later prefix reuse.
Move stable content ahead of the ID.
Verify improvement using cached-token counters.

questions.title: Every request to your chat service repeats the same long system prompt, and the engine has prefix caching on by default. What decides whether the next request reuses the work of the last one? How would you lay out the prompt, and how do you show a hit with a number instead of a guess?
questions.answer: The cache matches tokens from the first one onward and stops at the first difference, so a hit needs the same tokens in the same order at the start of the prompt. Put the parts that never change first, the parts that change per session next, and the question, the time and any request ID last. Prove the hit from the server: the cached_tokens field in the usage block, the #cached-token count in the prefill log line, or the prefix cache counters in /metrics.
followUps: Level 2: On vLLM every request starts with the same 20 tokens. How many come from the cache? Expected: 16, one full block; the last 4 are computed each time because only full blocks are cached.

Level 3: The prompt is stable, one server hits well, and the fleet still misses. Name two causes outside the prompt. Expected: a full pool that drops blocks before the next request arrives, and a router that sends a session to a server which never saw its prefix; sticky routing moved one report from 64.7 to 92.1 percent.

Level 3: Why does SGLang report 2,998 cached tokens for a 2,999-token prompt and never 2,999? Expected: the last prompt token always goes through prefill, because the model needs its logits to sample the first output token.

Level 4: A client writes a task-list snapshot at the end of the system prompt and updates it on every turn. What does the tree do? Expected: every update changes the system prompt, so every token after it misses, including the whole history behind it; in the manual's incident that invalidated more than 100,000 tokens per turn, and the fix is to move the snapshot behind the history or into request metadata.
wrongAnswers: "The cache is on, so repeated prompts hit it." The match is exact from the first token; a timestamp, a request ID or a reordered tool list near the start makes every later block miss, and one random ID at the start matched only 5 tokens of a 3,034-token prompt.
"Put the user question first so the model reads it first." The question changes on every request, so the shared system prompt behind it never matches; put the fixed part first and the question last.

"Turn the cache off for a fair benchmark." The cache is on in production, so the test must reset it between runs, not remove it; with it off the first token at 4,096 shared tokens took 13,353 ms on vLLM and 14,706 ms on SGLang.
"Measure the hit rate from the response time of the client." Read it from the server, in the usage block, the prefill line or the counters; a faster second response can also come from a warmer GPU.
keyPoints: Shared prefixes require identical starting tokens in identical order.
Place invariant prompt content first.
Put session fields next and question, time and request ID last.
Verify cached tokens in usage, prefill logs or metrics.

questions.title: You run the same evaluation twice at temperature 0 on a serving engine and the scores differ. You send one failing prompt alone and get one answer, then send it inside a busy batch and get another. Nothing in the request changed. Explain what did change, and what a seed can and cannot fix.
questions.answer: The batch changed the arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the kernels split their sums by the batch size, so the same request adds its numbers in a different order in a batch of 3 than in a batch of 30; a change in the last bit can flip the top logit, and every later token then follows a different text. The prefix cache does the same, because a request that reuses cached blocks runs a different prefill path, and so does the dtype. A seed fixes only the random draws of sampling, so it is not enough: offline, run the engine in one process with the same order; online, use the batch-invariant mode and pay its speed cost.
followUps: Level 2: Which comparisons in the manual's table gave the same text every time? Expected: a repeat after a cache flush against a fresh run, and a repeat with the cache off against the cache off, both 0 of 32 changed on both engines.

Level 3: Why can a warm prefix cache change a greedy answer when the model and the prompt are the same? Expected: a request that reuses cached blocks computes its prompt in a different path than a full prefill, so the logits differ in their last bits, and one changed token changes the rest; it changed 21 of 32 outputs on SGLang and 11 of 32 on vLLM.

Level 4: Under load two cache-off runs still differed. What does that say about the fix? Expected: the batch alone changed most outputs, 50 of 64 on vLLM, so a cache reset is enough only at one user; a live server needs batch-invariant kernels, and the manual did not test that mode at that load.
wrongAnswers: "Temperature 0 makes the output deterministic." Greedy picks the top logit, and the batch changes the logits in their last bits; the GB10 server gave two texts for one prompt at temperature 0 with nothing in the request changed.
"Set a seed and the outputs match." The seed only fixes the random draws; the vLLM seed defaults to 0 and cannot be unset, and the outputs still changed with the batch and the cache.

"Flush the cache before each run and you are done." At one user that was enough, 0 of 32 changed; at 64 users two runs with the cache off still differed in 50 of 64 outputs, because the batch changed the sums.

"Switch to FP16 for exact results." BF16 and FP16 round differently, so the same model writes different text in the two dtypes, 48 of 64 outputs for the 0.6B model; keep one dtype between runs you compare.
keyPoints: Batch-dependent floating-point reductions can change top logits.
Cache paths and dtype also affect arithmetic.
A sampling seed does not guarantee identical logits.
Use fixed offline execution or batch-invariant online mode at a speed cost.

questions.title: Two engineers benchmark the same server on the same day and report numbers that differ by a few percent. Both used standard benchmark clients. Before you look at the server, what about the clients could explain the gap, and what rules would you set for the team?
questions.answer: The client is part of the measurement. On one vLLM server the SGLang client read a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher and an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower than the vLLM client, the two clients sent different random prompts, and temperature 0.7 raised the time per token by 10 to 13 percent at one user against temperature 0. The rules: one client, one temperature, one prompt length distribution with the range ratio stated, a flush and a new seed per run, the clock recorded, and all of that written next to every number.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the default range ratio describe half the work? Expected: each length is drawn from 1 to the length asked, so the average prompt is about half of it; with 1.0 every prompt has the full length and the input token total in the report confirms it.

Level 3: Fixed lengths gave a late first token and a steady stream, mixed lengths the opposite. Which do you use? Expected: fixed lengths to compare two builds, because they repeat exactly; your real length mix before you set a latency target, because the two shapes measure two different servers.

Level 3: A teammate's hand-written timing loop reads 13 tokens per second where a hosted API reads 60. What is wrong with the loop? Expected: it counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate; a word is not a token and TTFT is not decode time, so use the benchmark client.

Level 4: At 16 requests per second the client reports a first token you do not believe. How do you check the client itself? Expected: a single-process client adds its own queue at high rates; run two client processes that each send half the rate and compare, and record the CPU use of the client.
wrongAnswers: "Both are standard clients, so the numbers are comparable." On one server the SGLang client read 3 to 10 percent higher first-token times and 2 to 8 percent lower throughput than the vLLM client; a gap of a few percent can come from the client alone.
"Temperature does not change speed." Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users over temperature 0.
"Set the input length to 512 and the prompts are 512 tokens." With the default range ratio of 0.0 the average prompt is about 256 tokens; pass 1.0 or state the distribution.

"A load tester that handles HTTP handles model traffic." A generic tool sends one prompt in a loop, which hits the prefix cache almost every time, and it does not read the token gaps of a stream; use a client that samples prompt lengths and counts tokens.
keyPoints: Use the same benchmark client across comparisons.
Fix temperature and prompt-length distribution.
Flush caches and use a fresh seed per run.
Record the GPU clock and all measurement settings.

questions.title: Your first concurrency sweep on an L4 shows a first-token median of 0.3 s up to 16 users and 1.8 s at 32, so you set the production limit at 20 users per replica. A second sweep with a reset before each run puts the first token at 1.6 s already at 16 users. Which sweep do you trust, and why do the two disagree?
questions.answer: Trust the sweep with the reset. The first sweep kept one server for all the user counts and sent the same first prompts at every count with a fixed seed, so below 32 users many requests found their prompt in the prefix cache and skipped the prefill. With the reset the median first token rose at every step, about 0.65 s at 4 users, 1.0 s at 8 and 1.6 s at 16, and the P99 ITL jumped from about 70 ms at 8 users to 522 ms at 16, so the knee on this card sits between 8 and 16 users, not between 16 and 32.
followUps: Level 2: Why did the time per token barely move between the flushed and the unflushed runs? Expected: a cache hit removes prefill work and leaves the decode work the same, so TTFT falls and TPOT moves by less than 15 percent.

Level 3: On the GB10 a single run read a faster first token at a cap of 32 than at a cap of 8. How is that possible? Expected: the runs shared one server and one seed, so the run at 32 found 64 of its 128 prompts in the cache from the earlier runs and half of its requests skipped prefill; three seeds on fresh servers put the first token back in order.

Level 3: The flush route on SGLang answered HTTP 400. What happened? Expected: the server flushes only when no request runs or waits; a request was still pending, so the flush did not run and the log says so, and the run must wait or restart the server.

Level 4: How would you make the warm-cache effect part of a benchmark on purpose? Expected: measure it as its own axis; record the cached tokens per run from the counters or the per-response field, and report a warm-cache row next to a cold row, each with its hit rate, instead of letting an unknown mix of the two set the knee.
wrongAnswers: "The jump from 0.3 to 1.8 s between 16 and 32 users is the knee." That sweep ran without a reset, so most requests below 32 users skipped their prefill; with a reset the P99 ITL jumped from about 70 to 522 ms between 8 and 16 users, and that is the knee.
"Turn the prefix cache off for benchmarks." Production runs with it on; reset it between runs, use a new seed per run and record the cached tokens instead.

"The time per token is inflated too, so throw the whole sweep away." A hit removes prefill work only; the time per token changed by less than 15 percent between flushed and unflushed runs, so the TPOT column stands and the TTFT column does not.
"The random dataset gives new prompts every run." With the same seed the client sends the same prompts; the dataset is random only across seeds, so use a new seed per run.
keyPoints: A reused fixed-seed workload can hit cached prefixes.
Trust the sweep that resets cache state.
Reset measurements showed rising TTFT with concurrency.
The stated card's latency knee lies between eight and sixteen users.

questions.title: Your server queues requests because the KV cache is full. Someone suggests --kv-cache-dtype fp8. What does it buy, what can it cost, and how do you check both before production?
questions.answer: An FP8 KV cache stores each key and value in 1 byte instead of 2, so the same memory holds twice the tokens: for Qwen/Qwen3-8B a token falls from 144 KiB to 72 KiB, and one GiB holds about 14,600 tokens instead of about 7,300. It can cost accuracy, because FP8 needs a scale per tensor and a checkpoint without scales runs with a scale of 1.0, and it can change the attention backend, which on our L4 broke the first start. Check it with an accuracy run on your own task and with the startup log: on 500 GSM8K questions our FP8 KV run scored 90.8 percent against 91.8 in BF16, with overlapping intervals.
followUps: Level 2: The pool has room and requests do not queue. Do you still switch? Expected: no; the cache dtype is a capacity decision, and with room in the pool it buys nothing and still carries the accuracy and backend risks.

Level 3: The scale warning prints although the checkpoint has k_scale tensors. What does it mean? Expected: the loader dropped the scales; at 0.31.0 one model family never loads its KV scales and the issue is open, so the server runs with a scale of 1.0 until you change the checkpoint or the version.

Level 3: Why did the first FP8 start fail on the L4 and not on a data center GPU? Expected: the default attention backend reads an FP8 cache only on Hopper and Blackwell data center GPUs, so vLLM fell back to a backend that compiles its kernels on the first start, and that build failed; the Triton backend reads FP8 and skips the build.

Level 4: The GSM8K check gave 91.8 against 90.8 percent, and the two intervals overlap. What can you conclude? Expected: this run did not show a difference and cannot rule out a loss of a few points; it is one model and one benchmark, so run the same check on your model and task, and expect a model with another attention layout to lose more.
wrongAnswers: "FP8 KV halves memory, so it doubles throughput." It doubles the tokens that fit; in the field report it was a few percent slower per token at every load both caches could run, and won only because the BF16 cache ran out at 64 requests.

"The checkpoint is FP8, so the KV scales are there." Weight scales and KV scales are different tensors; the FP8 checkpoint of Qwen3-30B-A3B lists weight scales and no k_scale or v_scale, so its cache ran with a scale of 1.0.

"Accuracy is a property of the model, so test it once." The loss depends on the model, the attention layout and the task; one family that needs calibrated scales lost accuracy with a scale of 1.0 while most models stayed close to BF16 in the same tests.
"The attention backend does not matter for a cache dtype." On the L4 the dtype change moved vLLM to another backend and the start failed; read the backend line after every change to the cache dtype.
keyPoints: FP8 halves KV storage from two bytes to one.
The stated model drops from 144 to 72 KiB per token.
Missing scales and backend changes can affect correctness or startup.
Check startup logs and task accuracy with uncertainty intervals.

questions.title: Speculative decoding promises several tokens per step with no change to what the model writes. Explain how the engine keeps that promise, where the speedup comes from, and why the gain shrinks as more users share the server.
questions.answer: A cheap proposer guesses the next few tokens, and the target model runs once over all the guesses and computes its own distribution at every position. A rejection sampler keeps each guess that the target supports, samples a correct token from the target at the first rejection, and stops, so one pass gives at least one token and at most the number of guesses plus one, with the same output distribution as plain decoding. The gain comes from idle GPU time: a small decode batch waits for memory, and as the batch grows that idle time goes away, so the checks of rejected guesses start to cost real compute.
followUps: Level 2: Which proposer needs no extra model, and when does it pay? Expected: n-gram, which matches the last tokens of the output against earlier text in the request; it pays for edits, quotes, code changes and extraction, and fails on open chat.

Level 3: Acceptance is high but the time per token did not fall. What does that tell you? Expected: the batch is already compute bound; the idle memory time that speculation uses is gone, so the checks cost as much as they save.

Level 3: With greedy sampling, how does the check decide at each position? Expected: a guess stays only if it equals the top token of the target there; the first mismatch is replaced by the target's token and the rest are dropped.

Level 4: Why can one verify pass never commit more tokens than the draft length plus one? Expected: the target computes a distribution at every draft position and one past the last guess, so when all guesses pass the sampler still draws one bonus token from that last distribution; at a rejection it samples a correct token there and stops.
wrongAnswers: "Speculation changes the output a little, so you trade some quality for speed." With greedy sampling a guess stays only if it equals the target's top token, and with random sampling the rejection rule keeps the output distribution equal to the target's, so the quality does not change, although one sampled run can differ from a run without speculation.

"The draft is where the speed comes from, so a faster draft always helps." The gain comes from idle GPU time in a small batch; a fast draft with low acceptance adds checks that cost compute, and at concurrency 20 one report lost a quarter of its throughput.
"Turn it on for the stress test too." At batch 1 one report more than doubled its speed and at concurrency 20 it was slower; the maintainer's answer was that speculation is for small batches.
keyPoints: A cheap proposer drafts several tokens.
The target evaluates all draft positions in one pass.
Rejection sampling preserves the target output distribution.
Speculation helps small bandwidth-bound batches more than large busy batches.

questions.title: You have twenty fine-tunes of one base model, each a LoRA adapter, and you want to serve them from one vLLM server. What do you set, what decides the cost, and what else in the server changes when LoRA is on?
questions.answer: Turn LoRA on at startup with --enable-lora, name the adapters with --lora-modules, and let each request pick one in its model field. Three limits set the cost: --max-loras, which defaults to 1 and caps the adapters that run in one batch, --max-lora-rank, which defaults to 16 and reserves memory for the largest rank, and --max-cpu-loras for adapters kept in CPU memory ready to load. LoRA also changes the prefix cache, because the adapter is part of every block key, so two adapters never share cached blocks, and it adds CUDA graphs per adapter, so startup takes longer and uses more memory.
followUps: Level 2: Two tenants send the same long system prompt through two different adapters. Does the second request hit the cache? Expected: no; the adapter is part of the block key in vLLM and of the tree key in SGLang, so two adapters never share blocks even for identical tokens.

Level 3: Requests for the second adapter wait although the GPU is idle. Why? Expected: the adapter cap defaults to 1, so only one adapter runs in a batch and requests for another adapter wait until that batch is done; raise it to the number of adapters that are busy at the same time.

Level 3: Why not set the rank limit to 256 to be safe? Expected: the server reserves memory for the largest rank it accepts, so a high limit takes memory from the KV pool for adapters you do not have; set it to your largest rank.

Level 4: You also want 4-bit weights for the base model. Which format, and what does it rule out? Expected: a GPTQ 4-bit base, because it supports LoRA adapters in vLLM with the Marlin kernels; the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026, so they are out until they do.
wrongAnswers: "One server per adapter is simpler." Each server would hold its own copy of the base model and its own pool; one base with adapters per request shares both, and requests for different adapters can run in the same batch.
"The default limits are fine." One adapter per batch makes requests for a second adapter wait, and a rank limit of 16 rejects a rank-64 adapter; set both from the adapters you serve.

"Enable runtime adapter loading so that operators can add adapters without a restart." The load route reads files from a path that the caller gives, so turn it on only when you trust every caller of the server.
"LoRA is free for the prefix cache because the base model is the same." The adapter changes the keys and values, so it is part of the block key, and two adapters never share cached blocks.
keyPoints: Enable LoRA at startup and name adapters.
Requests select an adapter in the model field.
Adapter count, maximum rank and CPU residency set resource costs.
Adapter-specific cache keys and CUDA graphs add memory and startup cost.

questions.title: Your first sweep on an L4 says that CUDA graphs do nothing: at one user the median per-token time is 103.4 ms with graphs and 103.4 ms without, and the three seeds at that cap spread from 10.0 to 14.9 tokens per second, half the median. What do you check before you report that graphs do nothing?
questions.answer: Check the GPU clock and the temperature during the run before you believe either number. The manual's L4 sat at 87 C with software thermal slowdown active and an SM clock of 360 MHz out of 2040 during that sweep, so the server under test was not the cause. A sweep with a cool-down to 72 C and the clock recorded gave 60.16 ms per token at one user against 103.38 hot, and 270.11 against 194.16 tokens per second at a cap of 32: the hot sweep reported up to 28 percent less throughput, with the same command on the same card.
followUps: Level 2: Which two columns do you add to every result row? Expected: the median SM clock and the highest temperature or the share of samples with the thermal flag, so that a reader can set aside hot runs.

Level 3: You locked the clock at 900 MHz and one run still reports 210 MHz. How? Expected: a lock sets the highest clock and cannot stop the GPU from throttling below it; set that run aside, repeat it after a cool-down, and compare only runs at the same clock.

Level 3: Under an open-loop overload the card finished fewer requests as you offered more. Why? Expected: the queue grew and the card heated, so the clock fell from 1,320 to 465 MHz and 70 percent of the samples showed thermal slowdown at 16 per second; on a passively cooled card overload costs throughput as well as latency.

Level 4: Your chassis cannot cool the card below 72 C. How do you still compare two configs? Expected: run both in one session and alternate them, record the clock for every run, set aside runs under a floor and repeat them, read ratios between runs at similar clocks rather than absolute times, and print the clock next to every number.
wrongAnswers: "The GPU shows 100 percent utilization, so it runs at full speed." Utilization says the GPU was busy, not how fast; the same card read 100 percent at 360 MHz of 2040 with the thermal flag active.

"A spread of half the median between seeds is normal noise." On a cool card the bands were inside about 10 percent of their medians; a spread of half the median is a sign of a changing clock, so read the telemetry.
"A clock lock makes every run comparable." It caps the clock and cannot stop a throttle; a run under the lock fell to 210 MHz and had to be set aside.

"Record the clock once at the start of the sweep." The clock fell from 1,320 to 465 MHz across one open-loop sweep as the queue grew; sample it once a second during every run and report the median per run.
keyPoints: Check GPU clock and temperature during each run.
Thermal slowdown can explain poor throughput.
Compare after cooling while recording clocks.
The stated hot and cool runs used the same card and command.

questions.title: Most explanations of continuous batching describe a prefill phase and a decode phase that take turns on the GPU. Describe what the vLLM scheduler does in one step instead. Where does chunked prefill come from in that design, and where do you read the value that controls it?
questions.answer: The scheduler asks the same question of every request: how many tokens does it still need to compute? Each step has a budget of tokens, set by --max-num-batched-tokens, and the running requests take their next token first. Waiting prompts fill the rest of the budget, so a long prompt is split over several steps, and chunked prefill needs no extra mechanism.
followUps: Level 2: Prefix caching is on, and a request with a 2,048-token prompt finds 1,024 tokens in the cache. What does the scheduler count for it? Expected: 1,024 tokens still to compute; the cache only lowers the count, and the same loop serves the request.

Level 3: A server with 121.69 GiB of unified memory logs a budget of 2,048. Why not 8,192? Expected: the default comes from the memory that vLLM reads, and the unified machine reads as small or unknown, so it gets the small value; read compile_ranges_endpoints before you change it.

Level 4: Speculative decoding is on with three draft tokens. How does the budget rule change? Expected: it does not; a running request now needs more than one token per step, so its count rises, and the budget is spent in the same order.
wrongAnswers: "Chunked prefill is a flag you turn on." It follows from the budget: a prompt that does not fit the rest of the budget gets part now and the rest later, so it is on by default and has no separate mechanism.
"New prompts go first so that the first token comes fast." Running requests take their tokens first so that a user who sees a stream keeps seeing it; a new prompt waits for the budget that is left.
"The budget is 2,048 on every GPU." It depends on the memory that vLLM reads: 2,048 below 70 GiB, 8,192 at 70 GiB or more, and 16,384 at 160 GiB or more, and the offline LLM class uses larger values.
keyPoints: Set each step's token budget with max-num-batched-tokens.
Schedule running requests' next tokens first.
Fill remaining budget with waiting prompt tokens.
Split long prefills over steps using the same budget.

questions.title: Explain how vLLM keeps the KV cache in GPU memory. Why does it not give each request its own buffer, how does it recognize a prompt it has seen before, and what happens when the memory runs out?
questions.answer: The KV cache is one pool of 16-token blocks, and a request takes blocks one at a time as it grows, mapped by a small block table. A buffer per request wastes memory twice: on length that the request never reaches, and on gaps between requests of different sizes. Each full block gets a hash that is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and a new request walks its chain and stops at the first miss. When no block is free, the scheduler preempts the newest request and computes it again later.
followUps: Level 2: Every request starts with the same 25 tokens. How many of them come from the cache? Expected: 16, one full block; the last 9 tokens are computed on every request because only full blocks are cached.

Level 3: Two tenants send the same system prompt. What can one learn about the other, and what field stops it? Expected: they share blocks, so the timing of one tenant can reveal what the other sent; a cache_salt per tenant goes into the hash, so the two never share a block.

Level 4: Under the default policy, which request does vLLM preempt when no block is free, and what does it cost?
