Expected: the newest running request; all of its blocks are freed, it goes to the head of the waiting queue, and its tokens are computed again from the start, which the preemption counter records.
wrongAnswers: "vLLM swaps preempted requests to CPU memory." Older versions could; the current engine only recomputes, because the documentation judges the recompute cheaper, and the cost shows in the time of that request and in the preemption counter.

"The prefix cache has its own memory budget." The cache is the pool; a freed block keeps its hash on the free list until a new block is needed, so a busy server keeps fewer old prefixes than an idle one.
"A block hash covers only its own 16 tokens." It is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and it also covers the adapter, the images and the salt.
keyPoints: Allocate KV memory as pooled 16-token blocks.
Map growing requests through block tables.
Chain full-block hashes to identify shared prefixes.
Preempt and later recompute the newest request when blocks run out.

questions.title: Your RL trainer shares its GPUs with the vLLM server that generates the rollouts. Between rollout steps the trainer needs the GPU memory back, and after each step the server needs the new weights. What does vLLM give you for this loop, and what can go wrong at the pinned version?
questions.answer: vLLM has development-mode routes for the loop: sleep mode frees GPU memory on /sleep and takes it back on /wake_up, /pause and /resume stop and restart generation, and a weight transfer runs through /init_weight_transfer_engine, /start_weight_update and /finish_weight_update, over NCCL between GPUs or through CUDA memory handles on one machine. At level 1 the sleep keeps the weights, and at level 2 it drops them too, which suits a step where the trainer sends new weights anyway. Three problems are known at 0.31.0: a level 2 wake does not reload a speculative draft, a level 2 sleep clears calibrated KV scales, and a weight update during sleep stops the engine, so wake first, reload, reset the prefix cache and read the acceptance counters.
followUps: Level 2: What is the difference between the two sleep levels? Expected: level 1 frees the KV cache and other memory and keeps the weights; level 2 drops the weights too, which suits a step where new weights arrive anyway and costs a reload.

Level 3: After a level 2 wake the output is correct but decode runs as slowly as with no speculation. Why? Expected: the weight reload covers only the target model, so the draft is not reloaded and the target rejects every draft token; no error appears, and the acceptance counters show it.

Level 3: The trainer's logprobs differ from the server's on every token. Bug or not? Expected: a small steady gap is normal because the kernels differ, 0.005 median absolute with raw logprobs; a growing gap means the weights did not arrive, and a constant offset near the log of the kept mass means the server returned processed logprobs under top-p while the trainer scored the full vocabulary.

Level 4: Order the steps of one RL iteration around these routes. Expected: pause or drain generation, sleep, train, wake, then start and finish the weight update and record the version, reset the prefix cache, reload the draft if speculation is on, read the acceptance counters, resume; never send weights while the server sleeps, because that stops the engine.
wrongAnswers: "Expose the sleep and weight routes on the public port." They exist only in development mode, and they free memory, replace weights and run methods on every worker; keep them on the trainer's network, bound to the local host when you test by hand.

"Send the new weights while the server sleeps to save time." At 0.31.0 that segfaults the engine; the API server stays up and every later request fails, so always wake before the trainer sends weights.

"Logprobs from the server and the trainer should match exactly." The kernels differ, so a small steady gap is normal; track it every step and treat a growing gap as a sign that the weights did not reach the generator.

"A level 2 wake restores the server to its state before the sleep." It reloads the target weights only; the speculative draft is not reloaded and calibrated KV scales were cleared on some checkpoints, so reload, reset the cache and read the acceptance after each level 2 wake, and on 0.31.0 a reload does not bring back the scales.
keyPoints: Sleep and wake routes release and reclaim GPU memory.
Pause and resume control generation during rollout loops.
Level two drops weights as well as cache state.
Wake before updating weights and check draft reload, KV scales and caches.

questions.title: You have a model that does not fit on one GPU, or you need more throughput than one GPU gives. Walk me through how you choose between tensor, pipeline and data parallelism, and what each one costs in communication.
questions.answer: Ask three questions. If the model fits on one GPU with room for the KV cache you need, use data parallelism, one full copy per GPU, and the output grows with the copies. If it does not fit, split it: tensor parallelism inside one machine when the GPUs have a fast link and the GPU count divides the attention heads, and pipeline parallelism when they do not or when the model needs more than one machine. Tensor parallelism talks after every layer, pipeline parallelism once per stage boundary, and data parallelism not at all between copies.
followUps: Level 2: Two GPUs in one host joined by PCIe only, and the model fits on one. What do you run? Expected: data parallelism, two full copies, because nothing moves between copies; tensor parallelism would pay after every layer over the slow link.

Level 3: The model needs two machines of 8 GPUs. How do you set the sizes, and what do you check first? Expected: pipeline size 2 for the machines and tensor size 8 inside each, with 8 dividing the attention heads; run the collective test on both machines first and keep the traffic on a private network, because it is not encrypted.

Level 3: Tensor parallelism on two GPUs where one is shared with another job. What does SGLang do at startup? Expected: it measures free memory on each rank, keeps the smallest, and stops if that is under 90 percent of the local free memory, because every rank holds the same share and pool; give the group whole GPUs.

Level 4: Why does tensor parallelism add no KV capacity when the attention keeps one latent per token? Expected: that attention stores one compressed latent per token that cannot be split across heads, so every rank keeps the full cache; attention data parallelism gives each group its own requests and cache, so capacity grows with the groups.
wrongAnswers: "Tensor parallelism is the default way to use more GPUs." It is the way to make a model fit; when the model fits, data parallelism adds output with no traffic between copies, and tensor parallelism over PCIe can cost more than it saves.

"More copies always mean more throughput." Only when every copy has about the same pool; a pair where one copy had an eighth of the pool served less than one card, because the round-robin controller fed it half the requests.
"Pipeline parallelism is only for several machines." Inside one machine it is the choice when the GPUs lack a fast link or when the GPU count does not divide the model evenly.
"Any GPU count works with tensor parallelism." The size must divide the attention-head count of the model; otherwise use a tensor size of 1 and put the whole count into the pipeline size.
keyPoints: Use data-parallel replicas when model and cache fit on one GPU.
Use tensor parallelism with fast links and divisible head counts.
Use pipeline parallelism across unsuitable links or multiple machines.
Compare per-layer tensor communication with per-stage pipeline communication.

questions.title: At 32 concurrent users your L4 chat service streams badly: the P99 inter-token gap is 613 ms, and your target is 100 ms or less per token with a first token within 1 second. A teammate proposes --max-num-seqs 16 so that each step holds fewer requests. What do you expect, and what does the measurement say?
questions.answer: A cap does not make room for more users; it only chooses who waits. With the cap at 16 and 32 users, each stream got a little smoother, a median ITL of 69.8 against 80.5 ms and a P99 ITL of 595 against 613, but half the users waited in the queue, the median first token went from 1.8 to 12.3 s, and output fell 38 percent to 171.8 tokens per second. At 64 users no cap that the manual tried brought the P99 ITL under 1.1 s, so the fix on this card is fewer users per replica, not a cap.
followUps: Level 3: The cap run had a higher clock than the default run. Why does that matter for the conclusion? Expected: a higher clock should help the cap run, so the clock does not explain its 38 percent lower output; the loss belongs to the cap.

Level 3: How does SGLang decide to admit a request, and what happens when its forecast is wrong? Expected: a new request must fit its uncached prompt plus its remaining max_new_tokens, and running requests hold back their remaining output times a ratio that starts at 0.7 and falls to 0.098 over 600 decode steps; when the forecast is too bold the scheduler retracts running requests to the queue and they prefill again.

Level 4: The pool has room, the tail gap is still over target, and a cap only moves the wait. What is left? Expected: the GPU is full; add a GPU or a replica and put fewer users on each, enforce the knee in the client or the gateway, and read the P99 ITL when you pick an engine, because at the same output the two engines differed about twofold on the GB10.
wrongAnswers: "A cap on running requests makes room for more users." It only chooses who waits; at 32 users the cap of 16 moved the wait into the queue, with the first token at 12.3 s, and cost 38 percent of the output.
"Lower the maximum model length to help the queue." The pool stays the same size, so it does not help when the cache usage is near full; add room with an FP8 cache or FP8 weights.

"Clients should ask for a large max_new_tokens to be safe." The admission forecast reserves it; a client that asks for 4,096 tokens and uses 200 makes the reservation of every new request about 20 times too big, so fewer requests are admitted.

"A queue means the server is broken." A long queue with fast tokens is admission control doing its job; the five admitted requests in the small-pool run got 24 ms per token while the median user waited 27.9 s, and a retraction, not a queue, is the alarm.
keyPoints: Concurrency caps move excess users into the queue.
Smoother decode can come with much slower first tokens.
The stated cap reduced output while half the users waited.
Use fewer users per replica when caps cannot meet latency targets.

questions.title: Your Qwen/Qwen3-8B server in BF16 fits on one L4, but only with a small KV pool. The model's publisher also offers an FP8 checkpoint. When does the FP8 checkpoint pay, what does it do to speed, and what does our GSM8K check say about the cost?
questions.answer: FP8 weights store most parameters in 1 byte instead of 2, so they free memory that the engine gives to the KV pool, and on a GPU with FP8 math they also speed up the matrix work. On our clock-locked L4 with the pool held fixed, the FP8 checkpoint gave 284.7 against 208.8 output tokens per second at 32 users, 36 percent more, and cut the time per token by 30 percent. On 500 GSM8K questions it scored 90.6 percent against 91.8 in BF16, 1.2 points lower with overlapping intervals, so the run did not show a loss and cannot rule out a few points.
followUps: Level 3: The pool was held fixed in the speed test. What did that hide, and what did it show? Expected: it hid the larger pool that FP8 frees, so the test shows only the change in speed; the gain in room comes from the bytes, and the SGLang run that let the pool grow went from 24,094 to 142,369 tokens with an FP8 cache too.

Level 3: Why was the one-user row not compared? Expected: the BF16 run fell to 210 MHz, below the 900 MHz lock, because the GPU throttled; a lock caps the clock and cannot stop a throttle, so the two runs were at different clocks.

Level 4: On the GB10 the FP8 pair nearly doubled the speed at every load, while a field report of an FP8 cache alone was a little slower per token. Reconcile the two. Expected: the GB10 decodes from a memory with modest bandwidth, so half the weight bytes gave almost twice the speed; an FP8 cache alone changes no weight bytes and adds the scale work, so it wins on capacity and not on speed per token.
wrongAnswers: "FP8 always speeds up decode." Only on a GPU with FP8 math, such as Ada, Hopper and Blackwell; on an A100 vLLM keeps the weights in FP8 and runs a weight-only kernel, so you keep the memory saving and expect less speed gain.

"Pass --quantization fp8 to be safe." vLLM reads the method from the checkpoint config, and in SGLang a flag that does not match the checkpoint raises at startup, so pass no flag for a published checkpoint.

"A 1.2 point drop on GSM8K means FP8 loses accuracy." The two intervals overlap, so this run did not show a difference; it also cannot rule out a loss of a few points, which is why you run your own prompts on both checkpoints.

"If FP8 is good, 4-bit is twice as good." A 4-bit model can lose more accuracy than an FP8 model, and the loss depends on the model and the method; use it when the model does not fit in FP8, such as a 14B model on a 24 GB card, and test it.
keyPoints: FP8 weights halve most parameter storage.
Freed memory can enlarge the KV pool.
FP8-capable hardware can also accelerate matrix work.
Measure throughput and task accuracy with intervals before judging the trade-off.

questions.title: You serve a chat model on one GPU. A load sweep shows output throughput that still rises at a cap of 64 concurrent requests, so the team wants to set the cap to 64. The product needs the first token in under one second and a steady stream of text after it. Which cap do you pick, and how do you defend it?
questions.answer: Pick the cap from goodput, not from throughput. Goodput counts only the requests that meet every latency target, so it falls to zero long before throughput stops rising. On the sweep in the SGLang manual, BF16 goodput was highest at a cap of 4 and was 0 from a cap of 8. Use the throughput curve only to explain the choice.
followUps: Level 2: What is the difference between throughput and goodput? Expected: throughput counts all tokens or requests per second; goodput counts only the requests that met every latency target.
Level 3: Why can a closed-loop cap never show a growing queue? Expected: each client waits for its answer before it sends the next request, so the server never receives more work than it finishes.

Level 3: FP8 holds the target at a cap of 16 and BF16 does not. What do you check before you switch the build? Expected: output quality on your own eval, and the KV pool size, because FP8 frees memory for a larger pool.

Level 4: The GPU gets hot at high load. How does that change your sweep? Expected: record the GPU clock and the thermal state with every run, and let the GPU cool to a fixed temperature before each run.
wrongAnswers: "Set the cap where throughput peaks." The throughput curve had no peak inside the sweep, and every BF16 request missed the target from a cap of 8.
"Use the median TTFT alone." A median can hide a slow half of the requests, and the time per token can fail while the first token is fast.
"Report goodput from one run." One run can be wrong for reasons you never see, so use three seeds and report the range.
keyPoints: Goodput counts requests meeting all latency targets.
Goodput can collapse while throughput still rises.
Choose the concurrency cap at goodput's peak.
Use throughput curves to explain rather than determine that choice.

questions.title: Your evaluation team wants bit-identical outputs from the live server and asks you to enable batch invariance for all traffic. What does it change, what does it cost, and what would you say?
questions.answer: The mode replaces the kernels that split their sums by the batch size with kernels that keep one reduction order, so one request gives the same logits alone and in a batch. It costs speed, most at low concurrency: on our L4 the small model paid 2.4 times the time per token at one user and 1.4 times at 32, and Qwen3-8B paid 1.4 times at 8 users with 27 percent less output. I would turn it on for evaluation and rollout servers and leave it off for production traffic, after I measured the cost at the concurrency we serve, because on SGLang with the default backend it also turns prefix caching off.
followUps: Level 3: Why did the relative cost shrink at higher concurrency? Expected: the invariant kernels give up the fast splits that an idle GPU would use, and that loss is a larger share of a small step; with more rows per step the fixed order costs a smaller share, 1.4 times at 32 users against 2.4 at one.

Level 3: On SGLang the 18 percent understates the cost for a chat workload. Why? Expected: with the default attention backend deterministic mode turns the radix cache off, so every repeated prefix pays its full prefill again; pick a backend that keeps the cache where the GPU supports it.

Level 4: Two servers both run the mode and still give different greedy text for one prompt. Name three causes. Expected: different hardware or engine version; a model path the mode does not cover, such as an attention layer that picks its own backend or a hybrid state-space layer; and kernel autotuning that picked different tactics on each start.
wrongAnswers: "The mode has no cost when the GPU is idle." The cost is largest at low concurrency, 2.4 times the time per token at one user on the small model, because the invariant kernels give up the fast splits that an idle GPU would use.

"Turn it on for production, because correctness comes first." Production traffic gains more from prefix caching and fast kernels than from identical bits; the manual's position is to use the mode for rollouts and evaluations and to measure the cost at the concurrency you serve.

"The flag covers every model." At 0.31.0 a model that picks its own attention backend skips the check, hybrid state-space layers are not covered, and a fix for expert models under compile is not in the next release; test the exact setup.

"The seed 42 makes sampled requests reproducible." It makes every request without a sampling_seed draw the same random numbers, which is reproducible and also identical across users; set a sampling_seed per request that must reproduce.
keyPoints: Batch-invariant kernels keep a fixed reduction order.
They stabilize logits across different batch sizes.
Measure the speed penalty at real serving concurrency.
Use for evaluation or rollouts and check prefix-cache backend effects.

questions.title: A vLLM server runs Qwen/Qwen3-8B with an EAGLE3 draft of depth 3. Over a run of answers near 2,000 tokens at 8 users, the counters show that the draft at position one was accepted with probability 0.77, position two with 0.54, and position three with 0.38. Estimate the mean number of tokens that one verify pass commits, and say what you would check before you rely on that gain for long answers.
questions.answer: Each verify pass commits the accepted drafts plus one bonus token from the target, so the mean acceptance length is one plus the sum of the per-position acceptance rates. With 0.77, 0.54 and 0.38 that is about 2.69 tokens per pass, which is the value vLLM reported on GSM8K in that run. Before I trust it on long answers I would read the acceptance of the longest answers alone, with real output lengths and without ignore-eos, because another study saw the acceptance fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 on answers that ran toward 20,000 tokens.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the bonus token always there? Expected: the target computes a distribution one position past the last accepted draft, so even when every draft is rejected the pass still writes one token of its own, as plain decoding would.

Level 3: The ShareGPT rates were 0.67, 0.42 and 0.26. What length do you get, and why is it below GSM8K? Expected: 2.35; open chat is harder for the draft to predict than math steps and code, so fewer drafts match the target.

Level 4: Acceptance was 3.2 at 1k input tokens and 1.2 at 10k on a draft with 2,048 positions. Cause and fix? Expected: the draft could not read past its position limit, so its guesses degrade with the prompt length; the rope scaling and the longer position count in the draft config fixed it, and the override variable only removes the check.
wrongAnswers: "The mean acceptance length is the mean of the three rates." It is the expected count of accepted drafts, the sum of the rates, plus the bonus token; 0.77 plus 0.54 plus 0.38 plus one is 2.69, not a value below one.

"An acceptance length of 2.69 means 2.69 times the speed." Each pass also pays the draft steps and the check; on the L4 the dense model gave each token 1.6 to 2.3 times faster and no more output from 32 users, because the draft took pool space.

"A long answer keeps the acceptance of a short one." In the manual's own test to 4,096 tokens it did, but another study saw it fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 toward 20,000 tokens, and a draft with too few positions fell from 3.2 to 1.2 with the prompt length; read your own long answers.

questions.title: You turn on an EAGLE3 draft for Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 and must set num_speculative_tokens. The draft config suggests a value, but you want to set it yourself. How do you choose, and how does the right value move with the number of users?
questions.answer: Set the depth yourself and sweep it at your real concurrency, because the depth that pays falls as more users share each step. On our clock-locked L4 at 32 users, depth 3 gave 333.6 output tokens per second against 208.8 with no speculation, and depth 5 fell back to 289.5, so the extra guesses cost more than they returned. At one user depths 3 and 5 tied, so start at 3 and move only on a measurement.
followUps: Level 3: Why did depth 5 lose to depth 3 at 32 users but tie at one user? Expected: at one user the step has spare compute, so two more guesses are nearly free; at 32 users the step is full, and each rejected guess takes compute from real tokens.

Level 3: The median time per token fell and users still said the stream felt uneven. Why? Expected: each step now sends several tokens at once, so tokens arrive in larger and less frequent groups; the median ITL rose from 84 to 133 ms at depth 3 with 32 users.

Level 4: Your load swings from 2 users at night to 32 by day. What do you set? Expected: sweep the depth at both loads, because the depth that pays falls with the batch; vLLM can set the depth per batch size, which the manual did not test, so measure before you trust it.
wrongAnswers: "Deeper is better, because more guesses mean more tokens per step." At 32 users depth 5 gave 289.5 tokens per second against 333.6 at depth 3; the extra guesses cost more compute than they returned.
"Leave the depth out and let the draft config decide." Then you do not know what runs; set it yourself so that the number in the command is the number you measured.

"Compare speculation with the baseline at one user and ship the ratio." The one-user baseline ran at 210 MHz while the EAGLE3 run ran near 1,400 MHz, so the ratio measured the clock; compare at the same clock and at the concurrency you serve.

"The gain on the random dataset transfers to chat." Synthetic prompts overstate the gain and the acceptance can fall on long answers; measure the acceptance on your own traffic with real output lengths and without ignore-eos.

questions.title: Long prompts make the stream pause for the other users of your SGLang server. A tuning page says to lower --chunked-prefill-size, so that decode steps run more often between the pieces of a long prompt. Would you follow it? What did the manual find when it tried, and what would you try instead?
questions.answer: Not without a measurement, because the small chunk did not help on either card in the manual's runs. On the GB10 at a low arrival rate a chunk of 1,024 made the P99 ITL worse, 1,977 against 929 ms with the default of 8,192, and at higher rates all chunk sizes tied. I would first try --enable-mixed-chunk, which puts the decode tokens into the prefill batch, and measure its trade: on the GB10 it cut the P99 ITL by 15 to 19 percent and at 1 and 2 requests per second it raised the median first token by 49 to 74 percent.
followUps: Level 3: Why would a small chunk cost more when the model routes each token to a few experts than on a dense model? Expected: each chunk reads the chosen expert weights again, so four chunks can read the experts four times; a dense model reads the same weights once per step either way.

Level 3: On the L4 neither flag moved the stream. Why not? Expected: the card could not keep up with the prompts, so prefill won every turn it could; a smaller chunk only added prefill turns ahead of the decode steps, and the fix is more prefill capacity or fewer long prompts per second.

Level 4: You raise the chunk to 8,192 on the L4 and the server dies at startup with an assert that asks you to report a bug. What happened? Expected: the prefill graph for 8,192 tokens needed more memory than the 2.33 GB that the pool left; the assert is the last line, and the out-of-memory line above it is the cause.
wrongAnswers: "Smaller chunks always smooth the stream." On the GB10 at 0.5 requests per second the 1,024 chunk raised the P99 ITL from 929 to 1,977 ms, and at higher rates the sizes tied.
"The mixed chunk is free." It traded a smoother stream for a slower first token: the median TTFT rose 49 to 74 percent at 1 and 2 requests per second on the GB10.
"The PyTorch assert at startup is a PyTorch bug." The real error is the out-of-memory line two lines above it; the prefill graph for the larger chunk did not fit in the memory that the pool left.
"A bigger chunk needs no more memory because the pool is the same." The pool stayed at 24,094 tokens, but the captured prefill graph for 8,192 tokens needed more than the 2.33 GB that remained.

questions.title: A teammate benchmarked EAGLE-3 on Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 with the random dataset and saw the time per token fall by half at 8 users. In production, with 32 concurrent chat users, the output throughput did not rise and the first token came later. The acceptance length in the log looks fine. What happened?
questions.answer: Two things, and the acceptance length hides both. On a 24 GB card the draft weights took pool space: the KV pool fell from 24,094 to 9,951 tokens, about 15 of the 640-token requests, so at 32 users most requests waited for a slot and the median first token went from 2,970 to 8,040 ms. The dataset also matters: at 32 users EAGLE-3 gave 1.6 times the output on GSM8K and code prompts and no more output on the random set or on ShareGPT, because the draft only pays when the GPU has idle time to spend on guesses.
followUps: Level 3: The log showed 2.73 accepted tokens per step whatever the load. Why did that not predict the throughput? Expected: acceptance measures how well the draft guesses, not whether the GPU has idle time for the guesses or whether the pool has room; the draft took pool space, the queue grew, so each token was faster and the server was not.

Level 3: Which startup lines should the teammate have read? Expected: the allocated KV cache line, 9,951 tokens against 24,094 without the draft, and the running-request cap of 48 that speculation sets when you do not.

Level 4: On the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B the gain held at 64 users. Why would an expert model behave differently? Expected: a dense model reads all its weights per step and a larger batch already uses the spare compute; the expert model reads only the experts that the step's tokens chose, and the verify pass scores four positions with weights it already read, so the gain held at 1.56 times or more; the manual calls this a reading from one model and one GPU.
wrongAnswers: "The acceptance length is fine, so speculation is working." It measures the draft's guesses, not the server; on the L4 each token came 1.6 to 2.3 times faster at every load and the server delivered no more tokens per second from 32 users.

"Random prompts are real text, so the benchmark is realistic." The random set cuts or repeats the first turn of ShareGPT conversations to 512 tokens with the end token ignored; on GSM8K and code prompts speculation gave 1.6 times the output at 32 users, and on ShareGPT it gave none.
"Raise --max-running-requests to let more users in." On the L4 the pool held about 15 requests, so a higher cap changes nothing; the pool was the limit, and the draft took nearly 60 percent of it.
"Use NGRAM instead, it needs no draft weights." It helped only on GSM8K and code, by about 1.1 to 1.2 times at 8 users, and on the other two sets it was slower with a P99 ITL of 244 to 779 ms.

questions.title: A teammate proposes --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 so that long prompts get their first token sooner. The server runs a model with mixture-of-experts layers on one card. Requests arrive at about half a request per second, with prompts between 1,024 and 4,096 tokens. What do you expect to change, and what would you measure before you accept the change?
questions.answer: A larger budget lets a long prompt finish its prefill in fewer steps, but each of those steps takes longer, and every running stream waits for it. At low load I expect a faster first token and a worse P99 ITL, and I would measure both with several seeds at the real request rate. On our GB10 at 0.5 requests per second, 16,384 raised the P99 ITL from 574 to 798 ms, while the first-token gain did not clear the seed spread.
followUps: Level 3: At the two higher rates the budgets tied. Why does the difference vanish as the rate rises? Expected: more requests share each step, so one long prompt fills a smaller share of the budget and its chunking matters less.

Level 3: Both budgets gave a later first token at the lowest rate than at the next rate up. How do you report that? Expected: all three seeds agreed, so it is not one slow seed; the cause was not found, so it stays an open result and no rule is built on it.

Level 4: Is there one budget that wins at every load? Expected: no; a large budget wins when prefill pressure is low and a small one when several prefills compete with streams, so the value must move with the load.
wrongAnswers: "A larger budget is free because the GPU has spare compute at low load." Each step with a bigger chunk takes longer and every running stream waits for it; the P99 ITL rose 39 percent at 0.5 requests per second.
"Set the budget once from the GPU size and leave it." The best value moved with the request rate in these runs, so measure at your real rate and again when the load changes.
"The drop from 1,145 to 906 ms proves the first-token gain." The seed ranges of the first token overlapped, so the cost is confirmed and the gain is not.

questions.title: You add a second L4 to an SGLang server with --dp-size 2 and expect about twice the throughput. The sweep shows less than one card gave: at 64 users the pair peaks at 64 tokens per second and falls to 42, and the P99 first token is 391 seconds against 33.4 on one card. Both copies loaded the weights without an error. What do you check, and what went wrong?
questions.answer: Read the KV Cache is allocated line of every DP rank before you trust the sum. On that pair the second card ran two pods of another team, so its copy had 3.17 GB free after the weights against 6.59 GB and a pool of 2,925 tokens against 24,094, an eighth of the first. The round-robin controller does not look at pools, so it sent every second request to the small copy, where 4 ran and 59 waited, while the large copy held one to three requests and used 2 to 7 percent of its pool.
followUps: Level 3: Why did the large copy sit almost idle while 59 requests waited? Expected: the benchmark is a closed loop with 64 open requests, round robin put half of them on the small copy, and the client could not send new work to the large copy until the small copy returned a slot.

Level 3: Why did a tensor split refuse the same pair while the data-parallel pair started? Expected: tensor parallelism checks that every rank has at least 90 percent of the local free memory, because every rank holds the same share and pool, and the shared card had 18.28 GB against the 19.53 GB required; data parallelism sizes each copy's pool on its own and has no such check.

Level 4: Routing by total tokens lifted the pair to 114.7 at 64 users. Is the problem solved? Expected: no; one card alone gave 250.9, the token-routed run also had a higher clock than the round-robin run so part of the gain is the card, and the fix is equal pools, with whole GPUs for each copy or separate servers behind a gateway with weights.
wrongAnswers: "Both copies loaded, so the second card is fine." The weights need 15.28 GB on each card; the pool is sized from what is left, and the shared card had 3.17 GB left against 6.59, an eighth of the pool.

"The controller balances load, so a slow copy gets fewer requests." The default round robin does not look at pools or queues; it alternated requests, so 63 of 64 open requests ended on the small copy.

"The pair is slower because of the clock, so run it again when the card is cool." The pair did run under the clock floor at 32 and 64 users, but it was already 16 to 41 percent slower up to 4 users, and the log shows 59 requests waiting on one copy; the pool explains the shape and the clock explains part of the size.

questions.title: Your chat users see a smooth stream until someone pastes a long document, and then every stream pauses while the server prefills it. A colleague proposes prefill-decode disaggregation: separate prefill servers and decode servers. When does that split pay, what does it not do, and how would you decide?
questions.answer: Split prefill from decode when the measured problem is the tail of the inter-token latency and long prompts cause it, because a prefill server then never shares a step with a stream. It does not raise throughput: the documentation says so, it costs a KV transfer for every request plus more servers and a router, and a 2025 study found that even the tail gain depends on the load and on the path that moves the cache. Decide with a measurement: one server first, then copies behind a gateway, and the split last, compared with the same GPUs run as plain servers at your real load.
followUps: Level 3: On the same GPUs, the split pair's first token arrives later than the plain server's. What do you suspect first? Expected: the transfer path, an old transfer library or a router timeout; one incident fixed it with an upgrade, and only the single-server baseline showed that the split made it worse.

Level 3: Prefill logs aborts at a load of 64 users and works at 4 to 7. Where is the fault? Expected: in the router or client timeouts, which aborted requests that were still running, not in the transfer; a later fix lengthened the router timeout.

Level 4: How do you pick the ratio of prefill to decode servers? Expected: from your prompt and answer lengths and your concurrency; long prompts with short answers need more prefill and the reverse more decode; one test found one prefill for three decode servers won at high concurrency and three to one or two to two gave a better first token at low concurrency, so measure both sides and move one server at a time.
wrongAnswers: "Disaggregation raises throughput." The documentation says it does not; it gives control over the first token and the stream as two numbers and costs a KV transfer per request and more servers.

"Send requests straight to the decode server to skip the router." The scheduler asserts that a bootstrap room exists and tells you to send requests to the router; the room is how the two servers find each other's half of one request.
"A failed transfer falls back to a normal prefill." The vLLM default policy fails the request; set the failure policy to recompute if you want the decode server to compute the prompt again.

"Chunked prefill already solves this." It makes the pause shorter but cannot remove it, because the chunk still shares the step with the running decodes; the split removes the sharing at the cost of a transfer and a second set of failures.

questions.title: Design the serving layer for a chat product on a fleet of L4 cards with Qwen/Qwen3-8B. The target is a first token within 1 second and 100 ms or less per token for the P99 user. Every request shares a 2,048-token system prompt, and sessions run for several turns. How many users per card, which precision, which caps, and what do you measure before launch?
questions.answer: Size from the pool and the knee, not from throughput. In BF16 the 24,094-token pool on an L4 holds about 37 requests of 640 tokens, and with a cache reset the P99 gap between tokens at 16 users was already 522 ms, so a BF16 replica meets the target for well under 16 users; the FP8 checkpoint with an FP8 cache grows the pool to 142,369 tokens and served 2.87 requests per second within the same target at 64 users, where BF16 served none. So I would serve FP8 after an accuracy check on our prompts, put the shared system prompt first so that the cache holds it, keep the pool large enough for the sessions that return, cap users per replica at the measured knee in the gateway, and run the sweep with a flush, a clock record and a mixed length distribution before launch.
followUps: Level 3: Why not take the user count from the throughput peak of the sweep? Expected: throughput peaked at 32 users while no request met the target there, and the knee with a reset was between 8 and 16 users; goodput at the target sets the limit and throughput only explains it.

Level 4: The product adds long sessions that return after minutes. What changes? Expected: the working set grows past the GPU pool, the default eviction drops each session just before it returns, and the hit rate collapses, about 1.5 percent at later turns in an 8,192-token pool; grow the pool first, route each session to the same replica, and add a host tier only when the working set is larger than the GPU pool and smaller than the GPU and host pools together.

Level 4: Traffic doubles for an hour. What protects the users? Expected: a limit at the gateway that sheds or queues above the knee, because the engine admits until memory runs out and a cap on the engine only moves the wait to the first token, and because a passively cooled L4 under overload also loses clock, from 1,320 to 465 MHz, so overload costs throughput as well as latency.
wrongAnswers: "Run 32 users per card; the sweep showed 275 tokens per second there." No request met the target at 32 users, where the P99 ITL was 613 ms; the knee with a cache reset was between 8 and 16 users.

"Keep BF16, FP8 is a quality risk we cannot take." On 500 GSM8K questions every FP8 interval overlapped BF16, and FP8 was the difference between zero and 2.87 requests per second within target at 64 users; run the check on your prompts and decide on evidence.
"Set the engine cap at the knee and you are done." The engine cap only chooses who waits and moved the first token to 12.3 s at 32 users; enforce the knee in the gateway and shed load above it.

"Benchmark with fixed 512-token prompts, that is the standard." Fixed lengths form waves and gave a first token of 1,996 ms with a P99 ITL of 82 ms, while mixed lengths gave 291 and 300 ms; test your real length mix before you set the limit.

questions.title: On one L4 with Qwen/Qwen3-8B and the same 24,096-token pool, a closed-loop sweep at 64 users gives vLLM 241 tokens of output per second and SGLang 257, so the engines tie on throughput. Yet the chat team says one of them is unusable at that load and the other is fine. What are they seeing, and which engine do you choose for chat?
questions.answer: They are seeing two different choices at a full pool. At 64 users vLLM ran 40 requests and kept 11 waiting with its pool 99.5 percent full, so its first token came 1.7 times sooner, 10,953 against 18,356 ms, but each new prefill shared the step with the running decodes and the P99 gap between tokens was 1,363 ms against 114 on SGLang, which ran 37 requests and kept 27 waiting. For chat, read the P99 ITL next to the first token at your real load and traffic shape, because the two engines pick different sides of that trade by default, and one flag on SGLang moved its side.
followUps: Level 3: Why did vLLM give the sooner first token and the worse stream at the same throughput? Expected: it admitted more requests, 40 against 37, and filled 99.5 percent of its pool while it prefilled new prompts at 460 tokens per second; each new prefill shared the step with the running decodes, so the streams stalled while the first tokens came sooner.

Level 4: With mixed prompt lengths vLLM led on the stream, and then SGLang tied it. What changed? Expected: the mixed-chunk flag put the running decodes into the prefill batch, so a new prompt no longer stopped the stream; the P99 ITL fell from 363 to 193 ms with mixed lengths, and the cost was a worse P99 ITL with fixed lengths, 81 to 203 ms, because whole waves then shared steps with decodes.

Level 4: A published comparison shows one engine 29 percent ahead. What do you ask before you believe it? Expected: the versions and the date, whether the workload matches yours including the share of repeated prefix, whether the memory budgets and context flags were matched, whether the concurrency passed the decode graph limit, whether the flags were mapped correctly, and who paid for the test.
wrongAnswers: "They tie on throughput, so pick either." At 64 users the P99 gap between tokens was 1,363 ms on one and 114 on the other at the same output; for chat that is the number the users feel.
"The engine with the sooner first token is better for chat." It bought the first token with stalls in the stream; the P99 ITL was 12 times higher, and no cap fixed it; read both numbers.

"The faster engine in the benchmark is faster." Compare only at matched pools and clocks; one published test left one engine at its automatic memory fraction and the other at 0.9 of GPU memory, so the two pools differed.

"The result transfers to our mixed traffic." The winner changed with the traffic shape: at a full pool and in waves one engine protected the stream, with mixed lengths the other led by default, and one flag removed that lead; measure your own length mix.

topics.title: GPU memory, quantization and hardware
topics.about: Where GPU memory goes, how quantization frees it, and how work splits across GPUs.

questions.title: How do weight-only and weight-activation quantization techniques like AWQ, GPTQ, and FP8 work?
questions.answer: Weight-only quantization compresses just the stored weights, which reduces size and memory with a simple process, and is common for GPU serving. Weight-activation quantization also quantizes activations at runtime. It can reduce computation further, but activations contain outliers that hurt accuracy if they are quantized naively. Methods such as SmoothQuant and AWQ handle this by protecting the salient weights and channels. Smaller models also need less memory bandwidth, which speeds up inference, so always measure accuracy against your speed gain.
keyPoints: Weight-only quantization compresses stored parameters.
Weight-activation quantization also compresses runtime activations.
Activation outliers require protection such as SmoothQuant or AWQ.
Measure accuracy alongside bandwidth and speed gains.

questions.title: How many parameters are in a fully connected layer from 4,096 inputs to 4,096 outputs, with a bias?
questions.answer: Weights: 4,096 × 4,096 = 16,777,216. Biases: 4,096. Total 16,781,312. A transformer block has several of these (the attention projections and the MLP), which is where most of a model's parameters live.
keyPoints: Multiply 4,096 input features by 4,096 outputs.
The weight matrix has 16,777,216 parameters.
Add 4,096 bias parameters for 16,781,312 total.
Transformer attention projections and MLPs contain several such layers.

questions.title: A 3×3 convolution takes 64 input channels to 128 output channels, with a bias. How many parameters?
questions.answer: Each output channel has a 3 × 3 × 64 filter, plus a bias: 128 × (576 + 1) = 73,856. The image size doesn't appear anywhere. A convolution's parameters are shared across every position.
keyPoints: Each output channel has a 3 by 3 by 64 filter.
Add one bias per output channel.
Compute 128 times 577 to obtain 73,856 parameters.
Spatial image size does not change shared convolution parameters.

questions.title: How much GPU memory do the weights alone of a 7-billion-parameter model take in bf16? (In GB, where 1 GB is 10⁹ bytes.)
questions.answer: bf16 uses 2 bytes per parameter: 7 × 10⁹ × 2 = 14 GB. That's only the weights. Serving also needs memory for the KV cache and activations, and training needs far more.
keyPoints: BF16 uses two bytes per parameter.
Seven billion parameters occupy 14 GB.
Serving also needs KV cache and activation memory.
Training requires more than weight storage alone.

questions.title: Training that 7B model with Adam in mixed precision: bf16 weights and gradients (2 bytes each), plus fp32 master weights and Adam's two moments (4 bytes each). How much memory before activations? (GB, 10⁹ bytes.)
questions.answer: Per parameter: 2 (weights) + 2 (gradients) + 4 (master copy) + 4 (first moment) + 4 (second moment) = 16 bytes. 7 × 10⁹ × 16 = 112 GB, before a single activation. That's why full fine-tuning a 7B model needs several GPUs or sharding (ZeRO, FSDP), and why LoRA is popular.
keyPoints: Count weights, gradients, master weights and two Adam moments.
The stated layout uses sixteen bytes per parameter.
Seven billion parameters need 112 GB before activations.
Use sharding or LoRA to reduce full-fine-tuning memory demands.

questions.title: Training runs out of memory at batch size 32. You want to keep an effective batch of 32. What do you do?
questions.answer: Activation memory scales with the micro-batch size. Gradient accumulation splits the batch, accumulates gradients over several forward/backward passes, then calls optimizer.step() once, which is mathematically the same update (apart from batch-norm statistics). Combine it with activation checkpointing (recompute activations during backward) and mixed precision if you need more room.
options: Lower the learning rate.
Use a smaller learning-rate warmup.
Gradient accumulation: run 4 micro-batches of 8, summing the gradients, then step once.
Train fewer epochs.
keyPoints: Activation memory scales with micro-batch size.
Accumulate gradients across multiple forward and backward passes.
Step the optimizer once per accumulated batch, with batch-norm caveats.
Add checkpointing and mixed precision for further memory savings.

questions.title: Each GPU processes a micro-batch of 8, you accumulate gradients over 16 micro-batches, and you train on 4 GPUs with data parallelism. What's the effective batch size?
questions.answer: Effective batch = micro-batch × accumulation steps × GPUs = 8 × 16 × 4 = 512. This is the number to use when you reason about the learning rate.
keyPoints: Effective batch multiplies micro-batch, accumulation steps and GPU count.
Use eight examples per micro-batch.
Sixteen accumulation steps across four GPUs gives 512 examples.
Use effective batch when reasoning about learning rate.

questions.title: You need to train on 1 billion tokens. Each GPU processes 50,000 tokens a second, and you have 8 of them. How many minutes does one pass take, ignoring overheads?
questions.answer: Throughput is 8 × 50,000 = 400,000 tokens a second. 1 × 10⁹ ÷ 400,000 = 2,500 seconds = 41.7 minutes. Real runs add data loading, evaluation, checkpointing and communication, so a budget 20–40% above this is common.
keyPoints: Eight GPUs at 50,000 tokens each give 400,000 tokens per second.
Divide one billion tokens by aggregate throughput.
The ideal run takes 2,500 seconds or 41.7 minutes.
Budget extra time for loading, evaluation, checkpointing and communication.

questions.title: Why do most large-model training runs now use bf16 rather than fp16?
questions.answer: Both are 16-bit. fp16 spends its bits on precision (10 stored mantissa bits) with a small range (max about 65,504). bf16 keeps fp32's 8-bit exponent, so its range matches fp32, and stores only 7 mantissa bits. Neural network training is far more sensitive to overflow and underflow than to low precision, so bf16 trains stably without loss scaling.
options: bf16 uses less memory than fp16.
bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so it rarely overflows and doesn't need loss scaling.
bf16 is more precise than fp16.
fp16 isn't supported on GPUs.
keyPoints: FP16 and BF16 both use sixteen bits.
FP16 has more mantissa precision but limited range.
BF16 uses the FP32 exponent range with seven mantissa bits.
BF16 avoids overflow sensitivity and usually needs no loss scaling.

questions.title: An image classifier scores 98% on validation and 81% on new photos. You find that augmented copies of the same originals appear in both the training and validation sets. What's the fix?
questions.answer: Any group of near-duplicates (augmentations, frames from the same video, photos from the same patient) must stay on one side of the split. Split first, by the group, then augment the training set only, ideally on the fly. Check for near-duplicates across splits with perceptual hashes or embedding similarity.
options: Stop augmenting.
Use a bigger validation set.
Use stronger augmentation.
Split by original image first, then augment only the training split.
keyPoints: Keep near-duplicate groups on one side of the split.
Split by patient, video or augmentation group first.
Augment training examples only, preferably on demand.
Check cross-split duplicates with perceptual hashes or embeddings.

questions.title: Why do activation outliers cause perplexity spikes in Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), and how does Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) mitigate them?
questions.answer: In large language models starting around 6 billion parameters, certain hidden state dimensions exhibit extreme activation values—often 20 to 100 times larger than normal activations. In Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), we quantize weights and activations on calibration data without full retraining. Because uniform quantization maps the entire dynamic range into a small integer grid (like INT8 with 256 levels), scaling down to accommodate these massive outliers crushes the precision of normal values, causing severe degradation and perplexity explosions. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) models quantization noise directly during fine-tuning. In the forward pass, weights and activations are quantized to low precision to simulate quantization error, but gradients in the backward pass are computed using the Straight-Through Estimator in FP32. The model weights learn to suppress activation spikes and distribute information across channels that tolerate low precision. The trade-off is compute cost versus precision: PTQ runs in minutes with zero labeled data, while QAT requires retraining cycles and labeled training sets.
followUps: How does SmoothQuant mathematically redistribute activation outliers into weight matrices prior to quantization?
Why do activation outliers concentrate in specific feature dimensions across all sequence tokens?
wrongAnswers: Clipping all activation outliers to zero during PTQ, which destroys essential linguistic representations and model coherence.
Assuming weights have large outliers, when transformer outliers are overwhelmingly concentrated in hidden activation states.
tradeOffs: PTQ quantizes models in minutes with minimal compute, but suffers accuracy loss when activation outliers exceed integer dynamic ranges.
QAT recovers full precision by adapting weights to quantization noise, but requires significant training compute and hyperparameter tuning.
keyPoints: Activation outliers expand quantization ranges and crush normal-value precision.
PTQ calibrates without full retraining.
QAT simulates quantization noise and uses a straight-through gradient estimator.
QAT adds retraining cost while improving tolerance to low precision.

questions.title: Compare weight-only quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) with weight-activation quantization (FP8, INT8) in terms of compute vs memory-bound inference.
questions.answer: The choice between weight-only quantization and weight-activation quantization depends on whether inference is memory-bandwidth bound or compute bound. In token generation decoding, the GPU loads billions of parameters to generate a single token, making execution memory-bandwidth bound. Weight-only quantization (such as AWQ or GPTQ at INT4) compresses model weights in VRAM by four times. During matrix multiplication, weights are transferred from GPU memory in 4-bit and dequantized into FP16 in registers before computation. This speeds up decoding significantly without quantizing activations. During prompt prefill or large-batch serving, matrix multiplications are compute-bound on tensor cores. Weight-activation quantization (such as FP8 or SmoothQuant INT8) quantizes both weights and activations. Matrix multiplications execute directly on dedicated low-precision tensor cores, doubling compute throughput. The trade-off is numerical sensitivity versus speedup profile: weight-only quantization preserves output quality easily and accelerates single-user decoding, while weight-activation quantization accelerates prefill compute but requires careful outlier management.
followUps: Why is token decoding memory-bound while prompt prefill is compute-bound?
How does Activation-aware Weight Quantization (AWQ) protect the top 1% most salient weight channels?
wrongAnswers: Expecting weight-only quantization to double matrix multiplication FLOP throughput on GPU tensor cores.
Applying INT4 weight-activation quantization without calibration, which results in catastrophic output collapse.
tradeOffs: Weight-only quantization accelerates memory-bound decoding and cuts VRAM usage with minimal accuracy loss, but does not accelerate compute-bound prefill.
Weight-activation quantization doubles tensor core compute throughput for large batches, but requires outlier suppression to avoid perplexity degradation.
keyPoints: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound while prefill and large batches are compute-bound.
Weight-only quantization reduces transferred weights and dequantizes for computation.
Weight-activation quantization uses low-precision tensor-core computation.
Quantizing activations requires careful outlier handling.

questions.title: What are the trade-offs of quantizing the KV cache to FP8 or INT4 in long-context transformer serving?
questions.answer: In long-context serving (such as 32k to 128k tokens), the KV cache consumes far more GPU VRAM than the model weights themselves. A 70-billion parameter model serving a single 64k request requires over 40 gigabytes of memory just for its KV cache in standard FP16. Quantizing the KV cache to FP8 cuts memory footprint in half, while INT4 reduces it by four times, enabling serving engines to support twice as many concurrent users or double sequence lengths on the same GPU. However, attention keys and values have differing numerical tolerances. Keys determine attention score distributions: quantizing keys too aggressively alters softmax probabilities, causing the model to miss needle-in-a-haystack facts across long contexts. Values directly scale the attended output vectors and are somewhat more tolerant of quantization noise. Modern runtimes apply per-token or per-head dynamic scaling factors. The trade-off is context concurrency versus retrieval accuracy: FP8 KV caching preserves virtually full model quality with 2x memory savings, whereas INT4 requires calibration and can impair long-context reasoning.
followUps: Why does quantizing attention keys cause more retrieval errors than quantizing attention values?
How do you implement dynamic per-token scaling for FP8 KV cache blocks in custom CUDA kernels?
wrongAnswers: Quantizing weights to 4-bit while leaving KV cache in FP16 for 128k context lengths, leading to immediate out-of-memory errors on concurrent batches.
Using static global quantization scaling for KV cache tensors across thousands of diverse document tokens.
tradeOffs: FP8 KV caching cuts memory by 50% with negligible loss in perplexity, enabling doubled batch concurrency.
INT4 KV caching delivers 4x memory compression, but requires per-channel scaling to prevent severe degradation on long-context retrieval tasks.
keyPoints: Long-context KV caches can dominate memory usage.
FP8 halves cache memory while INT4 reduces it further.
Key quantization perturbs attention scores and can harm retrieval.
Use dynamic scaling and validate concurrency gains against long-context quality.

questions.title: Compare per-tensor, per-channel, and per-token dynamic scaling factors for activation quantization in transformer inference.
questions.answer: Quantization maps continuous floating-point numbers to discrete integer grids using a scaling factor. The granularity of this scaling factor determines how well quantization handles variations across layers and tokens. Per-tensor scaling uses a single scale factor for the entire activation tensor. If a single token in a long prompt contains a large activation outlier, the entire tensor's scale factor expands, crushing the precision of all other tokens. Per-channel scaling computes a separate scale factor for each feature dimension across all tokens. This handles features that are consistently large across time, but cannot adapt when activations spike unexpectedly on specific tokens. Per-token dynamic scaling calculates the scale factor on the fly for each individual token vector during the forward pass. This isolates token outliers completely: an outlier token scales within its own vector without degrading adjacent tokens. The trade-off is kernel computation overhead versus quantization precision: per-token scaling requires computing vector maximums dynamically in SRAM, but it provides the highest accuracy retention for 8-bit serving.
followUps: How does fused kernel execution hide the reduction latency of calculating per-token dynamic scales?
When is grouped per-block scaling (e.g. block size 128) preferred over pure per-channel scaling?
wrongAnswers: Using a single static per-tensor scaling factor for activations across diverse multi-turn user requests.
Assuming per-token dynamic scaling requires a full extra memory round-trip to GPU DRAM, missing that reductions happen in on-chip SRAM.
tradeOffs: Per-token dynamic scaling isolates activation spikes to individual tokens, preventing global precision collapse with minimal accuracy loss.
Calculating scale factors dynamically in custom kernels adds minor reduction overhead compared to pre-computed static scales.
keyPoints: Per-tensor scales let a single outlier reduce precision for all tokens.
Per-channel scales handle consistently large feature dimensions.
Per-token dynamic scales isolate token-specific outliers.
Dynamic scale computation adds kernel overhead.

questions.title: How does QLoRA combine 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), double quantization, and paged optimizers to fine-tune large models on a single GPU?
questions.answer: Fine-tuning large models requires immense GPU memory to store model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states. QLoRA enables fine-tuning a 70-billion parameter model on a single 80-gigabyte GPU through three innovations. First is 4-bit NormalFloat: pre-trained neural network weights follow a zero-mean normal distribution. NF4 constructs an information-theoretically optimal quantile grid where each bin has equal probability under a normal distribution, achieving lower quantization error than standard linear INT4. Second is Double Quantization: quantizing weights into 64-element blocks requires storing floating-point scale factors. Double quantization quantizes these scale factors themselves into 8-bit integers, saving roughly 0.37 bits per parameter. Third is Paged Optimizers: when memory spikes during long-context gradient computation, memory blocks for the Adam optimizer are automatically paged over PCIe to host CPU memory. Low-rank adapter matrices (LoRA) remain in full 16-bit precision and receive gradient updates. The trade-off is fine-tuning memory versus training speed: QLoRA cuts memory by 4x, but dequantizing weights during forward and backward passes adds 20% to 30% execution time overhead.
followUps: Why must LoRA adapter weights remain in 16-bit precision rather than being quantized to 4-bit alongside the base model?
How does NF4 guarantee equal information density across all quantization bins for normally distributed weights?
wrongAnswers: Quantizing both the base model weights and the active LoRA adapter gradients to 4-bit, which causes training divergence.
Claiming QLoRA reduces inference latency compared to full models, missing that QLoRA is strictly a fine-tuning memory optimization.
tradeOffs: QLoRA reduces fine-tuning memory footprint by 4x, making frontier model tuning accessible on commodity GPUs.
On-the-fly dequantization of 4-bit weights into 16-bit registers during every forward and backward pass slows training throughput relative to native FP16.
keyPoints: NF4 uses a quantile grid suited to normally distributed weights.
Double quantization compresses the quantization scale factors.
Paged optimizers move optimizer memory to CPU during spikes.
Train full-precision LoRA adapters while accepting dequantization overhead.

questions.title: A teammate says: we quantized the 70B model to 4-bit, so it is 35 GB now and it fits on one 80 GB card with room to spare. What is missing from that sentence?
questions.answer: The KV cache. Weight quantization shrinks the weights, and the cache for the running requests is a separate budget that stays in BF16 or FP8 and grows with every token in flight; at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context the lesson puts it near 20 GB for a 70B model, plus about 5 GB of activations, so the total is about 60 GB on the 80 GB card. That 20 GB is the lesson's rough figure, so check it against the config: Llama-3.1-70B keeps 320 KiB per token in BF16, and 128 full 2k-token requests then need about four times the lesson's figure, which does not fit beside the weights on one 80 GB card. Count the weights, the cache at your peak concurrency and context, and the activations together, and read the pool size in the startup log after the start.
followUps: Level 1: Which three things take memory on a serving GPU? Expected: the weights, the KV cache for the tokens in flight, and the activations with the startup working memory; the engine gives the cache what is left after the other two.

Level 2: What does the KV cache grow with? Expected: the number of running requests and the context that each one holds, prompt plus output, so it grows with concurrency and with length, not with the weights.

Level 3: Quantizing the weights to 4-bit and quantizing the cache to FP8 are different decisions. Why? Expected: the weights are a fixed cost and their quantization changes the matrix math; the cache is per token and its quantization changes the attention values directly, so it needs its own accuracy check and its own scales.

Level 4: Where in the startup log do you confirm that the budget held? Expected: in the weight load line, the available KV cache memory line and the pool size line with its maximum concurrency; divide the pool by prompt plus output per user rather than by the maximum length.
wrongAnswers: "The model is 35 GB, so the rest is free for users." The KV cache and the activations take their share first; at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context the lesson puts the cache near 20 GB and the total near 60 GB.
"Quantizing the weights also shrinks the cache." The cache stays in its own dtype; it halves only if you quantize the cache, which is a separate choice with its own accuracy effect.
"The cache is small because the model is small." The bytes per token depend on the layers and the KV heads; a 30B expert model keeps 96 KiB per token and an 8B dense model 144 KiB.
keyPoints: Weight quantization does not shrink the separate KV budget.
KV usage grows with context and concurrent requests.
Recompute cache size from the actual model configuration.
Budget weights, peak cache and activations and inspect startup pool size.

questions.title: Your teammate starts Qwen/Qwen3-8B in BF16 on an L4 with no flags, and the start fails with an error about the KV cache and --max-model-len. The same command works on a larger card. Explain the failure with numbers, and say what you set.
questions.answer: The model config gives a context of 40,960 tokens, and vLLM takes that as the maximum length when you set none. At 144 KiB per token one request at that length needs 5.6 GiB of KV cache, and on a 24 GB card the 16.4 GB of weights can leave less than that, so the start check fails before the pool line prints. Set --max-model-len to the longest prompt plus answer that your users send; the pool stays the same size, and the limit only stops one request from claiming all of it.
followUps: Level 2: Does lowering the maximum model length give you more users? Expected: no; the pool stays the same size, and the limit only stops one request from taking all of it and lets the start check pass; more users need a bigger pool, from an FP8 cache, FP8 weights or a bigger card.

Level 3: The same model started last month and fails after an upgrade with the same flags. What do you check? Expected: the derived context length in the startup log; a release changed how the scaling method is read and shortened one model's length from 131,072 to 32,768, and a change the other way can make the check fail, so set the length yourself.

Level 4: Estimate the pool when the FP8 checkpoint replaces BF16 on the same card and the cache is FP8 too. Expected: the weights fall to 8.81 GB and leave 13.06 GB, and each token takes half the bytes, so the pool rose from 24,094 to 142,369 tokens in the manual's run.
wrongAnswers: "The card is too small for an 8B model." The weights fit with about 6.59 GB to spare; the check fails because one request at the default length of 40,960 tokens needs 5.6 GiB of cache, so set the length to what your users send.

"Raise the memory fraction to make it start." The gap between 5.6 GiB and the room left is larger than a fraction step can close on this card; the length is the lever, and a fraction set too high leaves nothing for the activations.
"Lower the maximum length to fit more users." It fits the start, not more users; the pool size does not change with the limit.
"The KV pool is sized from the weights." It is sized from what is left after the weights and the startup profile, so read the available KV memory line, not the parameter count.
keyPoints: The engine can inherit a 40,960-token model context limit.
At 144 KiB per token that needs about 5.6 GiB per request.
Weights can leave too little cache room on a 24 GB card.
Set max-model-len to the longest real prompt plus answer.

questions.title: You are given two model configs. Model A: 36 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128. Model B: 48 layers, 4 KV heads, head size 128, and almost four times the parameters. Estimate the KV cache bytes per token of each in BF16, say which one fits more users in a KV pool of the same size, and explain why the parameter count misled you if it did.
questions.answer: KV bytes per token are 2 times layers times KV heads times head size times bytes per value, where the 2 counts the key and the value. Model A, which is Qwen/Qwen3-8B, holds 2 x 36 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes, which is 144 KiB per token; model B, which is Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B, holds 2 x 48 x 4 x 128 x 2 bytes, which is 98,304 bytes or 96 KiB. The bigger model keeps fewer bytes per token and fits more users in the same pool, because the KV heads and the layers decide the cost and the parameter count does not. On one card the bigger model also needs room for weights almost four times larger, so its pool is smaller, and it can fit fewer users in total.
followUps: Level 2: Qwen3-0.6B has 28 layers and 8 KV heads with a head size of 128. What does one token cost, and what did the log say? Expected: 2 x 28 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes, 114,688 bytes or 112 KiB; the startup log printed bytes_per_slot=114688, so the formula and the log agree to the byte.

Level 3: A dense 70B model with 80 layers and 8 KV heads is split across 8 GPUs by tensor parallelism. What does each GPU hold per token? Expected: 320 KiB in total and 40 KiB on each GPU, because tensor parallelism splits the KV heads across the ranks.

Level 4: Why does the same split not help a latent-attention model? Expected: that attention stores one compressed latent per token, about 68.6 KiB for the 61-layer model, which cannot be split across heads; every rank stores the full latent, so eight GPUs hold eight copies and add no tokens.
wrongAnswers: "A bigger model always needs more KV cache per token." The layer count and the KV heads decide the cost; the 30B expert model keeps 96 KiB per token against 144 KiB for the 8B dense model.
"A small model needs a small cache." Qwen3-0.6B keeps 112 KiB per token, almost as much as an 8B model, because it has 28 layers and 8 KV heads.
"Tensor parallelism always adds KV capacity." It splits the KV heads of a grouped-query model, but a latent-attention model stores the full latent on every rank, so more ranks add no tokens.

"Count the weights and subtract from the card to get the cache." The engine also keeps a startup profile and graph memory; read the available KV memory and the pool size in the startup log, then divide by the bytes per token.
keyPoints: KV bytes equal two times layers, KV heads, head size and value bytes.
The stated 8B model needs 144 KiB per token.
The stated 30B model needs 96 KiB per token.
Total concurrency also depends on memory left after weight storage.

questions.title: A 14B model must run on a 24 GB card and does not fit in FP8 with a usable pool. You can choose AWQ, GPTQ, a checkpoint in the compressed-tensors format, bitsandbytes at load time, or a GGUF file. How do you pick, and what did the manual measure for each?
questions.answer: Pick a published 4-bit checkpoint over quantization at load time, and pick the format from the engine and the workload. For a GPU server AWQ with the Marlin kernels is the default, GPTQ when you also serve LoRA adapters on the base, and GGUF only for CPU or edge serving, because its kernels are not built for GPUs. The manual started an AWQ Qwen3-14B on an L4 with 9.44 GiB of weights and a pool of 36,272 tokens, loaded Qwen3-1.7B with bitsandbytes in 1.33 GiB against 3.22 GiB in BF16, which is 41 percent, and loaded a GGUF file of 0.55 GiB through a plugin that the documentation calls experimental.
followUps: Level 2: Why pick a published checkpoint over bitsandbytes at load time? Expected: load-time quantization adds load time and gives a checkpoint that nobody evaluated; a published checkpoint has a known method and often a published accuracy, and vLLM reads the method from its config with no flag.

Level 3: The bitsandbytes load saved 41 percent on a 1.7B model. Will a 14B model save the same share? Expected: not the same; the 41 percent includes the embeddings and the output layer, which stay in 16-bit, and they are a smaller share of a larger model, so the saving changes.

Level 3: You need LoRA adapters on the 4-bit base. Which format? Expected: GPTQ with the Marlin kernels, because it supports LoRA adapters in vLLM; the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026.

Level 4: A domain model quantized with AWQ on generic web text loses several points on its own eval. Why, and what do you do? Expected: AWQ picks the weights to protect from a calibration set, and generic text makes it protect the wrong ones for the domain; calibrate on hundreds of in-domain samples and test on the eval set before you ship.
wrongAnswers: "GGUF is the most popular format, so use it on the GPU server." It is the CPU and edge default; in vLLM it needs an experimental plugin, and its kernels are not built for GPUs, about 93 tokens per second on a 7B model in the lesson's numbers.

"Quantize at load time with bitsandbytes, it is one flag." Without the plugin the server stops with an unknown method error, and the result is a checkpoint that nobody evaluated; use a published AWQ or GPTQ checkpoint and test it.
"4-bit loses as little as FP8." A 4-bit model can lose more, and the loss depends on the model and the method; AWQ loses several points on math in the lesson, so run your own check.

"The memory saving is 41 percent for any model." The measured 41 percent is one small model with its embeddings and output layer in 16-bit; the share differs on a larger model, and the KV cache is separate from the weights.
keyPoints: Prefer a published four-bit checkpoint to load-time quantization.
Match the format to engine and workload.
The answer chooses AWQ with Marlin for GPU serving and GPTQ for LoRA.
It reserves GGUF for CPU or edge workloads.

questions.title: You enabled an FP8 KV cache on a checkpoint that ships calibrated scales, and accuracy on your eval dropped. The startup log contains a line about the scaling factor. What happened, how do you confirm it, and what are your options?
questions.answer: The server is running the cache with a scale of 1.0, because the loader did not use the scales in the checkpoint: vLLM prints Using KV cache scaling factor 1.0 when that is the case. SGLang prints Using FP8 KV cache but no scaling factors provided whenever no --quantization-param-path is passed, so its warning alone does not show which scales the server uses. Confirm the vLLM case by searching the weight index of the checkpoint for tensors that end in k_scale or v_scale; if they exist and vLLM still prints the warning, the loader dropped them, which at 0.31.0 happens for one whole model family and for one draft loader in open issues. The options are another checkpoint or version whose scales load, a scale file passed through the quantization parameter path on SGLang, or a BF16 cache until they do, with an accuracy run on your own task after each change.
followUps: Level 3: The checkpoint has one weight file and no index. How do you look for the scales? Expected: list the tensor names with the safetensors package instead of searching the index, and look for names that end in k_scale or v_scale.

Level 3: The warning prints, but your GSM8K run shows no loss. Are you done? Expected: no; 500 questions cannot rule out a loss of a few points, the loss depends on the model and its attention layout, and one family needed calibrated scales while most did not; run your own task and track the warning as a defect.

Level 4: Why do calibrated scales matter more for some attention layouts than for others? Expected: the scale maps the range of the keys and values into the FP8 range, and a layout whose values spread wider than the format clips or loses precision at a scale of 1.0; the vLLM team named one latent-attention family that did not work well uncalibrated while most models stayed close to BF16, so the layout and the calibration decide together.
wrongAnswers: "The checkpoint is FP8, so the KV scales are loaded." Weight scales and KV scales are different tensors, and a checkpoint with KV scales can still have them dropped by the loader; the warning tells you what the server uses.

"The warning is informational." On vLLM it means that every KV scale is 1.0, which the vLLM team treats as the worst case for accuracy; with scales in the checkpoint it means that the loader dropped them.

"A scale of 1.0 worked for Qwen3-8B, so it works." It gave overlapping intervals on 500 GSM8K questions for one model, which cannot rule out a loss of a few points, and another family lost accuracy at 1.0.

"Pass --quantization fp8 to load the scales." The weight method and the cache scales are separate; on SGLang the scales come from the checkpoint or from the quantization parameter path file, and a weight flag that does not match the checkpoint raises at startup.
keyPoints: Check whether KV scaling silently defaults to one.
Distinguish vLLM loader warnings from SGLang scale-path warnings.
Inspect checkpoint indices for k_scale and v_scale tensors.
Use working scales or BF16 and rerun task accuracy after changes.

questions.title: An SGLang server on a shared workstation ran for four minutes, and then a benchmark with 32 requests in flight crashed it with an out-of-memory error. The scheduler log just before the crash shows token usage: 0.05. Explain how the pool was 95 percent empty and the server still ran out of memory, and what you set.
questions.answer: The KV pool is sized once at startup from a snapshot of free memory, and the automatic fraction gave 87.2 percent of what was free to the weights and the pool. Thirty-two requests held 16,095 tokens, 5 percent of a 312,581-token pool, so the pool had reserved 33 GB and used under 2 GB, and the activations of the next forward pass needed memory outside the pool that the operating system no longer had. On a machine that runs anything else, pass --mem-fraction-static yourself; with 0.4 the same benchmark finished all 128 requests at concurrency 32.
followUps: Level 3: Why did the second start get a bigger pool than the first when nothing in SGLang changed? Expected: other programs used less memory at the second start, so the snapshot of free memory grew from 27.81 to 38.29 GB and the pool grew with it, from 24.25 to 33.39 GB at the same automatic fraction.

Level 3: What memory does the fraction cover, and what lives outside it? Expected: the weights plus the KV pool; activations, graphs, autotuning scratch and every other program live outside it, which is why a pool at 87 percent of free memory left nothing for the next forward pass.

Level 4: On a dedicated GPU, when do you raise the fraction and by how much? Expected: only when the scheduler log shows a full pool and retractions, in steps of 0.02; find the upper limit in staging with your longest prompts, run production one or two steps below it, and lower it when long prompts fail with out-of-memory errors in attention.
wrongAnswers: "A token usage of 0.05 means the server was nowhere near full." It means the pool was nearly empty; the pool had taken the memory and the activations outside it ran out, so an empty pool and an out-of-memory crash were the same event.

"Raise the fraction so that the pool is bigger and the crash goes away." The crash came from memory outside the pool; a bigger fraction takes more from the activations and the other programs, and 0.4 is what fixed it.

"The automatic fraction is tuned, so leave it." It assumes the machine belongs to the engine; on a shared machine the snapshot at startup does not hold for the life of the server, and when the capacity cannot be read it becomes 0.95 and fails on the first prefill.

"The pool line tells you the memory the server uses." The pool is the largest part and not the whole; one report measured 25 to 40 GB of short-lived allocations outside the accounting from the autotuner and the graph capture.
keyPoints: KV pools reserve memory at startup.
