A compound question gets decomposed, an ambiguous one gets disambiguated, an already-fine query passes through untouched — this per-query adaptivity is exactly what a single fixed prompted strategy applied to every query can't do.

questions.title: What is REFRAG, and what third option does it introduce beyond “include a chunk fully” or “don't retrieve it”?
questions.answer: REFRAG compresses every retrieved chunk to a single dense embedding by default, with a lightweight RL-trained policy selectively "expanding" only the chunks it judges important back into full raw tokens for that specific query. Standard RAG only has two states per chunk — fully included, or not retrieved at all — while REFRAG adds a third: "included, but compressed, with the option to zoom in," which is what lets it extend effective usable context roughly 16x at a comparable latency budget, instead of forcing a flat tradeoff between context breadth and decoding speed.

questions.title: What is Few-Shot Example RAG, and how does it differ from standard document RAG?
questions.answer: Instead of retrieving documents to ground a factual answer, it retrieves similar *past examples* (demonstrations) to populate a dynamic few-shot prompt for in-context learning — common in text-to-SQL and other structured-generation tasks where "show it a similar solved case" beats a static hand-picked few-shot set. The retrieval target is categorically different: not "facts relevant to this question" but "prior demonstrations whose pattern this new case should follow."

questions.title: What is Agentic Web RAG, and how does it differ from corpus-based RAG beyond “it searches the internet”?
questions.answer: It replaces a fixed, pre-indexed corpus with live web search and page fetching as the retrieval mechanism, which introduces problems corpus-based RAG doesn't have at all: source quality and reliability vary per result and have to be actively assessed, citation tracking has to be a first-class architectural component (not an afterthought) since users need to verify claims against live, changing sources, and the fetch layer itself is a real security surface — an attacker-controlled page can attempt prompt injection or redirect the fetcher to internal/unintended endpoints, which a closed, pre-vetted corpus simply can't do.

questions.title: A RAG answer has a citation next to every sentence. Which check tells you the claims are actually supported?
questions.answer: A citation just means the model pointed at *some* passage near the claim — it doesn't guarantee that specific passage actually entails the specific claim being made next to it. Real verifiability requires checking at the claim level: citation precision (of the passages cited, how many genuinely support the claim), citation recall (of the claims made, how many have any supporting citation at all), and attribution accuracy (does the cited passage actually say what the response claims it says, checked via NLI entailment) — three genuinely separate failure modes a model can hit independently even while technically "citing sources."
options: The answer's fluency.
Whether the cited documents were retrieved.
The number of citations per answer.
Claim-level attribution: does each cited passage actually entail the claim next to it?

questions.title: What is Privacy-Preserving RAG, and what are the main technical levers for keeping a corpus's content from leaking through the system?
questions.answer: Techniques span the whole pipeline: on-device or federated embedding so raw sensitive text never leaves a trust boundary, differential privacy noise added to retrieval signals or training data, and strict output filtering/redaction for PII before a response is returned. The hard part in an interview answer isn't naming the techniques, it's being honest that most of them trade real quality or latency for privacy guarantees — there's no free version of this, and the right combination depends entirely on the actual threat model (internal misuse vs. external breach vs. regulatory compliance).

questions.title: Why does standard RAG underperform specifically on tables, and what does Table-Aware RAG do differently?
questions.answer: Standard RAG treats a table as just another block of prose and chunks it by character count, which destroys the row/column structure that gives a table its meaning — a chunk boundary can split a row from its header, or merge unrelated rows together with no indication of which value belongs to which column. Table-Aware RAG's distinctive mechanism is structure-preserving linearization: explicitly parsing rows, columns, and headers into a structured representation first, then converting that structure back into text designed for retrieval and arithmetic reasoning — either full-table Markdown, or per-row chunks with the header re-attached to every single row so each chunk stays self-contained.
options: LLMs can't read tables.
Embeddings can't represent numbers.
Fixed-size chunking breaks rows and columns apart, separating values from their headers. Parse the table and keep the header with every row.
Tables are too short to be retrieved.

questions.title: What is Streaming/Real-Time RAG, and what's the core mechanism that separates it from standard batch-indexed RAG?
questions.answer: The distinctive mechanism is continuous, incremental index updates as new data arrives, rather than periodic batch re-indexing — new documents (or events) become searchable within seconds to minutes instead of waiting for the next scheduled rebuild. This matters for use cases like live news, fast-moving incident response, or trading desks, where a correct answer five minutes ago can be actively wrong right now, and a standard nightly-rebuild RAG pipeline's staleness window is itself the failure mode.

questions.title: What is LightRAG, and how does its dual-level retrieval differ from Microsoft GraphRAG's community-hierarchy approach?
questions.answer: LightRAG indexes at two levels simultaneously — fine-grained entity-level relationships for specific queries, and higher-level thematic summaries for broad ones — and lets a query mode choose which level (or both) to search, without needing GraphRAG's expensive community-detection clustering step at index time. The practical consequence is a meaningfully cheaper, faster index build, at the cost of GraphRAG's more thorough corpus-wide thematic coverage from pre-computed community summaries.

questions.title: Which query needs a knowledge graph rather than a vector index?
questions.answer: A vector index retrieves by embedding similarity, which is excellent for open-ended semantic queries but has no mechanism for following explicit entity relationships across documents — it can't natively answer "who leads the company that acquired the company that made this product." A knowledge graph stores entities and typed relationships explicitly, enabling that kind of multi-hop structured traversal directly, but it's a worse fit for free-form "find me things that feel similar to this" queries a graph has no edges to represent. Production systems commonly run both: vector search to find semantic entry points into the graph, graph traversal for the relational reasoning once you're in.
options: "What does our refund policy say about digital goods?"
"Summarise this report."
"Who leads the company that acquired the maker of this product?"
"Find complaints similar to this one."

questions.title: How do you handle entity resolution when the same real-world entity shows up under different names across documents?
questions.answer: A tiered approach, cheapest first: normalize surface forms (lowercase, strip punctuation, expand known abbreviations); apply a curated alias table for known synonyms (ticker symbols, legal name variants); use embedding similarity to cluster candidate names above a cosine threshold (roughly 0.92 is a common starting point); and for genuinely ambiguous remaining cases, prompt an LLM with surrounding context to make the call. Assign each resolved cluster a single canonical node ID and store every surface form as an alias on it, so future documents referencing any variant resolve to the same node.

questions.title: Why does source provenance on every graph edge matter operationally, not just for citation purposes?
questions.answer: Without knowing which source document produced a given edge, you can't incrementally update the graph when that document changes or gets deleted — you'd have no way to know which edges to remove, and would be forced to rebuild the entire graph from scratch on every single document change. With provenance tracked per edge, a document update becomes a targeted operation: delete that document's edges, re-extract from the new version, done — the difference between an incremental update pipeline and a full rebuild every time anything changes.

questions.title: Which question needs GraphRAG's global search rather than local search?
questions.answer: Local search behaves like standard knowledge-graph RAG: vector similarity finds entry-point entities, then it expands into their graph neighborhood to assemble context for one generation call — cheap and precise for entity-anchored questions. Global search instead map-reduces over pre-generated community summaries (computed once at index time via Leiden clustering): each relevant community summary independently produces a partial answer, and those partial answers get ranked and merged into one final response — costs more per query, but it's the only mode that can actually answer broad, thematic, corpus-wide questions, since the expensive summarization work was already paid for once upfront rather than repeated per query.
options: "What did Acme's CEO say about pricing?"
"Which contracts mention Acme?"
"When was Acme founded?"
"What are the main themes across all 5,000 interview transcripts?"

questions.title: When do you choose a knowledge graph over pure vector retrieval, as a real design decision?
questions.answer: When queries genuinely require multi-hop reasoning across named entities, when you need to retrieve by relationship type rather than general topical similarity ("find all companies Apple acquired"), when entity deduplication materially affects answer quality because multiple documents refer to the same thing inconsistently, or when the domain already has a well-defined ontology (medical codes, legal concepts, product hierarchies) a graph can map onto directly. Stick with vector retrieval when queries are primarily free-form/semantic, the corpus lacks any clear entity structure to exploit, or build time is genuinely constrained — a graph you don't have time to build and maintain correctly is worse than no graph at all.

questions.title: What's the “sliding window” memory problem, and how does compress-and-carry solve it?
questions.answer: A sliding window keeps only the last N turns verbatim — once it fills, older turns are simply dropped, and the system loses all memory of earlier conversation context, even context that might matter several turns later. Compress-and-carry periodically compresses older turns into a short running summary and carries that summary forward instead of the raw turns, so the context cost grows with summary length rather than linearly with session length — the tradeoff is the summary loses precision (exact quotes, fine phrasing nuance), which is why it's usually paired with a sliding window over the *most recent* few turns kept verbatim for immediate fidelity.

questions.title: How does MemGPT's approach to memory differ from a standard application-managed sliding window or summary?
questions.answer: Standard approaches manage memory entirely outside the model — the application layer decides what to keep, archive, or drop. MemGPT instead gives the model explicit memory-management tools (append to working memory, search archival memory, insert into archival memory) and lets the model itself decide when to invoke them, the same way it decides when to call a retrieval tool. The upside is the model can reason about *what's actually worth remembering* in a way a fixed window or summary rule can't ("this constraint will matter several turns from now"); the downside is added latency from the memory tool calls themselves, and the risk of the model mismanaging memory if those tool prompts aren't specified carefully.

questions.title: How would you implement cross-session personalization in a conversational RAG assistant without storing full transcripts?
questions.answer: After each session ends, run a lightweight extraction pass asking "what did we learn about this user's preferences, constraints, or domain knowledge this session," and store only those extracted facts in a per-user namespaced vector store — not the raw transcript. At the start of a new session, retrieve the most relevant stored facts for the opening query and inject them as a brief "user context" block in the system prompt. Storing semantic summaries rather than full transcripts is both cheaper and aligned with minimal-data-retention practice — you rarely actually need the verbatim history, just the durable facts it revealed.

questions.title: Turn 1: "Tell me about the March outage." Turn 3: "Did it affect enterprise customers?" Retrieval for turn 3 returns unrelated pages. What is the most likely cause?
questions.answer: It's when a multi-turn system's retrieval quality degrades specifically because follow-up queries lose the context that made them meaningful in isolation — "did it affect enterprise customers?" means nothing to a retriever without knowing what "it" refers to from three turns ago. The most common root cause is skipping query condensation/rewriting before retrieval: embedding the raw follow-up as-is, rather than first rewriting it into a self-contained query using the conversation history, almost guarantees the retriever searches on an under-specified or ambiguous version of what the user actually meant.
options: The follow-up was embedded as written, instead of being rewritten into a standalone question using the conversation.
Top-k is too low.
The index is stale.
The embedding model is too small.

questions.title: How does CLIP's training objective enable cross-modal retrieval without any manually labeled image-text pairs?
questions.answer: It trains contrastively on hundreds of millions of naturally co-occurring (image, alt-text) pairs scraped from the web — no manual labeling involved — with a loss that pulls each image's embedding close to its paired text embedding and pushes it away from the other images in the same training batch. Because both encoders are trained to land in the same shared vector space, a text query can be embedded and compared directly against image embeddings by ordinary cosine similarity at retrieval time, with no classification head or extra alignment step needed.

questions.title: Early fusion vs. late fusion for multimodal RAG — which do production systems actually use, and why?
questions.answer: Early fusion combines raw multimodal inputs before encoding, requiring one architecture capable of processing both modalities jointly from the start. Late fusion encodes each modality independently with its own best-in-class encoder (text with a strong text embedder, images with CLIP) and combines the resulting vectors afterward — and this is what production systems overwhelmingly use, because it lets you swap in the best available encoder per modality without retraining anything else, index everything in one shared vector store with a single ANN query across modalities, and add a brand-new modality later (audio, say) by adding one new encoder rather than retraining the whole system.

questions.title: How would you index a corpus of PDFs that mix prose, figures, and tables?
questions.answer: Parse each document and route by content type: text blocks chunked and embedded with a text encoder; figures extracted as images and embedded with CLIP (or captioned via a vision-language model and embedded as text, for cases where a text query is more likely than an image query); tables linearized to Markdown and embedded as text. Store everything in one index with a modality metadata field so retrieval can span all three at once from a single text query embedding — and flag any figure that has no surrounding caption text for manual review, since those are the hardest content type for a plain text query to ever surface via semantic similarity alone.

questions.title: How do you evaluate and tune cosine similarity thresholds in semantic vector caches to balance hit rate against false answers?
questions.answer: A semantic vector cache intercepts repeated LLM queries by comparing incoming query embeddings against cached query vectors. Because users rarely type identical queries character-for-character, exact string caches achieve low hit rates. Semantic caches use vector similarity to match paraphrases. Tuning the cosine similarity threshold is the critical trade-off. If the threshold is set too low (such as 0.85), queries with contrasting meanings or subtle domain differences match incorrect cached answers—such as returning an explanation of 'DDP' for a query asking about 'FSDP'. If the threshold is set too high (such as 0.99), even minor wording changes miss the cache, dropping hit rates down to exact-match levels. We evaluate thresholds empirically on historical query pairs using ROC curves, plotting false semantic match rates against cache hit rates. In production, thresholds are typically calibrated tightly between 0.94 and 0.97 using domain-tuned embedding models. The trade-off is cost savings versus answer correctness: semantic caching cuts 30% to 50% of LLM compute, but requires strict threshold validation to avoid returning false answers to subtly different questions.
followUps: Why do general-purpose embedding models struggle with negation queries in semantic caches?
How does semantic cache efficiency vary between consumer chat and structured enterprise search?
wrongAnswers: Using an arbitrary loose similarity threshold (e.g. 0.80) without validation, causing users to receive answers meant for different questions.
Relying entirely on exact MD5 string matching, achieving less than 5% cache hit rates on conversational traffic.
tradeOffs: Calibrated semantic thresholds catch diverse paraphrases that miss string caches, delivering major API cost savings.
Setting similarity thresholds too loose causes false semantic hits, delivering confidently wrong answers to subtle query variations.
keyPoints: Semantic caches match paraphrases using query-vector similarity.
Low thresholds admit incorrect matches while high thresholds lose paraphrase hits.
Tune thresholds on historical query pairs using ROC curves.
Balance compute savings against false semantic matches.

questions.title: How do you design asymmetric cache invalidation when underlying enterprise knowledge documents or database records update?
questions.answer: In enterprise RAG systems, knowledge documents are updated frequently—such as an HR policy revision or a corrected API documentation page. In a standard semantic cache, cached answers contain synthesized text derived from past versions of these documents. If the underlying document changes, cached answers become stale and incorrect, but the cached query vectors have no direct relationship to the document URLs. We design asymmetric cache invalidation using dependency tagging. When an answer is generated and stored in the semantic cache, the cache entry records metadata tags listing every source document chunk ID and database entity ID cited in the response. When our data ingestion pipeline detects an updated or deleted document, it publishes an invalidation event containing the modified chunk IDs. An asynchronous worker queries the cache metadata for all entries tagged with those chunk IDs and purges them immediately from the vector index. The trade-off is ingestion tracking overhead versus knowledge freshness: tracking provenance adds metadata overhead on cache writes, but it guarantees that stale information is purged as soon as source documents update.
followUps: How do you handle partial document updates where only one paragraph in a 50-page PDF is modified?
What happens if an invalidation worker experiences lag during a rapid batch document update?
wrongAnswers: Relying solely on simple time-to-live (TTL) expiration, allowing stale answers to persist for days after a critical policy is updated.
Flushing the entire enterprise cache whenever any single document updates, destroying cache hit rates for unrelated departments.
tradeOffs: Document-tagged cache invalidation guarantees knowledge freshness when enterprise source data changes, eliminating stale answers.
Maintaining dependency graphs between cached queries and source document IDs adds metadata complexity on cache writes.
keyPoints: Record source chunk and entity IDs with each cached answer.
Publish invalidation events when source documents change or disappear.
Purge entries tagged with modified IDs from the vector index.
Provenance metadata adds write overhead in exchange for freshness.

questions.title: How do you enforce security and multi-tenant isolation boundaries in a shared corporate semantic vector cache?
questions.answer: In an enterprise deploying a centralized semantic cache across multiple departments, users must never receive cached answers containing information they are unauthorized to see. For example, if an executive asks about upcoming layoffs and the answer is cached, an engineer asking a similar question must not receive the cached executive response. We enforce multi-tenant security isolation using partition keys and Access Control List (ACL) pre-filtering. Every semantic cache entry stores metadata containing the tenant ID, department code, and the minimum security clearance role required to view the answer. When a user submits a query, their authenticated JWT token is validated to extract their tenant ID and authorized role scopes. The semantic similarity search applies a hard boolean filter matching the tenant ID and role constraints before vector scoring. If no authorized match exists, the request bypasses the cache and invokes the RAG pipeline with user-specific permissions. The trade-off is cache hit sharing versus data privacy: strictly isolating cache partitions by user role prevents cross-tenant data leakage, but slightly reduces overall cache hit rates relative to an open unpartitioned cache.
followUps: How do you prevent cache timing attacks where an unauthorized user infers confidential facts from query response latency?
What happens if a user's permissions are revoked after an answer has already been cached?
wrongAnswers: Sharing a single un-partitioned semantic cache across all employees regardless of access permissions, leaking private data.
Filtering unauthorized cache hits after vector retrieval, which returns empty results when top matches are restricted.
tradeOffs: ACL-filtered vector cache search guarantees zero cross-tenant data leakage, ensuring compliance with enterprise security policies.
Partitioning cache entries by security boundaries reduces cache deduplication across teams that have partially overlapping access.
keyPoints: Store tenant and required-role metadata on cache entries.
Extract authenticated tenant and role scopes from validated tokens.
Apply authorization filters before vector scoring.
Bypass the cache when no authorized match exists, accepting fewer shared hits.

questions.title: Why do embedding models struggle with negation queries in semantic caches, and how do you prevent false positive cache hits on conflicting constraints?
questions.answer: Standard dense embedding models encode topical semantics rather than exact logical constraints. Because 'How do I enable two-factor authentication?' and 'How do I disable two-factor authentication?' share identical keywords and domain context, their embedding vectors usually end up very close. In a naive semantic cache, an inquiry asking how to disable a feature will hit the cached answer explaining how to enable it, producing a dangerous false positive hit. We prevent negation and constraint false positives using a hybrid verification stage. When a candidate cache hit exceeds the semantic similarity threshold, we do not return the answer immediately. We run a fast lexical constraint checker that compares boolean operators, negation words ('not', 'without', 'disable', 'never'), and named entities between the candidate query and the cached query. If conflicting polarities or mismatched entity constraints are detected, the cache hit is invalidated and the query routes to the full LLM pipeline. The trade-off is verification compute versus semantic safety: running lexical verification adds a few milliseconds to cache lookups, but it prevents catastrophic false positive answers on high-stakes queries.
followUps: How do fine-tuned cross-encoders compare against heuristic lexical checkers for verifying cache hit validity?
What other categories of queries (e.g. temporal dates, version numbers) exhibit semantic false positive risks?
wrongAnswers: Relying solely on dense embedding cosine similarity for semantic cache hits, returning opposite answers to negation queries.
Assuming that modern embedding models reliably encode boolean negation out of the box without special training.
tradeOffs: Hybrid lexical-semantic validation prevents false positive cache hits on negation queries, protecting users from opposite answers.
Running entity and negation checks on candidate cache hits adds a small parsing step to cache lookup latency.
keyPoints: Dense embeddings can place opposite intents close together.
Check negation, boolean constraints and named entities after similarity matching.
Reject hits with conflicting polarity or entities.
Route rejected hits to the full pipeline despite verification overhead.

questions.title: A retrieval pipeline uses one model to find candidate chunks and a second model to order them. Explain what each model sees as input, and why the second model does not run over the whole corpus.
questions.answer: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document on their own and compares the vectors, so every document vector is computed once at index time. A cross-encoder reads the query and one document together as a single sequence and outputs one relevance score, so it can see how the two texts interact. That score costs one forward pass for each pair, so the cross-encoder runs only on a short candidate list.
followUps: Level 1: Which of the two outputs can you compute before any query arrives? Expected: the bi-encoder document vectors; a cross-encoder score depends on the query.
Level 2: What caps the quality of the two-stage pipeline? Expected: the recall of the first stage at N, because the reranker can only reorder what the retriever returned.
Level 2: Does the order of the two texts in the pair matter? Expected: yes, the cross-encoder is not symmetric; feed the query first, or recall collapses.

Level 3: A team promises a p95 under 100 ms with a 22M parameter reranker. What do you plan first? Expected: memory, because the weights take 88 MB at float32, and batching, because scoring the N candidates one by one multiplies the latency by N.
wrongAnswers: "The cross-encoder is a better embedding model." It does not produce an embedding; it produces one score for one query and one document.
"Run the cross-encoder over every chunk for the best quality." On a 10 million document corpus that is 10 million forward passes per query.
"A larger reranker always wins." The 22M parameter class is the production point; larger models lose more latency than they gain and are kept for offline reranking or a very small K.

questions.title: A product team wants an assistant that answers questions about the internal policy wiki. One engineer proposes to tune the model on the wiki pages. Another proposes to search the pages at question time and paste the matches into the prompt. Which do you pick, and in which case would you still tune the model?
questions.answer: Pick retrieval for knowledge. The model never changes, the document store updates in minutes, and you can show the passages behind each answer. Tuning fits when you need a style, a tone or a reasoning pattern that a prompt cannot reach, not when you need facts.
followUps: Level 1: A policy page changes. What happens in each approach? Expected: with retrieval you re-index that page and the next answer uses the new text; with a tuned model the old fact stays until you train again.

Level 2: A legal reviewer asks which page an answer came from. Which approach can show it? Expected: retrieval, because the passages that went into the prompt are known and can be returned with the answer.

Level 2: Why is the privacy story different? Expected: with retrieval the pages stay in your store and only the matched chunks go to the model for one call; with tuning the content is inside the weights of the model you deploy.

Level 3: The answer is wrong even though the right passage is in the store. Which stage do you check first? Expected: retrieval, with recall at k, because the model cannot use a passage that the search did not return.
wrongAnswers: "Tune the model, because then it knows the documents." The weights hold a copy that goes stale, and nothing in the output says which page a fact came from.
"Retrieval is always better." A fixed style, a tone or a reasoning pattern is learned better by tuning than by a prompt.
"Skip the search and put the whole wiki in the prompt." The lesson budgets 2,500 to 5,000 tokens of retrieved text per query; a whole wiki does not fit, and unrelated text dilutes the prompt.

questions.title: A user reports that the document assistant gave a wrong answer. The pipeline has a chunker, a retriever, a reranker and a generator. You get one metric to look at before anything else. Which one, and why that one?
questions.answer: Recall at k on the retrieval stage. If the gold chunk is not in the top k, no reranker can bring it back and the generator usually lacks the evidence for the right answer, unless another chunk happens to hold it, so the later metrics are hard to read. Recall comes first in the order, but it is not a gate: when recall holds, or when another retrieved chunk holds the evidence, move on to the rank position and then to the generated text, because a failure there stays hidden otherwise.
followUps: Level 1: What does precision at k add once recall is fine? Expected: it shows how much of the returned list is noise, which matters when a wrong chunk poisons the answer or wastes tokens.
Level 2: Recall at 5 is fine but the gold chunk sits at rank 4 or 5. Which metric shows that, and which stage do you fix? Expected: MRR, and the reranker.

Level 3: Recall averages 90 percent and one team still complains every day. What is hidden? Expected: one query class that always misses; slice the qrels by class, such as literal, paraphrased and multi-topic, and report each slice.
Level 3: How do you keep the eval fast enough to run on every change? Expected: tiers, with a smoke set of 20 queries in CI, 200 nightly and 2000 weekly.
wrongAnswers: "Read the answer and judge it." The answer alone cannot tell which of the four stages failed.
"Precision at k, because the noise caused the wrong answer." Precision matters once the right chunk is present; a missing chunk is the first thing to rule out.
"Faithfulness, because the model hallucinated." A faithful answer to the wrong chunks is still wrong; faithfulness only grades the generator against what it saw.

questions.title: You write the search step of a retrieval pipeline. A teammate wants to rank chunks by the raw dot product between the query vector and each chunk vector. What do you use instead, and when is the dot product the right choice?
questions.answer: Use cosine similarity, which is the dot product divided by the lengths of the two vectors. It measures only the angle, so a long chunk and a short chunk compete on direction and not on size. The raw dot product is right only when the vector length carries meaning that you want to reward.
followUps: Level 1: What do the values 1, 0 and -1 mean for cosine? Expected: the same direction, orthogonal, and opposite directions.

Level 2: Your embedder returns unit vectors. Does the choice still matter? Expected: no, because with unit vectors the dot product and the cosine are equal, which is why the lesson normalizes and then uses a matrix product.
Level 2: Why does L2 distance treat a long and a short chunk differently? Expected: it measures the straight-line distance, so a longer vector sits farther away even when it points the same way.

Level 3: When would you keep the raw dot product on purpose? Expected: when the model was trained so that length carries a signal, such as more content in a longer document, and you want that signal in the rank.
wrongAnswers: "The dot product and the cosine give the same order." Only when every vector has the same length; otherwise longer vectors win on the dot product.
"A smaller cosine means a closer match." A larger cosine means a smaller angle; smaller is closer only for a distance such as L2.
"Use whatever the vector store defaults to." The measure must match how the vectors were produced and normalized, so check the embedder before the store.

questions.title: A team is about to index a new document corpus and asks you to review the chunker. They picked semantic splitting, 1000 tokens per chunk and 20 percent overlap, because a blog post recommended it. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: Start from the query type, not from a post. Factoid questions want 256 to 512 tokens, analytical or multi-hop questions 512 to 1024, and whole-section questions 1024 to 2048. Begin with recursive splitting at 512 tokens and no overlap, then measure recall at 5 on a 50-query set before you move any knob.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the chunk size depend on the kind of question? Expected: the chunk has to contain the answer with its context, and still be small enough that the top k is about the answer and not about the surrounding noise.
Level 2: The corpus is markdown API documentation. What do you try first? Expected: the structural header splitter, because the format carries explicit structure; drop or merge header-only chunks.
Level 3: Which two guards does every chunker need, whatever the strategy? Expected: a minimum and a maximum size, because chunks of 5 tokens or 5000 tokens both break retrieval.

Level 3: You switch the embedding model later. What do you run again? Expected: the chunking eval, because the winner depends on the corpus and the model, and semantic splitting moves its boundaries when the model changes.
wrongAnswers: "Semantic splitting is best because it follows meaning." It lost to recursive splitting at 512 tokens in the measured study, and it makes tiny fragments unless you set a floor.
"Overlap is a safety margin, keep it." The studies found that overlap often adds nothing, and it adds index cost in proportion to its size; justify any overlap with an ablation.
"Bigger chunks give the model more context." Quality drops around 2,500 tokens of context, and a chunk that covers many topics dilutes its own embedding.

questions.title: A proposal replaces the vector retriever with a cross-encoder that scores every chunk in a 10 million chunk index, so that nothing is ever missed. Estimate the work for one question, and say what you propose instead.
questions.answer: One forward pass per chunk means 10 million forward passes for one question, which no request budget allows. Keep a bi-encoder for the first stage, because its document vectors are computed once at index time, and run the cross-encoder on a pool of 50 to 200 candidates. The advanced RAG lesson puts the per-pair cost at 100 to 1000 times a bi-encoder comparison.
followUps: Level 2: Which part of the bi-encoder cost is paid once? Expected: the document embeddings, at index time; a query pays for one embedding and the comparisons.
Level 2: Why does the expensive model pay for itself on the top 50? Expected: 50 passes fit a request budget and the lift is concentrated in the final order of the candidates.
Level 3: The index doubles in size. Which stage grows in cost per query? Expected: the first stage, because it compares against every chunk; the reranker stays at N passes while N is fixed.

Level 3: At this scale the first stage itself is not a brute-force scan. What does it use, and what does that cost? Expected: an approximate nearest neighbor index, which trades a little recall for speed; the advanced RAG lesson notes that at 2 million chunks the error can push a relevant chunk out of the top k.
wrongAnswers: "Score everything, GPUs are fast." 10 million passes per question is not a latency a user waits for, and the lesson's model takes 88 MB before any batch.
"Precompute the cross-encoder score for every chunk." The score depends on the query, so there is nothing to precompute.
"Use a smaller cross-encoder over the whole corpus." Smaller rerankers lose quality faster than they save latency, and the pass count stays the same.

questions.title: Support agents search the knowledge base with the exact error code from a ticket, such as E-4021. The vector search returns articles about error handling in general and misses the one article that contains that code. What is happening, and what do you add?
questions.answer: The embedding model treats a rare code as noise, so the query vector lands near articles about errors in general and not near the one exact match. Add a lexical index with BM25 next to the vector index, run both for every query, and merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion. The exact token wins on BM25, and the fused list puts that article first.
followUps: Level 2: Why does BM25 give a rare code so much weight? Expected: the inverse document frequency factor; a term in few documents scores high and a term in most documents scores low.

Level 2: The code is in the ticket but in no article at all. What does each retriever return? Expected: BM25 contributes nothing for that term, and the dense retriever still returns neighbors that look plausible and are wrong, and the fusion keeps them; check that a retrieved article contains the code, and when none does, say that no retrieved article contains it.

Level 3: How do the paraphrased queries fare after you add the lexical index? Expected: they still win, because the fusion is rank based; in the demo the paraphrased query sat at BM25 rank 6 and dense rank 1 and fused to rank 1.
Level 3: The codes live in a short title field and the body is long prose. What do you tune? Expected: field weighting, which repeats the title tokens at index time so a title match counts more.
wrongAnswers: "Switch to a better embedding model." A rare code has no meaning to learn; the fix is a lexical signal next to the semantic one.
"Lower the similarity threshold so more articles come back." More neighbors on the wrong topic do not include the one exact match.
"Replace the vector search with BM25." Then the queries that share no words with the article fail; run both and fuse.

questions.title: Two answer-grade metrics sit in your RAG eval report: faithfulness and answer relevance. A teammate says they measure the same thing and wants to drop one. Explain what each one grades, and give one answer that scores high on one and low on the other.
questions.answer: Faithfulness asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevance asks whether the answer addresses the question. A grounded summary of the retrieved chunks that never gets to the question scores high on faithfulness and low on relevance, and a short direct answer from the model's own memory scores high on relevance and low on faithfulness.
followUps: Level 2: Which of the two catches a hallucination? Expected: faithfulness, because an invented fact has no support in the retrieved context.

Level 2: Low relevance with high faithfulness points at which stage? Expected: the query rewriter or the generation prompt; the context was about something else, or the answer drifted from the question.
Level 3: Why does neither metric need a reference answer? Expected: both are judged against the context and the question, which is what makes them usable on live traffic.

Level 3: What is the limit of the lesson's offline judge? Expected: it counts token overlap above a threshold, so it cannot read meaning; production uses a model judge, from a different family than the generator.
wrongAnswers: "They are the same, a faithful answer is relevant." A faithful answer can summarize the context and ignore the question.
"Relevance is enough when retrieval is good." Relevance never sees the context, so an answer from the model's own memory can be relevant and ungrounded.
"Faithfulness needs a gold answer." It is judged against the retrieved context, which is why it works on live traffic.

questions.title: A question asks what changed in the security policy last month. Your vector search returns a two-year-old security document because it is semantically close. Design the retrieval step so that this cannot happen, and say what else the same mechanism buys you in a regulated deployment.
questions.answer: Store metadata with each chunk, such as the source, the creation date, the category, the author and the version, and filter on it before the similarity search runs. For this question the filter is the security category and the last 30 days, so the old document is never a candidate. Under regulation the same pre-filter carries role labels and jurisdiction tags, so a user only retrieves chunks they are allowed to see.
followUps: Level 2: Why filter before the search and not after? Expected: the search space shrinks, which helps at scale, and an excluded document can never take a slot in the top k.
Level 2: Which fields do you store with each chunk? Expected: source, date, category, author and version, plus role and jurisdiction labels in a regulated setting.
Level 3: How do you test that the role filter holds? Expected: a probe set of cross-jurisdiction questions, which the capstone runs as a 20-question check scored pass or fail.

Level 3: Where does the filter sit relative to the reranker and the generator? Expected: before retrieval; the capstone filters, then runs hybrid retrieval, then the reranker gets the top 20 and the generator gets the top 5.
wrongAnswers: "Put the date into the query text so the embedding reflects it." An embedding does not enforce a date; a semantically close old document still scores high.
"Filter the results after the top k comes back." If the top k is all old documents the filter leaves nothing, and the right one never had a chance.
"Tell the model not to use documents from another jurisdiction." Access control belongs in retrieval, before the text reaches the prompt.

questions.title: You have a BM25 ranked list and a vector ranked list for the same query. An engineer proposes to merge them as alpha times the BM25 score plus one minus alpha times the cosine. What is wrong with that, and what do you do instead?
questions.answer: BM25 scores are unbounded and change with the corpus, while a cosine sits between -1 and 1, so a weighted sum needs a new alpha every time you re-index. Reciprocal rank fusion merges by rank instead: each document gets the sum, over the lists, of one over k plus its rank, with k at 60. Ranks are comparable across the two retrievers, so nothing has to be calibrated.
followUps: Level 2: What does the constant k control? Expected: how fast the contribution decays with rank; at 60, rank 1 gives 1/61 and rank 10 gives 1/70, so deep candidates still count.
Level 2: When would you lower k? Expected: when the top result of each list should dominate the fused order.

Level 3: You know BM25 is better on your corpus. How do you express that? Expected: a per-list weight that multiplies the rank contribution of the BM25 list; the decay shape and the scale-free property both survive.

Level 3: Why does the rank method survive a re-index when the weighted sum does not? Expected: ranks keep their meaning when the corpus changes, while BM25 scores and their spread move, so the tuned alpha no longer fits.
wrongAnswers: "Normalize both scores to a zero to one range and add them." The two distributions still differ per query and per corpus, so the tuned balance drifts after a re-index.
"Take the document with the highest score in either list." One unbounded BM25 score then dominates every query; ranks are the comparable unit.
"Fusion is only a tie-breaker between the two lists." In the demo it decides the top result on every query class; a document good in both lists beats one that is top in only one.

questions.title: Your chunker keeps a 100-token overlap between neighbor chunks. After the last corpus refresh the index size and the embedding bill both went up, and a teammate says the overlap must stay because it protects sentences that a boundary would cut in half. How do you settle it?
questions.answer: Settle it with an ablation, not an opinion. Run the same recall at 5 eval with the overlap at zero and at the current value on a stratified query set, and keep the overlap only if the number moves. The recent studies found that overlap often adds no measurable benefit, while it adds index cost in proportion to its size.
followUps: Level 2: Why did the fixed-window splitter need overlap? Expected: it cuts at a fixed count whatever the text, so a boundary can split a sentence; the repeated tail puts that sentence whole into the next chunk.
Level 2: What does a recursive splitter do instead? Expected: it splits on the paragraph, the line and the sentence separators in turn, so boundaries land on natural breaks.
Level 3: What rule does the chunker skill apply to overlap? Expected: default zero, and refuse any overlap above 20 percent without an ablation.

Level 3: The ablation shows a gain on one document type only. What do you ship? Expected: overlap for that type alone, with the ablation recorded, and a re-run when the corpus or the embedder changes.
wrongAnswers: "Overlap is free, embeddings are cheap." Every overlapped token is embedded and stored twice, so the index cost grows in proportion to the overlap.
"A blog post says 20 percent overlap." The studies found no measurable benefit in the measured case; the answer depends on your corpus, so measure it there.
"Remove it everywhere, no test needed." The ablation is cheap and the result is corpus dependent; a slice with real boundary losses would show up in it.

questions.title: Your pipeline offers three query rewriters: write a hypothetical answer and search with it, write several paraphrases and merge, or decompose it into sub-questions and merge. A user asks "what does our team do when uploads fail and the budget is gone?" Which rewriter fits, and when would each of the other two be the right pick?
questions.answer: Split it, because the question joins two topics with a conjunction, an upload failure and an exhausted budget, and no single chunk holds both. The hypothetical answer fits a jargon-heavy question whose words do not match the corpus vocabulary. Paraphrases fit a short question that could be asked in many equally good ways.
followUps: Level 2: What does a rewriter cost in latency? Expected: one model call before retrieval, 500 to 2000 ms for a hypothetical answer in the advanced RAG lesson, with the retrievals after it in parallel.

Level 2: The paraphrases come back nearly identical. What happens and what do you change? Expected: the merged list equals one retrieval; add a diversity instruction and drop near duplicates by Jaccard overlap.

Level 3: The splitter turns an atomic question into three parts. What is the damage and the guard? Expected: the same document comes back three times at a lower rank and the merge is worse; test that the parts are distinct before the fan-out.
Level 3: How does the end-to-end system choose without a human? Expected: heuristics on length, conjunctions and jargon ratio, or run all three and fuse.
wrongAnswers: "Always write the hypothetical answer, it is the strongest." It bridges a vocabulary gap and does nothing for a two-topic question; an invented identifier can also hurt the lexical side.
"A rewriter fixes a weak retriever." It only moves the query closer to the corpus voice; a chunker that cut the answer still loses.
"Split every query into sub-questions." Atomic questions get over-split and come back worse than the original.

questions.title: A new cross-encoder reranker lifts MRR on the offline fixture to a near-perfect value. In production the same reranker makes the top result worse than the retriever alone. List the causes you check, in order, and say how each one shows up.
questions.answer: Check the training data first: if the hand-labeled training pairs include the eval queries, the eval is a memory test and the lift is fake. Then check the pair order in production, because a cross-encoder is not symmetric and a swapped query and document collapses recall. Then check the candidate pool, because production candidates come from the real bi-encoder, and its recall at N caps what the reranker can see.
followUps: Level 2: How do you make the leak impossible? Expected: hold the eval queries out of the training triples strictly, even on a fixture, as the end-to-end lesson does.
Level 2: What does a swapped pair look like in the numbers? Expected: a collapse rather than a drift, because every score is computed for the wrong direction.

Level 3: Why does a synthetic candidate pool inflate the offline result? Expected: it can contain the gold chunk every time, while the real bi-encoder's recall at N caps what the reranker sees in production.
Level 3: Which one number do you log per query to catch the next regression? Expected: the rank-1 cross-encoder score; a top score below a corpus threshold marks an out-of-domain query.
wrongAnswers: "The production model is a different build." Check the data and the inputs before the weights; a leak and a swapped pair both reproduce with the same weights.
"The fixture is too small to mean anything." Size does not create a leak; overlap between training and eval queries does.
"Lower N in production to match the fixture." A smaller N lowers the recall cap and makes the pipeline worse.

questions.title: Design a question answering service over a company's internal documents: wikis, policies, contracts and support articles, a few hundred thousand pages, with weekly updates. Users are employees with different access rights. Walk through the pipeline, the evaluation, and the first three things you would measure in production.
questions.answer: Build two sides. The ingestion side parses each document, chunks it per document with a structure-aware splitter, embeds the chunks, and indexes dense vectors and a BM25 index with metadata and access labels on every chunk. The query side filters by access first, runs hybrid retrieval with rank fusion, reranks a candidate pool with a cross-encoder, and generates a cited answer with a refuse path. Prove it with a golden set labeled by domain experts and a retrieval eval that reports recall at k per query class, then measure retrieval quality weekly, faithfulness and citation correctness per turn, and cost per query in production.
followUps: Level 3: Where does access control live? Expected: in the retrieval filter, as role labels on chunks applied before the similarity search, and never in the prompt text.

Level 3: A document changes on Tuesday. What is stale and for how long? Expected: its chunks, until the next re-index; re-embed only changed documents, carry the version in the metadata, and watch the gap between source updates and index updates.

Level 4: How do you keep the model cost down at this volume? Expected: a cache-friendly prompt with the system prompt and policies first, the reranked context next and the question last; the capstone targets a 60 to 80 percent hit rate and a 3 to 5 times lower cost per query.

Level 4: The golden set passes and one department still reports bad answers. What do you do? Expected: slice the eval by document type and query class, add that department's real queries to the qrels, and check whether their documents are chunked by a splitter that fits their format.
wrongAnswers: "Put every document into one long prompt." Hundreds of thousands of pages do not fit, and the lesson budgets 2,500 to 5,000 tokens of retrieved text per query for a reason.
"Tune the model on the documents every week." It cannot cite, it goes stale between runs, and it cannot enforce access rights.
"Vector search alone is enough." Exact identifiers, codes and names need the lexical side; run both and fuse.
"Ship without a labeled set, the demo works." A demo on ten documents says nothing about hundreds of thousands of pages; label the golden set first.

questions.title: Your document assistant answers every question, including the ones the corpus does not cover, and the invented answers are the ones users remember. Design the path that lets the system say it does not know, and say how you measure that the path works.
questions.answer: Log the reranker's rank-1 score for every query and refuse when it falls below a corpus-specific threshold, instead of handing weak chunks to the generator. Tell the generator to answer only from the snippets, to cite every claim and to say it does not know when the snippets do not answer. Measure refusal calibration: on questions whose answer is not in the store, count how often the system refuses, and track the false confidence rate.
followUps: Level 3: Where does the threshold come from? Expected: the distribution of rank-1 scores on a held-out set with known in-corpus and out-of-corpus questions; it is specific to the corpus.

Level 3: What does the generator prompt need beyond "use only the context"? Expected: cite each claim with its anchor and say it does not know when the snippets do not answer; the explicit instruction cut hallucination by 40 to 60 percent in the question answering lesson.

Level 4: Too many refusals are also a failure. How do you balance it? Expected: track the false confidence rate on out-of-corpus questions next to the wrong refusal rate on in-corpus questions, and move the threshold on the held-out set.

Level 4: How does the citation post-filter work with the refusal gate? Expected: each claim is checked against the passage its anchor cites, and a claim with no anchor or with a passage that does not state it is dropped or re-asked, so a weak answer that passed the score gate cannot ship an unsupported claim.
wrongAnswers: "Tell the model to be careful." An instruction cannot see the retrieval scores; the first gate belongs before generation.
"Refuse when retrieval returns fewer than k chunks." A count is not confidence; weak chunks still fill k slots.
"Set the threshold once from the fixture." It is corpus specific and moves when the embedder, the reranker or the corpus changes.

questions.title: Take-home. You receive a corpus of a few hundred internal documents and a retrieval pipeline with two chunkers and two retrievers behind flags. Build the evaluation that tells the team which configuration to ship, and write up what the numbers mean. You have one evening.
questions.answer: Build a labeled query set first, stratified by query type, with gold document ids and gold answer text for each query. Run every configuration against the same set and report recall at 5 for each slice, plus MRR and the share of queries whose top 5 holds a chunk with the gold answer text, and read the spread between configurations. Label at document level so the same labels grade every chunker; if you label at chunk level, record the chunker in the qrels and relabel after any change of chunker.
followUps: Level 3: Why split the queries by type? Expected: factoid and multi-hop queries reveal different winners, and one average hides the class that loses.

Level 3: The labels were produced with chunker A. Can you reuse them for chunker B? Expected: only if the labels are at document or span level; chunk ids change with the boundaries, so record the chunker in the qrels and relabel otherwise.

Level 4: How do you justify the query count in the write-up? Expected: a 50-query stratified set for the first decision, then tiers of 20 queries in CI, 200 nightly and 2000 weekly, with a note on what each tier can and cannot detect.

Level 4: What do you refuse to conclude after one evening? Expected: anything about answer quality, because the eval grades retrieval; faithfulness and relevance need a judge, and a judge from the generator's own family is biased.
wrongAnswers: "I wrote ten questions myself and ran each configuration." Ten questions of one type cannot separate four configurations or expose a class that always misses.
"Here is the average recall for each configuration." One average hides per-slice winners and the class that fails.
"I changed the chunker and reused the chunk-level labels." Chunk ids no longer line up with the new chunks; label at document level, or relabel and record the chunker in the qrels header.

questions.title: After a release, the nightly RAG eval shows recall at 5 unchanged and still high, MRR down from last week, and faithfulness unchanged. Nobody touched the retriever. Which stage do you suspect, how do you confirm it, and what would other patterns have told you?
questions.answer: The reranker. On average the gold chunk still arrives in the top 5, so recall holds, but it sits lower in the list, so MRR falls, and the generator stays grounded in what it receives. Confirm it from the per-query trace: compare the rank of the gold chunk before and after the release, then look at what changed in the reranker, such as its weights, its candidate pool size, or the order of the query and the document in the pair.
followUps: Level 3: The trace shows the gold chunk at rank 3 only for literal identifier queries. What does the slice suggest? Expected: a change that hurt the lexical signal inside the pool for those queries; slice by class to find it rather than averaging it away.

Level 3: Which release changes can move MRR while recall at 5 stays fixed? Expected: anything inside the reranker: new weights, a smaller candidate pool, or the query and the document swapped in the pair.

Level 4: Faithfulness is also down while recall and MRR are fine. Where do you look? Expected: the generation prompt, and the judge itself, because a judge from the same model family grades its own output too kindly; hand-grade a sample.

Level 4: Why keep the per-query trace rather than the averages? Expected: a 90 percent average hides a class that always misses, and when a user complains you can find the matching qrel and see whether the eval would have caught it.
wrongAnswers: "The retriever regressed." Nobody touched the retriever and recall at 5 did not move; a flat average can still hide a query that lost its gold chunk, so check the per-query rank trace before you blame retrieval.
"The model started to hallucinate." Faithfulness did not move; the generator is still grounded in what it receives.
"Run it again, it is noise." The eval is offline and deterministic on the fixture; one metric down with the others flat points at one stage.

questions.title: You turned on the hypothetical-answer rewriter for a code search assistant. Questions about one subsystem got worse: the gold document, which sat at rank 2 before, now falls out of the top 10 on the lexical side. The hypothetical passages read well. What happened, and what do you change?
questions.answer: The model wrote a function name that does not exist in the index. The real symbol that carried the lexical match is gone from the rewritten query, the rest of the passage is generic prose that scores across many documents, and the dense side returns a plausible neighbor for the invented token. Cap the hypothetical at two or three sentences, lower the BM25 weight in the fusion for rewritten queries, and route queries that already contain a literal symbol past the rewriter.
followUps: Level 3: Why does a longer hypothetical make it worse? Expected: it collects more tokens that score on many documents; the lesson caps it at two or three sentences.
Level 3: Which queries should skip the rewriter? Expected: queries that already contain a literal symbol, because the lexical retriever ranks those first without help.

Level 4: How do you prove the fix rather than argue it? Expected: slice the eval by query class, compare recall per slice with and without the rewriter, and enable it only on the slices where it helps.

Level 4: Why does the dense side not rescue the query? Expected: the invented token still gets a plausible vector, so the dense retriever returns wrong neighbors that look right; the fusion fixes that only when the lexical side votes correctly.
wrongAnswers: "Tell the model not to invent names." It cannot know which names exist in your corpus; the lesson says the passage is wrong as a fact by design.
"Turn the rewriter off everywhere." It wins on queries whose phrasing does not match the corpus; route by query class instead.
"Raise the BM25 weight to get the lexical signal back." The lexical signal is the part the invented token broke; the lesson lowers the BM25 weight for the rewritten query.

questions.title: Your faithfulness score comes from a model that reads each claim next to the retrieved context and answers yes or no. The score has sat near the top for a month, yet reviewers keep finding invented facts in sampled answers. The generator and the judge are the same model. What is going on, and what do you change?
questions.answer: A judge from the same family as the generator grades its own output as more faithful than it is, so the number stays high while the samples show the truth. Switch the judge to a different model family or hand-grade a sample, and add a sample-level review, because a per-sentence check can pass while the whole answer misleads.
followUps: Level 3: How do you size the judge problem before you change anything? Expected: hand-grade a sample of claims and measure the disagreement between the judge and the human labels.
Level 3: Every sentence passes but the answer as a whole misleads. Which check catches that? Expected: a sample-level qualitative review in addition to the per-claim metric.

Level 4: Why can a high faithfulness score sit next to a useless answer? Expected: faithfulness compares the answer with the context and not with the question, so a grounded off-topic answer scores high on faithfulness and low on relevance.

Level 4: The team wants the strongest model available as judge, and it is also the generator. What do you say? Expected: pick the judge for independence first; a strong judge of its own family is still biased, so use another family and keep a human-graded calibration sample.
wrongAnswers: "The score is high, so the reviewers are wrong." The score is one model's opinion of its own family's output; the sampled answers are the ground truth.
"Make the judge stricter and the problem goes away." A stricter prompt or threshold does not remove a bias toward the judge's own family; only another family or a human sample does.
"Replace faithfulness with answer relevance." They measure different things; relevance asks whether the answer addresses the question and says nothing about grounding.

questions.title: You add a cross-encoder behind a hybrid retriever. The prompt receives K chunks. The team wants a rule for N, the number of candidates the reranker scores, and one engineer proposes a small N to protect the latency budget. How do you choose N, and what do you refuse?
questions.answer: Choose N from the recall curve of the reranked output and the latency budget together. Sweep N on a held-out query set; the lift saturates at a knee somewhere around 20 to 50 candidates, and past it every extra candidate costs a forward pass for nothing. Keep N at least three times K, because the reranker can only promote a chunk that the retriever put in the pool.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the curve flatten? Expected: past the knee the extra candidates are rarely relevant, so the reranker has nothing more to promote while each one still costs a forward pass.
Level 3: You cut N from 50 to 10 to save latency. What else moves? Expected: the recall cap, because the reranker cannot see a chunk outside the pool; run the eval again instead of assuming.
Level 4: The embedder is upgraded. Is the chosen N still valid? Expected: no; a new bi-encoder changes recall at N, so the sweep must run again before the release.
Level 4: How do you get the latency back without a smaller N? Expected: one batched forward pass for the N pairs, and a cache keyed on the query and the document id.
wrongAnswers: "Set N equal to K to save time." Then the reranker can only reorder the K chunks and never bring a new one in, so recall at K cannot move.
"The larger N, the better." Past the knee the lift saturates and each extra candidate costs one forward pass.
"Pick N once and keep it." N is pinned with the two models; a change in either one invalidates the choice.

questions.title: Your RAG eval reports high recall, high MRR, high faithfulness and high answer relevance, and the weekly drift dashboard is flat. Support still forwards a stream of wrong answers from one business unit. As the staff engineer on the system, what do you conclude, and what do you change in the eval program itself?
questions.answer: Conclude that the eval set does not represent that unit's traffic: all four metrics can be high on queries that nobody asks. Add their real queries to the qrels, slice every metric by query class and document type, and check whether their documents are chunked by a splitter that fits their format. Then change the program: tier the qrels, review them on a schedule so they do not rot, and treat a per-slice drop as a release blocker.
followUps: Level 3: Why can every metric be high while the answers are wrong? Expected: the metrics are computed on the eval set, and that set lacks the queries and documents where the failures happen.
Level 4: What is the first concrete change to the qrels? Expected: add that unit's real queries with expert-labeled gold ids and answers, tagged with query class and document type for slicing.

Level 4: How do you keep the qrels honest over time? Expected: a scheduled review, quarterly in the lesson, because gold answers drift as the corpus changes, plus a check that the chunker in the qrels header is the one in production.
Level 4: Why was the drift dashboard flat while quality fell? Expected: it tracks the same unrepresentative set every week; an alert on that set says nothing about traffic it does not contain.
wrongAnswers: "The metrics are high, so the complaints are user error." The metrics grade the eval set, not the traffic; the complaints are the missing data.
"Raise the thresholds." Tighter thresholds on the wrong queries still measure the wrong queries.
"Replace the eval with a bigger public benchmark." A public set has nothing from that unit; the fix is their real queries, labeled.

questions.title: A regulated-domain assistant serves analysts in two jurisdictions from one index. In a red-team probe, a question asked under one jurisdiction returned a contract clause that belongs to the other. The reranker and the generator behave as designed. Where is the leak, how do you close it, and how do you prove that it stays closed?
questions.answer: The leak is in retrieval: the jurisdiction tag was not applied as a pre-filter before the similarity search, so a semantically close chunk from the other jurisdiction entered the candidate pool, and nothing downstream is built to remove it. Close it by tagging every chunk with role and jurisdiction at ingestion and filtering on both before hybrid retrieval runs. Prove it with a cross-jurisdiction probe set in the red-team suite, scored pass or fail with a severity, and run before every release.
followUps: Level 3: Why can the reranker not catch the leaked clause? Expected: it only orders the candidates it receives, and a clause from the wrong jurisdiction is still relevant to the question.
Level 3: Why is the output guard not the fix? Expected: it scrubs personal data and blocks forbidden topics; it cannot tell which jurisdiction a clause belongs to.
Level 4: The tags exist and the leak persists. What do you check? Expected: whether the filter runs before retrieval or on the top k after it, and whether ingestion lets an untagged chunk in.

Level 4: How do you keep the proof current? Expected: run the probe set in the red team on every change to ingestion or retrieval, and show the leak count on the drift dashboard with a zero threshold.
wrongAnswers: "Add a sentence to the system prompt about the user's jurisdiction." The model cannot verify which jurisdiction a chunk belongs to; access control belongs in retrieval.
"Separate indexes solve it, no tags needed." Role filtering still needs labels, shared documents get duplicated, and the probe is still needed to prove the split holds.
"The red team passed once, so it is closed." One pass proves one build; the probe runs on every ingestion or retrieval change.

questions.title: Design a code search service that answers questions such as "how is the upload retry budget enforced" across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code, and that stays fresh on every push. What is different from document retrieval, and where does it break?
questions.answer: Chunk at syntax tree nodes, functions and classes, not at fixed windows, and give each chunk three retrievable forms: a dense code embedding, BM25 terms with the symbol name weighted above the body, and a one-sentence natural-language summary. Retrieve hybrid, rerank with a cross-encoder, and synthesize with mandatory file and line citations that a post-filter enforces. Freshness is the hard part: a push triggers a symbol-level diff so that only changed chunks re-embed and only affected cross-file edges recompute.
followUps: Level 3: Why three forms per chunk and not one good embedding? Expected: users ask how something is authorized while the code says check_permission; the summary bridges a vocabulary gap that neither the code embedding nor BM25 covers.

Level 3: What does the symbol graph buy at query time? Expected: expansion across repository boundaries, from a function to its callers and imports, so a question that spans several repositories finds the whole chain.
Level 4: Generated boilerplate enters the corpus. What happens and what do you do? Expected: near-duplicate code poisons retrieval; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them.

Level 4: What is the freshness target and how do you hold it? Expected: a 50-file push searchable in under 60 seconds on the 2M line fleet, by re-embedding only changed chunks and recomputing only affected edges.
wrongAnswers: "Chunk code every 512 tokens like prose." Fixed windows cut identifiers in half and separate a function from its signature; cut at syntax tree nodes.
"Re-index the whole fleet on every push." Two million lines per commit never catches up; diff at the symbol level.
"Citations are optional for code answers." The capstone rejects any claim without a file and line anchor; the post-filter drops or re-asks.

topics.title: Prompting and structured output
topics.about: Prompt design, context engineering, schemas, constrained decoding and function calls.

questions.title: How do you guarantee strict schema-compliant JSON outputs from an LLM in production?
questions.answer: The strongest guarantee is constrained decoding, where a grammar or JSON schema masks any token that would make the output invalid. You define the expected structure with a schema, for example using Pydantic, and pass it to the model. You still validate every response in your application, because a valid format can contain wrong values. If validation fails, retry automatically with the error message, with a limit on the number of retries.
keyPoints: Constrained decoding masks tokens that violate a schema.
Define the expected structure with a typed schema.
Validate response values in application code.
Retry validation failures with feedback and a fixed retry limit.

questions.title: When should you use chain-of-thought prompting and what engineering trade-offs does it introduce?
questions.answer: Use chain-of-thought for complex tasks that need several steps, such as multi-step maths, logic, or planning. It is rarely worth it for simple lookups or classification. It generates extra tokens, so it adds latency and cost. The written reasoning can also be wrong or may not reflect how the model actually reached its answer, so you should not treat it as proof. Keep the reasoning separate from the final answer, and evaluate whether it actually improves results on your task.
keyPoints: Use chain-of-thought for multi-step maths, logic or planning.
Simple lookups and classification rarely justify the extra tokens.
Reasoning adds latency and cost and is not proof.
Separate reasoning from the final answer and measure task gains.

questions.title: Your team adds "think step by step" to every prompt in the product, including a high-volume classifier and the calls to a reasoning model. Where does that help, where does it hurt, and why?
questions.answer: It helps on multi-step problems, where each reasoning token becomes context for the next one and the model computes its way to the answer. It hurts on simple recall and single-step classification, where it adds 50 to 200 tokens of reasoning per query for no gain, and on reasoning models, which already run a chain of thought internally and can get worse with the extra instruction. Pick the technique per task from the accuracy requirement, the latency budget and the cost.
followUps: Level 1: Why does writing the steps out raise accuracy? Expected: each reasoning token becomes context for the next token, so the model computes the answer in steps instead of in one pass.
Level 2: What does the classifier pay for the extra phrase? Expected: 50 to 200 tokens of reasoning per query, which at volume is cost and latency for no accuracy gain.
Level 2: Why leave the phrase out for a reasoning model? Expected: it already runs its chain internally before the answer, so the instruction is redundant and sometimes counterproductive.

Level 3: Is there a task where a single chain is worse than a plain answer? Expected: yes, the lesson's search puzzle, where the chain solved fewer cases than standard prompting and a tree search solved most.
wrongAnswers: "It never hurts, worst case it is neutral." It costs tokens on every call, and it lowered accuracy on the wide search puzzle and on reasoning models.
"Few-shot and chain of thought are the same thing." Few-shot shows examples; chain of thought shows reasoning; the two combine into few-shot chain of thought.
"Always run it at temperature zero." A single chain at zero is fine, but sampling several chains for a vote needs temperature above zero, or every sample is identical.
keyPoints: Reasoning tokens help solve multi-step tasks.
Simple recall and classification can gain no accuracy from extra reasoning.
Reasoning models may worsen with redundant chain-of-thought instructions.
Choose per task using accuracy, latency and cost requirements.

questions.title: A teammate turned on the provider's JSON mode and says the extraction output is now guaranteed. What does JSON mode guarantee, what does it not, and what do you turn on instead?
questions.answer: JSON mode guarantees that a finished output parses, nothing more; a response cut at the token limit can still fail, so check the finish reason first. It does not guarantee your keys, your types, your enum values or the absence of extra fields. Turn on the schema mode, where the provider takes a JSON Schema and constrains decoding to it, and keep a check on your side for the values that a schema cannot judge.
followUps: Level 1: Which failure remains under strict schema mode? Expected: a refusal, when the model decides the input does not fit the schema; handle it as a typed outcome, and route a response cut at the token limit to the error path.
Level 2: What does strict mode demand of the schema? Expected: every property required, additional properties forbidden, no unresolved references; otherwise the request is rejected with a 400.
Level 2: The output matches the schema and the price is wrong. Which layer failed? Expected: none of the format layers; the value is invented, and only a semantic check or an eval catches that.
Level 3: A field is sometimes unknown in the source text. How do you write the schema? Expected: allow null or a sentinel; a grammar that forces a value makes the model invent one, such as a date.
wrongAnswers: "JSON mode means the keys match my model." It only guarantees syntax; extra keys, wrong types and missing fields still happen.
"Adding 'respond in valid JSON' to the prompt is the same thing." A prompt-only approach is about 90 percent reliable and fails with fences, preambles and truncation.
"With schema mode I can drop validation." A schema cannot catch a wrong value with the right type; keep a semantic check.
keyPoints: JSON mode guarantees parsing only for completed output.
Check finish reason for truncation.
JSON mode does not enforce fields, types or enums.
Use schema-constrained decoding plus semantic value checks.

questions.title: Walk me through the three parts of a chat API call and what each one is for. Then tell me how you would get a model to return a JSON object with no preamble, without a structured output API.
questions.answer: The system message sets identity, rules and output constraints and persists across turns. The user message carries the task and changes every turn. The assistant prefill starts the model's reply for it, so a prefill of an opening brace makes the model continue as JSON with no preamble, on the providers that accept a partial assistant turn.
followUps: Level 1: Why does the system message come first? Expected: the model gives it the highest priority, and it stays constant while user turns change.

Level 2: What does the prefill save compared with an instruction to respond in JSON? Expected: the preamble and the code fence; the reply starts inside the object, so the parser sees JSON from the first character.

Level 2: Your system prompt has grown to 2,000 words of rules. What does the lesson say? Expected: over-constraining; the model spends its capacity on the rules instead of the task, and most tasks want a system prompt under 500 tokens.

Level 3: How do you write one prompt that behaves the same on several providers? Expected: plain English, an explicit format, XML style delimiters, the instructions at the start and the end, temperature zero while testing, and two or three examples.
wrongAnswers: "The system message is just the first user message." It is processed with a higher priority and persists while user turns change.
"A prefill works on every provider." Only some accept a partial assistant turn; elsewhere use the structured output mode.
"More rules in the system prompt means more control." Past a point the model spends its capacity on the rules; the lesson keeps most system prompts under 500 tokens.
keyPoints: System messages define persistent identity, rules and output constraints.
User messages carry the changing task.
Assistant prefill starts the generated reply.
An opening brace can suppress a JSON preamble where prefill is supported.
