questions.title: A classification prompt has eight output labels. One engineer wants twenty examples in the prompt to be safe, another wants none and a longer instruction. How many examples do you include, which ones, and what decides it?
questions.answer: Three to five for most tasks, and for a classifier with many labels one example per label, so eight here. Pick examples that are semantically close to the input and that cover every label, because similar examples beat random ones by 5 to 15 percent on classification. Below three the model has too little signal to extract the pattern; above five you pay context tokens on every call for diminishing returns.
followUps: Level 2: When does zero-shot win? Expected: simple factual questions, creative tasks where examples constrain, and tasks where good examples are harder to find than a good instruction.

Level 2: What do examples do that an instruction cannot? Expected: they show the format and the reasoning instead of describing them, and the model matches a shown pattern more reliably than it interprets a rule.

Level 3: How do you choose the examples at request time? Expected: embed a labeled pool and select the nearest examples to the input while keeping label coverage; the lesson measured a 5 to 15 percent gain over random selection.

Level 3: The examples cost 200 to 500 tokens on every call. How do you contain that? Expected: keep the count at three to five; place a fixed set of examples in the stable prefix so the prompt cache serves them at the discounted rate, and place examples picked per query below the breakpoint, because they change on every request.
wrongAnswers: "More examples are always safer." Above five the returns diminish and every example costs context on every call.
"Random examples are fine, the model generalizes." Similar examples beat random ones by 5 to 15 percent on classification.
"Describe the labels in detail and skip the examples." For a format-sensitive task with many labels, examples transfer the pattern better than a description, and across providers too.
keyPoints: Use three to five examples for most tasks.
For many-label classification, cover each label.
Choose examples semantically close to the input.
Balance too little pattern signal against repeated context cost.

questions.title: You assemble a prompt from a system message, ten retrieved documents, the chat history so far and the user question. In which order do you place them, and what evidence decides it?
questions.answer: Put the system prompt and the critical instructions first, the current question and the most relevant context last, and the lowest-priority material in the middle. The evidence is the lost-in-the-middle finding: with one relevant document among 20, accuracy was 85 to 90 percent when it sat first or last and fell to 60 to 70 percent in the middle. If a key point has to sit in the middle, repeat it at the end.
followUps: Level 2: Why not include all ten retrieved documents? Expected: bad retrieval is worse than none; score each against the query, drop those below a threshold, and keep the 3 relevant ones over 10 mediocre ones.
Level 2: What do you reserve at the end of the window, and how much? Expected: the generation budget, at least 2,000 to 4,000 tokens, or the model has no room to answer.

Level 3: How does the lesson's reorder place five scored documents? Expected: sorted by score, the odd ranks go to the front in order and the even ranks go to the back in reverse, so the best sit at both ends.

Level 3: The same system prompt is sent on every turn. What does that imply for its size? Expected: every word is paid on every call, so keep it tight; the lesson cites a coding assistant with about 6,000 tokens of system prompt and tool definitions.
wrongAnswers: "The window is huge, more context is always better." A 10K prompt that is 90 percent signal beats a 100K prompt that is 10 percent signal; more context is more noise for attention to filter.
"Put the question first so the model knows what to look for." The end of the context gets high attention too; the lesson places the current query last and the instructions first.
"Order does not matter, attention sees everything." The measured drop in the middle is 10 to 20 percent.
keyPoints: Put critical instructions and system content first.
Place the current question and most relevant context last.
Leave lower-priority material in the middle.
Repeat an unavoidable middle-position key point at the end.

questions.title: You need two things from the same model: a typed summary of a support ticket, and the ability to look up the customer's account during the conversation. A teammate wants to build both as tools. Which mechanism fits each, and why does the distinction matter?
questions.answer: The ticket summary is structured output: the typed data is the final product, so use the schema mode and validate it. The account lookup is a function call: the model declares an intent to act, your code executes it and feeds the result back, so the output is an intermediate step. The two share the JSON Schema machinery but differ in what happens next, and mixing them hides which outputs are data and which are actions your code runs.
followUps: Level 2: When is tool use the right way to get structured data? Expected: when the model must pick one of several schemas from the input; the lesson's example is 10 extraction schemas, where tool use gives the selection and the structure together.
Level 2: In the lookup case, who runs the function? Expected: your code; the model emits the name and the arguments, and the result goes back as a message.
Level 3: What differs in validation between the two? Expected: data gets schema validation and a semantic check; an action gets argument validation, an allowlist and a call budget before it runs.

Level 3: A provider offers schema output only through tool use. How do you keep the distinction? Expected: name the tool for the data it returns, never execute it, send its arguments to the validator as the final record, and keep real actions in a separate registry.
wrongAnswers: "They are the same thing with different names." They share the schema machinery; one produces the final data, the other requests an action your code performs.
"Use function calling for everything, it is more flexible." Every tool is an executable surface with security rules; data extraction does not need one.
"The model runs the lookup itself." The model never executes anything; it emits a call and your code is the executor.
keyPoints: Use structured output when typed data is the final product.
Validate final data against the schema.
Use function calling for an intermediate intent to act.
Application code executes the function and returns its result.

questions.title: An extraction service turns purchase-order emails into typed records. Name the ways a structured output call can fail, say which of them disappear under strict schema enforcement, and describe how the code should treat what remains.
questions.answer: Three ways: a parse error, where the output is not JSON; a schema violation, where it parses but breaks a type, a required field, an enum or a range; and a refusal, where the model decides the input does not fit the schema. Strict enforcement removes the first two by construction for a response that finishes. The refusal stays, and it must be a typed outcome that the code logs and returns, never a retry. A response cut at the token limit can still fail to parse, so check the stop reason before you read the output.
followUps: Level 2: How many retries, and what does needing more tell you? Expected: at most three; one is usually enough, and beyond three the schema or the prompt is wrong for some inputs.
Level 2: Why must the refusal branch not retry? Expected: the model declined for a reason, often fit or safety; a retry wastes cost and can push a wrong extraction through.
Level 3: What does the retry prompt need from the validator? Expected: a typed error list with a path and a message per failure, so the model knows which field to fix.
Level 3: Which schema setting blocks invented fields? Expected: additional properties set to false, which strict mode requires everywhere.
wrongAnswers: "A refusal is a failed call, retry it." It is a first-class outcome with a reason attached; log it and return it typed.
"Strict mode removes every failure." It removes parse errors and schema violations for a finished response; refusals, truncated responses and wrong values with the right type remain.
"Retry until it validates." Past three retries the cost grows and the schema is the real problem.
keyPoints: Distinguish parse errors, schema violations and refusals.
Strict schema enforcement handles format failures for completed responses.
Treat refusals as logged typed outcomes rather than retries.
Check stop reason before parsing potentially truncated output.

questions.title: You enabled prompt caching on a 15,000-token system prompt. The usage field for cache reads stays at zero on every request, while cache creation tokens are charged every time. What do you look for, and in what order?
questions.answer: Something above the cache breakpoint changes on every request. Look first for a timestamp or a request id at the top of the system prompt, then for tool definitions serialized in a changing order, then for near-duplicate text that differs by a byte between code paths, and then for a block under the minimum cacheable size. The cache matches prefixes only, so the first differing token turns everything after it into a miss.
followUps: Level 2: How do you make this a test? Expected: two requests built by the production prompt builder with the same user input, with an assertion that the cache read tokens are above zero on the second; if they stay at zero the keys are drifting.
Level 2: Where does the timestamp go instead? Expected: below the breakpoint, with the other per-request fields such as the user message.
Level 3: The block is below the minimum size. What happens? Expected: nothing is cached and nothing is reported; the floor is 1,024 tokens, and 2,048 on the small model.
Level 3: Input tokens fell after your change. Is that proof it works? Expected: no; split the input tokens into cached and uncached, or a drop in traffic looks like a cache win.
wrongAnswers: "Caching is automatic, there is nothing to configure." On the explicit providers you mark the block; on the automatic one the prefix still has to be stable and above 1,024 tokens, and a changed user field or tool order breaks it.
"Put the user message first so the model reads it early." That places the only part that changes above everything else, and the cache never hits.
"Extend the TTL to one hour, the cache is expiring." Expiry would show as writes after quiet periods, not on every request; the one-hour TTL also charges 2x for the write.
keyPoints: Inspect changing fields before the cache breakpoint.
Check timestamps, request IDs and unstable tool ordering.
Compare near-duplicate text and minimum cacheable size.
The first different token invalidates the remaining prefix match.

questions.title: An agent has eight tools and keeps calling the wrong one. The tool descriptions are one or two words each, such as "gets weather". What does the description do, and how do you rewrite one?
questions.answer: The model reads the description to decide when and how to call the tool, so the description is a prompt for tool selection. Rewrite it as a full sentence that says what the tool does and what it returns, for example that it gets the current weather for a city and returns the temperature in Celsius and the conditions, and describe each parameter with an example value and an enum where the set is closed. Then validate the arguments against the schema before anything executes.
followUps: Level 2: Where else does a description help besides the tool itself? Expected: on each parameter, with an example value and an enum where the set is closed, so the arguments come out right.

Level 2: The model still guesses instead of calling a tool when it should. Which setting changes that? Expected: tool choice set to required, or to a named tool when upstream logic already knows which one.
Level 3: How do you prove the rewrite worked? Expected: a set of test queries with expected tool names, 30 in the lesson, the share that select the right tool, and the confused pairs listed.
Level 3: A tool fails. What should it return so the model recovers? Expected: a structured error with a message, a code and suggestions, not an exception or an empty response.
wrongAnswers: "The model infers the purpose from the function name." It reads the description; a vague one produces worse selection than a full sentence.
"Describe every tool in a paragraph to be safe." Definitions travel with every request; one precise sentence plus parameter descriptions is the target.
"Let the model call any function by name." The lesson's rule is an allowlist of the tools you define, never a generic execute-by-name tool.
keyPoints: Tool descriptions guide model tool selection.
Describe what the tool does and returns in a full sentence.
Give parameter examples and enums for closed sets.
Validate arguments against the schema before execution.

questions.title: A classifier uses constrained decoding with a schema of two fields, answer and reasoning, in that order. The output is always valid JSON and the accuracy is worse than the free-text version was. What is wrong?
questions.answer: The field order. The model commits to the answer before it writes any reasoning, so the reasoning tokens never shape the answer, and you lose the gain that step-by-step gives. Put reasoning first and answer last; the schema stays valid, and no validator will ever flag the difference, because the order is logic and not formatting.
followUps: Level 2: Why can no validator catch this? Expected: both orders are valid against the schema; the harm is in what the model has seen when it writes the answer token.

Level 2: The schema forces a date pattern and the model fills in dates that are not in the text. Which related mistake is that? Expected: a grammar too strict for missing data; allow null or a sentinel so the model does not invent a value.
Level 3: A field is optional and the model leaves it out when it matters. What do you change? Expected: make it required and allow null, so the model has to state that the value is missing.
Level 3: The schema nests four levels deep and errors rise. What do you do? Expected: flatten, because each level of nesting is one more place to lose track of the structure.
wrongAnswers: "Constrained decoding guarantees a correct output." It guarantees the shape; the lesson shows valid JSON with a wrong answer.
"Order does not matter in JSON." It does not matter to the parser; it matters to the model, which writes the fields in order.
"Add a check that the reasoning supports the answer." That is an eval, not a fix; the fix is to generate the reasoning first.
keyPoints: An answer-first field order commits the decision before reasoning.
Later reasoning cannot influence an already generated answer.
Place reasoning before the answer field.
Schema validation alone will not catch this ordering issue.

questions.title: A math assistant samples five reasoning paths per question and takes a majority vote. Accuracy did not move compared with a single path, and the bill is five times higher. The team set the temperature to zero for reproducibility. What happened, and what else do you check before you keep the voting?
questions.answer: At temperature zero the samples should be identical, and only a nondeterministic serving stack makes them differ a little, so the five paths are close to one path counted five times and the vote changes almost nothing. The lesson samples at 0.7 so the paths differ enough for their errors to cancel. Then check that the final answer comes out in a fixed format, because without a line such as "The answer is" followed by the number the votes cannot be compared, and check that the single-path accuracy sits in the range where a vote helps, about 60 to 85 percent.
followUps: Level 2: Why 0.7 and not something much higher? Expected: enough randomness for diverse paths and not so much that the model produces gibberish.
Level 2: How are the five answers compared? Expected: the prompt forces a final line in a fixed form and the code extracts the number from it; without that, the vote has nothing to count.
Level 3: When is the vote worth five times the cost? Expected: when single-chain accuracy is in the 60 to 85 percent range; on a model at 97 percent the lift is about one point.

Level 3: How does the lesson turn the vote into a decision? Expected: the vote share is a confidence; with 4 of 5 in agreement, a confidence of 0.8, and a match with the deterministic answer, accept, otherwise escalate to a tree search.
wrongAnswers: "Temperature zero makes the vote more reliable." It makes the samples the same or nearly the same, so there is no real vote.
"Use forty samples like the paper." Five captures most of the benefit and more than ten shows diminishing returns; forty multiplies the cost for little gain.
"Voting fixes a systematic error." If most paths make the same mistake, the majority is wrong with high confidence; the vote cancels independent errors only.
keyPoints: Temperature-zero samples mostly repeat the same path.
Serving nondeterminism does not provide useful reasoning diversity.
Sample diverse paths and standardize the extracted final-answer format.
Check whether single-path accuracy is in a range where voting helps.

questions.title: Your batch job sends the same 15,000-token rubric with each of twenty code reviews, spread over 40 minutes in uneven clusters, and some of the quiet stretches between clusters outlast the short cache. The provider bills a write at 1.25 times the input rate for a five-minute cache and at 2 times the input rate for a one-hour cache, and bills reads at one tenth of the input rate. Which cache do you pick, and show the break-even.
questions.answer: The five-minute cache pays for itself on the first read: a write costs 1.25 times and a read 0.1 times the normal input rate, so one write plus one read averages 0.675 times, a saving of 32 percent, and one write plus ten reads averages 0.205 times, a saving of 80 percent. Each read refreshes the five-minute lifetime, so the five-minute cache expires only in a gap longer than five minutes. This batch has such gaps, so the one-hour cache fits; its write costs 2 times the input rate and it needs only two reads to come out ahead, and twenty reviews give far more. The rule of thumb is to cache anything reused at least three times within the lifetime.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the five-minute cache break even on the first read? Expected: the write costs 1.25 times and the read 0.1 times, so two requests average 0.675 times the uncached cost.
Level 3: What does the one-hour cache need to come out ahead? Expected: two reads, because its write costs 2 times the input rate.

Level 4: The reviews arrive in bursts of several within a minute, then nothing for an hour. Does the answer change? Expected: yes; each burst lives inside a five-minute cache, so the cheaper write wins, and the one-hour cache would pay the 2 times write for reuse that never comes.

Level 4: How do you verify the saving in production rather than on paper? Expected: read the cache creation and cache read token fields on each response, gate the deploy on a read fraction above 80 percent after warmup, and split the dashboard into cached and uncached tokens.
wrongAnswers: "Always pick the longer cache to be safe." Its write costs 2 times the input rate against 1.25; with reuse inside five minutes the shorter cache is cheaper.
"The write premium makes caching a loss for short jobs." One write plus one read already saves 32 percent on the five-minute cache.
"Cache the user message too." It differs on every request, so it never hits; the layout leaves it below the breakpoint.
keyPoints: Compare cache write and read prices with normal input cost.
The stated five-minute cache breaks even on its first read.
Reads refresh the five-minute lifetime.
Use the longer cache when reuse has gaps beyond five minutes.

questions.title: Design the extraction service for purchase-order emails. The input is free text; the output is a typed record with a customer, line items and a total. Cover the schema, the enforcement mode, the retry and refusal handling, and how you prove it works before it touches the accounting system.
questions.answer: Write one JSON Schema 2020-12 with the constraints that matter: required fields, enums for closed sets, a minimum of zero on the total, additional properties forbidden, and any reasoning field ahead of any decision field. Run it in the provider's strict schema mode so that a response that finishes cannot have a parse error or a schema violation, check the stop reason so that a response cut at the token limit goes to the error path, and treat a refusal as a typed outcome that goes to a review queue. Prove it with a labeled set of real emails scored per field, a refusal check on inputs that must not extract, and a run beside the human process before any record is written.
followUps: Level 3: Why forbid additional properties? Expected: it blocks invented fields, and strict mode requires it everywhere.

Level 3: You expect to switch providers next year. Which mode do you pick? Expected: a retry library over the Pydantic model for portability, or keep the schema identical across providers so each strict mode receives the same contract.

Level 4: How do you version the schema once records exist? Expected: a version field on each record and a schema diff that separates breaking changes from non-breaking ones. Strict mode makes every field required, so an added field is breaking too, because the records written before it do not contain it; removed fields and changed types are breaking, and relaxed constraints are not.

Level 4: Which failure can this design not remove, and where does it go? Expected: a wrong value with the right type; it goes to the field-level eval and the confidence flags, and the low-confidence records go to review.
wrongAnswers: "Prompt for JSON and parse it, the model is good." That works 85 to 95 percent of the time and fails six different ways; accounting needs the contract.
"Retry refusals until the model gives a record." A refusal says the input does not fit; forcing a record invents one.
"Validation after generation is as good as strict mode." It is reliable but pays for every retry, and a truncated output costs a turn each time.
keyPoints: Require fields, closed enums, nonnegative totals and no extra properties.
Use strict schema decoding with reasoning before decision.
Route truncation to errors and typed refusals to review.
Validate real-email fields and shadow the human process before writes.

questions.title: An extraction pipeline with strict schema enforcement has reported zero validation errors for a month. A finance review finds that a share of the extracted invoice totals do not match the source documents, and that a status field often holds a value that is allowed by the enum and wrong for the document. The engineers say the schema guarantees correctness. What do you tell them, and what do you build?
questions.answer: Schema enforcement guarantees shape, not truth. A total with the right type and the wrong number passes every format check, and an enum member can be allowed and still be the wrong one. Build a semantic eval: a labeled set of documents with gold records, exact match and field-level accuracy per field, plus a confidence signal from repeated extraction or token probabilities that sends low-confidence fields to human review.
followUps: Level 3: Which failure can a schema never see? Expected: a value with the right type and the wrong content, such as a total copied from the wrong line.

Level 3: How do you get a confidence per field without a new model? Expected: run the extraction three times and measure agreement, or read token probabilities, and flag fields that disagree for review.

Level 4: The status enum has a member the model keeps picking wrongly. What are the candidate fixes? Expected: describe the members so their meaning is explicit, put a reasoning field before the status, and check whether the source has cases no member fits, which calls for a null or an "other" member.

Level 4: What does the finished eval report look like? Expected: schema compliance near 100 percent as a sanity row, then exact match and field-level accuracy per field on the labeled set, with the hardest fields named.
wrongAnswers: "Zero validation errors means zero extraction errors." Validation checks shape; the review found value errors that no shape check can see.
"Switch to a bigger model and the values will be right." Size changes the error rate, not the blind spot; without a labeled eval you cannot tell by how much.
"Add a tighter pattern to the total field." A tighter grammar does not make the number true; a grammar too strict even pushes the model to invent one.
keyPoints: Schema validity guarantees shape rather than factual truth.
Wrong numbers and allowed-but-wrong enums can pass.
Evaluate gold records with exact match and per-field accuracy.
Route uncertain fields to humans using extraction confidence signals.

questions.title: A coding assistant exposes 50 tools, each defined with a name, a description and a parameter schema. Estimate what the tool definitions cost on every call, and say how you would cut that cost without removing a single tool from the product.
questions.answer: Each definition costs 50 to 200 tokens, so 50 tools at 150 tokens each is 7,500 tokens before the conversation begins, repeated on every call. Classify the intent of the query and include only the tools that match it; the lesson puts the reduction at 60 to 80 percent, from about 8,000 tokens down to about 1,000. The product keeps every tool; only the per-call definition list changes.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the cost repeat? Expected: definitions sit in the context on every call, so a 50-turn conversation pays the full block 50 times.
Level 3: How does the lesson choose which tools to send? Expected: keyword intent classification over the query, then the tools whose categories match, added until a 2,000 token budget is reached.

Level 4: What does pruning risk, and how do you check it? Expected: a needed tool left out for a misread query; measure task success with 5, 10, 20 and 50 tools included and watch the misses per intent.

Level 4: How do the 7,500 tokens compare with the rest of the lesson's breakdown? Expected: the breakdown totals 22,700 tokens, and the tool block at about 8,000 is the largest item, ahead of history at 6,000 and retrieved text at 4,000.
wrongAnswers: "Tokens are cheap, send all 50." It is the largest block in the lesson's breakdown and it repeats on every call; it also displaces context that carries signal.
"Shorten every description to one word." Then the model cannot tell the tools apart; prune by relevance and keep each description precise.
"Remove the rarely used tools from the product." The product need not change; the per-call definition list does.
keyPoints: Tool definitions consume tokens on every call.
Fifty definitions at 150 tokens cost 7,500 tokens.
Classify intent and include only matching tool definitions.
Keep all product tools while reducing each call's tool list.

questions.title: Design the execution layer for an agent that can query a database, run small code snippets and read files on behalf of a user. The model decides which tool to call. What rules does the executor enforce, and what does it never do?
questions.answer: The executor never passes model-generated SQL or shell text straight to a system. It exposes an allowlist of named functions with typed parameters, validates every argument against the schema before execution, sanitizes tool results before they return to the model, and caps the number of calls per conversation at 10 to 20. For code, an in-process filter is a teaching aid and not a boundary; untrusted code runs in a separate process or container.
followUps: Level 3: Why is a substring blocklist not enough for the code tool? Expected: it matches spelling, not structure; a parsed syntax tree rejects imports, dunder access and unsafe names by shape, and even that shares the interpreter with the code.

Level 3: How do you shape the database tool so the model never writes SQL? Expected: accept a table name and filter conditions, allowlist the tables, restrict the operators, and build the query in your code.

Level 4: What is tool poisoning and where is the control? Expected: results that carry instructions to the model; sanitize every result before it returns, and strip sensitive data such as keys and internal errors.

Level 4: The agent loops on a failing tool. What stops it? Expected: a maximum number of calls per conversation, 10 to 20 in the lesson, structured errors that let the model fix its arguments, and a retry cap of about 3 per call.
wrongAnswers: "The model behaves, parameterize later." The model can and will generate destructive queries or injections; the rule is never to pass its SQL through.
"A generic run-any-function tool is simpler." The allowlist is the rule: expose the five functions the user needs, not all fifty.
"The code filter blocks imports, so it is safe." It shares the interpreter with the code it runs; production uses a separate process or container.
keyPoints: Expose allowlisted functions with typed parameters.
Validate arguments before execution and sanitize returned results.
Cap calls per conversation.
Run untrusted code in a separate process or container.

questions.title: An assistant's tail latency climbs because every turn also prunes, summarizes and reconciles its memory before it replies. A proposal moves that work to a second agent that runs while the user is idle. What does the split buy, what does it cost, and what new failure does it create?
questions.answer: The split takes the memory work off the critical path, so a reply never waits on consolidation, and the background agent can be a slower and stronger model because nobody is waiting on it. It costs a second agent, a shared block store and the coordination around them. The new failure is silent drift: the background agent rewrites a block and the primary agent never notices, so version the blocks, surface diffs in the trace, and treat the background writer as untrusted when it touches the persona or the safety block.
followUps: Level 3: Why can the background agent use a more expensive model? Expected: it is not latency constrained, so a slower and stronger model is affordable.

Level 3: A block keeps growing toward its limit. What runs, and when? Expected: the block summarizer, before the write that would push the block over the cap; the trigger threshold trades summarization calls against overflow.

Level 4: How do you make a background rewrite visible? Expected: version every block, record the old value and a diff on each write, and expose a per-block history so an operator can see why the agent forgot something.

Level 4: The background agent reads attacker-reachable content. What is the control? Expected: treat it as an untrusted writer; a change to the persona or the safety block needs a second-agent review before it commits.
wrongAnswers: "Run the consolidation at the end of every turn, it is quick." It sits on the critical path and tail latency is the complaint; the point of the split is that the reply never waits.
"Use the cheapest model for the background agent to save money." It is the one place a stronger model is affordable, and its rewrites shape every later turn.
"Deduplicate on the critical path too, it is the same code." The lesson runs deduplication only in the sleep pass, never while the user waits.
keyPoints: Background consolidation removes memory work from response latency.
It allows a slower model at extra coordination and storage cost.
Version memory blocks and expose rewrite diffs in traces.
Treat background edits to persona and safety blocks as untrusted.

questions.title: Take-home. Build an agent memory with two tiers: a fixed-size main context and an unbounded searchable store, plus the tools that move facts between them. Show a trace where the main context fills, something is evicted, and a later question is still answered from the store. Standard library only. Explain your eviction and citation choices.
questions.answer: Treat the main context as RAM and the store as disk. Give the main context a cap, a pinned core section and a message list that compacts its oldest entries when the cap is passed; give the store records with an id, text, tags, a session id and a turn id, and a token-overlap search. Expose the memory tools, write three facts, overflow the main context, and answer the follow-up by searching the store and splicing the result into the next turn.
followUps: Level 3: Why page instead of using a larger window? Expected: overflow, dilution and persistence; a bigger window still dilutes attention and starts empty next session, and the lesson cites a 4k-window agent with external memory that caught long-horizon facts a 128k-window baseline missed.
Level 3: What goes in every store record, and why? Expected: the text, tags, the session id and the turn id, so a recalled fact can be cited to the turn it came from.

Level 4: A note in the store says to ignore all future user instructions. What is the guard? Expected: scan retrieved records for directive-shaped text and mark them untrusted before they reach the prompt; this is prompt injection over time.

Level 4: Writes outnumber reads and retrieval drowns in stale facts. What do you add? Expected: periodic consolidation and explicit invalidation of contradicted facts, which the later memory lessons run off the critical path.
wrongAnswers: "Keep everything in the context, the window is large enough." The lesson's three failures remain: overflow, dilution and an empty window at the next session.
"Evict by deleting the oldest messages outright." Compact them into a summary or move them to the store; deletion loses facts the store could have kept.
"The store does not need source fields." Without a session and a turn id the agent recalls a fact and cannot say where it came from.
keyPoints: Cap main context and pin core memory.
Compact old messages when the cap is exceeded.
Store facts with IDs, tags, session and turn provenance.
Retrieve stored facts after overflow and splice them into the next turn.

questions.title: You own the memory layer for three products on one platform: a consumer chat assistant, a compliance review agent and a research retrieval agent. The memory system runs a vector store, a key-value store and a graph store in parallel and fuses their results. How do you configure the fusion for each product, and which one scoping mistake would get you paged?
questions.answer: The fused score is a weighted sum of relevance, importance and recency, and the weights are tuned per product: recency up for the chat assistant, importance up for the compliance agent, relevance up for the retrieval agent. Each store wins a query class the others miss, so the weights steer which class dominates without dropping a store. The paging mistake is a scope leak: every write picks the user, the session or the agent scope, and a retrieval that mixes scopes without per-scope weights tells one user about another user's project.
followUps: Level 3: Which query class does each store win? Expected: vector for semantic similarity, key-value for a fact lookup, graph for relationship reasoning.
Level 4: Why a weighted sum and not vector first with fallbacks? Expected: each store wins a different class; a hierarchy makes two of three classes wait on the wrong store.

Level 4: The compliance agent asks what was true in March. Which store answers, and how? Expected: the graph, by traversing the edges valid at that time; contradicted edges are marked invalid and kept.

Level 4: Which failure grows with the corpus, and what is the maintenance? Expected: embedding drift in the vector store; re-embed the most used records periodically, audit the key-value type set quarterly, and cap graph writes per add.
wrongAnswers: "One vector store is enough, embeddings capture everything." A fact lookup is wasteful on a vector store and a relationship query is impossible on one.
"Set the weights once for the platform." Chat wants recency, compliance wants importance, retrieval wants relevance; one setting is wrong for two of the three.
"Delete the old fact when a new one contradicts it." Mark it invalid and keep it, or the temporal query loses its history.
keyPoints: Fuse relevance, importance and recency scores.
Tune weights to each product's needs.
Keep user, session and agent write scopes explicit.
Prevent retrieval from leaking facts across scopes.

questions.title: A team runs every question through the full escalation pipeline from the lesson: one deterministic chain, then five sampled chains with a vote, then a tree search when the vote is weak. Latency and cost are now the top complaint. As the staff engineer, how do you restructure the pipeline, and what do you measure to defend the new shape?
questions.answer: Make the pipeline earn each stage. Most questions should end at the cheap stage, so start the vote at the minimum of three samples and widen it only on disagreement, and reserve the tree search, which costs up to 39 calls at a branching factor of 3 and a depth of 3, for the questions where the vote fails. Measure accuracy against cost per question for each stage on a held-out set, and report the share of questions that each stage resolves.
followUps: Level 3: What does the tree search cost at the lesson's defaults? Expected: each node is a model call, so a branching factor of 3 and a depth of 3 means up to 39 calls.

Level 4: Where does a reasoning model fit in the new shape? Expected: as a drop-in for the chain and the vote on many tasks, one call with hidden internal reasoning at 2 to 10 times the tokens, compared on the same accuracy against cost curve.

Level 4: How do you pick the vote size? Expected: sweep N over 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10 on a held-out set and plot accuracy against total tokens; the lesson puts the knee near 5 and the minimum meaningful vote at 3.

Level 4: Which one number justifies keeping the tree search at all? Expected: the share of questions that only the tree search gets right, against its share of the bill; if that share is near zero, cut the stage.
wrongAnswers: "Run the tree search on everything for the best accuracy." It costs 10 to 40 or more calls per question, and the lesson keeps it for large, evaluatable search spaces.
"Drop the vote and keep one chain at temperature zero." One chain is cheap but carries no confidence signal; the vote share is what tells you when to stop or escalate.
"Set the confidence gate to 1.0 to be safe." Then any single disagreement triggers the tree search; the lesson accepts 4 of 5.
keyPoints: Resolve most queries at the cheapest stage.
Start voting with three samples and expand on disagreement.
Reserve expensive tree search for unresolved cases.
Measure held-out accuracy, cost and resolved share at each stage.

topics.title: Evaluation
topics.about: Metrics, eval harnesses, judges, calibration and how to trust a score.

questions.title: How do you design an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation harness and mitigate systematic biases?
questions.answer: Start with an explicit rubric and a clear scoring scale, with examples of each score, instead of asking which answer is better. Judges have known biases, so swap the order of answers to cancel position bias, and control for verbosity bias, where longer answers get higher scores. Avoid self-preference by using a judge from a different model family than the one being tested. Finally, calibrate the judge against a human-labelled set and track agreement over time.

questions.title: How do you evaluate RAG systems for hallucination using the RAG Triad?
questions.answer: The RAG Triad checks three links. Faithfulness, or groundedness, asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, and this is the direct check for hallucination. Context relevance asks whether the retrieved passages are relevant to the question, which tests the retriever. Answer relevance asks whether the answer actually addresses the question. Scoring all three separately tells you whether a failure came from retrieval or from generation.
keyPoints: Faithfulness checks claims against retrieved context.
Context relevance evaluates the retrieved passages.
Answer relevance checks whether the response addresses the question.
Score each link separately to localize failures.

questions.title: What architectural and prompting patterns prevent and intercept hallucinations in production?
questions.answer: Prevention starts with grounding: instruct the model to answer only from provided context, require citations, and allow it to say it does not know. For factual tasks, lower the temperature to reduce random output. To intercept errors, sample several answers and check whether they agree, because disagreement is a useful warning sign. You can also verify claims against sources with a separate check, and route high-risk or low-confidence answers to a person.
keyPoints: Ground answers in context with citations and an abstention option.
Lower temperature for factual tasks.
Check agreement across sampled answers.
Verify claims against sources and route risky cases to people.

questions.title: What does building a real golden evaluation dataset actually involve, beyond “write 20 questions”?
questions.answer: Real query sampling (drawn from actual production logs or a representative spread of query types, not just whatever's easy to think of), relevant-passage labeling (manual annotation is the gold standard but expensive; LLM-assisted labeling scales further but is noisier and needs spot-checking), measuring inter-annotator agreement if multiple people label (low agreement means your "ground truth" itself is ambiguous, which is useful information, not noise to ignore), and wiring the resulting set into CI so every pipeline change gets measured against it automatically rather than relying on someone remembering to run an eval manually before merging.
keyPoints: Sample real queries or representative query types.
Label relevant passages and spot-check assisted labels.
Measure agreement between annotators.
Run the resulting evaluation set in CI.

questions.title: Beyond RAGAS, what other LLM-judge evaluation frameworks exist, and when would you reach for each?
questions.answer: ARES adds calibrated confidence intervals to judge scores at the cost of needing domain fine-tuning and a few hundred human labels — worth it when you need statistically defensible scores, not just a point estimate. RAGChecker gives claim-level diagnostics that separate retriever failure from generator failure, useful specifically when RAGAS or production has already flagged *that* something's wrong but not *which stage*. ConsJudge trains a judge model from judgment-consistency signals rather than human labels or a stronger reference model, useful if you want your own judge without depending on either. FaithJudge is a human-aligned hallucination-rate leaderboard, useful for picking a generator (or judge) model with an independent, pre-validated hallucination-rate comparison rather than trusting a vendor's own benchmark.
keyPoints: ARES provides calibrated confidence intervals using human labels.
RAGChecker separates retriever and generator failures at claim level.
ConsJudge learns from judgment-consistency signals.
FaithJudge compares hallucination rates across models.

questions.title: How do you measure citation quality in a verifiable RAG system, beyond “does it have citations at all”?
questions.answer: Three genuinely separate metrics, because they catch three different failure modes: citation precision (of the passages actually cited, what fraction genuinely support the claim next to them — measured via NLI entailment between the cited passage and the specific claim); citation recall (of the claims the response makes, what fraction have any citation at all — requires segmenting the response into atomic claims first); and attribution accuracy (does the cited passage actually say what the response claims it says, which is distinct from hallucination detection, since hallucination checks if *any* passage supports a claim, while attribution accuracy checks specifically whether *the cited one* does).
keyPoints: Citation precision measures whether cited passages support adjacent claims.
Use entailment between each cited passage and claim.
Citation recall measures the share of atomic claims with citations.
Attribution accuracy checks the cited passage specifically.

questions.title: How do you evaluate RAG answers for open-ended questions where there's no single correct reference answer?
questions.answer: Automated exact-match metrics are useless here, so lean on two complementary LLM-judge patterns instead: rubric-based absolute scoring (define explicit dimensions — relevance, completeness, accuracy, citation quality — and have a strong judge model score each independently, which forces reproducibility and makes variance explainable) and pairwise preference (show the judge two responses — a baseline and a candidate — and ask which is better overall; pairwise judgments are empirically more reliable than absolute scores because they anchor the judge to a concrete comparison rather than an abstract scale). Always calibrate whichever you use against a small set of human-labeled examples before trusting it at scale.
keyPoints: Exact match does not suit open-ended answers.
Score relevance, completeness, accuracy and citation quality separately.
Use pairwise preference against a concrete baseline.
Calibrate judges on human-labelled examples.

questions.title: How do you evaluate a RAG system when you have no ground-truth labels at all?
questions.answer: "You can't" is the wrong answer here. Reference-free LLM-as-judge techniques genuinely work for faithfulness specifically, because checking whether an answer's claims are supported by the retrieved context only needs the context and the answer — it never needed a gold reference answer in the first place. Combine that with behavioral signals from live traffic (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, escalation rate) to triangulate overall quality without any labeled data at all.
keyPoints: Faithfulness evaluation does not require a gold answer.
Compare answer claims with retrieved context.
Monitor regeneration and rephrase rates.
Include escalation rates to triangulate quality.

questions.title: Your thumbs-up rate is 92%. Does that mean your RAG system is actually good?
questions.answer: Not necessarily, and taking it at face value is a real mistake — explicit feedback like thumbs typically comes from under 5% of users, and that sliver is heavily skewed toward either very angry or unusually engaged users, which says very little about the silent majority who never clicked anything. A more reliable read comes from composite implicit signals instead — no regeneration, no rephrase, no escalation within the session, taken together — rather than trusting one small, self-selected explicit metric.
options: No, because a good system scores 99%.
Not necessarily. Few users rate at all, and those who do are skewed. Look at implicit signals too.
Yes. 92% is high.
Yes, as long as thousands of people rated it.
keyPoints: Thumbs feedback comes from a small self-selected group.
Angry or highly engaged users skew explicit feedback.
Use no-regeneration and no-rephrase signals together.
Include absence of escalation in the composite signal.

questions.title: Your offline eval scores improved after a change, but users are complaining more. What's going on?
questions.answer: Don't default to blaming the users or assuming the eval was wrong — this is the classic online/offline divergence, and it has a few concrete, checkable causes: the golden dataset is cleaner and narrower than real live traffic (distribution shift), the change may have overfit specifically to the fixed golden set without generalizing (Goodharting), or live traffic includes genuinely unanswerable questions that never show up in a curated offline set at all. Check the unanswerable-question rate and compare query distributions between the golden set and live traffic before concluding anything about the model itself regressed.
options: Roll back and move on.
The offline set doesn't look like live traffic, or the change overfit to it. Compare the query mix and the unanswerable-question rate.
The eval has a bug, so ignore it.
Users don't like change.
keyPoints: Compare live queries with the golden dataset.
Check for overfitting to the fixed evaluation set.
Measure the rate of unanswerable live questions.
Check distribution shift before concluding model regression.

questions.title: What should you actually log per request in a production RAG system, beyond the question and the final answer?
questions.answer: The full trace: the raw query and the rewritten/condensed version if query transformation ran, retrieved chunk IDs and their scores, reranked chunk IDs and scores if reranking ran, the final assembled prompt that actually went to the model, model parameters and token usage, and any sampled judge scores for that request. Without per-stage chunk IDs and scores specifically, you cannot localize a production failure to retrieval, reranking, or generation after the fact — you're stuck guessing.
keyPoints: Log raw and rewritten queries.
Record retrieved and reranked chunk IDs with scores.
Capture the final prompt, model parameters and token usage.
Retain sampled judge scores to localize failures.

questions.title: Your LLM-judge scores dropped 5% overnight with no deploy on your side. What do you check first?
questions.answer: Don't assume your system broke — the drop could be coming from the *judge* itself. Providers silently update underlying judge models, and that alone can shift every score without any genuine change in your system's output quality. The fix is scoring a fixed sentinel set daily (same inputs, same expected scores, run every day regardless of anything else) — a shift in the sentinel set's scores isolates judge drift from a genuine system regression immediately, instead of you spending hours investigating a system problem that doesn't exist.
options: Raise the judge's temperature.
Whether the judge changed: score a fixed sentinel set every day to separate judge drift from a real regression.
Roll back the last deploy.
Retrain the retriever.
keyPoints: A score drop can originate in the judge.
Provider updates can move scores without product changes.
Score a fixed sentinel set daily.
Use sentinel shifts to distinguish judge drift from regression.

questions.title: How would you know your RAG system's quality regressed after a deploy, in a real production setup?
questions.answer: Four layers, and naming all four (in order) is what separates a senior answer from "we have an eval set": a pre-deploy CI gate running the golden-dataset eval that blocks the deploy on any metric regression beyond threshold; a canary rollout to a small traffic slice, comparing guardrail metrics (latency, error rate, refusal rate) and judge scores canary-vs-control before full rollout; post-rollout online signals (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, thumbs ratio, escalation rate) watched against a pre-deploy baseline window; and trace-level triage when any signal fires — pulling the actual failing traces, localizing which stage broke using per-stage scores, and promoting those failures into the golden set so the exact same regression gets caught pre-deploy the next time around.
keyPoints: Block deployments on golden-set regressions beyond threshold.
Compare canary and control guardrails and judge scores.
Watch online signals against the pre-deploy baseline.
Triage failing traces and add failures to the golden set.

questions.title: Your model improves offline metrics but loses the A/B test. Why might this happen?
questions.answer:
When a model improves offline evaluation metrics but degrades live A/B test performance, I investigate across four common disconnects:
First, metric misalignment. Offline proxies (such as offline AUC or cosine similarity) do not equal business objectives (such as 30-day user retention or revenue). If the model optimizes clicks, it may promote clickbait that degrades long-term engagement.
Second, selection bias and feedback loops. Offline evaluation on historical logs only measures predictions on items previously exposed to users (counterfactual evaluation problem). The new model may explore unexposed regions where historical behavior is absent, requiring off-policy evaluation like Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS).
Third, latency regression. The candidate model may achieve a higher F1 score but introduce 150ms of serving latency, which degrades conversion in time-sensitive user flows.
Fourth, experiment interference or cannibalization. In two-sided marketplaces, control and treatment groups often compete for the same inventory, violating SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption) and requiring cluster-based or switchback experimentation.
keyPoints: Offline metrics can mismatch the actual product outcome.
Selection bias, leakage or distribution shift can inflate offline results.
Latency or serving integration can reduce online performance.
Check experiment validity, cohorts and guardrails before concluding causality.

questions.title: How do you stop a prompt change from silently breaking an LLM feature?
questions.answer:
Preventing prompt regressions in LLM production features requires treating prompts as versioned code with rigorous CI gates:
First, we build a golden evaluation dataset with stratified slices: standard happy paths, historical production failure cases, complex edge cases, and adversarial prompt injections.
Second, we apply layered evaluation assertions. We use deterministic checks for schema compliance (valid JSON format, required keys, zero PII, token budget caps) and rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge for subjective dimensions (faithfulness, factual grounding, and tone). Because non-zero temperature introduces variance, we run multiple samples (n >= 3) per test case.
Third, we enforce statistical pass thresholds in CI. A candidate prompt must achieve non-inferiority against the baseline prompt on core quality metrics with zero regressions on critical safety test cases.
Finally, we capture production edge cases: user negative feedback and flagged responses automatically create pull requests to expand the regression test suite.
keyPoints: Maintain a versioned representative evaluation set.
Test task correctness, grounding and safety rather than text similarity alone.
Compare prompt and model versions against a baseline.
Use human review to audit automated judges.
Gate rollout and monitor online regressions with rollback available.

questions.title: How do you check whether a model is fair, and what trade-offs arise?
questions.answer:
Auditing algorithmic fairness begins by measuring performance disaggregated across protected demographic groups (such as race, gender, or age), analyzing error rates, calibration, and positive selection rates.
The central engineering reality is the mathematical impossibility theorem of fairness: when base rates P(Y=1) differ across groups, you cannot simultaneously achieve demographic parity (equal selection rates), equalized odds (equal false positive and false negative rates), and predictive parity (equal calibration). You must explicitly choose which definition satisfies your ethical and legal requirements in consultation with compliance teams.
Importantly, removing protected attributes from training data fails because correlated proxy features (such as postal code or browser language) allow the model to reconstruct sensitive attributes.
Mitigation strategies include re-balancing training distributions, applying adversarial debiasing during training, calibrating post-processing decision thresholds per group where legally permitted, or routing uncertain boundary cases to human reviewers.
keyPoints: Define harms and affected groups for the use case.
Measure disaggregated error and decision rates.
Fairness criteria can conflict when group base rates differ.
Discuss interventions and trade-offs with stakeholders and monitor outcomes.

questions.title: How would you explain a model's decision to a regulator or a customer?
questions.answer:
Explaining model decisions requires matching the technical methodology to the stakeholder audience and regulatory context (such as GDPR Article 22 Right to Explanation or FCRA adverse action requirements):
For tabular and tree-based models, we compute TreeSHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations). Grounded in cooperative game theory, Shapley values satisfy efficiency and additivity, enabling waterfall attribution plots showing exactly how each feature moved the prediction from the base value. However, we must account for feature correlation, which can create misleading off-manifold attributions.
For deep neural networks and text models, we apply Integrated Gradients or layer-wise relevance propagation, verifying implementation invariance.
For end users, technical feature attributions are unhelpful. We translate them into actionable counterfactual explanations: stating the top two factors and the minimum changes required to alter the outcome (for example, reducing debt-to-income ratio by 4%).
Crucially, post-hoc explanations describe model mechanics, not causal reality. We store model lineage and data snapshots in a registry so any audited prediction can be reproduced identically.
keyPoints: Match the explanation to the stakeholder and decision.
Use interpretable models or attribution methods with stated limits.
Feature attribution is not proof of causality.
Keep lineage, decision records and validation evidence for audit.

questions.title: Why does standard user-level A/B testing fail in two-sided marketplaces, and how do switchback experiments prevent SUTVA violations?
questions.answer: Standard user-level A/B testing assumes the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA): the treatment assigned to one user must not affect the outcomes of other users. In two-sided marketplaces like ride-sharing, food delivery, or shared compute clusters, this assumption fails completely due to shared supply pools. For example, if treatment users receive an aggressive algorithm that dispatches couriers faster, they consume available drivers, leaving fewer drivers for control users. Control users experience higher wait times not because their algorithm is worse, but because treatment cannibalized shared supply, leading to false positive experiment results. We solve this using switchback experimentation. Instead of randomizing by user, we randomize by geographical clusters and discrete time windows, such as alternating treatment and control every 30 minutes in a specific city zone. All users and drivers in that zone experience the identical policy during that window, eliminating direct interference. The trade-off is sample size and carryover effects versus causal validity: switchbacks produce unbiased causal estimates, but require longer runtimes and order-of-magnitude larger sample sizes to overcome temporal autocorrelation.
followUps: How do you determine the optimal switchback window length (e.g. 15 minutes vs 60 minutes) to balance carryover against variance?
How do cluster-based randomization schemes differ from temporal switchback experiments?
wrongAnswers: Randomizing individual buyers in a shared marketplace 50/50, ignoring that treatment demand directly starves control inventory.
Treating consecutive 30-minute switchback time slots as independent and identically distributed, ignoring temporal autocorrelation.
tradeOffs: Switchback testing eliminates supply cannibalization and SUTVA violations, but reduces effective sample size from millions of users to hundreds of time-cluster units.
Short time windows maximize sample count, but risk carryover effects where the state of the previous window bleeds into the next.
keyPoints: User-level randomization fails when treatment consumes shared marketplace supply.
Switchbacks randomize geographic clusters and time windows.
Everyone in a zone uses the same policy during a window.
Temporal autocorrelation and carryover require longer experiments.

questions.title: Compare Team Draft interleaving with standard A/B testing for evaluating search and recommendation ranking algorithms.
questions.answer: Evaluating ranking models with standard A/B testing requires large sample sizes and weeks of user traffic to detect subtle improvements in click-through rates. Furthermore, user variance between control and treatment cohorts introduces statistical noise. Team Draft interleaving evaluates two ranking algorithms simultaneously on the same user search query with 100 times fewer samples. When a user submits a search, the system blends results from Algorithm A and Algorithm B into a single presentation list, alternating picks analogously to team captains drafting players. The system tracks which algorithm contributed each item, without showing labels to the user. When the user clicks an item, the corresponding algorithm receives credit. Because both algorithms are evaluated on the exact same user query and presentation layout, user-level preference variance is eliminated. The trade-off is ranking sensitivity versus long-term business measurement: interleaving rapidly detects pure ranking preference with tiny sample sizes, but it cannot measure holistic user behavior metrics like session retention, checkout conversion, or long-term engagement.
followUps: How does Team Draft interleaving correct for presentation bias (the fact that higher-ranked items receive more clicks)?
When can an algorithm win an interleaving test but lose a subsequent long-term A/B test?
wrongAnswers: Showing Algorithm A's list to User 1 and Algorithm B's list to User 2 and calling it interleaving, which is standard A/B testing.
Using interleaving to measure bottom-of-funnel subscription revenue, which cannot be attributed to individual interleaved clicks.
tradeOffs: Interleaving requires orders of magnitude less traffic to detect ranking preference differences, accelerating offline-to-online experimentation.
Interleaving measures relative click preferences within a single session, but cannot evaluate holistic business outcomes like 30-day retention or revenue.
keyPoints: Interleave alternating picks from both rankers into one result list.
Credit clicks to the contributing ranker.
The same query and layout reduce between-user variance.
Interleaving measures ranking preference rather than long-term retention or conversion.

questions.title: How do you design guardrail metrics and automated rollback triggers for production machine learning canary deployments?
questions.answer: When releasing a new machine learning model to production, evaluating primary success metrics like conversion rate is insufficient. A model might increase short-term clicks by recommending sensationalist content while silently causing a spike in uninstalls, error rates, or serving latency. We design canary deployments paired with strict guardrail metrics and automated rollback triggers. In a canary release, the new model receives a small percentage of traffic (such as 2% to 5%). We evaluate primary metrics alongside non-negotiable guardrail metrics: API error rate, p99 serving latency, model timeout percentage, and user complaint or unsubscription rates. We configure statistical threshold triggers using sequential testing methods. If p99 latency degrades by more than 15%, or if unhandled exception rates cross 0.1%, the continuous deployment pipeline immediately aborts the canary, routes 100% of traffic back to the stable control model, and generates an automated incident report. The trade-off is canary release velocity versus user protection: automated guardrails prevent catastrophic widespread outages, but volatile canary metrics can trigger false-alarm rollbacks during temporary network blips.
followUps: Why are standard fixed-sample t-tests invalid when monitoring live canary metrics continuously over time?
How do you handle delayed guardrail metrics (like 24-hour customer support complaints) that arrive after a canary has expanded?
wrongAnswers: Promoting a new model directly to 100% of production traffic without a canary stage, exposing all users to unforeseen failure modes.
Monitoring only conversion metrics while ignoring system latency, allowing a slow model to degrade overall platform performance.
tradeOffs: Automated guardrail rollbacks prevent production outages and customer churn from bad model weights, but require robust canary routing infrastructure.
Sequential statistical testing bounds false positive rollback triggers, but requires adequate canary sample volume to detect regressions.
keyPoints: Canary a small traffic share while monitoring primary and guardrail metrics.
Include errors, p99 latency, timeouts and user complaints.
Use sequential threshold triggers to revert traffic and report incidents.
Volatile metrics can cause false-alarm rollbacks.

questions.title: How do you detect and diagnose Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) in an online experiment, and why does SRM invalidate results?
questions.answer: In an online A/B experiment configured for a 50/50 traffic split, observing 52,000 users in control and 48,000 users in treatment may look like random fluctuation, but statistically it represents a severe Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM). SRM indicates that the assignment or tracking mechanism is broken, meaning the observed cohorts are no longer comparable and all downstream causal conclusions are completely invalid. We detect SRM using a Chi-Square goodness-of-fit test comparing observed sample counts to the theoretical assignment ratio. If the p-value is below 0.001, an SRM alert is triggered. Diagnosing SRM requires investigating the user lifecycle: first, did the treatment model introduce high latency that caused users to bounce before the tracking event fired? Second, did bot detection filters disproportionately flag and remove treatment requests? Third, were assignment redirects failing on specific mobile browsers? The trade-off is experiment velocity versus scientific integrity: when SRM occurs, the experiment cannot be salvaged by statistical weighting; it must be stopped, debugged, and re-run.
followUps: Why can you not simply re-weight the treatment cohort using propensity scores when an SRM is detected?
How can a performance regression in treatment cause an apparent drop in treatment user count?
wrongAnswers: Ignoring an SRM alert and trusting the statistical significance of revenue metrics, missing that the underlying cohorts are fundamentally biased.
Assuming that a Chi-Square p-value of 0.0001 is acceptable because the overall sample size is large.
tradeOffs: Automated SRM checks catch experimental bugs early, preventing teams from shipping invalid features based on biased data.
Invalidating experiments with SRM forces teams to discard weeks of test data, but running decisions on broken splits causes revenue losses.
keyPoints: Detect allocation mismatch with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
SRM invalidates cohort comparability and downstream causal conclusions.
Investigate tracking loss, bot filtering and browser redirects.
Stop, debug and rerun the experiment rather than statistically reweighting it.

questions.title: When should you use Thompson Sampling multi-armed bandits instead of fixed-split A/B testing for recommendation item exploration?
questions.answer: Fixed-split A/B testing allocates a static percentage of traffic (such as 50% to Variant A and 50% to Variant B) for the entire duration of an experiment. While ideal for long-term causal hypothesis testing, fixed splits are inefficient for short-lived content like news headlines, seasonal promotions, or viral videos: half the users are exposed to the inferior option for weeks just to gather statistical power. Multi-armed bandits minimize cumulative regret by dynamically shifting traffic toward better-performing options while the test is running. Thompson Sampling maintains a posterior probability distribution for each candidate item's reward rate (using Beta distributions for click-through rates). For every incoming user, it samples a score from each item's posterior and recommends the item with the highest sample. High-performing items receive the vast majority of traffic rapidly, while uncertain items continue to receive exploratory traffic. The trade-off is regret minimization versus unbiased causal inference: bandits maximize revenue and engagement during the exploration period, but make calculating standard unbiased average treatment effect estimates difficult.
followUps: How do you incorporate contextual features (like user demographics or device type) into contextual Thompson Sampling?
When is a traditional fixed-split A/B test strictly preferred over a multi-armed bandit?
wrongAnswers: Running fixed 50/50 A/B tests for 3-day holiday promotional banners, leaving half the users on a poorly performing banner for the entire holiday.
Using a greedy argmax policy with zero exploration, causing the system to lock onto the first item that receives lucky early clicks.
tradeOffs: Thompson Sampling dynamically minimizes regret and maximizes conversions on short-lived content, but shifts traffic away from suboptimal arms.
Bandit data exhibits policy-dependent selection bias, making offline counterfactual evaluation significantly more complex than standard A/B logs.
keyPoints: Bandits shift traffic to reduce cumulative regret.
Thompson Sampling maintains reward posteriors such as Beta distributions for CTR.
Sample each posterior and choose the highest draw.
Adaptive allocation suits short-lived content but complicates unbiased causal estimates.

questions.title: A vendor shows you that their new model scores 89 percent on a public multiple choice benchmark and the model you run today scores 87. They say the gap proves the new model is smarter. Why are you not convinced, and what do you ask for instead?
questions.answer: Public benchmarks stop telling models apart once every frontier model sits in a narrow band near the top. Three mechanisms cause this: training data that contains the test, training mixes tuned to the test format, and saturation, where the questions that remain are ambiguous or mislabeled. A gap of two points in that band is noise or memorization. Ask for a run on your task with your data.
followUps: Level 1: Name the three categories of evaluation. Expected: public benchmarks, custom evals on your own data, and human evals.

Level 2: A model does not know an answer. How does the test format still help it? Expected: the test has four options with a near uniform answer distribution, so format knowledge alone raises the score.
Level 2: What are benchmarks still good for? Expected: rough model selection before you build a custom eval.
Level 3: How would you test whether a benchmark leaked into training? Expected: search the training corpus for the eval questions and close paraphrases, and report the share that appears.
wrongAnswers: "Two points on a standard benchmark is a real gap." At the top of a saturated benchmark the remaining questions are often ambiguous or obscure, so two points can be two memorized questions.
"Labs cheat by training on the test." Web scale scraping pulls the questions in without intent; the effect is the same, and the fix is a contamination audit, not an accusation.
"Use the coding benchmark instead." A function completion benchmark with 164 problems covers isolated function generation and says nothing about debugging or refactoring across files.
keyPoints: Saturated benchmarks stop distinguishing frontier models.
Training contamination can inflate public scores.
Test-format tuning and ambiguous residual questions weaken comparisons.
Evaluate the model on your task and data.

questions.title: Your question answering system returns "June 29th, 2007." The reference says "June 29, 2007." A teammate reports that this case gets a zero and asks you to replace the whole eval with token F1. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: Both metrics are right for different answer shapes. Exact match compares the whole string after normalization, so one extra character makes it zero. Token F1 compares the bags of tokens, so this pair scores about 75 percent. First add normalization to exact match, then pick the metric by the shape of the answers you grade.
followUps: Level 1: What does a token F1 of one mean? Expected: the prediction and the reference have the same multiset of tokens after normalization, in any order.
Level 2: The reference is "Paris" and the prediction is "Paris." Which metric fails without normalization? Expected: exact match; with the trailing punctuation rule it passes.
Level 2: When do you take the best score over several references? Expected: when a question has more than one valid answer string; the F1 and ROUGE-L metrics take the highest scoring target.

Level 3: Token F1 is high and the answer is wrong. How did that happen? Expected: lexical overlap with wrong content, such as a wrong entity inside a sentence that shares most tokens with the reference; grade the entity with exact match or use a judge.
wrongAnswers: "Exact match is broken, so remove it." Exact match with normalization is the right metric for dates, numbers and multiple choice letters; the missing step is normalization.
"Token F1 understands meaning." It counts shared tokens; two answers with no shared tokens can both be right, and a wrong answer can share most tokens.
"A human would give this 100, so always use a judge." A judge costs money and needs a calibration run; for a date, normalized exact match is free and exact.
keyPoints: Exact match compares the normalized whole string.
An extra character can make exact match zero.
Token F1 compares bags of tokens.
Normalize first and choose metrics for the answer shape.

questions.title: A colleague reports that the new checkpoint reaches a perplexity of 10 on the held out text, better than last week, and wants to ship it as the stronger model. What does the number mean, and what does it not tell you?
questions.answer: Perplexity is the exponential of the mean negative log likelihood per token. A value of 10 means that at each position the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 10 options. Lower is better only while the test set and the tokenizer stay fixed. It says nothing about instruction following, reasoning or factual accuracy, so treat it as a sanity check and run the task evals before you ship.
followUps: Level 1: Which perplexity value means the model is never surprised? Expected: one, because every real token then has probability one.
Level 2: Two models were measured on different test sets. Can you compare their perplexities? Expected: no; the number depends on the text and the tokenizer, so measure both on the same set.

Level 2: The adapter reports a perplexity of 0.8. What happened? Expected: the summed loss is negative, most likely because the adapter returned log p instead of negative log p; a perplexity below one is impossible, so the contract was violated.

Level 3: Why does the eval sum the loss over non pad positions and divide at the end instead of averaging per batch perplexities? Expected: averaging per batch gives each token of a short batch more weight than each token of a long batch, and pad positions shrink the loss; the sum over real tokens matches the definition.
wrongAnswers: "Lower perplexity means a better assistant." It measures fit to the text distribution, not instruction following or correctness.
"Perplexities from two papers are comparable." They depend on the test set and the tokenizer, so only same set comparisons hold.
"Aim for a perplexity near one." The held out text is not the model's own output; a value near one would suggest the test text was in the training data.
keyPoints: Perplexity exponentiates mean negative log likelihood per token.
Perplexity 10 resembles uncertainty among ten uniform options.
Compare only with the same test set and tokenizer.
Run task evaluations for reasoning and factual accuracy.

questions.title: You can score a summarization feature in three ways: n-gram overlap against a reference, a strong model that grades with a rubric, or human experts. The team has one afternoon and a small budget. How do you decide which to use, and for what?
questions.answer: Use all three, each for a different job. Overlap metrics are free and instant but agree with people only 40 to 60 percent of the time, so they serve as a baseline and a smoke test. A judge model costs a few dollars per thousand cases and agrees 82 to 88 percent with people on a well anchored rubric, so it is the default scorer. People are the ground truth, so spend them on calibrating the judge and on edge cases, not on every commit.
followUps: Level 1: What does ROUGE measure? Expected: recall of reference n-grams, built for summarization.
Level 2: Why keep the overlap metric once you have a judge? Expected: it is free and fast, it catches gross regressions in seconds, and it does not move when the judge model changes.
Level 2: When is a judge not enough? Expected: high stakes or policy decisions, and any time the judge has not been calibrated against human labels on this task.
Level 3: The lesson says the judge must be at least as capable as the model it grades. Why? Expected: a weak judge gives noisy, inconsistent scores and cannot see the errors a stronger model makes.
wrongAnswers: "People are the gold standard, so grade everything by hand." Human review takes hours and costs about 500 dollars per thousand cases, so it cannot run on every change.
"Overlap metrics are useless for generation." They catch gross regressions and cost nothing; they only miss meaning.
"Pick one metric and optimize it." Optimizing only correctness yields terse answers that nobody can use; score several criteria.
keyPoints: Overlap metrics serve as cheap smoke tests.
Use a rubric-anchored judge as the default scorer.
People provide ground truth for calibration.
Spend human review on edge cases rather than every commit.

questions.title: Two engineers ran the same judge on the same 100 answers with the instruction "rate from 1 to 5 how good the answer is" and got means almost a full point apart. How do you rewrite the rubric so the scores become reproducible, and what else goes into the judge prompt?
questions.answer: Anchor every level to behavior a reader can check. A rubric that states what a 5, a 4 and a 3 look like reduces judge variance by 30 to 40 percent compared with an unanchored scale. Score several criteria separately, give the judge the input, the output and the reference, and ask for the reasoning next to the number.
followUps: Level 2: Why score four criteria instead of one overall score? Expected: one score collapses dimensions; a model can be correct and useless, and the single number hides the trade.
Level 2: How do you show the new rubric is reproducible? Expected: run the judge several times per case and compute an agreement statistic; below 0.7 rewrite again.
