Level 3: The judge still wavers between 3 and 4 on many cases. What design change removes that? Expected: pairwise comparison, which only asks which output is better.

Level 3: One criterion has a reference answer and another has none. Does the rubric change? Expected: yes; correctness anchors to the reference, while helpfulness and safety anchor to properties of the output alone.
wrongAnswers: "Lower the temperature of the judge." A deterministic judge still applies a vague scale differently across cases; the rubric is the fix.
"Average more runs." Averaging noise costs money and leaves a scale that two readers interpret differently.
"One overall score is simpler." Simpler to read and wrong to optimize; the lesson warns that single metric optimization produces terse useless answers.
keyPoints: Anchor score levels to observable behavior.
Define what scores 5, 4 and 3 mean.
Score several criteria separately.
Supply input, output and reference with reasons beside scores.

questions.title: A prompt change scores 90 percent on your 50 case golden set, and the baseline scored 86 on the same set. The author wants to ship it as a four point win. How sure can you be, and what sample size would you need to make this call?
questions.answer: At 50 cases and 90 percent observed accuracy, the 95 percent interval runs from 78 to 97 percent, a 19 point spread. A four point gap sits well inside that spread, so the win cannot be told from noise. You need about 200 cases to detect a 5 percent change, and 500 or more when two systems are close.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the interval shrink slowly as you add cases? Expected: the width falls with the square root of the sample size, so four times the cases halve the width.
Level 2: The two runs used identical cases. Does that help? Expected: yes; a paired comparison on per case differences is tighter than two independent intervals.

Level 3: Which interval does the lesson use for a pass rate, and why? Expected: the Wilson interval, because it behaves correctly at small samples and extreme proportions where the normal approximation fails.

Level 3: You can afford 200 judge calls per run. How do you split them? Expected: a golden core, an adversarial slice and a sample of production traffic, versioned and fixed between the two runs you compare.
wrongAnswers: "Four points is four points." On 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide; a four point gap is noise.
"Run the same 50 cases three times." Repeating the cases measures the model's variance, not the population; the interval over cases stays wide.
"Always use a thousand cases." A thousand cases give a 3 point width but cost five times a 200 case run; use 200 for routine decisions and 500 or more for close calls.
keyPoints: Fifty cases give a wide accuracy interval.
A four-point gap can fall within sampling noise.
About 200 cases can detect a five-percent change.
Use 500 or more cases for close systems.

questions.title: You wrote a rubric, and a judge model now scores faithfulness for your retrieval system. The dashboard shows a high mean, and the team wants to use it as the release gate from Monday. What has to happen before this number can block or approve a release?
questions.answer: Calibrate the judge against people first. Hand label about 100 cases, score them with the judge, and compute the Spearman correlation between the two rankings. Below 0.7 the rubric needs work and the number is noise. Then freeze the judge model and version, and read the bottom scores as well as the mean.
followUps: Level 2: Why Spearman and not the mean difference between judge and human scores? Expected: Spearman compares rankings, so a judge that is harsh but orders the cases the same way still passes.
Level 2: What is the smallest hand labeled set the lesson accepts? Expected: it refuses a judge tested on fewer than 50 human labeled examples.

Level 3: The judge is the same model that writes the answers. What will the calibration run probably show? Expected: inflated scores by about 10 to 20 percent; switch the judge to another model family.

Level 3: The correlation passes, but the bottom decile holds confident wrong scores. Do you ship? Expected: no; the mean correlation can hide catastrophic failures, so inspect the lowest 10 percent before the number gates anything.
wrongAnswers: "The rubric is clear, so the judge is right." Length and family biases survive a clear rubric; only a correlation against human labels shows their size.
"It agrees with our old metric, so it is calibrated." The old metric may share the bias; calibrate against people.
"Calibrate once and keep upgrading the judge." Each judge version changes every score; freeze the version or rerun the baseline in parallel.
keyPoints: Hand-label about 100 calibration cases.
Compare judge and human rankings with Spearman correlation.
Rework the rubric when correlation is below 0.7.
Freeze judge version and inspect low scores as well as the mean.

questions.title: Overnight every metric on the eval dashboard moved by several points, up for some criteria and down for others, with no prompt change and no model change in the product. The last merged change switched the judge to the newest version of its model. What happened, and how should such a change be made?
questions.answer: The judge is part of the measurement, so a new judge version changes every metric at once while the product stands still. Freeze the judge model and version in the pipeline. When you upgrade, run the old and the new judge on the same baseline in parallel, calibrate the new judge against the human labeled set, and reset the baseline before you compare anything new.
followUps: Level 2: What else can move every score without a product change? Expected: an eval set edit without a version tag, or a change in how missing scores are counted.
Level 2: How do you tell a judge change from a product regression next time? Expected: the run metadata records the judge model and version, so a diff of the metadata answers it.
Level 3: The new judge correlates better with the human labels. Do you adopt it? Expected: yes, but rescore the stored baseline with it first so that old and new numbers share one judge.
Level 3: You must keep a trendline across the switch. How? Expected: score a fixed frozen set with both judges, publish the offset per criterion, and mark the switch on the chart.
wrongAnswers: "Newer judge, higher scores, ship it." The product did not change; the number did. A judge change needs a parallel baseline.
"Follow the newest judge version automatically." Automatic upgrades make every trendline meaningless; pin the version.
"A minor version does not need recalibration." Any version change can change the scores; rerun the correlation.
keyPoints: A judge upgrade changes the measurement instrument.
Freeze the judge model and version.
Run old and new judges on the same baseline.
Calibrate the new judge and reset the baseline.

questions.title: A faithfulness dashboard reports a mean of 0.85 over a thousand cases, above the 0.8 release threshold. Support tickets say the assistant invents policy details in some answers. The eval owner says the metric is green. Where do you look, and what do you change in the report?
questions.answer: A mean hides the tail. A mean of 0.85 is consistent with a 5 percent slice of catastrophic failures, and that slice is what becomes tickets. Sort the cases by score and read the lowest 10 percent. Then add a pass rate at a threshold and a bottom quantile alert to the report, next to the mean.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the lesson prefer the share of cases above a cutoff to the mean? Expected: it counts how many cases are good enough, so it measures reliability.
Level 2: The lowest cases all come from one category. What changes? Expected: the fix is local; report per-category scores and gate on the weakest category, not the aggregate.

Level 3: Missing scores from parse failures were dropped before averaging. What did that do? Expected: it raised the mean, because the worst outputs often fail to parse; count them as failures or report them separately.
Level 3: Which alert do you add to the release gate? Expected: a floor on the lowest 10 percent and a pass rate threshold, both next to the mean.
wrongAnswers: "The mean passed, so the release passed." A mean of 0.85 often hides a 5 percent catastrophic slice; the gate needs the tail.
"Raise the mean threshold to 0.9." A higher mean threshold still hides a small slice of zeros; add a distribution measure.
"The judge is noisy at the bottom, so ignore those cases." That is where the failures live; calibrate the judge on low scoring cases too.
keyPoints: A high mean can hide catastrophic failures.
Read the lowest-scoring ten percent of cases.
Report pass rate at a threshold.
Add a bottom-quantile alert beside the mean.

questions.title: A model card advertises a context window of one million tokens and a perfect score on a needle in a haystack test at that length. Your product asks the model to reconcile figures that appear in several places across a long contract. Does the card answer your question, and what do you measure instead?
questions.answer: No. A single needle test measures retrieval of one planted fact, and frontier models saturate it. Your task is multi hop aggregation, which degrades sharply past about 128k tokens on most models. Run a multi hop test at your target length and report two numbers: the effective retrieval length and the effective reasoning length.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a single needle pass not predict a three needle pass? Expected: several facts need attention at several positions at once; the multi needle test measures juggling, not retrieval.
Level 2: Which depths do you test? Expected: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0, because models under attend to the middle of the input.
Level 3: The planted fact uses the same words as the surrounding text. What goes wrong? Expected: retrieval becomes trivial lexical matching; use a needle with no literal overlap.
Level 3: What do you measure next to accuracy at the target length? Expected: time to first token and cost per query; a million token prompt can take 30 to 120 seconds to prefill.
wrongAnswers: "The vendor's score is independent evidence." Vendors publish their own scores; rerun on your task at your length.
"Pass at one million means pass at every shorter length and every task." Report the curve per task type; an aggregate hides large task level differences.
"Test the middle depth only." Many implementations do; the middle is where models under attend, so test five depths.
keyPoints: A single needle test measures one planted fact.
Single-fact retrieval does not establish multi-hop reasoning.
Test multi-hop aggregation at the intended context length.
Report effective retrieval and reasoning lengths separately.

questions.title: Your coding agent scores a pass at one of 0.6 on the fixture suite and a pass at five of 0.95. One manager reads this as a failing agent; another reads it as a passing agent. What does each number tell you, and what do you put in the report?
questions.answer: Pass at one says the first sample fixes the task on about six tasks in ten. Pass at five says that at least one of five samples passes on almost every task, so the right answer is usually within reach and the gap is selection. Report both, with the raw pass counts per task, because pass at k alone hides an agent that succeeds once in twenty tries.
followUps: Level 2: What do you need in production to turn a high pass at five into a high pass at one? Expected: a verifier that selects the passing sample, such as tests that run; without it the user gets the first sample.
Level 2: Why does the harness print raw pass counts next to the rate? Expected: to show variance per task and expose a task that passes once in many tries.

Level 3: The pass rate rose from Monday to Friday while five fixtures were renamed. Is it real? Expected: no; the task set changed, so the runs are not comparable, and the harness must run every fixture every time in a fixed order.
Level 3: Which three failure modes does the harness exist to prevent? Expected: unverified pass, undetected regression across tasks, and drift in the task set.
wrongAnswers: "Pass at five is the real score." It measures the ceiling with selection; users get one sample unless you build the selector.
"A pass at one of 0.6 means the agent is broken." It means the first sample fails on four tasks in ten; the high pass at five says the capability is there and selection is the gap.
"Trust the agent's own success report." Self reported success is the first failure mode the harness exists to remove; a deterministic verifier decides.
keyPoints: Pass at one measures first-sample task success.
Pass at five measures success in at least one of five samples.
A large gap indicates a selection problem.
Report both metrics with raw pass counts per task.

questions.title: Your product generates answers with one model, and your eval pipeline grades them using that same model plus a rubric. Scores rose after the last release and the team is pleased. A reviewer asks why the gain might not be real. What is the risk, and what do you change?
questions.answer: A model that grades its own family prefers its own style, so self evaluation inflates scores by about 10 to 20 percent. The rise can mean the judge likes the new outputs more, not that users do. Move the judge to a different model family, calibrate it against human labels, and score the baseline and the new version again under that judge.
followUps: Level 2: Which two other judge biases does the lesson name next to self preference? Expected: position bias in pairwise comparison and verbosity bias toward longer answers.

Level 2: The judge from another family is cheaper but correlates less with people. Which one do you take? Expected: the cheapest judge that still meets the calibration threshold; below the threshold the number is noise whatever the family.

Level 3: You cannot change the judge family this quarter. What limits the damage? Expected: calibrate against human labels and publish the correlation, normalize for length, and read only relative changes under the frozen judge.

Level 3: After the switch, how do you tell a real gain from a judge preference? Expected: both versions scored by the new judge, the difference with a confidence interval, and a human labeled slice of the cases that moved most.
wrongAnswers: "The judge has a rubric, so its family does not matter." The rubric does not remove the preference for its own style; the lesson measures a 10 to 20 percent inflation.
"Use the strongest model we have as the judge, which is the one we ship." Strength does not remove self preference; a different family at similar strength is the fix.
"Scores went up, so quality went up." The score is a proxy; the output may have moved toward what the judge rewards, such as length and tone.
keyPoints: A judge can prefer outputs from its own model family.
Self-preference can inflate evaluation scores.
Use a judge from another family and calibrate on human labels.
Rescore both baseline and candidate with that judge.

questions.title: Two papers report BLEU on the same test set. One says 28.3 and the other says 0.283. A third team reports a ROUGE-L score ten points below yours on the same outputs. Your manager asks which number is right. How do you answer?
questions.answer: All of them can be right for different metric setups. BLEU is a fraction, and one paper multiplies it by a hundred. ROUGE-L moves by ten points when one library lowercases and the other does not, or when the two tokenize differently. Read the metric setup before you compare, and in your own harness fix one tokenizer and one smoothing rule and pin them with tests.
followUps: Level 2: Why does clipping matter in BLEU? Expected: a candidate that repeats one matching phrase would inflate n-gram precision; clipping caps the count at the reference count.
Level 2: What does the brevity penalty do? Expected: it lowers the score of a candidate shorter than the reference, so a short output cannot win on precision alone.

Level 3: Why add one to the n-gram counts? Expected: a pair with no matching 4-gram would give a log of zero and a score of zero; smoothing keeps the geometric mean finite and barely moves long candidates.

Level 3: How do you keep your metric numbers comparable across a year of runs? Expected: pin the tokenizer and the smoothing in code, keep reference vectors in tests, and record the metric version with every leaderboard.
wrongAnswers: "Use the library everyone uses." Two libraries differ by ten points on the same outputs; you still need to know which tokenizer and casing each applied.
"BLEU is old, drop it." It still backs most published numbers; learn to read it, then layer model based metrics on top.
"Lowercasing cannot move a score by ten points." The capstone reports that it does for ROUGE-L across two libraries; casing changes which tokens match.
keyPoints: Metric scaling can explain different BLEU values.
Case handling and tokenization can move ROUGE-L.
Read metric configuration before comparing papers.
Pin tokenizer and smoothing rules with tests.

questions.title: You compare two prompt versions by showing a judge model both outputs and asking which one is better. Version B wins 70 percent of the pairs. You then swap the two outputs and version A wins most of them. What went wrong, and how do you run the comparison?
questions.answer: The judge has position bias: it prefers the option it reads first. Your first run measured the order, not the prompt. Score every pair in both orders, count a win only when the same version wins twice, and treat split decisions as ties. Then report the win rate with a confidence interval.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a pairwise comparison avoid rubric calibration problems? Expected: the judge only picks a winner and never places an output on a numeric scale.
Level 2: Version B is also longer. What else do you control? Expected: verbosity bias; normalize for length or exclude it in the rubric, then check whether the preference remains.

Level 3: After both orders, 40 percent of the pairs flip with the order. What does that tell you? Expected: the judge cannot tell the versions apart on those pairs; count them as ties and expect a win rate close to one half.
Level 3: How many pairs make a 55 percent win rate real? Expected: enough that the interval excludes one half; use a Wilson or bootstrap interval, and expect to need hundreds of pairs.
wrongAnswers: "The judge is random, so use a different judge." Position bias is systematic, not random; another judge has it too, and the protocol is the fix.
"Always put the baseline first." That fixes the bias in one direction and hides it; run both orders.
"Pairwise comparison is only for human raters." Judges run pairwise well once the order is randomized and both orders are scored.
keyPoints: Position bias can make the first answer look better.
Score each answer pair in both orders.
Count consistent wins and treat split decisions as ties.
Report win rate with a confidence interval.

questions.title: You must score generated code by running it. A teammate proposes a call to the interpreter's eval function inside the harness process with a try block around it. Design the execution contract instead, and say how a timeout, a crash and a denylist hit each appear in the result.
questions.answer: Run every candidate in a fresh interpreter subprocess with a wall clock timeout, an output cap and an import denylist, never in the harness process. The score is the fraction of assertions that pass. A timeout, a syntax error, an assertion failure and any other crash each map to a distinct exit reason, so a reviewer can tell a slow solution from a wrong one while the score for most of them is zero.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the denylist not the main control? Expected: determined code can escape any in process guard; the wall clock timeout and the output cap bound run time and output size whatever the code does. They do not bound memory or file writes, so production adds a read only file system and network isolation, or a container.
Level 3: A candidate prints inside an infinite loop. Which control fires? Expected: the output cap at 256 KB, recorded as an error with the detail output overflow; the timeout would fire later.

Level 4: How should the leaderboard treat timeouts, zero or missing? Expected: a documented choice; zero if slow code is wrong for the task, missing if you measure correctness alone, and the exit reason lets you report both.
Level 4: When do assertion strings stop being enough? Expected: when the eval should match production CI; replace them with real unit test files in a container and stop calling the strings tests.
wrongAnswers: "A try block around the call is a sandbox." It catches exceptions, not infinite loops, not file deletion, not memory floods.
"The denylist makes it safe." It is a conservative backstop; the capstone states that it is not bulletproof.
"Score a timeout as a crash." Keep them distinct in the exit reason; the score can be zero for both, but the reason tells you whether to raise the budget.
keyPoints: Run candidates in fresh interpreter subprocesses.
Enforce wall-clock timeout, output cap and import denylist.
Score the fraction of assertions that pass.
Record timeout, syntax error, assertion failure and crash separately.

questions.title: Your judge returns a JSON object with a score for each case. The pipeline parses it, and mean faithfulness rose from one week to the next with no change to the product. The logs show that the judge's output failed to parse on a growing share of cases. Explain the rise and fix the pipeline.
questions.answer: A parse failure becomes a missing score, and the aggregate silently drops missing scores. The cases that fail to parse are often the worst outputs, so dropping them lifts the mean. Catch the failure explicitly, record it as its own outcome, count it against the score or report it next to the mean, and alert when the failure share grows.
followUps: Level 3: Why are the failed cases not a random sample? Expected: the judge breaks its format most on long, odd or refused outputs, which are also the low scoring ones.
Level 3: Do you score a failed parse as a zero or leave it out? Expected: both, with the parsed share; a gate should treat a rising failure share as a failed run.

Level 4: How do you design the judge output so this cannot happen silently again? Expected: a strict schema, a validator that rejects anything else, a status field per case, and a run level parse failure metric with an alert.
wrongAnswers: "The mean rose, so quality rose." Nothing in the product changed; the denominator did.
"Retry until it parses." Retries without a record hide the failure and can change the score; record every retry and cap them.
"Exclude failures, they are judge bugs." The exclusion is biased toward bad outputs; the product number is wrong whatever the cause.
keyPoints: Parse failures can silently disappear from aggregates.
Dropping missing scores can inflate the mean.
Record parsing failures as explicit outcomes.
Count or report failures and alert on their share.

questions.title: You run three candidate models on the same fifty tasks and must publish a leaderboard with a winner. The means are 0.78, 0.75 and 0.10. The second team says their model is tied with the first. Design the aggregation and the statistics that settle it.
questions.answer: Report a mean with a bootstrap interval, a win rate, and a paired interval on the difference for each pair of models. Resample the tasks with replacement to get the interval on each mean. For the tie claim, bootstrap the per task difference between the first two models; if that interval includes zero, the leaderboard shows them as tied.
followUps: Level 3: Why bootstrap over tasks and not over predictions within a task? Expected: the unit of replication is the task; resampling within a task understates the variance across tasks.

Level 3: When does win rate rank differently from the mean? Expected: when one model wins many tasks by a little and loses a few by a lot; the mean punishes the big losses, the win rate counts the wins.
Level 4: Tasks come in families that share error patterns. What breaks? Expected: the tasks are not independent, so the interval is too narrow; resample families first, then tasks.
Level 4: One task's metric returns 0 to 100 instead of 0 to 1. What should the aggregator do? Expected: refuse the run; a silent rescale would hide the bug, and the metric must return a fraction.
wrongAnswers: "Two means with overlapping intervals are tied." The paired difference is the test; separate intervals can overlap while the difference excludes zero.
"Rank by win rate, it is robust." It loses magnitude; a model that wins every task by a hair and loses one badly looks perfect. Report both.
"Weight the tasks by importance now." The capstone counts every task the same; add weights only with a documented reason and keep the unweighted table.
keyPoints: Report bootstrap intervals around model means.
Report pairwise win rates.
Bootstrap per-task differences between models.
Treat models as tied when the difference interval includes zero.

questions.title: Design the evaluation gate that runs on every pull request that touches prompts or model code for a support assistant. Say what runs, what blocks the merge, what it costs per month, and how you stop the gate from blocking on noise.
questions.answer: Trigger on changes to the prompt and model paths, run a fixed versioned suite of about 200 cases through the proposed prompt, score four anchored criteria with a frozen calibrated judge, and compare with the stored scores of the last known good baseline. Block when any criterion drops beyond the threshold and the interval on the difference excludes zero, and store the results as artifacts. With a small judge tier a 200 case run costs about 4 dollars, so ten merges a week cost about 160 dollars a month.
followUps: Level 3: Why a path filter on the trigger? Expected: the eval costs money and minutes; run it when prompts or model code change, not on every commit.
Level 3: A criterion moved by 0.1 and the author calls it a regression. Expected: the threshold is 0.3 on the mean with intervals; 0.1 is inside noise at 200 cases, so report it and do not block.

Level 4: The gate blocks the merge and the author says the suite is stale. What is the process? Expected: suite changes are their own reviewed and versioned change; rerun the baseline when the suite version changes, and never edit the suite inside the failing pull request.
Level 4: How do you catch an aggregate improvement that regresses one category? Expected: a stratified per category report with intervals and a block rule on any category.
wrongAnswers: "Run the eval nightly instead." Nightly finds the regression after the merge; the lesson's story is 11 days of a shipped drop. Run before merge.
"Fifty golden cases are enough for a gate." At 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide, and a 5 percent regression cannot be detected.
"Use the newest judge model on each run." Judge changes move every score; freeze the judge and change it only with a parallel baseline.
keyPoints: Trigger evaluation on prompt and model changes.
Run a fixed versioned suite with a frozen calibrated judge.
Compare anchored criteria against the last good baseline.
Block meaningful regressions and store evaluation artifacts.

questions.title: Two harnesses in the repository compute pass at k. The first takes the empirical pass rate p and returns 1 - (1 - p) ** k. The second takes the sample count n, the pass count c and k, and returns 1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k). Read both. When do they agree, when do they differ, and which one goes in the report?
questions.answer: The first formula treats every draw as independent with success probability p and is a plug in estimate. The second counts the exact chance that k samples drawn from the n you ran contain at least one pass, and it is the unbiased estimator that code generation benchmarks use. They agree only as n grows large; for the samples you ran, the plug in is lower and noisier, and it extrapolates when k exceeds n. Report the unbiased one with the raw counts next to it.
followUps: Level 3: In the second function, why return one when n minus c is smaller than k? Expected: you cannot pick k failing samples from fewer than k failures, so every k subset contains a pass.
Level 3: Why compute the product in log space? Expected: binomial coefficients overflow for moderate n; the log of the ratio is a short sum of logs.

Level 4: A team ran five samples per task and reports pass at ten. What is wrong? Expected: k exceeds n, so nothing was measured; the second function falls back to whether any sample passed and the first extrapolates.
Level 4: Do the two functions agree on pass at one? Expected: yes; both reduce to c over n when k is one.
wrongAnswers: "They are the same formula." They agree only as n grows; for the samples you ran, the plug in is lower and noisier.
"Pass at k is the probability the agent is right." It is the chance that a set of k samples contains at least one pass; without a selector the user still gets one sample.
"More samples per task raise pass at one." They make the estimate more precise; the value is the per sample pass rate.
keyPoints: The plug-in formula assumes independent draws with success probability p.
The unbiased estimator samples k from the n observed runs.
The formulas agree only as n becomes large.
Report the unbiased estimate alongside raw counts.

questions.title: Your eval report shows two kinds of numbers: a pass rate, which is the share of cases that scored 4 or more, and a mean judge score on a 1 to 5 scale. A reviewer asks for error bars on both. Which interval do you use for each, and why not the same one?
questions.answer: Use a Wilson interval for the pass rate and a bootstrap interval for the mean score. A pass rate is a proportion, and the Wilson interval stays correct at small samples and near zero or one, where the normal approximation breaks. A mean of ordinal judge scores has no clean closed form, and the bootstrap resamples the scores with replacement and works with any distribution.
followUps: Level 3: What goes wrong with a plus or minus one standard error interval on a proportion? Expected: at small n or near zero or one it gives bounds outside the unit range and the wrong width; Wilson corrects both.
Level 3: What does a bootstrap assume? Expected: that the sample represents the population; it needs no distribution shape, but it cannot fix a biased or tiny sample.
Level 4: Two prompt versions ran on the same 200 cases. Which interval decides? Expected: an interval on the paired per case difference; two overlapping intervals do not prove equality.
wrongAnswers: "Plus or minus the standard error is fine." The normal interval fails at small samples and extreme proportions, exactly where releases are decided.
"Bootstrap works for the pass rate too, so use it everywhere." It works, but Wilson is closed form, cheap and built for proportions; keep the code auditable.
"Overlapping intervals mean no difference." Two separate intervals can overlap while the paired difference excludes zero; compare the difference.
keyPoints: Use Wilson intervals for pass-rate proportions.
Wilson handles small samples and extreme proportions.
Use bootstrap intervals for mean judge scores.
Bootstrap resamples observed scores with replacement.

questions.title: Your multiple choice eval reports an expected calibration error of 0.02 on a hundred predictions with ten bins, and the team calls the model well calibrated. What does that number measure, what does it miss, and which second number do you add?
questions.answer: ECE bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy, weighted by bin size. With ten bins and a hundred predictions you cannot tell 0.02 from noise, and inside one bin overconfident and underconfident predictions can offset each other in the bin average. Add the Brier score, the mean squared error between confidence and outcome per prediction, and report how many bins were populated.
followUps: Level 3: A predictor says one half on every item. What is its Brier score, and why? Expected: exactly 0.25, because the squared error is 0.25 whether the outcome is zero or one.

Level 3: Why can ECE be low while calibration is bad? Expected: inside one bin, overconfident and underconfident predictions offset each other in the bin means; the absolute gap stops cancelling only across bins, and Brier penalizes each prediction's error.

Level 4: Why is calibration a per model report and not a per task metric? Expected: the runner accumulates confidence and correctness pairs across the whole eval and computes it once; per task bins would be nearly empty.

Level 4: One model has higher accuracy and a worse Brier score than a rival. Which do you deploy? Expected: the capstone argues for the better calibrated one, because it reports its uncertainty reliably; confirm with the reliability diagram.
wrongAnswers: "An ECE of 0.02 means calibrated." On a hundred predictions with ten bins the value is inside the noise; report populated bins and collect a larger sample.
"Accuracy is enough." Two models with equal accuracy can differ in whether their confidence means anything; the capstone calls calibration the most ignored axis.
"Brier replaces ECE." They answer different questions; ECE shows the shape per bin and Brier the per prediction error. Report both with the diagram data.
keyPoints: ECE averages confidence-accuracy gaps across weighted bins.
Small samples make tiny ECE differences unreliable.
Opposite errors can cancel within a bin.
Add Brier score and report populated-bin counts.

questions.title: A colleague's perplexity eval computes the cross entropy at every position of every padded batch, averages it over the batch, exponentiates, and then averages the per batch values. The reported perplexity looks very good and gets better whenever the batch size grows. Read the description, name the bugs and give the correct computation.
questions.answer: There are three bugs: pad positions sit in the denominator, so the loss is diluted and the number improves with more padding, which is what a larger batch brings. Averaging per batch gives each token of a short batch more weight than each token of a long batch. And the targets must shift by one, because the logits at a position predict the next token. Sum the loss over real target positions across the corpus, count those positions, divide once, and exponentiate.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the off by one silent during training but fatal in the metric? Expected: the model still learns from misaligned targets and the loss keeps going down, but the metric no longer measures next token likelihood.
Level 3: The adapter returns per sequence means. Can the harness combine them? Expected: only with the token counts; a mean of means weights sequences equally instead of tokens.

Level 4: Perplexity on the held out set is far lower than on production text. What do you suspect? Expected: a tokenizer mismatch or a leak of the held out text into training; check both before you claim quality.
wrongAnswers: "Masking the loss is enough." The mask must also leave the denominator; counting pad positions dilutes the mean.
"Averaging per batch perplexities is close enough." It gives short sequences more weight per token and depends on the batch composition; the sum then divide form is the definition.
"A lower number is always a better model." It is a better fit to this text; it says nothing about the task.
keyPoints: Exclude padding from loss and token counts.
Avoid giving short batches extra weight.
Shift targets because logits predict the next token.
Sum real-token losses, divide once, then exponentiate.

questions.title: A leaderboard ranks your candidate models by one aggregate score, and the top model wins by a small margin. A colleague on the code team says that the top model is the worst of the three on their work. Both read the same report. How is this possible, what does the aggregate hide, and how do you publish so that both readers are served?
questions.answer: The aggregate is a weighted mean, so a model can win overall and lose in one category, and a small margin can sit inside the interval on the mean. Publish the per category means next to the aggregate, with intervals, and print the weights. If the leaderboard also mixes scales, a task with a wider range dominates the mean without anyone noticing.
followUps: Level 3: The code team wants the code category to count double. Do you change the headline? Expected: no; keep the unweighted table and, if agreed, add a second weighted view with its weights printed, as the capstone leaves weighting an explicit hook.

Level 3: The top two means differ by less than their intervals. What does the leaderboard show? Expected: the paired bootstrap of the per task difference; if it includes zero the two are tied and the rank order is a coin flip.
Level 4: Which single change to the report would have stopped this argument? Expected: per category means with intervals under the headline, so the code weakness was visible on the same page.
wrongAnswers: "The aggregate is the objective answer." It is the answer to one weighting; a different weighting is a different winner.
"Drop the aggregate and show only categories." The headline exists so people can decide; keep it, label its weights and put the categories under it.
"Rank by win rate instead." Win rate hides magnitude; publish both and the paired interval.
keyPoints: An aggregate can conceal category-specific losses.
Small margins may lie within uncertainty intervals.
Publish category means with intervals.
Print weights and check for mixed metric scales.

questions.title: A model you fine tuned jumped eight points on a public benchmark after you added a new web scraped corpus to the training mix. Leadership wants to announce it. Design the audit that tells you whether the jump is capability or leakage, and say what you would publish instead if it is leakage.
questions.answer: Audit for contamination before anyone announces anything. Search the new corpus for the benchmark questions and their close paraphrases and report the share found, then rerun the model on a versioned custom eval that the corpus cannot contain and diff the individual test cases against the previous model. If the overlap is material and the custom eval did not move, the jump is memorization, and you publish the custom eval result with the contamination share.
followUps: Level 3: The search finds exact matches for a small share and paraphrases for more. Which count? Expected: both; paraphrases leak the answer as well, so report exact and near matches separately with the method.
Level 3: The custom eval also rose. Is the jump real? Expected: more likely, if the suite is versioned, separate from training data and large enough that the rise exceeds its interval.

Level 4: How do you prevent the question next time? Expected: deduplicate training corpora against every eval set before training, keep eval data out of prompts and fine tuning data, and record the check in the training report.
wrongAnswers: "We did not include the benchmark on purpose, so it is clean." Web scale scraping includes it without intent; the lesson calls this the normal path to contamination.
"Eight points is too large to be noise." Noise is not the alternative; memorization is, and it produces large jumps.
"Announce the benchmark and add the caveat later." Publish the custom eval with intervals and the contamination share; a bare benchmark number is the claim you cannot defend.
keyPoints: Search new training data for benchmark questions and paraphrases.
Report the contamination share.
Rerun a versioned custom evaluation absent from training data.
Compare individual cases and publish custom results if gains are memorization.

questions.title: Your team will adopt a new model next quarter and needs a long context evaluation that runs again on every future upgrade. Design the battery for a product that answers questions over long documents and sometimes has to combine facts from several places: the tests, the sampling grid, the metrics, the cutoffs and the regression procedure.
questions.answer: Build a fixed in house harness with three parts: a needle grid over depth and length on your own documents, a multi hop variable tracing task at the same lengths, and a slice of real long document questions. Sample five depths at each length and record pass rates, time to first token and cost per query. Publish two cutoffs, the effective retrieval length at a 90 percent pass and the effective reasoning length at 70 percent, and rerun the same harness on every upgrade.
followUps: Level 3: Why a fixed harness instead of the newest public benchmark each time? Expected: a regression needs the same test on both models; a changing benchmark confounds the model change with the test change.

Level 3: The new model passes the needle grid at the target length but fails tracing at a quarter of it. What do you ship? Expected: the reasoning effective length as the product limit; chunk or retrieve beyond it and say so on the spec sheet.
Level 4: Prefill at the target length takes two minutes. Does it change the design? Expected: yes; the length budget is what the product can afford in latency and cost, not what the model can read.
wrongAnswers: "Run the needle test at the advertised length and stop." Needle only says nothing about multi hop; the lesson refuses it for any multi hop workload.
"Use the vendor's published long context scores." They are self reported; rerun independently on your use case.
"Test the middle depth at one length." Models under attend to the middle and degrade with length; one point hides both effects.
keyPoints: Test needle retrieval across context depths and lengths.
Include multi-hop tracing and real long-document questions.
Measure pass rates, time to first token and cost.
Publish separate retrieval and reasoning cutoffs and rerun on upgrades.

questions.title: Take home. We give you a small instruction tuned model, a held out corpus, a set of short factual prompts with gold answers, a set of open form prompts with reference answers, and no network access. Build an evaluation pipeline that reports more than one number and explains its aggregate, and describe how it would run in CI once a network and a judge model are available. What do you deliver, and what do you leave out on purpose?
questions.answer: Deliver one runnable file with four evals: held out perplexity with honest token accounting, normalized exact match on the factual set, token F1 on the open form set, and a deterministic mock judge on a 1 to 5 scale with the same interface a real judge will have. Report every per eval number, a weighted aggregate with the weights in a config, and per example records for diagnosis. Leave out the real judge, intervals on the aggregate and anything that needs a network, and say so in the readme.
followUps: Level 3: Why keep a mock judge in the deliverable at all? Expected: it fixes the interface and the aggregation path so the real judge is a one function swap, and it keeps the loop runnable offline.

Level 3: Why is the weighted mean a product decision? Expected: weights encode what the product values; the pipeline exposes them in config and reports every component so a reviewer can see what the aggregate hides.
Level 4: What is the first thing you add when a network appears? Expected: a real judge behind the same function, then a calibration run against hand labels before any of its scores gate anything.
wrongAnswers: "One accuracy number is the deliverable." A single metric never describes a model; the brief asks for several and for an explanation of the aggregate.
"Skip perplexity, it is not a task metric." It is the cheapest check that the model fits the language at all, and wrong accounting there is what a reviewer looks for.
"Hard code the weights." The weights are the product decision; expose them and print them next to the numbers.
keyPoints: Provide perplexity, normalized exact match and token F1 evaluations.
Use a deterministic mock judge with the real judge interface.
Report component scores, configured weights and per-example records.
Document omitted real judging, aggregate intervals and network dependencies.

topics.title: Multimodal
topics.about: How vision and language models join images and text, and how they are trained.

questions.title: Compare one-stage and two-stage object detectors. What is non-maximum suppression?
questions.answer:
Two-stage and one-stage object detectors represent an architectural trade-off between localization precision and inference latency:
Two-stage detectors (such as Faster R-CNN) first generate candidate regions of interest (RoIs) using a Region Proposal Network (RPN), extract pooled feature maps via RoIAlign, and then perform bounding box regression and classification. They excel at high accuracy on small or densely clustered objects, but operate at higher computational latency.
One-stage detectors (such as YOLO or SSD) frame detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly across dense spatial grids in a single forward pass, enabling real-time edge serving (60+ FPS).
Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) is the greedy post-processing step that eliminates redundant overlapping bounding boxes. It selects the highest-scoring prediction and drops all adjacent boxes whose Intersection-over-Union (IoU) exceeds a set threshold (typically 0.5). A known failure mode is suppressing true adjacent objects. Modern architectures like DETR bypass NMS entirely by formulating detection as set prediction via bipartite matching.
keyPoints: Two-stage detectors propose regions before classification and refinement.
One-stage detectors predict boxes and classes directly.
Non-maximum suppression removes overlapping lower-confidence detections.
Speed and small-object accuracy depend on architecture and workload.

questions.title: How do diffusion models generate images?
questions.answer:
Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a gradual noising process:
Forward Process: Gaussian noise is incrementally added to a clean image over T discrete timesteps according to a fixed variance schedule. Because the process is Gaussian, any noisy state x_t can be sampled directly from x_0 in closed form without iterating through intermediate steps.
Reverse Denoising: A neural network (traditionally a U-Net with attention, or a Diffusion Transformer like DiT) is trained with Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss to predict the exact noise vector added at timestep t, conditioned on the timestep embedding.
Latent Diffusion: Rather than operating in high-dimensional pixel space, models like Stable Diffusion operate inside a compressed latent space produced by a pretrained VAE, reducing compute requirements by 64x.
Controllability: Conditioning (such as text prompts) is injected via cross-attention. Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) dynamically interpolates between unconditional and conditional predictions during inference, trading sample diversity for strict prompt alignment. Modern samplers (such as DDIM or DPMSolver) solve the reverse differential equations in 20 to 30 steps rather than 1,000.
keyPoints: The forward process gradually adds noise to training images.
A neural network learns to predict noise or a denoising target.
Generation starts from noise and iteratively denoises.
Conditioning guides generation toward text or other inputs.
Sampling steps trade latency against quality.

questions.title: Design a real-time voice assistant. Where does the latency go?
questions.answer:
Designing a real-time conversational voice assistant requires keeping total glass-to-glass latency under 800ms—the boundary where human conversation feels natural:
Pipeline Architecture: The pipeline cascades Voice Activity Detection (VAD), Streaming Speech-to-Text (STT), LLM generation, and Streaming Text-to-Speech (TTS).
Streaming Strategy: We stream every intermediate boundary: partial audio chunks stream into STT; token streams emit from the LLM; and as soon as the first clause or punctuation boundary completes (5 to 8 tokens), tokens dispatch immediately to neural TTS chunk synthesis. This achieves sub-500ms Time-to-First-Audio (TTFA) before the LLM finishes the full response.
Endpointing Trade-off: Determining when the user finished speaking is the most critical balance. A short silence threshold (e.g., 400ms) cuts off thoughtful pauses; a long threshold (1,200ms) introduces noticeable delay. We use acoustic VAD paired with LLM completion probability to detect turn completion.
Barge-In: The client audio subsystem implements Acoustic Echo Cancellation (AEC). When user speech is detected during assistant playback, the client immediately cancels playback and interrupts server generation.
keyPoints: A voice pipeline includes capture, endpointing, recognition, generation and synthesis.
Streaming and overlap reduce time to first audible response.
Endpoint detection trades responsiveness against cutting off speech.
Support interruption and cancel obsolete generation or audio.
Measure end-to-end latency rather than just model inference time.

questions.title: How do you architect a streaming text-to-speech pipeline with chunked neural vocoders to achieve sub-200ms time-to-first-audio?
questions.answer: In conversational voice AI, waiting for an LLM to generate an entire sentence before beginning speech synthesis creates noticeable latency that breaks human conversational flow. We architect a streaming text-to-speech pipeline that operates concurrently with LLM token generation. As the LLM streams text tokens, a text normalizer accumulates tokens into grammatical phrase chunks (typically 4 to 8 words) delimited by commas or pauses. The phrase chunk is immediately dispatched to an acoustic model that generates mel-spectrogram frames. A lightweight neural vocoder—such as HiFi-GAN or a flow-matching vocoder—synthesizes raw 24kHz audio waveforms from the spectrogram in small chunks, streaming PCM audio frames over a WebSocket directly to the client browser. Audio playback starts on the client while downstream text is still being generated. The trade-off is time-to-first-audio versus prosody naturalness: streaming small phrase chunks achieves time-to-first-audio under 200 milliseconds, but synthesis models lack full sentence context, which can cause slight pitch and prosody discontinuities at phrase boundaries.
followUps: How do you handle audio phase alignment when stitching together streaming audio chunks in the client audio buffer?
What happens if the LLM token generation rate falls below real-time audio playback speed?
wrongAnswers: Buffering the entire LLM response text before initiating text-to-speech synthesis, forcing users to wait several seconds in silence.
Sending single-word chunks to the vocoder, causing unnatural robotic cadence and boundary clicks.
tradeOffs: Chunked streaming text-to-speech achieves sub-200ms time-to-first-audio, creating responsive real-time voice conversations.
Synthesizing speech in small phrase chunks reduces cross-sentence prosodic context, risking minor pitch glitches across boundaries.
keyPoints: Accumulate generated text into short grammatical phrase chunks.
Send phrases to an acoustic model and synthesize incremental audio with a vocoder.
Stream audio while the model continues generating text.
Smaller chunks reduce first-audio latency but weaken cross-phrase prosody.

questions.title: How do you tune Voice Activity Detection (VAD) pause thresholds to balance conversational responsiveness against interrupting user pauses?
questions.answer: In spoken conversational agents, determining when a user has finished speaking versus when they are taking a brief mid-sentence pause is the fundamental challenge of natural turn-taking. If the Voice Activity Detection (VAD) pause threshold is set too short (such as 300ms), the agent interrupts the user whenever they pause to think. If the threshold is set too long (such as 1,500ms), conversations feel awkward and sluggish. We implement a two-stage turn-taking architecture using a lightweight neural VAD model (like Silero VAD) paired with semantic end-of-turn classification. The VAD operates on 30-millisecond audio frames, outputting speech probabilities. We maintain a baseline silence threshold, typically calibrated around 600 to 800 milliseconds. When speech stops, the system passes the transcribed text transcript to a fast semantic end-of-turn classifier: if the transcript ends on an incomplete clause or trailing conjunction (like 'because...'), the system extends the pause threshold by another 700 milliseconds. If the transcript is grammatically complete, the agent responds immediately. The trade-off is conversational fluidity versus interruption risk: semantic turn-taking feels human, but requires sub-50ms classifier latency to avoid adding delay.
followUps: How do you calibrate energy-based versus neural VAD models in noisy acoustic environments (e.g. cafes)?
What role do acoustic pitch and prosody cues play in signaling turn completion in human speech?
wrongAnswers: Using a fixed 400ms silence threshold with no semantic context, causing the agent to constantly cut off users while thinking.
Using a fixed 2,000ms threshold for all turns, making the conversation feel unresponsive and broken.
tradeOffs: Semantic turn-taking combined with neural VAD allows natural human mid-sentence pauses without premature agent interruptions.
Extending pause thresholds on trailing conjunctions prevents interruptions, but delays response times if the user genuinely stopped speaking.
keyPoints: Combine neural VAD with semantic end-of-turn classification.
Distinguish reflective pauses from completed turns.
Extend the silence threshold for incomplete clauses.
Balance interruption risk against response delay and classifier latency.

questions.title: How do you manage sliding audio window overlap and prefix freezing in streaming speech-to-text (ASR) to prevent silence hallucinations?
questions.answer: Streaming speech-to-text models process continuous microphone audio in small increments to output text with minimal delay. However, splitting audio arbitrarily at chunk boundaries cuts phonemes in half, causing transcription errors. Furthermore, encoder-decoder ASR models (like Whisper) frequently hallucinate repetitive phrases when processing audio chunks containing pure ambient silence. We implement streaming ASR using sliding audio windows with boundary overlap and prefix freezing. The audio stream is accumulated in a growing buffer. At each step, we feed an audio window containing new audio plus 1 to 2 seconds of trailing overlap from the previous chunk. We align the new transcription with previous output, freeze the stable prefix that has repeated across consecutive passes, and emit only the finalized tokens. When our VAD flags that an audio chunk contains no human speech, we bypass model inference entirely, feeding pure silence tokens and clearing audio buffers to prevent hallucination loops. The trade-off is redundant audio compute versus boundary transcription stability: re-processing overlapping audio segments increases ASR compute by roughly 30%, but it eliminates boundary word mutilation.
followUps: How does CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) compare to autoregressive attention for streaming speech transcription?
What causes encoder-decoder models to loop phrases repeatedly when transcribing ambient background noise?
wrongAnswers: Chunking raw audio into disjoint 1-second chunks without overlap, causing words split across boundaries to be transcribed as nonsense.
Feeding non-speech audio into autoregressive models without VAD gating, triggering repetitive hallucination loops.
tradeOffs: Sliding window overlap and prefix freezing eliminate word clipping at chunk boundaries and stabilize streaming text output.
Re-processing overlapping audio segments consumes additional GPU compute compared to single-pass non-overlapping chunking.
keyPoints: Overlap adjacent audio windows to avoid splitting phonemes.
Align successive transcripts and freeze stable prefixes.
Use VAD to bypass silent chunks and prevent hallucination loops.
Overlap improves boundary stability but repeats compute.

questions.title: How do you design a rigorous Word Error Rate (WER) evaluation harness with text normalization to benchmark speech models across regional accents?
questions.answer: Evaluating speech recognition models across regional accents requires a standardized evaluation harness to prevent aggregate metrics from hiding performance disparities. Standard Word Error Rate computes Levenshtein edit distance on word tokens: substitutions plus deletions plus insertions divided by total reference words. However, raw ASR transcripts contain formatting artifacts like numbers, dates, contractions, and punctuation that distort WER if evaluated directly against ground truth. We apply a strict text normalizer before scoring: converting text to lowercase, expanding numbers to spoken words (e.g. '42' to 'forty-two'), stripping punctuation, and standardizing contractions. Crucially, evaluating an aggregate WER score across a pooled dataset hides severe accent bias: an overall WER of 8% can conceal that native speakers score 4% while non-native regional accents score 25%. We partition evaluation sets into stratified demographic cohorts across accents, background noise levels, and speaking rates, reporting per-cohort WER distributions and worst-case tail performance. The trade-off is normalization breadth versus semantic nuance: aggressive text normalization isolates acoustic recognition accuracy, but ignores capitalization and punctuation quality needed by downstream LLM prompts.
followUps: What is Character Error Rate (CER) and when is it preferred over Word Error Rate for non-concatenative or agglutinative languages?
How do you test speech recognition accuracy on domain-specific technical jargon and acronyms?
wrongAnswers: Evaluating raw un-normalized transcripts, penalizing models for formatting differences like 'Dr.' versus 'Doctor'.
Reporting only aggregate global WER, hiding that the model fails on non-native or regional accents.
tradeOffs: Standardized text normalization isolates phonetic speech accuracy from superficial casing and punctuation formatting differences.
Stratified cohort evaluation exposes regional accent performance gaps, preventing aggregate averages from masking real user failures.
keyPoints: Compute WER as substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by reference words.
Normalize case, numbers, punctuation and contractions before scoring.
Report separate accent, noise and speaking-rate cohorts.
Aggregate WER can hide severe regional-accent failures.

questions.title: How do you architect a full-duplex voice pipeline that supports user barge-in interruptions and acoustic echo cancellation?
questions.answer: In a natural conversation, a user does not wait for a speaker to finish a paragraph before interjecting; they interrupt or ask clarifications immediately. Half-duplex voice bots mute the microphone while speaking, preventing users from interrupting. A full-duplex voice architecture keeps the microphone active at all times while the agent speaks. This introduces acoustic echo: the agent's synthesized speech emitted from device speakers is picked up by the microphone and fed back into speech recognition, causing the agent to interrupt and transcribe itself. We solve this using WebRTC Acoustic Echo Cancellation (AEC) and hardware-level reference stream subtraction. The microphone input is scrubbed of the speaker output signal before reaching our VAD. When the VAD detects genuine user speech above an energy and duration threshold while the agent is speaking, a barge-in event fires immediately: the server halts downstream LLM generation, issues a cancellation signal to the streaming audio player to flush remaining buffers, and switches the agent into listening mode. The trade-off is barge-in responsiveness versus accidental interruptions: aggressive interruption thresholds cancel agent speech on faint background coughs or speaker echo leaks, while conservative thresholds make interrupting difficult.
followUps: How does WebRTC Acoustic Echo Cancellation (AEC3) mathematically model room impulse responses to cancel speaker echo?
What state cleanup is required when an agent's streaming audio is abruptly cut off by a user barge-in?
wrongAnswers: Muting the user's microphone during agent speech playback, forcing users into frustrating walkie-talkie style turn-taking.
Relying on software volume ducking alone without acoustic echo cancellation, causing the agent to transcribe its own speaker echo.
tradeOffs: Full-duplex barge-in allows immediate, natural interruptions, creating human-like conversational fluidity.
Acoustic echo cancellation leakage or overly sensitive VAD can cause the agent to interrupt itself on faint speaker reverberations.
keyPoints: Keep the microphone active while the agent speaks.
Remove speaker echo before speech detection using AEC.
On genuine user speech, cancel generation and flush playback buffers.
Thresholds trade responsive barge-in against accidental interruptions.

questions.title: A product manager asks how much of the context window one image uses in a LLaVA-style model with a 336-pixel encoder. Give the number, say where it comes from, and say how it changes with high-resolution tiling or with a query-based bridge.
questions.answer: One image costs 576 tokens: the encoder cuts the 336-pixel image into 14-pixel patches, a 24 by 24 grid, and the projector passes every patch token through. In a 2048-token context that leaves 1472 tokens for text; at 32k or 128k it is a small share. Tiling multiplies it: a 2 by 2 grid of 336-pixel crops plus one global thumbnail gives about 2880 tokens per image, and a 1 by 3 grid plus the thumbnail gives fewer, because it has one crop less. A query-based bridge compresses any image to a fixed 32 tokens, and a resampler to 64.
followUps: Level 1: Why does a higher input resolution raise the token count? Expected: the patch size is fixed, so more pixels per side means more patches per side, and the count grows with the square of the side.
Level 2: Which tasks justify the tiling cost? Expected: text in images, charts and documents; general scene questions gain little from it.
Level 2: When does the 32-token bridge win? Expected: when the token budget binds, as with long video or many images per prompt; for one image in a long context the compression buys little.

Level 3: How do you size the budget for video? Expected: tokens per frame times frames, so a compressing bridge or heavy frame sampling is the only way to fit minutes of video; count the tokens before you pick the bridge.
wrongAnswers: "An image costs one token, the placeholder." The placeholder is replaced by one embedding per patch token before the forward pass; the encoder grid sets the count.
"Higher resolution is free because the encoder is fixed." More patches means more visual tokens in the language model's sequence, and the language model's compute grows with them.
"The connector decides the quality, so pick the bridge first." At a fixed token count the connector barely matters; the token count and the encoder matter more.

questions.title: Draw the standard architecture of a vision-language model that answers questions about an image. Name its three parts, say what each one contributes, and say which part you would expect to train when a team fine-tunes on a few thousand labelled images.
questions.answer: A vision encoder, a projector and a language model. The encoder, a pretrained vision transformer, turns the image into patch tokens. The projector, a small two- to four-layer MLP or a query-based bridge, maps those tokens into the language model's embedding space, where they replace a placeholder token in the prompt. The decoder language model reads image tokens and text tokens as one sequence and writes the answer; in most fine-tunes the encoder and the language model stay frozen or get adapters, and the projector is where the training happens.
followUps: Level 1: Why does the projector need two layers and not one? Expected: one linear layer rotates and scales; the non-linearity between two layers lets the map bend, which is enough to align contrastive vision features to a language model's embeddings.

Level 2: What does the language model see where the image was? Expected: a run of embeddings, one per projected patch token, in place of the placeholder; the model treats them as tokens with no special handling.

Level 2: What does a bridge with a fixed set of learned queries change? Expected: it compresses the patch tokens to a fixed count, which saves context at the cost of a bottleneck; the MLP keeps every patch.
Level 3: Which part sets the ceiling on reasoning quality? Expected: the language model; the encoder can only feed it, so a larger language model lifts the benchmarks more than a cleverer bridge.
wrongAnswers: "The language model looks at pixels through cross-attention into the image." In this pattern the image enters as tokens in the input sequence; cross-attention bridges are a different family.
"Fine-tune the vision encoder first; it is the part that sees." The encoder is pretrained and frozen in stage one; the projector is where a small team's training budget goes.
"The projector must be a large network to carry the image." It is a two-layer MLP far smaller than the encoder in the capstone, and it trains in minutes.

questions.title: In the first training stage of most open vision-language models, both the vision encoder and the decoder are frozen, and only the small projector learns. A junior engineer asks why anyone would train the smallest part first instead of the parts that matter. Answer them.
questions.answer: The two big parts already work: the encoder represents images, and the language model writes text. What is missing is a translation between their two vector spaces, and that translation is small. Training only the bridge costs a few hundred steps on one GPU, cannot damage either pretrained part, and gives the language model inputs it can read before anyone unfreezes it. Unfreezing the language model comes in the second stage, once the bridge produces tokens that look like language.
followUps: Level 1: What does a frozen parameter mean in code? Expected: requires_grad=False, so the optimizer never sees it, and no memory goes to its gradient or optimizer state.

Level 2: Why pool the image tokens before the cosine loss in the capstone? Expected: the caption side is one vector, so the image side needs one vector too; the first token or the mean over all tokens are the usual choices.

Level 2: One linear layer would be smaller still. Why two? Expected: a single linear map can rotate and rescale but cannot bend; the GELU between two layers gives the one non-linear bend that aligns contrastive vision features to language embeddings.

Level 3: What breaks if you skip the alignment stage and start with instruction tuning with everything unfrozen? Expected: the language model receives unaligned inputs, and its gradients on a small set damage its text ability; the two stages exist to give it readable inputs first.
wrongAnswers: "Train the encoder; it is the part that sees." It already sees, and a small dataset cannot teach it more than it loses by overwriting features; the missing part is the translation.
"The projector is too small to carry an image." It does not carry the image; it maps tokens that already encode the image into the space the language model reads.
"Freezing is only a memory trick." Memory is one gain; the larger ones are stability, a clean training signal, and the ability to swap the language model.

questions.title: A product needs a model that reads screenshots and answers questions today, and might need to draw diagrams later. Two designs are on the table: an adapter model, where a vision encoder feeds projected tokens into a text-only decoder, and a model that turns images into discrete codes in the same vocabulary as text and trains one next-token loss over interleaved sequences. Compare them and pick for this product.
questions.answer: The adapter design is late fusion: images enter as projected continuous tokens or through cross-attention, the decoder reuses all its text pretraining, and the output is text only. The shared-vocabulary design is early fusion: a quantizer maps an image to discrete codes, the transformer trains one loss over text and image codes, and it can emit image codes, so it generates pictures. For a product that must read screenshots now, pick the adapter: it reuses more pretrained compute, has no quantizer ceiling for understanding, and is cheaper to serve; add the early-fusion model only when drawing becomes a real requirement, because its image quality is capped by the quantizer and each generated image costs a decoder pass over a thousand or more codes.
followUps: Level 2: Why can the adapter model not generate an image? Expected: its output head covers the text vocabulary only; images enter as embeddings and never exist as tokens it could predict.
Level 2: What is the shared vocabulary made of? Expected: text tokens, image codes and modality separators in one id space, so one embedding table and one output projection cover all of them.

Level 3: Where does the quality ceiling of the early-fusion model come from, and what moves it? Expected: the quantizer's reconstruction; a larger codebook and more codes per image raise it, as the next generation of tokenizers showed.

Level 3: A hybrid keeps images continuous and trains a diffusion loss on patches next to the text loss. What does it trade? Expected: no quantizer and higher image fidelity, against two losses on different scales to balance and a diffusion sampling loop at generation time.
wrongAnswers: "Early fusion is the future, so start there." For understanding alone it reuses less pretrained compute and caps quality at the quantizer; the adapter is the simpler, stronger choice until generation is required.
"The adapter can draw if you add a decoder head." Its images never exist as predictable tokens; drawing needs either image codes in the vocabulary or a separate generation model.
"The quantizer is a detail; the transformer does the work." In the early-fusion family the quantizer sets the ceiling on every image the model produces.

questions.title: A unified next-token model generates a 512 by 512 image as a sequence of discrete codes. Estimate how long one image takes at a typical decode speed, compare it with a diffusion model, and say what a four-second video clip at low resolution costs in codes. Then name the levers that change the answer.
questions.answer: The reference model's tokenizer reduces 8 by 8 pixels to one code, so a 512 by 512 image is 4096 codes; at about 30 codes per second that is about 2 minutes per image, against 2 to 5 seconds for a diffusion model of the same quality tier. A 4-second clip at 8 frames per second is 32 frames; with the same 8 times spatial reduction and a 4-frame temporal reduction, a 256 by 256 clip is 32 times 32 times 8, which is 8,192 codes. The levers are the codes per image, the decode speed through speculative decoding or the KV cache, and a different decoding scheme such as masked parallel decoding, which needs about 16 passes instead of one pass per code.
followUps: Level 2: Why does guidance double the cost? Expected: each step needs a conditional and an unconditional forward pass to mix.
Level 2: What happens to the per-image time at 1024 by 1024? Expected: four times the codes at the same reduction, so about four times the decode time; the lesson's exercise asks for that count.

Level 3: Where does the quality ceiling of this model sit, and what moved it up from the first shared-vocabulary model? Expected: in the tokenizer's reconstruction; four times the codes per image and a four times larger codebook lifted it to 30.5 dB.

Level 3: When do you still pick this over a diffusion model? Expected: when one model must understand and generate across image, video and text with one loss, and the latency budget allows minutes per image or a batch pipeline.
wrongAnswers: "An image is a few hundred tokens, like a VLM input." Those are projected encoder tokens for understanding; generation needs discrete codes at the tokenizer's density, 4096 for this image size.
"Diffusion is slower because it iterates." Diffusion takes a few dozen passes over all pixels at once; next-token generation takes one pass per code, thousands per image.
"A larger codebook makes generation faster." It raises the reconstruction quality; the pass count is set by the number of codes, not by the codebook size.

questions.title: Your 7B vision-language model trails a competitor on a multimodal reasoning benchmark by several points. The team's plan is a new connector design. Argue for or against, using what the ablation literature says about where the score comes from.
questions.answer: Against. Across the controlled studies, swapping the connector moved a reasoning benchmark by less than a point at a fixed token count, while swapping the encoder moved it by three or more, and doubling the language model from 7B to 13B added two to four points. The reasoning ceiling of such a model is the text reasoning ceiling of its language model; the visual side can only feed it. Spend the effort on the language model size, the encoder, the token count and the data before the connector.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a bigger language model help a visual task? Expected: the benchmark asks for reasoning over what the encoder saw, and the reasoning happens in the language model; the visual side sets what it knows, not how well it thinks.

Level 2: When would a connector change still be the right move? Expected: when the token budget binds, because then the connector decides how many tokens you can afford, which is the axis that matters most.

Level 3: Which benchmarks move with the encoder and which do not? Expected: vision-centric benchmarks, counting and grounding, move with a self-supervised encoder, by about 5 to 7 points in one study; the reasoning benchmark also moves, by 3 or more points for a stronger contrastive encoder, so the encoder matters for both kinds.

Level 3: Design the smallest ablation that settles this for your model. Expected: hold the data, the encoder, the token count, the resolution schedule and the training schedule fixed, swap the language model size in one run and the connector in another, and compare both with the baseline on the same eval.
wrongAnswers: "The connector is where the modalities meet, so it must matter most." Its measured share is about 5 percent of the variance; the token count and the encoder dominate.
"A better connector lets a small language model reason like a large one." The reasoning ceiling is the language model's; no bridge adds reasoning the language model does not have.
"More visual tokens always help." They help up to the sweet spot and then give diminishing returns at a growing compute cost; the gain is in the token count, not in the architecture that emits them.

questions.title: You are choosing the bridge between a frozen vision encoder and a language model that stays frozen, for a new product. One architect wants a query-based transformer that compresses each image to a fixed set of tokens. Another wants a plain MLP that passes every patch through. How do you decide?
questions.answer: Decide on the token budget, not on quality in the abstract. At a fixed number of visual tokens, the ablation studies find the connector architecture a wash, within about a point between an MLP on mean-pooled patches, a query bridge and a resampler; a full-patch MLP spends more tokens, so it sits at a different budget. The query bridge caps an image at 32 tokens whatever its resolution and costs 188M parameters plus a two-stage pretraining of its own; the MLP emits every patch, 576 for a 336-pixel image, with about 22M parameters and one language-modeling loss. Pick the compressing bridge when context binds, as with long video or many images; pick the MLP when quality per token and simplicity matter and the context is long enough.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the query bridge need a pretraining stage of its own? Expected: its queries start random and must learn to pull text-relevant content from the patches before the language model can use them; the MLP starts from patches that already carry the image.

Level 2: What do the three stage-one losses do? Expected: contrastive alignment of pooled queries with text, a matching classifier with hard negatives, and image-grounded text generation that forces the queries to encode what text needs.

Level 3: A team picked the MLP and now serves ten-minute videos. What do they hit first? Expected: the context; tokens per frame times frames exceeds any window, so they need heavy frame sampling or a compressing bridge after all.

Level 3: If the connector barely matters, where does the quality come from? Expected: the encoder, the token count, the data mix and the resolution schedule; the recipes lesson's decomposition puts the connector last.
wrongAnswers: "The query bridge is more advanced, so it gives better answers." At the same token count the two are within about a point; its advantage is compression, not quality.
"The MLP is always better because it keeps every patch." Keeping every patch costs tokens; with many images or video the context runs out before quality matters.
"Pick the bridge first and the encoder later." The encoder and the token count explain most of the variance; the bridge is the last knob to turn.

questions.title: A warehouse team wants a general vision-language model to answer "which shelf is the item on" and "is the box on top of or under the pallet" from camera frames. They plan to ship as soon as a demo works on ten images. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: Spatial relations are the weak spot of today's general-purpose vision-language models: on benchmarks of above and below, left and right, counting and distance they score about 50 to 60 percent, below human level. A demo on ten images proves nothing about that distribution. Build a labelled eval of a few hundred frames with the exact questions first, measure the model, and compare it with a specialised detection or depth model whose box geometry you post-process; if the general model stays, fine-tune it on the task and keep a human-review route for low-confidence answers.
followUps: Level 2: Why does a model that captions well fail at which object is on top? Expected: captions describe content, not geometry; the training pairs rarely contain precise relations, and fine position fades as the language model reasons over projected tokens.
Level 2: What does the detector route lose? Expected: the plain-language interface and the open vocabulary; it answers only the relations you compute from boxes, for the classes you labelled.

Level 3: How many frames does the eval need, and how do you decide? Expected: enough that each question type and each camera condition has tens of examples; a few hundred in total is the floor, and you grow it where the confusion matrix is unstable.
