Level 3: How does a stronger encoder change the picture? Expected: self-supervised encoders carry more dense spatial features and lead vision-centric benchmarks; swapping the encoder and retraining the projector is the lesson's hard exercise for these tasks.
wrongAnswers: "The demo worked on ten images, so it works." Ten images cannot cover the cameras, the lighting or the relation types; the benchmark figure for this kind of question is near a coin flip for some relations.
"A bigger VLM will fix spatial reasoning." Size lifts language reasoning more than geometry; the lesson's advice for pure spatial tasks is a specialised model.
"Fine-tune on the demo images." Tens of examples teach nothing and overfit; the fine-tuning route needs thousands of labelled frames and an eval that is separate from them.

questions.title: Take-home. You get a frozen vision encoder that emits 197 tokens of width 768 per image and a frozen text embedding table of width 512. Build the smallest module that lets the two talk, train it on paired samples, and ship tests that prove it works. Describe the design, the loss, how you train it, and the tests.
questions.answer: Pool the 197 image tokens to one vector, pass it through a two-layer MLP, 768 to 1024 to 512 with a GELU between, and compare it with the mean-pooled caption embedding through a cosine alignment loss, one minus the cosine. Train only the MLP, about 1.3M parameters, with the encoder and the table frozen, for a few hundred steps over a few dozen pairs. The tests: the output shape equals the text width, the frozen parts have no trainable parameters, the loss is zero on identical vectors and two on opposite vectors, a gradient reaches the projector after one backward pass, and the loss at the last step is lower than at the first.
followUps: Level 2: Why cosine and not mean squared error? Expected: alignment means the same direction in the joint space, not equal vectors; cosine is scale-invariant, so the projector is not punished for a norm the text table happens to have.
Level 2: What does a learned temperature on the cosine change? Expected: a sharper or flatter loss surface; too small gives noisy gradients and too large plateaus high, as the exercise shows.

Level 3: The capstone's run stops near 0.80 after 200 steps. Is that a floor? Expected: no; it is the loss of one run at 200 steps. The projector has 1024 hidden units for 32 pairs, so more steps or a different rate can push the loss lower; on natural pairs, the encoder features set how far the alignment can go.

Level 3: How does this module relate to a query-based bridge? Expected: that bridge ends in the same kind of projection to the text width; the difference is that it first compresses the tokens through learned queries instead of pooling.
wrongAnswers: "Fine-tune the encoder as well; it is only 86M parameters." The take-home gives frozen parts for a reason: a few dozen pairs cannot teach the encoder anything, and the test that checks the frozen table would fail.
"Use a single linear layer; it is enough for a rotation." The two bases differ by more than a rotation; the non-linearity is what lets one bend close the gap.
"Skip the tests; the loss went down." The loss can fall through a shape bug or a leak into the frozen parts; the tests pin the contract that the loss alone cannot.

questions.title: A model must take a prompt with any number of images, some small and some large, interleaved with text, and then caption the last image from a few in-context examples. Explain the module that makes the number and the size of the images manageable, and how a text token knows which image to look at.
questions.answer: A resampler with a fixed set of learned latent vectors turns the patch tokens of each image into a fixed number of visual tokens. In the reference design, 64 latents attend over however many patches the encoder produced, 196 for a small image or 900 for a large one, through six blocks of cross-attention and self-attention, and every image exits as 64 tokens of one width. Text tokens then read those tokens through gated cross-attention layers inserted between the frozen language model blocks, and a mask lets each text token attend only to the latents of the most recent image before it in the sequence.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the latent side supply the query vectors and the patch side the rest, not the other way around? Expected: the output has one row per query, so queries from the latents give a fixed number of rows; the reverse would give one row per patch again.

Level 2: What does the temporal encoding do for video? Expected: each frame gives the same 64 latents, so without a time signal the model cannot tell the first frame from the last; the encoding marks the frame index.

Level 3: Why mask to the most recent image instead of all preceding images? Expected: it keeps the shape each text token sees constant and matches the interleaved reading order, where a caption describes the image before it; seeing all images is the alternative with a different trade-off.

Level 3: A fine-tune of a model like this lost text-only quality. Where do you look? Expected: the gate; if it opened too wide too fast, visual noise overwrote the text residual stream, so compare the gate values by layer with the base.
wrongAnswers: "Pad every image to the same number of patches." Padding wastes compute on large images and loses detail on small ones; the resampler gives a fixed count without either.
"Let the text tokens attend to all image patches directly." The count then varies per image and per prompt, and a prompt with many images floods the attention; the latents keep it fixed.
"Initialize the gate open so that the model learns faster." An open gate at step zero destroys the frozen language model's text behavior; a start at zero is what preserves it.

questions.title: Token-by-token image generation used to mean predicting one code after another in raster order. A newer method predicts whole grids at increasing resolution instead. Explain what it predicts at each step, why that fixes the old method's main weakness, and how it compares with diffusion in the number of network passes.
questions.answer: Next-scale prediction tokenizes an image into a pyramid of grids, from one code up to the full latent resolution, with a residual quantizer so that the sum of the scales reconstructs the image. The transformer is causal across scales and parallel within a scale: given all coarser grids, it predicts every code of the next grid in one pass. That removes the raster-order problem, where an early corner code had to commit before any context existed. For a 256 by 256 image the reference uses about 10 scales, so generation is about 10 passes against 28 to 50 for a diffusion transformer, and all codes of a scale come out together.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the residual structure matter for the tokenizer? Expected: each scale encodes only what the coarser scales missed, so the sum reconstructs the latent and the scales are not redundant.
Level 2: What does a code at scale k see, and what may it not see? Expected: all codes at scales 1 to k, its own scale's positions included; nothing at finer scales.

Level 3: What happens to quality and cost as you add scales? Expected: finer residuals and better reconstruction, at the cost of one more pass per scale; the lesson's exercise sweeps 4 to 10 scales to find the knee.

Level 3: How would you add text conditioning? Expected: feed a pooled text embedding through adaptive normalization, as the hybrid variant in the lesson does, and measure the gain on text-aligned samples.
wrongAnswers: "It is diffusion with a different name." Diffusion iterates over noise levels on continuous latents; this iterates over resolution on discrete codes and predicts a whole grid per pass.
"Within a scale the codes still go one by one." The mask is bidirectional inside a scale, so one forward pass produces the whole grid.
"Raster order only costs speed." It also biases generation: an early code commits before the context that should condition it exists, which capped quality below diffusion at matched compute.

questions.title: Your deployed vision-language model answers questions about product photos. Support tickets say that it invents objects and misreads numbers, but the offline benchmark score is fine. Design the production monitoring and the response plan.
questions.answer: Treat hallucination as a production metric, not as a model property. Score every answer with a cross-modal error rate: embed the image and the generated text with an independent contrastive checker, and flag outputs where the text confidence is high but the image-text similarity is low. Track that rate per endpoint, per prompt type and per customer, alert on a rise, and route the flagged answers to human review instead of to the user. The team that introduced the metric cut its hallucination rate by about 35 percent this way, without a model change.
followUps: Level 3: Why an independent checker and not the model's own confidence? Expected: the model is confident when it hallucinates, which is the failure; the checker gives a second opinion that does not share the generator's blind spots.

Level 3: How do you set the two thresholds? Expected: label a few hundred answers as grounded or not, sweep the thresholds, and pick the pair that catches most hallucinations at a review load the team can afford.

Level 4: The rate rises for one customer only. What do you check? Expected: their image source: resolution, lighting, a new product line with text the model misreads; the per-customer split exists for that reason.

Level 4: How do you decide between a model change and a routing change? Expected: routing is cheap and immediate and protects users today; a model change needs grounded data and a re-measurement; do both in that order and let the metric arbitrate.
wrongAnswers: "Raise the benchmark score and the hallucinations will go away." The benchmark rewards plausible text; the production failure is confident text the image does not support, which the benchmark does not measure.
"Add a system prompt that says do not hallucinate." The model does not know when it hallucinates; a prompt does not create grounding, and only a measurement and a review route reduce the harm.
"Block every answer with a low image-text similarity." Low similarity with low confidence is often a right answer about a hard image; the signal is high confidence with low similarity.

questions.title: You pretrain an early-fusion model on interleaved text and image codes. The small runs are fine, but the large run's loss spikes and diverges after a while, and the attention scores climb from layer to layer. What is happening, and what did the published recipe change to make such a run converge?
questions.answer: Early-fusion training at scale is unstable because image codes and text tokens share one softmax and one residual stream, and their gradients and norms differ; the attention logits grow with depth until the softmax saturates and the loss blows up. The published recipe at 34B parameters diverged at several checkpoints without three changes: normalization of the query and key projections before the dot product, dropout after every residual addition rather than only after attention and the MLP, and pre-normalization on the residual branch plus an extra normalization on the skip connection of the last block. The training recipe is as much of the contribution as the architecture.
followUps: Level 3: Why does normalizing the queries and keys bound the logits? Expected: the dot product of two normalized vectors is bounded by their scale, so the logits cannot grow without limit as the residual stream grows.

Level 3: Why not lower the learning rate instead? Expected: a lower rate slows the growth but does not remove the mechanism; the norms still drift with depth, and the run pays in steps for a problem that normalization removes.

Level 4: What did the paper report at 34B without the changes? Expected: repeated divergence at several checkpoints, driven by growth of the attention logits, a norm explosion, which the three changes removed.

Level 4: How does the two-loss continuous design trade this problem for another? Expected: it removes the shared softmax over image codes but introduces two losses of different magnitude, where one head can dominate without careful loss weights and schedules.
wrongAnswers: "Early fusion is unstable by nature; use smaller models." The published recipe converged at 34B with the three changes; the instability is a recipe problem.
"Clip the gradients harder." Clipping bounds the update, not the logit growth that causes the saturation; the norms keep drifting under a clip.

"Use post-normalization everywhere; it is more stable." The recipe kept pre-normalization on the residual branch and added normalization where the norms grew: the queries, the keys, and the skip of the last block.

questions.title: You fine-tune a model built like Flamingo, with a gated cross-attention block after every few layers of a frozen language model, on a small captioning dataset. Captions improve, but text-only quality degrades: the model rambles on plain prompts and loses facts it knew. What is the likely cause, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: The gates opened too wide too fast. Each gated layer adds the hyperbolic tangent of a learned scalar times the cross-attention output to the residual stream; at zero the layer is a no-op and the model is the pretrained text model. A high learning rate on the gates, or no regularization, lets visual noise flood the residual stream even when the prompt has no image. Confirm it by reading the gate values per layer against the base and by running a text-only eval with the gates forced to zero; fix it with a lower rate or a schedule on the gates, a text-only data mix, and a check that the layers add nothing when no image is present.
followUps: Level 3: What does the residual connection buy once the gate is open? Expected: the text representation is never overwritten, only added to; even a fully open gate leaves the text path intact, which is why the fix is the schedule and not a redesign.

Level 3: How would you spot the same damage in a model that concatenates image tokens instead? Expected: there is no gate to read; the damage shows as a shift in the language model weights, so compare the text-only eval before and after, and freeze the language model or limit it to adapters.

Level 4: Design a unit test that catches this before training. Expected: build the block with alpha at zero and assert that the output equals the block output exactly for a text-only input, then set a large alpha and assert that a text-only input with an empty mask still equals the block output.

Level 4: How do you decide how many gated layers to keep? Expected: ablate the insertion frequency against caption quality and text-only quality on one eval; every fourth block is the reference, and fewer layers mean fewer places for noise to enter.
wrongAnswers: "The captioning data is too small; add more images." More caption data with no text-only prompts pushes the gates further the same way; the fix is the gate schedule and the data mix.
"Unfreeze the language model so that it can adapt to the visual input." That trades a schedule problem for catastrophic forgetting of the text model, which the frozen design exists to prevent.

"Replace gated cross-attention with the simpler concatenation design." The symptom is a schedule problem; the gate is the mechanism that protects the text model, and the simpler design has no such protection.

questions.title: You can spend your data budget on one of two things: have a strong proprietary model write captions for two million images, or pay people to describe seven hundred thousand images in detail by speaking for a minute or more about each one. Which do you choose for a new vision-language model, and what is the evidence?
questions.answer: Pay the people. The reference result is a model trained on 712K densely captioned images and no distilled captions that beat a much larger model on 11 of 11 benchmarks. Dense human captions carry 5 to 10 times the information of a short web caption and stay grounded in the image, while distilled captions inherit the hallucinations of the model that wrote them; about 12 percent of crawled pairs already describe things that are not in the image. Caption density beats caption quantity, which beats distillation convenience.
followUps: Level 3: Why did the speech-based collection matter? Expected: people say far more in a minute than they type, so the captions are long and specific at a cost that scales.

Level 3: How do you check that a synthetic caption is grounded? Expected: embed the image and the caption with a contrastive checker and flag low similarity, then read a sample; drop or rewrite the tail.

Level 4: How would you prove to a skeptic that the gain is data and not model size? Expected: the reference comparison beat a larger model; replicate at one size with two data mixes and the same encoder, connector and schedule.

Level 4: Where in the three-stage pipeline do dense captions pay most? Expected: alignment and the first instruction stage, where the projector and the language model learn what an image contains; task-specific data pays in the last stage.
wrongAnswers: "Two million captions beat seven hundred thousand; more data wins." The reference result beat a larger model with fewer, denser, grounded captions; volume of thin or hallucinated captions is no substitute.
"The strong model's captions are better than what annotators write." They are longer than web captions but not grounded; the model describes what it expects, and the student learns the same habit.
"Caption quality only matters for captioning tasks." The reference model gained on every benchmark, reasoning and reading included, because the alignment stage learned more about each image.

questions.title: Your team needs one open model for answering questions about images, text-to-image generation and inpainting, with a usable generation latency. One candidate generates images one code at a time; another denoises continuous patches; a third stays with discrete codes and fills them in parallel over a few passes. Compare the three on passes, training complexity and what comes for free.
questions.answer: Next-token generation over codes needs one pass per code, 1024 to 4096 passes per image, with one simple loss. Continuous diffusion in a shared transformer needs about 20 passes, but it trains two losses on different scales. Masked discrete decoding keeps codes and one cross-entropy loss, predicts all masked positions at once and commits the most confident ones each pass, so an image takes about 16 passes; inpainting is free, because the training objective is to fill masked codes from the rest. For a product that wants all three tasks in one open model at a usable latency, the masked discrete design is the fit, and the continuous design is the pick when fidelity is paramount.
followUps: Level 3: Why can the model not unmask everything in one pass? Expected: each masked position is predicted from a marginal that ignores the others, so the sampled codes do not agree; committing the confident ones first gives the rest conditioning.
Level 3: Why does a cosine schedule beat a linear one? Expected: it spends more steps at the mid-range ratios where each prediction is most informative, while a linear schedule plateaus earlier.

Level 4: Where does the per-step cost differ between masked discrete and continuous diffusion? Expected: both are full transformer passes, but the discrete head emits logits over the codebook while the continuous head regresses a velocity for every patch; the discrete pass is cheaper per step.

Level 4: What would make you give up the one-model simplicity for a specialist? Expected: a fidelity requirement above the tokenizer ceiling, or a latency budget that even sixteen full passes cannot meet, where a dedicated continuous generator wins.
wrongAnswers: "Masked decoding is diffusion, so it needs a noise schedule." It is discrete: positions are masked, not noised, and the schedule sets how many codes to commit per pass.
"Next-token generation is the fastest because each pass is small." Each pass is a full transformer pass over the sequence, and there are thousands of them per image.
"Inpainting needs a separate model." The masked objective is inpainting; masking a region at inference is the task the model trained on.

questions.title: You lead a small team training an open vision-language model. The first run lands well below the open-weight models of its size on a general benchmark and on a document-reading benchmark. You can afford three more full runs. Which three changes do you make, in what order, and what do you expect each to move?
questions.answer: Order the runs by the variance each axis explains. First, the resolution schedule and the token count: ramp from a low resolution to a high one and add image splitting for the document benchmark, where moving from 448 to 980 pixels added 3 to 5 points in the ablations. Second, the encoder: swap the common contrastive encoder for the stronger one, which added 3 or more points on the general benchmark, and concatenate a self-supervised encoder if grounding matters. Third, the data: replace distilled synthetic captions with dense human-written ones, which beat the distilled set on every benchmark in the reference comparison; leave the connector alone, because at a fixed token count it moves scores by about a point.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the document benchmark respond to resolution and the general one less? Expected: reading needs pixels per character; general questions need semantics that the encoder already carries at a low resolution.
Level 3: What does a resolution ramp buy over a flat high resolution? Expected: faster alignment early and a higher end point; the ablations show that flat schedules plateau at medium accuracy.

Level 4: You cannot get human captions in time. What is the next best data move? Expected: filter the distilled captions for grounding against the image with a contrastive checker and drop the ungrounded tail; density matters, but ungrounded density teaches hallucination.

Level 4: If a fourth run appears, is it the connector or the language model? Expected: the language model, if memory allows a larger one; it lifts reasoning by points, where the connector moves a fraction of one.
wrongAnswers: "Start with the connector; it is the cheapest to retrain." Cheap and useless: at a fixed token count it moves scores by about a point in every controlled study.
"Generate more captions with a stronger proprietary model." Distilled captions inherit hallucinations; the reference comparison shows dense human captions beating distillation across the board.
"Train longer at the same settings." The ablations put the gap in resolution, encoder and data, not in steps; more steps at a flat low resolution plateau.

questions.title: In the unified-generation family, the quality of a generated image is said to be capped by the tokenizer, not by the transformer. Explain why, show what moved the cap between two generations of models, and say which design avoids the cap entirely and at what cost.
questions.answer: A discrete image tokenizer is lossy: the decoder can only render what the codes carry, so the best image the model can ever produce is the tokenizer's own reconstruction of a real image. The first shared-vocabulary model used 1024 codes per 512 by 512 image from a codebook of 8192 and reconstructed at about 26 to 28 dB; the next generation used four times the codes, 4096, and a codebook four times larger, 32768, and reached 30.5 dB, close to the 32 dB of continuous latent diffusion. The design that avoids the cap keeps image patches continuous and trains a diffusion loss on them next to the text loss in one transformer; it drops the quantizer and gains fidelity, and pays with two losses on different scales to balance and a sampling loop at generation time.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the reconstruction score of the tokenizer the right number to read before you train the transformer? Expected: it is the ceiling; no amount of transformer scale lifts a generated image above what the decoder can render from the codes.

Level 3: What else besides the codebook and the code count lifts a tokenizer? Expected: the quantizer design; the newer models use an inverse-bottleneck quantizer family that uses the larger codebook well, where a naive larger codebook leaves codes unused.

Level 4: How does the attention mask differ in the continuous design? Expected: causal over text tokens, bidirectional among the patches of one image, text attends to images that closed before it, and image patches attend to the preceding text; a block-triangular mask.

Level 4: Which side of this trade-off does the masked discrete design sit on? Expected: discrete, with the tokenizer ceiling, but with parallel decoding in a few passes; it trades the fidelity of continuous diffusion for simpler training and fast sampling.
wrongAnswers: "Scale the transformer and the images get sharper." The transformer predicts codes; sharpness beyond the tokenizer's reconstruction does not exist in the codes to predict.

"A bigger codebook is enough." The code count sets the spatial detail and the codebook sets the value detail; the newer tokenizer raised both, and the quantizer design decides whether a large codebook is used.

"Continuous patches are strictly better, so discrete codes are obsolete." Continuous patches cost two losses to balance and a denoising loop per image; the discrete family keeps one loss and one decoder for every modality, which is why both survive.

questions.title: Design a vision-language model for an on-device mobile assistant that reads the phone screen and taps, types and scrolls. Keep the language model at about 2B parameters. Choose the encoder, the bridge, the resolution plan and the data mix, justify each choice with the ablation evidence, and name the capability you would guard against over-promising.
questions.answer: Encoder: the stronger contrastive encoder at native resolution, with a self-supervised encoder's features concatenated for a dense spatial signal, because the encoder explains about 20 percent of the variance and self-supervised features lead vision-centric tests. Bridge: a two-layer MLP, since the connector explains about 5 percent, with features from several encoder depths stacked so that fine position reaches the language model. Resolution: a ramp from low to high, with dynamic resolution up to about 1280 pixels on the long side, because screens are text-dense and reading gains most from pixels. Data: dense human descriptions of screens plus grounded action traces, not distilled captions; and guard the promise on spatial relations, where general models score 50 to 60 percent and the agent must hit the right element every time.
followUps: Level 3: Why stack shallow and deep encoder layers for an agent and not for a captioner? Expected: a captioner needs semantics; an agent needs where exactly, which the shallow layers carry and the last layer blurs.

Level 4: The language model is fixed at 2B. Which axis do you lean on hardest, and what is its limit? Expected: resolution and token count, because screens are text-dense; the limit is the latency per step on the device, which the token count sets.

Level 4: How do you make the agent robust to being wrong about an element? Expected: a read-back after each action that compares the new screen with the expected state, and a stop when they do not match; the model's own confidence is not a safe signal.

Level 4: What does the ablation evidence not tell you about this design? Expected: it comes from general benchmarks on datacenter GPUs; the device latency, the UI domain and the action format need your own ablation, one axis per run.
wrongAnswers: "Use a query-based bridge to save tokens on the device." It caps the tokens at a count too low for dense screen text, and the ablations put 64 tokens as too few for reading; spend tokens here and save elsewhere.

"Generate the screen descriptions with a strong proprietary model." Distilled descriptions inherit hallucinations, and an agent that taps a hallucinated element fails; dense human descriptions won the reference comparison.

"A 2B model with a great encoder matches a 70B agent." The language model sets the reasoning ceiling; frame the task as perception plus short actions and verify each step, instead of promising long reasoning.

questions.title: A design tool wants to ship, with open weights it can host, one model that answers questions about a user's image, edits a region of it on request, and generates a new image from text. The latency per image must stay in seconds, not minutes. Lay out the families you would consider, pick one, and state the test that would make you change the pick.
questions.answer: Three open families cover understanding and generation in one model: next-token prediction over discrete codes, which does everything with one loss but spends one pass per code and minutes per image; continuous patches with a diffusion loss next to the text loss, which gives the best fidelity in about 20 passes but trains two losses; and masked discrete decoding, which keeps one loss, fills an image in about 16 passes, and gets region editing free from its masking objective. For a tool that needs editing and a seconds-level latency with open weights, start with the masked discrete family. Change the pick if a fidelity eval on your own prompts shows the quantizer ceiling hurting, or if the latency budget cannot afford sixteen full passes; the continuous two-loss family then takes over, with editing done through conditioned denoising of the region.
followUps: Level 3: Which of the three tasks does the masked objective give for free, and why? Expected: region editing; training predicts masked codes from the rest, which is what an edit asks for.

Level 4: How do you do a region edit in the continuous design? Expected: keep the patches outside the region fixed across the denoising steps and denoise only the region, conditioned on the text and the context; it works, but it is a sampler you write, not a training objective.

Level 4: Why does the pass count become a serving parameter in the masked design? Expected: more passes commit fewer codes each and raise quality, fewer passes cut latency; the schedule is set at inference, so the product can trade them per request.

Level 4: What single measurement tells you that the quantizer is the bottleneck? Expected: the tokenizer's reconstruction of your real images; if the reconstruction already loses the detail your users care about, no generator on those codes can recover it.
wrongAnswers: "Ship the next-token model; one loss, one stack, no compromise." Minutes per image at the reference decode rate breaks the latency requirement, and a region edit regenerates codes in sequence.
"Fidelity decides, so take the continuous design." Fidelity is one requirement; editing and operational simplicity favor the masked design until an eval shows the ceiling hurting.
"Pick the model with the best benchmark score." The product needs three tasks, an edit path and a latency budget; a benchmark covers one of those at best.

questions.title: Explain how a single transformer can train the text objective of next-token prediction together with a denoising loss on images in one gradient step. Cover the input representation, the attention mask, how the loss is routed per position, and the balance problem that follows. Then say what a sibling architecture changed.
questions.answer: Text enters as discrete tokens through the embedding table; images enter as continuous 16 by 16 pixel patches through a linear projection, bracketed by image start and end tags. One forward pass runs over the mixed sequence, and the loss is picked per position: cross-entropy on the vocabulary head for text positions, and a flow-matching regression for image patches, which predicts the velocity from a noised patch toward the clean one at a sampled time. The mask is block-triangular, causal over text and bidirectional among the patches of one image, with text attending to images that closed before it and patches attending to the preceding text. Both losses backpropagate through the same weights, so their relative magnitude must be balanced by hand; the sibling architecture keeps the joint attention but gives text and image their own weights in every block.
followUps: Level 3: Why may image patches attend bidirectionally when text may not? Expected: text is generated left to right under teacher forcing, so a token must not see its target; an image is produced as one snapshot, and its patches have no order.

Level 4: How would you set the loss weights? Expected: measure the magnitude and the gradient norm of each loss on a held-out batch, scale them to comparable contributions, and tune from there against a text eval and an image eval together, because one can improve while the other regresses.

Level 4: What does the sampled time t do in the training loss? Expected: it picks how much noise the patch carries, so the model learns the whole path from noise to clean; at generation each step moves along that path.

Level 4: What does the sibling's per-modality weight set cost and buy? Expected: more parameters per block; it buys separate capacity for two very different input statistics and eases the balance, while the joint attention still lets the modalities condition each other.
wrongAnswers: "One transformer can only have one loss." The loss is a function of the outputs per position; routing a different loss to different positions is one summed objective with one backward pass.

"Use a causal mask everywhere for simplicity." Causal attention inside an image hides part of each image from its own patches and hurts generation; the mask must be bidirectional inside an image block.
"The two losses balance themselves because they share the weights." Shared weights are the problem: the larger loss dominates the shared gradient until you weight them.

topics.title: Agents
topics.about: The agent loop, tools, scope contracts, verification gates and why agents fail.

questions.title: How does an autonomous ReAct agent loop work and how do you prevent runaway execution?
questions.answer: A ReAct agent repeats a cycle of thought, action, and observation. The model reasons about what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, and continues until it can answer. Tools are defined with clear schemas, and their calls are parsed and validated before they run. To prevent runaway loops, enforce a maximum number of steps, plus time and cost budgets. Also detect repeated identical calls and break the cycle, then stop gracefully or hand off to a person.
keyPoints: ReAct cycles through thought, action and observation.
Validate tool calls against clear schemas.
Enforce step, time and cost budgets.
Detect repeated calls and stop or hand off gracefully.

questions.title: When should you build a multi-agent system versus a single agent with multiple tools?
questions.answer: Start with one agent, and add more only when you have a real need. Multi-agent designs help when one agent has too many tools to choose from accurately, or when unrelated context pollutes its prompt. A common pattern is a supervisor that routes work to specialised agents, each with a small tool set and focused context. The cost is that every extra agent adds model calls, latency, and new ways to fail, so measure whether quality improves enough to justify it.
keyPoints: Start with a single agent.
Split agents when tool choice or unrelated context becomes a problem.
Use a supervisor with focused contexts and tool sets.
Measure quality gains against extra latency, cost and failure modes.

questions.title: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a single LLM call?
questions.answer: A single LLM call takes input, produces output, and stops. An agent wraps the model in a loop where it can decide to call a tool, observe the result, and decide what to do next — potentially many times — before producing a final answer.
keyPoints: A single model call produces output and stops.
An agent wraps the model in a decision loop.
The loop can call tools and observe results.
Several iterations can precede the final answer.

questions.title: With function calling, who actually executes the function?
questions.answer: The model recognizes when a task needs external information or action and emits a structured request (a function name plus arguments) instead of a plain-text answer; the calling application actually executes it and feeds the result back into context.
options: Your application. The model only outputs the function's name and arguments.
The model runs it inside the API.
The provider runs it in a sandbox.
The user approves and runs it.
keyPoints: The model identifies the need for external information or action.
It emits a structured function request.
The request includes a function name and arguments.
The application executes the call and returns the result to context.

questions.title: What is the ReAct pattern?
questions.answer: Interleaving reasoning steps with actions and observations — think, act (call a tool), observe the result, think again — the foundational loop behind most tool-using agents.
keyPoints: ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions.
An action can call a tool.
The model observes the tool result.
The observation informs the next reasoning step.

questions.title: A task has twenty steps whose order is clear upfront, and each model call is expensive. ReAct, or plan-and-execute?
questions.answer: Produce a full multi-step plan upfront, then execute the steps (optionally re-planning if one fails), rather than deciding just the next single action at each turn like ReAct does. Better for tasks where seeing the whole shape of the problem upfront produces a more coherent plan than reasoning step-by-step in isolation.
options: Neither. Use a single prompt.
Either. They cost the same.
ReAct: decide each step after seeing the last result.
Plan-and-execute: plan once, then run the steps, replanning only if one fails.
keyPoints: Plan-and-execute produces a complete plan upfront.
Execute the planned steps after planning.
Replan when a step fails if supported.
Use upfront planning when seeing the whole task improves coherence.

questions.title: What is reflection / self-critique in an agent?
questions.answer: Having the model (or a separate call) evaluate its own prior output against the task and revise it before finalizing — a real accuracy lever for tasks where a first pass is often subtly wrong in a findable way.
keyPoints: Reflection evaluates a prior model output.
The same model or another call can perform the evaluation.
Check the draft against the task.
Revise detectable errors before finalizing.

questions.title: What's the difference between single-agent and multi-agent systems?
questions.answer: A single agent handles the whole task itself, with one growing context. Multi-agent systems split work across several agents (often with their own clean context windows), trading added coordination complexity for parallelism and per-subtask focus.
keyPoints: A single agent handles the whole task in one context.
Multiple agents split the work.
Separate contexts improve per-subtask focus.
Coordination complexity buys parallelism and focus.

questions.title: You're building a multi-agent system that has to be easy to debug when something goes wrong. Which topology?
questions.answer: Hierarchical (one orchestrator delegates to sub-agents and combines results — easiest to debug), peer-to-peer (agents talk directly as equals — more flexible, harder to guarantee convergence), and blackboard (agents read/write shared state, never talking directly — useful when the set of contributors isn't fixed in advance).
options: Peer-to-peer.
Blackboard.
A swarm where every agent can message every other.
Hierarchical: one orchestrator delegates and combines.
keyPoints: Hierarchical orchestration delegates and combines results.
Peer agents communicate directly as equals.
Blackboard agents communicate through shared state.
Topology trades debugging ease against flexibility and convergence.

questions.title: What is the supervisor / routing pattern?
questions.answer: A dynamic version of hierarchical delegation: a supervisor agent loops, re-routing between sub-agents based on intermediate results, instead of committing to one fixed delegation plan upfront like a static orchestrator would.
keyPoints: A supervisor performs dynamic hierarchical delegation.
It loops rather than following one fixed plan.
Intermediate results guide rerouting.
Sub-agents receive work as the supervisor adapts.

questions.title: Five AI apps each need the same 20 tools. Without a shared protocol, each app-tool pair needs its own integration. How many is that?
questions.answer:
5 × 20 = 100 separate integrations. With MCP, each app implements a client once and each tool a server once: 5 + 20 = 25. That N × M to N + M change is the problem MCP solves.

A standardized protocol for connecting an AI application to external tools/data sources, so one client implementation works against any MCP-compatible server instead of every app needing bespoke integration code per tool.
keyPoints: Five apps and twenty tools require 100 bespoke integrations.
MCP reduces that example to 25 implementations.
Each app implements a client once.
Each tool implements a compatible server once.

questions.title: What are the agent memory types?
questions.answer: Short-term: whatever fits in the current context window (conversation so far, tool results). Long-term: information persisted outside context, across sessions, typically an external store the agent retrieves from — turning memory into a retrieval problem.
keyPoints: Short-term memory lives in the current context.
Conversation and tool results consume short-term memory.
Long-term memory persists outside context across sessions.
Retrieve long-term information from an external store.

questions.title: What is context engineering, and how is it different from prompt engineering?
questions.answer: Prompt engineering is about writing and organizing instructions. Context engineering is the broader discipline of managing an agent's *entire* context state across a multi-turn task — conversation history, tool results, retrieved documents, memory, all of it — not just the instructions.
keyPoints: Prompt engineering organizes instructions.
Context engineering manages the entire multi-turn context.
Manage conversation history and tool results.
Include retrieved documents and memory in context management.

questions.title: A fact at the very start of a 120k-token context is recalled reliably, but the same fact in the middle often isn't. What's that called?
questions.answer: As the number of tokens in context grows, a model's ability to accurately recall and use any specific piece of it degrades — not because of position (that's "lost in the middle" specifically), but because of sheer token volume spreading attention thinner.
options: Lost in the middle: recall depends on where the fact sits.
Hallucination.
Catastrophic forgetting.
Context rot.
keyPoints: Recall can degrade as context token volume grows.
Token volume spreads attention more thinly.
Volume-related degradation differs from positional effects.
Lost in the middle names the positional problem specifically.

questions.title: Your agent's context fills with the full working traces of research sub-tasks, and later steps get worse. What's the standard fix?
questions.answer: A specialized sub-agent handles a focused sub-task in its own clean context, then returns only a condensed summary (often 1,000–2,000 tokens) to the parent — keeping the parent's context from filling up with the sub-agent's entire working trace.
options: Raise the temperature.
Delete the oldest messages.
Switch to a model with a longer context.
Run each sub-task in a sub-agent with its own context, and return only a short summary to the parent.
keyPoints: Give a specialist a focused subtask.
Let the sub-agent work in a clean context.
Return a condensed summary to the parent.
Keep the full working trace out of parent context.

questions.title: How do you prevent an agentic RAG loop from running forever (or effectively forever, on your bill)?
questions.answer: Combine four stopping conditions rather than relying on just one: a hard iteration cap as the absolute last resort (e.g. max 6 loops); a semantic-drift check that flags when the agent starts issuing near-duplicate retrieval queries (high cosine similarity to a prior query in the same loop signals it's spinning); a cheap sufficiency check, where a small model reads the accumulated context and outputs a simple yes/no on whether it's enough to answer; and a token/cost budget guard that stops before the context window or a spend limit is hit. In practice the sufficiency check fires most often in healthy operation — the hard cap and budget guard are safety nets for genuine edge cases, not the primary mechanism.
options: Several stopping rules together: a sufficiency check, a near-duplicate-query check, a token budget, and a hard iteration cap.
Tell the model to stop when it's done.
A wall-clock timeout only.
A hard cap of 50 iterations.
keyPoints: Set a hard iteration cap.
Detect near-duplicate retrieval queries as semantic drift.
Use a cheap context-sufficiency check.
Enforce token and cost budgets as safety guards.

questions.title: ReAct vs. Plan-and-Execute for agentic RAG — when do you reach for each?
questions.answer: ReAct interleaves reasoning and retrieval in a serial loop, where each observation informs the next step — highly adaptive, since it can change approach mid-loop, but every hop adds latency because steps can't run in parallel. Plan-and-Execute separates planning from execution: one call produces a full task list up front, then everything in it runs in parallel — faster when the task decomposes predictably, but brittle, since there's no replanning if the upfront plan turns out to be wrong partway through. Use ReAct when the query's scope is genuinely unknown and you need adaptive exploration; use Plan-and-Execute when the decomposition is predictable and latency matters more than adaptivity.
keyPoints: ReAct adapts each step using previous observations.
Serial ReAct hops add latency.
Plan-and-execute runs a predictable task decomposition in parallel.
Choose adaptivity or latency according to task uncertainty.

questions.title: What does a Reflection/Correction agent actually catch that a single-pass RAG system misses?
questions.answer: It re-reads the retrieved chunk it just cited alongside the model's own draft answer and checks whether the chunk *actually* supports the specific claim being made — not just whether some chunk was retrieved at all, but whether this particular sentence is traceable to this particular chunk's text. A single-pass system has no mechanism to catch the case where a plausible-sounding number or fact simply wasn't in the retrieved context at all; a reflection agent flags that case and can trigger a more targeted re-retrieval before the draft ever reaches the user.
keyPoints: Compare the draft claim with the chunk it cites.
Check support for the specific sentence, not just retrieval presence.
Flag plausible facts absent from the cited context.
Trigger targeted retrieval before showing an unsupported draft.

questions.title: How do you make an agentic RAG system observable in production, given that failures can be two or three hops removed from the wrong final answer?
questions.answer: Instrument three things specifically: per-iteration traces (log each step's query, which tool was called, a summary of the result, and tokens used, with an iteration index, so you can replay the whole chain); the *terminal reason* the loop stopped (reached a real answer, hit the iteration cap, tripped the drift check, or exhausted budget — distinguishing "answered correctly" from "gave up" is not optional for debugging); and user-visible citations tracing which retrieved passages actually contributed to the final answer. Without per-iteration traces specifically, debugging a multi-hop agent is close to impossible, because the root cause is routinely several steps upstream of where the wrong answer actually surfaces.
keyPoints: Log each iteration's query, tool, result summary and tokens.
Include iteration indices to replay the chain.
Record the terminal reason, including caps and budget exhaustion.
Expose citations to passages used in the final answer.

questions.title: How do you decide which agent framework to use for a given agentic RAG project?
questions.answer: Match the framework to what's actually hard about the use case, not to popularity — LlamaIndex if the core problem is RAG pipeline quality itself (chunking, indexing, retrieval); LangChain for general-purpose orchestration gluing together many different tool types; LangGraph or CrewAI when the design is genuinely multi-agent with distinct roles that need to converse or loop, and you want explicit, inspectable control over a cyclic execution graph; and for a single-agent, single-source system, consider skipping a framework entirely — a hand-rolled loop against the raw model API has less overhead and is easier to debug than an unnecessary abstraction layer.
keyPoints: Choose frameworks for the use case's actual difficulty.
Use LlamaIndex for RAG pipeline concerns.
Use LangChain for tool orchestration and graph frameworks for cyclic roles.
Consider a raw API loop for a simple single-source agent.

questions.title: Walk through a concrete example of why single-shot RAG fails on a genuinely compound question, and how an agentic version fixes it.
questions.answer: Take "my basement flooded from a burst pipe and my car got water damage, am I covered?" — single-shot RAG embeds the whole compound question once and runs one search, which creates three distinct failure points: if auto and homeowner's policies live in the same index, whichever has denser chunks near that embedding dominates the top-k and the other policy's relevant clause may not make the cut at all; even if both surface, nothing checks that the retrieved "water damage" clause actually addresses *flood* specifically (homeowner's policies typically exclude flood while covering other water damage — a distinction a single pass has no mechanism to check); and there's no re-query if the first pull is thin. An agentic version decomposes into policy-specific subqueries, retrieves each independently, and runs an explicit verification step checking for exactly this kind of nuance before synthesizing a final answer.
keyPoints: One compound-query embedding can favor one policy's chunks.
Retrieved water-damage text may not address flood exclusions.
Decompose into policy-specific searches.
Verify clause-level nuance before synthesizing an answer.

questions.title: How do you design an idempotency layer for agent tool execution to prevent duplicate side effects during retries?
questions.answer: An agent loop can retry a tool invocation if a network call times out or an execution step halts. Without idempotency, retrying an action like creating a database entry or sending a refund produces duplicate mutations. We generate a deterministic idempotency key before dispatching any tool. We construct the key by hashing the session identifier, the agent step index, the tool name, and the canonical JSON-serialized arguments with sorted keys. When a tool call arrives at our execution layer, we check a central key-value store for that key. If the key exists and the status is completed, we return the cached result immediately without re-executing the action. If the key is in progress, subsequent attempts wait; if it does not exist, we record the key, execute the tool, store the result, and set a time-to-live expiration. The trade-off is state management overhead versus mutation safety: storing idempotency keys requires distributed storage, but it prevents costly duplicate side effects during automatic retries.
followUps: How do you handle non-idempotent third-party APIs that do not support client-supplied idempotency keys?
What happens if an agent legitimately needs to execute the same tool twice in different steps of a task?
wrongAnswers: Generating random UUIDs as idempotency keys on every retry attempt, defeating the purpose of deduplication.
Hashing tool arguments without including the step index or session ID, incorrectly blocking repeated calls in later steps.
tradeOffs: Deterministic idempotency keys guarantee exactly-once tool semantics across network retries, but require central lock storage.
Setting key TTLs too short risks duplicate execution on delayed retries; setting them too long consumes unnecessary storage.
keyPoints: Hash session ID, step index, tool name and canonical arguments into an idempotency key.
Return cached results for completed keys.
Wait on in-progress keys and record new executions centrally.
Distributed key storage adds overhead but prevents duplicate side effects.

questions.title: How do you architect a least-privilege permission model for agent tool execution across read, write, and destructive actions?
questions.answer: We architect agent permissions using least-privilege capability tokens rather than granting broad administrative rights. We classify all tools into three distinct risk tiers. Tier 1 consists of read-only operations like searching documents or inspecting metrics, which execute automatically with no mutation risk. Tier 2 covers scoped idempotent mutations, such as drafting an email, writing to a staging database, or updating a ticket. Tier 3 includes destructive or high-impact actions, like deleting infrastructure, modifying production permissions, or transferring funds. When an agent session starts, it receives a scoped security token containing only the permissions required for that specific task. If the agent attempts to invoke a tool outside its granted scopes, the execution layer intercepts and rejects the call before it runs. The trade-off is agent autonomy versus security blast radius: strict permission boundaries restrict what an agent can accomplish without human approval, but they prevent catastrophic unauthorized actions.
followUps: How do you pass user-level permissions into agent tool calls in multi-tenant enterprise environments?
What mechanism should downgrade an agent's permissions if an injection attempt is detected?
wrongAnswers: Relying on system prompts to tell the model not to call dangerous tools, which is easily bypassed via prompt injection.
Granting the agent a global admin API key for all tools, exposing all databases to unintended modification.
tradeOffs: Fine-grained tool scoping bounds security blast radius, but requires maintaining permission registries and token validation logic.
Coarse permissions allow full autonomous problem solving, but expose production systems to destructive agent mistakes.
keyPoints: Use scoped least-privilege capability tokens.
Separate read-only, scoped mutation and high-impact tools into risk tiers.
Reject calls outside granted scopes before execution.
Permission boundaries limit autonomy while reducing unauthorized actions.

questions.title: When an agent determines it needs to invoke a high-impact tool, how do you suspend execution, request human approval, and resume deterministically?
questions.answer: When an agent decides to invoke a high-impact tool, it must not execute the action autonomously. Instead, the runtime suspends execution, serializes the agent state, and alerts a human reviewer. We implement this using a durable execution workflow. When a tool call hits a protected permission boundary, the runtime creates an approval request detailing the tool name, input arguments, and model reasoning. The agent state, including conversation history and tool outputs, is saved to persistent storage, and the execution thread halts cleanly. Once a human reviews the request and submits an approve or reject decision through a dashboard or messaging channel, the workflow engine wakes up, restores the agent state, and injects the human decision as the tool response. The trade-off is decision safety versus latency: human-in-the-loop elevation provides strong governance for irreversible operations, but waiting for human approval pauses the workflow and introduces state staleness if underlying data changes during the delay.
followUps: How do you handle workspace state drift while an approval request is pending for several hours?
What happens if the human reviewer modifies the tool arguments before approving the execution?
wrongAnswers: Holding open an active HTTP connection with a long timeout while waiting for human review, exhausting server connection pools.
Allowing the agent to continue executing downstream actions before the high-impact tool has been approved.
tradeOffs: Durable execution suspension eliminates active thread memory costs while awaiting human input, but requires persistent state serialization.
Human gates provide essential safety for irreversible mutations, but introduce minutes or hours of latency into autonomous workflows.
keyPoints: Suspend execution and persist agent state at a protected tool boundary.
Request approval with tool name, arguments and reasoning.
Restore state and inject the review decision as a tool response.
Approval delays can make underlying state stale.

questions.title: How does content-addressing tool arguments with SHA-256 enable safe result caching and replay across agent runs?
questions.answer: Content-addressed caching caches the results of pure, deterministic tool calls by hashing their inputs. When an agent invokes a tool like calculating an equation or running an exact database query, we serialize the argument payload into canonical JSON with sorted keys and compute its SHA-256 hash. We use the tool name combined with this hash as the cache key in an in-memory store. If the agent calls the same tool with identical arguments later in the session or across sessions, the execution engine returns the cached response in milliseconds without calling external services. Crucially, we mark tools explicitly as cacheable or non-cacheable: mutating tools, random generators, and live real-time feeds must bypass the cache completely. The trade-off is execution speed against cache freshness: content-addressed caching saves latency and API costs on expensive deterministic operations, but caching time-sensitive data can return stale facts if the underlying data source changes.
followUps: Why must non-deterministic tools like live web search or time checks be excluded from content-addressed caching?
How do you invalidate content-addressed tool caches when underlying database schemas update?
wrongAnswers: Caching the output of mutating tools (e.g. create_user or send_email), causing repeated calls to silently skip execution.
Hashing raw JSON strings without canonical key sorting, producing cache misses on semantically identical arguments.
tradeOffs: Content-addressed caching accelerates deterministic tool calls and eliminates duplicate API billing, but requires strict purity guarantees.
Canonical JSON serialization requires sorting keys and formatting floats uniformly to prevent hash mismatches.
keyPoints: Hash canonical JSON arguments with the tool name for deterministic tool caching.
Return cached results for identical inputs.
Bypass caching for mutations, randomness and live feeds.
Caching saves latency and cost but risks stale time-sensitive data.

questions.title: Where should policy enforcement sit in an agent runtime: in system prompt instructions, application middleware, or kernel-level tool sandboxes?
questions.answer: Policy enforcement must never rely on system prompt instructions alone. Prompt guidelines are advisory: adversarial user inputs, prompt injections, and hallucinated model outputs easily bypass instructions like 'never delete files'. Robust policy enforcement sits in application middleware and kernel-level sandboxes as defense in depth. First, application middleware intercepts the structured tool call after model generation but before execution. It validates arguments against a strict JSON schema, checks user authentication tokens, and verifies organizational rate limits. Second, if the tool requires executing code or filesystem operations, execution happens inside a sandboxed container with restricted Linux namespaces, read-only root filesystems, and strict network egress allowlists. The trade-off is system latency versus security guarantees: running pre-execution policy checks adds a few milliseconds to each tool step, but it guarantees that security policies cannot be bypassed by prompt injection.
followUps: How do you handle dynamic policy rules that depend on the runtime state of the enterprise database?
Why is prompt engineering considered an advisory guard rather than an enforcement mechanism?
wrongAnswers: Relying solely on system prompt instructions for security boundaries, which can be bypassed by indirect prompt injection.
Running untrusted code directly in the host agent runtime without OS-level namespace and filesystem isolation.
tradeOffs: Deterministic middleware policy checks guarantee enforcement independently of prompt injection, but add slight dispatch overhead.
Kernel-level sandboxing provides bulletproof operating system isolation, but adds container initialization latency.
keyPoints: Enforce policy after tool generation and before execution.
Validate schemas, authentication and rate limits in middleware.
Sandbox code and filesystem tools with restricted namespaces and egress.
System prompt instructions alone cannot enforce security.

questions.title: An agent executes three tools in sequence and fails on the third. How do you implement compensating transactions or a saga pattern to avoid leaving systems in a half-mutated state?
questions.answer: When an agent executes multiple sequential tools and fails midway, standard database transactions cannot roll back external API calls. We implement the saga pattern with compensating transactions. For every mutating tool in a sequence, we register a corresponding undo action. For example, if Step 1 books a flight and Step 2 reserves a hotel, but Step 3 fails to book the rental car, the runtime halts forward execution and executes compensating actions in reverse order: cancelling the hotel reservation and refunding the flight. If a compensating action fails, the runtime logs the error, marks the transaction as requiring manual intervention, and alerts an operator. The trade-off is recovery guarantees versus external side effects: compensating actions work well for reversible operations like database updates or booking reservations, but operations like sending an email or charging a payment card cannot be silently undone and require human reconciliation.
followUps: How do you handle a failure inside a compensating transaction itself?
What state must be preserved in the agent trace to allow resuming an interrupted saga?
wrongAnswers: Assuming distributed microservice tool calls can participate in a traditional ACID two-phase commit database transaction.
Ignoring tool failures and allowing the agent to proceed to subsequent steps after a mutation failed.
tradeOffs: The saga pattern provides robust distributed consistency across heterogeneous APIs, but requires implementing custom undo logic per tool.
Compensating actions cannot reverse real-world side effects like sent emails or SMS messages, requiring human escalation.
keyPoints: Register a compensating action for each mutating tool.
Stop forward execution on failure and compensate in reverse order.
Alert an operator if compensation fails.
Irreversible side effects require human reconciliation.

questions.title: An agent is granted permission to inspect and edit files in a workspace. How do you sandbox the execution environment to prevent path traversal and unauthorized exfiltration?
questions.answer: When an agent can view and edit files in a workspace, we must prevent it from traversing the directory tree to access sensitive host files like credentials or system binaries. We isolate the execution environment using containerized sandboxes with separate Linux mount and user namespaces. Inside the sandbox, the agent is restricted to an isolated workspace directory. In code, every file path requested by the agent is resolved to its canonical absolute path using realpath, and we verify that the resolved path starts with the workspace root, blocking path traversal tricks like dot-dot-slash or symlink redirections. We also enforce read-only mounts on system directories and block outbound internet access except for pre-approved package repositories to prevent data exfiltration. The trade-off is startup overhead versus isolation: lightweight process wrappers start fast but share kernel attack surfaces, while container sandboxes provide strong isolation at the expense of a brief startup delay.
followUps: How do you prevent an agent from exhausting disk space or memory inside a shared multi-tenant sandbox?
Why is checking '..' with string matching insufficient without calling realpath()?
wrongAnswers: Using simple substring checks like 'if .. not in path', which fails to catch symlinks pointing outside the workspace root.
Running the agent code execution tool under the host root user with read/write access to the host filesystem.
tradeOffs: Linux container sandboxing provides robust OS isolation, but adds startup and tear-down latency per agent session.
Restricting outbound network egress prevents data exfiltration, but blocks tools that require dynamic web access.
keyPoints: Isolate workspace access with mount and user namespaces.
Canonicalize requested paths and verify workspace containment.
Restrict system mounts and outbound network access.
Containers add startup overhead compared with lightweight process wrappers.

questions.title: How do you pass authentication credentials to agent-invoked tools without exposing long-lived API secrets to the LLM context window?
questions.answer: Long-lived API credentials, tokens, and database passwords must never be placed inside the prompt or model context window. If secrets appear in context, they can be leaked through prompt injection attacks or echoed in user responses. Instead, we use an execution proxy backed by a secure credential vault. The LLM only sees abstract tool definitions and parameters, such as a customer identifier or repository name. When the agent dispatches a tool call, the request routes to our backend execution proxy. The proxy verifies the agent session and user permissions, fetches short-lived credentials from the vault, injects the authentication headers into the outgoing HTTP request, and forwards the call to the external service. The model only receives the sanitized data response. The trade-off is architectural complexity: running an authenticated credential proxy introduces an additional network hop, but it ensures secret keys never enter the prompt.
followUps: How do you audit which specific user authorized an agent tool call that executed through the credential proxy?
What happens if a tool output accidentally includes sensitive tokens in its response payload?
wrongAnswers: Injecting AWS access keys or bearer tokens directly into the system prompt for the model to pass as tool parameters.
Storing API keys in plain text environment variables inside an unisolated agent sandbox.
tradeOffs: Proxy credential injection guarantees secrets never enter prompt context or model logs, but requires maintaining an authenticated gateway.
Short-lived scoped tokens bound blast radius if compromised, but require token refresh machinery.
keyPoints: Keep credentials out of prompts and model context.
Route tools through a proxy that checks session permissions.
Inject short-lived vault credentials into outgoing requests.
Return sanitized responses to the model despite the extra network hop.

questions.title: How do you set deterministic recursion depth and step count limits in an autonomous agent loop, and how should it fail?
questions.answer: Autonomous agents can get caught in infinite reasoning loops if a tool returns unexpected output or the model fails to satisfy its goal. To prevent runaway execution and unbounded cost, we enforce deterministic recursion depth and step count limits in the agent runtime. We initialize a step counter when the session begins. Every forward model call and tool execution increments the counter. If the step count reaches a maximum threshold, typically 15 to 25 steps depending on task complexity, the loop halts immediately. Rather than throwing an unhandled exception, the runtime catches the limit, constructs a structured failure payload explaining that the step budget was exhausted, and asks the model to summarize its partial progress. The trade-off is false-positive termination versus cost runaway: setting step limits too tightly aborts complex multi-step tasks prematurely, while setting them too high risks runaway billing on stuck agents.
followUps: How do you determine the optimal maximum step count for different categories of agent tasks?
How should an agent preserve its work if the user wants to grant additional steps upon hitting the limit?
wrongAnswers: Using a while True loop with no step counter or timeout, allowing stuck agents to loop until API rate limits or budget exhaustion.
Throwing an uncaught fatal exception when the limit is hit, discarding all intermediate reasoning and tool results.
tradeOffs: Hard step limits provide an absolute safety ceiling against runaway spend, but can terminate complex valid tasks before completion.
Graceful degradation with partial progress reporting gives users actionable summaries rather than abrupt system crashes.
keyPoints: Enforce deterministic step and recursion limits in the runtime.
Increment the counter for model calls and tool executions.
Halt at the limit and return a structured partial-progress summary.
Tight limits may terminate valid complex tasks prematurely.

questions.title: An agent repeatedly queries a search tool with minor wording changes without making progress. How do you detect and break semantic execution loops?
questions.answer: An agent can get stuck repeating the same failed action with minor phrasing variations, such as slightly tweaking a search query without learning from previous misses. We detect and break these loops using state hashing and semantic distance tracking. For exact loops, we maintain a rolling history of tool calls and hash the tool name alongside its arguments. If the identical hash appears more than twice in recent history, an exact loop is detected. For semantic loops where the agent rephrases arguments, we embed recent inputs and measure cosine similarity; if consecutive queries have near-identical semantic embeddings without new information, we flag a semantic cycle. When a loop is detected, we intercept execution and inject a system intervention message prompting the agent to reflect on its failure or try an alternate strategy. If the loop persists, the runtime terminates the task. The trade-off is exploratory flexibility versus loop prevention: aggressive cycle detection can interrupt legitimate iterative refinement, so detection thresholds must require multiple consecutive repetitions.
followUps: What embedding similarity threshold reliably separates repetitive loops from legitimate iterative query refinement?
How do you detect cyclical multi-tool loops (e.g. Tool A -> Tool B -> Tool A -> Tool B)?
wrongAnswers: Checking only exact argument string equality, which misses queries that differ by a single synonym or punctuation mark.
Terminating the agent on the first detected similarity without providing a corrective prompt to steer the model.
tradeOffs: Semantic similarity tracking catches subtle paraphrased loops that bypass exact string hashing, but requires embedding compute per step.
Intervention prompts guide models to recover autonomously, but consume prompt tokens and can fail if the model lacks alternate tools.
keyPoints: Hash tool names and arguments to detect repeated exact calls.
Use embedding similarity to detect rephrased queries without new information.
Intervene with an alternate-strategy instruction and terminate persistent loops.
Require repeated cycles to avoid interrupting legitimate refinement.

questions.title: How do you implement execution budget limits that halt an agent when cumulative token spend or step costs exceed thresholds?
questions.answer: To prevent an agent from burning through financial budgets during long-running tasks, we enforce a strict execution budget guard in the runtime. We assign each session a maximum spending cap in dollars and tokens. Before dispatching any model call, the runtime estimates the cost of the input context; after the call, it tallies the exact prompt and completion tokens returned in the provider usage metadata and calculates cumulative spend. If the running total crosses a warning threshold, such as 80% of budget, the runtime can switch from a frontier model to a smaller, cheaper model for remaining steps. If cumulative spend reaches 100%, the execution engine immediately intercepts the loop, prevents further API calls, and returns a structured response summarizing the work completed and reporting that the budget limit was reached. The trade-off is task completion versus financial predictability: hard budget cutoffs prevent unexpected cloud bills, but complex tasks that genuinely need more compute will halt unfinished unless dynamic budget approvals are supported.
followUps: How do you calculate real-time cost when an agent uses multiple different model providers with differing pricing tiers?
What mechanism allows a user to approve a budget extension dynamically in an interactive session?
wrongAnswers: Relying solely on post-hoc billing alerts from cloud providers, which report spend hours after an agent has burned the budget.
Tracking only request counts without counting token usage, failing to catch prompts with massive context windows.
tradeOffs: Strict budget guards prevent catastrophic billing spikes from runaway loops, but can truncate valid high-value complex tasks.
Dynamic model downgrading (falling back to cheaper models) stretches budgets, but risks reasoning quality degradation.
keyPoints: Assign session spending caps in dollars and tokens.
Estimate input cost before calls and tally provider usage afterward.
Switch to a cheaper model near the warning threshold.
Block further calls at the cap and summarize completed work.

questions.title: When an external tool called by an agent hangs or encounters high latency, how do you enforce non-blocking timeouts and handle cancellation?
questions.answer: When an agent calls an external API or executes code that hangs indefinitely, the agent thread can block forever, holding memory and stalling the user. We wrap every tool execution in an asynchronous non-blocking timeout using asyncio.wait_for or equivalent timer guards. We set distinct timeouts based on tool type: fast API lookups time out in a few seconds, while heavy code execution or data processing jobs are allocated longer windows. If the timer expires before the tool finishes, the runtime cancels the future, sends a termination signal to the underlying subprocess or closes the HTTP connection, and returns a structured timeout error to the agent context. This lets the agent decide whether to retry with different parameters, try a fallback tool, or report an error. The trade-off is premature timeout versus hanging resources: setting timeouts too aggressively cancels long-running valid operations, but letting tools hang degrades system responsiveness and exhausts worker threads.
followUps: How do you ensure a cancelled subprocess actually terminates and does not become an orphaned zombie process?
What information should the timeout error message provide to the LLM to help it recover?
wrongAnswers: Executing tools synchronously on the main agent event loop, causing a single hanging API call to freeze the entire application.
Catching a timeout but failing to kill the underlying spawned process, creating zombie processes that exhaust host memory.
tradeOffs: Non-blocking async timeouts keep the orchestrator responsive and prevent worker thread exhaustion, but require clean subprocess cleanup.
Overly aggressive timeouts cancel legitimate slow batch computations, while lax timeouts leave users waiting.
keyPoints: Wrap tool execution in non-blocking timeouts tailored to tool type.
Cancel the future and terminate the subprocess or connection on timeout.
Return a structured timeout error for retry or fallback decisions.
Aggressive timeouts can cancel valid long-running work.

questions.title: What runtime guard should intercept an agent when it invokes a non-existent tool or provides malformed arguments, and how should the error be fed back?
questions.answer: Large language models frequently hallucinate non-existent tool names or generate JSON arguments that violate the expected schema. If the execution runtime blindly attempts to dispatch an unknown tool, it crashes with runtime exceptions. We intercept all model outputs at a pre-dispatch validation layer. When the model outputs a tool call, we validate the requested tool name against the registered tool catalog and parse its arguments against the tool's JSON Schema. If the tool does not exist or arguments fail validation, we catch the error before execution. Instead of terminating the session immediately, we inject a structured error message into the conversation history: 'Tool X does not exist. Available tools are: A, B, C.' We permit up to two corrective retries. If the model continues hallucinating invalid tools, we abort the loop cleanly. The trade-off is self-correction capability versus wasted tokens: allowing retries lets models fix minor syntax errors on their own, but repeated retries consume prompt tokens when a model genuinely lacks the necessary tools.
followUps: How do you design JSON schema descriptions to minimize model argument formatting errors?
What threshold of consecutive validation failures should trigger immediate task termination?
wrongAnswers: Crashing the server with an unhandled KeyError when an unknown tool name is encountered.
Allowing unlimited validation retries, letting the agent get stuck in an endless loop generating invalid arguments.
tradeOffs: Detailed schema validation feedback allows models to self-correct minor parameter mistakes autonomously.
Allowing multiple retries on invalid tools burns prompt tokens and latency if the model fundamentally lacks capability for the task.
keyPoints: Validate tool names against the registered catalog before dispatch.
Validate arguments against the tool JSON Schema.
Return structured errors and allow two corrective retries.
Abort cleanly if invalid calls persist.

questions.title: In a multi-agent system where Agent A delegates to Agent B, how do you prevent cascading retries and thundering herd failures across subagent trees?
questions.answer: In multi-agent systems where supervisor agents delegate sub-tasks to specialized subagents, a failure in a leaf agent can trigger rapid retries that cascade upstream, causing a thundering herd that saturates downstream services.
