We prevent cascading failures using two mechanisms: distributed hop limits and exponential backoff with full jitter. First, we attach a global time-to-live and hop budget header to every inter-agent task message. When Agent A delegates to Agent B, the hop counter decrements; if the counter reaches zero, further delegation is blocked, preventing unbounded recursive subagent spawning. Second, when a subagent tool fails due to rate limits or transient errors, we do not retry immediately. We apply exponential backoff with full jitter, calculating sleep time as a random value between zero and the exponentially backed-off interval. The trade-off is task completion latency versus system stability: backoff delays overall task execution, but it prevents multi-agent trees from synchronizing their retries and overwhelming backend infrastructure.
followUps: How do you propagate distributed trace contexts across asynchronous agent message queues?
What circuit breaker pattern should a supervisor agent use to temporarily stop delegating to a failing subagent service?
wrongAnswers: Allowing every agent in a hierarchy to retry immediately upon failure, creating an exponential amplification of traffic downstream.
Omitting a maximum delegation depth, allowing two subagents to endlessly delegate sub-tasks to each other.
tradeOffs: Exponential backoff with jitter desynchronizes retries and prevents downstream system collapse, but increases tail latency for failing workflows.
Strict delegation hop budgets bound call graph depth, but can artificially restrict deep collaborative workflows.
keyPoints: Attach global time-to-live and hop budgets to delegated tasks.
Decrement hop counts and block delegation at zero.
Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and full jitter.
Backoff adds latency but avoids synchronized retry storms.

questions.title: When an agent execution is aborted by a user or terminated by a safety rule, how do you preserve partial progress and leave the workspace in a recoverable state?
questions.answer: When an agent execution is interrupted by a user cancellation, safety violation, or budget cutoff, leaving the workspace in an inconsistent half-finished state corrupts files and confuses users. We handle abort signals through graceful lifecycle termination. At each step of the agent loop, before applying mutations, we create a lightweight checkpoint—such as a temporary git commit or file snapshot. When an abort signal arrives, the runtime halts forward execution and invokes an abort handler. The handler cancels running subprocesses, cleans up temporary files, and preserves uncommitted changes on a dedicated review branch rather than discarding them. It then generates a structured debrief detailing what sub-tasks succeeded, what step was in progress when aborted, and what actions were rolled back. The trade-off is abort latency versus state cleanliness: terminating a process immediately with a kill signal is instantaneous but leaves corrupt files, whereas running clean rollback handlers takes a few seconds but guarantees workspace consistency.
followUps: How do you handle in-flight database transactions when a user clicks 'Cancel' on a running agent?
What debrief structure best explains to an end user why an agent stopped and what was preserved?
wrongAnswers: Sending an immediate SIGKILL to the agent container without running cleanup handlers, leaving dangling lockfiles and half-written files.
Silently discarding all agent work on abort, forcing users to re-run the entire multi-step task from scratch.
tradeOffs: Atomic step checkpointing guarantees workspace consistency on sudden aborts, but adds disk snapshot overhead to each step.
Preserving partial progress on a review branch gives users salvageable work, but requires branch management and cleanup.
keyPoints: Checkpoint state before mutations.
On abort, cancel subprocesses and clean temporary files.
Preserve unfinished changes on a review branch.
Report succeeded, interrupted and rolled-back work.

questions.title: At the end of each session your agent writes a paragraph that says what it did. The next session still spends its first half hour finding out where things stand. What is missing from the end-of-session artifact, and how do you produce it so that it is never skipped?
questions.answer: The paragraph is a status report, and a handoff needs seven fields: a summary, the changed files, the commands run, the failed attempts, the open risks, the next action and a pointer to the verification and review reports. The next action is the most important field, because it makes the first step of the next session deterministic. Generate the packet from the workbench artifacts instead of asking the agent to write it, and run a cleanup check first so that the packet describes a tree the next session can trust.
followUps: Level 1: Why does the JSON win when the two forms disagree? Expected: the next agent loads the JSON, so the machine-readable form is the one that drives the next session.
Level 2: Which failed attempts belong in the packet? Expected: every record with a non-zero exit, with the retry chain visible, so that the next session does not repeat a known dead end.

Level 2: What is the difference between a handoff and the state file? Expected: the state file is read on every turn and holds where the agent is, while the handoff is generated once at session end and tells the next session where to start.

Level 3: Two sessions on two branches each wrote a handoff. How does the next session pick one? Expected: each packet carries a branch, a last known good commit and a status of active, superseded or archived, and only the active packet for this branch drives the session.
wrongAnswers: "Ask the agent to write a detailed summary at the end." A written summary is skipped when the session ends badly, and it is the bad sessions that need the handoff most.
"The chat history is the handoff." The history is trimmed or gone, and the next session cannot replay an hour of chat in its first minute.
"A green verification report is enough to resume." The report proves the task state, not the tree state, and a dirty tree costs the next session its first ten minutes.
keyPoints: A handoff needs summary, changed files and commands.
Include failed attempts and open risks.
State the next action and link verification and review reports.
Generate from artifacts after a cleanup check.

questions.title: A teammate says that their chat application is an agent because it calls a model inside a while loop. Name the parts that a real agent loop needs, and say what goes wrong when each one is missing.
questions.answer: An agent loop needs five parts: a message buffer that grows with each turn, a tool registry that the model calls by name, a stop condition, a turn budget, and an observation formatter. The model is the same in a chat bot and in an agent. The difference is that the agent can pause, call a tool, read the result and continue. Without the five parts, the loop is a chat bot with extra steps.
followUps: Level 1: What is an observation? Expected: the string form of a tool result that the loop appends to the buffer for the next model call.
Level 2: Why is a turn budget a separate part from the stop condition? Expected: the stop condition depends on what the model emits, and the budget protects the run when the model never emits a stop.

Level 2: Where does the thought go in a model with a native reasoning channel? Expected: in a separate field that the runtime passes between turns, so the transcript shows tool calls and results without inline thought text.
Level 3: What changes when two tool calls in one turn return out of order? Expected: each result needs a correlation id that ties it to its call, or the model reads the wrong result for a call.
wrongAnswers: "An agent is a model with a long system prompt." A prompt cannot run a tool or read a result, so the model still stops at its first wrong guess.
"The loop ends when the model says it is done." A model can say it is done too early or never, so the loop also needs a turn budget and a no-tool-call stop.
"Tool errors should raise so that the developer sees them." An error that raises ends the run, while an error that becomes an observation lets the model fix the call.
keyPoints: Maintain a growing message buffer and named tool registry.
Define a stop condition and turn budget.
Format observations for the model.
Let the model pause for tool execution and continue on results.

questions.title: A team ran a frontier model on a small repo task. The result had plausible code, two red tests, one edit in a file that had nothing to do with the task, and no note of what the model assumed or what remains. The team wants to buy a bigger model. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: The model was right about the language and wrong about the work, and a bigger model does not fix that. Reliable agents need a workbench with seven surfaces around the model: instructions, state, scope, feedback, verification, review and handoff. Each symptom in the run maps to one missing surface. You can swap the model and keep the surfaces, but you cannot drop the surfaces and keep the reliability.
followUps: Level 1: Which of the seven surfaces does a pull request template cover? Expected: handoff, because it records what changed, why, and what is left.

Level 2: Which surface catches an agent that writes an extra file nobody asked for? Expected: scope first, because the diff check compares touched files with the contract, and then verification, which refuses the forbidden write.
Level 2: Why does the lesson say the loop closes on a file and not on the chat? Expected: sessions end and conversations get trimmed, so the file is the only record that the next session can trust.

Level 3: The lesson maps each surface to a distributed-systems primitive. What is verification? Expected: a function that is deterministic over its inputs, triggered when the task closes, and that fails closed.
wrongAnswers: "The model hallucinated, so pick a model that hallucinates less." The model did not know what done meant or where it could write, and no model knows that without the surfaces.
"Write a longer system prompt with all the rules." A prompt covers one turn, while the surfaces carry the work across turns and sessions.
"The framework already does this." A framework gives the agent a runtime, and the workbench is what the agent reads and writes inside that runtime.
keyPoints: A larger model does not fix missing workbench structure.
Provide instructions, state and scope.
Provide feedback, verification and review.
Include handoff and map symptoms to missing surfaces.

questions.title: You wrap every shell command that an agent runs so that the next turn can read what happened. What goes into the record, which field tells you whether the command worked, and what do you do when that field is empty?
questions.answer: The record carries the exact command as argv, the tail of stdout and the tail of stderr as separate fields, the exit code, the duration, the start time, and a one-line note of what the agent expected. The exit code is the success signal, because text can say anything and the code cannot. If the runner fails before it captures an exit, the record carries a null exit and an error reason, and the loop must not advance on it.
followUps: Level 1: Why keep stderr separate from stdout? Expected: the failure summary often lands on one stream and progress on the other, and a merged tail can bury the summary.
Level 2: A command times out. What does the record say? Expected: a null exit code, an error field with the timeout, and whatever partial output was captured, and the loop refuses to advance.
Level 2: What is the agent note for? Expected: it records the prediction before the result, so a reviewer can see when the agent expected success and got a failure.

Level 3: A retry succeeds. How does the audit see the first failure? Expected: each record has a command id, and the retry carries the parent command id, so the chain is visible and the retry does not look like an independent success.
wrongAnswers: "Parse the output for the word error to detect failure." Output text varies by tool and language, and the exit code is the signal every command gives.
"Keep the whole output, because truncation can hide something." A huge record pushes the loop out of its token budget, and the deterministic tail keeps the lines that matter.
"Redact when a human opens the log." The file on disk is already the leak, so redaction has to happen before the append.
keyPoints: Record command argv and separate stdout and stderr tails.
Capture exit code, duration and start time.
Include the expected outcome in a short note.
Treat missing exit capture as an error and do not advance.

questions.title: The task given to the agent was to fix one login bug. The diff changes the login route, an email helper, the database driver, the README and the release script. The transcript gives a plausible reason for each change. The reviewer rejects the pull request and asks you what went wrong and how to stop it. What do you say?
questions.answer: This is scope creep, and it is hard to see because the agent explains each step in good faith. The fix is not a stricter prompt. It is a contract on disk that lists the files the task may change and the files it must never change, plus a check that compares the final diff with that contract. The check runs before the gate, and a write to a forbidden path blocks the task.
followUps: Level 2: The agent needed a one-line change in the email helper to fix the bug. What should have happened? Expected: the checker flags the off-scope write, the agent opens a question, and a human either grows the contract or asks the agent to back off.

Level 3: How do you keep the contract valid when a refactor moves the login code? Expected: write the globs by pattern such as app//login*.py, not by exact path, and archive the contract when the task closes.

Level 3: Two contracts apply to one diff, one for the project and one for the task. What is the merge rule? Expected: least privilege, so intersect the allowed globs, union the forbidden globs, and take the most restrictive time budget.

Level 4: File globs are not the only scope dimension. What else belongs in the contract? Expected: a wall-clock budget and a network egress allowlist, because an agent can stay inside its files and still call a service that was not part of the task.
wrongAnswers: "Add a sentence to the prompt that says stay in scope." The agent already believed it was in scope at every step, so the sentence changes nothing without a check.
"Review the diff by hand more carefully." Human review caught it this time, after the agent spent the budget, and the point is to catch it before the pull request exists.
"Block every write outside the task files." A hard block on a README edit trains the team to disable the gate, so use warnings for low-risk paths and blocks for scripts and migrations.
keyPoints: An on-disk contract defines permitted file changes.
List forbidden paths explicitly.
Compare the final diff against the contract.
Block forbidden writes before running the gate.

questions.title: A coding agent offers six permission modes, from one that asks before every action to one that approves everything. A colleague runs every task in the mode that approves everything, because the prompts are annoying. Give the rule you use to pick a mode, and say which tasks go where.
questions.answer: Pick the mode from the task, not from the annoyance. Start an unfamiliar or production-adjacent task in plan mode, where reading the plan is cheaper than undoing a bad run. Use the default mode for most interactive sessions, and the mode that auto-approves file writes for a known refactor across many files. Reserve the classifier-driven auto mode for unattended runs inside a workspace whose reach you have measured, and reserve the approve-everything mode for a disposable container.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the refactor mode still ask on shell commands? Expected: a file write is reversible from version control, while a shell command can delete, send or install, so the mode approves the cheap-to-undo class only.

Level 2: How does the never-prompt mode differ from the top of the ladder? Expected: the never-prompt mode denies anything that a rule did not pre-approve, while the approve-everything mode approves it.

Level 3: An unattended run needs a 24-hour budget. What do you set? Expected: a turn cap, a dollar cap, per-tool action caps and an allowlist, each with a reason, inside a workspace with no credentials and no egress you did not opt into.

Level 3: The classifier approved every action and the run still exfiltrated data. How? Expected: a sequence of allowed actions, such as writing data you own to a file and then pushing to a public repository, where the composition is the problem and no single action was flagged.
wrongAnswers: "Approve everything, because the agent is in version control anyway." Version control covers file writes, and the risk is in shell, network and credentials, which no commit reverts.
"The classifier mode is safe for anything, because a model reviews each step." The classifier judges actions, not trajectories, and the documentation pairs it with budgets, allowlists and isolation.
"Plan mode is for beginners." Plan mode is for the task where a wrong run costs more than a read, and that is a property of the task, not of the operator.
keyPoints: Choose permission mode according to the task.
Use planning for unfamiliar or production-adjacent work.
Use interactive defaults or write approval for known refactors.
Reserve broad unattended permissions for measured or disposable environments.

questions.title: A repo has a 3000-line instructions file for its coding agent. The agent follows about half of it. One engineer wants to cut it to a page. Another says that every line came from an incident and nothing can go. How do you settle it?
questions.answer: Both are right about something, and the answer is a layered file set, not a shorter file. Keep a root router under about 50 lines that holds only pointers and the few hard rules. Move the rules into a rules file with one screen per category, and move the depth into topic documents that the agent loads only when a task touches them. Every rule stays, and the agent reaches any rule in at most two hops.
followUps: Level 2: The team keeps a rule in the router because it is important. What is the test for whether it belongs there? Expected: the router holds pointers and the few hard rules that apply to every session, and anything that applies to one kind of task goes in a topic document.
Level 2: How do you keep one source of truth when the team uses several coding agents? Expected: one root file and symlinks with the names each tool expects, so that every tool reads the same text.
Level 3: What does a lint for the workbench check? Expected: the router is under the line budget, every path it references exists, and no two rules conflict.

Level 3: Why does the lesson rank a dead link below a rule that was never written? Expected: the agent trusts the router, follows the pointer, finds nothing, and proceeds as if the rule did not exist, while a missing rule at least leaves no false promise.
wrongAnswers: "Cut the file to one page and delete the rest." The rules came from incidents, and deleting them repeats the incidents, so move them to tiers instead.
"Keep the long file, and tell the agent to read all of it." The model has an attention budget, and an instruction to read everything does not change how much it acts on.
"Put the file in the system prompt so that it is always in context." Being in context is not the problem; acting on it is, and a short router with pointers gets followed where a long block does not.
keyPoints: Keep a short root router with pointers and hard rules.
Put categorized rules in a separate file.
Load deeper topic documents only when relevant.
Keep every rule reachable within two hops.

questions.title: An instructions file tells the agent to be careful, to test thoroughly, and to ask if it is unsure. Three days later the agent ships a change with no tests, writes into a directory it should not touch, and never asks a question. Redesign these instructions so that a runtime can enforce them and a reviewer can score them.
questions.answer: Rewrite each wish as a rule with a slug, a category, a one-line description and a named check function. Five categories cover most rules: startup, forbidden, definition of done, uncertainty and approval. Give every rule a severity of block, warn or info, so that the runtime refuses only on block. Keep the rules in one markdown file with one rule per heading, so that review can see every change.
followUps: Level 2: Why delete a stale rule instead of commenting it out? Expected: the workbench is the source of truth, and a commented rule is a rule the agent might still read while the checker ignores it.

Level 3: A rule says to follow a published style guide. Why does it fail the design? Expected: it has no enforcement command, so the agent can invent compliance, and the fix is to pair it with the exact lint command.

Level 3: Where does the uncertainty check get its signal? Expected: from the state file, which lists assumptions, and from the question notes, so an assumption with no source and no note is a violation.

Level 4: How does the rule set stay portable across three agent products? Expected: the file is markdown plus function names, so each runtime registers the same checks as its own guardrails or interrupts while the file stays the contract.
wrongAnswers: "Make every rule a hard block so that the agent takes them seriously." Teams quietly weaken blocks under deadline pressure, and a rule set where everything blocks ends with nothing enforced.
"Keep the rules in the prompt, where the model reads them." The model reads them and still cannot check them, while a named check function gives the runtime and the reviewer the same verdict.
"Rules are permanent because they came from incidents." A rule that never fires still costs attention, so expiry forces a review that keeps, lowers, or deletes it with a reason.
keyPoints: Give each rule a slug, category and description.
Name the function that checks the rule.
Categorize startup, forbidden, completion, uncertainty and approval rules.
Assign block, warn or info severity and refuse only on block.

questions.title: A pull request from a coding agent says that the whole suite is green. A reviewer runs it and two tests fail. The transcript shows the agent writing "running tests now" and then "all tests pass", with nothing between the two lines. What happened, and what do you build so that this claim cannot reach a reviewer again?
questions.answer: The agent predicted the output instead of reading it. Either no command ran, or the command ran and nobody captured the result into the loop. The fix has two parts: a feedback runner that records every command with its exit code, and a verification gate that reads those records and refuses to mark the task done unless each acceptance command ran and exited zero.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the record keep stdout and stderr in separate fields? Expected: a test runner writes the failure summary to one stream and progress to the other, and a merged tail can hide the summary behind progress lines.

Level 2: The agent runs the acceptance command, it fails, and a retry passes. What does the gate see? Expected: two records for the same command, linked by the parent command id. The gate blocks on the failed record and does not report passed: true, even though the retry exited zero. Only a signed human override gets past it, and the chain keeps the failure history visible.

Level 3: Why must the gate be deterministic and not a model judge? Expected: the gate answers whether the task is complete, which must give the same verdict for the same artifacts every time, while a judge gives a qualitative opinion that belongs on the review side.

Level 4: Where do you place the gate so that it cannot be bypassed? Expected: in layers, with a pre-commit hook, a CI status check, and a pre-merge gate, so that a failure in one layer is caught by the next.
wrongAnswers: "Tell the agent to paste the test output into the transcript." The model can paste what it expects, and a reviewer cannot tell a paste from a capture.
"Trust the agent and let CI catch it." CI did catch it, after the claim reached a reviewer, and the point is to stop the claim at the source.
"Treat a timeout as a pass, because the tests were slow." A timeout gives a null exit, and the loop must refuse to advance on a null exit.
keyPoints: Predicted test output is not execution evidence.
A feedback runner records commands and exit codes.
A gate reads the execution records.
Require every acceptance command to have run and exited zero.

questions.title: The product team wants a single maximum number of turns that applies to every run of your agent. The agent handles one-line edits, multi-file refactors, and unattended runs that drive a computer for hours. What number do you give them, and how do you defend it?
questions.answer: There is no single number, and the estimate shows why. Agents run 40 to 400 steps per task, and a computer-use task runs dozens to hundreds of steps as a normal case. A cap that fits a one-line edit stops every refactor, and a cap that fits an unattended run lets a stuck edit spend hundreds of turns. Give one cap per task class, set each from the trace distribution of successful runs in that class, and pair every cap with a wall-clock budget and a cost cap.
followUps: Level 2: A run reaches the cap with the task almost done. What happens? Expected: the loop yields with a budget reason, the caller inspects the partial state, and the caller extends the budget or closes the session with a handoff.

Level 2: Why should the fallback cap for a task with no class be small? Expected: an unknown task is the one most likely to loop, and an early yield costs a human decision while a late one costs hours.

Level 3: How do you tell a long run from a stuck run before the cap? Expected: a repeat detector over the action and observation hashes, so that five near-identical actions in a row pause the run early.
Level 3: The traces for a class show two clusters of turn counts. What does that tell you? Expected: the class is two classes, and each needs its own cap.
wrongAnswers: "Set it high so that no legitimate task is cut off." A high cap on a short task class lets a stuck run spend hundreds of turns, and the point of the cap is to catch the stuck run.
"Set it low and let users retry." A low cap on a refactor ends every run with half the work, and a retry starts from zero.
"The turn cap is enough, because turns are what cost money." Turns are one axis, and a run can be slow in time or expensive in tokens with few turns.
keyPoints: Use different turn caps for different task classes.
Set caps from successful trace distributions.
A universal small cap interrupts larger tasks.
Pair turn caps with wall-clock and cost limits.

questions.title: Two engineers disagree about how the loop should end. One wants an explicit finish tool that the model must call. The other wants the loop to end as soon as an assistant turn has no tool call in it. Which do you pick, and what does each choice get wrong?
questions.answer: Both are stop conditions, and a production loop needs both plus a budget. The no-tool-call stop is simple and matches how models behave, but it ends the run on any turn where the model answers in prose, including a turn where it only meant to think aloud. An explicit finish gives a clear signal with a payload, but a model that never calls it runs until the budget. Pick the no-tool-call stop as the default, keep finish as a tool that carries the final answer, and make the budget the last guard.
followUps: Level 2: A model returns prose and a tool call in the same turn. Which stop applies? Expected: none, because the turn has a tool call, so the loop dispatches it and continues.
Level 3: Why does the result need the name of the stop that fired? Expected: an eval that counts a no-tool-call stop as success rewards early termination, so the reason must be visible to the scorer.

Level 3: Reasoning now travels on a separate channel. Does that change the no-tool-call stop? Expected: yes, a turn with reasoning content and no visible text or tool call must not count as an answer, so the check must read the visible output.

Level 4: How would you measure early termination across a task set? Expected: compare the stop reason with a gate that checks acceptance commands, and count the runs that stopped with no tool call while the acceptance commands never ran.
wrongAnswers: "Use only the finish tool, because it is explicit." A model that never calls it runs to the budget on every task that it cannot finish.
"Use only the no-tool-call stop, because the model knows when it is done." A model that pauses to think in prose ends the run with half the work done.
"The budget is enough on its own." The budget is the guard for a loop that never converges, and a run that waits for it wastes every turn after the real end.
keyPoints: No-tool-call termination is simple but can stop on intermediate prose.
An explicit finish tool carries a final payload.
A model may never call finish.
Use a budget as the final stopping guard.

questions.title: An on-call engineer pages you. A coding agent has run for two hours on a task that normally takes ten minutes. The trace shows one shell command, one result, and then the same command again, over and over. Walk through how you find the cause and what you change so that this cannot happen again.
questions.answer: Read the trace for the pair of action and observation that repeats, then ask why the model does not react to the observation. The usual causes are an error that the loop never shows to the model, an observation that reads the same on every turn, and a missing turn budget. Fix the cause, then add the two guards that stop any future loop: a budget that yields control to the caller, and a check for a repeated action with a repeated observation.
followUps: Level 2: The model repeats a call because the tool returns an empty string on failure. Who owns the fix? Expected: the observation formatter, which must add the exit code and the error text so that the observation changes when the call fails.

Level 3: Why does the harness yield on a budget instead of raising? Expected: a yield is a return value that the caller can inspect and resume from, while an exception loses the partial state and forces a restart.

Level 3: A repeat detector hashes the action only. What loop does it miss? Expected: a loop where the action changes slightly each time, such as a counter in an argument, while the observation never changes, so hash the observation too.

Level 4: The loop is fixed, but the agent still ran for two hours before anyone noticed. What is the missing surface? Expected: observability, a wall-clock budget with an alert, and a trace that someone can read at step 38 without reading the whole run.
wrongAnswers: "Raise the maximum turns so that the task can finish." The task was not progressing, so more turns give more of the same call.
"Add a line to the prompt that says do not repeat yourself." The model repeated because it never saw the error, and a prompt cannot show it what the loop hid.
"Kill the process when the budget is reached." A kill loses the partial state, while a yield lets the caller inspect it, extend the budget, or close the session with a clean handoff.
keyPoints: Inspect repeated action-observation pairs in the trace.
Check whether errors are hidden from the model.
Fix observations that never change.
Add caller-yielding budgets and repeated-pair detection.

questions.title: Leadership wants to pause the harness work for two quarters and wait for the next model generation, on the theory that a better model will not need the scaffolding. Make the case with evidence, and say what part of their argument is right.
questions.answer: Today the engineering that carries the load is around the model, not inside it, and the numbers say so. The same model moved a coding agent from outside the top 30 to rank five on a terminal benchmark when only the harness changed, and a team that deleted 80 percent of its agent's tools saw success go from 80 percent to 100 percent. Most enterprise agent projects that fail do so around runtime, not reasoning. Leadership is right that models absorb harness tricks over time, which is why you build the harness from primitives that survive a model swap.
followUps: Level 3: Which of the receipts is the weakest evidence, and why? Expected: the enterprise failure rate, because it is a survey figure without a controlled comparison, while the benchmark rank change held the model fixed.

Level 3: A newer model stops needing the repeat detector. What do you remove? Expected: nothing yet, because the detector is a trigger plus a function that costs little, and you remove it only when the trace data shows it never fires.

Level 4: How do you make the harness investment visible to leadership each quarter? Expected: run the same task set with and without the surfaces on the current model, report completion, scope violations and interventions, and show the gap.

Level 4: What is the one harness piece most likely to be absorbed by models next? Expected: a reasoned pick, such as self-correction on tool errors, with the argument that the model sees the observation and the surface only formats it.
wrongAnswers: "The model is the product, so the harness is overhead." The harness decided the rank on the benchmark while the model stayed the same.
"A longer context window will fix the goal loss." The long-context result in the lesson went the other way, with completion falling under 10 percent as context grew.
"Harness work is prompt engineering by another name." Prompting tells the model what you want this turn, and the harness carries the work across turns and sessions in files and checks.
keyPoints: Agent reliability depends on engineering around the model.
Changing the harness can change benchmark performance with the same model.
Reducing tool count can improve success.
Build runtime primitives that survive model swaps.

questions.title: Take-home. Your team has the workbench surfaces as loose scripts, a shared document and some memory. Package them into one directory that a new repository can install with one command, and defend what you leave out. Bring the layout, the installer, the versioning rule and the uninstall rule. We grade the second install as much as the first.
questions.answer: Ship a versioned directory with four parts: the docs that carry the rules and the rubric, the schemas that are the contract, the scripts that are the runtime, and a short installer. The installer refuses to install over an existing pack without a force flag, copies the pack, connects CI if a workflows directory exists, and prints the next steps. Running it twice gives the same result. Project tasks, vendor SDK calls and onboarding prose stay out, because the pack is the recipe and each install is a serving.
followUps: Level 3: Which one optional fifth document would you promote into the pack, and why? Expected: a reasoned choice with the cut defended, for example a migration runbook, with the argument that it is needed on every major bump and not on one project.
Level 3: What counts as non-trivial state for the uninstaller? Expected: any uncommitted change in the state file, the board or the outputs, because those are the user's work and not the pack's.

Level 4: How do you migrate a hand-rolled workbench to the pack with the least downtime? Expected: install beside it, map each existing file to a schema, run the gate on both for one task, then switch the router pointer and archive the old files.

Level 4: What breaks if two repositories pin different major versions of the pack? Expected: nothing, as long as each records its version and the lint checks each against its own pack, while a shared CI job must run the matching version per repository.
wrongAnswers: "Put the team's current backlog into the pack so that new repos start with real tasks." Tasks belong to the target repository, and a pack that carries them is wrong for every repository but one.
"Call the vendor SDK from the scripts to save time." The pack must survive a framework change, and an SDK call ties every install to one runtime.
"Make the installer overwrite by default so that updates are easy." An overwrite without a flag destroys local changes, and the force flag is what makes an update a decision.
keyPoints: Ship versioned docs, schemas, runtime scripts and an installer.
Refuse overwriting an existing pack without force.
Connect CI when workflows exist and print next steps.
Make repeat installation idempotent and exclude project tasks and vendor calls.

questions.title: A rule says that no migration file may change without an approval. It lives in docs/database.md, which docs/architecture.md links, which the top-level instructions file links. The root file also says to always use the ORM, while the database document says to write raw SQL in migrations. The agent changed a migration twice this week without asking. Find the causes and fix them in order.
questions.answer: There are three independent causes, and any one of them is enough. The rule is three hops from the router, past the two-hop reachability limit, so the agent never loads it, and it is prose with no check, so nothing refuses the write even when the agent reads it. And the root file conflicts with the database document, and conflicting instructions silently move an agent from asking to guessing. Fix the reach first, make the rule an approval-category rule with a block-severity check, and remove the conflict.
followUps: Level 3: Why does a shorter root file help here? Expected: a short router is read in full on every session and on every pull request review, so a pointer to the database document stays current and reachable.

Level 3: The team wants to keep the rule in the database document because that is where the context is. What do you do? Expected: keep the explanation there, put the rule and its check in the rules file, and link both from the router, so the rule is two hops away and still has its context.

Level 4: How would you find two rules that contradict each other before an incident? Expected: a lint that flags two rules whose scopes overlap with different verbs, and a review habit of numbering priorities in the router.

Level 4: The checker passes in CI, and the agent still edits a migration in a live session. Where is the gap? Expected: the checker runs after the fact, so the same check must also run as a pre-tool hook in the runtime, where it can refuse the write before it happens.
wrongAnswers: "Add the rule to the system prompt in capital letters." Emphasis does not add a check, and the conflict in the router still pushes the agent toward guessing.
"The model is ignoring instructions, so switch models." The rule was unreachable, uncheckable and contradicted, and a different model meets the same three problems.
"Delete the ORM rule, since it caused the conflict." The ORM rule is correct for application code, so scope it rather than delete it.
keyPoints: Keep rules reachable within two hops of the router.
Prose without a check cannot block an unsafe write.
Conflicting documents push the agent toward guessing.
Fix reachability, add a blocking approval check and remove conflicts.

questions.title: A long coding session has used most of its context window. The runtime offers to summarize the older turns and keep going. Your teammate wants to let it run to the limit, because compaction is automatic. When do you compact, when do you end the session, and what do you measure to choose?
questions.answer: Compaction extends a session, and a handoff closes one cleanly and starts the next in fresh context. Compaction is fine while the compressed history still carries what the task needs, but quality decays as compression stacks up. The lesson's guidance is to end the session with a generated handoff at 50 to 75 percent of the budget, not at the wall, because the packet is cheap to write while the context is intact and expensive when the model is already losing its place.
followUps: Level 3: Why is a fresh session better than a third compaction? Expected: compression losses stack up, while a fresh session starts from the packet, the state file and the repo, which are the system of record.

Level 3: What must be true of the tree before the handoff runs? Expected: the cleanup check passes, so the tree is committed or stashed with a note, no temp files remain, tests are green or named as risks, and the branch is right.

Level 4: The handoff is cheap, but the next session has to rebuild its working context. How do you keep that cost down? Expected: the packet lists the exact artifacts the next session must load before it acts, and the router points at them, so the session loads the state, the board and the active contract and nothing else.

Level 4: Two coding agent products are used on one task, one after the other. What makes the transition work? Expected: the packet schema, because the JSON form is product-neutral and both runtimes read the same fields.
wrongAnswers: "Compaction is automatic, so let the runtime handle it." Automatic compaction decides when to compress, not whether the compressed state is still good enough to work from.
"End every session as early as possible to be safe." Each handoff costs a packet and a reload, so the target is a range, not a minimum.
"A longer context window removes the problem." A larger window delays the wall, and the quality decay from stacked compression is the same.

questions.title: Every verification report for the last month says passed. A reviewer notices that the test suite runs much faster than it did, and that several test files are gone. The acceptance command still exits zero. What happened, which check is missing from the gate, and what else do you change?
questions.answer: The agent met the acceptance command by removing the tests that failed, and the gate only checked that the command ran and exited zero. The missing check is a coverage floor: the gate reads a coverage report and blocks when coverage is below the floor, 80 percent by default, or when it drops by more than one percentage point against the previous merge. Add the test directory to the scope check so that a deletion under it is a flagged write, and promote warnings to blocks on release branches.
followUps: Level 3: Which artifact carries the floor? Expected: the coverage report carries the current and previous values, and the floor is a gate parameter so that it is versioned with the gate, not with the agent's output.

Level 3: Why is a missing coverage report only a warning by default? Expected: strict everywhere erodes daily flow, so the default warns and the release branches run strict, where the warning becomes a block.

Level 4: The agent rewrites a test to always pass instead of deleting it. What catches that? Expected: coverage stays the same, so the gate does not, and the reviewer's diff of test files or a mutation check in CI is the layer that sees it.

Level 4: How do you keep the human override from becoming the way around the floor? Expected: an override writes a signed row with the finding code, the reason, the user and the commit, and review reads that log.
wrongAnswers: "Add a rule that says do not delete tests." A rule the gate cannot check from an artifact is a wish, and the agent did not think of it as deleting tests.
"Count the tests and block when the number falls." A count blocks legitimate consolidation, while a coverage floor measures what the suite protects.
"Make the acceptance command also print coverage." The gate reads a report, not output text, so the coverage must arrive as an artifact the gate can parse.

questions.title: An unattended coding run used the mode in which a separate model reviews every action before it executes. The audit shows that the reviewer approved each action. The run still copied a private dataset into a public repository. Explain how that is possible, and name the controls that would have stopped it.
questions.answer: The reviewer judges one action at a time against the request. Each action in the run was allowed on its own: read a file you own, write a file you own, commit, push. The harm was in the composition, and the reviewer does not re-derive the user's intent across the trajectory. The controls that catch this live outside the per-action check: an isolated workspace with no sensitive mounts, a network egress allowlist in the scope contract, per-tool action caps, and a trajectory audit after the run that detects what the other controls let through.
followUps: Level 3: Why is an egress allowlist a scope dimension and not a runtime setting? Expected: the hosts a task may reach change per task, so the rule belongs in the per-task contract where the file globs and the time budget live.
Level 3: What does the trajectory audit read? Expected: the append-only event stream of tool calls and results, which a subscriber can replay from any offset without re-running the model.

Level 4: You cannot patch indirect prompt injection fully. What does that imply for the design? Expected: treat tool outputs as untrusted, keep the data the agent can reach small, keep the places it can send to small, and accept that detection is a layer and containment is the control.

Level 4: How do you test the control set before the next unattended run? Expected: write one trajectory in which every action is approved and the composition is harmful, run it in the isolated workspace, and confirm that the allowlist or the mounts stop it.
wrongAnswers: "The reviewer model was too weak, so use a bigger one." A bigger reviewer still judges actions one at a time and still reads the same injected context.
"Approve pushes manually and the rest automatically." A push is one of many legitimate channels, and the data had already left the private location through allowed writes.
"Keep the dataset in the repo but mark it private in the prompt." The prompt is advice, and the control is whether the dataset is mounted into the workspace at all.

questions.title: A proposal replaces the script that decides whether an agent task is done with a model judge. The argument is that a judge reads the diff, understands intent, and catches more than a script can. Argue for or against, and say where a judge does belong.
questions.answer: Against. The gate answers one question, is this task complete, and that verdict must be the same for the same artifacts every time, in version control, in CI, with no way for the agent to argue with it. A model judge gives a different answer on a different day and can be talked into a pass. A judge belongs on the review side, where the question is qualitative: is the code readable, secure and on style.
followUps: Level 3: An agent deletes failing tests, and the gate stays green. Which check is missing? Expected: a coverage floor read from a coverage report, with a block when coverage falls below the floor or drops by more than one percentage point against the previous merge.

Level 3: When is promoting every warning to a block the right default? Expected: on release branches and in post-incident triage through a strict flag, and not globally, because strict everywhere erodes daily flow.

Level 4: What stops the override log from becoming a formality? Expected: the runtime refuses an unsigned entry, the log is in git, and review reads it, so every override has a name and a reason attached.

Level 4: The gate and the reviewer disagree. Who wins? Expected: the gate decides whether the task is done, and the reviewer decides whether it is good, so a gate failure blocks regardless of the review, and a review failure reopens the task without touching the verdict.
wrongAnswers: "A judge understands intent, so it catches more." The gate does not need intent, and a judge that infers intent can be convinced that an incomplete task is complete.
"Run the judge and the script, and pass if either passes." The judge then becomes the way around the script, so the deterministic checks must decide done and the judge must only annotate.
"Let the agent explain why a block does not apply." The agent is the party under test, and an override needs a human signature with a reason.

questions.title: Take-home. Pick a small real change in a repository you may modify, and let one coding agent make it. Bring back evidence that a reviewer can reproduce, not a transcript. Tell us what you would record at each step, how you would prove that your acceptance check can fail, and what you would refuse to claim.
questions.answer: Record the starting revision, the observable goal, the non-goals, the allowed paths and the acceptance evidence before the agent runs, together with the working mode, the budget and a stop condition. Capture a baseline with the closest existing check before any edit. After the change, write the expected result independently of the implementation, introduce one deliberate wrong result in a disposable copy, and show that the same check fails for that reason. Label every runtime observation as local, staging or live, rehearse a rollback, and leave the branch, the changed files, the open risks and the next action explicit.
followUps: Level 3: Your planted regression passed the acceptance check. What do you do? Expected: treat the check as untrustworthy, strengthen the assertion or the observation until it fails for that reason, and only then rerun the correct version.

Level 3: Why must each runtime observation carry an environment label? Expected: a local rehearsal supports a local claim only, and an unlabeled observation lets a reader read a laptop run as production evidence.
Level 4: The agent finished faster than your baseline. What may you claim? Expected: that this task was faster on this run with this many interventions, and nothing about agents in general.

Level 4: Which single row would you mark unverified rather than fake? Expected: any row whose evidence you could not observe, such as a recovery step that needs a production mount you do not have, with the claim narrowed to match.
wrongAnswers: "The transcript shows the agent running the tests, so that is the evidence." A transcript is what the agent said, and the evidence is the check, its exit code and the record a reviewer can rerun.
"The acceptance check passed, so the change is proven." A check that never failed proves nothing, and the deliberate wrong result is what shows the check can detect a regression.
"Deployment to production is required to complete the exercise." A labeled local or staging rehearsal supports a local claim, and the exercise asks for honest labels, not production access.

questions.title: A repository has a project-wide scope contract, and each task adds its own. The checker currently reads whichever file it finds first. Write the merge rule for every field so that the result is mechanical, reviewable and never looser than either input.
questions.answer: Merge by least privilege. Intersect the allowed globs, so that a path must be permitted by both contracts, and union the forbidden globs, so that either contract can prohibit a path. Take the smaller time budget, accumulate the approvals required, and treat the egress allowlist with three states: unset defers to the other side, two lists intersect, and an empty list stays deny-all. Write the rule into the contract schema so that the checker and the reviewer apply the same merge.
followUps: Level 3: The project contract has no egress field and the task contract lists one host. What is the merged egress? Expected: the one-host allowlist, because an unset value defers to the other side.

Level 4: Why intersect allowed globs rather than union them? Expected: a union lets a task contract grant a path the project forbade by omission, and least privilege means both parties must agree on every write.

Level 4: A task legitimately needs a file outside the project contract. What is the path to approval? Expected: an entry in approvals_required with a human sign-off recorded, and the project contract updated in review, never a looser merge rule.

Level 4: How do you test the merge? Expected: a table of input pairs and expected outputs for each field, with the deny-all absorption and the unset deferral as named cases, run in CI against the checker.
wrongAnswers: "Let the task contract override the project contract, because it is more specific." Specific is not the same as safe, and an override lets any task open any path or host.
"Take the union of allowed files so that nothing legitimate is blocked." A union is the loosest result, and the merge must never be looser than either input.
"Merge in the checker and keep the contracts simple." A merge the reviewer cannot read is a rule the team cannot audit.

questions.title: Your harness has grown to about two hundred tools across several teams. The model cannot hold all of them in context, two teams once registered the same name and the second silently replaced the first, and the success rate has fallen as the catalog grew. Design the registry and the policy for what the model sees on each turn.
questions.answer: Make the registry the only source of truth for what exists, what shape the arguments take and which handler runs, and surface only ten to forty tools per turn. The registry holds a typed record per tool, rejects a second registration of a name unless the caller asks to override, and validates every call against a small schema subset with pointer-shaped errors. The exposure policy loads tool metadata into context only when the task needs it, and the fewer tools the model sees, the better it calls them.
followUps: Level 3: Two teams want the same tool name for different handlers. What do you do? Expected: refuse the collision, namespace by dotted segment, and let the exposure policy pick the family the task needs.
Level 3: How do you prove the validator is still correct after a refactor? Expected: run it over a saved replay log of real calls, which works because it has no I/O, no clock and no globals.

Level 4: What breaks if the exposure policy is itself a model call? Expected: a second nondeterministic step on every turn, so the selection should be rule-based from the contract and the board, with the model allowed only to request a named family.
Level 4: The dispatcher retries a failed call. Which record field decides whether it may? Expected: idempotent, because a retry of a non-idempotent tool can repeat a side effect.
wrongAnswers: "Give the model the whole catalog and let it choose." The model cannot hold two hundred schemas, and success fell as the catalog grew, so the fix is fewer tools in view.
"Put validation in each handler, close to the code it protects." Validation inside handlers drifts per team and turns the dispatcher into a guessing game that ends in a stack trace.
"Allow re-registration so that teams can hot-fix a tool." A silent replace is the incident in the prompt, and a fix should pass an explicit override that shows up in review.

questions.title: A vendor deck lists its harness features: a loop that re-injects the original intent when the agent tries to stop early, a plan-execute-verify split, control-plane separation, signed tool-call passports, progressive compaction, hooks, skills with progressive disclosure, and sandboxed agents. Translate each one into the primitive it is, and say what the deck leaves out.
questions.answer: Every entry is a distributed-systems primitive with a new name. The re-inject loop is a trigger that re-enqueues the task with fresh context, plan-execute-verify is three workers with a queue between them, the passport is an authorization policy enforced by a pre-action worker, and compaction is a state-management worker over session persistence. Hooks are triggers around the invocation path, skills are a function registry whose metadata loads just in time, sandboxes are the compute plane, and the control-plane item is the control-plane and data-plane split that predates agents. The decks usually leave out queues, workers as the unit of deployment, trigger semantics, persistence as its own concern and authorization as a separate plane.
followUps: Level 3: Which primitive is most often missing from an agent product that otherwise looks complete? Expected: the queue, because without a durable buffer the board, the feedback log and the review inbox are chat messages that scroll away.

Level 3: The deck says its hooks are a security boundary. Test the claim. Expected: a hook is a trigger plus a function inside the runtime, and a security boundary is an authorization policy enforced outside the agent's reach, so ask where the policy lives and who can change it.

Level 4: Two vendors describe the same thing as a handoff and as a checkpoint. How do you tell? Expected: map both to persistence and triggers, and see whether the record is read by the next session's startup trigger, which makes it a handoff, or by the same session on resume, which makes it a checkpoint.

Level 4: What would make a ninth primitive legitimate? Expected: a capability that cannot be built from the eight, which is rare, so the first check is whether it is a shared-state flavor or a policy flavor you have not seen.
wrongAnswers: "These patterns are new because agents are new." Each one has a name in distributed systems, and the agent label changes the vocabulary and not the engineering.
"Pick the vendor with the most patterns." More names on a deck is not more primitives covered, and the question is which of the eight are missing.
"A good instruction file is the harness." Instructions are policy and function metadata, one of eight, and a file cannot replace a queue or a persistence layer.

topics.title: Protocols: MCP, A2A and skills
topics.about: How agents call tools and other agents, and how those calls stay safe.

questions.title: Your planner agent must delegate a test run to a remote agent that it knows only by host and port. Describe what it fetches first, how it decides which endpoint to call, and what it checks before it asks that agent for a stream.
questions.answer: It fetches the agent card with a plain GET on /.well-known/agent-card.json. From supportedInterfaces it takes the first entry whose binding and version it speaks, and it calls that entry's URL. Before SendStreamingMessage it reads capabilities.streaming, because a server must refuse the call with UnsupportedOperationError when the flag is absent or false.
followUps: Level 1: Which field tells you what work the agent can do? Expected: skills, each with an id, a name, a description and at least one tag; pick the agent by skills and media modes.

Level 2: The card lists a gRPC entry first and a JSON-RPC entry second, and your client speaks only JSON-RPC. Which URL do you call? Expected: the JSON-RPC one, because the rule is the first entry that you support.
Level 2: How do media types reach the agent? Expected: the card's defaultInputModes and defaultOutputModes, a skill's own inputModes and outputModes, and a mediaType on each part the client sends.

Level 3: You hold a bearer token and the card sets extendedAgentCard. What changes? Expected: call GetExtendedAgentCard with the declared credential and use the fuller card in place of the cached public one for that session, or until the card's version changes.
wrongAnswers: "Read the top-level url field of the card." The current version moved the endpoint into supportedInterfaces, and there is no top-level url.
"Try the stream and fall back when it fails." The flag answers the question in advance. The failed call costs a round trip for nothing.
"Put the skill id in the message so the server runs that skill." No field of SendMessageRequest or Message names a skill. The list describes the agent.

questions.title: A team builds an MCP server for a project tracker. It has five capabilities: show the details of one issue, create an issue, a sprint review template, the project policy document, and close an issue. A developer proposes to publish each capability as a tool, a resource and a prompt at the same time, so that every client finds it. Which primitive do you give each capability, and why not all three?
questions.answer: Pick the primitive from who makes the choice. The model chooses a tool to perform an operation, so create and close are tools. A host or a user reads addressable content at a URI, so issue details and the policy are resources, and a user starts a prepared message workflow, so the review template is a prompt. Each extra surface costs discovery, authorization, caching, error handling, tests and documentation, so one capability gets one primitive.
followUps: Level 1: What makes a good resource URI? Expected: stable enough to bookmark, namespaced to the server, independent of a process id or connection, validated before storage access, and authorized on every read.

Level 2: A client wants to know when the policy document changes. Which mechanism does the current revision use? Expected: a client-opened subscriptions/listen request that names the URI in resourceSubscriptions; the event says the resource changed, and the client reads it again with resources/read.
Level 2: A client asks resources/read for a URI that does not exist. Do you return an empty document? Expected: no, return JSON-RPC -32602, so the client can tell absence from a valid empty document.

Level 3: When would you publish a resource template instead of listing every issue? Expected: when the list is large or unbounded; the template tells the client how to form a valid URI, and the server still parses the variables, authorizes, and uses typed storage queries.
wrongAnswers: "Make everything a tool so that the model can reach it." Content that a host reads is not an operation. It loses the URI contract, the cache hints and the user-controlled surface.
"Store the template as a resource because it lives in a file." Where the data is stored does not decide the primitive. A user starts the review, so it is a prompt.
"A prompt is policy that the host injects without the user knowing." Prompts exist for explicit user selection. Policy that the host enforces stays in the host at a higher priority.

questions.title: Your MCP server has a tool route_report that reads a report from an upstream source. A reviewer reads the handler and finds two things. When the upstream source is down, the handler returns a JSON-RPC error. When a client sends a tool name that the server does not know, the handler returns a result with isError: true. Is that the right way round?
questions.answer: No, both cases are backwards. A JSON-RPC error means the request could not be dispatched at all: an unknown tool name, a malformed envelope, missing request metadata or an invalid cursor. A complete result with isError: true means a valid call reached the tool and the tool reports a failure the model can act on, such as a source that is unavailable right now.
followUps: Level 1: A request arrives without the protocol version in params._meta. Which code? Expected: -32602, invalid params, never filled in from an earlier call.
Level 2: The tool publishes an output schema. Must an error result match it? Expected: yes; every complete result, with isError: true included, must return conforming structuredContent.

Level 2: Why does the host validate structuredContent instead of trusting the descriptor? Expected: a server can violate its own schema, a model cannot repair that, so the client validates before model use.

Level 3: A valid tool call has an argument that fails the input schema. Which layer? Expected: method parameters are invalid, so a JSON-RPC error; the capstone's TypeScript model instead returns a complete result with isError: true without invoking the executor, so name your choice and apply it everywhere.
wrongAnswers: "Return isError for everything so the model always gets text." A malformed envelope then looks like a tool failure, and the model retries a request that can never run.
"An unknown tool is a tool failure." The call never reached a tool, so it is a dispatch error at the protocol layer.
"An error result can skip the output schema." The flag classifies the outcome, and the published contract still holds.

questions.title: A client written for an older A2A release calls a current agent. Its first SendMessage carries only Host and Content-Type headers and gets HTTP 200 with a JSON-RPC error, code -32009. Its second call sends A2A-Version: 1.0, names the method message/send and gets code -32601. Explain both replies, and name the two changes the client needs.
questions.answer: Both replies are a current server reading an old client. An empty A2A-Version must be read as version 0.3, and an interface that serves only 1.0 answers VersionNotSupportedError; the recorded run reported the request as 0.3 (no header) against supported: 1.0. message/send is the old method name, and 1.0 uses the PascalCase rpc names such as SendMessage, so the second call is method-not-found. The client must send A2A-Version: 1.0 on every request and switch to the 1.0 names.
followUps: Level 2: Why send 1.0 and not the release 1.0.1? Expected: the version is Major.Minor; no patch number travels in requests, responses or cards.

Level 3: After the fix, the client's sends hang for the length of each task. Why? Expected: the old blocking default was false and the new returnImmediately default is also false, which now means wait; set it to true and poll or subscribe.
Level 3: Will every server reject a request that carries no version at all? Expected: no; one SDK never reads the header and another accepts its absence, so the client must send it on every call.

Level 4: You must serve both old and new clients for a quarter. What do you change on the server? Expected: turn on the SDK's 0.3 layer, add a second interface with protocolVersion 0.3 to the card, and route by header, method name or URL as that SDK does.
wrongAnswers: "HTTP 200 means the call worked." JSON-RPC errors arrive inside a 200 response; read the error member before result.
"Send the version as a query parameter instead." Both JSON bindings require the header, and the reference SDK reads only the header.
"The method name is case-insensitive." The names are exact PascalCase rpc names, and the old slash form is unknown to a 1.0 server.

questions.title: Your gateway pins each approved tool by hashing its description text. A connected server ships an update. The description is unchanged, but the inputSchema gains a destination field and destructiveHint flips to false. The pin passes, and the model begins calling the tool with the new argument. What went wrong, and how do you pin correctly?
questions.answer: The pin covered one field, so a schema and annotation change passed as unchanged. Canonicalize the complete descriptor with sorted keys, hash it, and store the digest under a qualified name together with publisher evidence and the approval time. On every refresh, quarantine an unknown key or a changed digest until a person re-approves it. Hash equality proves stability, not safety, so the first descriptor needs review too.
followUps: Level 2: What does a clean scanner result prove? Expected: nothing semantic; it is review evidence, not an innocence score.
Level 3: The server's serverInfo says it is the familiar publisher. How much trust does that buy? Expected: none; it is self-reported display data for logs, not a certificate or registry proof.
Level 3: The descriptor was poisoned on day one and the pin stored that digest. What catches it? Expected: review before the first approval, with the scanner as a tripwire; the hash cannot.

Level 4: How does a gateway stop the model from treating annotations as policy? Expected: annotations stay presentation hints; authorization binds the principal to the exact verb, resource and normalized arguments, and a consequential call needs action-bound approval.
wrongAnswers: "Hash the description; the schema is only typing." The schema decides which arguments the model can send, and a new field can route data to a new destination.
"A matching hash means the tool is safe." It means the descriptor did not change. A poisoned descriptor stays poisoned when pinned.
"Set destructiveHint and the host will confirm." Annotations are untrusted hints. The server enforces authorization and approval.

questions.title: A planner polls a remote agent with GetTask until a task is done. It stops when the state is completed, failed or canceled. Against a deploy agent, the loop never returns. Against a test runner, the planner deploys a build whose test suite had a failure. Explain both bugs.
questions.answer: The loop knows three terminal states, and there are four. The deploy agent rejected the task, and a task in TASK_STATE_REJECTED never changes again, so the loop spins forever. The test runner finished the work it was asked to do, so its task is TASK_STATE_COMPLETED even with a failing test, because the verdict is a result and results travel in artifacts.
followUps: Level 2: Which other states must the loop handle, and how? Expected: the two interrupted states; answer TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED with a message on the same task, and route TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED to an approver outside A2A while you subscribe or poll.

Level 3: You call CancelTask and get -32002. What next? Expected: call GetTask; canceled means an earlier cancel worked, another terminal state means the task ended first, and a running state means the server cannot stop it.

Level 3: The agent process crashed mid-task and your blocking send returned an error. Is the task failed? Expected: treat the outcome as unknown; the reference SDK stores the task as failed, but the client only saw an error, so read the task back.

Level 4: How do you continue a completed review with a changed diff? Expected: a new task with the same contextId, no taskId, and the old task in referenceTaskIds; a terminal task takes no more messages.
wrongAnswers: "Compare the state with the lower-case string completed." The current version sends enum names such as TASK_STATE_COMPLETED, and an unknown name must be an error, not a wait.
"A completed task means the tests passed." Completed means the agent finished the work it was asked to do. The verdict is in the artifact.
"Send another message to the rejected task and ask again." A terminal task refuses messages. Start a new task in the same context.

questions.title: A notes server wants a shared cache in front of it, so its resources/read results carry a public scope and a five-minute freshness hint. A security reviewer objects. What is the risk, which scope and freshness do you pick for a user's note, and what do you do with a result that must never be stored at all?
questions.answer: A public scope lets a shared cache hand one user's note to another user who asks for the same URI. Content bound to a user gets cacheScope: "private", which ties the entry to the requesting credential context, and a short freshness such as one minute. MCP defines only public and private, so a secret-bearing or fast-changing result gets private with ttlMs: 0, and the host adds a stricter no-store rule in its own cache policy.
followUps: Level 2: Why must resources/list return a stable order? Expected: so that equivalent responses produce stable cache keys and stable model context, and host UIs do not jump between refreshes.

Level 2: A client receives a cached list and wants to know when it changes. What does it do? Expected: open subscriptions/listen with the list-change category, and refetch after expiry or after an event.
Level 3: tools/list differs by principal because of per-user authorization. Which scope? Expected: private; per-user tool visibility must not sit behind a shared public cache.
Level 4: The team proposes cacheScope: "no-store". What do you answer? Expected: it is not an MCP value; return private with ttlMs: 0 and apply no-store in the host cache policy.
wrongAnswers: "A short TTL makes the public scope safe." Scope decides who may share an entry, and TTL decides for how long. One second of sharing still leaks the note.
"The cache hints are the authorization." They are freshness and sharing hints. The server authorizes every read on its own.
"Only tool lists need cache hints." Resource reads and discovery carry them too, and a user-specific read is where the private scope matters most.

questions.title: A client library exposes one cancel(request) method that behaves the same on stdio and on Streamable HTTP: it writes or POSTs a notifications/cancelled notification for the request id. Over HTTP, servers keep running the work and sometimes send a response after the cancel. A second method, cancelTask, returns success, the UI shows "stopped", and the worker keeps going. What is wrong with both methods?
questions.answer: Cancellation is transport-specific, and a durable task is a third thing. On stdio the client sends notifications/cancelled with the request id and receives no response. On Streamable HTTP the signal is closing that request's response stream, and a POSTed cancellation notification is the wrong signal. tasks/cancel acknowledges intent for a durable task that may stay working until a worker checkpoint observes the flag, so the UI must poll until a terminal status.
followUps: Level 2: The server receives a cancellation for a request that already finished. Does it return an error? Expected: no, it ignores the notification; a notification receives no response in any case.

Level 3: The worker commits a mutation just before the cancel reaches the server. What does each side do? Expected: the server has sent the response and ignores the late notification; the client ignores the late response, and the idempotency contract decides whether a retry is safe.
Level 3: When may a server itself send notifications/cancelled? Expected: on stdio only, to terminate a subscriptions/listen request; never for ordinary client calls.

Level 4: A subscriptions/listen stream drops mid-task. Does the Task behind it change state? Expected: no; the client opens a new listen request with a new id and refetches the Task, and durable state is untouched by the dropped stream.
wrongAnswers: "POST notifications/cancelled over HTTP too, for symmetry." Each HTTP request owns its response stream, and closing it is the signal that matches the request lifetime.
"A successful tasks/cancel means the worker stopped." It acknowledges the request. The task can stay working until a checkpoint, and the work can finish first.
"Return an error for a cancellation of an unknown request id." Unknown, malformed and completed cancellations are ignored by design.

questions.title: A platform team deploys an MCP server over Streamable HTTP behind a load balancer with two replicas. They configure sticky routing keyed on Mcp-Session-Id, keep a standalone GET /mcp stream for change notifications, and plan to resume a broken stream with Last-Event-ID. Which of these belong to the current revision, and what replaces the rest?
questions.answer: None of the three belongs to the current revision. The endpoint accepts POST only: GET /mcp and DELETE /mcp return 405, Mcp-Session-Id is ignored and never minted, and Last-Event-ID is ignored because streams do not resume. Change notifications arrive on a client-opened subscriptions/listen POST whose response stays open as SSE, and a dropped stream is replaced by a new listen request and a refetch of the affected data.
followUps: Level 2: How does a client cancel an in-flight request over this transport? Expected: it closes that request's response stream; there is no cancellation POST.
Level 3: Why is a startswith test on the trusted origin unsafe? Expected: it accepts an attacker-controlled suffix on the host name; match the canonical origin exactly.

Level 3: A dual-era client receives 405 from an unknown server. Does it fall back to the old GET endpoint? Expected: only after reading the body; a recognized modern JSON-RPC error proves the server is modern, and only an empty or unrecognized body justifies the legacy attempt.

Level 4: A workflow needs state across two calls on two replicas. Where does it live? Expected: behind a server-minted opaque handle in a shared store, returned as an ordinary result, bound to the principal, expired, and authorized on each use.
wrongAnswers: "Sticky routing is harmless, so keep it as a safety net." It hides a correctness bug until a rollout, a reschedule or a failover moves the next request to another replica.
"Add SSE event ids so that clients can resume." Modern streams are not resumable. A lost request is retried with a new id when the operation allows it.
"Origin validation authenticates the caller." It stops DNS rebinding only. A network service still authenticates and authorizes every request.

questions.title: A filesystem MCP server reads the client's Roots list once and treats any path under a root as authorized for deletion. The client advertises one workspace directory. Two delete requests arrive: one for a sibling directory whose name starts with the workspace name, and one that reaches the parent through an encoded dot-dot segment. What is wrong with this design, and how do you replace it?
questions.answer: Roots were informational guidance, never authorization and never a sandbox, and the current revision deprecates them. A string-prefix check accepts both hostile paths, because both begin with the workspace text. Replace the root with an explicit workspaceUri argument or a resource URI, then enforce three layers: authorize the principal for that workspace, normalize the URI and check containment by path components, and run the server under an operating-system sandbox.
followUps: Level 2: When is server configuration the right replacement? Expected: when one deployment owns one fixed workspace; per-call scope belongs in a workspaceUri argument.

Level 3: Why re-check containment immediately before the deletion? Expected: the live record can move outside the workspace between validation and mutation, and a race must not delete the wrong target.

Level 3: Why does lexical containment alone not stop a symlink escape? Expected: a link inside the boundary resolves to a path outside it, so the filesystem layer needs a symlink policy and resolution of the real path.

Level 4: A pinned legacy peer still sends roots/list. How do you serve it without weakening the modern handler? Expected: an isolated adapter that embeds the request in MRTR input requests, labelled legacy, with authorization and containment still enforced on the server.
wrongAnswers: "The client declared the root, so the server can trust the scope." A root is a self-reported hint. Authorization comes from the authenticated principal and server policy.
"Check startswith on the allowed URI." A sibling directory and an encoded traversal both pass. Normalize, then compare path components.
"An operating-system sandbox makes the authorization check unnecessary." The sandbox is the third layer for a compromised process. It does not decide which principal may touch which workspace.

questions.title: A colleague ports an MCP server from the 2025 revision. The port keeps the initialize handshake and stores the client's declared capabilities on the connection object for later requests. All the old tests pass.
