What breaks under the current revision, and where does the metadata have to live instead?
questions.answer: The current revision has no handshake and no protocol session. A server that remembers capabilities from an earlier message can apply the wrong permissions or the wrong wire shape to the next request, which may come from another client on the same process or land on another worker. Every request carries io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities in params._meta, and the server validates them on each request and forgets them after it answers.
followUps: Level 2: Is clientInfo required, and can you authorize on it? Expected: it is recommended, not required; it is display and debugging data and never a credential.
Level 2: A client sends tools/list without calling server/discover. Does the server reject it? Expected: no; the request carries its version and capabilities, so discovery is not a gate.
Level 3: What does closing stdin or ending an HTTP response terminate? Expected: transport activity only; there is no protocol session to end, and the next request must still describe itself.

Level 4: Where does a multi-step workflow keep its state now? Expected: behind a server-minted opaque handle in a shared durable store, returned as a normal result, bound to the authenticated principal, expired, and authorized on every use.
wrongAnswers: "Stateless means the server cannot keep any state at all." Durable application state behind an explicit handle is allowed. Only hidden protocol context is removed.
"Send initialize first to be safe with every server." A current server must not receive initialize by default. Legacy is a documented fallback for a pinned peer.
"The connection identifies the client, so one capability check per connection is enough." Two clients can share one process or HTTP worker in sequence, and a remote request can land on any replica.

questions.title: Over Streamable HTTP, a client calls charge_account. A reverse proxy buffers the response stream, the client reaches its timeout and disconnects, and the server commits the charge a moment later. The client sends the call again with a fresh JSON-RPC id, and the customer is charged twice. The team proposes to deduplicate on the JSON-RPC id. Design the fix.
questions.answer: A JSON-RPC id correlates one message and never identifies a business operation, so two ids are two charges to the server. Add an application idempotency key to the arguments, and make the server store the key, a fingerprint of the arguments and the committed result in one atomic durable transaction. The same key with the same arguments returns the stored result, and the same key with different arguments is rejected.
followUps: Level 3: The same key arrives with a different cents value. What happens? Expected: the server compares the argument fingerprint and rejects the call, because one key must not alias two business intents.

Level 3: Two workers see the key missing at the same instant. What prevents two charges? Expected: the key claim, the effect and the result commit in one atomic durable transaction; a check-then-write sequence cannot.

Level 4: The charge is executed by an external payment provider. Does the local ledger make it atomic? Expected: no; either the provider accepts the same idempotency key, or a transactional outbox bridges the local commit to the remote effect.

Level 4: The client reconnects a dropped subscriptions/listen stream. Does it resend the lost charge? Expected: no; it opens a new listen request, refetches authoritative state, deduplicates by stable identifiers, and never replays an unsafe mutation because a response was lost.
wrongAnswers: "Deduplicate on the JSON-RPC id." Ids correlate messages, and a retry carries a new id by design.
"Set idempotentHint and let clients retry freely." Annotations are untrusted hints. The application contract and the ledger decide retry safety.
"Check the key, run the charge, then store the result." Two workers can both miss the key, and a crash between the effect and the store leaves the retry ambiguous.

questions.title: Your client watches a long test run over SendStreamingMessage. After four frames the connection drops, while the agent keeps working and appends more lines to the log artifact. Design the recovery: how the client learns what it missed, how it rebuilds the log, and how it knows when to stop reconnecting.
questions.answer: Nothing is replayed, because a stream is a live view and the specification defines no cursor. The client calls SubscribeToTask with the task id, and the first frame must be a Task snapshot that already holds every chunk written while the client was away. The client replaces its partial artifact with the snapshot's copy and appends the frames that follow. When a later subscribe answers UnsupportedOperationError, the task is terminal, so the client stops reconnecting and reads the final task with GetTask.
followUps: Level 3: Why replace the artifact from the snapshot instead of merging? Expected: missed chunks never replay and the snapshot is the stored copy, so a merge would duplicate parts.

Level 3: The stream closes right after a status frame in TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED. Is the task over? Expected: no; the close ended the reading, so call GetTask and answer the question on the same task.

Level 4: The last status message said "done" but no terminal state arrived before the close. What do you trust? Expected: the state from GetTask; a task is finished only when a terminal state is recorded, never on the close or on prose.

Level 4: How does lastChunk relate to the end of the task? Expected: it closes one artifact only; the recorded stream carried two more frames after a lastChunk, and a canceled task can store an artifact that never got one.
wrongAnswers: "Reconnect with a last event id so that the server replays." The specification defines no cursor and no replay. SubscribeToTask starts with a snapshot instead.
"The close means the task finished." Servers close at different states. Confirm the state with GetTask before you stop.
"Keep the chunks you had and append the snapshot's." That duplicates parts. The snapshot replaces your copy, and the following frames append.

questions.title: A test run outlasts any connection your planner can hold open, so you want a webhook. Compare a webhook with polling and with streaming for this case. Then list the receiver's duties, given that the agent promises only to try each delivery at least once, and that the config operations return the stored webhook credentials to anyone who can call them.
questions.answer: Register the config inline in SendMessage with returnImmediately: true, so that no event escapes before the config exists, and close the connection. Delivery is at least once, so a notification can arrive twice or, after an outage, not at all: the receiver answers 2xx, checks the task id, processes idempotently, and reads the task with GetTask before it acts. Put the secret your receiver checks in authentication, because token has no standard header, and restrict who can call the four config operations, because a read returns the credentials in clear.
followUps: Level 3: An artifactUpdate with append: true arrives twice. Why can you not apply it twice? Expected: it duplicates parts, and there is no delivery id to deduplicate on, so read the task instead.
Level 3: The receiver was down for a minute. What did it miss? Expected: possibly everything, because no SDK retries; read the task when the receiver returns.

Level 4: Why must the agent reject a webhook URL inside a private range? Expected: the agent calls that URL for every later event of the task, so an outside caller could aim the agent's requests at an internal service.
Level 4: Who may call ListTaskPushNotificationConfigs, and why? Expected: only the task's owner, because the reply returns credentials and token unchanged.
wrongAnswers: "Register the webhook after the task starts with the create operation." Events before the config exists are lost. Inline registration leaves no gap.
"Authenticate on the token header." The specification gives token no transport, and the SDKs use two header names. Put the secret in authentication and check Authorization.
"Apply each notification as it arrives." Duplicates and lost deliveries both happen. The stored task is the source of truth.

questions.title: A document MCP server runs as two replicas behind a load balancer. Its draft_create tool keeps the new draft in a dictionary inside the process and returns {"ok": true}. The next call, draft_append, fails about half the time with "no draft", and the failures stop when the operator turns on sticky routing. Explain the failure, say why the operator's fix is wrong, and redesign the two tools.
questions.answer: The first call created the draft in the memory of one replica and returned no name for it, because the design assumed the connection identifies the draft. The second call is a fresh POST that can land on the other replica, which has valid protocol metadata and no way to load the draft. Sticky routing hides the bug until a restart, a rollout or a failover moves the next request. Return a server-minted opaque handle from draft_create, keep the draft in a shared durable store, and make draft_append take the handle as an ordinary argument.
followUps: Level 3: Where may replica memory still be used? Expected: as a cache of the stored record, never as the only copy required for correctness.
Level 3: How do you test that the fix holds? Expected: alternate replicas for consecutive calls and run many concurrent requests; every append must find its draft without affinity.

Level 4: What does the handle need beyond being random? Expected: binding to the authenticated principal and tenant, expiry, authorization on each use, and concurrency plus idempotency rules for appends.

Level 4: Why not carry the draft in requestState instead of a store? Expected: requestState suits a short input-required continuation; a durable draft needs shared persistence, and a client-echoed value is not storage.
wrongAnswers: "Sticky routing fixed it, so ship it." Affinity breaks on restart, rollout, reschedule or failover. Correctness must not depend on which replica answers.

"Replicate the dictionary between the two processes." That hides protocol context in a store as a substitute for the removed session. The fix is an explicit handle and shared storage the client can name.
"Use Mcp-Session-Id to find the draft." The current revision ignores that header and never mints it.

questions.title: A gateway in front of an MCP server authorizes each tools/call by reading the Mcp-Name header and checking it against the caller's role. The origin server behind it executes params.name from the JSON body. An attacker sends Mcp-Name: notes.read with a body whose params.name is notes.delete. The gateway also rejects an unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version before it looks at anything else. Walk through what happens, and give the validation order you would ship.
questions.answer: The gateway approves a read while the origin runs a delete, because two components decide from two different fields. Ship one fixed order: validate the JSON-RPC and metadata types, compare every mirrored header with the body, and only after equality is proven check whether the matched version is supported. A disagreement is HTTP 400 with -32020 even when one of the two version values is unsupported, so the request dies before a backend is selected, a role is checked or a rate-limit token is spent.
followUps: Level 3: Header and body both say version 2027-01-01. Which response? Expected: HTTP 400 with -32022 and data {"supported":["2026-07-28"],"requested":"2027-01-01"}.

Level 3: Mcp-Name carries a resource URI with non-ASCII characters. How does the server compare it? Expected: the client sends the exact base64 UTF-8 sentinel, and the server decodes it before comparing with params.uri.

Level 4: Why must the mismatch check run before a rate-limit token is consumed? Expected: a rejected request should cost nothing and leave its own evidence; otherwise an attacker spends quota or triggers policy against the wrong object.

Level 4: The attacker's request also carries a valid bearer token. Does that change the outcome? Expected: no; the wire validation fails first, and authentication tells you who sent a malformed request, not that it may run.
wrongAnswers: "Trust the header, because the gateway routes on it." The body is what executes. The two must be proven equal before either is used for a decision.
"Check version support first so that bad clients fail fast." A mismatch must return -32020 even when a version is unsupported; support is checked only after equality.
"Header values are case-insensitive like header names." Values are case-sensitive, and a name that differs in case is a different name.

questions.title: Your agent host launches several MCP servers over stdio. One is current. One is an old archive server that understands only initialize. One is current but slow to start. A teammate proposes a simple rule: send server/discover, and on any error or timeout send initialize. Design the startup so that the slow server is never downgraded and the archive server still works.
questions.answer: Treat an ambiguous signal as ambiguous. A timeout, a connection close, an empty response or an unrecognized error does not identify an era, so the client fails closed unless that exact peer is configured with allow_legacy=True. A recognized modern error such as -32022 proves the server is current and forbids initialize. For the archive peer on the allowlist, send one initialize under a transport-enforced deadline and select the legacy era only after a structurally valid positive result.
followUps: Level 3: The allowlisted archive peer answers -32022 to discovery. Which era? Expected: current; a recognized modern error forbids the legacy probe, so choose from data.supported and retry with a new request id.
Level 3: The initialize probe times out. What state is the peer in? Expected: unknown and unavailable; no era is selected and notifications/initialized is never sent.

Level 4: A legacy server accepts tools/list before initialization. Why does that make discovery-first safer on stdio? Expected: the ambiguous success would hide the era; server/discover creates a clean era boundary before any operation.

Level 4: The archive process crashes and restarts. Do you reuse the cached legacy era? Expected: no; discard the peer-era cache, rediscover, relist, reopen subscriptions, and retry only safe operations with new ids.
wrongAnswers: "Any error from discovery means the server is old." A malformed request, an overloaded server, a dead process and an old server can all produce the same timeout or close.
"Send initialize first; a current server will reject it." Sending initialize to a current server is a downgrade and must never be the default path.
"A method-not-found error proves the server is legacy." It only makes an allowlisted peer eligible for one bounded probe; the positive evidence is a valid initialize result.

questions.title: A tool that deletes notes, notes_delete, finds three notes that match the title the user gave. Design the confirmation flow under the current MCP revision: how the server asks the user to pick one and confirm, how the answer comes back, and what stops a client from answering a different question or replaying one confirmation with changed arguments.
questions.answer: The server answers with a result typed input_required that embeds an elicitation/create form request listing the three candidate ids and a confirm boolean, plus an integrity-protected requestState. The client shows the form and retries the original tools/call with a new request id, echoing requestState and the inputResponses. The server signs the state over the principal, the method, a digest of the arguments, the candidate set, the phase and an expiry, verifies the echo, checks that the chosen id was in the signed set, re-authorizes the workspace and re-checks containment, and consumes a one-time nonce in a shared replay store before it deletes.
followUps: Level 3: The client declares {"elicitation": {"url": {}}} only. What does the server do? Expected: return -32021 with the required form capability in data; it must not embed a mode the current request did not declare.

Level 3: The user dismisses the dialog. Which action, and what happens to the state? Expected: cancel; nothing is mutated and the state stays retryable until it expires, unlike decline, which is terminal.

Level 4: Two server instances share the note store. How do you stop both from executing one confirmation? Expected: a shared replay store with an atomic nonce claim coupled to the mutation; the lesson's test runs two server objects against one state.
Level 4: A note moves outside the workspace after the form was shown. What catches it? Expected: the live record check and the containment re-check before mutation, not the signed state alone.
wrongAnswers: "Keep the candidate list in server memory keyed by the connection." There is no session, and the retry can reach any instance. The candidates travel inside the signed state.
"The host validated the form, so the server can trust the content." The client controls everything it sends. The server validates the schema and the candidate set again.
"Ask for the user's password in the form as the confirmation." Form mode must not carry secrets. An external credential flow uses URL mode and binds the browser user to the same principal.

questions.title: You run the official A2A conformance kit against your server twice. The first run scores 32.3 percent. After a two-line change to the kit's own JSON-RPC client, the second run scores 66.7 percent: 62 PASS, 31 FAIL, 11 SKIPPED and 25 NOT TESTED of 129 requirements. Your manager asks how conformant the server is. Estimate the real figure and defend every adjustment you make.
questions.answer: Neither percentage measures the server alone. The first run lost 63 of 85 JSON-RPC records because the kit posted to the card URL with a trailing slash, which is the kit's defect. In the second run, 21 of the failures are skips inside a test body that the tagged kit records as FAIL, so under the main-branch rule the run reads 62 PASS, 10 FAIL and 32 SKIPPED, or 86.1 percent, and of those ten failures three belonged to the server: the missing REST push routes and, at SHOULD level, the missing Cache-Control and ETag on the card.
followUps: Level 3: Why do the percentages leave out the SKIPPED and NOT TESTED rows? Expected: those rows carry no verdict, so a percentage over them would reward a card that declares few capabilities.

Level 4: The push requirements pass on one binding and fail on the other. How do you classify that? Expected: a kit defect, because the JSON field names must be camelCase and the kit sends task_id; keep the requirement as passing in your own ledger with the evidence.
Level 4: What did the one real failure teach about cards? Expected: a capability flag is a promise for every declared binding, so the REST side needed the four push routes the card advertised.

Level 4: Which checks do you add that the kit lacks? Expected: owner scoping of tasks, a resent messageId, append to an unknown artifact, the REST subscribe verb, and pagination with the returned token.
wrongAnswers: "Report the second percentage as the conformance figure." It counts kit skips as failures and the kit's snake_case parameters as your bugs.
"Report full conformance after fixing the missing routes." The two SHOULD gaps remain, and a quarter of the requirements were never tested.
"The kit is the specification." It departs from the canonical error table in six places; the specification wins, and the kit's README itself calls SHOULD an expected failure.

questions.title: Take-home. Build the admission module of an MCP gateway. It takes the tools/list results of several servers and produces an admitted set, a rejected set and an audit trail. It must page through every list completely, pin each descriptor, qualify names before it merges, reject a descriptor that mirrors a sensitive parameter into a header or places x-mcp-header anywhere but a direct top-level property, validate structured results against output schemas on the invoke path, and emit header audit events that carry names and never values. Describe your design, the tests you ship, and the evidence a reviewer should expect.
questions.answer: Run the five gates in order and keep them separate. Discover with an opaque cursor loop that stops only when nextCursor is absent or null; admit each descriptor against a canonical whole-descriptor digest, a full schema-tree walk for x-mcp-header, and a sensitive-name policy; qualify every tool as <server>.<tool> before the merge; and validate structuredContent against the published output schema before anything reaches the model. Tests prove that one rejected descriptor does not block valid tools, that an empty-string cursor continues, that an annotation under oneOf, items or $ref is rejected, and that a changed inputSchema fails the pin. The evidence is the page trace, the admitted and rejected sets, the digest ledger and redacted audit events.
followUps: Level 3: Why not stop pagination when a page's tools array is empty? Expected: emptiness is the server's choice; continue while nextCursor is present and not null.

Level 4: Two servers return byte-identical descriptors under different names. What does the ledger hold? Expected: two qualified keys with two digests; the same digest under different keys is fine, and a different digest under the same key is the rug pull.
Level 4: The scanner flags a legitimate warning sentence in a description. What happens? Expected: review, not automatic rejection; the scanner is a tripwire and a human approves the full descriptor.

Level 4: A descriptor passes every check and is poisoned from day one. What catches it? Expected: nothing automatic; the design needs a review queue before the first pin, because hash equality proves stability and not safety.
wrongAnswers: "Hash the description; schemas rarely change." Schema and annotation changes are the rug pull; pin the whole canonical descriptor.
"Trust the server's deterministic order and skip the sort." Local registry order must not depend on process startup timing; sort before you merge.
"Log header values to make debugging easier." A mirrored value can be routing data or, in a bad descriptor, a secret; audit names and rejection categories only.

questions.title: You deploy a remote MCP server that accepts tokens from two authorization servers, one for staff and one for partners. Design the client enrollment, the per-request token validation and the key handling so that three things hold: a token minted for a sibling MCP server is refused, a signing key rotation causes no outage, and a client steered to a hostile token endpoint never hands over its authorization code.
questions.answer: Publish RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata that names both issuers, and treat that list as the issuer allow-list. Enroll a client with its pre-registered credentials when it has an explicit relationship with that issuer, otherwise with a Client ID Metadata Document when the issuer advertises support, and use deprecated dynamic registration only as an explicit fallback with the correct application_type. On every request validate the pinned iss, an aud equal to this server's canonical resource URI, exp and the scope the tool needs; answer 401 for an invalid token and 403 with insufficient_scope for a valid token that lacks the scope. Refresh the JWKS on a schedule and re-fetch once on an unknown kid, and let the client record the issuer before it redirects and compare the RFC 9207 iss in the authorization response exactly before it redeems the code.
followUps: Level 3: Why is a per-connection token check not enough? Expected: there is no protocol session; every request carries its own bearer token and is validated on its own.

Level 3: A scope step-up is needed for one tool. What does the server return? Expected: 403 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope" naming the scope and the resource_metadata URL; the client obtains consent and retries with a new request id.

Level 4: Two concurrent step-ups produce two tokens with different scopes. Which does the validator use? Expected: the token presented on the request, never a lookup of "the user's current scope", which would open a time-of-check race.

Level 4: The partner issuer changes its issuer URL in discovery. What may the client reuse? Expected: only a portable CIMD URL; prior issuer-minted credentials, registration tokens and access tokens are refused, and the client re-enrolls.
wrongAnswers: "Any token from our own identity provider is fine." A token minted for a sibling server passes the issuer check; only the audience check refuses it.
"Fetch the JWKS once at boot." The validator rejects every token after the next rotation until a restart; refresh on a schedule and once on a miss.
"Fall back to dynamic registration when CIMD validation fails." A security failure must not select a weaker enrollment path; the fallback is an explicit configuration decision.

topics.title: Multi-agent systems
topics.about: Supervisors, handoffs, shared memory, consensus and the failure modes of agent teams.

questions.title: Compare hierarchical supervisor architectures with peer-to-peer agent choreography in multi-agent systems. How do you prevent deadlocks?
questions.answer: In multi-agent systems, agents must coordinate to complete complex workflows. In a hierarchical supervisor architecture, a central coordinator agent receives the primary user request, decomposes it into sub-tasks, assigns work to specialized worker agents, synthesizes their results, and maintains global state. Communication is strictly vertical: workers report only to the supervisor. In peer-to-peer agent choreography, agents communicate directly with each other via message buses or direct calls without a central controller, negotiating responsibilities dynamically. Supervisor patterns provide predictable execution, centralized budget tracking, and deterministic debugging, but the supervisor can become a reasoning and token bottleneck. Peer-to-peer patterns allow organic problem solving, but risk circular message storms and deadlocks where Agent A waits for Agent B while Agent B waits for Agent A. To prevent deadlocks, we enforce strict acyclic message graphs using hop counters and timeout deadlines. The trade-off is coordination predictability versus emergent autonomy: supervisors guarantee deterministic completion, while peer choreography offers flexibility for collaborative research tasks.
followUps: How do you implement distributed cycle detection across asynchronous peer agent message queues?
When does a supervisor agent decide to replace an underperforming worker agent rather than retrying?
wrongAnswers: Allowing peer agents to send unbounded synchronous messages to each other without timeouts, leading to circular deadlocks.
Treating multi-agent coordination as a single un-partitioned prompt where all agent personae speak in a shared context window.
tradeOffs: Hierarchical supervisors eliminate circular deadlocks and simplify trace debugging, but create a single point of failure and higher token overhead.
Peer choreography allows flexible emergent problem solving, but requires distributed deadlock detection and hop budgets.
keyPoints: Supervisors decompose tasks, delegate and maintain global state.
Peer choreography communicates directly without a central controller.
Supervisors can bottleneck while peer messaging risks storms and deadlocks.
Bound peer communication with hop counters and timeout deadlines.

questions.title: How does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardize cross-agent tool discovery and execution compared to bespoke JSON-RPC schemas?
questions.answer: When multiple agents collaborate across distributed services, integrating tools using custom JSON-RPC schemas creates an exponential integration problem: every agent framework requires custom glue code to discover and invoke another framework's tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes three core primitives over JSON-RPC transports: Tools, Resources, and Prompts. Tools define executable functions with strict JSON Schema arguments; Resources expose read-only contextual data like files and documentation; Prompts provide standardized parameterized workflow templates. When an agent connects to an MCP server, it invokes tools/list to dynamically discover available capabilities, their schemas, and required permissions without hardcoded client integrations. The client handles execution isolation and security approval, while the server executes the action. The trade-off is protocol framing overhead versus ecosystem modularity: MCP adds a layer of standardized JSON-RPC framing, but it allows any agent runtime to immediately use any tool server across organizations with zero custom adapter code.
followUps: What is the difference between MCP Server-Sent Events (SSE) transports and standard stdio transports?
How do you enforce authentication and access control when an agent calls an external remote MCP server?
wrongAnswers: Hardcoding custom HTTP endpoints and ad-hoc schemas for every single tool in each agent codebase, creating technical debt.
Assuming MCP allows tools to execute code directly inside the host LLM without external runtime sandboxes.
tradeOffs: MCP provides standardized, dynamic tool discovery and uniform permission models, enabling plug-and-play tool integration across vendors.
Standardized protocol abstractions introduce minor JSON-RPC serialization overhead compared to direct in-process function pointers.
keyPoints: MCP standardizes Tools, Resources and Prompts over JSON-RPC.
Discover tool capabilities and schemas through tools/list.
Clients handle isolation and approval while servers execute actions.
Standard framing adds overhead but reduces custom integration code.

questions.title: How do you propagate distributed trace contexts across asynchronous multi-agent delegation trees using OpenTelemetry?
questions.answer: When an agent delegates a task to multiple subagents across message queues or asynchronous HTTP calls, debugging failures without distributed tracing is nearly impossible. A bug in a third-tier subagent appears as an opaque failure in the top-level supervisor. We implement distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry context propagation. When the root agent receives a request, it initializes a root span with a unique trace ID. When delegating a task to another agent, the client injects standard W3C Trace Context headers—traceparent and tracestate—into the outgoing message payload or HTTP headers. The recipient subagent extracts these headers and starts a child span linked directly to the parent span. In the span metadata, we record the agent's role, the prompt token count, tool execution parameters, and model completion tokens. The trade-off is telemetry overhead versus operational visibility: trace propagation adds small payload headers and requires centralized trace storage, but it visualizes the entire execution waterfall, isolating the exact subagent that stalled or hallucinated.
followUps: How do you correlate distributed traces with financial cost and token consumption metrics per tenant?
What happens to trace context when an agent execution is suspended for hours awaiting human approval?
wrongAnswers: Logging agent execution using isolated, un-correlated log lines with no shared trace ID, making it impossible to reconstruct call trees.
Passing trace context in the conversational prompt text where the LLM can alter or erase trace headers.
tradeOffs: OpenTelemetry context propagation makes complex asynchronous agent graphs visible and debuggable, but increases telemetry storage volume.
Logging full prompts and tool outputs inside trace spans provides rich debugging, but requires strict PII scrubbing to prevent data leakage.
keyPoints: Start a root span and propagate W3C trace context on delegation.
Subagents extract headers and create linked child spans.
Record roles, token counts and tool parameters in span metadata.
Centralized tracing adds overhead but exposes stalled subagent calls.

questions.title: How do you implement optimistic concurrency control and file locks when multiple agents collaborate on a shared codebase workspace?
questions.answer: When multiple autonomous agents work simultaneously in a shared workspace—such as one agent writing unit tests while another refactors application code—uncontrolled concurrent writes cause race conditions where one agent silently overwrites another agent's edits. We implement optimistic concurrency control backed by cryptographic file hashing. Before an agent begins editing a file, it reads the content and captures its SHA-256 hash as a version tag. When the agent finishes generating its changes and submits the update, the execution runtime checks whether the current file on disk still matches the original version tag. If the hash matches, the write commits atomically and the version updates. If another agent modified the file in the interim, the hash check fails: the runtime rejects the write, returns a concurrency conflict error, and provides the current file diff to the agent, prompting it to re-apply its changes on top of the latest version. The trade-off is merge retry overhead versus workspace integrity: optimistic concurrency allows parallel agent collaboration with zero lock contention, but highly active files require retry handling when conflicts occur.
followUps: How do you handle workspace conflicts when an agent renames or deletes a file that another agent is editing?
How can operational transformation or Git-style three-way merging automate conflict resolution for non-overlapping edits?
wrongAnswers: Allowing multiple agents to write directly to shared disk files with no version checks or locks, corrupting codebases.
Holding long-lived exclusive file locks across multi-minute LLM generation steps, causing severe multi-agent pipeline stalls.
tradeOffs: Optimistic concurrency control allows multiple agents to work in parallel without blocking locks, but requires agents to handle write conflict retries.
Pessimistic file locking prevents conflict retries, but can cause agents to sit idle waiting for locks to release.
keyPoints: Capture the file's SHA-256 hash before editing.
Check the original version hash before an atomic write.
Reject conflicts and provide the current diff for reapplication.
Optimistic concurrency avoids locks but requires conflict retries.

questions.title: A new multi-agent framework ships every few months, each with its own vocabulary. Give the method you use to understand a new one quickly, and name the part of every such system where the hard bugs live.
questions.answer: Map the framework onto four primitives: the agent, the handoff, the shared state and the orchestrator. Every framework picks a default on each axis, and the rest is surface syntax. The agent is a system prompt plus tools and is stateless, the handoff is a structured transfer of control, the orchestrator decides who runs next, and the shared state is the only stateful part of the system. That is where the difficult bugs sit: memory poisoning, message ordering, versioning and write contention.
followUps: Level 1: Two agents have the same prompt and the same tools. How do they differ? Expected: they do not, because everything that looks like per-agent state is in the shared state or the handoff.

Level 2: Name the three ways a handoff is implemented. Expected: a tool that returns the next agent, a graph edge selected by a condition, and a selector function that picks the next speaker from a pool.
Level 2: Full pool or projected state, which scales further and what does it cost? Expected: projected state scales further, and it costs an up-front schema so that each role's view is defined.
Level 3: Before adopting a framework, what do you write first? Expected: its four-primitive mapping, and if you cannot write it, the docs are incomplete or the framework is inventing a primitive.
wrongAnswers: "Each framework has its own architecture, so learn them one at a time." The architectures are points in one four-axis space, and learning the axes once reads every release.
"The agents hold the memory." The agent is stateless by definition, and memory lives in the shared state or in the handoff payload.
"The orchestrator is the smart part, so pick the framework with the best one." The orchestrator is a scheduler with four flavors, and the choice depends on how much you trust the model to route.

questions.title: Your single agent does well on small tasks. Pointed at a codebase of 200 files in three languages, with tests that need infrastructure and an external API to research first, it stops making progress. The team proposes a model with a bigger window. What is the ceiling it hit, and would a bigger window remove it?
questions.answer: The task exceeds what one loop, one window and one system prompt can carry, and a bigger window only moves one of three limits. Context saturates as tool results pile up, so details from an early turn are gone by turn 30, and one prompt that asks the model to research, code, review and test produces an agent that does each one poorly. One loop reads file A, then B, then C, with no parallelism. The fix for all three is to split the work so that each agent has one job, one window and one prompt.
followUps: Level 1: Which of the three limits does parallelism address? Expected: the sequential bottleneck only, because reading three files at once does not shrink any one window or sharpen any one prompt.

Level 2: Why does a specialized prompt improve each stage? Expected: a prompt that covers one role can be specific about inputs, outputs and what to ignore, while a prompt for four roles has to be generic.
Level 2: What is the cost that the split always adds? Expected: more total tokens, because each agent is a separate model call, plus latency and coordination logic.
Level 3: Where does information get lost in a multi-agent split? Expected: at every agent boundary, where one agent's full context is compressed into a message for the next.
wrongAnswers: "A bigger context window solves it." The window moves one limit and leaves role confusion and the serial loop untouched.
"A longer, more detailed system prompt covers the roles." A single prompt that covers four roles is the cause of role confusion, not the cure.
"Always split, because specialists are better." Below about 20 tool calls and 100k tokens, the split adds cost and bugs for no gain.

questions.title: A research system with one lead agent and several worker agents beat a single agent on an internal evaluation by a wide margin. Explain the mechanism, and say which single variable explains most of the gain.
questions.answer: The lead plans and decomposes the question, each worker gets a fresh window for one narrow sub-question, and the lead synthesizes the worker summaries without ever reading the raw sources. Three mechanisms carry the gain: fresh context per worker, a narrow prompt per role, and workers that run at the same time. The variable that explains most of it is total token usage, which the lesson's source puts at 80 percent of the variance on one browsing benchmark. A worker that does not carry the lead's planning tokens has room to read.
followUps: Level 1: Why does the lead not read the raw sources? Expected: so that its window stays free for planning and synthesis, and so that each source is read once by the worker who owns it.
Level 2: When does the pattern lose to a pipeline? Expected: when step two needs step one's output, because then there is no parallel work and the extra agents only add tokens.
Level 2: What does the lead do when two workers disagree? Expected: it re-asks or notes the disagreement in the answer, and never picks one side in silence.

Level 3: A worker drifts beyond its sub-question. What stops it? Expected: an explicit scope in its prompt, a timeout at about twice the median worker runtime, and a token cap, after which the lead re-spawns with a narrower question or proceeds without it.
wrongAnswers: "The lead is a bigger model, so it is smarter." The gain tracks token usage, and the workers do the reading; a bigger lead alone changes nothing about context.
"Multi-agent is cheaper because workers are small." It costs about 15 times the tokens, and it is worth it only when the task value covers that.
"Give the lead the raw sources too, so it can check the workers." That fills the lead's window with what the workers already read and removes the fresh-context advantage.

questions.title: Three agents share a memory on a research task. A retrieval agent reads a page and writes that a study found a 42 percent improvement. The page says 4.2 percent. A summarizer builds on the entry, an analyst recommends adoption on the strength of the number, and the final report cites it. No agent crashed and no test failed. What is this failure called, why is it structural, and what are the three changes that stop it?
questions.answer: This is memory poisoning. One agent's hallucination entered the shared state, and every agent downstream read it as a verified fact, so the error was turned into evidence as it moved. It is structural because any shared memory without provenance and without an independent verifier will do this eventually. The three changes are provenance on every write, an append-only log where corrections supersede instead of overwrite, and at least one read-only verifier that re-fetches sources and reports on a separate channel.
followUps: Level 2: Why does provenance help a reader who cannot re-fetch the source? Expected: the reader can see that one claim rests on one retrieval with no citation, and weigh it lower than a claim with a source and a verifier flag.

Level 2: What does the analyst do when it sees a flag on the entry it depends on? Expected: it withholds the recommendation or writes it with the flag attached, and the final report carries a retraction instead of the number.

Level 3: Which of the three changes would topic partitioning of the memory replace? Expected: none, because partitions limit which agents read an entry, and a poisoned entry in one topic still poisons everyone subscribed to it.

Level 3: The verifier itself hallucinates a mismatch. What is the damage? Expected: a false flag on a correct entry, which a human on the verification channel can clear, and no new false fact in the pool because the verifier cannot write.
wrongAnswers: "Add a line to every prompt that says to verify numbers." The summarizer and the analyst had no source to verify against, only the shared entry, and a prompt does not give them one.
"Let the verifier correct the entry in place." An in-place correction destroys the audit trail and gives the verifier a write handle that a poisoned pool can turn against it.
"Switch from a shared pool to passing messages." Messages are shared state with extra copying, and a wrong number in a message poisons the receiver the same way.

questions.title: A team added an ensemble to a question-answering task: five agents on the same model debate until they agree, then answer. Accuracy fell below the single agent. They want to add more agents. What went wrong, and what would you change first?
questions.answer: Whether debate helps depends on structure, not on the count: who talks to whom, how many rounds, whether the agents are different, and whether anyone argues against. Five copies of one model share their errors, so the vote is correlated, and debate until agreement rewards the most confident agent through conformity. Change the composition before the count: start from self-consistency with one strong model, then swap one agent for a different base model, bound the rounds at two or three, and add a judge that does not vote.
followUps: Level 2: Why does adding a sixth copy of the same model not help? Expected: it adds one more correlated sample, so the shared bias gets one more vote.
Level 2: What does the judge do that the voters cannot? Expected: it scores the final consensus without having taken a position, so conformity pressure does not move it.

Level 3: When is plain self-consistency the right final answer? Expected: a simple task with a clean ground truth, where five samples of one strong model are as accurate as any ensemble and far cheaper.

Level 3: The task is opinion-shaped. What happens to the vote? Expected: agents converge on the most confident-looking answer rather than the most correct one, so a vote is an opinion poll and should be labeled as one.
wrongAnswers: "Add more agents until the vote stabilizes." A stable wrong vote is still wrong, and past about four agents on a graph the cost grows faster than the quality.
"Let them debate until they agree, because agreement means confidence." Unbounded debate rewards conformity, and the agreed answer is the loudest one, not the right one.
"Use the same model at different temperatures for diversity." That is self-consistency, and the systematic bias of the model survives every temperature.

questions.title: A paper reports that its multi-agent coding system beats single agents by a wide margin on a well-known software engineering benchmark. Your team wants to adopt the architecture. What do you ask before you believe the number?
questions.answer: Ask which benchmark and which split, whether the benchmark was released after the model's training cutoff, what the comparison baseline was, how many trials were run, how many task types were covered, and what the result cost in tokens and wall-clock. The split matters most: frontier models score about 23 percent on the uncontaminated split of that benchmark against more than 70 percent on the older split, so a number without its split says nothing.
followUps: Level 2: Why compare a coordination system against random guessing? Expected: if the system cannot beat random by a wide margin, the task may be ill-posed, as the multimodal coordination results showed.
Level 2: What does milestone achievement measure that final success does not? Expected: partial progress, so a system that gets most of the way is distinguished from one that fails at the start.

Level 3: How do you check contamination yourself? Expected: compare the benchmark's release date with the model's training cutoff, and withhold a slice of tasks from any tuning set in your own evaluations.

Level 3: The paper's score is reported without a primary source from the model's vendor. How do you treat it? Expected: as preliminary, and you do not make a production decision on it until an independent run reproduces it.
wrongAnswers: "A wide margin on a known benchmark is enough to adopt." Without the split, the baseline, the trials and the cost, the margin is a headline, not evidence.
"Multi-agent always helps on coding tasks." The medical and multimodal results show domains where it did not, and the coding gain depends on the split and the scaffolding.
"Our internal benchmark is less rigorous than a public one." A public benchmark informs, and only an internal one reflects your production distribution and your cost constraints.

questions.title: A team proposes a five-agent pipeline, with a planner, a retriever, a writer, a critic and a formatter, for a summarization feature that one agent handles today in a dozen tool calls. The argument is that specialists produce better output. How do you decide, and what will the pipeline cost that the slide does not show?
questions.answer: Keep the single agent unless the task fails one of three tests: it needs more context than one window holds, it needs different prompts at different stages, or it has work that can run at the same time. A dozen tool calls on a task that fits in one window passes none of them. The pipeline adds a lossy compression step at each of four boundaries, coordination logic that has its own bugs, at least five serial model calls of latency, and five times the token cost.
followUps: Level 2: The critic sends the draft back to the writer. What does that do to the latency? Expected: each round adds two more serial model calls, so the loop must have a cap on rounds.

Level 2: Which single split would you accept first, if any? Expected: a critic with an adversarial prompt, because it is the one role that needs a different system prompt, and only if the eval shows a gain.

Level 3: Why is the boundary between agents described as lossy compression? Expected: the receiving agent sees only the message, not the sender's tool results and reasoning, so any detail that was not written into the message is gone.

Level 3: How does the choice change if the summaries must be produced under a strict latency target? Expected: serial stages are the enemy of latency, so stay single or fan out only the parts that run in parallel.
wrongAnswers: "Specialists always beat a generalist." Specialists win when the task fails one of the three tests, and this task fails none.
"More agents means more checks, so quality goes up." Each boundary loses information, and a critic that never sees the sources cannot check them.
"Token cost does not matter at our scale." Five agents multiply the bill and the latency on every request, and that is a product decision, not a detail.

questions.title: A team of four agents shares one message log, and every agent reads all of it. The team is about to grow to a few dozen agents, and the context each agent carries is already large. Compare keeping the single log with moving to topics that agents subscribe to, and say how you would handle several agents writing at once.
questions.answer: A full pool is simple, transparent and easy to inspect, and it stops scaling at about 10 agents because each agent's window fills with the others' work. A blackboard with subscriptions routes only the relevant messages to each agent, so it scales further, and it costs an up-front schema that makes the topics meaningful. Many systems mix the two: a small pool at the planning layer and blackboards below it. For writes, most systems serialize through one writer, because model calls are slow enough that contention is rare.
followUps: Level 2: A planning layer of three agents and a worker layer of thirty. Which topology where? Expected: a full pool for the three planners, who need to see each other, and blackboards for the workers, who need only their topics.

Level 2: Which poisoning scenarios does topic partitioning make harder? Expected: a poisoned entry reaches only the subscribers of its topic, so cross-topic spread is cut, while subscribers of that topic are poisoned the same way.

Level 3: When would you move from a single writer to optimistic versioning? Expected: when writes are frequent enough that the coordinator's queue adds visible latency, which is rare while each write follows a slow model call.

Level 3: What goes wrong when you add a blackboard without a schema? Expected: topics are named ad hoc, agents subscribe to the wrong ones or to everything, and you rebuild the full pool with more code.
wrongAnswers: "Keep the pool and give agents bigger windows." The pool grows with every turn from every agent, and a bigger window delays the limit without removing it.
"Pass messages directly between agents instead of sharing state." Direct messages are shared state with extra copying, and they lose the inspectable log.
"Partition by topic and the poisoning problem is solved." Partitions limit the spread, and an entry with no provenance and no verifier still poisons every subscriber of its topic.

questions.title: A swarm runtime uses one thread per in-flight model call. At peak it holds about 10,000 calls at once. Estimate the memory the threads take before any work is done, say what those threads are doing most of the time, and say what you would change.
questions.answer: A thread stack is about 1 MB, so 10,000 threads need about 10 GB of memory for stacks alone, before the first token arrives. Those threads are idle about 99 percent of the time, waiting for the next token from a model service. Move the model calls to cooperative fibers through asynchronous I/O, where the same 10,000 calls fit in one process, and keep threads or processes only for CPU-bound work such as embeddings.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the thread count matter more than the request count? Expected: each thread holds a stack whether or not it is doing work, so memory scales with concurrency, not with throughput.

Level 2: What breaks if you run the embedding step on the asynchronous loop? Expected: a CPU-bound task blocks the loop, so every waiting call stalls behind it, which is why CPU work goes to threads or processes.

Level 3: The memory fits after the change. What is the next limit? Expected: the model service's rate limits and the queue depth, so the runtime needs back-pressure and a lease per run rather than more concurrency.

Level 3: How do you prove the change before you ship it? Expected: run the lesson's comparison on your own call shape, measure wall-clock and peak memory for both versions at the same concurrency, and keep the numbers next to the decision.
wrongAnswers: "Add memory until the threads fit." Memory for idle stacks is waste, and the next peak needs more, while fibers remove the cost.
"Make the threads smaller with a reduced stack size." A smaller stack is still a stack per idle call, and the idle time stays at 99 percent.
"Use fibers for everything, including embeddings." A CPU-bound step on the cooperative loop blocks every waiting call, so the CPU layer keeps threads or processes.

questions.title: A support system uses handoff-driven orchestration: each agent is a prompt plus a set of tools, and one of the tools returns another agent. The trace shows the triage agent handing a user to billing, billing handing the user back to triage, and the two repeating until the round cap ends the run. The user never got an answer. Why does this happen, and what is the cheap fix?
questions.answer: In this pattern the routing lives in the prompts, and the current agent picks its successor with a tool call. The triage prompt says that a billing question goes to billing, and the billing prompt says that anything outside its tools returns to triage, and the user's message satisfies both. Nothing persists between handoffs, so the new agent starts from its prompt and the history and does not know that the same handoff already failed. The cheap fix is a loop detector on the last few handoffs that forces an exit to a fallback agent, plus a trace event for every handoff.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the billing agent not notice that it already sent this user back once? Expected: it is stateless and starts from its prompt plus the history, and nothing in the loop reads the history for a repeated handoff.
Level 2: What should the fallback agent do? Expected: answer with what it can, or hand the case to a human with the trace, and never hand off to either agent in the loop.

Level 3: How do you choose what context moves on a handoff? Expected: full history when the case is short, a summary written by the outgoing agent when it is long, and never nothing, because the incoming agent then repeats the questions.

Level 3: How does a group chat with a selector avoid this specific loop? Expected: the selector sits outside the agents and can see the alternation, while in the handoff pattern the agent that is looping is the one making the decision.
wrongAnswers: "Raise the round cap so the agents have time to settle." The cap is what ended the loop, and more rounds give more of the same two handoffs.
"Tell triage never to accept a handoff from billing." That blocks a legitimate return when billing really cannot help, and the fix is clear ownership plus a detector.
"Switch to a graph framework and the problem disappears." A graph can encode the same cycle with two edges, and the loop detector is useful in both.

questions.title: Four agents, a coder, a reviewer, a tester and a researcher, share one conversation. You must decide how the next speaker is chosen on each turn. The options on the table are a fixed rotation, a model that reads the recent messages and picks, and letting the current agent name its successor. Compare them and say what you would ship with each.
questions.answer: A fixed rotation is deterministic and cheap, and it gives the coder the turn when the topic is a legal question. A model selector is context-aware, and it costs one extra model call per turn, picks differently on identical input, and tends to favor one agent. A handoff by the current agent keeps the routing in the prompts with no external manager, and it is the pattern that loops when two prompts disagree. Most production chats use a selector with fallback rules, a round cap, a termination signal and a log of every selection.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the model selector need a log of its input as well as its output? Expected: the choice depends on what the selector saw, and without the input a reviewer cannot tell whether the pick was wrong or the pool was.

Level 2: What does a verifier-based termination add over a sentinel token? Expected: the chat stops when a check passes, not when an agent claims it is done, which removes early termination by a confident agent.

Level 3: Which of the three makes prompt injection worse, and why? Expected: the handoff pattern, because the deciding tool call is made by the agent that just read the injected text, while an external selector can apply rules the agents do not control.

Level 3: How does a custom selector fix the hot-speaker problem without losing context awareness? Expected: let the model propose, then apply a rule that caps consecutive turns per agent and forces the verifier or a quiet agent in.
wrongAnswers: "Use the model selector, because it understands the conversation." It also adds a call per turn, picks inconsistently, and favors one agent unless rules and a balance metric constrain it.
"Round-robin is fair, so it is safe." Fair turns are not useful turns, and a coder speaking on a legal question wastes a round and adds noise to the pool.
"Let the agents decide among themselves." That is the handoff pattern, and it is the one that forms cycles and that an injected message can steer.

questions.title: Your multi-agent prototype runs in one process with an in-memory event loop. In production, runs last hours while they wait for human input, worker processes crash and lose everything, peak load is ten times the average, and users are charged per run so a retried side effect is a double charge. Design the layer that goes under the agents, and say what you would build first.
questions.answer: Put a durable execution layer under the agents: persist the full run state after each step under a run id, so that when a worker crashes its lease expires and any other worker resumes from the last checkpoint. That needs serializable state, a deterministic resume, and idempotent side effects. For the charge, use a deduplication key per run and an outbox so that side effects are written as intent first and executed once, use asynchronous I/O for the model calls, and deploy new versions beside old ones so that in-flight runs are never killed. Build the simplest version first, a web service with a relational database, and adopt a workflow engine when a measured problem demands it.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the model call the hard part of deterministic resume? Expected: it is not deterministic, so the resume must replay the recorded result of the call rather than make it again.
Level 3: What does the lease do? Expected: it marks a run as owned by one worker for a bounded time, so a crash frees the run for another worker without two workers running it at once.

Level 4: How do you test the outbox? Expected: run the same side effect twice through the executor and assert one external call, then crash the executor between the effect and the mark and assert that the compensation or the idempotent redo leaves one effect.

Level 4: Which feature of a workflow engine is hardest to replicate by hand, and is that a reason to adopt it? Expected: a reasoned pick such as durable timers for hour-long waits or compensation policies, with the rule that adoption follows a measured failure of the simple design.
wrongAnswers: "Retry the whole run from the start when a worker dies." That repeats every side effect that already happened, which is the double charge in the prompt.
"Use a thread per run; it is simpler." Threads idle while they wait for tokens, and at ten thousand concurrent calls the stacks alone exhaust memory.
"Adopt a workflow engine on day one to be safe." The simple design carries about a hundred concurrent runs, and the engine's ceremony costs time until a measured problem pays for it.

questions.title: A three-level agent hierarchy reviews a contract. The top manager splits the work into an engineering branch and a legal branch, each with its own sub-manager and workers. The final report is complete and confident, and it contains finance findings where the legal review should be. Nobody asked a finance question. Trace the failure and say what you change in the design.
questions.answer: The top manager mislabeled the legal branch as finance when it decomposed the task. The sub-manager did what it was given, the workers did finance work well, and the top synthesizer reported finance findings. The error surfaced only at the top, one level away from any point where a human could have caught it. The design fixes are a depth cap of two, provenance on every synthesis, a logged decomposition that is checked against the original question, and a canary worker that is always asked the user's question unchanged.
followUps: Level 3: How many levels did the error travel before the output diverged from the question? Expected: one, because the mislabel happened at the top and every level below executed it faithfully, which is why the depth cap is two.
Level 3: The canary's answer and the merged answer differ. What does the manager do? Expected: stop, record both answers with provenance, and escalate to a human or re-decompose, never merge the two.

Level 4: How do you detect meaning drift between levels? Expected: compare each node's summary with the leaf outputs it cites, and flag a summary that changes the modality of a claim, such as unverified becoming false.

Level 4: The reconciliation loop keeps hitting its step limit. What does that tell you? Expected: the limit is now a hyperparameter that hides a disagreement, so either the decomposition is wrong or the question has no single answer, and the top must report the disagreement.
wrongAnswers: "Add a fourth level to check the third." More levels hide more errors from observability, and the fix is fewer levels with provenance.
"Tell the sub-manager to double-check the task it receives." The sub-manager had no access to the original question, and a canary worker is the mechanism that gives it one.
"Use a bigger model for the top manager." A bigger manager still re-derives the structure each turn from its context, and the mislabel is a context drift, not a capability gap.

questions.title: A payment service starts failing about 10 percent of its requests. Within minutes the inventory service, which never failed, is down, and the order agents that call both are stalled. The payment service itself recovered on its own. Explain the chain, name the failure family, and say what you add so that it cannot repeat.
questions.answer: This is a retry storm, a cascading reliability failure. The order agent retried each failed payment, each retry ran a fresh inventory check, inventory saw twice its normal load and began to time out, every order then retried the inventory check as well, and inventory saw ten times its load and fell over. The fix is classical: a circuit breaker on every outbound call that opens when the downstream error rate passes a threshold and serves a cached or default result, plus a capped retry budget per request.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the inventory service fail when payment is the one with errors? Expected: the order agent's retry loop re-runs the inventory check on every payment retry, so inventory's load tracks payment's failures.
Level 3: What does the breaker serve while it is open? Expected: a cached or default result that the order agent can act on in a degraded mode, so the user gets a slower answer instead of none.

Level 4: Where does the breaker threshold belong, and who owns it? Expected: in the caller's configuration per downstream service, owned by the team that runs the caller, and reviewed when the dependency's normal error rate changes.

Level 4: How do you test the fix without a production incident? Expected: a simulator that injects a 10 percent failure rate downstream and measures total calls with and without the breaker, as the lesson does.
wrongAnswers: "Add exponential backoff to the payment retries." Backoff slows the storm and does not cap it, and the inventory check still runs on every retry.
"Scale the inventory service to absorb the peak." The peak is ten times normal and made of wasted retries, and scaling pays for the storm instead of stopping it.
"This is a model problem, so improve the agent's prompt." No model decision is in the chain, and a prompt cannot see the error rate of a downstream service.

questions.title: You are adding a checking agent to a team that shares a memory. A colleague wants the checker to fix wrong entries directly, because that is the simplest design. Specify the checker: what it reads, what it may write, where its results go, and what it can and cannot protect against. Defend the restrictions.
questions.answer: The checker reads the shared memory like every other agent, re-fetches the sources that entries cite, and compares. It has no write handle to the shared memory, only to a separate verification channel that a human or a decision agent reads. It cannot stop a bad entry from being written, and it can be fooled by an entry that cites no source, but its verdicts can never become a shared fact. A checker that writes into the memory is poisoned by the same memory it checks, and then its verdicts carry the poison further.
followUps: Level 3: The verifier flags an entry that the analyst already used. What happens to the analyst's entry? Expected: it stays in the log, a new entry can supersede it with the finding as the reason, and the final report carries the retraction.
Level 3: How many verifiers do you deploy? Expected: at least one, and more if the pool is partitioned by topic, with each verifier subscribed to the topics it can check.

Level 4: How do you keep the verifier's source access independent? Expected: it fetches from the original location with its own tools, not from a cache that a writer filled, otherwise it checks the entry against a copy of itself.

Level 4: What metric tells you the verifier is doing useful work? Expected: the share of writes that are supersessions and the share of flagged entries, read together, with a rising flag rate as an early sign of a writer that hallucinates.
wrongAnswers: "Let the checker fix the entry, since it has the source." The fix overwrites the audit trail and gives the checker a write path that a poisoned pool can turn against it.

"A second reviewer agent that reads the pool is enough." A reviewer that only reads the pool compares entries with each other and inherits the same poisoned facts; the verifier must re-fetch the source.

"Route the verifier's findings into the pool so every agent sees them." The findings then become shared facts, and a wrong finding poisons the pool in a new way; the finding on the verification channel, keyed by entry id, is the visible signal, not a new entry in the pool.

questions.title: In a lead-and-workers research system, two workers answered overlapping sub-questions with numbers that contradict each other. The final report contains one of the numbers and no mention of the other. The user found the second number in a source and asks why the report hid it. Where did the system fail, and what do you change?
questions.answer: The lead resolved a synthesis conflict by picking one side in silence, which the lesson calls the worst failure in this pattern, because the user never learns that a disagreement happened. Two upstream causes made it likely: the decomposition gave two workers the same ground, and no worker had a scope that stopped it from drifting into the other's territory. The fix is a lead that detects contradiction between worker outputs and either re-asks with a narrower question or writes the disagreement into the answer, plus provenance on every synthesized claim.
followUps: Level 3: Why is a silent pick worse than a wrong pick with a note? Expected: a noted disagreement lets the reader check the sources, while a silent pick presents an unresolved fact as settled.
Level 3: The re-ask adds a round and the latency target is tight. What do you do? Expected: surface the disagreement in the answer instead of re-asking, and record the key for a later run.
Level 4: How do you test the conflict detector? Expected: feed it worker outputs with a planted contradiction on one key and matching values on others, and assert that exactly that key is flagged.

Level 4: The two workers agree and are both wrong. What catches that? Expected: nothing in the lead, because agreement is not correctness, so an independent verifier with its own source access has to check the claim.
wrongAnswers: "Add a rule to the lead's prompt that says be careful with numbers." The lead did not know a conflict existed, and a prompt does not compare worker outputs.
"Trust the worker with the higher confidence." Confidence is not correctness, and the user still never learns that a disagreement happened.
"Run three workers per sub-question and take the majority." A majority can be wrong together, it triples the cost, and the overlap that caused the conflict stays in the plan.

questions.title: Take-home. Design a research system in which one lead agent plans and several workers search in parallel, for a product where users ask open questions and expect a cited answer. Deliver a design document with the lead and worker prompts in outline, the shared memory, the failure modes you expect and the mitigation for each, the operational limits, and the cost model. Say what you would cut if the budget were halved.
questions.answer: The lead decomposes the question into sub-questions, scales the number of workers to the question's complexity, and synthesizes the worker summaries without reading raw sources. Each worker has a fresh context, an explicit scope, a timeout at about twice the median runtime and a token cap. Shared memory carries provenance on every entry, is append-only, and is checked by a read-only verifier that re-fetches sources and reports on its own channel. Every outbound call sits behind a circuit breaker, the system is deployed with versions side by side, and the cost model states up front that the pattern spends about 15 times the tokens of a single agent.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the lead never read raw sources, even to check a worker? Expected: its window is for planning and synthesis, and the check belongs to the verifier, which re-fetches the source without writing to the pool.

Level 3: A worker returns a summary with no source. What does the design do with it? Expected: provenance marks the entry as uncited, the lead weighs it lower, and the verifier cannot check it, so the answer either omits it or labels it.

Level 4: Which one component would you keep if you could keep only one beyond the lead and the workers? Expected: the read-only verifier with provenance, because a cited answer that is wrong is the failure the product cannot survive.

Level 4: How do you know the system is still working next quarter? Expected: the golden set run weekly, the supersession and flag rates, the agreement rate across parallel workers, and the quarterly audit.
wrongAnswers: "Give every worker the full conversation so it has context." That spends the fresh-context advantage and copies the lead's planning into every window.
"Let the lead resolve conflicts by picking the better-written answer." A silent pick hides the disagreement from the user, and the design must re-ask or surface it.
"Skip the verifier, because the lead already reads the worker summaries." The lead compares summaries with each other, not with the sources, and shared summaries can share a hallucination.

questions.title: A multi-agent product has been in production for two quarters. Failures arrive as a stream of unrelated tickets and nothing gets fixed systematically. Design the audit that turns the stream into a ranked list of fixes, and say which failure class you would weight most heavily even if it is not the most frequent.
questions.answer: Sample about 1000 real execution traces each quarter, categorize every failure into the three root categories of the published taxonomy and the five groupthink patterns, compute the failure rate per category, rank the mitigations by how many failures each would remove, and commit to two or three for the quarter. Weight verification gaps most heavily even though they were the smallest category by count, because they are silent: a plausible wrong output produces no exception, no alert and no ticket until a human notices.
followUps: Level 3: Why sample traces instead of auditing tickets? Expected: tickets are the loud failures, and the silent ones never produce a ticket, so a stratified sample is the only way to see them.

Level 3: Which single proxy would you instrument first? Expected: agreement rate across parallel agents, because a sharp rise signals conformity and a sharp fall signals drift, and both precede visible errors.

Level 4: The audit finds that specification problems dominate. What is the cheapest fix? Expected: a pre-flight check of the task definition by a separate agent before dispatch, with role contracts that include what each agent does not do.

Level 4: How do you keep the audit from becoming a report nobody acts on? Expected: the failure budget with a stop-shipping rule, owners per mitigation, and the re-audit date on the calendar before the quarter starts.
wrongAnswers: "Fix the most frequent category first." Frequency is not cost, and the silent verification gaps cost more per failure than the loud specification problems.
"Audit once a year, when the system is stable." Categories shift as the system grows, and a year of unranked failures is the stream you started with.
"Add more agents to check each other." Agents that share a model share their blind spots, and the check that matters is an independent verifier with its own source access.

questions.title: Five agents answer the same factual question and vote. Three of them run the same base model and agree on a wrong answer, and the two others are right. Majority vote picks the wrong answer. A colleague says that classical fault-tolerant consensus solves this. Explain why it does not, which assumptions break, and what the recent agent-specific protocols change.
questions.answer: Classical consensus tolerates fewer than a third of nodes behaving arbitrarily, and it assumes that faults are independent, that honest nodes are correct, and that a ground truth exists. Three agents on a shared base model share their faults, an honest model still hallucinates, and on some questions the agents define the truth. The agent-specific variants weigh each vote by a confidence probe, aggregate leaderless proposals by a geometric median, or split agents into a core and an edge with learned trust weights. None of them makes agreement equal correctness, so the consensus output still goes to an independent verifier.
followUps: Level 3: Does the geometric median rescue this case? Expected: no. The median discounts outliers and moves toward the dense cluster, which helps only while the wrong cluster is under half. Here three of five votes are wrong, so the dense cluster is the wrong one and the median selects it.

Level 3: The three wrong agents are also the most confident. What now? Expected: no aggregator fixes a wrong cluster that is both larger and more confident, so the system needs diversity of base models or an independent verifier.
Level 4: Why bound the rounds at two or three? Expected: agents that observe earlier rounds start to mimic each other regardless of truth, so more rounds reward conformity.
Level 4: What do you monitor in production? Expected: the agreement rate, where a sharp rise means conformity and a sharp fall means model drift, and the minority clusters with their provenance.
wrongAnswers: "Use the classical protocol with a two-thirds quorum." Three honest agents that share a hallucination form the quorum, and the protocol agrees on the wrong value.
"Add more copies of the same model until the majority is right." More copies of one model add more correlated votes, and the wrong cluster grows with them.
"Consensus means the answer is correct." Agreement and correctness are different measurements, and the consensus output needs a verifier that is independent of the ensemble.

topics.title: Sandboxes
topics.about: Isolation for agents that run code or drive a computer, and the policy around it.

questions.title: Inside a Docker sandbox the agent runs as uid 1000 in the sudo and docker groups, and docker version answers with a server. A teammate concludes that the sandbox is no safer than a container running as root. Where is the wall, and what does the agent own inside it?
questions.answer: The wall is the hypervisor line under the guest kernel, not the user inside. The documentation puts it plainly: the agent is a non-root user with sudo rights inside the VM, the hypervisor boundary isolates the agent, and privilege separation inside the VM does not. Everything below that line belongs to the agent, including a private Docker Engine whose images never appear in docker ps on the host, and the host offers no Docker API to the sandbox at all.
followUps: Level 1: The agent runs docker build and the host's docker ps shows nothing. Why? Expected: the engine and its image store live inside the VM; the host daemon is a different engine.

Level 2: A compiled tool crashes inside with a page-size error. What is different about the guest? Expected: the guest kernel uses 16 KiB pages, which getconf PAGESIZE reports as 16384, and sbx diagnose compares the mkfs.erofs block size against it.
Level 2: Name each path by which something from the host enters the VM. Expected: the workspace mount, the proxy for network, secret sentinels, the MCP gateway URL and the forwarded SSH agent.
Level 3: Which registered MCP server is not covered by the wall? Expected: one added with --command, which runs on the host as your user and is not under network policy.
wrongAnswers: "sudo inside means root on my laptop." The user inside is a guest user; the hypervisor is the control, and the docs say privilege separation inside is not.
"The sandbox shares my Docker daemon." Each sandbox runs its own Docker Engine, and the host offers no API to the VM.
"It needs no account because it runs without Docker Desktop." sbx runs without Desktop and still refuses to create a sandbox without a sign-in; the FAQ gives the reasons.
