Standard preventions: request coalescing/single-flight (only the first miss actually recomputes; concurrent requests for the same key wait on that result instead of duplicating the work), a lock around the recompute-and-write step so only one caller repopulates the entry, probabilistic early expiration (recompute slightly before the real TTL, with increasing probability as expiry nears, to spread refreshes out instead of letting them all cliff-edge together), and proactive cache warming ahead of a known traffic spike or right after a deploy/restart.
options: Too many distinct keys.
The cache grows until it runs out of memory.
Stale entries get served after an update.
A hot entry expires and many concurrent misses all recompute it at once. Prevent it with request coalescing and staggered or early refresh.
keyPoints: Concurrent misses can duplicate expensive recomputation.
Coalesce same-key requests with single-flight.
Lock cache recomputation and writes.
Spread refreshes with early expiry and warm caches before spikes.

questions.title: Which of these should you not cache?
questions.answer: Four cases: when responses are genuinely personalized or user-context-dependent (a cached answer for one user is simply wrong for another); when the knowledge base updates more frequently than your cache TTL (you'd be serving stale answers by design); when the query distribution is long-tailed enough that nearly every query is unique (hit rate approaches zero, so the caching infrastructure adds complexity for essentially no benefit); and when a strict freshness SLA requires every answer to reflect the absolute latest documents, which any caching layer structurally works against.
options: The KV cache of the shared system prompt.
Answers personalised to the user's own account or permissions.
FAQ answers keyed by document version.
Embeddings of documents that never change.
keyPoints: Avoid shared answer caching for personalized responses.
Do not let cache lifetime outlast knowledge freshness.
Near-unique queries make cache infrastructure low value.
Strict latest-document requirements conflict with stale cached answers.

questions.title: What's a production “router + fallback” pattern for a RAG system, and what should the router itself cost?
questions.answer: A practical router has three parts: a rule-based pre-filter for deterministic cases (explicit entity codes route to an exact-match path, greetings route to a cached response), a lightweight classifier for genuine semantic intent classification on everything else, and confidence-based promotion — even if the router initially classifies a query as simple, if the retrieved results score poorly, it falls through to a more thorough tier automatically rather than returning a weak answer. The router itself should stay cheap and fast (under roughly 50ms added latency, a tiny fraction of a cent per call) to remain a net positive; track tier distribution as an ongoing KPI, since a creeping share of traffic landing in the expensive tier can mean either the router is miscategorizing or the real query mix has genuinely shifted.
keyPoints: Route deterministic cases with cheap rules.
Classify remaining semantic intent with a lightweight model.
Promote weak retrieval results to a more thorough tier.
Keep routing cheap and monitor expensive-tier traffic share.

questions.title: What's the fan-out/fan-in pattern in RAG, and what's RAG-Fusion a special case of?
questions.answer: Multiple retrieval strategies (or query reformulations, or retrievers over different sub-corpora) run in parallel — fanning out — and their results get merged into one ranked list — fanning in — typically via Reciprocal Rank Fusion since it handles differently-scaled result lists without needing score calibration. RAG-Fusion is exactly this pattern specialized to one specific fan-out source: multiple LLM-generated rephrasings of the same query, rather than multiple genuinely different retrieval strategies or sub-corpora.
keyPoints: Run retrieval strategies or sub-corpus searches in parallel.
Merge their results into one ranked list.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion handles differently scaled rankings.
RAG-Fusion fans out LLM-generated reformulations of one query.

questions.title: What is “conversational context drift” as a distinct failure mode, and how do you detect it before it causes a bad answer?
questions.answer: It's specifically when a multi-turn system's retrieval degrades because a follow-up query has lost the context that made it meaningful, as opposed to a single-turn retrieval failure which has nothing to do with conversation history at all. Detect it proactively by monitoring the similarity between a condensed/rewritten follow-up query and the raw retrieval results it produces — a sharp drop in retrieved-result relevance scores right after a topic-shift-shaped follow-up is a strong leading indicator, worth catching before it ever reaches a visibly wrong answer.
keyPoints: Follow-up queries can lose the context needed for retrieval.
Distinguish conversational loss from single-turn retrieval failure.
Compare condensed-query similarity with retrieved results.
Alert on sharp relevance drops after topic-shifting follow-ups.

questions.title: Your RAG system's p99 latency just doubled with no obvious deploy. How do you debug it?
questions.answer: Localize before you guess: check whether it's a specific pipeline stage (a slow vector DB index after a cold start or node change, a reranker that started receiving a larger-than-usual candidate set, a prompt-caching cache-miss spike from a prefix that stopped matching) versus a traffic-mix shift (a sudden influx of queries that route to a more expensive tier or trigger more retrieval hops). Pull per-stage latency from your traces rather than only looking at end-to-end p99 — "it got slower" isn't actionable, "retrieval p99 tripled specifically" is.
options: Add a cache.
Break p99 down by pipeline stage from traces, and check whether the traffic mix shifted.
Move to a faster LLM.
Roll back the latest deploy.
keyPoints: Use trace-level latency to locate the slow stage.
Inspect vector database changes and reranker candidate counts.
Check for prompt-prefix cache misses.
Compare traffic tiers and retrieval-hop mix before choosing a fix.

questions.title: What's the real difference between retrieval failure's observable symptoms and its root causes, and why does that distinction matter for debugging?
questions.answer: Symptoms are what users or monitoring actually see — irrelevant answers, "I don't know" responses, low confidence scores; root causes are what actually produced them — embedding-space mismatch between query and document vocabulary (the semantic gap problem), a chunking strategy that split the relevant fact across a boundary, a stale index missing recently-added content, or a mis-tuned top-k. The distinction matters because the same symptom can have several different root causes, and the fix for each is completely different — treating a symptom (e.g. "just add more context") without finding the actual root cause routinely makes things worse, not better.
keyPoints: Irrelevant answers and low confidence are symptoms.
Check embedding vocabulary mismatch and chunk boundaries.
Check stale indices and top-k configuration.
Find the cause before adding context or changing the pipeline.

questions.title: What's cascading retrieval failure, and how is it different from a single, isolated retrieval miss?
questions.answer: It's when one technique's failure actively propagates and amplifies through the rest of the pipeline rather than staying contained — the canonical example is HyDE: if the generated hypothetical document is itself subtly wrong, the system doesn't just fail to retrieve the best chunk, it confidently retrieves chunks relevant to the *wrong* hypothetical, which can look more convincing (and be harder to catch) than a normal low-relevance-score miss. In multi-hop RAG the same shape shows up as a wrong intermediate fact at hop one actively steering every subsequent hop further from the correct answer, rather than each hop failing independently.
keyPoints: One stage's error can amplify through later stages.
A wrong HyDE document retrieves evidence for the wrong hypothesis.
Convincing wrong-context retrieval may evade simple relevance checks.
Wrong intermediate facts can steer every later retrieval hop.

questions.title: What's a stale index problem in production, and what's the actual fix — beyond “just re-index more often”?
questions.answer: A naive fix (more frequent full rebuilds) doesn't scale and still leaves a staleness window between rebuilds. The real fix is detecting exactly which documents changed — via a content hash or modification timestamp tracked per source document — and re-embedding only those, incrementally, continuously, rather than paying the cost and staleness window of a periodic full rebuild. Also worth naming explicitly: staleness interacts with other failure modes, since a stale index can produce a confident, well-formed, entirely outdated answer that looks indistinguishable from a correct one until someone checks the document's actual current version.
keyPoints: Full rebuilds remain costly and leave staleness windows.
Track per-document hashes or modification times.
Re-embed changed documents incrementally and continuously.
Recognize that stale evidence can produce confident outdated answers.

questions.title: What causes embedding mismatch in production, and what are its observable symptoms?
questions.answer: Root causes span several dimensions: a domain shift the original embedding model was never trained for, a language the model has weak coverage of, an architecture change when swapping embedding models without fully re-embedding the existing index (leaving old and new vectors geometrically incompatible in the same store), or simple model-version drift over time. The symptom is usually subtle rather than catastrophic — retrieval quality silently degrades in a way that looks like "the model got worse at understanding queries" when it's actually a mismatch between how the query and the stored documents were embedded, not a quality regression in either encoder individually.
keyPoints: Domain and language shifts can weaken embedding alignment.
Changing models without re-embedding mixes incompatible vectors.
Model-version drift can also cause mismatch.
Distinguish query-document embedding mismatch from encoder quality decline.

questions.title: What is a feature store, and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: A feature store centralizes the definition, computation, and storage of ML features across offline training and online serving. It solves two critical production issues: training-serving skew—where training uses batch SQL while serving computes features via Python microservices with differing logic—and point-in-time leakage, by performing AS OF time-travel joins so training instances only see features available before the event timestamp. Architecturally, it couples an offline store (Snowflake, BigQuery, or Parquet on S3) optimized for high-throughput batch reads with an online key-value store (Redis, DynamoDB) optimized for sub-10ms point lookups. The trade-off is infrastructure complexity: maintaining streaming pipelines (Flink/Kafka) to keep the online store synchronized with batch updates introduces synchronization lag, operational overhead, and storage costs. For teams without real-time feature requirements or feature reuse across models, a database view and a lightweight Redis cache are far simpler.
keyPoints: A feature store shares feature definitions across training and serving.
Point-in-time joins avoid using future feature values.
Offline storage supports training and online storage supports low-latency retrieval.
Freshness and consistent transformations reduce training-serving skew.

questions.title: Offline AUC is 0.92 but production performance is poor. How do you investigate?
questions.answer:
When offline AUC is high but online performance collapses, training-serving skew is the primary suspect. I triage this systematically across three vectors:
First, feature pipeline skew. I log raw inference feature payloads with request IDs and compare them against features generated by the training pipeline for the exact same entity and timestamp. Computing Population Stability Index (PSI) or Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests across feature distributions quickly pinpoints discrepancies, such as missing value imputations or differing library versions between Python training and C++/Go serving.
Second, temporal data leakage. I check if training features inadvertently incorporated information from after the label event, such as a user's 30-day aggregate containing the target transaction.
Third, feedback loops and distribution shifts. If the production model's own predictions influence user interactions, historical offline splits fail to simulate live policy changes.
Before rolling out, running the candidate model in shadow mode and validating feature parity against production logs prevents these discrepancies from reaching users.
keyPoints: Compare production features and transformations with training.
Check label definition, leakage and point-in-time correctness.
Check distribution shifts and serving errors before blaming model capacity.
Evaluate representative cohorts with the production decision threshold.

questions.title: Explain data drift and concept drift. How do you monitor when labels are delayed?
questions.answer:
Data drift occurs when the input distribution P(X) changes while the conditional relationship P(Y|X) remains constant—for instance, a marketing campaign shifts user demographics. Concept drift occurs when the underlying relationship P(Y|X) shifts—such as macroeconomic changes causing users with high credit scores to suddenly default.
When ground-truth labels are delayed by weeks or months (such as credit defaults or fraud chargebacks), we cannot measure accuracy directly. Instead, we monitor inputs and outputs:
First, we track Population Stability Index (PSI) and two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests on top-ranked features; a PSI exceeding 0.2 indicates significant shift requiring investigation.
Second, we monitor prediction score distributions and calibration drifts against historical baselines.
Third, we track short-term proxy signals, like click-through or engagement rates, that correlate with downstream conversion.
The trade-off is alert fatigue: feature drift alerts are noisy. We tier alerts by feature importance and business impact, triggering automated retraining only when core drivers show structural movement.
keyPoints: Data drift changes input distributions.
Concept drift changes the relationship between inputs and targets.
Unlabelled drift signals do not prove quality degradation.
Use proxy signals while labels are delayed and evaluate outcomes when labels arrive.

questions.title: Compare shadow, canary and blue-green deployment for an ML model.
questions.answer:
For model releases, shadow, canary, and blue-green deployments balance verification fidelity against risk and infrastructure cost:
Shadow deployment mirrors live production traffic asynchronously to the candidate model without serving its outputs to users. It provides zero-risk verification of latency, GPU memory, and prediction sanity against production traffic, but cannot measure user behavioral impact and incurs 2x inference compute cost. Writes and external mutations must be mocked.
Canary deployment routes a small slice of live traffic (e.g., 2% to 5%) to the new model, measuring real conversion metrics and p99 latency against the champion. It risks user experience for that slice if the model is degraded, but bounds the blast radius.
Blue-green deployment maintains two identical production environments, switching load-balancer traffic instantly. It provides immediate zero-downtime cutover and instant rollback, but requires 2x full infrastructure footprint.
In production, we chain them: shadow for performance and stability, followed by canary with automated metric circuit-breakers for business impact.
keyPoints: Shadow traffic evaluates a model without affecting user decisions.
Canaries expose a limited share of real traffic.
Blue-green deployment switches between prepared environments.
Define monitored guardrails and a rollback path before rollout.

questions.title: How do you decide when to retrain a model?
questions.answer:
We decide when to retrain by balancing the economic cost of model decay against the financial and compute cost of retraining and validation.
To determine policy, we first backtest model performance across historical time windows to measure decay rate. Rapidly decaying domains (like fraud or ad bidding) require continuous or daily retraining; structural domains (like credit scoring or document classification) require monthly cadences.
Operationally, we combine a scheduled cadence with event-driven triggers based on statistical drift thresholds (PSI > 0.2) or drop in proxy metrics.
Every retraining pipeline must execute automated gates before deployment: schema validation on input data, a fixed golden test set evaluation, and a champion-challenger backtest on out-of-time data.
The critical trade-off is avoiding automated retraining on corrupt data. If an upstream logging failure causes missing features, blindly retraining bakes the corruption into the model weights. The pipeline must fail closed on data contract violations rather than automatically retraining.
keyPoints: Retraining decisions depend on measured quality and changing data.
Scheduled retraining and drift-triggered retraining have different costs.
Validate a candidate on recent representative data before promotion.
Keep lineage and a rollback path for each promoted model.

questions.title: How do you make model training reproducible?
questions.answer: Version code, data and configuration together, and record them with each model, using tools such as Git, DVC and MLflow. Pin dependencies in a container and log seeds and hardware. Full bit-level determinism on GPUs is costly and rarely needed, so aim to reproduce results within a small tolerance. Save the exact train and test splits, and a model registry should link every deployed model back to its run.
keyPoints: Version data, code, configuration and model artifacts.
Record environment, dependencies and random seeds.
GPU operations can remain nondeterministic despite fixed seeds.
Track experiments and verify reproducibility within an explicit tolerance.

questions.title: A new model degrades conversion by 3% in production. What do you do in the first hour?
questions.answer:
In the first hour of a 3% production conversion drop, the priority is immediate containment:
Minute 0 to 5: Roll back traffic immediately. In a mature model registry and serving setup, rollback is a routing pointer change at the API gateway or feature flag level, diverting 100% of traffic back to the previous champion model artifact within seconds. Never attempt to debug a live degraded model in production.
Minute 5 to 20: Verify containment. Confirm conversion rates recover and verify secondary health metrics—p99 latency, error rates, and fallback activations.
Minute 20 to 60: Isolate root cause. Freeze telemetry logs and slice metrics across dimensions: user cohort, client version, device type, and geography. Determine whether the degradation was model-driven (poor predictions on specific segments) or infrastructure-driven (feature store timeouts causing default fallbacks).
Afterward, conduct a blameless post-mortem and implement preventative gates, such as tighter canary alert thresholds and segment-level regression tests in CI.
keyPoints: Stop the rollout or roll back to a known good model promptly.
Verify the business metric and inspect affected cohorts.
Check model, data and feature versions and recent changes.
Preserve evidence and investigate the cause after containing harm.

questions.title: How would you serve an LLM on Kubernetes, and how do you autoscale it?
questions.answer:
Serving an LLM on Kubernetes requires treating GPU workloads differently from standard stateless microservices:
First, pod configuration. We pin dedicated GPUs using nvidia.com/gpu: 1 resource limits, mount a high-speed shared PVC or local NVMe daemonset to pre-cache model weights, and configure startup probes with a 5-minute timeout to allow weights to load into VRAM before accepting traffic.
Second, autoscaling. Horizontal Pod Autoscalers (HPA) driven by CPU or memory are ineffective because GPUs run near 100% compute during batching. Instead, we use KEDA to autoscale on inference queue depth, active concurrent requests, or KV cache memory utilization from vLLM/TGI metrics.
Third, lifecycle management. LLM cold starts take several minutes, so we maintain pre-warmed standby capacity. When scaling down, we implement graceful termination with preStop lifecycle hooks that drain in-flight streaming requests before terminating the pod. The API gateway handles load balancing with round-robin routing aware of model replica capacity.
keyPoints: GPU requests require device plugins and suitable scheduling.
Model loading and GPU memory affect readiness and capacity.
Autoscale using queue depth or latency rather than CPU alone.
Account for slow cold starts with warm capacity.
Manage batching and resource limits to control throughput and latency.

questions.title: How do you stop bad data from breaking a production model?
questions.answer: Validate at pipeline boundaries: schema, ranges, null rates, row counts, freshness and distributions, using tools such as Great Expectations or TFX Data Validation. Fail closed for training so a bad batch cannot produce a bad model. For serving, fall back to safe defaults and raise an alert. Assign owners to upstream data contracts, because most incidents begin with an upstream change that nobody announced.
keyPoints: Validate schema, ranges, missingness and freshness at ingestion.
Quarantine or reject invalid data before it reaches the model.
Monitor distribution changes and pipeline health.
Version data contracts and alert an accountable owner.

questions.title: What is point-in-time correctness in feature stores, and how do AS OF joins prevent data leakage during offline training set generation?
questions.answer: Point-in-time correctness ensures that when generating training data for past events, the feature values matched to each label reflect exactly what was known at the historical moment the event occurred. Without this, offline models suffer from temporal data leakage. For example, if predicting loan default at the application timestamp of June 1st, using a feature computed on July 1st that reflects subsequent missed payments leaks the future label into training, producing an artificially high validation score that collapses in production. Feature stores solve this using AS OF time-travel joins. Each feature update in the offline store is recorded with an observation timestamp. When generating training sets from an observation table containing entity IDs and event timestamps, the feature store joins the latest feature value whose timestamp is strictly less than or equal to the event timestamp. The trade-off is query complexity and storage volume versus model reliability: maintaining immutable temporal feature logs requires partitioned time-series storage, but it guarantees zero future leakage in training.
followUps: How do you handle late-arriving event data that updates historical feature values retroactively?
What is the difference between event time and ingestion time in feature store tables?
wrongAnswers: Joining historical training events against the current snapshot of a database table, causing severe temporal data leakage.
Assuming that training-serving skew only occurs in online serving, ignoring that offline training datasets can leak future states.
tradeOffs: AS OF joins eliminate temporal leakage and guarantee training-serving feature equivalence, but require partitioned event-time storage.
Computing time-travel joins over billions of historical records requires distributed query engines like Spark or Snowflake.
keyPoints: Use only feature values known at the historical decision time.
Future feature values leak labels and inflate offline scores.
AS OF joins select the latest feature timestamp no later than the event.
Immutable temporal logs add storage and query complexity.

questions.title: How does a modern feature store maintain parity between low-latency online stores (Redis) and high-throughput offline stores (Snowflake)?
questions.answer: A core problem in production machine learning is training-serving skew, where features used in offline training are computed with batch SQL queries while features used in live online serving are re-implemented in Python or Java microservices with differing logic. Over time, subtle logic divergences cause live model performance to degrade. A feature store maintains parity through a single canonical feature definition. Developers write transformation logic once—such as aggregations or windowed counts—in a declarative framework. The feature store engine compiles this definition into two execution paths: a batch pipeline that computes historical features and writes them to an offline warehouse (like Snowflake or BigQuery) for training, and a streaming pipeline that computes live updates and writes them to an in-memory key-value store (like Redis or DynamoDB) with sub-10ms lookup latency for online serving. The trade-off is infrastructure management versus feature consistency: managing dual storage layers adds operational complexity, but it guarantees that live model scoring receives mathematically identical features to training.
followUps: How do you test and verify that features served from Redis match features queried from Snowflake?
What happens when an offline batch backfill overwrites recent streaming updates in the online store?
wrongAnswers: Writing feature computation SQL for offline training and separate Python code for online serving, creating training-serving skew.
Querying the offline analytical warehouse directly during live user inference, causing 5-second latency timeouts.
tradeOffs: Single-source feature definitions eliminate training-serving skew, but require maintaining dual storage layers and synchronization pipelines.
Streaming ingestion keeps online feature values fresh in real time, but introduces small synchronization lag relative to batch updates.
keyPoints: Separate offline and online implementations can diverge and cause serving skew.
Define feature transformations once in a canonical framework.
Compile definitions into historical batch and live streaming paths.
Dual warehouse and key-value storage adds operational complexity.

questions.title: How do you design a streaming feature pipeline with Kafka and Flink to serve rolling window aggregations with sub-10ms point lookups?
questions.answer: Real-time machine learning models—such as fraud detection or dynamic pricing—rely on up-to-the-minute behavior features, like the number of credit card transactions in the last ten minutes. Standard batch pipelines run hours too late to detect active fraud attacks. We architect a real-time streaming pipeline using Kafka, Apache Flink, and Redis. Raw application events are published to a distributed Kafka topic. A stateful Flink streaming job consumes the event stream and maintains rolling window aggregations in memory, utilizing Flink's managed state and RocksDB state backend. As transactions arrive, Flink updates sliding-window counts and sums, and immediately writes the updated feature vectors to an in-memory Redis cluster partitioned by user entity ID. When a transaction inference request arrives at the model service, it performs an MGET lookup on Redis, retrieving all pre-computed features in under five milliseconds. The trade-off is streaming operational complexity versus feature freshness: running stateful stream processors requires managing checkpointing and out-of-order events, but it delivers sub-second feature freshness to online scoring.
followUps: How do you handle out-of-order events or network blips in Flink using watermarks?
What eviction and TTL policies ensure Redis memory does not fill up with inactive user entities?
wrongAnswers: Computing rolling window aggregates dynamically from raw transaction logs during the live inference API call, blowing past latency SLAs.
Using stateless stream consumers that query an external database on every event to calculate sliding sums, creating database bottlenecks.
tradeOffs: Flink stateful stream processing delivers real-time rolling aggregates to Redis with sub-second freshness, but requires 24/7 stream cluster operations.
Pre-computing features into Redis decouples inference latency from feature aggregation complexity, but increases memory storage costs.
keyPoints: Publish raw events to Kafka.
Use stateful Flink windows to compute rolling features.
Write updated vectors to Redis by entity ID for inference lookups.
Manage checkpoints and out-of-order events to maintain freshness.

questions.title: How do you monitor feature drift in production feature stores using Population Stability Index (PSI) and Wasserstein distance?
questions.answer: Machine learning models degrade silently when the distribution of live input features shifts away from the distribution observed during training. Because ground-truth labels often arrive weeks late, monitoring feature drift provides an early warning system before model accuracy collapses. We monitor feature drift by comparing the distribution of live online features served over a sliding window against the baseline training distribution. For categorical features, we compute the Population Stability Index (PSI): we bucket feature values and sum the difference between actual and expected percentages multiplied by the natural log of their ratio. A PSI below 0.1 indicates stability, while a PSI above 0.25 flags significant distributional drift requiring attention. For continuous numeric features, we compute the Wasserstein or Earth Mover's Distance, which measures the minimum work required to transform one probability distribution into another. The trade-off is detection sensitivity versus alert fatigue: calculating statistical distances over small windows catches sudden data corruption quickly, but natural weekend or seasonal shifts can trigger false positive alerts unless baselines adapt.
followUps: How do you distinguish between covariate shift (feature distribution changes) and concept drift (relationship to target changes)?
What automated retraining trigger should execute when a critical feature's PSI exceeds 0.25 for three consecutive days?
wrongAnswers: Monitoring only model prediction output distributions while ignoring input feature drift, missing upstream pipeline bugs.
Computing drift metrics on static single-day snapshots without accounting for weekly seasonality or holiday traffic patterns.
tradeOffs: Distributional drift monitoring catches upstream data pipeline corruptions and behavioral shifts before labels arrive, preventing silent model failure.
Setting PSI alert thresholds too sensitive causes false-alarm fatigue on benign seasonal shifts, while loose thresholds miss genuine drift.
keyPoints: Compare sliding-window live feature distributions with training baselines.
Use PSI for categorical features and Wasserstein distance for numeric features.
Feature drift can warn before delayed labels arrive.
Small windows increase sensitivity but can alert on seasonal changes.

questions.title: How do you architect a dual token-bucket rate limiter that enforces Tokens Per Minute (TPM) and Requests Per Minute (RPM) simultaneously?
questions.answer: In multi-tenant LLM gateways, rate limiting based solely on request counts is dangerous: a user sending ten requests of 100,000 tokens consumes vastly more GPU compute than a user sending ten requests of 50 tokens. Conversely, limiting only tokens allows a flood of tiny requests that overwhelm HTTP connection pools. We architect a dual token-bucket rate limiter that enforces Requests Per Minute (RPM) and Tokens Per Minute (TPM) concurrently. Each tenant is allocated two independent token buckets. The RPM bucket tracks discrete request allowances and refills at a fixed rate per second. The TPM bucket tracks token volume and refills proportionally based on token limits. When a request arrives, the gateway estimates the token size (prompt tokens plus requested max completion tokens) and attempts to acquire tokens from both buckets atomically. If either bucket has insufficient tokens, the request is rejected with an HTTP 429 status code indicating which limit was breached. The trade-off is quota predictability versus request queuing: dual enforcement protects both connection pools and GPU memory, but requires client SDKs to handle retry backoff gracefully.
followUps: How do you reconcile the TPM bucket when a model completes generation using far fewer tokens than the requested maximum?
How do you configure tenant burst capacities to accommodate legitimate batch jobs without degrading interactive users?
wrongAnswers: Rate limiting solely on raw HTTP request counts without tracking token volume, allowing one user to exhaust cluster GPU memory.
Checking RPM and TPM sequentially in separate un-locked operations, creating race conditions under high concurrent traffic.
tradeOffs: Enforcing both RPM and TPM protects API gateways from connection saturation and GPU clusters from memory exhaustion simultaneously.
Reserving max completion tokens up front prevents over-subscription, but can temporarily block concurrent requests from users who finish early.
keyPoints: Enforce both request and token quotas for each tenant.
Estimate prompt plus maximum completion tokens before admission.
Acquire from both buckets atomically.
Return HTTP 429 identifying the exhausted limit and require client backoff.

questions.title: How do you implement distributed sliding-window rate limiting in Redis using sorted sets and atomic Lua scripts?
questions.answer: Fixed-window rate limiters suffer from the boundary burst problem: if a user is allowed 100 requests per minute, they can send 100 requests at 11:59 and another 100 requests at 12:00, sending 200 requests across two seconds and overwhelming backend services. A sliding-window log provides smooth, continuous rate enforcement. In a distributed gateway fleet, we implement this using Redis sorted sets and atomic Lua scripts. For each tenant, the Redis key stores a sorted set where each member and score is the microsecond timestamp of an approved request. When a new request arrives, our Lua script executes three steps atomically: first, it removes all entries with timestamps older than current time minus the window duration using ZREMRANGEBYSCORE. Second, it counts the remaining elements in the set with ZCARD. Third, if the count is below the allowed limit, it adds the current timestamp with ZADD and returns an allowed response; otherwise, it calculates the retry-after delay from the oldest element and returns a rejected response. The trade-off is Redis memory footprint versus rate smoothness: sliding logs eliminate burst spikes completely, but storing individual timestamps consumes more memory in Redis than simple integer counters.
followUps: How does a sliding-window counter approximate a sliding log with fixed memory footprint?
What happens to rate limiting if the Redis cluster experiences a failover or network partition?
wrongAnswers: Using simple Redis INCR with EXPIRE, which creates fixed-window boundary spikes that allow double the rate limit across window edges.
Executing the remove, count, and add commands across multiple separate network round-trips to Redis, causing race conditions.
tradeOffs: Sliding-window logs eliminate boundary burst spikes completely, providing smooth, continuous rate enforcement across distributed nodes.
Storing every request timestamp in a Redis sorted set consumes O(N) memory per client, requiring TTLs to clean up expired sets.
keyPoints: Fixed windows allow bursts at window boundaries.
Store approved request timestamps in Redis sorted sets.
Atomically remove expired entries, count and admit with a Lua script.
Compute retry-after from the oldest entry at the cost of per-request storage.

questions.title: When upstream LLM providers return HTTP 429 rate limit errors, how do you implement priority load shedding to protect critical production traffic?
questions.answer: During peak traffic or upstream provider degradations, third-party LLM APIs frequently return HTTP 429 rate limit errors. If an application gateway treats all traffic equally, critical interactive user requests fail alongside low-priority background jobs. We implement priority load shedding at our API gateway. We classify all incoming requests into three priority tiers: Tier 1 is interactive customer-facing requests where latency directly impacts user experience; Tier 2 is asynchronous business workflows like email generation or batch document processing; Tier 3 is offline tasks like evaluation runs, synthetic data generation, and internal analytics. When upstream 429 responses or queue latencies cross threshold limits, the gateway activates load shedding: it immediately drops or defers Tier 3 batch jobs into durable message queues with exponential backoff. If pressure persists, it throttles Tier 2 jobs, preserving 100% of available upstream capacity for Tier 1 interactive users. The trade-off is background job processing delay versus customer experience protection: non-critical tasks experience processing backlogs, but customer-facing applications remain responsive during external provider crises.
followUps: How do you determine when to restore normal traffic processing after upstream 429 errors subside?
What backoff strategy should background workers use when consuming deferred tasks from the queue?
wrongAnswers: Retrying all failed requests immediately upon receiving an HTTP 429 error, creating a retry storm that worsens upstream throttling.
Treating internal test and eval runs with the same priority as paying end users, causing customer outages during benchmark testing.
tradeOffs: Priority load shedding preserves uptime for interactive user experiences during provider capacity crises, but delays background batch jobs.
Durable queue buffering ensures dropped lower-tier requests are eventually processed without data loss once capacity recovers.
keyPoints: Prioritize interactive traffic over asynchronous workflows and offline jobs.
Trigger load shedding on upstream 429s or excessive queue latency.
Defer low-priority jobs into durable queues with backoff.
Throttle the next tier if pressure persists to preserve interactive capacity.

questions.title: How do you implement token reservation and reconciliation for streaming LLM responses to prevent quota overshoots?
questions.answer: In streaming inference, token counts are unknown when the request starts because generation length depends on model decisions and stop sequences. If a gateway only debits tokens after generation finishes, a user with ten tokens remaining in their quota can initiate ten concurrent streaming requests that each generate 1,000 tokens, overshooting their quota by 10,000 tokens. We implement token reservation and reconciliation. When a streaming request arrives, the gateway inspects the prompt length, adds the requested max_tokens, and reserves that total from the tenant's token bucket up front. If the tenant has insufficient tokens, the request is rejected immediately. As the stream executes, if the user aborts the connection or the model emits an early stop token, the stream terminates. Upon completion, the gateway reads the exact token count reported in the final stream chunk, calculates the difference between reserved tokens and actual tokens consumed, and immediately credits the unused tokens back to the tenant's bucket. The trade-off is temporary quota reservation contention versus financial overdraft protection: reserving max tokens up front prevents unauthorized over-generation, but can temporarily block concurrent requests from users until short generations finish.
followUps: How do you handle token reconciliation if the gateway server crashes in the middle of an active streaming response?
What default reservation limit should you apply if a client does not specify max_tokens in their API request?
wrongAnswers: Debiting tokens only after the stream finishes, allowing malicious users to launch massive concurrent streams that blow past quotas.
Permanently deducting max_tokens without refunding unused capacity when a short answer finishes early.
tradeOffs: Up-front token reservation guarantees tenants cannot exceed billing quotas across concurrent streams, but requires atomic reserve and credit logic.
Over-reserving max_tokens can temporarily throttle legitimate concurrent requests until actual usage is reconciled.
keyPoints: Reserve prompt plus max completion tokens when a stream starts.
Reject requests whose tenant cannot cover the reservation.
Reconcile actual usage and refund unused tokens on completion or abort.
Upfront reservations prevent overdrafts but temporarily block concurrency.

questions.title: Your new prompt scores higher than the old one on your labeled set. A product manager asks why you still want a randomized online test before the full launch. Give the two-minute version.
questions.answer: An eval tells you whether the model can do the task on a fixed, labeled distribution. A randomized test with live users tells you whether users notice and care. A prompt can win on the labeled set and move no product metric, or move it the wrong way. You need both: the eval blocks a regression before any user sees it, and the experiment confirms the product effect after.
followUps: Level 1: Name one metric an experiment produces that an eval cannot. Expected: a user-level metric such as retention, conversion or the thumbs-down rate.

Level 2: The canary passed, and the experiment shows a small drop in conversion. Ship? Expected: not by default. Write the escalation criterion before the test starts, and treat a negative primary metric as a stop.
Level 2: When do you skip the experiment after a canary? Expected: when the new version is an improvement of the same behavior, not an alternative with a different cost curve or tone.

Level 3: Why does model non-determinism change the sample size? Expected: identical inputs give different outputs, so the effective sample is smaller than the nominal one. The lesson multiplies the required sample by about 1.3 to 1.5.
wrongAnswers: "The eval set is larger, so it is more reliable." The eval set is fixed and labeled, and it measures correctness, not what users prefer.
"Run the experiment and skip the eval to save a week." Without the eval, a regression reaches users before anyone can see it.
"If the eval and the experiment disagree, the experiment is wrong." They measure different things. A correct answer that users dislike is a real result.
keyPoints: Offline evals test capability on fixed labelled data.
Randomized live experiments measure whether users benefit.
An offline prompt win may fail to improve product metrics.
Use evals before deployment and experiments afterward.

questions.title: A teammate wants to skip the canary. The new model ran in shadow for a week with no errors and a flat bill, so they call it proven. What does that week show, and what does it leave open?
questions.answer: Shadow mode copies the production requests to the candidate and logs its outputs, and no user sees them. It shows that the candidate does not crash, does not refuse more often, does not cost more and does not write longer answers. It cannot show that users prefer the answers, because no user read one. Shadow is a smoke test, and the canary is the first quality test.
followUps: Level 1: Which signal does shadow give that an offline eval does not? Expected: the behavior of the candidate on the real request mix, including cost and output length per request.

Level 2: Shadow shows the cost per request is 40 percent above production. What do you do? Expected: stop before any canary. A cost more than 20 percent above the baseline is a gate breach, and a model that breaks the unit economics is a rollback case.
Level 2: Why can shadow not measure user feedback? Expected: no user sees the candidate output, so there is nothing for a user to rate or report.

Level 3: Shadow doubles the load on your model service. How do you keep it affordable? Expected: send a fixed share of requests to the candidate instead of all of them, and log the same metrics for that share.
wrongAnswers: "Shadow passed, so the quality is fine." Shadow has no user, so it measures cost, length, errors and refusals only.
"Shadow is a canary at zero percent." A canary returns the candidate output to real users and gates on their feedback. Shadow never returns an output to a user.
"A week in shadow replaces the offline eval." The eval judges correctness on a labeled set. Shadow records behavior on live traffic. They answer different questions.
keyPoints: Shadow mode copies production requests to a hidden candidate.
Log crashes, refusals, cost and output length.
Hidden outputs cannot establish user preference.
Use a canary to test visible quality effects.

questions.title: You add tracing to an agent. In one run it calls a model API twice, runs two tools inside its own process and sends one request to a tool server on another machine. Which of these operations get a CLIENT span, which get an INTERNAL span, and why does anyone care?
questions.answer: A call that leaves the process gets a CLIENT span: the two model API calls and the request to the remote tool server. The agent loop step and a tool that runs in your own process get INTERNAL spans. The kind tells a backend the direction of each call, so it can show which operations left the process and which did not.
followUps: Level 1: What joins the spans into one tree? Expected: one shared trace id, and a parent span id on every child.
Level 2: The agent calls a hosted agent service instead of a local one. What kind is that span? Expected: CLIENT, because the agent runs in another process.
Level 2: Which attribute lets a dashboard split cost by provider? Expected: gen_ai.provider.name, and multi-provider dashboards break when it is missing.
Level 3: A sub-agent runs inside the same process. Does it start a new trace? Expected: no. It is a child span under the parent agent span, so the whole run stays in one trace.
wrongAnswers: "Every tool call is a CLIENT span." A tool that runs in your process is INTERNAL. Only the call that leaves the process is CLIENT.
"The kind is decoration." Backends read the kind to show direction, and the conventions set it per span category.
"Start a new trace for each tool call, for isolation." Separate traces lose the parent link, so you cannot see which step caused the call.
keyPoints: Use CLIENT spans for calls leaving the process.
Model API calls are CLIENT operations.
Remote tool-server calls are also CLIENT operations.
Use INTERNAL spans for agent steps and in-process tools.

questions.title: A new team wants to run its first chaos experiment against the model service next week. What do you check for before you agree, and what goes wrong when one piece is missing?
questions.answer: Five things have to be in place: service level indicators with objectives, observability with traces, metrics and logs, an automated rollback, structured runbooks and an on-call owner. Each one lets you measure the experiment, stop it or repair the damage. When one is missing, the experiment is not a test. It is an incident that you scheduled.
followUps: Level 1: Which experiment goes first, and why? Expected: kill one decode replica under steady traffic, because it tests rerouting and recovery with a small blast radius.
Level 2: Name one failure a generic network chaos tool cannot reproduce for a model service. Expected: a KV cache eviction storm under burst load, or a prompt that stalls the tokenizer.

Level 2: Why does the rollback matter more than the dashboard during an experiment? Expected: the dashboard shows the harm, and the rollback stops it. Without the rollback the harm continues until someone fixes it by hand.

Level 3: The team wants staging only. When is production the right place? Expected: when staging cannot reproduce the traffic shape, the cache state or the provider behavior, and only with the safety guards in place.
wrongAnswers: "Skip the prerequisites and learn by doing." Without an SLO, a rollback and an on-call owner, the experiment is an outage that you caused on purpose.
"A dashboard is observability." Chaos needs traces, metrics and logs with trace-id correlation, so that you can tell experiment failures from natural ones.
"Run the biggest experiment first to find the biggest risk." Start with one replica kill, then grow the blast radius.
keyPoints: Define service indicators and objectives before chaos tests.
Provide traces, metrics and logs.
Have automated rollback and structured runbooks.
Assign an on-call owner to stop or repair failures.

questions.title: Your service handles 1,000 requests per minute. The canary opens at one percent, and the gate runs every five minutes. About how many data points does one gate check see, and which gates can you trust at this step?
questions.answer: One percent of the 1,000 per minute is 10 requests per minute to the canary, so a five-minute window holds about 50 points and a fifteen-minute window about 150. That is enough to read latency and error rates, and far too few to read user feedback. Gate the first step on latency, cost, errors and output length, and apply the feedback gate at a later step.
followUps: Level 2: At which step does the user feedback gate become usable? Expected: at 10 percent, where the canary sees about ten times more points per window.
Level 2: Why does a longer window not fix the first step? Expected: a longer window adds points slowly, and a regression runs for the whole window before the gate can fire.

Level 3: Traffic falls to a tenth at night. How does the plan change? Expected: the same share gives about one request per minute, so lengthen the dwell, start at a higher share, or run the ramp during the day.

Level 3: A breach must hold for two windows before the gate fires. What does that cost? Expected: a real regression keeps running through both windows until the halt, so the rule trades fewer false alarms for a longer exposure.
wrongAnswers: "One percent is safe, so the gates work at one percent." The share is safe for users, and most gates are blind at that sample size.
"Check every minute for faster detection." A one-minute window at this step holds about ten points, which cannot give a percentile.
"Start at 25 percent for better statistics." A quarter of the users see the new model before any gate has fired once.
keyPoints: One percent of 1,000 requests per minute is ten canary requests.
Five and fifteen minutes provide about fifty and 150 observations.
Early samples support latency and error checks rather than user feedback.
Gate latency, cost, errors and length first, then feedback later.

questions.title: You are about to share a public link to a model demo. Every request that reaches the model costs money. Design the sequence of checks a request passes before the model runs, and give the HTTP status for each refusal.
questions.answer: Run the cheap checks first and the paid step last. Refuse an oversized body from its Content-Length header before you read it, check the access token, take one token from the client's rate bucket, parse and validate the JSON, charge the daily usage cap, and only then call the model. Each refusal returns a JSON error with a stable code, a message and a hint, and the statuses in that order are 413, 401, 429, 422 and 503.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the usage cap come after the field checks? Expected: so that only valid requests count against the day's total.
Level 2: Why refuse on the header before reading the body? Expected: it stops a large upload before the server spends memory and time on it.

Level 3: Behind a reverse proxy one heavy user gets everyone rate limited. Why? Expected: every request arrives from the proxy address, so all clients share one bucket. Read the client address from the proxy's header, and trust it from the proxy only.

Level 3: What does the server do with a refused body before it answers 413? Expected: it reads and discards up to 64 KiB, because a close with unread data can trigger a TCP reset and the client loses the reply.
wrongAnswers: "Validate the text first, then check the size." Reading the body before the size check spends the cost that the check exists to avoid.
"A rate limit is enough, skip the cap." A per-client limit bounds each client. A hundred clients under the limit still spend the whole budget.
"Return 500 with the stack trace, developers can read it." A stranger cannot act on a stack trace. An error needs a code, a fact and one next action.
keyPoints: Reject oversized bodies before reading them.
Check authentication and rate limits before JSON validation.
Apply the daily usage cap before the paid model call.
Return stable structured errors with the appropriate status code.

questions.title: Your eval scores have been flat all year. A product owner tells you that what users ask has changed a lot since spring. How do you detect that change from telemetry, and what do you do with the result?
questions.answer: Embed the prompts, pool them per week, and compare the week with a trailing baseline using a population stability index or a KL divergence. A rising score means the input distribution moved, even when the scores on your fixed eval set did not. Alert above a threshold, then sample and label prompts from the new distribution, refresh the eval set, and recheck routing and prompts against it.
followUps: Level 2: What is the difference between a PSI on prompts and a falling eval score? Expected: the PSI measures the inputs, the eval measures the model on fixed inputs, and the first can move while the second stays flat.
Level 2: Why run the detector per application id? Expected: a global score averages the drift away, and the per-application view shows which surface moved.
Level 3: What goes wrong with a one-week baseline? Expected: weekly seasonality looks like drift, and the baseline moves along with the inputs it should measure.

Level 3: The PSI crossed the threshold after a marketing campaign. Is that a problem? Expected: it is a real shift in the inputs. The question is whether quality held on them, so sample, label and evaluate.
wrongAnswers: "Flat eval scores mean no drift." The eval set is fixed, so it cannot see the inputs change.
"Compare the raw prompt strings." Wording varies on every request. Embeddings capture the topic distribution.
"Alert on any score above zero." Small values are noise. The capstone's threshold is 0.2.
keyPoints: Embed prompts and pool them by week.
Compare with a trailing distribution using PSI or KL divergence.
Alert when the drift score crosses a threshold.
Label shifted traffic, refresh evals and recheck routing and prompts.

questions.title: Your service makes more than a million model calls a day. Keeping every trace now costs more than the model calls themselves. Design a retention policy that keeps the traces you will need during an incident and drops the rest.
questions.answer: Sample by rule, not by a flat rate. Keep every errored trace and every high-cost trace, keep a small share of the successes, and keep the aggregates always. Make the decision at the collector with a tail sampler after the trace completes, so that the rule can see the status and the cost. The capstone keeps all errored traces and 10 percent of the successes.
followUps: Level 2: Why does head sampling lose the errors? Expected: it decides before the span ends, so it cannot see the status.
Level 2: What survives from a dropped trace? Expected: the metrics. Counters and histograms count every request, whether or not its trace is kept.

Level 3: Your eval jobs run over the sampled traces. What bias do they inherit? Expected: a sample that keeps all errors overweights failures, so weight by the inverse sampling rate or evaluate the stratified share only.

Level 3: The collector runs out of memory during a burst. Why, and what do you change? Expected: tail sampling buffers whole traces until they complete. Cap the buffer, shorten the decision wait, and shed with a head rule under pressure.
wrongAnswers: "Sample 5 percent of everything." Most of the errors you need in an incident are gone, and the aggregate tells you only that they happened.
"Keep everything for a week, then delete it." A week of full traces at this volume is the cost you are trying to remove.
"Traces are enough, drop the metrics." A percentile over an hour needs every request, which only a histogram gives.
keyPoints: Keep every error and high-cost trace.
Sample only a small share of successful traces.
Retain aggregate metrics always.
Use tail sampling after completion so status and cost are known.

questions.title: Your trace backend can store the full prompt and completion on every model span. The support team wants it on, because they debug tickets from traces. The security team wants it off. What do you decide, and how do you still give support what they need?
questions.answer: Keep content capture off, which is the default the conventions recommend. Store prompts and completions in your own store, with access control and a retention period, and record a reference id on the span. Support follows the id from the trace to the content, and the trace backend never holds customer data.
followUps: Level 2: Which spans may carry raw content when capture is on? Expected: none in production. Keep one rule, references only, so nobody has to decide per span.

Level 3: A developer turns capture on in staging for a day. What is the risk? Expected: staging often replays production prompts, and the backend keeps them for its retention period. Use synthetic prompts or scrub before export.
Level 3: How do you keep the content store from becoming the same leak? Expected: access by role, an audit log of reads, a retention period, and redaction of known patterns before the write.
wrongAnswers: "Turn it on, the trace backend is internal." Internal operators read traces, and the backend's retention is not your policy.
"Store a hash of the prompt on the span." A hash shows a repeat but gives support nothing to read. A reference id into a controlled store does both.
"Keep the content on the span and strip personal data with a regex." Patterns miss, and the span is still the wrong store with the wrong retention.
keyPoints: Leave prompt and completion capture disabled in spans.
Store content separately under access control.
Set a retention period for the content store.
Put a reference ID on spans for authorized support lookup.

questions.title: After a routine upgrade of the tracing SDK, the token usage panels show zero for every model, while request counts and latency panels look normal. Nothing else was deployed. Where do you look first?
questions.answer: Look at the attribute names on the spans the service emits now. The GenAI conventions are still marked as in development, and they have renamed attributes before: the input token count moved from gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens to gen_ai.usage.input_tokens. If the SDK emits the new name and the dashboard queries the old one, every token panel reads zero while counts and latency keep working. Pin the conventions version you emit, and set the stability opt-in so that the names do not move under you.
followUps: Level 2: Why did the count and latency panels keep working? Expected: they use span counts and span timing, which do not depend on an attribute name.
Level 3: How do you catch the next rename before production? Expected: a test on emitted spans that asserts the canonical attribute names, run on every dependency upgrade.
Level 3: Should the dashboard read both the old and the new name? Expected: yes for a transition window, as a sum of both. Then remove the old one, so that a future regression stays visible.

Level 4: The backend maps the attributes into its own schema. Does that protect you? Expected: only when the mapping follows the same conventions version. A mapping built for the old name shows the same zero, so test the end-to-end path.
wrongAnswers: "The models stopped reporting usage." The provider responses did not change. The span emitter did.
"The backend lost data during the upgrade." The latency panels prove the spans arrive. Only one attribute is missing from the query's point of view.
"Roll the SDK back and stay there." A pinned conventions version and a test let you upgrade on purpose instead of never.
keyPoints: Inspect currently emitted span attribute names.
Input-token attributes can change across convention versions.
A dashboard querying the old name can show zero tokens.
Pin emitted convention versions and stability opt-ins.

questions.title: Last quarter a bad model launch took three hours to undo, because the only way back was a new deployment. You own the release path now. Design it so that the next time, the way back takes seconds. Name the pieces and say what each one holds.
questions.answer: Separate the policy from the model. Keep the traffic split in a feature flag that a configuration change flips, and keep the model in a registry under a pinned digest that never upgrades on its own. A rollback is then two actions: revert the flag, and point the pin at the previous digest, which also restores the prompt and template version pinned with that model. Nothing is rebuilt and nothing is redeployed.
followUps: Level 2: Why pin the model by digest and not by tag? Expected: a tag can move to a new build. A digest is immutable, so the rollback target is exactly the model that ran before.
Level 2: What else must revert together with the model? Expected: the gate thresholds, and any prompt or template version that shipped with the model.
Level 3: How do you know the path works before you need it? Expected: rehearse it in staging on every release and time it end to end, against a target such as the lesson's 60 seconds.

Level 3: The new model needs a new engine image. Does the flag still work? Expected: yes, when both images run side by side and the flag chooses between them. The old deployment stays alive until the new one has held at 100 percent.
wrongAnswers: "Roll back by redeploying the previous image." A redeploy takes hours, and the lesson's point is to separate the rollback from the deployment.
"Delete the old model a day after the launch." The old model must stay available until the canary has held at full traffic through every gate.
"A fast rollback makes the gates unnecessary." The gates decide when to roll back. The fast path only limits the damage once they fire.

questions.title: An experiment assigns users evenly to control and variant. After a week the dashboard shows 47 percent of users in control and 53 percent in the variant, and the variant is ahead on the primary metric. What do you conclude, and what do you do next?
questions.answer: Do not read the result. A configured even split that delivers 47 to 53 over a week of traffic is a sample ratio mismatch, which means the assignment or the logging is broken and the two groups are no longer comparable. Find the cause in the assignment path, fix it, and start the experiment again.
followUps: Level 2: Why hash the user id instead of drawing an arm at random on each request? Expected: the same user lands in the same arm on every request, so the experience is consistent and the exposure count is per user.
Level 3: Name two causes that put more users in the variant than in control. Expected: a logging failure that drops control exposures, or a variant path that treats bots or retries differently.
Level 3: Can you correct the mismatch statistically and keep the result? Expected: no. The mismatch shows that the groups are not comparable, and no correction restores the randomization.
wrongAnswers: "Three percent is within noise." Over a week of traffic, that gap under a fair split is very unlikely, and the mismatch check exists to flag exactly this case.
"The variant wins by more than the gap, so ship it." The gap can be correlated with the outcome, so the lift can be the dropout itself.
"Drop variant users until the groups match." Removing users after the fact adds a second bias on top of the first.

questions.title: Your demo streams tokens to the page over server-sent events. Users report that the page sometimes shows half an answer and then stops, with no message. The server log shows a model exception on exactly those requests. Why does the user see nothing, and how do you fix the protocol?
questions.answer: The server sends the status line with status 200 before the first token. When the model fails after that, the status cannot change, so the client sees a stream that ends early and nothing else. Send an error event inside the stream, and make the page show that event as an error. Also stop the generator when the client disconnects, so that a closed tab stops the model.
followUps: Level 2: Why can the server not send a 500 when the model fails halfway? Expected: the status line went out before the first token, and a response has one status.
Level 2: A user closes the tab halfway through. What should the server do? Expected: the write fails with a broken pipe, the handler closes the generator, and the model stops.

Level 3: Why does the page buffer the bytes instead of parsing each chunk as an event? Expected: a chunk can end in the middle of an event, so the reader keeps the partial text until the blank line arrives.
Level 3: What goes into the error event besides the message? Expected: a stable code that tests can compare, a hint with one action, and the request id that joins the report to a log record.
wrongAnswers: "Buffer the whole answer and return JSON instead." That removes streaming, and the user waits for the last token on every request.
"Send the error text as another token." The page cannot tell an error from model output, and the done event never arrives.
"Retry the request on the server when the model fails." The user already has half an answer. A retry duplicates output and doubles the cost.

questions.title: An incident triage agent proposes a root cause for every alert. The on-call team stopped trusting it after several confident wrong answers. Which pattern from the SRE lesson raises the trust in its output, and what does the team do when the pattern says the agent is unsure?
questions.answer: Run two models independently on the same incident. When they agree on the root cause, confidence is high. When they disagree, the system escalates to a person with both hypotheses and their evidence visible, instead of picking one. The pattern filters invented root causes at a low cost, and the disagreement itself tells the responder that the incident is uncertain.
followUps: Level 2: Why is a split verdict useful to the responder? Expected: it marks the incident as uncertain and gives the responder two candidate causes with their evidence.
Level 3: Both models agree and both are wrong. How do you catch it? Expected: require each hypothesis to cite evidence that the responder can check, and keep the human approval before any action.

Level 3: What does the pattern cost? Expected: two model runs per incident plus the latency of the slower one, which is small next to the first twenty minutes of a manual investigation that the lesson says are automatable.
wrongAnswers: "Ask one model twice at temperature zero." A repeat of the same model shares its blind spots. The pattern needs independent analyses.
"Let an agreed hypothesis trigger the fix on its own." Agreement raises confidence. The person still approves the action, and only narrow actions are automated at all.
"Disagreement proves the agent is useless." It means the incident is uncertain, which is exactly when a person should look.

questions.title: You run a canary for a new model. The team wants a rule that stops the rollout when the canary and the baseline differ on any metric. Design the gates so that they catch a real regression and let a healthy rollout through.
questions.answer: Write each gate as a multiplier above the baseline, never as equality. Gate on five metrics: latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, output length distribution and user feedback rate. Put every threshold above the run-to-run variance, which the lesson measured at up to 15 percent on identical inputs, and hold each step long enough to collect the samples the gate needs.
followUps: Level 3: How do you learn the size of the noise before the canary starts? Expected: run two canary arms of the same baseline and record the spread of each metric between them.

Level 3: User feedback at the first step is too thin to gate on. What do you do? Expected: gate the early steps on latency, cost, errors and length, and apply the feedback gate from the step that has enough samples.

Level 4: A gate fires at one step, and the metric is normal again on the next check. Continue or halt? Expected: halt and look. A gate that flaps sits inside the noise or sees an intermittent regression, and both need a decision before more users see the model.
wrongAnswers: "Stop on any difference from the baseline." Two runs of the same model differ, so that rule stops every rollout.
"Gate on the mean latency." A mean hides the tail. Gate on the percentiles.
"Allow zero cost increase." A better model can cost more. The lesson sets the breach at 20 percent, and the product decides whether the gain pays for it.

questions.title: Your team must choose an observability stack for a new model service. Half the team wants an all-in-one platform with evals, prompt versions and session replays. The other half wants a thin gateway that records every call and nothing more. How do you decide, and which pattern lets you avoid the choice?
questions.answer: Decide on four axes: the framework you run on, the license you can accept, the budget, and whether you must self-host. A bundled development platform fits a team that iterates on prompts and needs evals tied to traces. A gateway or telemetry tool fits a team that needs portable instrumentation that does not depend on a framework. The pattern that avoids the choice is to emit OpenTelemetry spans with the GenAI conventions from every call and ship them to more than one place: a gateway for day-to-day, an eval platform for regressions, and an archive for long-term analysis.
followUps: Level 3: Why instrument at the SDK layer rather than inside the framework? Expected: framework hooks tie you to the framework. The SDK layer keeps working when you change frameworks or add a second one.
Level 3: What breaks when prompt versions are not tied to traces? Expected: when production regresses you cannot bisect to the prompt change that caused it.

Level 4: You ship the same spans to two backends. What do you check so that they agree? Expected: the same conventions version, the same sampling rules on both exporters, and one source of truth for cost attribution, so that two dashboards do not show two bills.
wrongAnswers: "Pick the tool with the most features." Features you do not use cost money and couple you. Pick on stack, license, budget and hosting.
"Tracing is enough, evals can come later." Traces without evals are logs with a price. A regression hides in them until a user reports it.
"The gateway records every call, so skip the platform." A proxy sees calls, not agent steps or sessions. It misses the multi-step traces that an agent regression needs.

questions.title: A regression ships. One of your prompts starts to leak fake customer identifiers in about one answer in a hundred. Design the observability pipeline so that an alert reaches a person within five minutes of the first bad answer, and say what each stage adds to that clock.
questions.answer: Instrument every model call with GenAI-convention spans and ship them over OTLP to a collector. Run a cheap pattern check on every output at the collector, run a judge over the sampled traces on a short schedule, write the scores back as eval spans, export the aggregates as metrics, and alert when the leak score crosses a threshold. The five minutes are the sum of the scrape interval, the judge batch window and the alert routing, so each stage has to be short, and the sampler must keep enough traffic to see a one-in-a-hundred event. The five-minute target covers only the leaks that the pattern flags or the sampler keeps.
followUps: Level 3: Which stage usually dominates the five minutes? Expected: the judge batch window. A job that runs every fifteen minutes cannot meet a five-minute target.

Level 3: The sampler drops nine of every ten successes. What happens to detection when the leak rate is one percent? Expected: it sees one leak in a thousand answers, so at low traffic the detection takes longer. Keep every trace that a cheap pattern check flags.
Level 4: How do you prove the pipeline meets the target? Expected: inject the regression on purpose, as the capstone does, and measure the time from the deployment to the alert.
wrongAnswers: "Run the judge on every trace." At volume that costs more than the model calls. Sample, and filter with a cheap check first.
"A daily eval report is enough." A day of leaked identifiers is the incident. The target is minutes.
"The pattern check catches everything." Patterns miss paraphrases. The judge catches what the pattern misses, and the pattern keeps the judge affordable.

questions.title: A product manager reads the experiment dashboard every morning and wants to end the test on the first day the variant looks significant. Twenty other experiments run this quarter under the same plan. What is wrong with it, and what do you offer instead?
questions.answer: A fixed-sample test assumes one look at a sample size chosen in advance. Looking every day and stopping at the first significant result gives noise many chances to cross the line, so the false positive rate climbs. Offer a sequential test, which stays valid under repeated looks and still allows an early stop on a clear winner. Across many experiments, correct for multiple comparisons, and reduce variance with pre-experiment data so each test needs fewer samples.
followUps: Level 3: Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg for the quarter? Expected: Bonferroni when any false launch is costly, Benjamini-Hochberg when you accept a controlled share of false discoveries in exchange for power.
Level 3: What does CUPED need, and what does it give? Expected: it needs a pre-period metric for each unit, and it gives a tighter estimate from the same traffic.

Level 4: A new model needs a larger sample than the quarter allows. What do you change? Expected: pick a primary metric with lower variance, apply CUPED, or extend the test. Do not shorten it by stopping early under a fixed-sample procedure.
wrongAnswers: "Stopping early is fine when the p-value is small." Under a fixed-sample test, a small p-value on the first day is partly selected noise. Only a sequential procedure keeps that stop valid.
"Run all the tests at 95 percent and ship the winners." About one winner is a false positive by chance. Correct for multiple comparisons.
"A longer test is always more reliable." Longer helps only if the assignment is sound. Check the sample ratio first.

questions.title: During a provider slowdown, the provider began to return rate-limit errors. Within minutes your own service ran out of memory and crashed, although your incoming traffic had not changed. Reconstruct what happened, and fix the retry policy.
questions.answer: The gateway retried every rate-limited call, and each waiting retry kept its connection, its buffers and its request state in memory. The retries multiplied the in-flight concurrency several times over the real traffic, and the memory went with it. Fix the policy with exponential backoff and jitter, a small fixed number of attempts, a cap on in-flight requests, and a fallback chain that fails over instead of waiting.
followUps: Level 3: Why does backoff alone not stop the memory growth? Expected: backoff spreads the retries in time, and each waiting retry still holds its state. The fix needs a bound on in-flight requests.
Level 3: What does a queue do that a retry does not? Expected: it stores the request without a connection or a worker, and it gives the user a progress message instead of a timeout.

Level 4: The fallback model is cheaper and weaker. Who decides that it is acceptable, and how do you watch it? Expected: the product owner names the paths that may degrade. Log the fallback rate per path, and alert when it stays high.
wrongAnswers: "Retry faster so the queue drains before memory runs out." Faster retries raise the request rate against a provider that is already limiting you.
"Raise the maximum retries so users never see an error." Each attempt holds memory. More attempts multiply the in-flight state.
"The provider caused the outage, there is nothing to fix here." The provider caused the errors. The retry policy turned them into an outage.

questions.title: A vendor demo shows an operations agent that repairs incidents on its own. Your director asks which actions you would let such an agent take on the model service without a person in the loop. Draw the line and defend it.
questions.answer: Allow a narrow set that was approved in advance: restart a pod, revert one named deployment, scale a pool inside approved bounds, and flip an approved feature flag. Keep everything that changes the shape of the system behind a person: topology, resource limits, new code, access rights and databases. The agent proposes, a person approves the judgment calls, and the safe set grows only as the agent builds a record.
followUps: Level 3: Why is a scale-up inside bounds safe while a resource limit change is not? Expected: the bounds were approved in advance and the action reverses cleanly. A limit change alters how every pod runs and can trigger the next incident.

Level 3: What has to be true before the agent may run an action unsupervised? Expected: a structured runbook, a verify step with a success criterion, an audit record, and a record of proposals that matched the human decision.

Level 4: The agent restarted the busiest pod during a load spike because a probe failed. Was that inside the rules? Expected: the action was allowed and the trigger was wrong. A restart under load drops the running requests, so the rule needs a condition on load and on the probe type, not only on the action.
wrongAnswers: "If the agent is accurate enough, let it do everything." Accuracy on past incidents does not bound the damage of one wrong broad action.
"No automation until the agent is perfect." A restart and a revert are safe today, and they remove the first part of most investigations.
"An approval step makes the agent useless at night." The agent still does the investigation. The person approves one proposed action instead of starting from the dashboards.

questions.title: Your agent uses three tool servers over the MCP protocol. Two of them speak streamable HTTP, and one runs as a local subprocess over stdio. Design how a single trace id reaches all three, and say what each server has to do when it arrives.
