questions.answer: For the HTTP servers, inject the W3C traceparent header into every request, as any traced HTTP client does. The stdio transport has no headers, so put the same value into the _meta field of each JSON-RPC request until the protocol adds a standard field for it. Each server reads the value, opens its own span as a child of that context, writes the trace id into its logs, and passes the context on if it calls anything else.
followUps: Level 3: A server ignores the _meta field. What do you see in the trace? Expected: the server's work shows up as a separate trace or not at all, and the client span shows the duration but not where the time went.

Level 3: Which span records the hang, the client span or the server span? Expected: both. The client span shows the wait from the agent's side, the server span shows what the server did, and the gap between them is the transport.

Level 4: Another team operates one tool server. What do you ask them to commit to? Expected: accept the context from headers or _meta, continue the trace instead of starting one, log the trace id, and export spans to a backend that both teams can read.
wrongAnswers: "Log a request id and join the logs later." A request id has no parent-child structure and no timing. A trace has both.
"The stdio server is local, so it does not need tracing." The hang in the lesson was in a local server's cold start. Local does not mean fast.
"Put the trace id into the prompt so the model carries it." The model is not a transport, and a changing value in the prompt also breaks the prefix cache.

questions.title: Take-home. You receive a candidate model, a baseline model, and one week of production request logs with the latency, the token counts and the user feedback of each request. Deliver a rollout plan and a simulator that executes it: a shadow phase, a canary ramp with gates, and a rollback. Inject at least two regressions and show where the plan halts for each one. The logs hold user feedback only for the responses that users saw, so state how the simulator produces feedback for the candidate.
questions.answer: Build a simulator that replays the logs through both models, computes the five gate metrics per step, and advances the ramp only when every gate holds for the required number of windows. Set each threshold above the baseline's own run-to-run variance, which you measure by replaying the baseline against itself. Inject a cost regression and a quality regression, and show the step at which each one halts and the rollback that follows.
followUps: Level 3: The feedback regression was caught late. Is the plan wrong? Expected: no. It shows the limit of the feedback gate, and the fix is a longer dwell at the step where feedback first has samples, or a proxy metric with more volume.

Level 4: The candidate has the same cost and tone as the baseline. What changes in the plan? Expected: skip the A/B step after the canary, which the lesson makes optional for an improved version of the same behavior.
Level 4: What from the simulator survives into production? Expected: the gate evaluation code and the noise-floor measurement, which become the canary controller's checks.
wrongAnswers: "Use the lesson's thresholds as they are." The lesson's numbers are defaults. The floor comes from your own baseline.
"Advance the ramp on a fixed schedule." A ramp that moves on the clock ignores whether a gate had enough samples.
"Model the rollback as a redeploy." The simulator should model the mechanism you will use, and a redeploy is the mechanism the lesson tells you to remove.

questions.title: You run a chaos experiment in production. One model provider returns rate-limit errors for part of the fleet, so that you can watch the fallback. Alerts start to fire while it runs. Design the safety plane that keeps this from turning into an incident, and explain how on-call tells an experiment failure from a natural one.
questions.answer: Three guards sit in the safety plane: a burn-rate alert that pauses the experiment when the daily error-budget burn passes twice the expected rate, suppression windows that silence the non-experiment alerts inside the blast radius, and a tag on the trace id of every error that the experiment causes. On-call reads the tag. An untagged error inside the window is natural and gets the normal response.
followUps: Level 3: Why gate at twice the expected burn and not at any burn? Expected: an experiment is meant to spend some budget. The gate catches the case where it spends far more than planned.

Level 4: The burn keeps rising after the pause. What does that tell you? Expected: the cause is natural, or the experiment broke something that does not recover on its own. Run the incident response and roll back the last change.

Level 4: How do you pick the blast radius for a provider outage experiment? Expected: a share small enough that the fallback capacity covers it, written into the experiment definition and reviewed with on-call.
wrongAnswers: "Silence all alerts during the experiment." A natural incident in the same window goes unseen. Silence only the blast radius, and keep tagged errors visible.
"Run it in staging, so no safety plane is needed." Staging cannot show the fallback under real traffic. The safety plane is what makes production acceptable.
"The burn-rate alert is the kill switch." The alert pauses the experiment. The kill switch stops it at once, and it should be a separate manual control.

questions.title: A model trained on your logs, GPU temperatures and error patterns predicts most outages ten to fifteen minutes before they happen. The team wants to ship it as a dashboard panel. Design what the system does with a prediction, and defend the design.
questions.answer: A prediction with no action is a dashboard, and nobody watches a dashboard at three in the morning. Write a policy per prediction class: page the on-call, drain the suspect node or pool before it fails, or scale within approved bounds, and record every prediction with its outcome. Start with the page, measure the precision on live incidents, and promote a class to an automatic drain only when its false alarm rate is acceptable and a person has approved that drain as a pre-approved action in the runbook.
followUps: Level 3: What does a false alarm cost under each policy? Expected: a page costs sleep, a drain costs capacity for the drain time, and a scale-up costs money. Pick the policy per class from that cost against the cost of the outage.

Level 4: The lead time is ten minutes and a replacement replica takes longer to warm. What changes? Expected: keep a warm spare or act earlier on a weaker signal. A drain with no warm replacement moves the outage instead of preventing it.
Level 4: How do you know the predictor still works after the service changes? Expected: track precision and recall per class on live incidents, and retrain when the input distribution shifts.
wrongAnswers: "Ship the panel and let on-call decide." At night nobody watches a panel. The lesson's point is that a prediction without an action is a dashboard.
"Automate the drain for every prediction from day one." A false alarm then costs capacity, and nothing has measured the false alarm rate on your traffic.
"The research number means we will prevent most outages." The number was on a test set. Your precision in production is unknown until you measure it.

topics.title: Cost and capacity
topics.about: Caching, routing, batch APIs, cold starts and the cost of each request.

questions.title: How does Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) allocate multi-tenant cluster compute when teams have heterogeneous GPU, CPU, and memory demands?
questions.answer: In multi-tenant clusters, teams have diverse resource requirements: some jobs need high GPU count with low CPU, while others require high host memory and multiple CPUs per GPU. Simple slot-based scheduling leads to starvation and poor utilization. Dominant Resource Fairness calculates each tenant's dominant share: the fraction of the total cluster capacity allocated to them for their most heavily consumed resource. For example, if Team A uses 10% of total cluster GPUs and 30% of total CPU, their dominant resource is CPU and their dominant share is 30%. The DRF scheduler always picks the tenant with the lowest dominant share and allocates resources to their next waiting job, ensuring max-min fairness across multiple heterogeneous resources. The trade-off is cluster-wide throughput versus per-tenant fairness: DRF guarantees that no team starves and encourages honest resource requests, but prioritizing the tenant with the lowest share can leave GPUs idle if that tenant's jobs cannot utilize available hardware.
followUps: How does DRF handle gang-scheduled distributed training jobs where all workers must launch simultaneously?
What happens when dominant resources fluctuate dynamically during training (e.g. data preprocessing spikes)?
wrongAnswers: Allocating resources based solely on GPU counts while ignoring CPU and memory, leading to node memory exhaustion and hung jobs.
Assuming DRF always yields maximum cluster FLOP utilization, ignoring that fairness often conflicts with packing efficiency.
tradeOffs: DRF guarantees multi-resource max-min fairness and sharing incentive, but can achieve lower overall GPU utilization than greedy schedulers.
Tenants can game allocation by misrepresenting secondary resource requirements unless resource usage is strictly enforced.
keyPoints: Compute each tenant's largest fraction of cluster resources as its dominant share.
Schedule the tenant with the lowest dominant share next.
DRF balances heterogeneous resources with max-min fairness.
Fair allocation can leave GPUs idle when the selected jobs cannot use them.

questions.title: When partitioning an NVIDIA A100 or H100 across multiple inference workloads, what are the trade-offs between Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) and Multi-Process Service (MPS)?
questions.answer: Multi-Instance GPU and Multi-Process Service represent two distinct approaches to sharing a large GPU like an NVIDIA A100 or H100 across multiple inference jobs. Multi-Instance GPU partitions the physical GPU at the hardware level into up to seven independent GPU instances, each with dedicated streaming multiprocessors, memory controllers, and isolated high-bandwidth memory. MIG provides strict hardware fault isolation and predictable performance: if one container crashes or runs out of memory, it cannot affect adjacent instances. Multi-Process Service, by contrast, is a software-level server that multiplexes multiple CUDA processes onto a single shared GPU context. MPS eliminates CUDA context switching overhead and dynamically shares all GPU resources, maximizing utilization for small, bursty workloads. The trade-off is isolation versus flexibility: MIG offers guaranteed hardware isolation and deterministic latency but locks memory into rigid partition sizes, while MPS shares all memory dynamically but lacks memory fault isolation—a memory crash in one process can take down all co-located workloads.
followUps: When is it appropriate to use MPS inside an individual MIG slice?
How does CUDA context switching latency compare between time-slicing and MPS?
wrongAnswers: Claiming MPS provides hardware-level memory protection, when a single CUDA memory fault under MPS terminates all co-located processes.
Believing MIG partitions can be resized dynamically on the fly without stopping running GPU workloads.
tradeOffs: MIG guarantees hardware-level fault and memory isolation, but only supports static, fixed-size slice configurations.
MPS allows dynamic, fine-grained resource sharing with high GPU utilization, but lacks memory fault isolation across tenants.
keyPoints: MIG hardware partitions provide dedicated compute and memory resources.
MPS multiplexes processes through a shared GPU context.
MIG offers predictable isolation with rigid partition sizes.
MPS improves dynamic utilization but lacks memory fault isolation.

questions.title: When a high-priority production job preempts a low-priority research job on a shared GPU cluster, how do you guarantee checkpoint integrity without wasting progress?
questions.answer: When a high-priority production inference job or priority training run needs compute on a shared GPU cluster, the scheduler preempts lower-priority batch jobs. If preemption kills a job abruptly, hours of training progress are lost. We implement graceful preemption using Unix termination signals and atomic checkpointing. When the scheduler decides to reclaim a node, it does not issue an immediate kill signal; it sends a SIGTERM or custom preemption signal and grants a grace period, typically 60 to 120 seconds. The training loop catches this signal, completes the current backward pass, writes model weights and optimizer states to local NVMe storage, and performs an atomic rename of the checkpoint directory to prevent corrupt partial writes. Once the write completes, the job exits cleanly with code zero, signaling the scheduler that resources are released. The trade-off is scheduling latency versus lost compute: providing a checkpoint grace period slightly delays the start of high-priority jobs, but it saves days of wasted GPU hours on interrupted training runs.
followUps: How do you ensure checkpoint writes are atomic so that a crash during the save does not corrupt the last valid checkpoint?
What happens if a training step takes longer than the scheduler's preemption grace period?
wrongAnswers: Issuing an immediate SIGKILL to preempted jobs, destroying in-memory training states and corrupting half-written checkpoints.
Writing checkpoints directly over slow cloud object storage during the preemption window, exceeding the grace period timeout.
tradeOffs: Graceful termination signals allow saving full state, but delay resource acquisition for high-priority incoming workloads.
Writing checkpoints to local NVMe is fast enough for 60-second grace windows, but requires an asynchronous background sync to network storage.
keyPoints: Send SIGTERM with a grace period before reclaiming a training node.
Complete the current backward pass and save weights and optimizer state.
Atomically rename the checkpoint to prevent partial writes.
Checkpointing delays high-priority work but preserves training progress.

questions.title: How do you design a token-bucket or credit-based quota system for multi-tenant LLM inference to prevent burst starvation across teams?
questions.answer: In a multi-tenant LLM serving platform, treating all requests equally leads to starvation: a single team sending large prompt batches can monopolize GPU memory and degrade latency for interactive users. We implement a two-tier token bucket quota system that separates prompt prefill tokens from generated output tokens. Prefill computation is compute-heavy and dominates latency, while decode token generation is memory-bandwidth bound. We allocate each tenant a bucket that refills at a sustained rate per second with a configurable burst limit. When a request arrives, the gateway estimates the prompt token count and reserves initial capacity. If the tenant has exhausted their token bucket, their requests are queued or throttled with HTTP 429 responses rather than blocking the GPU engine. The trade-off is strict budget isolation versus cluster utilization: rigid per-tenant rate limits prevent noisy neighbors and guarantee fair service, but if one team is idle, their unused capacity cannot be utilized by busy teams unless dynamic borrowing is supported.
followUps: How do you accurately deduct tokens when generated sequence lengths are unknown before inference completes?
How do you implement burst borrowing where teams can exceed quotas when overall cluster load is below 50%?
wrongAnswers: Rate limiting solely on raw HTTP request counts without tracking token volume, allowing one request with 100k tokens to monopolize the GPU.
Allowing unconstrained token bursting, enabling a single team's batch script to cause latency spikes for all interactive users.
tradeOffs: Separating prompt prefill quotas from decode token quotas prevents prefill compute spikes from starving interactive decoding.
Strict per-tenant rate limiting guarantees service predictability, but leaves GPU capacity idle if active tenants hit their caps while others sleep.
keyPoints: Separate prefill and decode token quota buckets.
Give tenants sustained refill rates and configurable burst limits.
Reserve prompt capacity before admitting work.
Queue or reject exhausted tenants, with borrowing needed to reuse idle quotas.

questions.title: In a shared inference cluster, what causes GPU VRAM fragmentation across dynamic request batches, and how do modern memory allocators mitigate it?
questions.answer: In transformer inference, each active request stores key and value tensors for every token in GPU memory. In traditional serving runtimes, memory for this KV-cache is allocated contiguously for the maximum possible sequence length. Because request lengths vary widely and are unpredictable in advance, contiguous allocation leads to severe internal and external memory fragmentation—often wasting 60 to 80 percent of GPU memory on unreserved space. PagedAttention solves this by allocating the KV-cache in non-contiguous, fixed-size blocks, typically 16 or 32 tokens per block, analogous to virtual memory paging in operating systems. A block table maps logical sequence tokens to physical memory blocks anywhere in GPU memory. When a sequence generates a new token, the runtime allocates a physical block only when the current block fills. The trade-off is small index lookup overhead versus massive memory savings: managing block tables introduces minor software scheduling overhead, but it virtually eliminates memory fragmentation, allowing serving engines to increase batch sizes and throughput significantly.
followUps: How does PagedAttention enable zero-copy memory sharing during parallel sampling and beam search?
What is the impact of block size (e.g. 16 vs 32 vs 64 tokens) on internal memory fragmentation and kernel efficiency?
wrongAnswers: Pre-allocating max_sequence_length contiguous memory buffers for every incoming request, wasting up to 80% of VRAM on ungenerated tokens.
Relying on standard PyTorch memory caching for dynamic inference requests, which cannot prevent external fragmentation under variable token lengths.
tradeOffs: PagedAttention eliminates external memory fragmentation, boosting inference batch size and concurrency by 2x to 4x.
Block-level non-contiguous memory access requires specialized CUDA kernels to maintain high memory bandwidth utilization.
keyPoints: Contiguous maximum-length KV allocation wastes memory through fragmentation.
Allocate non-contiguous fixed-size KV blocks on demand.
Map logical sequence tokens to physical blocks with a block table.
Block-table lookups add overhead while enabling larger batches.

questions.title: How do you allow teams to burst beyond their baseline GPU quota during idle cluster periods without risking noisy neighbor interference on latency-critical workloads?
questions.answer: To maximize expensive GPU utilization, clusters should allow teams to burst beyond their baseline quotas when cluster resources are idle, without risking performance regressions on mission-critical workloads. We implement this through priority tiers and quality-of-service node pools. Production services run on dedicated, non-preemptible nodes with strict resource limits and CPU core pinning to ensure steady tail latency. Opportunistic burst workloads run on separate pooled nodes using lowest-priority preemptible classes. When a team with burst permissions submits extra jobs, the scheduler places them on idle GPUs but labels them as immediately revocable. If a higher-priority production workload demands those GPUs, the burst jobs receive a preemption signal and release the resources within seconds. The trade-off is cluster utilization versus execution predictability: allowing opportunistic bursts raises cluster GPU utilization from 50% to over 85%, but teams using burst compute must design their jobs to tolerate frequent interruptions and restarts.
followUps: How do you prevent a bursting workload from saturating shared host memory or PCIe bandwidth on multi-GPU nodes?
What metric should trigger automated throttling of burst workloads before production tail latency degrades?
wrongAnswers: Co-locating un-throttled batch burst jobs on the same physical GPUs as production inference services, causing latency spikes.
Permitting burst jobs without preemption mechanisms, causing production deployments to stall waiting for batch runs to complete.
tradeOffs: Opportunistic burst scheduling drives GPU utilization up to 85%+, but requires all burst jobs to be designed for frequent preemption.
Isolating latency-critical services on dedicated hardware guarantees flat tail latencies, but sacrifices fractional hardware sharing.
keyPoints: Protect production workloads with dedicated non-preemptible pools.
Place opportunistic bursts in low-priority preemptible pools.
Reclaim burst allocations when higher-priority work needs resources.
Burst users must tolerate interruptions and restarts.

questions.title: How do you design an automated GPU reclamation controller that detects idle development notebooks and reclaims allocations without disrupting active debugging?
questions.answer: In machine learning organizations, developers frequently launch interactive GPU notebooks, run a few experiments, and leave the instance allocated overnight while doing zero computation, locking tens of thousands of dollars of hardware. We implement an automated reclamation controller that monitors both kernel compute activity and network socket traffic. Checking memory allocation alone is insufficient, because an idle PyTorch notebook retains allocated GPU memory indefinitely. The controller inspects GPU compute utilization via nvidia-smi: if active GPU compute remains below 1% for an extended window, such as two hours, it checks whether any active WebSocket or HTTP sessions are interacting with the notebook. If both compute and user traffic are zero, the controller sends an automated alert with a link to extend the session. If the user does not respond within thirty minutes, the container state is checkpointed and the GPU allocation is released back to the shared pool. The trade-off is developer convenience versus hardware cost: automated reclamation occasionally interrupts a developer who stepped away for lunch, but it prevents massive idle GPU spend across large engineering teams.
followUps: Why is checking GPU memory allocation misleading when attempting to detect idle PyTorch sessions?
How do you handle background jobs that intentionally sleep between batch data syncs?
wrongAnswers: Checking only memory usage (e.g. nvidia-smi memory used), assuming non-empty memory means active computation.
Immediately killing containers without warning, causing developers to lose unsaved notebook cell outputs and progress.
tradeOffs: Automated idle reclamation recovers 20% to 40% of wasted enterprise GPU spend, but requires tuning idle timeouts to avoid annoying developers.
Checkpointing container disk state ensures developers can resume work seamlessly, but requires persistent volume storage per user.
keyPoints: Monitor compute activity and notebook network traffic rather than memory alone.
Check prolonged low utilization for absence of active user sessions.
Warn users and offer a session extension before reclamation.
Checkpoint inactive containers and release GPU allocations.

questions.title: Compare Kubernetes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator against Slurm for managing large-scale distributed training and inference clusters.
questions.answer: Slurm and Kubernetes represent two different philosophies for managing GPU clusters. Slurm was built for high-performance computing batch workloads. It excels at gang scheduling: if a distributed pre-training run needs 128 GPUs, Slurm ensures all 128 GPUs across 16 nodes are allocated and launched at the exact same second, with direct bare-metal network topologies and near-zero orchestration overhead. However, Slurm lacks native support for auto-scaling HTTP services, dynamic ingress routing, and cloud-native rolling updates. Kubernetes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator is built for microservices and cloud infrastructure. It excels at hosting model serving endpoints, auto-scaling inference replicas based on request traffic, rolling out canary deployments, and integrating with enterprise logging and monitoring stacks. The trade-off is workload fit versus operational overhead: Slurm is simpler and more efficient for pure distributed training runs, while Kubernetes is far superior for production inference and web platforms, requiring specialized gang schedulers like Volcano to handle large-scale distributed training.
followUps: How does Kueue improve Kubernetes scheduling for multi-node distributed training jobs?
What network plugin configurations are required in Kubernetes to support native InfiniBand SR-IOV?
wrongAnswers: Attempting to manage production low-latency LLM serving APIs with auto-scaling using batch Slurm job submission scripts.
Running multi-node distributed training on vanilla Kubernetes without gang scheduling, leading to deadlocks where incomplete pods hold GPUs.
tradeOffs: Slurm offers native, zero-overhead gang scheduling and topology awareness for batch training, but lacks modern service routing and auto-scaling APIs.
Kubernetes provides rich cloud-native APIs, service meshes, and auto-scaling for inference, but requires specialized operators (Volcano, Kueue) for gang training.
keyPoints: Slurm suits batch training with gang scheduling.
Kubernetes suits autoscaled inference, ingress and rolling deployments.
Kubernetes needs specialized gang schedulers for large distributed training.
Choose orchestration by workload and operational overhead.

questions.title: A team runs its nightly report pipeline through the same synchronous endpoint as the chat product, because the pipeline is production. How do you classify model workloads, and where does this one belong?
questions.answer: Sort every workload by the latency its user accepts, not by where it runs. Interactive work has a user waiting for the first token and stays synchronous with prompt caching, and semi-interactive work returns in minutes through an async queue. Anything whose user can wait for the full promise belongs on the batch API, which gives a 50 percent discount with a return promised within 24 hours and typical in a few hours. The nightly report is batch when a return at the 24-hour limit still meets its deadline, or when a synchronous fallback covers a late batch.
followUps: Level 1: Which question sorts a workload into a lane? Expected: what a wait of a day means to this user. If they would not notice, it is batch.

Level 2: A user clicks refresh on a health report and waits ten minutes without complaint. Which lane? Expected: semi-interactive at most, and batch if the report can arrive by mail. Shipping it synchronous is the partial-interactivity trap.

Level 2: Why does the lesson call batch asynchronous rather than slow? Expected: the promise is a return within a day, and the typical return is a few hours, because the provider runs it when capacity is idle.
Level 3: What breaks when you write one batch client for two providers? Expected: the file formats differ, so you need an adapter per provider.
wrongAnswers: "It runs in production, so it is interactive." Production is where it runs. The lane comes from the latency the user accepts.
"Batch means the answer takes a day." The promise is within a day. The typical return is a few hours.
"A 50 percent discount is not worth the complexity." On a shared prefix it stacks with caching to about a tenth of the synchronous cost, which the lesson calls the cheapest lever that nobody pulls.

questions.title: Finance asks for the cost per million tokens as the key metric for the model service. You push back. What metric do you propose instead, and what must every call record so that you can compute it?
questions.answer: Propose a cost per product outcome: per resolved ticket, per generated article, per successful agent task or per session minute. A price per million tokens is the vendor's unit, and it says nothing about whether the spend produced anything. To compute the outcome metric, stamp every call at creation with the user id, the task id with its route, and the tenant id, split the tokens into prompt, tool, memory and response, and join the cost to the outcome event.
followUps: Level 1: Why does the token price alone mislead? Expected: it says nothing about tokens per outcome. A cheaper model that needs twice the tokens per task costs more per task.
Level 2: Why split the tokens into four layers? Expected: one bucket hides whether prompt bloat, tool results, memory or output drives the spend, so you cannot choose the right fix.
Level 2: Why stamp the call at creation instead of tagging the bill later? Expected: the provider line item has no user, task or tenant on it, and retroactive attribution always misses cases.

Level 3: Which attribution pattern is the most accurate, and what does it need? Expected: the telemetry joiner, which joins trace ids to billing. It needs the trace id on every call and a billing export with the same key.
wrongAnswers: "Tokens are what we pay for, so tokens are the metric." They are the vendor's unit. The business pays for outcomes, and a cheaper token can mean a more expensive task.
"Tag the cloud bill by team like any other resource." A model call is a transaction, not an asset. The line item has no team on it unless the call stamped one.
"Per-tenant cost is enough." Per-task shows which feature to fix and per-user shows abuse. The lesson instruments all three.

questions.title: A teammate says the service already has caching, because the provider's prompt cache is on. The bill barely moved. Which two kinds of cache exist in a model service, what does each one skip, and why does one of them do nothing for a question that users keep asking?
questions.answer: There are two layers. The provider's prefix cache reuses the attention state of a prompt prefix that an earlier request computed, so the repeated opening tokens get cheaper, but the model still runs. An application-level semantic cache embeds the request and returns a stored answer when a similar question was answered before, so the model call is skipped. The prefix cache cannot serve a repeated question, because the user's part of the prompt still differs token by token and the model still generates the answer.
followUps: Level 1: Which cache returns an answer without running the model? Expected: the semantic cache. The prefix cache still runs the model on the uncached tokens and generates the output.
Level 2: Every user asks a different question under the same system prompt. Which cache helps? Expected: the prefix cache, because the shared prefix is identical and the questions are not.

Level 2: What decides whether a semantic cache is worth adding? Expected: the hit rate on your own traffic, which ranges from about 10 percent on open chat to about 70 percent on structured support, and the cost of a wrong hit.

Level 3: Why does the exact cache refuse to serve a call above temperature zero? Expected: the stored answer was one sample. A call that asks for variation would get a replay instead, which changes the behavior the caller asked for.
wrongAnswers: "The prefix cache returns the same answer for the same question." It reuses the attention state of the prefix. The model still generates every token.
"A semantic cache is a prefix cache with fuzzy matching." It sits in your application, keys on embeddings and skips the model. The prefix cache sits at the provider and keys on exact tokens.
"One cache is enough." They cover different reuse, identical tokens against identical meaning, and the lesson combines them.

questions.title: Last month a bug in a retry loop spent the whole monthly model budget in two days, and nobody saw it until the invoice. Design the controls that stop the next one, with the thresholds and what each threshold does.
questions.answer: Put a cost tracker on every call and a ladder of thresholds on top of it. At 70 percent of the budget alert, at 85 percent throttle so that every request goes to the cheapest model, and at 95 percent stop so that only cached answers are served and new calls are refused. In front of the ladder, add a rate limit and a daily spend cap per tenant, and a kill switch that pauses a tenant whose spend jumps far above its own history.
followUps: Level 2: Why three thresholds and not one hard stop? Expected: the alert gives people time, the throttle buys more time at lower quality, and the stop protects the budget. One hard stop surprises users with no warning.
Level 3: What changes for users during the throttle step? Expected: quality, because every request goes to the cheapest model. The service stays up while the spend slows.

Level 3: Why is the kill switch relative to the tenant's history? Expected: tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A z-score catches a jump for a small tenant and ignores a normal day for a large one.

Level 4: The retry bug spent the budget in two days. Which control fires first? Expected: the daily spend cap or the z-score kill switch fires on the first day. The monthly ladder would only have warned at 70 percent.
wrongAnswers: "Set a hard limit at the provider and stop there." The provider limit stops every tenant at once with no warning. The ladder degrades first and isolates the tenant.
"An alert to the team channel is enough." The incident is a bug at night. The throttle and the stop act without a person.
"Check the budget nightly." A retry loop spends a day's budget in minutes. The tracker has to run on every call.

questions.title: Your provider charges a 25 percent premium to write a prefix into its cache, and it bills a cache read at a tenth of the normal input price. The cache lives for five minutes. A one-hour variant costs twice the normal input price to write. How many reads does each variant need to pay off, and what rule do you give the team?
questions.answer: With the five-minute cache, one write and one read average 0.675 of the normal cost per request, a saving of about 32 percent, so the cache pays off on the first read. One write and ten reads average 0.205, about 80 percent saved. The one-hour cache charges 2x for the write, so that block needs two reads before it comes out ahead. The rule: cache anything you expect to reuse at least three times inside its lifetime.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the five-minute cache pay off on the first read? Expected: the write premium is a quarter and the read saves nine tenths, so the two together already average below the normal price.
Level 2: When does the one-hour cache make sense? Expected: a batch job that reuses the prefix across runs more than five minutes apart, more than five times.
Level 3: Input tokens are down and the bill is flat. What is wrong with the dashboard? Expected: it does not split cached from uncached input, so a drop in traffic looks like a cache win.

Level 3: Ten parallel requests share a prefix that nobody has cached yet. What happens to the arithmetic? Expected: all ten pay the write premium and none reads, so the cache costs more than no cache. Send one request first, then the rest.
wrongAnswers: "Caching always saves money." A prefix written once and never read costs 25 percent more than no cache.
"Pick the one-hour cache, it lasts longer." It writes at twice the normal input price, so a block read once costs more than without the cache.
"Mark the whole prompt as cacheable." The user message changes every time, so the match ends at the first differing token, and a block below the minimum size does not cache at all.

questions.title: Your SLA is a P99 time to first token under 320 ms. The model alone measures 300 ms at P99. You are choosing a gateway to put in front of it. Which classes of gateway fit in the budget, and what do you do when the one you want does not?
questions.answer: The gateway has at most 20 ms at the tail. An edge-managed gateway at 1 to 3 ms and a high-performance gateway at 3 to 8 ms fit, a lightweight proxy at 5 to 15 ms fits with little margin, and a control-plane gateway at 20 to 40 ms does not. If you need the features of the slow one, split the roles: keep the fast gateway on the request path, run the heavy features out of band, or buy the budget back from the model with a faster first token.
followUps: Level 2: Why measure the gateway at P99 and not at its median? Expected: the SLA is a P99, and the gateway's tail adds to the model's tail.

Level 3: The slow gateway's value is PII redaction. How do you keep it inside the budget? Expected: keep the redaction inline because it must run before the provider sees the prompt, move observability and audit off the path, and then measure whether the remaining overhead fits.
Level 3: Traffic will triple next year. Which class survives? Expected: the lightweight proxy breaks down around 2000 requests per second, so plan the move to the high-performance class before that.
wrongAnswers: "Every gateway adds a few milliseconds, pick on features." The lesson's overheads run from 1 to 40 ms, and 40 ms is twice this budget.
"Put the gateway behind the model, not in front." The gateway routes and falls back before the model. Behind the model it protects nothing.
"Add the gateway's median to the model's P99." Two tails do not add that way. Measure the gateway's own tail under load.

questions.title: A dashboard panel shows the prefix cache hit rate of a self-hosted server at 94 percent. Over the same run, the server's counters say that it computed 104,057 prompt tokens and took 182,079 from the cache. Both readings come from one scrape of the same endpoint. Which one do you trust for a cost decision, and why do they differ?
questions.answer: Trust the counters. The gauge holds the hit rate of the last prefill interval that the scheduler logged, and at idle it keeps the value from the last batch, which was a shared-prefix benchmark. The counters add up every prefill token since the server started, and their ratio over the whole run is 0.636, not 0.942. For a cost decision, compute the rate from the counters over a time window.
followUps: Level 2: What does a gauge answer, and what does a counter answer? Expected: a gauge answers what happened in the last interval. A counter answers how much happened since the start, and a rate over a window turns it into a trend.

Level 3: Why can the counter-based rate overstate the hits after retractions? Expected: the hit modes add raw hit counts, so a retracted request that runs again counts its cached tokens twice, while the input mode excludes the re-count.
Level 3: Which gauges may page you, and under what rule? Expected: queued requests above zero and token usage near one, only when the condition holds for several minutes, never on one scrape.

Level 4: A panel on this server shows utilization at zero during an outage. Why? Expected: that gauge stays at zero at the pinned version because of a known regression, so the panel shows an idle fleet. Read the HELP text and the code before building on a metric.
wrongAnswers: "The gauge is the newest value, so it is the most accurate." It is a snapshot of one interval, and it keeps its last value at idle.
"Average the two numbers." They answer different questions, and the counters already contain the whole run.
"The real rate is lower, so turn the cache off." A rate of 0.636 means a third of the prompt tokens were computed. The fix is the prompt layout or the routing, not the cache.

questions.title: An agent fans out ten tool calls at once for every user question. All ten share the same long system prompt, and prompt caching is on. The bill is several times what the cache should allow, and the usage fields show cache writes on nearly all calls and almost no cache reads. What is happening?
questions.answer: All ten requests reach the provider before the first one has finished writing the prefix into the cache. Each one sees a miss, each one pays the write premium, and none of them reads. The fix is sequential-first: send one request alone, let its cache write land, then fan out the other nine. It adds about one write latency to the first tool call and removes the inflation.
followUps: Level 2: How do you tell the fan-out trap from dynamic text in the prefix? Expected: both show writes and no reads. After the fan-out trap, a later sequential request with the same prefix reads. With dynamic text, nothing ever reads.
Level 3: How do you fix the fan-out without adding latency for the user? Expected: warm the prefix with one call when the session starts, so the first fan-out already reads.

Level 3: Does a self-hosted prefix cache have the same trap? Expected: the lesson says the self-hosted caches follow the same prefix pattern at your own compute, so measure the cached tokens on a fan-out before you assume they are shared.
wrongAnswers: "Caching is on, so the provider should deduplicate them." Writes are per request, and the cache can be read only after the first write has landed.
"Shorten the system prompt." That lowers every bill a little and leaves ten writes and zero reads in place.
"Turn caching off, it costs more." It costs more only because of the arrival pattern. Sequential-first turns ten writes into one write and nine reads.

questions.title: Two inference platforms quote you for the same open model. One bills per million tokens. The other rents a dedicated GPU by the minute. Your traffic is steady through the working day and near zero at night. Which pricing wins, and what number decides it?
questions.answer: Sustained utilization decides it. Per-token billing charges only for what you use, so it wins when traffic is bursty or low and a dedicated GPU would sit idle. Per-minute billing charges for wall-clock time, so it wins once you keep the GPU busy, and the lesson's rule of thumb puts the crossover near 30 percent sustained utilization. A load that runs only in the daytime sits near that line, so measure your utilization over a full week before you sign.
followUps: Level 2: Why does per-token pricing cost more per token than your own GPU time at high utilization? Expected: the platform's margin and its idle time are built into the per-token rate. At high utilization you pay for idle that you do not have.
Level 2: What changes when you scale the dedicated GPU to zero at night? Expected: you stop paying for the night and buy a cold start every morning, so the first requests of the day pay in latency.

Level 3: Why is the dedicated option faster at the tail? Expected: shared on-demand capacity competes with every other customer's traffic, and dedicated capacity does not. That is the gap the lesson on managed platforms measures between reserved and on-demand first-token latency.

Level 3: How does a fine-tuned model change the comparison? Expected: a per-token platform may serve the fine-tune at the base rate or charge a premium for it. A dedicated GPU serves it at the same hourly price either way.
wrongAnswers: "Per-token is always cheaper because you never pay for idle." Above the utilization crossover, the per-token rate carries the platform's idle and margin, and your own GPU is cheaper.
"Dedicated is always cheaper at scale." Only when you keep it busy. A daytime-only load leaves it idle half the time.
"Compare the headline prices." The two prices have different units. Only your traffic profile turns them into a bill.

questions.title: Your semantic cache serves 20 percent of requests at a similarity threshold of 0.95. A teammate lowered it to 0.85 in staging. The hit rate rose to 50 percent, and a few cached answers did not fit the question asked. Which threshold do you ship, and how do you decide?
questions.answer: Ship the threshold whose wrong hits you can afford, and measure that instead of guessing. A wrong cached answer is a correctness failure that a user sees, while a miss costs one model call. Keep the strict threshold on the general path, and lower it only where the answers are interchangeable or where a disclaimer is acceptable. A vendor's accuracy figure describes how often a hit was appropriate, not how often your traffic hits, so label pairs from your own traffic at both thresholds.
followUps: Level 2: Why is the accuracy number in a vendor's brochure not your hit rate? Expected: accuracy says how often a returned hit was appropriate. The hit rate says how often there was a hit at all, and it depends on your traffic.
Level 2: What does a miss cost, and what does a wrong hit cost? Expected: a miss costs one model call. A wrong hit costs a wrong answer in front of a user, which the product has to price.

Level 3: How do you lower the threshold without lowering the correctness of the strict path? Expected: a two-tier scheme, with strict matches served as they are and medium matches served with a disclaimer, and the tier logged so that satisfaction can be compared.
Level 3: Why do code questions hit so rarely? Expected: a small variant in a code question changes the correct answer, so similar text is not similar intent.
wrongAnswers: "Lower the threshold, the savings are bigger." A wrong hit is a correctness failure that a user sees. Its cost is not one model call.
"Raise the threshold until no hit is ever wrong." The hit rate then approaches the exact-match rate, and the cache stops paying for itself.
"Use the vendor's accuracy number as the hit rate." The figure describes match correctness, not how often your traffic hits.

questions.title: Your serverless endpoint scales to zero overnight. The first request in the morning waits minutes while a 70B model loads, and the product wants the first token within two seconds. One engineer wants a replica that never sleeps. Another calls that a GPU burning money all night. Settle it.
questions.answer: Both are right, and the decision is arithmetic per path. A warm replica costs one GPU hour every hour whether anyone calls or not, and it removes a cold start of several minutes for a large model. An interactive path with a tight first-token target on a large model needs the warm replica, while a small model with a cold start of seconds, or a background path that tolerates minutes, scales to zero. Then shrink the cold start itself, so that fewer paths need a warm replica at all.
followUps: Level 2: Which paths get a warm replica first? Expected: the interactive ones with a tight first-token target on a large model, such as live chat or a voice agent.

Level 2: Whose cold start is cheaper to hide, a small model's or a large one's? Expected: in proportion, the large one's. For a small model you pay a full GPU hour to avoid seconds, and for a large one the same hour avoids minutes.

Level 3: Name two mitigations that remove whole phases of the cold start. Expected: a pre-seeded node image removes the image pull, and a GPU memory snapshot removes most of the weight load and the init.

Level 3: What is the break-even request rate for a warm replica? Expected: the rate above which the cost of cold starts, in requests that miss the target, exceeds the hourly price of the idle GPU. The lesson's simulator computes it.
wrongAnswers: "Keep one warm replica everywhere, it is the simple answer." It is one GPU hour every hour per product. Five products idle all night cost thousands of GPU hours a month.
"Scale to zero everywhere and let the first user wait." A first-token wait of minutes on an interactive path is an outage, not a wait.
"A bigger GPU loads faster." The load is bound by the storage and the copy path. The fix is where the weights live and whether a snapshot exists.

questions.title: Your model service runs as a plain Deployment with an autoscaler on CPU use. During a traffic spike the autoscaler added replicas late, kept adding them while the new pods were still loading weights, and a liveness probe restarted the busiest pod in the middle of the spike. Redesign the scaling and the probes.
questions.answer: Scale on the engine's own signals, not on CPU: the count of waiting requests and the KV cache usage say that a server is saturated long before CPU does. Give the startup probe a window longer than your measured cold start, so that a loading pod is neither sent traffic nor restarted, and make the liveness probe cheap, so that a busy server does not lose its busiest pod to a probe that waited in the queue. Keep the weights and the compile cache on persistent storage, so that a new replica is ready in a fraction of the time.
followUps: Level 3: Which pair of readings says the pool is the bottleneck, not the batch limit? Expected: waiting requests above zero with cache usage near one. With cache usage below 0.9, the batch size or the token budget limits admission instead.

Level 3: Why does a generating health probe hurt under load? Expected: its request waits in the queue like any other, times out, and marks a busy server unhealthy. In one incident each failed probe also left an orphan request behind.

Level 4: How do you keep the autoscaler from overshooting during a cold start? Expected: a stabilization window at least as long as the measured cold start, a cap on replicas added per step, and a shorter cold start from persistent weights and compile caches.

Level 4: What does a scale-down need so that no request is lost? Expected: remove the pod from the load balancer, send SIGTERM to the main process only, and a grace period at least as long as the longest request at the output cap.
wrongAnswers: "Scale on GPU utilization instead of CPU." Utilization can read high while requests wait and low while the pool is full. The queue and the cache usage are the signals the engine exposes for this.
"Make the liveness probe stricter so that bad pods restart faster." Under load a strict probe restarts healthy, busy pods. The fix is a cheap probe and a long startup window.
"Add replicas faster to beat the spike." Replicas that take minutes to load add nothing during the spike and cost money after it. Shorten the cold start and keep a warm margin.

questions.title: Six months ago a cascading router cut the bill by more than half with no measurable quality loss. Since then the escalation rate has crept from 8 percent to 22 percent, and a sales engineer reports that a competitor's demo now answers better than your product. Diagnose it.
questions.answer: The traffic drifted and the router did not. Its classifier learned the question mix of six months ago, users now ask longer and harder questions, and the cheap model's first pass fails its own confidence check more often, which is what the rising escalation rate records. Quality fell silently on the requests that were not escalated. Gate every route with online quality metrics, retrain the classifier on current traffic, and treat an escalation rate above about 30 percent as proof that the cheap model is over-routed.
followUps: Level 3: Why did the offline eval not catch the loss? Expected: the eval set was built from the old distribution. It scores the model on questions that users no longer ask.

Level 3: Which online metric gives the earliest warning? Expected: the escalation rate per route. It rises as the cheap model fails its own confidence check more often, before the thumbs or a judge sample show the loss.

Level 4: The provider updated the cheap model behind the same alias. How do you know? Expected: a step change in escalations or judge scores on a date with no deploy on your side. Pin the model version and log the served model on every call.

Level 4: Where do you set the alarm on the escalation rate? Expected: near the design target, about 10 percent escalated for the cascade pattern, with the lesson's 30 percent as the hard line for over-routing.
wrongAnswers: "The cheap model got worse, swap it." Possible, and the first suspect is the router's stale classifier against drifted traffic.
"Quality is fine, the eval score did not move." The eval set comes from the old distribution and cannot see the new questions.
"Raise the confidence cutoff so that more goes to the frontier model." That buys quality back at a cost without finding the cause. Retrain the router and gate it online.

questions.title: A nightly pipeline summarizes 50,000 documents, and every call opens with the same system prompt. It runs synchronously against a provider for four hours and costs about 2,000 dollars a night. Estimate what the same job costs on the batch API with the system prompt cached, and say when you would move it onto your own GPU instead.
questions.answer: Batch gives a flat 50 percent discount on input and output tokens, and the cached system prompt makes the repeated input about ten times cheaper after the first write. Stacked, the lesson's worked example lands at about 180 dollars a night, near 9 percent of the synchronous bill, from three configuration changes. Move the job to your own GPU when it runs every night at high utilization and the shared prefix is short, so that neither discount has much to work on, and size that run by raising concurrency until the output stops growing.
followUps: Level 3: Which of the two discounts applies to output tokens? Expected: only the batch discount. Caching lowers the price of repeated input and does nothing for generated tokens.

Level 3: The first call in each batch pays a cache write premium. Does that change the estimate? Expected: not at this volume. One write at a quarter more, against tens of thousands of reads at a tenth of the price.

Level 4: When does a reserved GPU beat batch plus cache? Expected: when the job keeps the GPU busy every night, the shared prefix is short and the outputs are long, so the two discounts have little to work on. The lesson's exercise computes the break-even prefix length.

Level 4: How do you find the right concurrency for the job on your own GPU? Expected: pass the whole list to the offline engine or the batch command, raise concurrency until the output tokens per second stop growing, and raise the token budget. The manual's card peaked near 32 concurrent requests.
wrongAnswers: "Batch alone gets you to a tenth of the cost." Batch alone halves the bill. The other factor is the cached shared prompt.
"Caching saves the same on output as on input." The cache reuses the prompt's attention state. Every output token is generated and billed in full, less the batch discount.
"Batch is too slow for a nightly job." The promise is a day and the typical return is hours. Submit a day ahead, or keep a synchronous fallback for the rare late batch.

questions.title: A pod serving an MoE model on a unified-memory machine took about eight minutes from start to ready. Break that time into its parts, say which parts a restart can skip, and estimate what a warm restart looks like on the same machine.
questions.answer: Most of the time was the weight load. The manual's log shows about 330 seconds to copy 57 GiB of weights into memory on that machine, one tensor at a time from a file-backed page. The engine init took 127.54 seconds, and it holds the two CUDA graph captures of 39 and 38 seconds and a compile share of 18.67 seconds. A restart reuses the compile cache and nothing else, so a warm restart on that machine is only a little shorter than the cold one, unless the weights are staged in host memory or a process snapshot exists, which a field report took from a cold start of 695 seconds to 9.6 seconds.
followUps: Level 3: Which phase dominates on this machine, and why? Expected: the weight load at about 330 seconds, because each tensor is copied from a file-backed page, which is slow on this platform.
Level 3: What does a persistent compile cache save on a restart? Expected: the compile share of the engine init, 18.67 seconds here. The weight load and the graph captures remain.

Level 4: How do you get the restart under a minute? Expected: a process checkpoint or GPU memory snapshot with the weights staged in host memory, which the field report took to 9.6 seconds. A faster disk alone does not get there.

Level 4: What does an eight-minute start imply for the probes and the autoscaler? Expected: a startup probe window longer than eight minutes, a stabilization window at least as long, and a warm replica for the interactive path.
wrongAnswers: "The compile is the slow part, use eager mode." The compile share was 18.67 seconds of an eight-minute start, and eager mode costs decode speed on every request afterwards.
"A faster GPU loads faster." The load was bound by the copy path from the file view, not by the GPU.
"Restart often to pick up configuration changes." Each restart pays the full load. The manual's advice is to start once and keep the server running.

questions.title: A self-hosted server shows its KV pool near full for hours while the request rate is normal. A few requests have been generating for many minutes each, and the users behind the other requests wait. What is going on, and what do you change tonight and tomorrow?
questions.answer: A handful of requests are in a generation loop. Every token of a running request stays in the pool until the request ends, so a request that never stops grows until it crowds out the rest. Tonight, cap the output length so that every request ends, and add a presence penalty for the workloads that loop. Tomorrow, set the shutdown grace period from the new cap, because a request that runs to the cap decides how long a graceful restart takes.
followUps: Level 3: Why does a looping request hurt other users and not only itself? Expected: the pool is shared. A request that never ends keeps its slots, so new requests wait or running ones are retracted.
Level 3: How do you find the looping requests after the fact? Expected: requests that finished with the length reason at the cap, grouped by tenant and prompt template.

Level 4: Why does the cap on output length come first, before you pick how long a drain may take? Expected: the grace period must outlast the longest request, and the longest request runs to the cap. The manual's arithmetic gives more than 18 minutes for 32K tokens at 30 tokens per second.

Level 4: The long answers are legitimate agent sessions. What then? Expected: grow the pool with an FP8 KV cache or more memory, lower the concurrency cap, and keep an output cap that the product agreed to.
wrongAnswers: "Restart the server to clear the pool." Every running request fails, and the loops come back on the next prompt.
"Raise the memory fraction." A larger pool delays the symptom. A request with no cap fills any pool.
"Lower the temperature to stop the loops." Sampling settings change the odds of a loop. Only a cap guarantees that a request ends.

questions.title: You add a second serving replica to double capacity. Throughput rises, but the first-token time of long chat sessions gets worse, and the cache hit rate on both servers falls. Explain the cause, and design the routing so that the second replica stops undoing the cache.
questions.answer: Each replica has its own KV cache, and a router that spreads requests at random or in turn sends turn five of a chat to the replica that never saw turns one to four. That replica prefills the whole history again, which is the prefix miss the cache exists to avoid. Route each conversation back to the replica that holds its prefix with a cache-aware policy that remembers which server saw which text, with a load-balance check in front of it. Then read the hit rate on the servers themselves, because the router's record is a guess.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the router check load balance before the prefix match? Expected: a prefix-first policy would send every long conversation to one hot server. The imbalance test sends the request to the least-loaded server when the gap is large.

Level 3: Which traffic should not use the cache-aware policy? Expected: batch traffic with unique prompts. A match rate under the threshold gives no affinity, so a load-based policy does the same work with less state.

Level 4: One server's hit rate stays low although the gateway routes its conversations there. Why? Expected: the gateway's tree records where it sent text, not what the server still holds. The server evicted the prefix, so the request prefills. Read the server's own counters.

Level 4: You upgrade the router without touching the engine. What do you measure? Expected: throughput and hit rate of the router and the engine as one system, because a router change alone halved throughput in a reported incident.
wrongAnswers: "Add a replica and each server's hit rate stays the same." Each replica has its own cache, and random routing splits every conversation across both.
"Hash the user id to a server and be done." It keeps a user on one server and ignores load. The manual's gateway balances first, so a hot user cannot saturate one replica with no relief.
"Turn on in-server data parallelism instead of a gateway." Its default method is round robin, which ignores prefixes, which is the problem you are solving.

questions.title: A teammate raised the memory fraction of a self-hosted server and grew the KV pool by 63 percent. The closed-loop benchmark at 64 concurrent users did not move. They want to revert the change, because the extra memory bought nothing. What do you tell them, and which measurement settles it?
questions.answer: The benchmark never filled the pool, so the extra memory had nothing to do. At 64 users the running requests held about 11 percent of the pool, and throughput stayed within 2 percent. Under an open-loop overload the same pool mattered: at the smaller fraction the pool was 96 percent full with requests waiting outside it, and the larger pool completed about a third more requests per second. Size the pool from token usage at peak load, bursts included, and read it from the scheduler's decode lines, not from a closed-loop sweep.
followUps: Level 3: Why did the closed-loop sweep never fill the pool? Expected: each client waits for its answer before it sends the next request, so the server never holds more work than it finishes.
Level 3: Which log lines tell you the pool is the limit? Expected: token usage near one in the decode lines, a queue above zero, and retractions.

Level 4: On a shared machine, what does an oversized pool cost? Expected: memory that other programs cannot use. The manual's machine had a guard that paused the scheduler when the pool allocation grew by tens of gigabytes in seconds.

Level 4: The two overload runs were a day apart. How much of the gain do you trust? Expected: the mechanism, from the lines that show one pool full with requests waiting and the other with room. The size of the gain needs a same-day repeat.
wrongAnswers: "The pool did not matter, revert it." It did not matter under a load that never filled it. The overload filled it and completed a third more requests per second.
"Give the pool as much memory as possible." On a shared machine that memory is taken from other programs, and past the point where the pool fills it buys nothing.
"Throughput at 64 users is the capacity number." Capacity shows under an arrival rate above the service rate, which a closed loop cannot produce.

questions.title: Take-home. You receive one day of request logs from a multi-tenant assistant. Each record follows the lesson's attribution trace: a trace id, a timestamp, the tenant, the user, the task id and its route, the model, the token counts for each of the four layers in the lesson's trace, whether the input was cached, and whether the task was resolved. You also receive the daily spend of each tenant over the previous weeks, as the baseline for the kill switch. Build a simulator that attributes spend by tenant, task and user, splits the tokens into layers, computes a cost per resolved task per tenant, and enforces a rate limit, a daily spend cap and a kill switch. Inject one abusive tenant and show when each control fires.
questions.answer: Price every call from a pricing table, roll the cost up by tenant, by task with its route and by user, and split the tokens into prompt, tool, memory and response so that the report names the layer that drives each tenant's spend. Compute the cost per resolved task from the outcome field, not from the token totals. Implement the ladder from the lesson: a rate limit at 2 to 3 times the expected peak, a daily cap at 1.5 to 3 times the contracted ceiling, and a kill switch on a spend z-score above 4 against the tenant's own baseline. Show the abusive tenant hit the rate limit first, then the cap, then the kill switch when its spend jumps far above its history.
followUps: Level 3: Why is the kill switch relative to each tenant's history instead of a fixed amount? Expected: tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A fixed amount pauses a large tenant on a normal day and never fires for a small one.

Level 4: Your largest tenant is unprofitable in the report. What do you propose? Expected: three interventions ordered by customer impact, such as caching and routing on their heaviest task, then a quota change, then a price change at renewal.

Level 4: Which five views would you put on the dashboard first? Expected: spend per tenant over time, the per-tenant spend divided by resolved tasks, the layer split per task, the top users by spend, and the enforcement events timeline.
wrongAnswers: "Attribute the bill by dividing it by seats." That hides the heavy tenants and the heavy features, which is what the exercise is for.
"One token bucket for everything." A single bucket cannot say which layer or tenant to fix, and it cannot carry a per-tenant cap.
"Fire the kill switch at a fixed dollar amount." Tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A fixed amount is wrong for all but one of them.

questions.title: You run three tiers on a serverless GPU platform: paid users on a live chat, trial users on the same chat, and a nightly batch pipeline. Design the warm-pool policy per tier, show the arithmetic behind it, and say what you would measure after a month to revisit it.
questions.answer: Give the paid chat one or two warm replicas, because its first-token target cannot absorb a cold start of minutes on a large model. Give trial users a smaller margin, or let them ride on the paid pool's spare capacity, and let the batch pipeline scale to zero, because it tolerates a cold start of several minutes. The arithmetic is the hourly GPU price times the idle hours against the requests that would miss the target during a cold start, and after a month you compare the measured utilization, the cold-start count and the missed-target count per tier.
followUps: Level 3: Why not give trial users the same warm pool as paid users? Expected: a warm replica costs a month of GPU hours whether trial traffic arrives or not. The decision is the conversion loss from a cold start against that cost, and the month of measurement answers it.
Level 4: How does a 15 second cold start change the policy? Expected: tiers that tolerate seconds scale to zero, so the warm pool shrinks to the paths with targets of a second or two.
Level 4: Which signal says a warm replica count is too low? Expected: the share of requests that miss the first-token target during scale-outs, together with the cold-start count per day.
wrongAnswers: "Warm replicas for every tier, the cost is small." One replica per product is a month of GPU hours each. Five products idle come to thousands of hours.
"Scale trial to zero, those users are free." A cold start of minutes on the first trial session is a lost conversion. Measure it before you decide.
"Keep the batch pipeline warm so that it finishes earlier." Batch tolerates minutes. A warm GPU for it is paid idle time for the rest of the day.

questions.title: The CTO wants every product-critical model call to survive a full outage of one provider, with no redeploy and without doubling the bill. Design the setup: where the second provider sits, how a request moves between the two, what has to be identical on both sides, and what the design costs.
questions.answer: Put a gateway in front of the application with one model alias per use case, a priority list of two providers behind each alias, and a fallback rule on server errors and rate limits with a bounded retry budget. Keep the cacheable prefix layout, the tool order and the output schema identical on both providers, so that a failed-over request can hit the second provider's cache once that prefix is cached there, and still parses. The steady-state uplift is small, because the gateway sends traffic to the preferred provider most of the time, and the real price is paid in evals and prompt tests that run twice.
followUps: Level 3: Why does the second provider cost little in steady state? Expected: the gateway sends most traffic to the preferred provider. The second one carries traffic only during failures and drills.

Level 4: What breaks first on a failover without the identical prefix layout? Expected: the cache on the second provider misses on every request, so the outage hour costs full price and the first-token time jumps.

Level 4: Which failures trigger the failover, and which do not? Expected: server errors, rate limits and timeouts on the primary. Not a guardrail block or a malformed response, which would fail the same way on the second provider.
wrongAnswers: "Two providers double the bill." The second provider carries traffic only during failures. The gateway routes to the preferred one the rest of the time.
"Tune a separate prompt per provider." Then every change ships twice and the fallback path drifts. Keep one layout and one eval set for both.
"Fail over on any error." A guardrail block or a schema error repeats on the second provider and doubles the cost of a request that should fail fast.

topics.title: Safety
topics.about: Reward hacking, prompt injection, jailbreaks, refusals and safety gates.

questions.title: How do you defend production LLM applications against prompt injection and data exfiltration?
questions.answer: Treat all outside text as untrusted data, not as instructions. Separate it from system instructions with clear delimiters, and remember that this reduces risk but does not eliminate it. Indirect injection can arrive through retrieved documents or web pages, so sanitise that content and give tools the least privilege possible, with approval for risky actions. Add classifiers before and after the model to catch attacks and unsafe output, and detect and redact personal data on both input and output.
keyPoints: Treat external text as untrusted data.
Delimit it from system instructions without claiming complete protection.
Apply least privilege and approvals for risky tool actions.
Classify unsafe content and redact personal data on input and output.

questions.title: Why does simple input sanitization fail as a defense against prompt injection in RAG, and why does hardening the system prompt also fail?
questions.answer: Sanitization fails because an attacker can rephrase malicious instructions in countless ways that never match a fixed filter pattern — "ignore previous instructions" gets blocked, but a thousand semantically-equivalent rewordings don't. System-prompt hardening fails for a more structural reason: when a retrieved document contains conflicting instructions, the model has no principled way to always weight the older, more abstract system prompt over the more recent, more specific instruction sitting right in its context — in practice, the more recent and specific instruction often wins, regardless of which one the system intended to be authoritative.
keyPoints: Fixed sanitization patterns miss paraphrased attacks.
Attackers can preserve malicious meaning while changing wording.
Retrieved instructions can compete with system instructions in context.
System-prompt hardening cannot guarantee priority under every conflict.

questions.title: What does an actual defense-in-depth strategy against prompt injection in a RAG system look like, given no single defense fully solves it?
questions.answer: Layer multiple partial defenses rather than relying on one: structural separation (clearly delimit retrieved content from trusted instructions, e.g. with XML-style tags the model is prompted to treat context as data, never as commands), content filtering at ingestion (flag documents containing injection-like patterns without necessarily auto-blocking them, since false positives on legitimate content are a real cost), sandboxed extraction for any document-processing step that itself executes code or fetches further content, output inspection for signs an injection succeeded, and privilege separation so even a successful injection can't take an action beyond what that specific context should ever be allowed to do. The honest framing for an interview: this raises the cost and reduces the success rate of an attack, it does not eliminate the risk — claiming a "solved" defense is itself a red flag in an answer.
keyPoints: Separate retrieved data from trusted instructions.
Filter ingestion and sandbox executable document processing.
Inspect outputs and restrict privileges.
Layer partial defenses while acknowledging residual injection risk.

questions.title: Design a RAG system over SharePoint-style documents that must respect existing, possibly-changing document permissions. Walk through it.
questions.answer: Seven steps, in order: clarify requirements first (single org or multi-tenant, how fresh must permission checks be — minutes or seconds, what scale of users/groups); ingestion via a connector that produces chunks plus embeddings plus resolved per-chunk ACL metadata; identity resolution where the user's group memberships get expanded at query time and cached with a short TTL; retrieval that pre-filters *inside* the ANN search itself on tenant and permission match, not after; a late-binding permission re-check against the authoritative source on the final top-k right before generation, failing closed on any gap; permission-awareness extended beyond retrieval itself (ACL-aware citations, permission-scoped cache keys, a zero-retention LLM endpoint); and an audit layer logging user, applied filter, and chunk IDs per query, plus periodic cross-tenant probe tests. Naming the two-gate model explicitly — a cheap metadata pre-filter plus an authoritative late-binding check — and the staleness window between them is what distinguishes a senior answer from "just add a metadata filter."
keyPoints: Resolve tenant identity and per-chunk permission metadata.
Pre-filter inside ANN search with current group memberships.
Recheck final chunks against authoritative permissions and fail closed.
Scope caches and citations to permissions and audit cross-tenant behavior.

questions.title: Retrieval is correctly filtered by permissions. Then a "related documents" feature follows links from the retrieved chunks to other documents. What's the risk?
questions.answer: Any stage added after the ACL gate that touches document content can reintroduce a leak even though retrieval itself was correctly filtered — a reranker that re-queries the index for more candidates without reapplying the filter, a semantic cache that returns an answer generated under a different, broader-permission user's session, a "related documents" link-expansion step that follows references from an authorized chunk into an unauthorized one, or a summarization-memory layer that condensed an earlier, more-privileged session into context reused later. The principle worth stating explicitly: authorization has to be enforced at the *last* point document content enters the prompt, and every component between retrieval and generation has to be either ACL-aware itself or provably content-blind.
options: Lower recall.
It can pull in documents the user isn't allowed to see, because it runs after the permission filter.
Answers get slower.
Duplicate chunks.
keyPoints: Later pipeline stages can reintroduce unauthorized content.
Reranking and link expansion must preserve ACL checks.
Caches and memory must respect the current permission scope.
Enforce authorization at the last content entry into the prompt.

questions.title: Why is filtering the LLM's output for restricted content the wrong place to enforce access control, versus filtering what gets retrieved?
questions.answer: By the time restricted content reaches the model it has already crossed the trust boundary — it may be logged or retained by the model provider regardless of what the final visible output ends up saying. Output filtering also depends on correctly recognizing and stripping every possible leak after the fact (often via a second LLM-as-guard), and that detection step is bypassable the same way any LLM behavior is bypassable. Filter what goes in — what gets retrieved — not what comes out.
keyPoints: Restricted context crosses the trust boundary before output exists.
Providers may log or retain restricted inputs.
Post-generation leak detectors are bypassable.
Filter retrieval inputs before they reach the model.

questions.title: An approximate search returns the top 100 candidates, then a permission filter keeps only documents this user may see: 2% of the corpus. If permissions are unrelated to relevance, how many results are left on average?
questions.answer:
100 × 0.02 = 2 results, and often zero. Filtering after an approximate top-k throws away almost everything for users who can see little. That's why the fix is to filter during the search, or partition by permission.

When a user can legitimately see only a tiny slice of the corpus, HNSW's greedy graph traversal can get stranded in regions where almost no node satisfies the filter, since most of the graph's edges lead toward ineligible vectors the traversal has no reason to route around. Fixes: use a filterable-graph engine that builds extra links specifically to keep filtered traversal connected, fall back to brute-force scan below some match-ratio threshold where approximate search would otherwise fail, or move to per-tenant/per-permission-class index partitions so the permission boundary *is* the partition boundary rather than a predicate layered awkwardly on top of one shared graph.
keyPoints: Post-filtering one hundred results at two-percent visibility leaves about two.
Filter during search or partition by permissions.
Filtered HNSW traversal can lose connectivity.
Use filterable graphs or brute-force fallback for tiny eligible sets.

questions.title: What's the security risk of semantic caching specifically in a multi-tenant RAG system, beyond the obvious “wrong answer served”?
questions.answer: Beyond a naive cross-tenant leak (Tenant A's cached answer served to Tenant B's semantically-similar query), there are two subtler ones: a timing side-channel, where a cache hit (fast) versus a cache miss (slow) lets one tenant infer whether another tenant has previously queried a given topic, purely from response latency; and document-ID leakage in cache metadata, where an implementation that caches retrieved chunk IDs alongside the answer exposes *which documents are relevant to a topic* even if the answer text itself is withheld. The fix for all three is the same: namespace every cache key by tenant/user ID and include a hash of the current permission set in the key, not just the query embedding.
keyPoints: Cross-tenant answer reuse can leak cached content.
Hit latency can reveal another tenant's query history.
Cached chunk IDs can reveal relevant document identities.
