questions.title: Design an internal AI assistant over 10 million company documents with access control.
questions.answer:
An enterprise RAG system over 10 million documents must prioritize security and access control above raw retrieval:
Access Control: Permissions (ACLs) must be enforced at retrieval time, never as an LLM post-filter. Document chunks inherit security tokens (user, department, role group IDs) stored in the vector database metadata. Queries inject the authenticated user's active directory groups into the vector database filter, ensuring forbidden documents never enter the retrieval context.
Ingestion & Parsing: Documents (PDFs, spreadsheets, presentations) pass through layout-aware parsers (extracting tables and hierarchy), followed by semantic chunking. An asynchronous Change Data Capture (CDC) pipeline syncs document updates and immediate deletions.
Retrieval & Generation: We combine BM25 and dense embeddings via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, followed by a cross-encoder reranker to pick the top 5 chunks. The system prompt requires citations with exact source links and instructs the model to refuse to answer if retrieved context is insufficient.
Evaluation: We track retrieval Recall@K and answer faithfulness using automated LLM-as-a-judge pipelines on a curated golden dataset of internal queries.
keyPoints: Ingest, chunk and index documents with ownership metadata.
Enforce user permissions during retrieval and before returning evidence.
Combine retrieval and reranking to select relevant context.
Generate grounded answers with citations and an abstention path.
Evaluate retrieval and answer quality separately and maintain index freshness.

questions.title: Design a platform that serves LLMs for 50 internal teams.
questions.answer:
An internal LLM gateway serving 50 teams acts as a centralized control plane for cost, reliability, and security:
Authentication & Routing: Teams access a unified OpenAI-compatible API using scoped API keys. The gateway routes requests based on intent and cost tier: lightweight classification and extraction to small 8B models, complex reasoning to frontier models.
Resilience & Failover: The gateway manages provider redundancy. If a primary provider returns 429 or 500 errors, the gateway automatically falls back to an alternative region or secondary provider with exponential backoff and circuit breaking.
Caching & Cost Management: Exact match and semantic caching (using Redis vector search) serve repeated queries at zero GPU cost. The gateway enforces per-team token budgets and rate limits (token bucket algorithm), logging prompt/completion token counts for monthly departmental chargebacks.
Security & Observability: Streaming responses pass through real-time PII redaction and prompt injection filters. We separate interactive user traffic from background batch jobs to prevent batch processing from degrading interactive p99 latency.
keyPoints: Centralize authentication, model access and per-team quotas.
Route requests using quality, latency and cost requirements.
Apply rate limits, batching or caching where appropriate.
Track token usage and costs per team.
Provide isolation, safety checks, observability and fallback behavior.

questions.title: Estimate the GPU cost of serving 1,000 requests per second with an LLM.
questions.answer:
To estimate the infrastructure cost for 1,000 requests per second, we must explicitly state model parameters and operational assumptions:
Assumptions: Assume an 8B parameter instruction model quantized to FP8, served on NVIDIA H100 GPUs using continuous batching and PagedAttention. Average prompt length is 1,000 tokens, and average completion length is 200 tokens.
Throughput: Serving 1,000 RPS generates 200,000 output tokens per second. An H100 GPU running an FP8 8B model under optimal continuous batching achieves approximately 2,000 generated tokens per second while maintaining a time-per-output-token (TPOT) under 30ms.
GPU Sizing: Sizing purely on output tokens: 200,000 / 2,000 = 100 H100 GPUs. Adding 30% headroom for peak diurnal traffic spikes, KV-cache memory pressure, and node redundancy requires approximately 130 GPUs.
Financials: At cloud pricing of roughly $2.50 per H100 GPU-hour on 1-year reserved instances, 130 GPUs cost $325 per hour, or approximately $234,000 monthly.
Optimization: We reduce this cost by implementing prompt prefix caching for shared system instructions, semantic caching, and dynamic autoscaling during off-peak hours.
keyPoints: Request rate alone is insufficient; input and output token distributions are needed.
Separate prefill work from autoregressive decode work.
Benchmark throughput under the required latency target.
Estimate replicas from capacity and add utilization or redundancy headroom.
Multiply GPU count by time and price and include operational overhead.

questions.title: Design a visual defect detection system for a factory line.
questions.answer:
Visual defect detection on a manufacturing line succeeds or fails on physical environmental control before software:
Physical Setup: Standardizing lighting (polarized LED rings, dome lights to remove reflections) and using telecentric lenses to eliminate perspective distortion yields far greater improvement than changing neural network architectures.
Edge Architecture: Inspection must match line speed (often 50-100ms per part). We deploy optimized inference engines (TensorRT on industrial edge PCs or Jetson modules) running directly on the factory floor, isolating the line from cloud network dependency.
Modeling: Defective units represent less than 0.1% of production, making standard supervised classification impractical due to extreme class imbalance. We deploy patch-based unsupervised anomaly detection (e.g., PatchCore) trained purely on normal parts, paired with a lightweight detector for known defect categories.
Operational Strategy: We set an asymmetric decision threshold: false rejects are acceptable for secondary human inspection, but false escapes (shipping a defective part) must approach zero. Unconfident predictions route to an operator verification UI, and confirmed edge cases automatically feed into an active learning dataset for retraining.
keyPoints: Collect representative labelled defects and normal examples.
Select classification, detection or segmentation to match the task.
Use representative holdouts to test rare defects and shift.
Fit capture, inference and actuation within line timing.
Monitor false rejects and missed defects with human review and retraining.

questions.title: How do you prevent one customer's data from leaking to another in a multi-tenant AI product?
questions.answer:
Multi-tenant LLM isolation requires strict defense-in-depth across authentication, data storage, runtime caching, and model context:
Identity & Storage: Tenant identity is cryptographically verified at the API gateway and propagated via signed tokens. In the storage layer, relational metadata enforces Row-Level Security (RLS). In vector databases, enterprise tenants are isolated via separate collections or dedicated namespaces, and metadata query filters unconditionally restrict vector retrieval to tenant_id == current_tenant. Access control is never delegated to LLM prompt instructions.
Cache Isolation: Prompt caching and KV-cache reuse must be explicitly scoped by hashing the tenant ID into the cache key: cache_key = hash(tenant_id + prompt_prefix). Sharing intermediate KV-cache states across tenants allows cross-tenant memory snooping.
Context Sandboxing: Retrieved documents are treated as untrusted input. We wrap external text in structured XML tags and apply input guardrails to prevent indirect prompt injection from overriding system instructions or exfiltrating other tenants' data.
Verification: CI pipelines execute automated cross-tenant security probes—attempting to retrieve across tenant boundaries—asserting that leak rates remain exactly zero.
keyPoints: Enforce tenant identity and authorization on every data access.
Partition or filter retrieval and caches by tenant.
Use least-privilege tool access and keep secrets out of prompts.
Test cross-tenant access and prompt-injection failures.
Record auditable access and isolate training or logging data.

questions.title: How do two-tower retrieval models use in-batch negatives for training, and how do you correct for item popularity sampling bias?
questions.answer: Two-tower models perform large-scale candidate retrieval by mapping user context and candidate items into a shared embedding space using separate user and item neural networks. In a production catalog of 100 million items, computing full softmax over all items is computationally impossible. In-batch negative sampling solves this: within a training mini-batch of B user-item interaction pairs, the positive item for User i serves as a negative item for all other B minus one users in that same batch. This allows computing B-by-B dot products efficiently using a single matrix multiplication without sampling explicit negatives from disk. However, in-batch negative sampling introduces popularity bias: popular items appear more frequently in user interactions, meaning they are sampled as negatives far more often than rare items, causing the model to penalize popular items unfairly. We correct this using logQ correction: we compute each item's marginal sampling probability Q and subtract the log of Q from the raw dot product logit before applying cross-entropy loss. The trade-off is computational efficiency versus negative hardness: in-batch negatives provide fast O(B^2) training samples, but lack challenging hard negatives unless paired with dedicated hard negative mining.
followUps: How do you incorporate hard negatives (e.g. items displayed but not clicked) alongside in-batch random negatives?
Why is approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search needed during online serving of two-tower models?
wrongAnswers: Training two-tower retrieval with pure random uniform negatives sampled from the catalog, which are too easy and fail to separate subtle categories.
Omitting logQ correction on in-batch negatives, causing the retrieval model to systematically under-recommend popular items.
tradeOffs: In-batch negative training achieves massive sample efficiency via matrix multiplication, but requires logQ correction to avoid popularity distortion.
Batch size directly determines the negative sample pool: small batches lack diversity, while massive batches require distributed negative sharding.
keyPoints: Separate user and item towers map inputs into a shared embedding space.
In-batch positives serve as negatives for other users via B-by-B dot products.
Subtract log sampling probability Q to correct popularity-biased negatives.
Add hard-negative mining when in-batch negatives are too easy.

questions.title: How does Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) balance competing user engagement objectives (clicks, completion, watch time) in ranking stages?
questions.answer: In production recommendation systems, ranking models must predict multiple distinct objectives simultaneously: the probability of a click (CTR), the probability of video completion, and expected continuous watch time. Optimizing for clicks alone promotes clickbait that users quickly abandon, hurting retention. Hard parameter sharing—where all tasks share lower layers and split into task-specific heads—suffers from negative transfer when tasks conflict (such as clicking versus finishing a 30-minute video). Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) uses multiple shared expert sub-networks, but gives each task its own gating network. For Task A, its gating network computes a softmax over all experts, determining how much to weight each expert's representation for its specific prediction; Task B learns completely different gating weights over the same shared experts. Experts naturally specialize in distinct representations without interference. The trade-off is parameter scale and inference latency versus prediction accuracy: MMoE eliminates negative transfer across competing business metrics, but increases model parameter size and scoring compute relative to single-task models.
followUps: How do you combine multiple predicted probabilities (e.g. pCTR, pComplete, expected_watch_time) into a final single ranking score?
What is Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE) and how does it improve on MMoE by separating shared and task-specific experts?
wrongAnswers: Training separate standalone deep neural networks for every single business metric, duplicating feature extraction and doubling serving latency.
Forcing all tasks into a single shared dense backbone with no task-specific gating, causing negative transfer that degrades completion prediction.
tradeOffs: MMoE decouples task learning and prevents negative transfer across conflicting objectives, while sharing common underlying representations.
Multiple gating networks and expert matrix multiplications increase inference FLOPs during high-throughput heavy ranking stages.
keyPoints: Competing ranking objectives can cause negative transfer under hard sharing.
MMoE shares expert networks but gives each task its own gate.
Task-specific softmax gates weight shared expert representations.
More experts increase parameters and inference compute.

questions.title: Compare Deep Interest Network (DIN) attention over user history with static user embedding features in real-time recommendation ranking.
questions.answer: Traditional recommendation ranking models compress a user's entire historical interaction sequence into a single fixed-length embedding vector using average pooling or sum pooling. This creates a severe information bottleneck: a user's diverse interests (e.g. electronics, running shoes, and cooking knives) are averaged together into a single vector that cannot adapt when the user is currently evaluating a specific candidate item. The Deep Interest Network (DIN) replaces static pooling with candidate-aware local activation attention. When scoring a candidate item—such as a pair of running shoes—DIN computes soft attention weights across all items in the user's recent history relative to the candidate. Past running shoe purchases and sports apparel receive high attention weights, while unrelated cooking knife purchases receive near-zero weights. The resulting user representation adapts dynamically for every candidate scored. The trade-off is model expressiveness versus ranking serving latency: DIN dramatically improves ranking accuracy and click-through rates, but running attention over hundreds of historical items for thousands of candidates increases ranking latency significantly.
followUps: How does the Behavior Sequence Transformer (BST) utilize multi-head self-attention over user interaction histories?
How do you truncate or bucket long user interaction histories to meet strict sub-50ms ranking SLAs?
wrongAnswers: Averaging a user's entire past 500 clicks into a single static embedding vector, washing out specific intent when evaluating niche candidates.
Assuming sequential attention models can be computed during candidate retrieval across 100 million items, confusing retrieval with ranking.
tradeOffs: Candidate-aware attention dynamically highlights relevant historical interests for each candidate item, boosting click-through prediction.
Computing attention across user history for hundreds of candidate items increases ranking phase inference latency relative to static vectors.
keyPoints: Static pooled histories collapse diverse interests into one embedding.
DIN attends to history relative to each candidate item.
Candidate-aware weights emphasize relevant past interactions.
Per-candidate history attention increases ranking latency.

questions.title: How do you design a cold-start exploration pipeline using LinUCB contextual bandits to discover engagement on newly published items?
questions.answer: When a creator uploads a new video or a merchant lists a new product, collaborative filtering models have zero user interaction history for that item. If the recommendation engine relies purely on historical click signals, new items receive zero impressions and remain permanently cold. We solve this using a cold-start exploration pipeline powered by Linear Upper Confidence Bound (LinUCB) contextual bandits. For each new item, we represent user and item features in a shared context vector. LinUCB assumes expected reward is linear in context features and maintains a ridge regression model along with a covariance matrix capturing parameter uncertainty. When a user requests recommendations, LinUCB estimates the item's expected reward and adds an exploration bonus proportional to parameter uncertainty. An item with zero impressions has wide confidence bounds and receives an exploration boost. As users interact with the item, uncertainty shrinks, and the item transitions into standard ranking models based on its true performance. The trade-off is short-term engagement versus catalog vitality: exploratory impressions slightly reduce immediate click rates, but discover viral content and prevent creator churn.
followUps: How do you transition an item from the bandit exploration tier to the mainstream collaborative filtering index?
What happens if an exploratory item receives early clicks due to clickbait and how do you prevent runaway exploration bonuses?
wrongAnswers: Randomly inserting new items into all user feeds without context, annoying users and ruining personal recommendations.
Waiting for search queries alone to surface new items, leaving 90% of new catalog items un-discovered.
tradeOffs: Contextual bandits provide mathematically bounded regret while rapidly exploring new items, solving cold-start organically.
Allocating a fixed percentage of inventory (e.g. 5%) to exploration sacrifices a fraction of short-term conversion for long-term discovery.
keyPoints: New items lack the history needed by collaborative filtering.
LinUCB uses context features with ridge regression and parameter covariance.
Add an uncertainty-based exploration bonus to expected reward.
Exploration trades immediate clicks for discovering new items.

questions.title: Compare Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) with Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) for diversity re-ranking in recommendation trays.
questions.answer: If a recommendation heavy ranker scores items independently, the top-10 list often consists of near-identical items (such as ten consecutive iPhone phone cases), creating a redundant, boring experience for the user. Diversity re-ranking balances individual item relevance with catalog diversity across the final presentation slate. Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) is a greedy heuristic that iteratively selects the next item by maximizing a linear combination of its relevance score minus a penalty for its maximum similarity to already-selected items. MMR is fast (quadratic in slate size) and simple to tune with a single lambda parameter, but it only considers pairwise similarity. Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) model diversity globally as the volume spanned by item feature vectors in a Hilbert space. The probability of selecting a subset is proportional to the determinant of its similarity kernel matrix: highly similar items collapse the determinant volume to zero, while diverse, orthogonal items maximize volume. The trade-off is computational speed versus slate diversity elegance: MMR runs in a few milliseconds and is standard in production, while DPP provides global diversity guarantees at the expense of higher algorithmic complexity.
followUps: How do you determine the optimal diversity penalty without hurting overall platform click-through rates?
What categories of recommendations (e.g. news vs music playlists) require higher diversity penalties?
wrongAnswers: Showing the raw top-10 items straight out of the ranking model without diversity re-ranking, resulting in redundant homogeneous slates.
Applying diversity filters that replace high-relevance items with completely irrelevant random items, destroying user trust.
tradeOffs: MMR provides intuitive, low-latency greedy diversity tuning with a single lambda trade-off parameter.
DPP optimizes global slate diversity mathematically through matrix determinants, but is computationally heavier during fast re-ranking stages.
keyPoints: MMR greedily trades relevance against similarity to selected items.
DPP scores subsets through a similarity-kernel determinant.
Similar items reduce determinant volume while diverse items increase it.
MMR is simpler and faster; DPP adds global diversity with more complexity.

questions.title: A product owner asks your team for "a model" to decide which support tickets get escalated. Before you design anything, what questions decide whether this should be a learned model at all, and what would make you answer with a rule instead?
questions.answer: I ask whether a short rule already reaches the goal, whether labels exist or can be collected, whether anyone will act on the prediction, whether the data at decision time holds the signal, and whether one error is acceptable. A model loses when a few conditions stay correct and explain themselves, when there are no labels, or when the cost of building and running the system exceeds the value of the better decisions. A model wins when the rule has grown long and fragile, because a learned model is easier to update than a complex heuristic.
followUps: Level 1: Where do labels for ticket escalation come from, and what is their delay? Expected: from past escalation decisions or outcomes, which arrive after the ticket closes; the delay sets how fresh the training data can be.
Level 2: The team has no escalation history at all. What do you build first? Expected: the rule, with logging of the decision and its inputs, so labels start to accumulate.

Level 2: A regulator requires that every escalation decision be explainable. What changes? Expected: either keep the rule or restrict the model to interpretable forms such as a small tree or a linear model.
wrongAnswers: "A model always beats a rule given enough data." The rule can win when the features carry weak signal, and the lift must be measured, not assumed.
"Collect data later; ship the model first." Without labels there is nothing to train on and nothing to evaluate against.
"The heuristic baseline is just a sanity check." It is the real competitor and the safe default for failures.
keyPoints: Check whether a short rule already meets the goal.
Confirm labels, usable decision-time signal and an action on predictions.
Compare model cost and error tolerance with decision value.
Prefer a learned model when heuristics become long and fragile.

questions.title: You built a small web demo of a model for reviewers. Three months later a colleague asks whether it is "production". How do you tell, and what changes when the answer is yes?
questions.answer: A demo serves known people in short sessions from one process. It has become a product when people outside the team use it every week, when someone asks for an uptime target or reports an outage, when users want to sign in or see history, when the weekly model cost is a budget line, or when the input is covered by a contract or a law. At that point the demo moves onto the production stack with authentication, fallback models, tracing, and cost tracking per user.
followUps: Level 1: Which single signal is the strongest? Expected: an outage report, because it means someone depends on the demo and expects availability.
Level 2: The weekly model cost appears in a budget. What control replaces the daily cap? Expected: per-user quotas and billing, so the total is attributed and limited per tenant.
Level 2: Regulated data starts arriving in the input. What must the log do? Expected: keep no input text and no client address, with a retention period and access control on the records.
wrongAnswers: "It is production when it runs on a server instead of a laptop." Where it runs does not decide; who depends on it does.
"Add a disclaimer that it is a demo." A disclaimer does not stop traffic, cost or outages.
"Keep the demo and build the product separately later." The signals mean the demo already carries product risk now.
keyPoints: External recurring users and uptime expectations signal product needs.
Sign-in, history, model budgets and regulated inputs add production obligations.
Add authentication, fallback models and tracing.
Track model cost per user.

questions.title: A data scientist reports a churn classifier with an AUC of 0.91. Three months after launch, nobody on the retention team uses the scores. The algorithm was fine. Name the design decisions that were missing, and say which metric should have been reported instead.
questions.answer: The failures happened before training: nobody named the action a score starts, the scores arrived weekly while the team called customers daily, a feature leaked the label through the cancellation reason, and nobody compared the model with the rule the team already used. AUC averages over every threshold including ones never used; the decision was to contact the top 5 percent each night, so the right offline number was precision in that top 5 percent, paired with online, business and guardrail metrics.
followUps: Level 1: Why is a 30-day churn label slow to evaluate? Expected: the label arrives at the end of the horizon, so the business metric lags the launch by at least that long.
Level 2: Which guardrail would catch a model that saves users at any price? Expected: offer cost per saved user.
Level 2: The heuristic baseline beats the model by a small margin. What ships? Expected: the rule, because it is cheaper to run and explain, unless the model clears the minimum lift.
wrongAnswers: "A higher AUC would have fixed adoption." Adoption failed on freshness, action and trust, not on ranking quality.
"Business metrics are enough; skip the offline one." The business metric arrives weeks later and is noisy; the offline metric gates the launch.
"Guardrails are a product concern, not a model concern." A model that moves a guardrail the wrong way is rolled back no matter its offline score.
keyPoints: Define the action and match score delivery to the decision cadence.
Check cancellation-related label leakage and compare the existing rule.
Measure precision in the top five percent rather than relying on AUC.
Pair offline metrics with online, business and guardrail metrics.

questions.title: A chat feature expects 10,000 daily active users with 5 queries each, about 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query, at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens. Measured cache metrics give a 35% hit rate. Walk me through the monthly estimate, and say which number you would attack first.
questions.answer: The traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and a 35% cache hit rate leaves 32,500 that reach the model. Over 30 days that is $3,656 of input and $3,900 of output, about $7,556 a month, against $11,625 without the cache, so the cache saves about $4,070. Output tokens cost four times more per token, so after the hit rate the output length is the number to attack, with a maximum output tokens limit and tighter prompts.
followUps: Level 2: Which single metric on the dashboard tells you the estimate holds? Expected: cost per request, which combines token counts and prices and has a target under $0.01.

Level 2: The cache hit rate drops to zero after a prompt template change. Why? Expected: the cache key is the query embedding and the response was generated with the old template; stale entries are invalid or the time to live cleared them.

Level 3: How does prompt caching on the stable prefix change the input line? Expected: the system prompt and fixed instructions are billed at a discount when they repeat, so the effective input price per query falls without changing the token count.
Level 3: What does a per-user daily cap protect that a per-request cost target does not? Expected: the total from one heavy user; many cheap requests still sum to a large bill.
wrongAnswers: "Multiply users by a cost per user from a vendor page." The bill comes from tokens per query, queries per user and the hit rate; each is measured.
"Caching saves money only on exact repeats." A semantic cache matches similar queries by embedding, which is why the hit rate reaches a third of traffic.
"Input tokens dominate because there are more of them." At these prices and lengths the output line is larger even though there are fewer output tokens.
keyPoints: Apply the cache hit rate before calculating billable model traffic.
A 35 percent hit rate leaves 32,500 daily model queries.
The answer's monthly input and output costs total about $7,556.
Limit output length because output tokens cost more per token.

questions.title: A payment risk model scores every transaction. Labels arrive weeks later as chargebacks. Design the monitoring: what you watch, how you compare windows, which statistics you compute, and how you keep the alert rate low enough that people read the alerts.
questions.answer: Monitor four layers: system health, input distributions, prediction distributions, and outcomes once labels arrive. Compare a fixed reference window with sliding current windows, with the Population Stability Index and the two-sample KS statistic for numeric features and a chi-square test with Cramér's V for categorical ones. Alert only when a corrected p-value and an effect size both pass and the condition persists for consecutive windows, and send warnings to a dashboard rather than to a person.
followUps: Level 2: Why fix the reference window instead of sliding it too? Expected: a sliding reference follows the drift and hides it; the reference changes only at retraining.

Level 2: A clean window shows a tiny chi-square p-value. Why is it a warning and not an alert? Expected: the effect size is below threshold, so the policy logs a warning; the p-value alone is not enough.

Level 3: Labels arrive 500 events late. How does the outcome monitor handle that? Expected: it joins labels as they arrive and computes metrics on the labeled part, always looking that far into the past.
Level 3: Which drift stays invisible to this whole design except the last layer? Expected: concept drift, where the inputs do not change and only outcomes reveal the new relation.
wrongAnswers: "Alert on any p-value below 0.05." With many features and hourly checks that is dozens of false alarms a day and people stop reading.
"Watch accuracy; it is the only metric that matters." Accuracy arrives after the label delay; input and prediction monitors give the early warning.
"Retrain on a schedule and skip monitoring." A schedule retrains when nothing changed and waits when something did.
keyPoints: Monitor system health, inputs, predictions and delayed outcomes.
Compare fixed reference and sliding current windows with statistical tests.
Require corrected significance, effect size and persistence before alerting.
Send warnings to a dashboard rather than paging a person.

questions.title: Design the request path of a chat service that calls a hosted model. Users leave when nothing appears for a few seconds, the provider returns rate limits and server errors at night, and the vector store behind retrieval sometimes times out. Cover what the user sees, how you retry, and what happens when each part fails.
questions.answer: Stream tokens over server-sent events so the first token appears in a few hundred milliseconds even though the full answer takes seconds. Retry provider failures with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at three retries, then fall through an ordered chain of models to a cached answer and finally a short unavailable message. Secondary systems degrade instead of failing the request: no retrieval context when the vector store is down, a direct model call when the cache is down, and a clear message when a guardrail blocks.
followUps: Level 2: Why add jitter to the backoff? Expected: many clients that fail at once would otherwise retry at the same instants and reproduce the overload.
Level 2: Why is a guardrail block not retried? Expected: the input is the problem; retrying the same input gives the same block and spends a call.
Level 3: The fallback model has a different price. Where does that show up? Expected: in the cost tracker per request and per model, so the dashboard shows the cost of the outage, not only its rate.
Level 3: The stream has started and the model fails. What can the server still do? Expected: send an error event inside the stream, because the HTTP status is already committed.
wrongAnswers: "Retry until the provider answers." Unbounded retries pile up during an outage; cap them and fall through the chain.
"If retrieval is down, fail the request so the answer stays grounded." A secondary system must not take down the primary flow; answer with reduced context and log it.
"Buffer the whole response and send it at once for simplicity." The user sees nothing for seconds and leaves; the total time is the same either way.
keyPoints: Stream responses over server-sent events for early first tokens.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter up to three retries.
Fall through models, cached answers and an unavailable response.
Degrade secondary cache and retrieval failures gracefully.

questions.title: You have a small pretrained language model and 800 labeled text messages, half spam and half not. Design the classifier: what you keep, what you replace, which of two training regimes you choose, how you split and evaluate, and when the other regime would win.
questions.answer: Keep the pretrained body and replace the vocabulary head with a linear layer to two classes over a mean-pooled, mask-weighted sequence vector. With 800 examples, train the head only with the body frozen: it is fast, light on memory and rarely overfits, and on this fixture it reaches about 0.9 precision and 0.85 recall after twenty epochs. Full fine-tuning takes about three times longer and lands within a couple of points either way; it starts to pay off at the scale of 80,000 examples or when the domain drifts far from the pretraining text.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the frozen body rarely overfit here? Expected: only the head's few parameters move, so the model cannot memorize 640 examples through the body.
Level 2: Why stratify the split? Expected: so the test set keeps the class balance and precision and recall mean what they say.

Level 3: Precision matters more than recall for this product. What changes in the design? Expected: the decision threshold on the spam logit, chosen on a validation split held out from the 640 training messages to trade recall for precision, so the 160 test messages stay untouched for the final numbers; the training regime stays the same.

Level 3: The messages are in a domain the body never saw. Which regime and why? Expected: full or partial fine-tuning, because the frozen features do not carry the domain and the head alone underfits.
wrongAnswers: "Train a small classifier from scratch; the model is tiny anyway." That wastes the pretraining and 800 examples are too few to learn the language from zero.
"Always fine-tune everything for the best accuracy." On small data full tuning overfits and forgets, for a result within a couple of points of the head alone at three times the cost.
"Use the last token's hidden state without a mask." Padded sequences then pool a padding position; the mask must select the last real token or weight the mean.
keyPoints: Replace the vocabulary head with a two-class linear head over masked mean pooling.
Freeze the pretrained body for the small 800-example dataset.
Head-only training reduces time, memory and overfitting risk.
Full fine-tuning becomes more useful with more examples or domain shift.

questions.title: A new version of a chat prompt looks better in a notebook. Design how it reaches users: the stages, how users are assigned, what you measure at each stage, and when it rolls back automatically.
questions.answer: Run it in shadow first, on all traffic, logging its answers without showing them, and compare quality metrics with the current prompt. Then route a small share of users to it, 10% in the lesson, and widen in steps to 25%, 50% and 100% while the metrics hold. Assign by a deterministic hash of the user id so each user sees one version, and roll back automatically when the new version's error rate reaches twice the old one over a window of requests.
followUps: Level 2: Why hash the user id and not pick randomly per request? Expected: a user then gets one consistent version across a session and the assignment is reproducible from the log.
Level 2: What does shadow mode not tell you? Expected: how users react to the new answers; it only compares logged outputs and system metrics.

Level 3: The new prompt costs more per request but scores higher. Who decides? Expected: a guardrail on cost per request decides whether it can ship at all; the quality gain against the cost is then a product decision with both numbers on the table.

Level 3: How do you keep the control and the variant from sharing a cache entry? Expected: include the prompt version in the cache key, otherwise a hit returns the other version's answer and the comparison is corrupted.
wrongAnswers: "Ship to everyone and watch the dashboard." A regression then hits every user before the dashboard moves.
"Assign per request at random for a cleaner statistic." Users see both versions in one conversation and the logged metrics mix them.
"Shadow mode is enough; skip the canary." Shadow mode never shows the output to a user, so it cannot measure user reaction.
keyPoints: Run the prompt in shadow before exposing its answers.
Roll out to increasing user shares while quality metrics hold.
Assign versions by deterministic user-ID hash.
Roll back automatically when the new error rate doubles over a request window.

questions.title: A feed ranking score must be no more than two hours old for 5,000,000 items, and the serving peak is 120 requests per second. Price batch and online serving with the lesson's cost model, pick one, and say what would flip the choice.
questions.answer: With a one-hour batch job and a two-hour staleness limit, the job must run every hour, which the lesson's cost model prices at 24.0 runs per day over 5,000,000 items for $48.50 a day. Two online replicas sized for 120 peak QPS cost $24.00 a day and serve the freshest data. Online wins here; the choice flips when the freshness limit relaxes enough to cut the runs, or when peak traffic grows enough to need many replicas.
followUps: Level 2: Why is the online plan at its minimum here? Expected: two replicas is the availability floor, and 120 peak QPS fits inside what two replicas handle, so traffic does not drive the count.
Level 2: The job takes longer than the staleness limit. What does the planner return? Expected: infeasible; no schedule satisfies the limit, so the budgets or the job must change.

Level 3: Design the hybrid. Expected: batch scores known items on the relaxed schedule, online scores new items and requests that need fresh data; price it as the sum of a cheaper batch plan and a small online tier.

Level 3: Which design document check does this feed? Expected: the serving-fit check, which prices the chosen mode against the staleness, latency and cost budgets and fails a mode that misses any of them.
wrongAnswers: "Batch is always cheaper." Batch cost scales with runs per day times entities; a tight freshness limit makes it the expensive plan.
"Online is always fresher, so always better." Fresher costs replicas, and a nightly process cannot use freshness it does not read.
"Pick by model accuracy." Accuracy is the same in both plans; the choice is about freshness, latency and cost.
keyPoints: Account for job duration when satisfying a batch staleness limit.
Hourly batch runs cost more than two online replicas in this example.
Online serving provides fresher data for the stated traffic.
Relaxed freshness or higher peak traffic can reverse the cost choice.

questions.title: A subscription company with 2,000,000 users wants to reduce churn. The retention team can send a save offer to a small share of users each night. Design the system end to end: the prediction, the decision, the serving mode, the baselines, the rollout, and the failure defaults. State the load and the budgets you assume.
questions.answer: The task is binary classification: the probability that a user cancels in the next 30 days, so that the nightly job can pick the top 5 percent for an offer. Nightly scores for every user fit batch inference; the lesson's cost model prices one run a day over the user base at under one dollar, while an online service sized for 40 peak QPS costs $24.00 a day for a freshness nobody needs. The model must beat the idle-days rule by a set lift, ship through shadow and canary stages, and fall back to that rule when anything fails.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the majority baseline score zero? Expected: F1 counts positive predictions, and the majority class is "stays", so there are none.

Level 2: The retention team wants hourly freshness. What changes? Expected: more runs per day raise batch cost in proportion, and the online path becomes cheaper at some point; price both with the cost model.

Level 3: How do you keep the model from learning its own interventions? Expected: a random holdout that never receives offers, plus logging of score and decision so training can separate influenced from clean rows.
Level 3: What is the safe default when the model service is down during the nightly run? Expected: serve the last good scores for a fixed window, then fall back to the idle-days rule.
wrongAnswers: "Serve it online so scores are always fresh." The decision runs once a night; online replicas cost more for freshness the process cannot use.
"Use AUC as the offline metric." The decision uses one threshold; precision in the contacted share is the metric that matches it.
"Retrain monthly on all users." Treated users carry the intervention in their labels; without a holdout the model degrades with each retrain.
keyPoints: Predict 30-day churn and select the top five percent nightly.
Use batch scoring because fresher online scores are unnecessary.
Require lift over the idle-days heuristic.
Roll out through shadow and canary with heuristic fallback.

questions.title: Design the feature layer for a churn model. Training needs the value of each feature for millions of user and time pairs. Serving needs the latest value for one user in a few milliseconds. Name the parts, explain how a training row gets its features, and show with the lesson's numbers what goes wrong without the right join.
questions.answer: One registry holds each feature definition with its entity, window, default, TTL and version, and both paths compute from it. An offline store keeps the full history with event timestamps for training and backfills; a materialization job copies the latest value per entity into an online key-value store with a TTL. A training row takes the latest feature row at or before its label time, inside the TTL. Without that point-in-time join the lesson's demo looks better offline, 0.948 against 0.893, and worse on new data, 0.763 against 0.876, because the newest snapshot leaks the answer.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the leaked model look better offline? Expected: the feature contains the outcome, so the offline split rewards it; on new data the information is not there.
Level 2: What does the TTL do in the join, and relative to what time? Expected: it drops a feature row too old for the label; the age is measured from each label time, not from the query time.

Level 3: Two teams compute the same feature in two services. Which skew cause is that, and how does the registry remove it? Expected: two code paths; both services call the registry definition instead of their own copy.
Level 3: Fresher serving features turn out to hurt. Why? Expected: the model trained on weekly snapshots, so values up to six days old are what it learned; staleness skew runs both ways.
wrongAnswers: "Join labels to the feature table on the user id." That returns the newest value and copies the outcome into the input.
"Fresher features are always better at serving time." The model learned the freshness of its training data; a different age is skew.
"Snapshots every day remove the problem." Daily snapshots reduce staleness but the join still needs the as-of rule and the TTL.
keyPoints: Keep feature entity, window, default, TTL and version in one registry.
Store timestamped history offline and materialize latest values online.
Join training features at or before label time within their TTL.
Latest-snapshot joins leak future information and degrade new-data performance.

questions.title: A reviewer and a customer want to try your model from a link, on a phone, without your notebook. Each model call costs money. Design the demo: the input contract, the order of the checks, the controls for a public link, and what the log is allowed to keep.
questions.answer: Write the contract first: a string of 1 to 500 characters with no control characters, a model call with a known cost, and an output that includes a JSON error with a hint. Run the checks in order of cost, body size, access token, per-client token bucket, input validation, daily cap, and only then the model call. Return a stable error code with a message, a hint and a request id, and log the route, the status, the latency and the input length with a keyed hash of the client, never the text or the address.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the daily cap run after validation and not before? Expected: so only valid requests count against the budget; a rejected request should not spend it.

Level 2: Behind a reverse proxy every request has the proxy's address. What breaks? Expected: all users share one bucket; read the client address from a header that only your proxy sets and trust it from nowhere else.
Level 3: Why send the input in a POST body instead of the URL for the event stream? Expected: servers and proxies write URLs into access logs, so a GET would store user text.

Level 3: A framework builds the page for you. Which controls are still your job? Expected: the rate limit, the cost cap and log privacy; the frameworks save work on the form and the streaming, not on the risks of a public link.
wrongAnswers: "Validate in the browser with a maximum length attribute." The browser helps honest users only; the server repeats every check.
"A rate limit per client is enough to control cost." It bounds each client, not the sum; the daily cap bounds the total.
"Log the full request so you can debug reports." The log then holds user text and addresses; a request id joins a report to a record without either.
keyPoints: Define bounded validated input and structured output errors.
Run cheap checks before the model: size, auth, quota, validation and daily cap.
Return stable codes with hints and request IDs.
Log operational metadata and keyed client hashes without raw text or addresses.

questions.title: A team trains and aligns models in a multi-stage pipeline and ships the result to serving. Design the evaluation platform that decides whether an artifact is shippable: what it reads, what a gate is, which two gates catch most disasters, how it handles a failed gate, and how a third party replays a decision.
questions.answer: The platform reads a manifest that describes the run completely, with a seed, a code revision, and an input and output hash for every stage, and it evaluates numeric gates that were written before the run started. A regression gate holds the new model to the previous one on core benchmarks and catches training bugs; a KL budget gate caps how far the aligned policy drifted from its reference and catches alignment overcooking. A failed gate holds the run for a named reviewer whose override is logged in the manifest, and anyone can replay the decision because the eval report is content-addressed and the eval data hash is part of it.
followUps: Level 3: Why must the thresholds be written before the run? Expected: a threshold chosen after seeing the scores is moved to pass the model; a gate is only a gate if it can fail.
Level 3: A change to the eval set invalidates what? Expected: only the ship decision; the eval data hash changes, the report is recomputed, and the training artifacts stay valid.

Level 4: The quantized model passes every gate except the safety refusal rate, which rose slightly. What do you ship? Expected: nothing without a logged override; the gate exists for the serving artifact, and the lesson's recipe keeps safety evals on a higher-precision quantization where deltas matter.

Level 4: How does the platform stop a model trained through the wrong stage from reaching the gate? Expected: typed artifacts and typed stage signatures, so a preference-tuned checkpoint cannot be fed into the supervised path and the mismatch fails at plan time.
wrongAnswers: "Have a reviewer look at samples and sign off." Subjective sign-offs are not gates; a gate is a number that can fail, and the reviewer's role is the logged override.
"Rerun training to confirm a result." Pre-training costs weeks; replay checks hashes and metrics against the manifest instead.
"One benchmark is enough if it is the right one." The regression set and the KL budget catch different failures, and a safety gate catches a third.
keyPoints: Describe runs with manifests, seeds, revisions and stage hashes.
Freeze numeric evaluation gates before execution.
Gate core regressions and policy KL drift separately.
Log named-reviewer overrides and content-address reports for replay.

questions.title: Design the service behind a chat product with 10,000 daily active users who send about 5 queries each, with roughly 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query. Users must see a response start quickly, the tail must stay bounded, and the product has a unit cost target. Lay out the request path, the components, the budgets you hold each one to, and how you would scale it.
questions.answer: The request enters through a gateway that authenticates and rate limits per user, passes input guardrails, is matched against a semantic cache, and on a miss goes to the model with streaming, then through output guardrails, an eval logger and a cost tracker. The budgets are a median under 2s, a p99 under 10s, a cache hit rate above 30%, a guardrail block rate under 5%, and a cost per request under $0.01. At 50,000 queries a day this runs on a few async servers behind a load balancer; the servers are I/O bound, so a single async process holds a hundred or more concurrent requests and scaling means more servers, not more cores.
followUps: Level 3: A user pastes a document far longer than the context window. Where is that caught? Expected: at the maximum input token limit before the model call, with a clear error, not at the provider.

Level 3: Why does cost per user matter when cost per request is already under target? Expected: a few heavy users dominate the bill; per-user tracking and a daily cap move them to a cheaper model or stop them.

Level 4: The provider has a regional outage during the daily peak. Walk the request path. Expected: backoff and retries on the primary, fall through the chain to a second model, then cached answers for repeated queries, then an unavailable message; the cost tracker shows the fallback's price and the dashboard shows the step that answered.

Level 4: How do you prove the service meets its budgets before the first user? Expected: a load test at 100 concurrent users against the staging stack with the dashboard metrics as pass criteria, plus a shadow run of the prompts on logged traffic.
wrongAnswers: "Scale the model servers first." The service is I/O bound at this traffic; the gateway, cache and async servers are the design, and the model is a dependency.
"Skip the cache; the model is the product." A third of the traffic repeats, and the cache is the largest single saving in the bill.
"The p99 is a vendor problem." Timeouts, maximum tokens, streaming and the fallback chain are what bound the tail on your side.
keyPoints: Authenticate, rate-limit, guard inputs and check cache before model inference.
Stream model output through guardrails, evaluation logging and cost tracking.
Set latency, cache-hit, block-rate and per-request cost budgets.
Scale I/O-bound asynchronous servers behind a load balancer.

questions.title: A team wants to adapt an open model in the 8B class to its own domain and serve it at a measurable cost per million tokens. Design the pipeline so that one command runs it end to end: the stages, the hardware per stage, the data hygiene, the ablations you require, the serving measurements, and what the release must include.
questions.answer: Five stages, each with a config file in version control: data preparation with deduplication, a quality filter, personal data scrubbing and a contamination check against the eval sets; supervised fine-tuning for 2-3 epochs on 8xH100 with a cosine schedule and packed sequences; one epoch of preference tuning on 4xH100 with a swept beta; quantization into three formats; and serving with speculative draft heads and autoscaling on queue wait. The deliverable is an ablation table of base, SFT only, SFT plus DPO and SFT plus GRPO on the task benchmarks, serving numbers at batch 1, 8 and 32 with the draft acceptance rate and cost per million tokens, a safety pass rate, and a model card with seeds, configs and commit hashes.
followUps: Level 3: Why does preference tuning need fewer GPUs than SFT? Expected: it runs one epoch on a much smaller set of pairs, and the capstone sizes it at half the SFT hardware.

Level 3: Which stage gets rerun when the safety eval fails on the quantized model? Expected: quantization and serving only; the pipeline lesson's rollback invalidates the failed stage and its descendants.

Level 4: The acceptance rate on domain traffic is far below the number from generic chat data. What does that do to the design? Expected: the latency budget was set on the wrong number; retrain the draft heads on domain data or size serving without the speculation gain.

Level 4: A smaller model with a low-rank adapter matches quality at a tenth of the memory. How does the pipeline change? Expected: the SFT stage swaps to adapter training with the same data and eval gates, and the quantization and serving stages consume the merged weights unchanged.
wrongAnswers: "Skip the contamination check; the data is internal." Internal data copies public text all the time, and one leaked test set makes the whole eval table meaningless.
"Report the final model against the base and stop." Without the per-stage ablation nobody knows whether preference tuning helped or hurt.
"Measure serving at batch one only." Throughput and cost per million tokens come from batched decoding; batch one measures latency, not economics.
keyPoints: Version configurations for data preparation, SFT, preference tuning, quantization and serving.
Deduplicate, scrub personal data and check evaluation contamination.
Compare base and tuned variants in an ablation table.
Report serving throughput, draft acceptance, cost, safety and model provenance.

questions.title: A payment service must approve, review or block each payment within 100 ms, at 400 requests per second at peak. Fraud labels arrive as chargebacks weeks later. Design the system: the task, the serving mode and its sizing, the data and label plan, the rollout, the failure defaults, and the two things that will quietly break it after launch.
questions.answer: The task is binary classification of fraud probability with two thresholds that split the score into approve, review and block, served online because the decision needs the data of the request. At 400 requests a second and 50 ms per request about 20 requests are in flight at any moment, so the service is small, and the budget leaves room for a feature fetch plus the model. Chargeback labels come weeks after the payment, so training uses a time split and features that exist at payment time, and the rollout goes shadow, then canary on a small share, with the heuristic rule as the default on timeout. The two quiet failures are the feedback loop, where blocked payments never get a label, and concept drift, where the same basket changes its fraud risk and only outcome monitors see it.
followUps: Level 3: Why does a time split matter more here than a random split? Expected: a random split leaks future tactics into training and overstates performance on the next month's fraud.
Level 3: The review queue grows after launch. Which guardrail caught it and what do you adjust? Expected: the review rate guardrail; move the review threshold, not the model.

Level 4: The random non-blocking share costs real fraud losses. How do you size it? Expected: as the smallest share that keeps enough labeled fraud examples from the blocked region to retrain; price it as the cost of clean data against the cost of a model that drifts blind.

Level 4: Retraining on the last quarter's labels after a tactic change makes the model worse. Why? Expected: concept drift; most of the labels still describe the old relation, so new labels must be collected before retraining helps.
wrongAnswers: "Precompute fraud scores nightly for every card." The payment did not exist last night; the decision needs request-time data.
"Retrain weekly on all blocked and approved payments." Blocked payments have no outcome, so the training set drifts toward the model's own decisions.
"Watch feature drift and you will see the fraudsters change." Concept drift leaves inputs unchanged; only outcomes show it.
keyPoints: Use online fraud scoring with approve, review and block thresholds.
Train with time splits and payment-time features because labels are delayed.
Roll out shadow then canary with heuristic fallback on timeout.
Monitor blocked-payment feedback loops and outcome-based concept drift.

questions.title: An engineering organization wants to ask questions across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code and get answers that cite file and line. The index must stay fresh on every push. Design the ingestion, the retrieval, the answer step, the freshness path, and the evaluation, with the budgets you would commit to.
questions.answer: Parse each file into function and class nodes and chunk at those boundaries, give each chunk a dense embedding, sparse terms and a one-sentence summary, and store a graph of imports and calls between chunks. A query runs dense and sparse search in parallel, merges and deduplicates, reranks the top 50 with a cross-encoder to keep 10, and hands those to a long-context model that must cite every claim by file and line; uncited claims are dropped. A push triggers a symbol-level diff so only changed chunks re-embed, with a budget of under 60 seconds for a 50-file push. Quality is measured on 100 labeled cross-repo questions with MRR@10, nDCG@10, citation faithfulness and p50 and p99 latency.
followUps: Level 3: Why chunk at syntax nodes instead of fixed token windows? Expected: a window cuts functions in half and mixes neighbors; a node is one coherent unit with a stable symbol name to cite and deduplicate on.

Level 3: What does the reranker add that the two retrievers cannot? Expected: it scores each query and candidate pair together, which is more accurate than cosine on separate embeddings, at a cost that only the top 50 can afford.

Level 4: Generated boilerplate makes up a fifth of the corpus. What happens and what do you change? Expected: retrieval poisoning, where near-duplicate generated code crowds the results; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them.

Level 4: A question needs code from four repositories. Which component carries that? Expected: the symbol graph expands the candidate set across import and call edges, so the reranker sees chunks from repositories the first search missed.
wrongAnswers: "A million-token context window replaces retrieval." Context helps but does not rank; cross-repo questions still need retrieval and citations.
"Dense embeddings alone are enough for code." Exact symbol names need the sparse index, and the summary catches intent that the code text does not state.
"Re-index the fleet on every push to keep it simple." Reprocessing 2M lines per commit blows the freshness budget; the diff keeps the index consistent at a fraction of the work.
keyPoints: Chunk code at function and class boundaries with embeddings, sparse terms and summaries.
Fuse dense and sparse results, deduplicate and cross-encode a narrowed set.
Require file-and-line citations and drop uncited claims.
Re-embed changed symbols and evaluate retrieval, faithfulness and latency.

questions.title: A payment model's accuracy, measured as labels arrive, fell from 0.946 to between 0.76 and 0.79. The feature monitors and the score distribution stayed quiet the whole time. The team proposes retraining on the last quarter of labeled data tonight. What happened, why did the monitors miss it, and is the proposal right?
questions.answer: The relation between inputs and labels changed while the inputs themselves did not, which is concept drift. Input and prediction monitors compare distributions of features and scores, so a change in the conditional label distribution is invisible to them, and only the outcome monitor can see it, after the label delay. Retraining tonight on the last quarter is the wrong move: most of those labels still describe the old relation, so the model relearns it; collect labels from after the change first, then retrain on them.
followUps: Level 3: Which signal could you add that reacts before the labels? Expected: none for pure concept drift; a proxy such as a review queue outcome or a faster partial label is the only earlier signal.

Level 3: How does a performance estimator that uses predicted probabilities behave here? Expected: it assumes the calibration still holds, so it misses concept drift; the lesson notes that such estimators handle covariate shift and not concept drift.

Level 4: How do you choose how many post-change labels are enough? Expected: enough to test the retrained model on a recent held-out slice with a tolerance you set in advance; the test on recent labels is the gate, not a count.

Level 4: After retraining, the input monitors start to alert on the clean reference. Why? Expected: the reference window was not reset to the new training data, so it compares live traffic with an old distribution.
wrongAnswers: "The feature monitors are broken; nothing changed in the inputs." They worked as designed; the inputs did not change, the labels did.
"Retrain on everything so the model sees the new pattern." The old labels outnumber the new ones and the model relearns the old relation.
"Shorten the windows to catch it faster." Smaller windows add noise and false alarms; the lag here comes from the label delay, which windows cannot remove.
keyPoints: Concept drift changes the input-label relationship without necessarily changing inputs.
Input and score monitors can miss the changed conditional label distribution.
Outcome monitoring detects it only after labels arrive.
Collect post-change labels before retraining instead of relearning old-quarter relationships.

questions.title: A churn model scored well offline and does worse than the older, simpler model on live traffic. Serving features are computed by another team's service. You have a sample of logged serving requests. Design the triage: which comparisons you run, in which order, what each one isolates, and what the fix looks like for each cause you find.
questions.answer: Compare the same entity and time across three pairs. The online store read against the training join tests the whole system and should show zero skew when both read one definition. A fresh computation against the training join isolates staleness, and the second team's code path against a fresh computation isolates code differences such as window boundaries and defaults. Each pair gives a mismatch rate and a mean absolute difference per feature, and the fix for every cause is the same shape: one registry definition that both paths call, with logged serving features checked against it.
followUps: Level 3: Which comparison would you run first with one hour available? Expected: the first one; if the store read matches the training join, the system is consistent and the problem is elsewhere, and if not, every downstream check is moot.

Level 3: The defaults differ only for new users. Why does the mismatch rate understate the damage? Expected: the rate is low because new users are few, but the difference per mismatch is huge, so the model's output for every new user is wrong.

Level 4: The other team cannot change their service this quarter. What do you do? Expected: log their served features, train the next model on those logged values so training matches serving, and keep the skew check running so the gap is visible.

Level 4: How does a created timestamp enter the triage? Expected: a backfill written today can read late-arriving data, so a strict join also drops rows created after the label time; otherwise the training path itself is skewed.
wrongAnswers: "Fresh serving features are always better than training snapshots." The model learned the training freshness; a different age is skew in either direction.
"A mismatch rate under a few percent is fine." A small rate with a large mean difference, as with the defaults, still breaks every affected prediction.

"Compare offline accuracy with live accuracy and call it drift." Drift is a change over time; skew is a difference between two readers of the same feature at the same time, and the three comparisons tell them apart.
keyPoints: Compare online reads with training joins for matching entities and times.
Compare fresh computation with joins to isolate stale features.
Compare alternate code paths with fresh computation to isolate logic differences.
Use one registry definition and verify logged serving features against it.

questions.title: You are the reviewer for ML design documents before any training starts. A team hands you a document for a payment fraud check that proposes batch scoring, where one job takes an hour, with a three-minute staleness limit, reports an offline AUC, lists a majority-class baseline, and has no rollout section. Walk me through your review: the sections you expect, which gaps block, how you score it, and what you tell the team.
questions.answer: The document needs nine sections, and six items block a review because each one makes the system unsafe or useless: the decision that uses the prediction, a business metric, a heuristic or current-system baseline, confirmation that every feature exists at prediction time, a shadow or canary stage with a rollback, and a default action for every failure. This document fails at least three of them: the only baseline is trivial, there is no rollout and no rollback, and the serving choice fails the fit check because batch cannot meet a limit of three minutes when one job takes an hour. I send it back with the blocking list first, and I ask for precision at the decision threshold instead of AUC.
followUps: Level 3: The team says the majority baseline is enough since it scores zero on F1. Why is that the wrong baseline? Expected: it is the trivial one and usually weak; the heuristic or current system is the real competitor and the one the lift is measured against.

Level 4: Why does the serving fit check belong in a document review rather than in load testing? Expected: it is arithmetic on stated budgets and prices, so it catches an infeasible design before a line of serving code exists.

Level 4: The document proposes a hybrid serving mode. What does the checker do and what do you do? Expected: the lesson's cost model has no hybrid plan, so the check fails until a hybrid plan is added; ask the team to price the batch and the online parts and add the plan.

Level 4: What is the one non-blocking section you would still refuse to skip for a fraud system? Expected: feedback loops, because blocked payments never get a label and the model drifts toward its own decisions without a clean sample.
wrongAnswers: "A strong offline metric compensates for a missing rollout." A model with no shadow stage and no rollback reaches users with no way back; that is why rollout blocks.
"Score the document and pass it at a high enough total." One failed blocker fails the review regardless of the total.
"Serving mode is an implementation detail for later." The fit check shows batch cannot meet the limit at all, which changes the architecture and the cost.
keyPoints: Require a decision, business metric and meaningful baseline before review.
Confirm features exist at prediction time and serving meets freshness constraints.
Require rollout, rollback and default failure actions.
Ask for precision at the operating threshold rather than AUC alone.

questions.title: A twelve-stage training pipeline runs from tokenizer to inference server, and the pre-training stage costs weeks and millions of dollars. Before the run starts you must write what happens when each stage fails. Lay out the plan, explain how the orchestrator computes what to rerun, and say what "reproduce the run" can and cannot promise.
questions.answer: Sort the stages by the cost to rerun them: tokenizer, evaluation, quantization and the server are cheap and rerun in hours, supervised tuning and alignment take days, so the base checkpoint is kept and only those stages rerun, and pre-training takes weeks and a budget in the millions, so the plan is the last good checkpoint plus revised downstream stages. The rerun set falls out of the typed, hashed dependency graph: invalidate the failed stage and every descendant. A replay promises the same code, recipe and source data hashes and the same headline metrics, not bit-identical weights or the same output hashes.
followUps: Level 3: Why not name artifacts by version string? Expected: two artifacts can share a name and differ in content; the hash is the identity, and a name like latest is a trap.

Level 4: The reward model and the DPO policy both depend on the SFT checkpoint. What can run in parallel and what must wait? Expected: the two can run together after SFT; the refined policy waits for both, and its input hash must be a deterministic combination of both outputs.

Level 4: A corrupted checkpoint is discovered after alignment finished. Which plan applies? Expected: the expensive class; take the last good pre-training checkpoint and rerun the medium and cheap stages, never the full pre-training.

Level 4: A teammate reports that their replay has different weights. Is the run broken? Expected: not by itself; compare the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics, and only a mismatch there means the run is not reproduced.
wrongAnswers: "Rerun from the start to be safe." The expensive stage costs weeks; the typed graph tells you exactly which stages are invalid.
"Keep the latest checkpoint file and overwrite it each step." A mutable name cannot be verified or replayed; content addressing is what makes the rollback set trustworthy.

"If the weights are not bit-identical, the pipeline is not reproducible." Distributed training is not deterministic; reproducibility is defined on the code, recipe and source data hashes and the metrics.
keyPoints: Choose reruns by stage cost and preserve expensive base checkpoints.
Invalidate a failed stage and all descendants in the hashed dependency graph.
Rerun cheaper downstream stages when possible.
Replay promises the same recipe and data with comparable metrics, not identical weights.

questions.title: Three systems retrain monthly on their own production data: a churn model that sends save offers, a fraud model that blocks payments, and a ranking model that orders a feed. Each one gets a little worse after every retrain. Explain the shared cause, design the data layer that prevents it, and say what each training row must carry for the fix to work.
questions.answer: Each model's decisions change the data that trains its next version, which is a feedback loop. Offers keep users who would have churned, so high-risk users look loyal; blocked payments never get a chargeback, so fraud disappears from the blocked region; the feed shows only its top items, so only those collect clicks. The fix is to keep data the model did not influence: a random holdout that never receives the intervention, a small share of random decisions, and a log that stores the score and the decision with every row, joined to features as of the decision time so training can separate influenced from clean data.
followUps: Level 3: Why is a time split alone not enough here? Expected: the recent period is also influenced by the deployed model; time ordering prevents future leakage but not intervention bias.

Level 4: The random non-blocking share costs real fraud. How do you argue for it? Expected: as the price of clean labels against the cost of a model that drifts blind; size it to the minimum that keeps enough labeled fraud from the blocked region.

Level 4: How does the exposure loop in ranking differ from the other two? Expected: the label is never collected rather than hidden; random exposure of lower-ranked items is the only way to learn their click rate.
Level 4: A retrain evaluated on the holdout is worse than on the full set. Which number do you trust? Expected: the holdout; the full set rewards the model for agreeing with its own past decisions.
wrongAnswers: "More training data fixes a drifting model." The new data is influenced; more of it entrenches the loop.
"A random train and test split shows the real performance." Both halves are influenced; only a holdout that never saw the intervention is clean.
"Log the decision later from the outcome table." The decision and the assignment must be recorded at decision time, with the features as of that time, or the join leaks the outcome.
keyPoints: Model interventions change the data used to train later versions.
Keep a random holdout or small random-decision share free of model influence.
Log scores and decisions with each row.
Join decision-time features to distinguish influenced and clean data.

topics.title: Coding
topics.about: Write the code that the lessons build. Each item links to a practice task with checks.

questions.title: Implement k-means from scratch in NumPy. What would you test?
questions.answer: Initialize k centroids, preferably using k-means++. Loop: compute distances with broadcasting, assign each point to its nearest centroid, recompute means, and stop when assignments stop changing or at a maximum iteration count. Handle empty clusters by reseeding them. Test with clearly separated synthetic blobs, k equal to one, a fixed seed, and a check that within-cluster error never increases between iterations.
keyPoints: Assign each sample to its nearest centroid using vectorized distances.
Recompute cluster means and iterate to convergence.
Handle empty clusters and reproducible initialization.
Test known clusters, degenerate inputs and multiple restarts.

questions.title: Implement scaled dot-product attention in PyTorch and explain the tensor shapes.
questions.answer: Given Q, K and V with shape batch, length, dim: scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k). Apply the mask by filling blocked scores with negative infinity before softmax on the last dimension, then return weights @ V. Output shape matches V's. For multi-head, reshape to batch, heads, length, head dim. Common bugs are masking after softmax and applying softmax to the wrong dimension.
keyPoints: Compute query-key scores with compatible batch, head and sequence axes.
Scale logits by square root of key dimension.
Apply the mask before softmax over the key axis.
Multiply attention weights by values to produce output.
Test shapes, masks and numerical stability.

questions.title: Write precision, recall and F1 from scratch, and handle the edge cases.
questions.answer: Count true positives, false positives and false negatives. Precision is TP over TP plus FP, recall is TP over TP plus FN, and F1 is their harmonic mean. Guard every division against zero, and state the convention you use, usually returning zero. For multi-class work, explain macro averaging, which treats classes equally, against micro averaging, which treats examples equally. Test with all-negative predictions and no positive labels.
keyPoints: Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP.
Recall is TP divided by TP plus FN.
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
Define zero-denominator behavior explicitly.
Test perfect, all-negative and no-positive-prediction cases.

questions.title: Find the top k most frequent items in a very large stream. What is your approach?
questions.answer: If it fits in memory, count with a hash map and keep a min-heap of size k, which takes O(n log k) time. If it doesn't, use an approximate sketch such as Count-Min with a heap, or Misra-Gries, which accept a bounded error for fixed memory. On a cluster, count by key with map-reduce, then merge. State your accuracy needs first, since they determine the design.
keyPoints: Exact counts require memory proportional to distinct items.
A size-k heap selects top counts efficiently after counting.
Approximate sketches or heavy-hitter algorithms bound memory.
Explain approximation error and whether a second pass is available.

questions.title: An interviewer gives you a coding problem you haven't seen. How do you work through it?
questions.answer: Restate it and ask about input size and edge cases. Give the brute-force solution and its complexity, then improve it. Most problems at ML roles use hash maps, two pointers, sliding windows, heaps, binary search, BFS or DFS, and basic dynamic programming. Talk as you work, write clean code, then test with a small example and an edge case. A working simple solution beats an unfinished clever one.
keyPoints: Clarify constraints and input or output behavior before coding.
Start with a correct baseline and explain its complexity.
Choose a data structure using the constraints.
Test edge cases and reason through correctness.
Explain improvements and trade-offs while implementing.

questions.title: Using SQL, find each user's most recent purchase and their 7-day rolling spend.
questions.answer: Use window functions. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchased_at DESC) and filter to row 1 gives the latest purchase. For rolling spend, aggregate to one row per user per day, then use SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Days with no purchases need a calendar join, or the seven rows will span more than seven days.
keyPoints: Use row numbering partitioned by user and ordered by descending time for latest purchases.
Define a deterministic tie-breaker for equal timestamps.
A seven-day window is a time range rather than seven rows.
Aggregate per user without losing required row-level information.
Test missing dates and multiple purchases on the same day.

questions.title: Implement a token-aware recursive text chunker in Python with configurable overlap and sentence boundary preservation. What would you test?
questions.answer: We chunk text by counting tokenizer subwords rather than raw characters or words. If you slice on raw characters, you break multi-byte UTF-8 sequences and split subword tokens in half, corrupting embeddings and overflowing model context windows. We implement a recursive hierarchy.
