We try paragraph boundaries first, fall back to sentence endings, and split on words only as a last resort. When accumulating text into a chunk, once the next sentence would exceed the token limit, we emit the chunk, retain a trailing overlap window of tokens, and continue. For testing, we verify edge cases: documents smaller than a single chunk, individual sentences longer than the chunk limit where word splitting is forced, unicode emojis and accents, and exact overlap continuity between adjacent chunks. The main trade-off is latency against precision: running the BPE tokenizer over every boundary is slower than raw string slicing, but it guarantees chunks never exceed context limits.
followUps: How would you optimize tokenizer calls if chunking a 100 MB text corpus?
What happens if a single Markdown table or code block exceeds the maximum token limit?
wrongAnswers: Chunking by character length (e.g. text[:500]) and assuming each token is four characters. This causes token truncation, invalid UTF-8 fragments, and context window overflows.
Splitting strictly on full stops without handling abbreviations (e.g. 'e.g.', 'U.S.') or numbers ('3.14'), fragmenting sentences prematurely.
tradeOffs: Token-exact counting guarantees chunks fit context windows, but invoking the BPE tokenizer for every sentence boundary adds CPU latency compared to character slicing.
Larger overlap (e.g. 20%) preserves cross-chunk reasoning at the expense of duplicate storage and redundant vector search scoring.
keyPoints: Count tokenizer subwords rather than raw characters.
Split by paragraphs, then sentences, then words as needed.
Emit at the token limit and retain trailing overlap.
Test oversized sentences, small documents, Unicode and overlap continuity.

questions.title: Implement Okapi BM25 scoring from scratch in Python given inverted document frequencies, term frequencies, and document lengths. What edge cases must you handle?
questions.answer: Okapi BM25 scores how relevant a document is to a query by combining inverse document frequency with saturated term frequency. In standard TF-IDF, repeating a keyword ten times gives ten times the score. BM25 caps that growth: the first few occurrences provide the strongest signal, and additional mentions quickly level off. We also normalize by document length so longer documents are penalized and do not win simply by having more words. For the inverse document frequency term, we use the standard plus-one floor formula to prevent negative scores when a word appears in more than half of the corpus. In code, we handle empty documents, queries with zero matches, and unseen vocabulary terms. The trade-off is lexical precision versus semantic understanding: BM25 requires zero GPU compute and excels at exact keywords like part numbers, but it misses synonyms and cross-lingual meaning entirely.
followUps: Why does BM25 saturate term frequency while standard TF-IDF grows linearly?
How do you combine BM25 scores with dense embedding cosine similarity without one dominating the other?
wrongAnswers: Using linear term frequency without saturation, causing keyword-stuffed documents to dominate search results.
Omitting the plus-one floor in Robertson IDF, resulting in negative relevance scores for frequent query terms.
tradeOffs: Robertson IDF with the plus-one floor guarantees strictly positive scores, whereas raw Robertson IDF turns negative for ubiquitous terms.
BM25 captures exact lexical keywords with zero GPU compute, but cannot capture semantic synonyms or cross-lingual intent.
keyPoints: Combine inverse document frequency with saturated term frequency.
Normalize by document length so length alone does not dominate.
Handle empty documents, unmatched queries and unseen vocabulary.
BM25 favors exact lexical matches but misses semantic synonyms.

questions.title: Implement a two-stage reranker pipeline in Python that scores candidate passages with a cross-encoder and blends semantic and lexical scores. How do you test it?
questions.answer: In two-stage retrieval, we use a fast first stage to fetch initial candidates, and then pass each candidate through a cross-encoder to rerank them. A bi-encoder embeds the query and passage separately, so they cannot interact until cosine similarity. A cross-encoder concatenates the query and passage together into a single transformer, letting every query token attend to every document token across all layers. We normalize the first-stage scores to zero and one, compute the cross-encoder logit, and blend them with an interpolation weight. To test this, we feed synthetic pairs: one with exact keyword matches in the wrong context, and one with rich semantic relevance but no keyword overlap. We verify that the cross-encoder down-ranks the keyword decoy and that score blending produces no missing values. The trade-off is accuracy against latency: cross-encoders give superior relevance ranking, but quadratic self-attention over every candidate makes reranking hundreds of passages too slow for interactive search.
followUps: How do you calibrate the interpolation weight between lexical and cross-encoder scores?
Why can we not run cross-encoders directly over the entire document corpus of millions of passages?
wrongAnswers: Concatenating raw BM25 scores (unbounded) with cross-encoder probabilities (0 to 1) without normalization, letting lexical scores dominate.
Assuming bi-encoders and cross-encoders have identical accuracy, ignoring that bi-encoders compress entire passages into a single static vector.
tradeOffs: Cross-encoders achieve significantly higher ranking precision via all-to-all token attention, but compute scales quadratically with candidate count.
Min-max score normalization is simple but sensitive to outlier first-stage scores; sigmoid normalization bounds outputs reliably.
keyPoints: Cross-encoders jointly attend to concatenated query and passage tokens.
Rerank candidates after a fast first-stage retriever.
Normalize and blend retrieval scores with cross-encoder logits.
Test keyword decoys while accounting for per-candidate latency.

questions.title: Implement a streaming JSON output parser in Python that extracts complete key-value pairs from an LLM token stream before the closing brace arrives. What are the failure modes?
questions.answer: When an LLM streams JSON, waiting for the final closing bracket delays the first user render. A streaming JSON parser reads tokens character by character as they arrive, maintaining a small state machine. We track brace depth for objects, bracket depth for arrays, a boolean flag for whether we are inside a string, and escape backslashes. When we are at the top object depth and encounter an unquoted colon, we capture the key. As soon as a terminating comma or closing brace completes a scalar value, we emit that key-value pair immediately to downstream UI components. Key edge cases include numbers split across token boundaries, escaped quotation marks inside string values, and unexpected model truncation where a trailing string never closes. The trade-off is time-to-first-render versus parser complexity: streaming partial objects gives an interactive user experience, but downstream consumers must gracefully handle partial trees if the stream disconnects midway.
followUps: How would you handle nested JSON objects and arrays in a streaming parser?
What happens if the model emits leading explanatory text or markdown code fences before the opening brace?
wrongAnswers: Calling json.loads() repeatedly on every arriving token chunk, causing O(N^2) JSONDecodeError exceptions on partial strings.
Splitting on commas with regular expressions, which breaks on commas embedded inside quoted string values.
tradeOffs: Streaming partial key-values minimizes perceived latency for end users, but partial JSON parsing requires maintaining complex state machines.
Early emission risks emitting incomplete nested structures if the model stream aborts midway through generation.
keyPoints: Track object depth, array depth, string state and escapes incrementally.
Emit completed scalar key-value pairs before the full object closes.
Handle numbers split across chunks and escaped quotes.
Downstream consumers must tolerate partial output after truncation.

questions.title: Implement an evaluation harness in Python that computes macro and micro Precision, Recall, and F1 across multi-label classification outputs without using scikit-learn.
questions.answer: In multi-label classification, each instance can belong to several classes at once. Our evaluation harness tallies true positives, false positives, and false negatives for every class independently, without relying on external libraries. We compute two views: micro and macro metrics. For micro-averages, we sum all true positives and divide by total predictions globally across all classes. This gives every individual prediction equal weight, meaning dominant classes heavily influence the result. For macro-averages, we calculate precision, recall, and F1 per class first, and then take their unweighted mean. This treats every class equally regardless of frequency. The trade-off is frequency balance versus rare class visibility: micro-F1 reflects overall user traffic volume, whereas macro-F1 exposes whether the model fails on critical rare classes.
followUps: When would you prefer macro-F1 over micro-F1 in an enterprise intent classification system?
How do you compute sample-averaged F1 and how does it differ from micro and macro F1?
wrongAnswers: Treating multi-label evaluation as binary classification by flattening predictions without grouping by class, corrupting per-class metrics.
Dividing by zero when a rare class has zero predictions without handling the edge case, crashing the evaluation harness with ZeroDivisionError.
tradeOffs: Micro-averaging weights every instance equally, making it ideal for aggregate traffic accuracy; macro-averaging weights every class equally, exposing performance on rare classes.
Zero-division handling requires explicit policy: returning 0.0 when a class has zero positive predictions prevents NaN propagation.
keyPoints: Tally true positives, false positives and false negatives per class.
Micro metrics pool counts across classes.
Macro metrics average per-class precision, recall and F1 equally.
Macro-F1 reveals rare-class failures hidden by traffic-dominated micro metrics.

questions.title: Implement an asynchronous dynamic batching queue in Python that groups incoming concurrent inference requests by maximum batch size and timeout.
questions.answer: A dynamic batcher groups concurrent inference requests into single batches before calling a GPU model server. We run an asynchronous queue with two release conditions: maximum batch size and a short timeout window, typically a few milliseconds. When a request arrives, we push it onto an internal queue and wait. If the queue reaches the target batch size, we pop all requests and dispatch immediately. If traffic is light, the timer fires and we dispatch whatever requests have arrived, padding tensor inputs to matching sequence lengths. We return an awaitable future to each caller so responses route back to their specific connection. The trade-off is throughput versus individual request latency: batching maximizes GPU tensor core utilization and lowers cost per token, but the first request in a batch waits for the queue window to fill, slightly increasing tail latency.
followUps: How do you adjust the batch timeout dynamically based on current queue depth and traffic volume?
What happens if one request in a batch fails during model execution?
wrongAnswers: Processing each request immediately in a separate thread without batching, resulting in 100% memory bandwidth stalls on GPU tensor cores.
Using a fixed sleep timer rather than event-driven dispatch, forcing every request to experience maximum wait time even when batches are full.
tradeOffs: Dynamic batching drastically increases GPU saturation and overall system throughput, but introduces artificial queuing delay for early-arriving requests.
Padding variable-length inputs in a batch wastes compute on padding tokens; bucketing by sequence length mitigates this.
keyPoints: Queue concurrent requests asynchronously.
Dispatch when maximum batch size or timeout is reached.
Pad inputs and map responses back through caller futures.
Batching improves utilization but adds waiting latency.

questions.title: Implement a thread-safe token bucket rate limiter in Python supporting burst capacity and continuous fractional refill without polling threads.
questions.answer: A token bucket rate limiter controls traffic while allowing controlled bursts. Instead of running background worker threads that sleep and poll, we calculate token refill lazily on each request. Each bucket stores its capacity, the refill rate per second, current token balance, and the timestamp of the last check. When a request arrives under a thread lock, we calculate how much time passed since the last request, add elapsed time multiplied by the refill rate to our tokens, and cap the total at maximum capacity. If we have at least one token, we decrement and allow the request; otherwise we reject it with a retry-after estimate. The trade-off is burst accommodation versus downstream overload: token buckets handle legitimate user bursts smoothly, unlike fixed-window counters that produce edge-of-window spikes, but if downstream LLM APIs are already saturated, burst allowances can temporarily overwhelm backend connections.
followUps: How do you extend this in-memory implementation to work across distributed API gateway instances?
How do you handle token rate limiting where different requests consume differing numbers of tokens (e.g. prompt length)?
wrongAnswers: Spawning a background daemon thread with time.sleep() to increment tokens, which wastes CPU cycles and drifts over time.
Omitting concurrency locks, causing race conditions where concurrent requests double-spend tokens.
tradeOffs: Lazy timestamp-based refill eliminates background thread CPU overhead and sleeps, but requires thread locking around timestamp updates.
Token buckets support bursty client traffic gracefully, unlike sliding window logs which require storing timestamps for every individual request.
keyPoints: Store capacity, refill rate, balance and last-check time.
Refill lazily from elapsed time and cap at capacity.
Lock refill and debit together for thread safety.
Reject exhausted requests with retry-after estimates while controlling bursts.

questions.title: Implement a Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming client in Python with reconnection logic, buffer management, and event-type dispatch.
questions.answer: Server-Sent Events deliver real-time model tokens over a persistent HTTP connection using a text stream format. An SSE client reads raw byte chunks and accumulates them into an internal string buffer. The protocol specifies that events are separated by double newlines, while individual fields start with prefixes like 'data:' or 'event:'. When the buffer contains a double newline, we extract the complete block, parse the fields, deserialize JSON payloads, and dispatch them to the subscriber. If the network drops, the client reconnects automatically with exponential backoff and sends the last observed event identifier in the Last-Event-ID header to resume without losing tokens. The trade-off is framing simplicity versus binary payload efficiency: SSE runs over standard HTTP with no WebSocket handshake, making it easy to proxy and inspect, but parsing string lines adds CPU string-splitting overhead compared to binary protocols like gRPC.
followUps: How do you handle a scenario where an SSE chunk is split in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character?
What is the difference in proxy buffering behavior between chunked transfer encoding and SSE?
wrongAnswers: Assuming each read() chunk from the socket represents exactly one complete SSE event, which corrupts multi-line payloads.
Failing to track Last-Event-ID on reconnects, causing dropped or duplicated tokens during network blips.
tradeOffs: SSE operates over standard HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 without WebSocket upgrades, simplifying proxy traversal and firewall rules.
Text-based line framing introduces string parsing overhead compared to binary streaming protocols like gRPC or WebSockets.
keyPoints: Buffer incoming bytes until a complete double-newline-delimited SSE event arrives.
Parse event fields and deserialize data payloads.
Reconnect with exponential backoff and Last-Event-ID.
HTTP text framing is easy to proxy but adds string-processing overhead.

questions.title: Implement batched cosine similarity and squared Euclidean distance in NumPy without nested Python loops. When does cosine equal Euclidean distance?
questions.answer: We implement batched similarity in NumPy using matrix multiplication. For cosine similarity, we normalize input matrices across their embedding dimension by dividing by their L2 norms, and then compute the dot product matrix. For squared Euclidean distance, we expand the binomial theorem: squared distance equals norm of u squared plus norm of v squared minus two times their dot product. When vectors are unit-normalized to length one, squared Euclidean distance simplifies directly to two minus two times cosine similarity. In that case, ranking by cosine similarity and ranking by Euclidean distance produce identical orderings. The trade-off is magnitude information versus directional semantic similarity: normalizing vectors removes vector length, which is beneficial when comparing text passages of differing lengths, but harmful if embedding magnitude encodes confidence or popularity.
followUps: How do you compute top-K nearest neighbors without sorting the entire N-by-M similarity matrix?
Why is squared Euclidean distance preferred over raw Euclidean distance in vector index retrieval?
wrongAnswers: Using nested for-loops over all vector pairs, resulting in O(N*M) Python interpreter overhead that fails to scale.
Claiming cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are always equivalent, ignoring that un-normalized vectors produce conflicting rankings.
tradeOffs: Matrix multiplication vectorization achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over nested loops by utilizing optimized BLAS libraries.
Unit-normalizing vectors simplifies distance math to dot products, but permanently discards embedding norm information.
keyPoints: Normalize embedding rows and use matrix multiplication for cosine similarity.
Compute squared distance from norms and dot products.
Unit-normalized squared distance equals two minus twice cosine similarity.
Normalization discards magnitude information that may encode confidence.

questions.title: Implement a semantic vector cache in Python with time-to-live expiration and cosine similarity threshold matching.
questions.answer: A semantic vector cache stores previous query embeddings alongside their generated answers to intercept redundant LLM calls. When a user submits a query, we embed it and compare it against cached query vectors using cosine similarity. If the highest similarity exceeds an exact threshold, such as 0.95, and the entry has not exceeded its time-to-live expiration, we return the cached response immediately without calling the model. We evict stale entries on access or through a periodic sweep. The trade-off is cache hit rate versus answer correctness: an exact string hash guarantees zero false semantic matches but yields few hits, while a semantic cache catches rephrased queries. However, if the similarity threshold is set too low, the cache returns answers for queries with subtle semantic differences, such as negations or conflicting constraints.
followUps: How do you handle cache invalidation when underlying knowledge documents update?
How does semantic caching interact with temperature > 0 and user personalization?
wrongAnswers: Relying solely on MD5/SHA256 string hashing for LLM caching, which misses identical user queries with minor punctuation changes.
Setting a loose similarity threshold (e.g. 0.80), causing the cache to return answers that contradict the user query.
tradeOffs: Semantic matching catches diverse natural language paraphrases that miss exact string caches, saving substantial API spend.
Setting the cosine threshold too low causes semantic drift, returning cached answers to subtly different questions.
keyPoints: Compare query embeddings with cached vectors using cosine similarity.
Return a hit only above the threshold and before TTL expiry.
Evict expired entries on access or by sweep.
Low thresholds confuse negation or constraints despite better paraphrase hits.

questions.title: Implement Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) in Python to merge ranked lists from multiple search algorithms.
questions.answer: We merge ranked candidate lists using Reciprocal Rank Fusion without relying on raw score calibration. Because keyword retrievers like BM25 yield unbounded positive scores while dense retrievers return cosine similarities between 0 and 1, direct score arithmetic produces distorted rankings. We iterate through each searcher's ordered results, taking 1-based ranks. For each document, we accumulate 1 / (60 + rank). We sort the resulting fused list by reciprocal score descending, breaking ties by document identifier ascending. Testing covers identical rankings, disjoint lists, differing list lengths, and stability under edge-case ties. The trade-off is ranking stability against loss of score margin: RRF discards the confidence spread between adjacent items, treating the gap between rank 1 and 2 identically whether the score delta was massive or negligible.
followUps: Why is the smoothing constant k conventionally set to 60?
When would min-max score normalisation be preferred over reciprocal rank fusion?
wrongAnswers: Adding raw BM25 and dense similarity scores together directly, allowing the uncalibrated BM25 scale to decide the entire order.
Using 0-based rank indexing without a smoothing constant, causing a division by zero on the top document.
tradeOffs: RRF requires zero calibration across disparate score distributions, but completely discards intra-ranking score confidence intervals.
Adding an empirical smoothing constant k=60 prevents top-ranked outliers from dominating the ensemble.
keyPoints: Fuse ranks rather than uncalibrated raw retriever scores.
Sum 1/(60 + one-based rank) for each document.
Sort by fused score with document-ID tie breaking.
Test disjoint lists and ties while recognizing score margins are discarded.

questions.title: Implement exponential backoff with full jitter in Python to desynchronize retry storms on rate-limited model endpoints.
questions.answer: When remote LLM endpoints return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, clients retrying with fixed intervals or pure exponential backoff synchronize their requests into destructive thundering herds. We implement exponential backoff with full jitter. For each attempt index from zero to attempts minus one, we calculate the exponential ceiling as min(max_delay, base_delay * 2^attempt). We then draw a uniform random float between zero and this ceiling using a seeded pseudorandom generator. Testing covers attempt zero base scaling, capping at max_delay, zero attempts returning empty lists, and uniform delay distribution under load. The trade-off is bounded completion latency against server recovery: full jitter maximizes randomness to disperse request spikes, but individual retries may occasionally draw very short delays near zero.
followUps: What is the mathematical difference between Full Jitter, Equal Jitter, and Decorrelated Jitter?
How do circuit breakers complement exponential backoff during prolonged infrastructure outages?
wrongAnswers: Using deterministic exponential backoff without jitter, which causes all concurrent failed callers to sleep for the exact same duration and crash the service again simultaneously.
Setting unbounded exponential growth without a max_delay cap, causing subsequent retries to sleep for days.
tradeOffs: Full jitter minimizes thundering herd collisions on shared model gateways, but introduces variable request latency for end users.
Setting a strict max_delay cap protects user turnaround times at the expense of giving downstream servers less recovery time.
keyPoints: Compute each retry ceiling as min(max_delay, base_delay times two to the attempt).
Draw full-jitter delays uniformly between zero and that ceiling.
Test cap behavior, zero attempts and seeded reproducibility.
Jitter disperses synchronized retries but can yield near-zero waits.

questions.title: Implement an autonomous agent execution loop in Python with step budgets, loop detection, and token limits.
questions.answer: We build an autonomous agent runner with deterministic execution guardrails to prevent infinite recursion, runaway token expenditure, and repeated identical tool calls. The runner receives a task and an environment interface. At each iteration, we check whether our step budget has expired. We maintain an in-memory history of tool call signatures composed of the tool name and sorted JSON arguments. If a tool call repeats an identical signature and fails consecutively, we flag an active loop and abort. We track total token consumption across prompt and completion turns, breaking if the budget is breached. Testing covers normal single-step answers, multi-turn tool loops terminating within limits, repeated tool invocation detection, and graceful budget exhaustion returns.
followUps: How do you differentiate between legitimate iterative search queries and infinite loops in agent traces?
What fallback strategy should the agent execute when its step budget is exhausted?
wrongAnswers: Running a while True loop with no maximum iteration ceiling, allowing the agent to burn API credits indefinitely on ambiguous prompts.
Checking for loops using raw output string equality instead of normalized tool arguments, causing subtle whitespace differences to bypass detection.
tradeOffs: Strict step and token budgets guarantee bounded cost and latency, but prematurely abort complex multi-step reasoning tasks.
Signature-based loop detection prevents cycling on failing actions, but requires deterministic argument serialization.
keyPoints: Check step and total token budgets during every iteration.
Track tool signatures using names and sorted JSON arguments.
Abort repeated consecutive failed tool calls.
Test graceful budget exhaustion and normal completion.

questions.title: Implement an idempotent tool call wrapper in Python to prevent duplicate side-effects during agent retries.
questions.answer: When autonomous agents invoke state-mutating external tools such as charging a card or dispatching a refund, network dropouts leave the caller uncertain whether the action committed remotely. We wrap tool execution in an idempotency manager. Each tool request provides an idempotency key and argument payload. Before dispatching, we query an idempotency registry. If the key has not been seen, we execute the tool, store the normalized parameter hash and response payload, and mark it executed. If the key is seen with identical parameters, we immediately return the cached response without re-executing. If the key is reused with mismatched parameters, we raise an idempotency conflict. Testing verifies single execution, duplicate caching, parameter conflict detection, and missing key validation.
followUps: How do you manage TTL expiration for idempotency records in high-throughput distributed systems?
Why must the parameter payload be cryptographically or deterministically hashed alongside the key?
wrongAnswers: Retrying failed tool calls without an idempotency key, causing payment gateways to process multiple real financial transactions.
Treating identical keys with different arguments as valid cache hits, executing the wrong action with old outputs.
tradeOffs: Enforcing idempotency keys guarantees at-most-once side-effects across retries, but adds storage overhead for session state.
Parameter conflict validation prevents accidental key collision bugs, but requires deterministic JSON serialization.
keyPoints: Look up the idempotency key before executing a mutating tool.
Store a parameter hash and result after first execution.
Return cached results for matching duplicate parameters.
Reject reused keys with different parameters and validate missing keys.

questions.title: Implement a tool call parser in Python that extracts function names and JSON arguments from model output.
questions.answer: We parse tool calls from conversational model outputs supporting both structured code fences and inline JSON invocations. The parser checks if the output contains a tool invocation marker. If wrapped in markdown code fences, we extract the inner text; otherwise we slice from the first opening brace to the last closing brace. We parse the payload with json.loads, validating that it contains a tool name and arguments dictionary. If parsing fails or required fields are absent, we return None or raise structured syntax errors so the agent loop can prompt the model for immediate self-correction. Testing covers fenced JSON, unfenced JSON, conversational preamble stripping, and malformed syntax.
followUps: Why should tool schemas specify argument types and strict validation in the prompt?
How does streaming tool call parsing differ from batch post-generation extraction?
wrongAnswers: Using regular expressions to extract argument values with naive string splitting, failing on nested dictionaries or escaped quotes.
Crashing the entire agent service when the model outputs invalid JSON instead of catching the error and prompting for repair.
tradeOffs: Parsing tool calls with strict JSON validation prevents malformed execution, but requires dedicated error-recovery loops.
Allowing inline and fenced formats increases extraction resilience, but requires careful delimiter slicing.
keyPoints: Extract JSON from code fences or inline invocation text.
Validate the parsed tool name and arguments dictionary.
Return structured parse errors for model correction.
Test preambles, fenced output and malformed syntax.

questions.title: Implement hybrid retrieval fusion with min-max score normalisation across dense and keyword scores.
questions.answer: Hybrid retrieval merges keyword BM25 results with dense semantic embeddings to combine exact keyword recall with conceptual semantic understanding. Because BM25 scores can exceed 30 while cosine similarities sit between 0 and 1, naive addition allows keyword scores to override the semantic ranker. We normalize both score distributions separately to [0.0, 1.0] using min-max scaling, assigning 1.0 when all scores in a list are identical. We then blend scores using a weighting coefficient alpha: score = alpha * dense_norm + (1 - alpha) * bm25_norm. Documents missing from either retriever are assigned zero for that retriever. Testing verifies normalisation stability, alpha boundary weights, tie-breaking, and empty input handling.
followUps: How do you tune the alpha parameter between lexical and dense retrieval for technical code search?
When does reciprocal rank fusion outperform min-max score blending in production search?
wrongAnswers: Adding raw BM25 scores directly to dense embedding cosine similarities without normalisation.
Dividing by zero when all candidate documents from a retriever have identical scores.
tradeOffs: Min-max normalisation preserves relative score distances within each retrieval method, but is sensitive to outlier scores.
A configurable alpha weighting slider allows tuning domain-specific lexical versus semantic importance.
keyPoints: Normalize dense and BM25 scores separately to zero through one.
Blend normalized scores with alpha and one minus alpha.
Assign zero for documents missing from a retriever.
Test equal-score lists, alpha boundaries, empty inputs and ties.

questions.title: Assemble context from retrieved chunks within a token budget and merge contiguous passages in document order.
questions.answer: Retrieved chunks arrive sorted by relevance score, but feeding them to a model in score order fractures reading continuity: chunk 3 may appear before chunk 2, and disjoint snippets confuse long-context attention. We implement a two-phase context assembler. First, we select chunks greedily by score descending until our token budget is reached, skipping any chunk that would cause an overflow. Second, we re-order the selected chunks by original document identifier and character position, merging adjacent chunks from the same source document into unified passages. Testing verifies score-ordered budget selection, source order restoration, adjacent passage joining, and token counting.
followUps: Why does presenting context in original reading order improve LLM factual recall compared to score order?
How do you handle middle-loss context effects in large prompt windows?
wrongAnswers: Concatenating chunks directly in retrieval score order, interleaving disconnected paragraphs and confusing the language model.
Discarding the entire selection when a large chunk exceeds the remaining token budget instead of skipping it to fit smaller candidates.
tradeOffs: Restoring source order and merging neighbours improves model reasoning and reduces token overhead from repeated headers.
Greedy score selection within token budgets maximizes prompt information density while preventing context overflow.
keyPoints: Select chunks by descending relevance within a token budget.
Skip chunks that would overflow the budget.
Restore document and character order after selection.
Merge adjacent selected chunks and test continuity and token counts.

questions.title: Drop near-duplicate chunks before indexing using word shingles and Jaccard similarity.
questions.answer: Enterprise document stores and web crawls contain extensive duplicated boilerplate: identical copyright notices, header navigation bars, and copy-pasted setup guides. Indexing every duplicate floods retrieval top-k with redundant copies of the same text. We implement pre-index deduplication using word shingles. We convert each chunk into a set of lower-case 3-word n-grams. We walk chunks sequentially, computing Jaccard similarity against already-retained chunk shingle sets: intersection size divided by union size. We discard any candidate whose similarity exceeds our deduplication threshold. Testing verifies exact duplicate filtering, boilerplate variant detection, distinct word order preservation, and short chunk handling.
followUps: Why is word-level shingling superior to full-text hashing for identifying boilerplate variants?
How do you scale shingle-based deduplication from thousands of chunks to billions using MinHash LSH?
wrongAnswers: Using MD5 or SHA-256 exact hashing, which fails to detect near-duplicates that differ by a single whitespace character or date.
Deduplicating after retrieval inside the query path instead of pruning redundant chunks during ingestion.
tradeOffs: Pre-index shingle deduplication frees vector index capacity and prevents top-k answer crowding, but adds ingestion CPU overhead.
3-gram shingles preserve word order and phrase structure while ignoring superficial formatting changes.
keyPoints: Represent chunks as lowercase three-word shingle sets.
Compare candidates with retained chunks using Jaccard similarity.
Drop chunks above the duplicate threshold before indexing.
Test exact duplicates, boilerplate variants and short chunks.

questions.title: Verify citations in generated RAG responses against retrieved source passages.
questions.answer: A retrieval-augmented generation response that displays bracketed citations like [1] or [2] implies factual grounding in specific retrieved passages. If the model hallucinates non-existent source indices or leaves claims uncited, users are misled. We implement an automated citation validator. We split the candidate response into sentences. We extract bracketed citation markers using regular expressions and parse all referenced source numbers. We verify each number against the bounds of the provided sources list (1 to N), flagging any non-existent indices as invalid. We identify all sentences lacking citations. Testing verifies valid citations, out-of-range index detection, multi-source brackets, and uncited sentence tracking.
followUps: How do you verify whether a cited source passage actually supports the claim made in the sentence?
What user experience should you show when an answer has valid citations but partial factual hallucination?
wrongAnswers: Trusting model-generated citation brackets without validating that the referenced document index actually exists in the prompt context.
Stripping all citations from the UI instead of flagging unverified sentences for revision.
tradeOffs: Automated citation index verification cheaply eliminates out-of-bounds hallucinations before rendering responses in UI.
Flagging uncited sentences enables targeted secondary verification or model regeneration.
keyPoints: Split responses into sentences and extract bracketed source numbers.
Validate citation indices against the available source list.
Flag uncited sentences as well as out-of-range references.
Test multi-source brackets and valid citations.

questions.title: Implement single-token decoding with a key-value (KV) cache for autoregressive transformer inference.
questions.answer: During transformer autoregressive generation, recomputing keys and values for all previous sequence tokens at every decode step results in quadratic O(N^2) compute complexity. We implement single-step KV cache decoding. For the incoming token representation, we project Query, Key, and Value matrices. We append the new key and value vectors to historical cache tensors along the sequence dimension. We compute attention between the single-step query vector and all cached keys, scale by square root of head dimension, apply softmax, and multiply across cached values. Testing verifies cache tensor concatenation shapes, single-step attention weighting, projection dimension consistency, and recurrent state accumulation.
followUps: Why does KV caching convert decode phase computation from compute-bound to memory-bandwidth-bound?
How do PagedAttention and vLLM eliminate memory fragmentation in multi-user KV caches?
wrongAnswers: Recomputing full sequence self-attention from scratch at every generated token, wasting over 90% of GPU compute in decode phases.
Allocating static contiguous maximum-context memory for every request, causing severe out-of-memory errors on concurrent serving.
tradeOffs: KV caching reduces generation step compute from O(N) to O(1) FLOPs, but consumes extensive GPU VRAM that bounds serving concurrency.
Appending keys and values recurrently requires efficient memory allocation to avoid cache tensor reallocation overhead.
keyPoints: Project the incoming token into query, key and value vectors.
Append new keys and values to historical cache tensors.
Attend the new query over cached keys with head-dimension scaling and softmax.
Test concatenation shapes and recurrent cache accumulation.

questions.title: Write the one line that applies a sampling temperature to a vector of logits, then tell me what happens to the distribution as the temperature goes toward zero, equals one, and goes above one.
questions.answer: Divide the logits by the temperature before the softmax. Near zero the division stretches the gaps between logits, so the largest one takes almost all the mass and sampling becomes greedy. At one the model's own distribution is used, and above one the gaps shrink, the distribution flattens, and rare tokens are drawn more often.
followUps: Level 1: Why does temperature zero need a special case in code? Expected: division by zero; implement it as argmax rather than dividing.
Level 2: A product wants deterministic output. Is temperature zero enough? Expected: it removes sampling randomness, but ties and numeric differences across batches can still change the argmax.

Level 2: How does temperature interact with a top-p cutoff? Expected: the cutoff must run on the temperature-scaled probabilities, otherwise it cuts the distribution at temperature one and the setting does less than expected.
wrongAnswers: "Temperature scales the probabilities after the softmax." Scaling probabilities and renormalizing changes nothing; the division happens on the logits.
"A higher temperature makes the model smarter." It only flattens the distribution, which trades repetition for more mistakes.
"Temperature one means no sampling." It means sampling from the unchanged distribution; greedy is temperature zero or argmax.

questions.title: You get a corpus as a dictionary from words, each a tuple of byte ids, to the number of times the word occurs. Write the training loop that produces an ordered list of merges, and state the three rules that make the loop deterministic. Then tell me what the loop must not do to the caller's data.
questions.answer: Each step counts every adjacent pair inside each word, weighted by the word frequency, picks the pair with the highest count, rewrites every occurrence of that pair into one new id, and records the merge. The three rules are: pairs never cross a word boundary, ties go to the smallest pair in tuple order, and the loop stops when no pair repeats. The input dictionary and its tuples are never changed; the loop builds a new corpus each step.
followUps: Level 2: Why does the symbol count fall as training proceeds, and what does that do to the cost of a step? Expected: each merge shortens words, so the pair count over the corpus shrinks and later steps are cheaper.
Level 2: What does the tie rule protect? Expected: reproducibility; the same corpus must give the same merge list on every machine.
Level 3: Two words merge into the same tuple after a step. What must the new dictionary do? Expected: add their frequencies together instead of keeping only the last one.
Level 3: How does the vocabulary size relate to the number of merges? Expected: the base byte block plus one id per merge, plus any reserved special ids.
wrongAnswers: "Count each pair once per word." Frequency weighting is what makes common pairs win early.
"Take the first pair with the maximum count." Dictionary order is not stable across inputs, so the tokenizer becomes irreproducible.
"Keep merging until the budget is spent." A pair that appears once gains nothing and wastes vocabulary.

questions.title: The reference small GPT configuration uses a learned position embedding of shape 1024 by 768. Replace it with a sinusoidal table computed at construction time, add it to a batch of token embeddings, and tell me by how much the parameter count changes and why the model still forwards.
questions.answer: Build a table with one row per position and one column per feature, where column 2i holds the sine and column 2i + 1 holds the cosine of the position divided by the base raised to 2i over the model width. Register it as a buffer, slice the first T rows at each forward and add them to the token embeddings without changing the caller's array. The table has the same shape as the learned one, so the forward pass is unchanged, and the count drops by 786,432 parameters because the table is no longer learned.
followUps: Level 2: Why interleave sine and cosine rather than put them in two halves? Expected: a checkpoint trained with the interleaved layout expects each pair of neighbor columns to form one rotation, and the two layouts are not interchangeable.
Level 2: What does the base control? Expected: the lowest frequency, and so the longest position range before the slowest columns repeat.

Level 3: Which position scheme does the assembly lesson say turns this model into the next model family? Expected: a rotary scheme applied inside attention replaces the additive table and leaves the block and the head unchanged.
Level 3: A fixed table has no parameters; what does the model lose? Expected: the ability to learn position features from data, in exchange for a table that extends to any length at construction.
wrongAnswers: "Register the table as a parameter so the optimizer can refine it." Then it is a learned table again and the count does not drop.
"Start positions at one so the first row is not all zeros and ones." The reference starts at zero; row zero is the code of position zero.
"Use the same exponent for sine and cosine columns but a different base." Both columns of a pair share one angle; only the function differs.

questions.title: Given the logits of the last position, a temperature, a value of k and a seeded random generator, write the function that draws the next token. State the order of the operations, how ties are broken, and how the draw uses exactly one random number.
questions.answer: Divide the logits by the temperature, keep the k largest and set the rest to negative infinity, take the softmax, and draw one index from the result. Ties keep the lower index. The draw calls the generator once, takes the cumulative sum of the probabilities in vocabulary order, and returns the first index whose cumulative value exceeds the random number.
followUps: Level 2: What does top-k one produce? Expected: greedy decoding, the argmax every time.

Level 2: Why must the filter run before the softmax and not after? Expected: zeroing probabilities after the softmax leaves a distribution that does not sum to one unless it is renormalized; masking the logits does that for free.

Level 3: The assembly lesson keeps the context inside a fixed length during generation. How? Expected: when the prompt plus generated tokens exceed the context length, the oldest tokens are dropped so the active window fits.

Level 3: How do you make two runs with one seed produce the same text? Expected: the same generator, one draw per step, the same tie rule and the same temperature; any extra draw shifts every later token.
wrongAnswers: "Call the generator's choice function with the probabilities." It works, but it consumes draws differently across versions and breaks the one-draw contract that the tests pin.
"Apply the temperature after the filter." The filter then selects tokens at temperature one and the setting changes less than intended.
"Sort descending by reversing an ascending sort." Equal logits then keep the higher index, which contradicts the tie rule.

questions.title: Before a long training run you are asked to pick the peak learning rate for a warmup and cosine schedule. Write the sweep that trains a small seeded model at each candidate rate, decides which runs diverged, picks the best stable rate and reports the smallest rate that diverged. State what "diverged" means in code.
questions.answer: Run the same seeded training loop once per candidate rate and record the final loss and the loss history. A run diverged when its final loss is not finite or when the loss grew over the run, not only when it became NaN. The best rate is the lowest final loss among the stable runs, with the smaller rate on a tie, and the smallest diverging rate is reported as the ceiling, because it bounds how high the peak can go.
followUps: Level 3: Two rates give the same final loss. Which one do you pick? Expected: the smaller one; it has more margin to the divergence ceiling.

Level 3: Why does the practice compare the first diverging rate with two over the top curvature of the loss? Expected: for a quadratic loss, gradient descent is stable only below that bound, so the measured ceiling should land near it and a mismatch points at a bug in the sweep.

Level 4: Warmup is set as an absolute count of steps. Why does the sweep on a short run then mislead the long one? Expected: the same count is a much smaller fraction of a long run, so the long run sits at the peak almost at once; set warmup as a fraction of total steps.
wrongAnswers: "Pick the rate with the lowest loss across all runs." A NaN or a climbing run must be filtered first, otherwise the argmin can return a diverged rate.
"A run diverged only if the loss is NaN or infinite." A finite loss that grew over the run is a divergence the long run will also show.
"Sweep the warmup length first since it protects the start." The peak is the most sensitive knob; the warmup fraction is tuned after it.

questions.title: Write a training loop for a table of next-character logits: one row per context character, one column per next character. Train it with gradient descent on a text, under a fixed step budget and a seeded generator, until its held-out NLL is lower than a model that ignores the context. Tell me what the held-out check must look like for the comparison to mean anything.
questions.answer: Build the pairs so that the current character is the context and the following character is the target, compute the log-softmax over each row, and descend the mean of the negative target log-probabilities over the training pairs within the step budget. The held-out check scores a fixed split that training never saw, with the same loss definition for the bigram and the unigram baseline, and the model only passes when its held-out value is lower than the baseline's. Reproducibility comes from drawing the initial table from the generator that the caller passes, not from a global one.
followUps: Level 3: Why return log-probabilities and not raw logits from the scoring function? Expected: the loss needs a normalized distribution per row; raw logits are not comparable across contexts.
Level 3: The model beats the baseline on training text and loses on held-out text. What happened? Expected: it memorized the training pairs; a held-out split exists to catch exactly that.

Level 4: How does this toy loop map onto the full training loop in the lesson? Expected: the pair construction is the shift-by-one, the row lookup is the forward, the held-out check is the fixed evaluation, and the budget is the step count of the schedule.
wrongAnswers: "Evaluate on the training text to save time." The comparison then measures memorization and the baseline comparison means nothing.
"Draw the initial table from the global random state." Two runs with one seed then differ, and the test for reproducibility fails.
"Train until the loss stops improving." The budget is part of the contract and an open-ended loop hides a slow or stuck run.

questions.title: Design and implement a tokenizer for a small language model: train it on a corpus, encode fresh text, decode ids back, and reserve two special tokens for document boundaries and padding. State the guarantees the test suite must pin, and explain how the special tokens survive both training and inference without ever being merged.
questions.answer: The base symbols are the 256 raw bytes, so every input has an encoding before any merge and decoding always terminates in bytes. Training runs on pre-tokenized chunks that never contain the special strings, so no merge can produce or consume a special id. At inference a matcher splits the text on the special strings first, maps each one to its reserved id, and runs the merge table on the text between them in training order. The suite pins the round trip on unseen text, on text with multi-byte characters, and on text that contains a literal special string with the flag off.
followUps: Level 3: Why are the first 256 ids reserved for bytes rather than for the characters of the corpus? Expected: any input, including text in scripts the corpus never had, can then be encoded without an unknown token.

Level 4: Where do chat template markers fit in this design? Expected: they are special tokens like the boundary token, matched exactly before the merges, with fixed ids that the model was trained on; a wrong template puts the input outside the training distribution.

Level 4: How do you protect a deployed model from a tokenizer that drifts? Expected: hash the merge table and the special-token map, and check the hash in the pipeline before training and before serving; a different table decodes different ids.
wrongAnswers: "Add the special tokens to the corpus so the model learns them." Then they can be merged with neighbors and stop being single ids.
"Match special strings after the merges." The merges have already split the string into byte pieces, so the matcher never sees it.
"Decode by looking up a string per id in a dictionary." Ids are bytes, and a multi-byte character can be split across ids; concatenate bytes first, then decode.

questions.title: You have a trained model with 64 query heads and 64 key and value heads, and you want to serve it with 8 key and value heads to shrink the cache. Write the function that pools the key projection of the checkpoint into groups, say by what factor the cache memory for keys and values falls, and explain why the pooled model needs more training before it is usable.
questions.answer: Group g of the new projection is the mean of the consecutive heads g r to g r + r - 1, where r is the number of query heads per group, taken over the columns of the projection matrix. The cache holds keys and values for 8 heads instead of 64, so that memory falls by a factor of eight. The mean of several heads is not a head the model was trained with, so quality drops until a short continued training run adapts the query heads to their shared group.
followUps: Level 3: Why pool consecutive heads and not every eighth head? Expected: the attention reads group h floor-divided by r for query head h, so the pooled heads must be the ones that will share a group.

Level 4: How does the cache saving change when the model is served with a longer context? Expected: it does not change as a factor; the saving is per token, so the absolute bytes saved grow with the number of tokens held.

Level 4: The multi-head latent variant compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent. What does it trade for the extra saving? Expected: compute, because the latent must be projected back to full keys and values at attention time.
wrongAnswers: "Pooling is lossless since the mean preserves the average key." The individual heads are lost; the queries were trained against them, so quality drops until the model is adapted.
"The cache shrinks by the ratio of query heads to total heads." Only key and value heads live in the cache; the factor is the old count of key and value heads over the new count.
"Sum the heads so no information is lost." The sum scales the keys by the group size and pushes the scores out of the range the softmax was trained for.

topics.title: Behavioral
topics.about: Framing work, planning from evidence, delegation and turning feedback into a system.

questions.title: Walk me through the most impactful ML project you led.
questions.answer: Use a clear shape: the business problem and metric, the baseline, your role, key decisions and alternatives you rejected, what failed, and the measured outcome. Senior interviewers will probe, so know your data size, latency, cost, evaluation method and what you would change now. Say I for your own decisions and we for the team's. Prepare one project deeply enough to discuss for 30 minutes.
keyPoints: State the business problem, baseline and success metric.
Explain personal technical decisions and constraints.
Describe measured outcomes and how attribution was checked.
Explain trade-offs, failures and what changed afterward.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you decided not to use ML, or to use a simpler model.
questions.answer: Show judgment. Describe the problem, then how you compared a simple rule or baseline with a complex model on accuracy, cost, latency and maintenance. Give numbers, such as a rules system reaching most of the value in two weeks. Explain how you convinced people who wanted something more advanced, and what would have changed your decision. Interviewers look for evidence over enthusiasm for technology.
keyPoints: Compare a simple baseline with ML using the actual product need.
Account for data quality, operating cost and maintenance.
Explain the evidence behind choosing the simpler approach.
Define when future evidence would justify adding ML.

questions.title: Tell me about a model that failed in production. What did you do?
questions.answer: Pick a real failure with consequences. Explain how it was detected, how you limited the damage, the root cause and the lasting fix, such as a new monitor or release check. Take ownership without blaming others. A blameless account that produced a system change is much stronger than a story with no mistakes. Quantify the impact, and say what you now do differently.
keyPoints: Describe the failure and its observable impact.
Explain containment or rollback before extended diagnosis.
Trace the cause using evidence rather than hindsight.
Describe prevention and what was learned without blaming others.

questions.title: How do you handle a product manager who wants a launch date your model can't safely meet?
questions.answer: Translate risk into business terms and bring options, not just a no. For example, offer a limited launch to low-risk users, a human review step, or a simpler first version, each with its risk and timeline. Agree a metric that defines ready. If leadership accepts a risk, record the decision and set monitoring and rollback. Seniors are judged on keeping trust while finding a way forward.
keyPoints: Clarify launch goals and quantify the specific risk.
Present evidence and options such as reduced scope or staged rollout.
Agree measurable launch criteria and communicate ownership.
Escalate unresolved high-impact risk with a clear recommendation.

questions.title: As a senior engineer, how do you raise the quality of your team's ML work?
questions.answer:
As a senior engineer, I raise team engineering quality by institutionalizing rigorous systems and multiplying collective output rather than acting as a gatekeeper:
First, engineering scaffolding. I introduce standardized production checklists: experiment design templates with pre-registered hypotheses and power calculations, automated offline evaluation harnesses in CI, and deployment runbooks covering canary metrics and rollback procedures.
Second, pedagogical code and design reviews. I focus reviews on architectural trade-offs, failure modes, and data leakage rather than stylistic nitpicks. I frame feedback as architectural questions to build junior engineers' mental models.
Third, technical direction. I help the team prioritize the highest-impact problems, identifying when a simple heuristic or linear baseline delivers 80% of business value faster than a complex deep learning architecture.
Success is measured by systemic outcomes: reduced incident frequency, faster time-to-production for new models, and junior engineers independently driving complex technical designs.
keyPoints: Set shared review, testing and evaluation standards.
Coach teammates through concrete technical decisions.
Create reusable tools or practices that reduce repeated failures.
Measure team outcomes and balance guidance with autonomy.

questions.title: You are told to use AI to reduce support costs, with no further detail. What do you do?
questions.answer: Clarify first: how much is spent now, which ticket types drive it, and what quality is acceptable. Analyse the data before choosing a method. Propose a small test, such as drafting replies for one common category with human review, and define success and guardrails. Compare build and buy, and estimate cost per ticket. Then scale what works. Interviewers want structured thinking, not an immediate architecture.
keyPoints: Clarify support costs, user needs and the success metric.
Inspect workflows and data before selecting a model.
Compare automation with simpler process improvements.
Run a scoped pilot with quality and escalation guardrails.
Measure cost reduction alongside customer outcomes.

questions.title: What separates a senior ML engineer from a mid-level one in interviews?
questions.answer: Seniors start with the business problem and metric, state assumptions, and compare options with numbers instead of naming tools. They discuss failure modes, cost, monitoring and rollback without being asked. They know their past projects in depth, admit what they don't know, and explain trade-offs clearly. They also show ownership beyond code, such as influencing direction, handling ambiguity and helping others improve.
keyPoints: Senior engineers frame ambiguous problems and own outcomes.
They explain system trade-offs and production failure modes.
They use evidence to connect technical work to business impact.
They raise team quality through influence and mentoring.

questions.title: Your session ends without warning in the middle of a multi-step change, and a colleague picks it up the next morning. What must they be able to find, and where?
questions.answer: They need to see which items are done, which proof ran for each one, which files changed, which dependencies are now unblocked, and what the next safe item is. That state lives next to the work, in the repository, as small items with explicit proof, not as checked boxes inside a chat.
followUps: Level 1: Where do you keep the plan? Expected: in the repository next to the work, as the source of truth, with any rendering such as a Markdown view generated from it.
Level 2: An item is marked done but has no proof recorded. What does the colleague do? Expected: treat it as not done and run its proof; a box without proof is a belief.
Level 2: Why does item size matter for resumption? Expected: a small item either finished or did not; a large half-done item forces the next person to reconstruct where it stopped.
wrongAnswers: "Write a summary message at the end of the session." The session can end before the summary; the state must exist as the work proceeds.
"The git log is enough." Commits show what changed, not which proof ran or which item is next.
"Only the person who started can finish it." That is the failure the plan should prevent.

questions.title: A product manager asks you to build an incident assistant for the on-call team. You have one week. Before you plan any work, what do you ask, and what do you write down first?
questions.answer: The request names an artifact, not a result. I write an outcome frame first: who has the problem, when it happens, what they do today, which observable state must improve, which limits are fixed, and which nearby work is out of scope. Then I check the frame for a product form, a model or an architecture that no evidence supports yet.
followUps: Level 1: How do you tell an outcome from an output? Expected: an outcome names an observable change for a user; an output names an artifact such as a page, a tool or a model.

Level 2: The manager insists on a chat interface. Where does that go in the frame? Expected: into the constraints only when policy or compatibility fixes it, with the reason written down; otherwise it waits for evidence.
Level 2: Name two non-goals that keep the first slice small. Expected: no automatic fix of the incident and no new alert routing, for example; each one must be concrete enough to reject work.

Level 3: What is the first observation that would show the desired outcome is wrong? Expected: a measured time to find the failing service that is already short, which means the frame targets a problem that does not exist.
wrongAnswers: "Start with the interface and refine the goal later." The interface is one output. It ties the team to the first artifact before anyone knows what must improve.
"Constraints are implementation details for later." A build that reaches the outcome and breaks a constraint has not reached the outcome.
"Non-goals are optional." Without them, a useful slice grows into a platform before the first result is measured.

questions.title: A teammate, or a coding agent, hands you this plan for a change to a public API: update the endpoint, add tests, update the documentation. They want approval to start. What do you ask for before you say yes, and what would make you reject the plan outright?
questions.answer: That list repeats the request in future tense. I ask for five things on each item: a stable identifier, the smallest change, the repository facts that justify it, the items it depends on, and the exact check that closes it. I reject a plan with a duplicate identifier, an item without evidence or proof, a dependency on an unknown item, a cycle, or an irreversible step scheduled before the uncertainty it depends on is resolved.
followUps: Level 2: One item lists two proof commands. What do you do? Expected: split it into two items, because one item needs one clear completion proof.
Level 2: Two items depend on each other. What does that usually hide? Expected: an unresolved product or design disagreement; the cycle is the symptom, the missing decision is the cause.

Level 3: The plan sits in a chat thread as checked boxes. Why is that a problem? Expected: a session can end at any moment, and another person cannot see which proof ran or which item is now unblocked; the plan belongs next to the work.
Level 3: A migration item needs a human approval. How do you express that in the graph? Expected: as an explicit item with the approval as its proof, which every dependent item waits for.
wrongAnswers: "Trust the author and review the result instead." Rework found at review time costs more than a plan rejected before editing.
"A longer plan is a better plan." Length adds nothing; evidence and proof on each item do.
"Dependencies are obvious from the order of the list." Prose order hides which steps can run together and which must wait.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you defined how a project would be judged before you had any results. What did you write down, and what did you refuse to leave open until later?
questions.answer: I start from the goal, derive the questions it raises, and only then pick the smallest metrics that answer them. Each metric gets a direction, a threshold, a window, a source and a population before any value is observed, and each outcome metric is paired with a guardrail and a counter-metric. I also write the pass, fail and ambiguous decisions in advance, because a team that sees the result first moves the threshold to protect the build.
followUps: Level 2: A metric is easy to collect but cannot change the decision. What do you do with it? Expected: remove it; measurement answers a decision, it does not decorate a dashboard.
Level 2: Give a counter-metric for the incident tool. Expected: review time added for the incident commander, or escalations that moved to another team.
Level 3: The outcome metric passes and the guardrail fails. What is the verdict? Expected: fail; a fixed constraint that broke means the outcome was not reached.

Level 3: Results come back ambiguous. What was already written for that case? Expected: the next step, such as a larger replay set, decided before the result so nobody argues the threshold afterwards.
wrongAnswers: "Pick the metric after you see what the system can do." The threshold then moves to protect the build and the measurement decides nothing.
"One good outcome metric is enough." Without a guardrail, a fast but unsafe result passes.
"Run a live pilot since the implementation is ready." Readiness is not a reason to expose users; the cheapest evidence that answers the decision comes first.

questions.title: You join a team with a quarter-long roadmap for an assistant that recommends a next action to on-call engineers. The roadmap lists features in priority order. Tell me how you decide what to work on in week one, and why it may not be the first roadmap item.
questions.answer: A roadmap hides uncertainty inside features. I rewrite the features as falsifiable assumptions about value, usability, feasibility, viability and safety, then score each one on impact, uncertainty and irreversibility. Week one goes to the cheapest decisive test of the highest open risk, which is often not the top roadmap item.
followUps: Level 2: The highest-risk assumption is tested and holds. What changes? Expected: it moves from open to tested with its evidence attached, and the next experiment targets the next highest open risk.
Level 2: Which assumption class do feature lists most often omit? Expected: safety, the question of whether the feature can fail without unacceptable consequence.

Level 3: The roadmap owner says the ranking already reflects risk. How do you check? Expected: compare the risk ranking with the roadmap order and explain each mismatch; where they differ, one of them is wrong about the evidence.
Level 3: Write a threshold that would stop the build. Expected: for example, fewer than a stated share of engineers in the replay trust the read-only recommendation enough to act on it.
wrongAnswers: "Build the first roadmap item; the order was agreed." Agreement on order is not evidence that the riskiest assumption holds.
"Ship something small and see what happens." A small build without a claim, a threshold and a next decision learns nothing.
"Risk is just how likely it is to fail." Impact and irreversibility change the order even when the probability is the same.

questions.title: A customer lead spends an hour describing how their support team handles a refund request. You now have to decide what the first version of an assistant does. Tell me how you treat that hour of description, and what you do next.
questions.answer: An interview is reported behavior, which is the third rung of a four-rung ladder. I label every claim from the hour by its rung, then look for direct evidence for the claims that matter most: a trace, a recording, a ticket or a completed form. The steps that stay unproven remain visible as open claims instead of turning into requirements.
followUps: Level 2: The lead says "we always check the order history first." How do you confirm that? Expected: ask for a recording or a log of three real cases and mark the claim as reported until one of them shows it.
Level 2: What is the direct-evidence ratio and why track it? Expected: the share of workflow steps backed by observation or an artifact; a low ratio means the model of the workflow is mostly belief.
Level 3: You can only observe the happy path. What is the risk? Expected: the exception path, where most failures live, stays unshaped, so the assistant breaks at the handoff that matters.

Level 3: A proposed feature removes a visible step. What do you check before you accept it? Expected: whether hidden work behind that step still exists, so the feature only moves the effort somewhere invisible.
wrongAnswers: "The customer knows their process, so the interview is the requirement." A description is reported behavior; it is useful but it does not prove what happens.
"Average the descriptions from several people into one workflow." An averaged workflow can describe nobody; the variants must stay separate until their cause is known.
"Infer the missing steps from similar teams." Inference is the weakest rung and must stay labeled as a guess.

questions.title: Two senior analysts on the same team show you how they triage a flagged transaction. Their steps differ in order, in the tools they open, and in who they ask before they act. Your deadline allows one workflow in the first version. What do you do with the disagreement?
questions.answer: I keep both variants separate until I know why they differ. The difference can come from different roles, different risk levels, a legacy process next to a current one, a difference in expertise, or a real policy disagreement, and each of those leads to a different product. An averaged workflow can describe nobody, so the first version targets one variant on purpose and names the other as a known gap.
followUps: Level 2: One analyst asks a supervisor before acting and the other does not. What is that step? Expected: an authority boundary; the build must respect it, and the two variants may differ in risk level or role.
Level 2: You can only ship one path. How do you choose? Expected: by the risk and the frequency of each variant, with the other recorded as a named gap, not by averaging.
Level 3: The owner says both are fine. What do you record? Expected: that the policy allows both, with the evidence, so the assistant does not force one on everybody.

Level 3: How do you keep the second variant from disappearing from the plan? Expected: write it as a non-goal with its reason and a review point, so it stays visible as a decision instead of an omission.
wrongAnswers: "Merge the two into one standard process." The averaged workflow may describe nobody and breaks at the handoff.
"Follow the more senior person." Seniority is not evidence; the cause of the difference decides.
"Treat the extra steps as optional and skip them." The extra step is often the exception path that carries most of the risk.

questions.title: For the third time this month you have told a coding agent not to edit the project README during a feature change. Each time it apologized and fixed the run. Tell me what you do now, and why the fix is not a better prompt.
questions.answer: A correction that lives in chat fixes one run. I treat the repeat as evidence about the work system: the scope boundary was not executable. I find the cause behind the symptom, then put a control at the earliest layer that can stop the recurrence, which here is a scope or permission policy rather than another paragraph in the instructions. The control gets an owner, a verification and a date to review or retire it.
followUps: Level 2: Two corrections use different words for the same cause. How do you keep them from becoming two rules? Expected: normalize them to a stable fingerprint of the cause, so they collapse into one control without merging unrelated failures.
Level 2: A first-time failure deleted customer data. Does it wait for recurrence? Expected: no; consequence weighting lets a severe first occurrence be promoted at once.

Level 3: When would you remove the control you added? Expected: when the architecture changed, a stronger executable control replaced it, the failure has not recurred across a meaningful window, or the control blocks more legitimate work than the risk it prevents.
Level 3: What is the smallest system you aim for? Expected: the smallest set of controls that preserves the hard-won judgment, not the longest instruction file.
wrongAnswers: "Add the rule in capital letters at the top of the instructions." The instruction already existed; a louder copy still depends on the agent reading it.
"Promote every correction so nothing is lost." Controls accumulate, conflict and bloat context; promotion needs recurrence or consequence.
"The agent is the problem, switch models." The boundary was not executable; a different model meets the same missing control.

questions.title: Your team agrees to ship a minimum viable version of a new assistant. Three proposals are on the table: a polished interface on synthetic data, a working data pipeline with no interface, and a read-only replay over ten real incidents. Which one do you argue for, and how do you justify the choice?
questions.answer: I argue for the replay over real incidents. Small is useful only when the slice proves something that matters, so I first write the required proof set from the highest-risk open assumptions and reject any candidate that does not cover it. The polished page over fake data and the pipeline without users each remove the exact uncertainty the team needs to test.
followUps: Level 2: The replay fails. Name two valid next moves. Expected: change the target user or situation, or test a different mechanism; both were written in the stop rule before the build.
Level 2: Why does a replay beat a live pilot here? Expected: it produces reversible evidence about trust and identification without exposing real users to a system nobody has measured.

Level 3: A reusable component would speed up all three proposals. When does it get built? Expected: after the slice has produced decisive evidence; building platform machinery first is the platform minimum.
Level 3: How do you keep the replay from becoming a demo? Expected: a repeatable measurement with a threshold decided in advance, not a persuasive walkthrough.
wrongAnswers: "The smallest build is the one with the fewest features." Smallness is measured by the evidence gained, not by the feature count.
"Build the interface first so stakeholders can see progress." A persuasive artifact without a measurement is the demo minimum.
"If the slice fails we iterate." Without a written stop rule, every result leads to more building and nothing was tested.

questions.title: Tell me about a project where the evidence turned against your plan. What did you do inside your own authority, and how did you present the situation to the person who had to decide?
questions.answer: I separate what I observed from what was reported and what I inferred, name the setback and the evidence that changed my understanding, and move the reversible work I am allowed to do while the blocked decision waits. Then I write a short brief for the decision owner: the user problem and the new evidence, at least two options including a cheaper manual or no-build option where it is credible, the tradeoffs in quality, effort, cost and risk, my recommendation with its remaining uncertainty, and the decision needed with its owner and date.
followUps: Level 3: Why include a no-build option whenever it is credible? Expected: narrowing the workflow or keeping a manual step can be the better decision; without that option the brief only asks for permission to continue.

Level 3: What goes next to each number in the outcome comparison? Expected: the sample counts, the exclusions and the evidence links, with the same metric definition and comparable windows for baseline and follow-up.

Level 4: A simulated walkthrough passed every step. What claim can you make? Expected: a bounded learning claim only; unobserved real-user behavior stays a named gap with the next observation needed to close it.
Level 4: How do you turn the setback into a change in how the team delivers? Expected: pick one process improvement with an owner and a review date, then keep, revise or retire it on evidence.
wrongAnswers: "Wait for the decision before doing anything." Reversible, authorized work can move forward; only the blocked decision waits.
"Present the recommendation alone to keep it simple." The owner needs the options and the tradeoffs to make a decision rather than approve a conclusion.
"Report the measured gain and leave out the review time." The complete task includes human review and correction; a faster model can still make the task slower.

questions.title: You discover that a weekend prototype you shared internally is now used every day by another team, with production data, and someone just reported an outage to you. Walk me through what went wrong before this moment and what you do in the first week.
questions.answer: The system drifted across stages. It gained users, data and authority without gaining ownership, and nothing in the system itself marked it as a prototype. In the first week I make the stage observable in configuration, access control, telemetry and documentation, cut the production data path until a named owner accepts it, and decide with that team whether the right next stage is a bounded pilot or a stop.
followUps: Level 3: The other team says the outage shows the tool is valuable. How do you answer? Expected: value is a reason to run a bounded pilot with an owner, not a reason to keep an unowned system on production data.
